sections.overview: Isotactic polypropylene (iPP) is the stereoregular propylene-homopolymer subfamily made with stereospecific catalyst systems. Its isotactic chain arrangement supports crystallization, and different crystal forms can be produced by a material's thermal and deformation history.
sections.history: The isotactic branch of polypropylene is associated especially with Giulio Natta’s 1954 stereospecific-polymerization work and the industrial lineage that became part of LyondellBasell. The ability to organize propylene units regularly made crystalline polypropylene a practical material. Later developments concentrated on selective catalysts and more efficient polymerization, broadening applications in molded goods, packaging and fibers. Modern Spheripol technology illustrates this continuity: successive catalyst generations reduced processing complexity while extending the homopolymer and copolymer product range. These are developments of isotactic manufacture, not new dates of invention for the original chain structure.
sections.nomenclature: iPP or i-PP identifies the isotactic polypropylene stereochemical form, not all polypropylene or a propylene copolymer. Polymer grade, molecular weight, additives, and crystal form are additional descriptors of a particular isotactic-PP material rather than alternate names for the tacticity-defined subfamily.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Isotactic polypropylene is prepared by stereoselective coordination polymerization of propylene; catalyst and donor selection control tacticity, so this entry is narrower than polypropylene made by any route. One industrially framed example uses Ziegler–Natta catalyst in a liquid hydrocarbon slurry containing a donor agent, with polymer formed in two or more reactors in series. A separate catalyst-system example polymerizes propylene homopolymer with a magnesium/titanium Ziegler–Natta component, external donor, dialkylaluminum hydride, and trialkylaluminum; hydrogen is used there as a molecular-weight control. These are cited route examples, not required ingredients or operating conditions for every isotactic polypropylene grade.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Isotactic polypropylene (iPP) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic whose crystalline lamellae and intervening amorphous, tie-chain network produce a stiff initial response followed by yielding, necking or strain localization, plastic flow, orientation and strain hardening. In tension, cavitation and stress whitening can accompany yield; under sustained load it creeps and relaxes, and a notch, high rate, low temperature, weld line, large spherulite or oxidative damage can make fracture more brittle. Mechanical behavior is not fixed by the repeat unit alone. Stereoregularity and stereodefects, molecular mass and distribution, crystal fraction, lamellar thickness, tie-molecule density, spherulite size, alpha/beta/gamma crystal form and mesophase content all matter. Cooling rate, pressure, nucleating or clarifying agents, annealing and physical aging establish that morphology; molding shear or drawing adds orientation and directional properties. Temperature and loading rate control yield and post-yield flow, while fillers, fibers, impact modifiers, recycled content and thermal or ultraviolet aging can alter stiffness, strength, fatigue, impact response and elongation. Caelers and co-workers give a bounded polymorph comparison for a SABIC iPP homopolymer with weight-average molar mass 320 kg/mol and dispersity 5.4. Approximately 1 mm compression-molded alpha-iPP sheets were melted at 230 °C, held under about 5 MPa for 10 min, cold-pressed at 25 °C for 3 min and stored at room temperature for two months. Dumbbell specimens stretched at 12 micrometres per second yielded at 32.0 MPa at 25 °C, 22.3 MPa at 50 °C, 12.6 MPa at 80 °C and 8.4 MPa at 110 °C. Under separate room-temperature uniaxial compression at 10^-3 s^-1, the alpha form had an estimated strain-hardening modulus of 2.2 MPa; beta- and gamma-rich preparations gave 4.2 and 3.5 MPa, respectively. Those values isolate one resin and deliberately prepared crystal morphologies, not a family range. As a separate current commercial benchmark, LyondellBasell lists typical values for Moplen HP501H polypropylene homopolymer used in injection and compression molding: tensile modulus 1450 MPa, tensile stress at yield 33 MPa, strain at yield 9%, strain at break greater than 50%, notched Charpy impact 8 kJ/m2 at 23 °C using a Type 1 edgewise specimen with notch A, and ball-indentation hardness 72 MPa. The public product page does not report tacticity, specimen preparation, tensile rate, conditioning, or variability, so these values remain specific to that grade and must not be transferred to fibers, films, foams, filled compounds, recyclate, or differently crystallized moldings.
sections.processing:
Commercial isotactic polypropylene homopolymers are melt-converted by injection molding; sheet, profile, cast-film, blown-film, and biaxially oriented-film extrusion; tape and fiber spinning with drawing; thermoforming; and welding. INEOS notes that ordinary polypropylene normally needs no predrying, although filled grades can require it, and emphasizes controlled melt temperature, pressure, fill rate, mold cooling, shrinkage, and residence time. Film and fiber operations deliberately use quenching and subsequent orientation; surface printing or coating generally requires prompt flame or corona treatment. Repeated heat histories can reduce molecular weight, so regrind level and time at temperature must be qualified for the grade and article.

As a bounded laboratory example, Caelers and co-workers made roughly 1 mm sheets from a SABIC isotactic-PP homopolymer by compression molding at 230 °C and 5 MPa for 10 min, followed by cold pressing at 25 °C for 3 min; the sheets were stored for two months before test-specimen preparation. These settings were chosen to prepare controlled polymorphic specimens and do not define an industrial iPP molding window. The INEOS guide's temperatures and draw ratios are likewise supplier starting guidance whose suitability depends on melt-flow grade, additives, equipment, cooling, orientation target, and allowable residence time.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Isotactic polypropylene is a stereoregular polypropylene whose methyl groups are arranged predominantly on the same side of the backbone, enabling semicrystalline chain packing. Crystalline form, orientation, and nucleation history produce polymorphic structures that can differ between processing histories.
sections.properties: The semicrystalline morphology gives isotactic polypropylene low density, useful stiffness, chemical resistance, electrical insulation, and fatigue resistance. Crystallinity, molecular mass, tacticity, orientation, additives, and cooling history control shrinkage, clarity, impact response, creep, and thermal behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Isotactic PP underpins the crystalline homopolymer grades used for rigid packaging, household goods, fibers and electrical or automotive parts. Tacticity describes chain structure; commercial application selection also depends on molecular weight and additives.

Purchasing. For conversion, specify a commercial PP homopolymer grade and its required processing behavior. INEOS supplies homopolymer pellets through direct or distributor channels, including bulk truck and rail shipments.

Scale and evidence limits. No independently separated isotactic-PP purchase total was established. Broad PP statistics include copolymers and other grades and cannot be treated as a measured total for this structural subtype.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Repeated processing of Novatec MA3 PP homopolymer produces radicals, yellowing and changes in stereoregularity and mechanical behavior; it does not identify a complete small-molecule product inventory.

Timescales: Up to five extrusion passes used an approximately 1 min barrel residence and approximately 210 °C die-exit resin temperature.

Environmental persistence: This isotactic-PP processing study does not measure environmental mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Melt re-extrusion and injection remolding are demonstrated on the named grade; repeated passes progressively change properties.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Isotactic PP melt processing involves hot surfaces, pressurized resin and possible fumes. As polypropylene-family context, HSE lists formaldehyde, acrolein and acetone among products detected when PP is heated above its recommended processing range. The mixture depends on temperature, residence time, stabilizers and other ingredients. LyondellBasell’s polyolefin guide adds guarding, spill control and eye/hand protection for film equipment; the actual grade and operation determine the control measures.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Unfilled isotactic polypropylene can be notch-sensitive and less impact-tough at low temperature than impact-modified grades; oxidation and repeated heat history can reduce molecular mass. Tacticity, comonomer, filler, nucleant, orientation, weld lines, and cooling rate make grade and article geometry essential to any comparison.

sections.overview: Syndiotactic polypropylene is the stereoregular polypropylene subfamily produced by syndiospecific coordination-insertion polymerization of propylene. The alternating stereochemical arrangement distinguishes this material from the other polypropylene tacticities and is associated with polymorphism and reversible structural transitions.
sections.history: Syndiotactic polypropylene had a different development path from the dominant isotactic material. Early syndiospecific catalyst work established that alternating stereochemistry was possible, but later metallocene chemistry made much higher stereoregularity accessible. John Ewen and Abbas Razavi’s Fina patent lineage, with a 1988 priority date, documents a major step in that development. Their work linked catalyst symmetry and polymer microstructure to a distinct crystalline polypropylene. The patent discusses uses in shaped articles, fibers and films. It records a technical milestone and intended applications; it does not establish that syndiotactic grades displaced isotactic polypropylene on a comparable commercial scale.
sections.nomenclature: sPP is the abbreviation for syndiotactic polypropylene. This record covers propylene polymers with the syndiotactic boundary; isotactic and atactic polypropylene, stereoblock materials, and polypropylene copolymers are not alternate names for this subfamily.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Syndiotactic polypropylene (sPP) is made by coordination–insertion polymerization of propylene with a catalyst whose stereochemical environment favors alternating placement of the pendant methyl groups along the chain. Modern routes use stereorigid, often bridged and C_s-symmetric, metallocene complexes of zirconium or hafnium activated by methylaluminoxane, modified methylaluminoxane, a noncoordinating borate/borane ion-pair reagent, or another organoaluminum component. Catalyst ligand symmetry and substitution are the primary tacticity controls; temperature, monomer purity, comonomer level, hydrogen, catalyst loading, and residence time regulate syndiotacticity, molar mass, and productivity. One cited industrial patent uses a crosslinked metallocene plus an aluminoxane, ion-pair-forming compound, or organoaluminum cocatalyst and permits solution, slurry, or gas-phase propylene polymerization, optionally with a particulate support. A distinct earlier patent describes low-temperature propylene polymerization with a stereorigid cationic metallocene having dissimilar substituted cyclopentadienyl rings and a weakly coordinating counteranion; trialkylaluminum is an optional cocatalyst. Liquid propylene can serve as monomer and medium, or an inert hydrocarbon solvent can be used. Supported catalysts and prepolymerization are manufacturing variants. Hydrogen or temperature changes provide molar-mass control. This entry concerns polypropylene whose principal stereoregularity is syndiotactic; isotactic, atactic, and deliberately stereoblock products require different catalyst-site control and are not synonyms.
sections.mechanicalProperties: sPP mechanical behavior depends on stereoregularity, molar mass, polymorph and crystallinity, thermal history, temperature, and the degree and direction of orientation. Unoriented sPP can show incomplete elastic recovery, whereas stress-relaxed fibers drawn to 400–600% have reported tension sets below 10%, attributed to a reversible crystal–crystal transition. In a separate tensile/drawing study, melt- or solution-crystallized sPP films reached draw ratios of 5–10; the maximum drawn-film modulus and strength were 3.0 and 0.33 GPa. Those values belong to highly drawn, morphology-specific films and must not be read as isotropic resin properties.
sections.processing:
Syndiotactic polypropylene (sPP) can be melt converted by injection molding, compression molding, extrusion, and melt spinning. Its lower melting range and different crystallization kinetics and polymorphism distinguish it from ordinary isotactic polypropylene, so an iPP setup should not be transferred without grade trials. Pellet feed consistency, melt temperature, residence time, shear, mold or die temperature, cooling rate, take-up speed, draw ratio, and later annealing determine crystallinity, crystal form, orientation, elastic recovery, shrinkage, and dimensional stability. In molding, pressure and cooling establish morphology and weld-line behavior; in spinning, air quench, godet speed, wind-up tension, and any subsequent drawing determine partial or full orientation. Polymerization tacticity control belongs in Synthesis; melting, shaping, quenching, drawing, winding, and annealing belong here.

Amer, van Reenen, and Mokrani provide a bounded molding example for their commercial sPP and 50/50 polypropylene blends. They injection-molded 20 mm by 1.5 mm disks on a HAAKE MiniJet II at 190 °C and 200 bar; separate DMA specimens were melted for 8 min at 180 °C and pressed at 180 °C and 5 MPa. These are laboratory specimen settings for the named materials, not a universal sPP molding window. A distinct fiber patent describes metallocene sPP pellets heated for extrusion at about 190–230 °C, metered to a spin pack, air-quenched, finished, passed over godets, and wound with little additional drawing. Its claimed partially oriented yarn process uses 700–3500 m/min forward spinning and a draw ratio below 1.2, with the disclosed sPP having at least about 90% syndiotactic r diads and 75% r-pentads. Those values are specific to that fiber process and polymer definition.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Syndiotactic polypropylene (sPP) is a stereoregular polypropylene whose crystallization route and polymorphism govern oriented morphology.
sections.properties: Drawn sPP fibers show reversible crystal transitions and drawing-dependent tensile response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. A documented commercial syndiotactic example is TotalEnergies 1251, listed for film and sheet extrusion. It is described as a syndiotactic random copolymer, so its applications do not establish a market for a chemically pure syndiotactic PP homopolymer.

Purchasing. The manufacturer provides product-contact and ordering channels for grade 1251. Buyers seeking homopolymer specifically must verify composition and tacticity rather than assuming that every syndiotactic PP listing has that scope.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separately reported annual production, purchases or consumption was established for syndiotactic PP. The supplier listing confirms a narrower commercial grade and application, without market tonnage or minimum order quantity.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Melt-state oxidation can cleave syndiotactic PP chains. A study of purified polymers showed much less molecular-mass loss for syndiotactic than isotactic PP in air, but increasing oxygen pressure accelerated degradation of syndiotactic PP. Individual volatile products were not resolved.

Timescales: The comparison included 200 °C treatment for 30 min and oxygen-pressure variation. It is a melt-aging experiment, not an outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The measured molecular-mass change does not establish environmental mineralization or a disappearance time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For syndiotactic PP, general polypropylene reclamation practice supplies a useful starting point: regrind compatible, segregated scrap and melt-mix it with virgin polymer. A directly measured PP-family example used a random copolymer over repeated extrusion cycles and showed that thermomechanical degradation changes viscosity and tensile response. This supports monitoring oxidation and processing history, but its quantitative results cannot be assigned to sPP, whose tacticity changes crystallization and oxidation behavior. A direct sPP waste-recovery trial remains a narrower evidence need.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Syndiotactic PP melt processing involves hot surfaces, pressurized resin and possible fumes. As polypropylene-family context, HSE lists formaldehyde, acrolein and acetone among products detected when PP is heated above its recommended processing range. The mixture depends on temperature, residence time, stabilizers and other ingredients. LyondellBasell’s polyolefin guide adds guarding, spill control and eye/hand protection for film equipment; the actual grade and operation determine the control measures.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Values belong to specified stereoregularity, drawing, crystallization, and fiber or film history; they do not describe all PP.

sections.overview: Random propylene–ethylene copolymer is a polypropylene-based copolymer in which ethylene-derived units are distributed along the propylene-rich chain. Its ethylene content and sequence distribution distinguish it from polypropylene homopolymer and block copolymers.
sections.history: Random propylene–ethylene copolymers grew out of the post-1950s polypropylene industry as manufacturers used comonomers to adjust an otherwise crystalline homopolymer. Their history is a sequence of catalyst and reactor improvements rather than a single independently documented invention. LyondellBasell’s Spheripol documentation describes successive high-selectivity catalysts and bulk/gas-phase process refinements that support commercial random-copolymer manufacture. Alongside broader polypropylene developments such as Spherizone in 2002, these tools widened the range of packaging and molded products that manufacturers could design. A particular process launch dates an industrial capability, not the first synthesis of all random propylene copolymers.
sections.nomenclature: PP-R and PPR are common abbreviations for random propylene–ethylene copolymer. The name describes a random copolymer architecture, not a physical mixture of polypropylene and polyethylene.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Random propylene–ethylene copolymer is made by coordination copolymerization of a propylene-rich feed with a smaller, controlled ethylene feed so that ethylene-derived units are statistically incorporated along the same predominantly propylene chain. Supported stereospecific Ziegler–Natta catalysts commonly combine a magnesium-chloride-supported titanium component, an organoaluminum cocatalyst, and internal or external electron donors; metallocene single-site catalysts are another route. The comonomer/propylene feed ratio governs incorporated ethylene, while hydrogen acts as a chain-transfer agent for molar-mass control. One cited patent performs propylene/ethylene copolymerization in successive gas-phase stages and varies ethylene and hydrogen between stages while retaining random-chain architecture. A distinct patent uses a slurry reactor followed by gas-phase copolymerization with a Ziegler–Natta procatalyst, cocatalyst, external donor, and hydrogen. Liquid-propylene bulk, loop-slurry, and stirred or fluidized gas-phase reactors are manufacturing variants. The defining distinction from a heterophasic impact copolymer is that ethylene is incorporated within the propylene copolymer chains rather than chiefly forming a separately produced rubber phase. Reactor staging may broaden composition or molar-mass distributions without by itself changing that boundary.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Random propylene–ethylene copolymers are semicrystalline thermoplastics in which statistically distributed ethylene counits interrupt regular isotactic-propylene sequences. Relative to a comparable polypropylene homopolymer, this usually lowers crystallinity, melting point, yield stress, and modulus while increasing flexibility and tensile ductility; the impact response depends on grade and temperature and should not be conflated with the separate rubber-phase toughening mechanism of heterophasic or block copolymers. Under tension PP-R can yield and draw, while long-term pipe loading is viscoelastic and creep- and oxidation-sensitive. Ethylene content and sequence distribution, tacticity, molecular weight and distribution, nucleation and α/γ crystal balance, crystallinity and lamellar morphology, cooling or annealing history, flow-induced orientation, weld lines, wall geometry, temperature and loading rate, fillers and pigments, and stabilizer type, concentration, dispersion, and depletion all affect performance. Hot water and warm air can consume different antioxidants in pipe walls, so short-term coupon data do not establish hydrostatic lifetime.

For one bounded grade example, SIBUR's September 2023 technical sheet identifies PP R003 EX/1 as a low-flow propylene–ethylene random copolymer stabilized for extruded PPR80 pressure pipe. Its typical GOST results are 23 MPa tensile yield stress and 12% elongation at yield at 50 mm/min, 650 MPa flexural modulus at 50 mm/min, and notched Izod impact strength of 10.0 kJ/m^2 at 23 °C but 2.5 kJ/m^2 at −20 °C. The document does not report specimen preparation or conditioning, and labels the values non-specification typical data. They therefore describe this pipe grade and show the importance of test temperature; they are not a PP-R family range.
sections.processing:
Random propylene–ethylene copolymers (PP-R) are melt thermoplastics converted by injection molding; pipe and profile, sheet, cast or blown-film extrusion; blow molding; and melt spinning into multifilament or nonwoven products. A grade must be matched to the route because ethylene content, molecular-mass distribution, nucleation, stabilizers, and melt flow alter crystallization rate, sealability, melt strength, stiffness, shrinkage, and cycle time. Pellets normally need no drying when clean and properly stored, but surface moisture or condensation can disrupt feeding or appearance; concentrates and clean regrind should be metered uniformly. Extrusion control includes screw geometry and compression, feed-throat stability, melt temperature and pressure, shear heating, screen and die condition, drawdown or blow-up ratio, chill-roll or air cooling, take-up, and orientation. Injection molding additionally depends on shot-to-barrel sizing, residence time, filling and packing through gate freeze, balanced mold cooling, and sufficient crystallization before ejection. Excess melt temperature, oxygen exposure, or residence can oxidize polypropylene, while inadequate cooling and uneven orientation promote sink, warpage, gauge variation, and anisotropy. Polymerization and comonomer incorporation belong in Synthesis; this section begins with PP-R pellets and covers their preparation and shaping.

Formosa's polypropylene guide provides supplier starting guidance, not a universal PP-R window. For single-screw sheet extrusion it recommends an L/D ratio of 24:1–30:1, compression ratio of 3:1–4:1, and melt temperature about 200–250 °C, while noting that drying is generally unnecessary. A distinct open study supplies an article-conversion example without claiming a family window: Traxler and co-workers used the named Borealis RD204CF random-copolymer grade R8 to injection mold the study's tensile and Charpy specimens alongside matched-flow polypropylene materials. The Formosa machine ranges and the study's specimen route should not be transferred unchanged to pressure-pipe, film, fiber, or packaging grades.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PP-R is a propylene-rich random copolymer with ethylene units disrupting polypropylene crystallinity.
sections.properties: Ethylene content and molecular architecture control impact response and pipe performance.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Random propylene–ethylene copolymers are used in clear packaging and molded containers; random PP offerings also include other comonomers, so product composition must be verified for this entry.

Purchasing. Purchase the specified ethylene-containing random grade through a PP producer or distributor. INEOS lists random-copolymer pellets among its bulk truck and rail deliveries; composition and intended application remain grade-specific.

Scale and evidence limits. No separate purchased or consumed tonnage was established for the ethylene-containing random subset. Supplier-wide PP volumes combine homopolymer, random and impact grades.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hot chlorinated water depletes stabilizers and produces lower-molecular-mass chains in tested PP-R pipe grades. The alpha- and beta-nucleated grades differ in chain loss and embrittlement; a complete small-molecule product inventory was not measured.

Timescales: For 100 µm specimens at 60 °C in water containing 5 mg/L free chlorine, total embrittlement occurred after approximately 1,500 h for the alpha-nucleated grade and 2,000 h for the beta-nucleated grade.

Environmental persistence: These accelerated, thin-specimen embrittlement endpoints are not whole-pipe lifetimes or environmental mineralization times.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical recycling of random PP is directly demonstrated by repeated extrusion and blending with virgin resin. La Mantia and co-workers used Hostalen PP H5416 random copolymer for five successive single-screw extrusion cycles, then studied blends made with a 30 wt% reprocessed fraction and 70 wt% virgin resin. The stated barrel profile was 180–210–240–270 °C at 60 rpm. Viscosity declined with repeated processing, and the authors stress that mixing rules depend on preservation of chemical and morphological compatibility. These laboratory results support controlled reuse of compatible scrap, not unlimited recycling without property change.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Random propylene–ethylene copolymer melt processing involves hot surfaces, pressurized resin and possible fumes. As polypropylene-family context, HSE lists formaldehyde, acrolein and acetone among products detected when PP is heated above its recommended processing range. The mixture depends on temperature, residence time, stabilizers and other ingredients. LyondellBasell’s polyolefin guide adds guarding, spill control and eye/hand protection for film equipment; the actual grade and operation determine the control measures.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Pipe-aging data concern specified antioxidant packages and grades.

sections.overview: Heterophasic polypropylene copolymer is a multiphase impact-polypropylene material in which sequential polymerization produces polypropylene fractions together with a propylene–ethylene elastomer fraction. The dispersed elastomer phase distinguishes the material from a simple propylene homopolymer.
sections.history: Heterophasic polypropylene developed as producers combined a polypropylene matrix with an elastomeric phase to broaden the material’s impact performance. It is a reactor-made multiphase material class, with no single first-invention date established by the sources used here. LyondellBasell documents the role of gas-phase copolymerization stages and successive Spheripol catalyst generations in expanding impact-copolymer production. Such process development supported the polypropylene industry’s expansion in automotive parts, appliances and other molded goods. The 2002 Spherizone milestone provides a later example of producers changing reactor architecture to gain additional control over product architecture.
sections.nomenclature: The record covers the heterophasic or impact-copolymer form of polypropylene, also denoted PP-B or HECO. These terms identify a multiphase copolymer architecture; they should not be used for an arbitrary random polypropylene copolymer or a particular filled injection-molding grade.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Heterophasic polypropylene copolymer is a reactor-made multiphase polypropylene material, not a simple mechanical blend. It is commonly prepared by sequential polymerization: a propylene-rich matrix fraction is first made, then ethylene with propylene and/or an alpha-olefin is polymerized in the presence of that first fraction to create a dispersed rubbery copolymer phase. Documented multistage routes use stereospecific Ziegler–Natta catalyst systems with titanium-containing procatalyst, organoaluminum cocatalyst, and optional electron donor; slurry/bulk and gas-phase stages can be combined. One recent three-stage example forms initial propylene copolymer fractions then makes a propylene–ethylene elastomer in a further gas-phase stage. Reactor sequence, comonomer feeds, catalyst/donor system, hydrogen use, and phase proportions are composition-specific. Subsequent compounding, filler addition, or molding is outside this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Heterophasic polypropylene copolymers are multiphase thermoplastics in which a semicrystalline isotactic-polypropylene matrix supplies stiffness and yield strength while dispersed ethylene-propylene rubber, commonly with polyethylene-rich inclusions, promotes energy absorption and ductile fracture. Relative to polypropylene homopolymer, the characteristic design tradeoff is higher impact resistance, especially below room temperature, against lower tensile and flexural stiffness. Their response is strongly temperature- and rate-dependent: notches, rapid loading, thick sections, weld lines, or temperatures near and below the matrix and rubber transitions can shift a molding from yielding and plastic deformation toward brittle fracture. The balance depends on matrix tacticity, molecular mass, crystallinity and molecular-mass distribution; rubber fraction, ethylene content, molecular mass and glass-transition temperature; dispersed-particle size, shape, internal core-shell structure, spacing and interfacial adhesion; and any polyethylene, external elastomer, filler, reinforcement, nucleating agent, or peroxide modification. Melt viscosity ratio and deformation during compounding or molding govern the resulting phase morphology, while cooling rate, annealing, orientation, specimen thickness, notch geometry, strain rate and test temperature govern the measured result. Increasing rubber fraction can produce a brittle-to-tough transition but generally lowers modulus; higher-molecular-mass phases and a fine, well-adhered dispersion can improve toughness. Talc or glass fiber can raise stiffness and dimensional stability, but filler loading, dispersion and coupling determine whether strength rises and impact resistance is retained. As one bounded commercial example, SOCAR Polymer reports typical values for its phthalate-free CB 1200 MO injection-molding heterophasic copolymer grade: flexural modulus 1200 MPa by ISO 178 at 2 mm/min, tensile modulus 1100 MPa by ISO 527 at 1 mm/min, tensile stress at yield 23 MPa and elongation at yield 6% by ISO 527 at 50 mm/min, and notched Izod impact strength of 10 kJ/m2 at 23 °C and 5 kJ/m2 at -20 °C by ISO 180. The sheet does not identify specimen molding history, geometry, conditioning, or replicate statistics, and labels these as typical rather than specification values; they therefore characterize CB 1200 MO only, not the family or filled, oriented, recycled, weathered, or differently processed articles.
sections.processing:
Heterophasic polypropylene copolymer is a melt-processable thermoplastic used for injection molding, extrusion, thermoforming, and (for suitable grades) compression molding. Pellets normally need no routine drying when kept dry, but moisture, contamination, and any filler or regrind package should be checked before molding; grade molecular mass, rubber-phase content, filler loading, and mold geometry change the usable window. Compounding or regrinding should provide enough distributive mixing to retain a fine rubber dispersion while avoiding excessive residence time, shear heating, and oxidative degradation.

A bounded supplier example is SCG's EL-Pro P740J impact-copolymer grade: its technical sheet recommends a 230–270 °C melt, 25–70 °C mold, fast injection, 40–70 rpm screw speed, and injection/packing/back-pressure settings expressed as 40–80%/30–60%/10% of machine maximum. Those values apply to that grade and machine/product context, not to every heterophasic PP. A separate PP injection guide gives broader compound guidance (about 200–250 °C mass temperature for PP variants, 20–90 °C mold temperature depending on reinforcement, and residence time below 10 min) and notes that drying, moisture, shrinkage, and cooling depend on formulation and part geometry. These sources support melt conversion; reactor polymerization of the heterophasic material belongs in Synthesis.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Heterophasic polypropylene is a multiphase material with a crystalline polypropylene-rich matrix and a dispersed rubbery ethylene/propylene-rich phase, commonly made in sequential reactors. The dispersed phase toughens the matrix while particle size, composition, and interfacial structure control the balance of stiffness and impact response.
sections.properties: The two-phase morphology provides improved impact toughness and low-temperature ductility compared with many polypropylene homopolymers while retaining polypropylene's low density and melt processability. Stiffness, shrinkage, weld-line response, and impact behavior depend on rubber content, particle morphology, crystallinity, fillers, and processing orientation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Heterophasic PP is used where molded articles require impact toughness. SOCAR CB1200MO is specifically documented for crates, housewares, rigid packaging and automotive battery cases.

Purchasing. The CB1200MO sheet lists pellets in 25 kg bags, with 1,250 kg per pallet, or 1,000 kg bulk bags by agreement. Select an impact grade suited to the molding or compounding application.

Scale and evidence limits. These package sizes span tens of kilograms to roughly a tonne and document delivery units, not annual purchases. No reliable separate global purchased or consumed tonnage was established for heterophasic PP.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In Novatec BC03AD block PP, repeated processing changes the PP matrix while thermo-crosslinking in the ethylene–propylene rubber phase modifies the overall response.

Timescales: The study used up to five extrusion passes with approximately 1 min residence and approximately 210 °C die-exit temperature.

Environmental persistence: The measured property changes cannot be converted to an outdoor disappearance or mineralization time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Re-extrusion and remolding were demonstrated for this heterophasic grade. Rubber-phase changes mean recyclability must be qualified by composition and processing history.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Heterophasic PP melt processing involves hot surfaces, pressurized resin and possible fumes. As polypropylene-family context, HSE lists formaldehyde, acrolein and acetone among products detected when PP is heated above its recommended processing range. The mixture depends on temperature, residence time, stabilizers and other ingredients. LyondellBasell’s polyolefin guide adds guarding, spill control and eye/hand protection for film equipment; the actual grade and operation determine the control measures.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Impact and stiffness trade off with rubber fraction and morphology, and the result is sensitive to cooling, flow direction, weld lines, filler dispersion, and notch geometry. A reactor-grade copolymer, a mineral-filled compound, and a finished molded part should not be treated as equivalent materials.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Sequential polymerization forms a polypropylene-rich matrix and an ethylene/propylene rubber phase. Olefin first coordinates to an active metal site and then inserts into the metal–carbon bond of the growing chain. The longer metal-bound chain can coordinate and insert another monomer; catalyst environment and feed selection govern the resulting sequence and stereochemistry. The staged feeds create different polymer populations and phases; successive reactor stages do not by themselves establish a covalent block sequence.

sections.overview: Poly(1-butene) is the PB-1 coordination-polymerized homopolymer of 1-butene. Its catalyst system and polymerization conditions can produce stereoregulated material, while comonomer-containing polybutene materials are separate composition scopes.
sections.history: Poly(1-butene) belongs to the first wave of stereospecific polyolefins. LyondellBasell traces its discovery to Giulio Natta’s research group in 1954 and industrial introduction in Europe to the mid-1960s. Flexible pressure piping became an important early application, with subsequent development directed toward hot- and cold-water systems. The company’s later PB-1 business also developed packaging, polymer-modification and adhesive uses. This history connects an early catalyst discovery to decades of pipe-grade development; the performance of a particular pipe system still depends on its resin generation, fittings and installation.
sections.nomenclature: PB-1 is the abbreviation used for poly(1-butene), also called polybutene-1. This record is the 1-butene homopolymer; copolymers, particular pipe compounds, and their crystallization histories are not alternate names for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(1-butene) (PB-1) is made by coordination polymerization of 1-butene. Stereospecific Ziegler–Natta catalyst systems are used to favor isotactic material, while polymerization medium, temperature, hydrogen, and any alpha-olefin comonomer are route-specific controls of molecular mass, tacticity, and product form. One suspension-process example combines a titanium-based transition-metal component with an organoaluminum cocatalyst and conducts 1-butene polymerization in liquid isobutane; the source notes optional hydrogen for molecular-mass control. A separate catalyst patent describes a MgCl2-supported titanium component, aluminum-alkyl cocatalyst, and optional electron donor, including gas-phase and slurry variants. These are coordination-polymerization examples; they do not imply that copolymer recipes or crystallization histories are intrinsic to every PB-1 grade.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(1-butene) (PB-1) is semicrystalline and polymorphic, so stiffness, stress relaxation, and tensile response depend on crystal modification, crystallinity, molecular orientation, thermal history, temperature, and copolymer content. Open studies of isotactic PB-1 connect mechanical response to crystal-phase composition and the rigid/amorphous physical-network structure; a stress-relaxation study specifically identifies orientation and transformation from crystal form II to form I as part of the response. These dependencies make fresh versus aged or differently processed PB-1 specimens non-interchangeable.

A bounded pipe-system endpoint is Buteline's PB-1 pipe, which is stated to use Basell PB-1 granules: its design sheet lists hydrostatic design stress of 7.6 MPa at 20 °C and 3.5 MPa at 80 °C. These are manufacturer design values for pipe service, not tensile-test values for the polymer family; pipe geometry, extrusion history, pressure-test duration, and compound details limit transferability.
sections.processing: Poly(1-butene) (PB-1) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic processed by extrusion of pipe, tubing, film, and profiles, by melt spinning, and by injection molding with conventional polyolefin equipment when the grade and tooling are appropriate. Pellets should be kept dry and clean; melt temperature, shear, line speed, draw-down, and cooling must be coordinated because freshly formed PB-1 is soft and crystallizes slowly, changing from the initially formed phase II toward the stiffer phase I during aging. In a bounded LyondellBasell pipe-resin guide, small-pipe extrusion uses approximately 180–200 °C melt temperature and 10–12 °C cooling water, with immediate spray quenching, water pre-sizing, vacuum sizing, and controlled draw-down; the guide warns that higher temperature can cause sticking while lower temperature can increase machine-direction orientation. An independent melt-spinning study used commercial homopolymer PB0110M and 4.3 mol% ethylene copolymer PB8220M: pellets were vacuum-dried at 80 °C for 10 h, extruded through a single-screw/spin-pack system with a 110–260 °C barrel range, and wound at 7 or 10 m min−1; hot-pressed films were melted at 180 °C for 10 min and aged one week. These settings are grade- and article-specific, and the ethylene copolymer example is not identical to the homopolymer family. Butene-1 polymerization and catalyst chemistry belong in Synthesis; this section covers pellet handling, melt shaping, spinning, cooling, aging, and post-processing.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(1-butene) is a semicrystalline polyolefin with polymorphic crystal forms.
sections.properties: Crystallization history, molecular weight, and orientation govern its response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PB-1 is used for hot-water pipe systems, fittings, peelable packaging, hot-melt adhesives and polyolefin modification. These uses link the resin to building services, packaging converters and adhesive formulators.

Purchasing. LyondellBasell offers both homopolymer and random copolymer PB-1 resins through its product-information channel. Specify whether the order concerns resin for pipe, film modification or adhesive formulation; finished piping systems are a different purchase.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was established in the checked material. The supplier portfolio documents commercial end uses, not industry-wide volume or a standard order size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Isotactic PB-1 film oxidation proceeds through hydroperoxide formation and chain scission, with carbonyl-containing material accumulating. The Toyo Soda study identified acetaldehyde, ethanol, water, acetic acid and propionic acid in collected volatiles; it also reported formaldehyde and tentatively assigned methyl ethyl ketone.

Timescales: Product collection used approximately 2 g polymer under flowing oxygen for 7 h at 170 °C, with a 130 °C comparison. Oxygen-uptake experiments used 130–180 °C and showed a film-thickness effect. These accelerated oxidation conditions are not a service-life or environmental-decay clock.

Environmental persistence: Chain scission, oxygen uptake and volatilization do not establish complete mineralization in soil or water. The study does not provide an environmental half-life for PB-1 articles.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: PBPSA describes inline recycling of PB-1 production residues during pipe manufacture. This documents production-scrap recovery; it does not establish a broad post-consumer pipe collection stream.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PB-1 oxidation experiments demonstrate that severe hot-oxygen exposure can generate volatile oxygenated compounds, including aldehydes, acids and water. These laboratory products are not a measured exposure level during ordinary use. For industrial handling, the polyolefin-processing guidance on hot melt, pressurized equipment, ventilation and prevention of prolonged overheating is applicable as family context; the supplied grade’s stabilizers and processing window remain important.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Pipe and drawn-filament results are grade- and process-specific.

sections.overview: Poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) is PMP, a coordination/insertion homopolymer of the sterically demanding alpha-olefin 4-methyl-1-pentene. Catalyst and solvent choices in documented routes affect molecular mass and stereoregularity.
sections.history: ICI introduced poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) as TPX in 1965, according to a contemporary UNIDO paper. Mitsui Chemicals subsequently became a major developer and producer of the material. Its commercial development has emphasized an unusual combination of transparency, heat resistance and release behavior. Established uses include laboratory vessels, electrical insulation, rubber-hose mandrels and release films. More specialized applications include hollow fibers and processing aids for electronics. These applications explain its place as a specialty polyolefin rather than a direct replacement for commodity polyethylene or polypropylene.
sections.nomenclature: PMP is the abbreviation used for poly(4-methyl-1-pentene), also called poly-4-methyl-1-pentene. This record is the homopolymer of 4-methyl-1-pentene; copolymers, grades, and downstream molded or drawn forms are not aliases for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) is a coordination/insertion homopolymer of 4-methyl-1-pentene. The sterically demanding alpha-olefin makes catalyst structure important for activity, molecular weight, and isotactic stereoregularity. One documented route uses a single-site bridged imine-amido catalyst to coordinate and insert 4-methyl-1-pentene in toluene; other routes use aluminum-chloride catalyst systems in halogenated solvent. Catalyst/activator, solvent, monomer-to-catalyst ratio, reaction temperature, and termination are bounded experimental or industrial route choices rather than a universal polymerization recipe. The polymer is distinct from a cyclic metathesis-derived material, and extrusion or other final conversion is not treated as synthesis here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic polyolefin with a bulky isobutyl side group. The isotactic homopolymer can be comparatively stiff but brittle, while small amounts of other alpha-olefins are used commercially to disrupt packing and improve toughness and elongation. Its response is viscoelastic and strongly temperature dependent around the amorphous-phase transition: modulus and tensile strength can fall markedly as temperature rises even though the crystalline phase remains. Tacticity, comonomer identity and fraction, molecular weight, crystal form and crystallinity, tie-chain and amorphous-chain entanglement density, physical aging, and additives therefore matter. Melt-draw ratio, cooling rate, annealing, film or fiber orientation and thickness, loading direction, strain rate, and test temperature can change yield, strain hardening, recovery, and failure.

An open film study provides a bounded processing example rather than a bulk-material constant. It used a Mitsui extrusion grade with melt-flow index 9 g/10 min at 260 °C/5 kg, number-average molecular mass 180,000 g/mol, and weight-average molecular mass 622,000 g/mol. T-slot films were cast through a 270 °C die onto a 100 °C chill roll. At melt-draw ratio 40 the 50 μm film, tested at 60 °C and 50 mm/min, had 665 MPa tensile modulus, 15.8 MPa yield stress, and 27.8% elastic recovery after the stated 50%-strain hold/release cycle. Raising the draw ratio to 164 produced a 15 μm film with 147 MPa modulus, 7.2 MPa yield stress, and 44.8% recovery under the same method. The opposing changes were attributed to fewer crystalline tie chains but greater amorphous entanglement and orientation; they must remain limited to this grade, extrusion-cast geometry, draw history, loading direction, and elevated-temperature protocol.
sections.processing:
Poly(4-methyl-1-pentene) is a high-melting thermoplastic that can be injection molded, extruded into sheet and profile, melt-cast into film, melt-spun into fiber, and solution-cast for specialized thin films and composites. Melt processing requires equipment capable of its elevated melt temperature and careful control of residence time, oxidation, die and chill-roll temperatures, draw ratio, and cooling. Flow-induced crystallization and drawing strongly alter lamellar orientation, thickness, shrinkage, and film mechanics; blends and filled compounds require separate compatibility and dispersion work.

Yin and co-workers provide a bounded extrusion-casting example for a Mitsui extrusion-grade PMP with melt-flow index 9 g/10 min at 260 °C/5 kg, melting point 234 °C, and reported molar masses. They used a T-slot die at 270 °C and a chill roll at 100 °C, then varied melt-draw ratio from 40 to 164 to make films about 50 to 15 micrometres thick. Increasing draw transformed the morphology from spherulitic toward oriented lamellae and changed crystallinity and elastic response. Those temperatures and draw ratios are specific to that grade, die/roll setup, and hard-elastic-film experiment, not a universal PMP window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PMP is a semicrystalline branched polyolefin with low density and distinctive crystal structure.
sections.properties: Optical, thermal, and mechanical behavior depend on crystallinity and orientation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PMP is used for laboratory equipment, heat-resistant food containers, cosmetic packaging, LED molds and release films for electronics or synthetic-leather manufacture. Mitsui’s TPX examples also include hose-production mandrels and sheaths.

Purchasing. Mitsui supplies TPX in pellet form with distinct grades for molding, film and other conversion routes. Request the grade appropriate to the application; the marketed PMP family includes composition-dependent commercial materials.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate purchased or consumed tonnage was established from the checked manufacturer page. Its application and grade listings should not be read as a quantitative ranking of markets.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A patent demonstrates controlled molecular-mass reduction of PMP during co-extrusion with a selected polypropylene; the recovered material remains a polymer mixture rather than identified environmental metabolites.

Timescales: Its DX820/HP461Y example uses a 4:6 mass ratio, 250 °C outlet temperature and 200 rpm; no environmental degradation time is established.

Environmental persistence: Molecular-mass reduction during extrusion is not mineralization or proof of biodegradability.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent establishes a controlled chain-reduction method for virgin resins. Application to post-consumer PMP reclamation and commercial waste recycling remains unverified.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For poly(4-methyl-1-pentene), polyolefin-processing guidance provides useful workplace context: protect against hot melt and equipment, control pressure and moving machinery, and remove processing fumes. HSE stresses actual temperature and residence time when assessing emissions; its polyethylene and polypropylene product lists should not be treated as measured PMP emission compositions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Film results are processing-specific and cannot represent all PMP grades.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Coordination addition consumes the terminal alkene while retaining the branched side chain. Olefin first coordinates to an active metal site and then inserts into the metal–carbon bond of the growing chain. The longer metal-bound chain can coordinate and insert another monomer; catalyst environment and feed selection govern the resulting sequence and stereochemistry.

sections.overview: Cyclo-olefin polymer (COP) is a family of cyclic-olefin polymers, commonly made by ring-opening metathesis polymerization followed by hydrogenation. The record covers COP materials as a family and distinguishes this ROMP-derived route from addition-copolymerized cyclic olefin copolymers (COC).
sections.history: The modern commercial COP history is illustrated by Zeon’s hydrogenated cyclic-polymer materials. Zeon completed its ZEONEX plant at Mizushima in November 1990 and began selling ZEONOR in September 1998. Optical applications were particularly important because dimensional stability and low moisture uptake complemented transparency; medical and industrial molded parts broadened the market. Zeon’s history therefore records a transition from cyclic-monomer chemistry to precision-use plastics. These milestones date specific commercial families, while COP as a broader chemical category can include materials with different research and production lineages.
sections.nomenclature: COP is the abbreviation used for cyclo-olefin polymer in this record. It denotes a family/material class rather than one commercial grade or one fixed cyclic-olefin composition; COC, the addition copolymer of an acyclic and cyclic olefin, is outside this record's boundary.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cyclo-olefin polymer (COP) is commonly made by ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) of cyclic-olefin feedstocks followed by hydrogenation of the unsaturated polymer backbone. Unlike ethylene/norbornene COC addition copolymerization, ROMP opens the cyclic alkene and leaves backbone double bonds before the hydrogenation stage. A documented academic example uses a ruthenium Grubbs catalyst to ROMP strained bicyclic monomers and then hydrogenates the main-chain double bonds; changing comonomer feed changes the polymer composition. A Zeon patent likewise describes hydrogenating norbornene ring-opened polymer with hydrogen and a homogeneous or heterogeneous hydrogenation catalyst, and identifies vinyl/diene additions as molecular-weight modifiers during ring opening. These route-specific examples should not be read as a specification for every commercial COP grade.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cyclo-olefin polymers (COPs) are amorphous engineering thermoplastics. Their measured tensile and impact response depends on the named grade and test configuration, as well as the molded article geometry; numbers from one resin or tube should not be treated as a family-wide design range.

A supplier comparison of optical ZEONEX COP grades reported ISO 527 tensile moduli of 2530 MPa (K26R), 2570 MPa (K22R), 2650 MPa (T62R), and 2960 MPa (360R), with corresponding tensile strengths of 54, 72, 67, and 37 MPa. These are separate grade values from the supplier table, not a universal COP interval.

For a bounded article-level durability example, an independent study injection-molded Zeonex 690R COP blood-collection tubes (4 and 9 mL) and drop-tested water-filled, stoppered 10 mL tubes vertically onto linoleum. Table 2 reports zero breaks among 24 COP tubes at both 36 and 48 inch drop heights. That result describes this molded tube geometry, fill state, orientation, and visual breakage criterion rather than a standard bulk impact property.
sections.processing:
Cyclo-olefin polymer can be injection molded into optical, medical, and precision articles and hot-embossed or thermally bonded as sheet for microstructured devices. ZEON's molding guide treats the settings as product-specific: ZEONEX grades are preheated for 4–10 h at the listed grade temperature to remove dissolved air rather than simply to remove absorbed water, while overly long heating can discolor the material. For optical molding it recommends excluding oxygen with nitrogen at the hopper and barrel because oxidation at melt temperature can produce burning, discoloration, and contamination. Its listed ZEONEX examples span cylinder and mold settings that change by grade, so those tables should not be read as a family-wide window.

A separate bounded study hot-embossed COP sheet at 180 °C and 103 kPa for 5 min using a powder-reinforced PDMS mold constrained in an aluminum frame. Omitting either reinforcement or the frame produced inconsistent or distorted microscale features; patterned and unpatterned sheets were subsequently thermally bonded into chips. The temperature, pressure, time, and mold constraint are specific to that sheet-scale microfluidic experiment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cyclo-olefin polymers are cyclic-olefin-derived materials whose ring-containing repeat units and polymerization route control glass formation and optical morphology.
sections.properties: COP grades are transparent, low-moisture-absorbing thermoplastics with grade-dependent optical and thermal behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Optical COP grades are used in smartphone lenses and other precision optics, serving imaging and electronics supply chains. Zeon links the application to transparency, low optical dispersion and grades suited to intricate molded lenses.

Purchasing. Purchase a specified optical COP resin grade through the manufacturer’s contact channel, distinguishing optical requirements and molding behavior. Optical-grade resin is a different purchase from a finished lens or film.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate purchased or consumed tonnage was established from the checked optical product source. This documents a specific commercial use without estimating the entire COP market.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A COP-based development adhesive retained bond properties during heat and humidity aging; the supplier does not identify a degradation-product inventory for COP in this document.

Timescales: For the LS adhesive, the supplier reports retained shear/peel performance after 2,000 h under specified heat/humidity tests, and retained shear strength after 2,000 h at 100 °C. These are grade-specific retention tests.

Environmental persistence: Resistance to hydrolysis and retained bonds do not establish environmental disappearance or mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Zeon’s 2024 report records completion of a dedicated COP recycling plant and preparation for operation. This documents industrial development at the report date; it does not demonstrate general post-consumer COP collection.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: ZEON’s ZEONEX molding guide describes nitrogen sealing of the hopper to limit oxidation and cautions that the surrounding nitrogen concentration must be monitored with adequate room ventilation. This adds a gas-handling consideration to the hot-melt operation. Processing fume controls should follow the grade and actual temperature/residence history, as set out in HSE plastics guidance.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: ZEONEX technical data describe named optical grades, while microfluidic reports use particular COP grades and molding methods; their values do not apply to all COP chemistries.

sections.overview: Cyclic olefin copolymer is a family of olefin copolymers incorporating cyclic olefin units, commonly made from ethylene with monomers such as norbornene or tetracyclododecene. Its composition is set by the cyclic comonomer and copolymerization route.
sections.history: Cyclic olefin copolymers became commercially important when catalyst advances enabled controlled incorporation of cyclic and linear olefins. TOPAS traces its lineage to Hoechst research in the early 1990s and a commercial plant at Oberhausen in 2000. The business later passed through Ticona/Celanese to Daicel and Polyplastics in 2006. Early development targeted transparent, dimensionally stable products, including optical data storage and lenses; pharmaceutical packaging, diagnostic disposables and barrier films became important markets. These dates describe the TOPAS industrial lineage rather than the first laboratory preparation of every cyclic olefin copolymer.
sections.nomenclature: COC abbreviates cyclic olefin copolymer. The name covers a composition-variable copolymer family, not one defined repeat-unit sequence, and should not be silently merged with cyclic olefin polymers made by different polymerization routes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) denotes addition copolymers in which an acyclic olefin, commonly ethylene, is copolymerized with a cyclic olefin such as norbornene or tetracyclododecene. This is coordination-insertion polymerization: the cyclic olefin double bond is consumed during chain growth while the cyclic ring framework is retained in the chain, distinguishing the route from ring-opening metathesis routes used for many cyclo-olefin polymers. Group 4 molecular catalysts, including titanium- and zirconium-based systems, are documented for ethylene/cyclic-olefin copolymerization; catalyst structure and cocatalyst choice govern cyclic-monomer incorporation, sequence distribution, and molecular weight. A Polyplastics patent route uses a metal-containing catalyst, with aluminoxane or borate cocatalyst options, to copolymerize ethylene and a norbornene monomer while limiting polyethylene-like byproduct. The cited conditions describe particular catalyst systems, not a universal COC formulation.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cyclic olefin copolymers (COCs) are amorphous engineering thermoplastics whose tensile response is grade- and molding-history-dependent. In injection-molded parts, flow-induced orientation and the associated birefringence can vary through the plate; reported tensile values therefore need the grade, specimen location or orientation, and test method rather than being combined into a universal COC range.

A bounded supplier example is TOPAS 6017S-04, an injection-molding COC grade. Its technical data sheet reports an ISO 527-3 tensile modulus of 3000 MPa at 1 mm/min, tensile stress at break of 58 MPa at 5 mm/min, and strain at break of 2.4% at 5 mm/min. These are values for that named grade and test configuration, not for all COCs.

An independent study of injection-molded COC plates measured tensile moduli of 1991–2040 MPa, tensile strengths of 56–58 MPa, and elongations at break of 3.3–3.5% at three plate positions. The position-dependent results reinforce that an injection-molded article's local orientation and geometry affect the measured response.
sections.processing:
Cyclic olefin copolymer grades can be injection molded, extruded as film, sheet, or profile, and converted by blow molding or injection-blow molding; films may also be stretched above the grade's glass-transition temperature. Standard thermoplastic equipment is usable, but melt and mold temperatures, flow, and permitted residence time vary with grade. TOPAS guidance says routine predrying is generally unnecessary, while surface-moist pellets may be dried at 80 °C and high-surface-quality molding may require grade-specific predrying; it also warns that excess melt temperature or residence time can yellow the resin and that undersized gates can cause shear heating.

Hot embossing and thermal bonding provide a separate article route for microfluidic structures. In one bounded example, 1.5 mm mcs-COC-13 sheet with a reported glass-transition temperature of 142 °C was embossed against an epoxy mold for 10 min at 160 °C and 2.3 MPa, then held under pressure for another 15 min while cooling. The embossed substrate was cleaned, dried, and thermally bonded to another COC plate for 30 min at 130 °C and 2.3 MPa. These conditions belong to that sheet, mold stack, and device geometry, not to every COC grade.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cyclic olefin copolymers (COCs) are copolymers of ethylene or another alpha-olefin with cyclic olefins such as norbornene or tetracyclododecene; comonomer content determines the specific COC architecture.
sections.properties: Molded COC response varies with grade, molecular architecture, and plate position produced during injection molding.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. COC is used in healthcare packaging and diagnostic components, optical parts and packaging films. The TOPAS portfolio distinguishes molding grades from grades used in films and blends.

Purchasing. Buy a named COC grade from TOPAS or its commercial supply channel according to the part, sterilization or barrier requirements. A generic cyclic-olefin label does not specify the grade needed for an application.

Scale and evidence limits. The September 2019 brochure describes the Oberhausen, Germany plant that started in 2000 with annual capacity of 30,000 tons, as reported in the source. This places a documented production installation in the tens-of-thousands-of-tons-per-year range; it is historical plant capacity, not present production or annual purchases. No separately verified COC consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The TOPAS COC supplier documents adverse effects of prolonged direct sunlight on resin properties, while visible light produces little or no change. The guide does not identify the individual chemical degradation products.

Timescales: The guide supplies no transferable outdoor degradation time; formulation and exposure must be specified.

Environmental persistence: Hydrolytic and chemical resistance do not establish environmental mineralization. The cited document leaves a COC-specific mineralization lifetime unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The supplier describes flotation separation of COC-based shrink sleeves from PET bottles because their densities differ. This is a packaging separation/recycling example; it does not demonstrate closed-loop recovery for every COC article.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The TOPAS COC brochure identifies dust and volatile exposure during processing as matters for workplace control and refers users to the grade-specific safety data sheet. HSE guidance adds temperature control, avoidance of excessive residence time and suitable ventilation for melt operations. Optical clarity or chemical resistance of a finished COC article does not by itself characterize exposure during manufacture.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Coordination addition incorporates the cyclic olefin while retaining its ring framework. Olefin first coordinates to an active metal site and then inserts into the metal–carbon bond of the growing chain. The longer metal-bound chain can coordinate and insert another monomer; catalyst environment and feed selection govern the resulting sequence and stereochemistry. In this addition route, the norbornene double bond is consumed while its bicyclic skeleton is retained.

sections.overview: Ethylene–vinyl acetate copolymer is the EVA random copolymer of ethylene and vinyl acetate made by high-pressure free-radical polymerization. Vinyl-acetate content produces a family ranging from flexible thermoplastics to elastomer-like grades, while crosslinking or foaming is a separate formulation step.
sections.history: EVA developed as an ethylene copolymer offering flexibility and adhesion useful in many formulations. DuPont’s ELVAX was imported by the Mitsui Japanese venture from 1962, followed by domestic EVAFLEX production in 1965. This is an international commercialization milestone rather than EVA’s first synthesis. The subsequent product range served footwear and packaging foams, hot-melt adhesives, agricultural and protective films, electrical-wire coverings and molded goods. Development of different vinyl-acetate contents and processing grades allowed these markets to diverge while retaining the same basic ethylene–vinyl acetate chemistry.
sections.nomenclature: EVA and EVAC are abbreviations used for ethylene–vinyl acetate copolymer. The record is the uncrosslinked copolymer family and its grade variation; polyethylene, ethylene–vinyl alcohol (the hydrolyzed derivative), and a crosslinked or foamed article are related but not aliases for the base copolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–vinyl acetate copolymer (EVA) is produced by radical copolymerization of ethylene and vinyl acetate. High-pressure free-radical processes are documented in tubular and stirred-autoclave reactors, using organic peroxide initiators; a continuous route separates unreacted monomer from the polymer and recycles monomer to the reactor. A more recent tubular-reactor patent uses staged mixed initiators and reactor-temperature feedback for the same two monomers. These examples show that initiator identity, staged injection, pressure, temperature, and vinyl-acetate feed are process controls that can be varied for a target grade, rather than family-wide constants. EVA crosslinking or curing after polymerization is a separate formulation step and is not included in the synthesis description.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–vinyl acetate copolymer (EVA) spans flexible thermoplastics and elastomer-like grades. Tensile and impact response depend on vinyl-acetate content, melt-flow grade and molecular architecture, specimen form, and whether the material is crosslinked or filled; values for a high-VA adhesive grade or crosslinked formulation are not universal EVA values.

A bounded commercial example is EVATANE 40-55, a random EVA with 38–41 wt% vinyl acetate. Its technical data sheet lists tensile strength at break of 7 MPa and elongation at break of 900–1100%, determined to ISO 527/ASTM D638. These values apply to the named high-VA grade only.

An open study of radiation-crosslinked EVA reports that vinyl-acetate content and crosslinking change dynamic-mechanical behavior. This reinforces the need to identify both composition and crosslink state when comparing EVA mechanical results.
sections.processing:
EVA can be processed on conventional thermoplastic equipment by extrusion, film and coating operations, injection molding, and related routes, but the usable window shifts with vinyl-acetate content and melt index. Celanese's extrusion guide says lower-MFR, higher-viscosity grades generally need higher temperatures, while higher-VA grades melt at lower temperatures and can be run cooler to reduce tack and sticking. Its nominal extrusion examples are about 150, 175, or 205 °C depending on grade and melt index; it recommends a water-cooled feed throat, monitoring head pressure and motor amperage, and generally keeping EVA below 220 °C because degradation can eliminate acetic acid and corrode equipment. These are general starting guidelines, not universal grade specifications.

For injection molding, flexible/high-VA grades can be tacky, so mold-release and ejector design matter, and long residence time or excessive pressure can promote frozen-in strain. SK Functional Polymer's EVATANE 28-800 sheet independently advises conventional thermoplastic equipment, avoiding melt temperatures above 230 °C, and purging after a run; it also calls for protection from heat, humidity, and UV during storage. The 230 °C limit and purge advice apply to that named grade and should be confirmed for other EVA formulations, especially crosslinked or foamed compounds.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EVA is an ethylene copolymer containing vinyl-acetate units; acetate content disrupts polyethylene crystallinity and controls morphology and softness.
sections.properties: Vinyl-acetate content, molecular weight, additives, and crosslinking determine flexibility, adhesion, crystallinity, and thermal response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. EVA grades serve packaging and adhesives. Evatane 40-55 is a documented high-vinyl-acetate grade for hot-melt and solvent-based adhesives, inks and foams for the shoe industry.

Purchasing. Purchase a specified EVA grade by vinyl-acetate content and melt flow through its producer or material supplier. SK Functional Polymer offers Evatane resins; the 40-55 technical sheet identifies a particular high-vinyl-acetate grade rather than an interchangeable family specification.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed EVA tonnage was established from the checked sources. Packaging, adhesive and footwear grades cover different formulations, so their volume shares cannot be inferred from the existence of a product catalog.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: EVA thermal breakdown begins with loss of acetic acid and formation of an unsaturated polymer intermediate; further heating breaks the remaining backbone into smaller hydrocarbons. The cited photovoltaic-encapsulant study does not identify every final hydrocarbon.

Timescales: Nitrogen thermogravimetry of the studied waste-module encapsulant used 0.5–5 °C/min heating rates and found two main mass-loss stages spanning approximately 276–372 °C and 372–495 °C. These are programmed-heating results, not environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: Thermal mass loss does not establish biodegradation. Crosslinking, vinyl-acetate content and the module construction limit transfer to other EVA materials.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Pyrolytic removal of EVA can enable recovery of glass and other photovoltaic-module components. The cited kinetic study supports process development for destructive delamination; it does not demonstrate recovery of reusable EVA polymer.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: EVA overheating can release acetic acid as acetate groups are eliminated; the cited photovoltaic-encapsulant thermal study demonstrates that pathway for its particular waste-module material. During extrusion or hot encapsulation, fume assessment therefore needs the actual EVA formulation, curing package and thermal history. HSE recommends controlled temperature/residence time, trained purging and ventilation appropriate to the process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited technical sheets apply to named EVATANE grades, while radiation work examines a crosslinked EVA. Grade and crosslink state must be retained when interpreting properties.
