sections.overview: Poly(vinyl formal) (PVFM) is a PVA-derived vinyl acetal made by formalization with formaldehyde in aqueous acid conditions. The resulting material can retain other vinyl-alcohol-derived groups, so its formalization state is part of the particular product definition.
sections.history: Poly(vinyl formal) was already a practical electrical-insulation material during the Second World War. The Powerhouse museum preserves a 1943 specimen made by Australian General Electric and describes its display as an example of a material that could replace rubber in wire covering. That surviving industrial object provides a firm date and named manufacturer for an early application. It also shows how wartime material shortages encouraged the use of vinyl-derived plastics. The collection does not establish the first synthesis or complete international commercialization history of poly(vinyl formal), so 1943 is an application milestone rather than an invention date.
sections.nomenclature: PVFM and polyvinyl formal identify the formaldehyde-derived vinyl acetal, not PVA or the butyraldehyde-derived PVB material. Trade or application-specific coatings based on poly(vinyl formal) are formulations of the base polymer and should not replace its chemical name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(vinyl formal) is a PVA-derived polyvinyl acetal: it is made by formalizing PVA with formaldehyde under acid catalysis, not by polymerizing vinyl fluoride. The PVA can be fully or partly saponified, so retained acetate and hydroxyl groups depend on the precursor and formalization extent. A Kuraray aqueous route uses formaldehyde, acid, and metal chloride; the metal chloride and phase behavior control high formalization while avoiding intermolecular acetal crosslinking in that specific route. A Monsanto source identifies Formvar as formaldehyde condensed with partially hydrolyzed poly(vinyl acetate), retaining acetate and hydroxyl groups. Filled or networked compositions are composition-specific derivatives, not a general assertion about this polymer.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(vinyl formal) is ordinarily a partially acetalized poly(vinyl alcohol), so commercial and experimental materials retain different fractions of vinyl-formal, vinyl-alcohol, and sometimes vinyl-acetate units rather than sharing one invariant repeat composition. At ambient conditions an unplasticized, sufficiently formalized material can behave as a stiff glassy film, with an initial elastic response followed by yielding and plastic deformation; coatings, porous products, plasticized grades, and ultrathin membranes can respond very differently. Degree and distribution of acetalization, precursor-PVA molar mass and hydrolysis, residual hydroxyl and acetate content, plasticizer or solvent residue, water uptake and humidity, porosity, film thickness, orientation, thermal and drying history, and residual stress all affect modulus, yield, toughness, and creep. The retained hydroxyl groups enable hydrogen bonding and make conditioning especially important, while blending or crosslinking changes both interfacial load transfer and mobility.

A bounded numerical example comes from freestanding Vinylec E poly(vinyl formal) membranes only 10–100 nm thick. Films were spin-coated from 0.25 wt% solution in ethyl lactate, baked for 1 minute at 50 °C, released in water, mounted over circular holders, dried overnight under ambient conditions, and indented with a 2 mm sapphire sphere at about 45% relative humidity. For one 100 nm film, finite-element optimization of the indentation response gave a 3.28 GPa elastic modulus, 0.0018 pre-strain, and, in a bilinear fit, a 43.50 MPa yield strength with 100 MPa tangent modulus. These are model-derived membrane parameters under biaxial indentation, not a bulk-resin tensile dataset; the study also shows that neglecting residual pre-strain can produce much higher apparent moduli. An independent melt-blending study confirms that acetalization level, retained hydroxyl interactions, formulation, conditioning, and phase morphology materially change PVFM-containing specimens, but it does not provide a transferable neat-PVFM tensile endpoint.
sections.processing:
Poly(vinyl formal) (PVFM, often encountered in Formvar-type materials) is most commonly article-formed from solution as electrical wire enamel, protective coating, adhesive layer, or free-standing support film. Resin and any curable co-resins are dissolved and mixed to the target viscosity, filtered or deaerated as needed, applied by dies, rolls, dipping, or casting, and passed through staged ovens to remove solvent and, for reactive enamels, cure the coating. Repeated thin passes may be used on wire. Selected PVFM compositions can also be dried, compounded in the melt with a compatible polymer, pelletized or chopped, and compression- or injection-shaped. Resin acetal/hydroxyl content, molecular mass, solvent balance, solids and viscosity, coat concentricity, line speed, oven gradient, volatile removal, cure residence, blend feed dryness, mixing sequence, shear, and melt residence all need formulation-specific control. Network-forming reactions belong in Synthesis; coating, drying, cure schedule, and melt shaping belong here.

A General Electric wire-enamel patent supplies a bounded coating-and-cure example. Its Example 3 used a 50:50 blend of the stated low- and higher-molecular-mass Formvar grades in a specified phenolic/melamine/polyisocyanate enamel, coated a 40.3 mil copper wire to a 3 mil coating at 46 and 54 ft/min, and used a tower reported at 250 °C at the bottom and 500 °C at the top. Those severe oven settings belong only to that historical reactive enamel and line. In a distinct melt-compounding study, Han and co-workers first made a masterbatch containing 70 wt% of their PVFM in PPC in a 60 cm³ Haake mixer at 200 °C and 60 rpm for 7 min with a 55 g charge, cut it into small pieces, then diluted it with PPC to 30–50 wt% PVFM under the same mixing conditions and stored samples in a sealed desiccator. The two-step sequence addressed the components' large melt-flow mismatch and is not a general neat-PVFM molding prescription.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PVFM is a poly(vinyl acetal) derivative whose formal-acetal content follows conversion conditions.
sections.properties: Film and blend mechanics depend on acetalization, molecular weight, and modifiers.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Poly(vinyl formal) is used for support films on transmission-electron-microscopy grids and for specialty wire-insulation and protective coatings. The laboratory application uses a thin film supporting fragile specimens.

Purchasing. Polysciences sells Formvar 15/95 as powder, including catalog item 00631-100 in a 100 g package, with online ordering and a separate bulk-quotation channel.

Scale and evidence limits. The documented 100 g unit demonstrates a sub-kilogram laboratory purchase scale. It does not measure industrial demand; no reliable separately reported worldwide annual purchase or consumption figure was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For synthesized poly(vinyl formal), formal rings suppress hydroxyl-elimination behavior relative to PVA in thermogravimetry. The cited study does not identify a complete PVF degradation-product inventory.

Timescales: Neat PVF was compared with PVA during programmed heating; the reported thermal improvement cannot supply an outdoor degradation time.

Environmental persistence: The biodegradable character of the PPC blend partner does not establish that the PVF component mineralizes. PVF-specific environmental timing remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A PVFM-production patent documents reclamation of process solvent: vapors from spray drying the resin solution are condensed and rectified so that acetic acid can be reused. This is a manufacturing resource-recovery step, not conversion of PVFM back to PVA or formaldehyde. For the powder itself, SPI’s Formvar SDS recommends collecting spills without a dust cloud and retaining material for recycling or appropriate disposal. A demonstrated end-of-life route for recovering polymer from PVFM coatings remains unresolved in the cited sources.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: SPI’s 2015 Formvar powder SDS warns of dust-cloud explosion potential and recommends minimizing airborne powder, controlling ignition sources and using local extraction at open equipment. It lists less than 0.1% residual formaldehyde for that TEM-grid-coating product; that composition is not a specification for all PVFM resins. Eye protection and controls matched to any casting solvent are needed when preparing films.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Ultrathin-film and PPC-blend data are not general neat-PVFM properties.

sections.overview: Polystyrene (PS, PSt) is the styrene homopolymer, which can be produced by aqueous suspension or living anionic polymerization. Its molecular weight, tacticity, and any additive package distinguish a commercial resin or molded article from the base polymer.
sections.history: Polystyrene’s history begins with Eduard Simon’s 1839 observation of styrene forming a solid material. BASF developed industrial production in 1930, following styrene work at Ludwigshafen in 1929; Dow introduced Styron in 1937. It grew into solid molded products and expanded materials for packaging, household articles and insulation. The EPA’s 1980 account records an established producer base including Dow, Monsanto and BASF. Copolymers and rubber-modified products became neighboring branches of styrenic materials. The BASF milestone identifies industrial development rather than the earliest observation of styrene forming a solid polymer.
sections.nomenclature: PS and PSt identify polystyrene itself, not rubber-modified high-impact polystyrene, styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer, or an expanded-foam article. Those related materials contain additional phases, comonomers, or processing-defined structures and require their own names.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polystyrene is produced by addition polymerization of styrene. The dominant family chemistry is free-radical polymerization, which can be run in bulk, solution, aqueous suspension, or emulsion. Peroxide or azo initiators generate radicals; heat can also initiate styrene in bulk. In suspension polymerization, styrene droplets are dispersed in water with a protective colloid or suspending agent and polymerize into beads, while staged initiator addition helps manage conversion and heat generation. One cited patent documents aqueous suspension polymerization with peroxides dosed during reaction. A distinct patent demonstrates living anionic polymerization of styrene with sec-butyllithium in a hydrocarbon medium; exclusion of water and other protic impurities preserves active chain ends. Initiator concentration and monomer/initiator ratio control molar mass in the anionic route, and sequential monomer addition can form blocks, although ordinary polystyrene requires only styrene. Chain-transfer agents, regulator feeds, or reactor staging are route controls rather than changes to the repeat unit. Rubber modification and styrenic copolymers are separate compositions or families.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polystyrene (PS) is an amorphous, glassy thermoplastic under ordinary room-temperature service, so its tensile and fracture response is sensitive to molecular mass, thermal and physical-aging history, temperature and strain rate, molding-induced orientation and residual stress, specimen geometry, and crazing. Rubber modification (HIPS), plasticization, recycled content, and mineral or nanoscale fillers create materially different products and must not be collapsed into a single PS value. In one study of unfilled PS film specimens, tensile testing gave strength at break 56 ± 1 MPa, Young's modulus 1.6 ± 0.1 GPa, and strain at break 5.6 ± 0.2%; the same study found that filler identity and loading changed the response. Independently, injection-molded recycled HIPS from electronics waste had room-temperature ISO 527 tensile strength 40.1 ± 0.87 MPa, modulus 3460 ± 49 MPa, and break strain 1.5 ± 0.06% at 5 mm min−1; the study also tested its temperature and tuff-filler dependence. The numerical values are therefore for the named unfilled research material and recycled-HIPS comparator, not universal values for GPPS, HIPS, expanded PS, or filled/recycled grades.
sections.processing:
General-purpose polystyrene (GPPS), high-impact polystyrene (HIPS), and filled PS compounds are melt converted by injection molding and extrusion into profiles, film, and sheet; suitable grades are also blow molded or injection-blow molded and extruded sheet is thermoformed. Grade selection matters because molecular mass, rubber modification, filler, melt flow, heat resistance, and melt strength change filling, drawdown, sag, and cooling. PS absorbs little bulk water, so routine drying is usually unnecessary, but pellets carrying condensation or stored outdoors should be dried; color concentrates and clean regrind should be mixed consistently and contamination from incompatible polymers purged. In injection molding, cylinder/nozzle temperature, screw speed and back pressure, shot size and residence time, injection and hold profile, gate and vent design, and uniform mold cooling govern fill, weld lines, sink, shrinkage, frozen orientation, residual stress, and warpage. Extrusion requires stable melt temperature and pressure, controlled shear, clean streamlined dies, limited drawdown, uniform roll or air cooling, and matched take-up; sheet gauge and orientation then carry into thermoforming. Uniform sheet heating, sag and stretch control, tool temperature, cooling, and demolding govern wall distribution and distortion, while blow-molding grades require sufficient parison melt strength. Excess temperature or residence time can cause yellowing, volatiles, odor, and degradation. Styrene polymerization and rubber-phase formation belong in Synthesis; this section covers compounding and shaping existing resin.

Numerical guidance is bounded to its source. The BASF Polystyrene/Styrolux guide recommends drying outdoor-stored material at 60–80 °C for 2–3 h or using vacuum-vented extrusion, and its route guidance applies to the named BASF GPPS and HIPS grade portfolio rather than every PS. In a distinct open experiment, Moskalyuk and co-workers compounded PS 585 with the study's fillers in a 5 mL twin-screw microcompounder at 220 °C for 10 min and 50 rpm, injected the melt into an 80 °C die, and allowed the removed die to cool in room-temperature air. Their selected 200–220 °C melt-processing range and below-100 °C mold constraint, as well as the strong filler-dependent viscosity and agglomeration behavior, apply only to PS 585 and those nanocomposite formulations and laboratory equipment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polystyrene is the styrene homopolymer; molecular weight and chain architecture depend on the suspension or anionic polymerization route.
sections.properties: Unfilled PS tensile behavior differs from filler-containing materials, and rubber-modified HIPS is a separate multiphase polystyrene material.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polystyrene is used for packaging, appliances and insulation. Resin grades and foamed products address different requirements, so general-purpose PS, impact-modified PS and expanded materials should be distinguished when comparing products.

Purchasing. INEOS Styrolution offers a polystyrene portfolio through its sales specialists and electronic ordering channel. Purchase the required resin grade or converted foam or sheet rather than treating every PS product as an equivalent feedstock.

Scale and evidence limits. Plastics Europe’s preliminary 2023 world fossil-based PS-plus-expanded-PS category is about 22 million tonnes. This combined production estimate is not a neat-PS purchase total.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Controlled depolymerization of polystyrene produces styrene-rich oil that can be distilled to recover styrene monomer. INEOS Styrolution reports this pathway for post-consumer PS in the ResolVe project; the source does not provide a complete inventory of ambient weathering products.

Timescales: The project varied reactor temperature, throughput, residence time and vacuum pressure. Its public summary does not provide a transferable conversion time or environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Chemical monomer recovery does not establish a soil, marine or landfill mineralization time. Environmental weathering and fragmentation need separate fate measurements.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Major recovery routes include sorting and mechanical reprocessing, solvent dissolution followed by polymer purification, and thermal depolymerization followed by styrene distillation and repolymerization. The supplier describes these as complementary routes with different maturity and feedstock constraints. Its ResolVe project demonstrated post-consumer PS depolymerization; contamination affected yield, and bromine-containing traces remained when legacy flame-retarded material was treated.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For PS heated above its recommended processing range, HSE identifies styrene and aldehydes among the measured fume components. This is an overheating context, not a migration value for a finished article. Extrusion, molding, recycling and purging need control of temperature/residence time and appropriate ventilation, with the actual pigments, flame retardants and other ingredients included in the assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Pure-PS controls, recycled HIPS, and filler composites are not interchangeable; grade, additive, thermal history, specimen geometry, temperature, and test rate determine the reported result.

sections.overview: High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is a rubber-modified polystyrene material produced by polymerizing styrene in the presence of dissolved rubber. Grafting and phase inversion generate the characteristic rubber-modified morphology.
sections.history: The British Plastics Federation dates commercial high-impact polystyrene to 1949. Rubber modification addressed the brittleness of ordinary polystyrene and expanded molded and sheet applications. By the EPA’s 1980 industry survey, packaging and consumer products were established uses. HIPS is consequently a postwar development branch of polystyrene whose rubber phase and manufacturing details matter, rather than a separate monomer invention.
sections.nomenclature: HIPS names the rubber-modified polystyrene material, not general-purpose polystyrene or the rubber feedstock alone. The rubber type, grafting conditions, and resulting morphology are formulation and grade variables; they should be retained when identifying a particular HIPS product.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is a rubber-modified polystyrene made by polymerizing styrene in the presence of a dissolved elastomeric rubber, commonly polybutadiene or a styrene–butadiene rubber. The resulting material contains a polystyrene matrix and a dispersed rubber-rich phase with polystyrene grafting; it is not simply a dry blend of the two polymers. During solution or bulk polymerization, homopolymerization of styrene and grafting onto unsaturation in the rubber occur together, and phase inversion changes the morphology from a rubber-continuous to a polystyrene-continuous system. Documented processes control initiators, conversion, temperature, shear, and phase inversion to set rubber-particle morphology. These conditions are process examples rather than a universal HIPS recipe; extrusion and molding occur after the material has been made.
sections.mechanicalProperties: High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is polystyrene modified with a rubber impact modifier; the commercial record for RP-HIPS specifically identifies a butadiene-rubber modifier.  Accordingly, the stiffness--impact balance is formulation- and grade-specific, and the two commercial records below differ in recycled content and melt-flow range.  As a bounded fresh-grade example, ASCHEM HIPS 825E, identified for extrusion and thermoforming with melt-flow rate 4.0 g/10 min (200 °C/5 kg), reports typical ASTM D638 tensile strength 20 MPa, elongation at break 44%, and tensile modulus 2,090 MPa; its notched Izod impact is 135 J/m at 23 °C by ASTM D256.  The supplier marks these as typical rather than specification values.  Separately, The Plastics Group lists a reprocessed RP-HIPS grade (melt-flow range 3--8) at 73 °F with 3,600 psi tensile strength, 20% elongation at break, 260 kpsi tensile modulus, and 2.0 ft-lb/in notched Izod impact; that product-specific record should not be used to infer values for virgin HIPS grades.
sections.processing:
High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is converted by injection molding and by extrusion into sheet or profile followed by thermoforming. The rubber-modified amorphous melt is generally easy to process, but feed moisture/volatiles, colorant dispersion, gate size, mold temperature, cooling, and residence time affect molded stress, weld lines, shrinkage, and surface quality. Regrind and additive packages should therefore be kept within the grade supplier's limits.

Americas Styrenics' EB6400 sheet gives a bounded grade example: injection molding uses approximately 199–249 °C barrel zones, 213–243 °C nozzle, 2–12 bar back pressure, and 60–150 °F (16–66 °C) mold-surface temperature; its extrusion guidance gives approximately 193–232 °C melt, 199–232 °C die, 66–104 °C polish rolls, and 10–21 MPa head pressure. The same guide recommends a mixing head or static mixer for colorants/additives and warns that sheet orientation above 30% sharply reduces brittleness/tear performance. Independently, an open thermoforming study used HIPS sheet temperatures of 130–170 °C and mold temperatures of 30, 60, or 80 °C; a plug mold and suitable mold temperature improved wall-thickness uniformity. These are EB6400- and experiment-specific settings, not universal HIPS windows; styrene/rubber polymerization is upstream Synthesis rather than Processing.
sections.structureAndMorphology: HIPS is a polystyrene matrix modified with a dispersed rubber phase, typically polybutadiene, formed by grafting and/or physical phase separation during polymerization or compounding. The rubber particles absorb impact energy while the glassy polystyrene matrix provides shape and surface finish.
sections.properties: Compared with general-purpose polystyrene, HIPS has improved impact toughness and resistance to crack propagation while retaining low density, rigidity, and easy melt processing. The tradeoff is reduced transparency and often lower heat resistance or stiffness than unmodified polystyrene, with properties set by rubber content and morphology.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. HIPS is used for yogurt cups, refrigerator liners and molded refrigerator parts, toys and office articles, serving packaging and appliance manufacturers.

Purchasing. Specify an extrusion or injection-molding HIPS resin grade, including any required gloss or stress-cracking performance; INEOS Styrolution’s portfolio separates these options.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable HIPS-only annual purchased or consumed tonnage was established. Aggregate polystyrene statistics also cover other PS materials and should not be assigned entirely to the impact-modified subset.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Repeated melt processing of recovered HIPS changes melt flow and article properties. The cited e-waste study measures processing performance and does not resolve a complete molecular degradation-product inventory.

Timescales: Washed electronic-waste HIPS was followed from first-cycle flakes through fourth-cycle material, with filament extrusion at 195 ± 5 °C. Cycle count is a processing history, not an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Retained printability and changes in material properties do not establish soil or aquatic mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical recovery by washing, drying, extrusion and 3D printing was demonstrated for electronic-waste HIPS. Several measured properties remained comparable to commercial filament through the fourth cycle; performance depends on direction, property and waste composition, so this is not a universal four-cycle guarantee.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For HIPS processing, the polystyrene phase makes PS fume guidance relevant as family context: HSE identifies styrene and aldehydes when PS is overheated. The rubber phase and additive package mean that list is not a complete HIPS emission analysis. Temperature/residence-time control, suitable extraction and planned purging are practical controls for molding and reprocessing.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Impact performance depends on rubber particle size, grafting, rubber type, matrix molecular weight, orientation, thickness, and temperature. HIPS is combustible and can degrade under excessive heat or weathering; a flame-retarded, colored, foamed, or recycled grade should not be assumed to match a base resin.

sections.overview: Styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer is a thermoplastic copolymer containing styrene and acrylonitrile units. Its acrylonitrile content differentiates it from polystyrene and contributes to the material family’s performance balance.
sections.history: SAN was an established commercial copolymer by the EPA’s 1980 survey, which lists Dow Tyril, Monsanto Lustran SAN and ARCO/Polymers Luran. Its later development continued in transparent household components. A specific 2022 milestone is Bear Electric’s selection of INEOS Styrolution Luran SAN C for food processors, yogurt machines and filter kettles. Related grades serve drinkware, blenders and coffee-machine water containers. These sources trace industrial suppliers and sustained application development; they do not establish a unique first laboratory synthesis of SAN.
sections.nomenclature: SAN abbreviates styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer. The name denotes a styrene/acrylonitrile copolymer, not ABS, which additionally contains a butadiene-rubber phase.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–acrylonitrile (SAN) is formed by free-radical copolymerization of styrene and acrylonitrile. Industrial routes include continuous bulk or solution polymerization and aqueous suspension or emulsion polymerization. In continuous bulk manufacture, a styrene/acrylonitrile feed can include a small amount of solvent, a peroxide or azo initiator, and a mercaptan chain-transfer agent; the viscous polymer solution is then devolatilized to recover unreacted monomers and solvent. One cited patent example continuously polymerizes styrene and acrylonitrile in ethylbenzene with a peroxide initiator and n-dodecyl mercaptan before vacuum devolatilization. A distinct historical patent uses aqueous suspension polymerization and adjusts styrene feed during conversion to compensate for monomer reactivity and acrylonitrile partitioning, then strips residual acrylonitrile with inert gas. Monomer ratio and feed profile control incorporated acrylonitrile and compositional drift; initiator level, temperature, residence time, and chain-transfer agent regulate conversion and molar mass. SAN is the ungrafted binary copolymer. ABS, ASA, or other rubber-modified materials add a dispersed elastomeric phase or grafting step and are not synonyms for SAN.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SAN is an amorphous random styrene/acrylonitrile copolymer that is typically stiff but has limited unmodified elongation and notch impact. Acrylonitrile fraction, molar mass, residual stress and moisture, injection or extrusion history, temperature and rate, and rubber, fiber, or alloy modifiers determine the strength–toughness tradeoff. NETZSCH describes unfilled SAN as having an elastic modulus near 4 GPa. For Taitalac 1200 SAN, the producer reports at 23 °C ASTM D638/5 mm min⁻¹ yield and break stresses of 700 and 690 kg/cm² (about 68.6 and 67.7 MPa), 5% break elongation, and ASTM D790/2.8 mm min⁻¹ flexural modulus 34,000 kg/cm² (about 3.33 GPa). These are average values for that named resin and test configuration, not a SAN-family range.
sections.processing:
Styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer (SAN) is an amorphous thermoplastic converted primarily by injection molding; suitable grades are also extruded or compounded as blends, alloys, and glass-fiber-reinforced materials. Pellets should be protected from moisture and dried when storage or handling has allowed uptake. Melt and mold temperature, screw speed and back pressure, injection speed and pressure, gate design, reinforcement, wall thickness, residence time, and cooling determine fill, transparency, surface quality, shrinkage, residual stress, and warpage. High speed can help fill because SAN solidifies quickly, but the machine window must be adjusted for the selected acrylonitrile content, molar mass, reinforcement, pigment, and part geometry. Copolymerization belongs in Synthesis; pellet preparation, compounding, molding, and cooling belong here.

Taita Chemical's injection guide gives a bounded supplier window for its general-purpose TAITALAC 1200(Z) and 1400(N/Z) SAN grades: dry at 80–85 °C for 2–4 h, use a 205–235 °C nozzle, a 40–70 °C mold, 50–70 psi back pressure, and 30–100 rpm screw speed, with moderate-to-moderately-high injection pressure and moderate-to-fast injection. The sheet explicitly calls these reference conditions that require equipment and molding adjustment. Autodesk's independent Moldflow material reference gives broader SAN starting guidance of 80 °C drying for 2–4 h, 200–270 °C melt temperature (230–260 °C for most applications), 40–80 °C mold temperature, 35–130 MPa injection pressure, and high injection speed; it also recommends at least 60 °C molds for reinforced grades. These are separate technical starting windows, not a family specification or a reason to combine their endpoints into one universal range.
sections.structureAndMorphology: SAN is a styrene/acrylonitrile thermoplastic copolymer.
sections.properties: Acrylonitrile content and molecular weight affect heat, stiffness, and chemical behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. SAN is used for water tanks, food-storage products, blender components, industrial battery components and cosmetic articles, serving appliance, packaging and electrical markets.

Purchasing. Specify a SAN molding or extrusion grade, such as a member of INEOS Styrolution’s Luran range; distinguish SAN from the separately listed alpha-methylstyrene-containing high-heat materials.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable SAN-only annual purchased or consumed tonnage was established. The grade portfolio demonstrates commercial availability but provides no mass-based end-use split or standard order quantity.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Pyrolysis of SAN-dominant printer waste produces oils rich in styrene and toluene, with ethylbenzene, α-methylstyrene, phenol and heavier aromatic products also identified. This waste-specific study characterizes the hydrocarbon oil fraction; it does not provide a complete nitrogen-containing product inventory or natural-weathering leachate profile.

Timescales: The study treats 2 g cryomilled waste portions in a preheated tube furnace at 800, 1000 or 1200 °C under argon flowing at 1 L/min. Collection continues until emissions stop, about 5 min under that apparatus protocol.

Environmental persistence: High-temperature oil formation does not determine persistence in soil, freshwater or seawater. No ambient mineralization or disappearance time is established by this experiment.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The study demonstrates laboratory thermochemical conversion of SAN-rich electronic waste into oils requiring subsequent separation or upgrading. It does not demonstrate a closed SAN-to-SAN recycling loop or commercial deployment of that process.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: SAN melt operations need a formulation-specific fume assessment. HSE plastics guidance explains that emissions vary with polymer ingredients, actual melt temperature and residence time, and calls for reliable temperature control, ventilation and trained shutdown/purging procedures. Its polystyrene fume examples provide styrenic-family context, but do not determine the complete emission mixture of the acrylonitrile-containing copolymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Supplier data apply to named SAN grades.

sections.overview: Acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene copolymer (ABS) is a family of multiphase, rubber-toughened styrenic thermoplastics made from acrylonitrile, styrene, and a butadiene-derived rubber component. Its SAN-rich matrix, rubber-particle morphology, composition, grafting, additives, and manufacturing route vary among commercial resins, so ABS is not one fixed formulation or property envelope.
sections.history: The British Plastics Federation records ABS production in 1948, during the postwar expansion of styrenic plastics. Rubber toughening of a rigid styrene–acrylonitrile phase supported drainpipes, appliances, automotive parts and luggage. By 1980, the EPA listed Borg-Warner Cycolac, Monsanto Lustran, Dow, BFGoodrich and Uniroyal among producers. These commercial histories concern evolving rubber-modified material architectures; they should not be read as one immutable three-monomer formulation.
sections.nomenclature: ABS names the acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene material family, not the SAN matrix alone, a single polymer sequence, or a particular molding grade. The abbreviation covers commercially variable graft- and phase-structured resins; rubber type and amount, SAN composition, additive package, route, and grade remain material-specific descriptors.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis:
ABS is a family of rubber-toughened styrenic materials rather than a single, fixed statistical terpolymer. Its principal feeds are styrene, acrylonitrile, and butadiene, normally first converted to a polybutadiene rubber substrate. The resulting material commonly contains a styrene–acrylonitrile (SAN)-rich continuous phase and a dispersed butadiene-rubber phase; SAN formed during manufacture can be grafted to the rubber as well as present in the matrix. Rubber fraction, SAN composition, grafting, particle morphology, and molar-mass control are therefore material-definition variables.

In an emulsion ABS/SAN route, butadiene is first free-radically polymerized as an aqueous polybutadiene latex. Styrene and acrylonitrile are then emulsion-polymerized in the presence of that substrate with emulsifiers and initiators to make graft rubber. A separately prepared SAN latex or solid can be combined with the graft material before or after coagulation; the resin is then washed or dewatered and finished with stabilizers or other additive packages as needed. The 1991 EPA process survey documents these as historical industrial flows, not as evidence of current market prevalence. A later INEOS Styrolution patent illustrates one specific variant: a small-particle butadiene latex is agglomerated and then grafted with staged styrene/acrylonitrile feeds using a redox initiator followed by a potassium-persulfate boost. Its particle sizes, feed proportions, temperatures, and residual-monomer objective belong to that claimed process only.

In mass or solution ABS manufacture, a monomer-soluble polybutadiene is dissolved in styrene and acrylonitrile, and free-radical polymerization forms SAN while also grafting SAN onto the rubber. As conversion rises, phase inversion produces rubber-rich particles in a SAN-rich matrix. Historical EPA flow descriptions place prepolymerization before bulk polymerization, followed by vacuum devolatilization, monomer recovery and recycle, and pellet finishing. A BASF patent gives a bounded continuous example using successive low-back-mixing reactor zones, tert-butyl-perester initiation, and mercaptan chain-transfer control; its monomer ratios, rubber loading, temperatures, solvent option, and phase-inversion conditions are not universal ABS specifications.

Suspension routes are also documented historically for specialized ABS: lightly crosslinked, monomer-soluble polybutadiene is dissolved in styrene and acrylonitrile, prepolymerized with a radical initiator and chain-transfer agent, then dispersed in water to complete polymerization before bead washing, dewatering, and drying. These upstream synthesis and resin-recovery operations are distinct from grade-specific extrusion and molding conditions, which belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
ABS is a multiphase material with a continuous styrene–acrylonitrile (SAN) phase and dispersed, grafted polybutadiene (PB) rubber particles. The rubber phase alters craze initiation and shear-band development under load, while particle type, size and distribution, composition, SAN molar mass, grafting, rubber crosslinking, and SAN inclusions can change the resulting response. These relationships describe a variable ABS family rather than a universal property range.

A controlled mass-polymerized ABS study illustrates the effects of specimen geometry, molding history, and annealing. Magnum 3404 ABS pellets were dried for 3 h at 80 °C and injection molded into ISO 527 Type 1A and 1BA bars with a default injection velocity of 60 mm s⁻¹ in a steel mold. The reported barrel-zone temperatures were 220/230/240/250 °C and the mold temperature was 70 °C. Tensile testing used 7–10 specimens per variation and changed crosshead speed after 0.3% extension; for Type 1A bars, the speeds were 1 mm min⁻¹ and then 50 mm min⁻¹. Regular injection-molded Type 1A bars had a reported yield stress of 38.9 ± 0.1 MPa, compared with 38.1 ± 0.1 MPa after vacuum annealing at 110 °C for 6 h. Under a geometry-scaled test protocol, the smaller Type 1BA bars gave 41.5 ± 0.2 MPa before annealing and 41.1 ± 0.4 MPa after annealing at 110 °C for 5 h. These values are specific to the named grade, molding conditions, geometries, and tensile protocols; their differences show why results from nominally similar ABS specimens should not be collapsed into a family-wide range.

For a commercial comparison, SABIC lists typical properties for CYCOLAC EX75, a Region Asia multi-purpose extrusion ABS grade. ASTM D638 Type I testing at 5 mm min⁻¹ lists tensile yield stress of 39 MPa, tensile break stress of 33 MPa, and tensile modulus of 2130 MPa. The same sheet lists ASTM D790 flexural yield stress of 73 MPa and flexural modulus of 2400 MPa at 1.3 mm min⁻¹ with a 50 mm span, plus ASTM D256 notched Izod impact of 421 J m⁻¹ at 23 °C. The sheet labels these as typical values and does not report specimen preparation or conditioning; they are grade-specific data, not family constants. Charpy and Izod results, and values measured at different loading rates or specimen geometries, should not be combined into a single ABS range.
sections.processing:
ABS is an amorphous, rubber-modified thermoplastic commonly converted by injection molding and melt extrusion. Extrusion can produce profiles, sheet, or filament; sheet may then be thermoformed, while filament may be used in fused-filament fabrication. Conversion begins with resin, compound, sheet, or filament feed preparation. Clean storage, drying or moisture control, melt temperature, shear and residence time, pressure and holding, die or mold temperature, cooling, and formulation all affect filling, surface quality, residual stress, shrinkage, warpage, and repeatability. Polymerization, rubber grafting, resin recovery, and resin-manufacture pelletization belong in Synthesis; compounding belongs here only when it prepares an article-conversion feed.

Injection conditions are grade- and tool-specific. Toray's TOYOLAC ABS guidance recommends pellet moisture no higher than 0.1% and preferably no higher than 0.05%, hot-air drying at 80 °C for 3–6 h or 90 °C for 2–3 h, cylinder settings generally in the 210–240 °C range, and mold temperatures of 40–80 °C. Its grade table gives narrower examples: standard grades at 80–90 °C for 3–5 h, 220–240 °C cylinder temperature, and 40–80 °C mold temperature; heat-resistant grades use 90–100 °C for 3–5 h, 240–260 °C cylinder temperature, and 40–80 °C mold temperature. Toray also advises sufficient injection pressure and holding time to limit warpage and shrinkage. These settings apply to the named TOYOLAC portfolio and are not a universal ABS window.

An open Taguchi study of CHIMEI POLYLAC PA-709S examined neat ABS and ABS/carbon-fiber insert specimens on a Haitian MA1200 III injection machine. Its factor ranges were filling pressure of 104–118 MPa, packing pressure of 96–100 MPa, filling time of 1–3 s, packing time of 0.5–2.5 s, and melt temperature of 228–232 °C. The study used 4.5 mm test specimens and a purpose-built mold, so these settings are a bounded experimental example rather than portable production guidance for other ABS grades, formulations, or part geometries.

A 3devo laboratory report gives a distinct extrusion example for Magnum 3513. Pellets were dried at 80 °C for 1 h; the trial began with all four heaters at 240 °C and ultimately produced 1.75 mm filament through a 2 mm nozzle with H4/H3/H2/H1 set to 215/225/235/245 °C, a 4.3 rpm screw, and 50% fan speed. The report warns that ABS grades behave differently and that excessive heat can cause foaming or discoloration; its settings apply only to that grade, machine, nozzle, and filament target.

For thermoforming, ABS sheet is a distinct feed form. Arla Plast's sheet guidance recommends pre-drying ABS at 70–80 °C where required, a 150–180 °C sheet-heating range, and a maximum sheet temperature of 185 °C. It reports a minimum vacuum of 500 mm Hg (0.066 MPa), cooling before demolding, and ABS mold shrinkage of approximately 0.3–0.7%. These values cover the named Arla ABS sheet grades rather than injection-molding pellets.

Reprocessing should distinguish clean production regrind from mixed or post-consumer ABS. In an open study of Formosa AF3560 virgin ABS and ABS recovered from rigid tablet casings, extrusion used a 20 rpm feeder, 300 rpm screw, and barrel zones from 90 to 210 °C; injection used 1600 bar pressure, 30 s mold cooling, and barrel zones from 160 to 205 °C. After six extrusion and reinjection cycles, the virgin ABS melt-flow index increased by approximately 11%, while the WEEE-derived ABS showed a different flow and impact response. These results are bounded to the named virgin grade, WEEE source, equipment, and recycling history and do not establish a safe number of cycles for ABS generally.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ABS commonly comprises a glassy styrene–acrylonitrile-rich matrix containing dispersed butadiene-rich rubber particles. SAN can be grafted to the rubber phase as well as present in the matrix; particle size, internal particle structure, grafting, rubber microstructure, and phase proportions depend on route and grade.
sections.properties: ABS combines the glassy SAN-rich matrix's stiffness and melt processability with rubber-phase impact modification. Toughness, stiffness, flow, surface appearance, heat response, and aging behavior vary with rubber fraction and morphology, SAN composition and molar mass, stabilizers, pigments or flame retardants, and thermal and mechanical history.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. ABS supplies durable molded products, including appliance and electronics housings and automotive parts. It is selected as a formulated grade for the required impact behavior and surface finish.

Purchasing. INEOS Styrolution markets ABS through sales and electronic-order channels, including distinct standard and specialty offerings. Specify the grade, color and conversion route, rather than only the ABS family name.

Scale and evidence limits. The INEOS Styrolution–Sinopec plant inaugurated in Ningbo, China, in November 2023 had 600,000 tonnes per year of ABS nameplate capacity. This single-site capacity is of order one million tonnes per year; it is not actual production or global purchases.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: ABS can undergo thermo-oxidative degradation during melt processing and heat aging, with the butadiene-rich rubber phase particularly susceptible. In a controlled study of two commercial mass- and emulsion-polymerized ABS resins melt-blended at 220 °C, processing reduced markers of the polybutadiene phase and increased yellowing; antioxidant package and production route changed the response. This is evidence for processing- and formulation-dependent stability, not a universal ABS service-life prediction.

Timescales: Repeated UVA-aging and recycling experiments show exposure- and stabilization-dependent changes; no single ABS service-life or environmental lifetime is established.

Environmental persistence: Rubber-phase oxidation and surface embrittlement are not evidence of complete mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: ABS can be mechanically recycled when the incoming stream is identified, sorted, and kept sufficiently compatible for remelting, but prior use, additives, contamination, and cumulative heat and shear history limit direct transfer of virgin-grade expectations. In one open study of black ABS recovered from rigid tablet casings, six extrusion and reinjection cycles increased melt-flow index and affected impact response while tensile, flexural, and thermal results remained broadly stable for that material set. Those outcomes apply to the named WEEE stream and process, not to all recycled ABS or mixed electronic-plastic fractions. Repeated extrusion/injection molding can redistribute damaged surface material and recover some mechanical response. Antioxidant restabilization improves thermal-oxidative resistance in the cited commercial-ABS study.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: HSE reports styrene, phenol and butadiene among fume components for the fire-retarded ABS example in its plastics-processing guidance. This composition applies to that formulation and overheating context, rather than every ABS grade. Control actual melt temperature and residence time, extract processing fumes and account for flame retardants, pigments and recycled feed when setting workplace controls.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Commercial ABS is not a single property envelope. Rubber fraction and particle morphology, SAN composition and molar mass, grafting, additives, color and flame-retardant package, moisture and thermal history, molding orientation, and reprocessing history can change flow, surface quality, aging, and mechanical response. Recycled WEEE ABS adds prior-use, stream-purity, and additive-history uncertainty. The historical survey, patents, supplier guides, and individual experiments in this entry are bounded examples rather than universal manufacturing, property, or processing specifications. Health, safety, and regulatory coverage remains an explicit research gap.

synthesisRoutes.title: Rubber latex → SAN graft concentrate → ABS
synthesisRoutes.scopeNote: INEOS Example 1 grafting, followed by the separately sourced historical ABS blending stage. The patent rubber starts from 90:10 butadiene:styrene; its rubber segment below shows only the butadiene-derived motif.
synthesisRoutes.conditions: Aqueous emulsion; staged radical initiation; grafting at 68 °C
synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical addition converts vinyl groups into carbon–carbon chains. SAN growth and rubber grafting produce a multiphase material. The product segment identifies SAN chemistry; it does not locate an individual graft bond or impose a SAN sequence.

reagents.name: Potassium persulfate
reagents.detail: Late conversion boost: 0.1 parts per 100 parts rubber solids plus graft monomers in Example 1.

steps.title: Prepare and agglomerate the rubber
steps.body: The patent polymerizes the rubber feed with persulfate and mercaptan, then agglomerates the latex with aqueous acetic anhydride and restabilizes with KOH.

steps.title: Initiate and feed SAN monomers
steps.body: At 68 °C, charge the initial styrene/acrylonitrile portion over 15 min. Add CHP and the separate redox solution over 5 min; hold 1 h. Feed the remaining monomers and CHP over 3 h.

steps.title: Boost conversion and recover concentrate
steps.body: Add KPS over 10 min; hold 1 h at 68 °C. Cool, stabilize, acid-precipitate, wash and dry the graft powder.

steps.title: Formulate the ABS resin
steps.body: The historical EPA flow combines graft material with separately prepared SAN, then finishes the resin. The required matrix fraction depends on the selected grade.

synthesisRoutes.limitations: Procedure outline, not a complete batch recipe. Use the patent for all charges and controls. No separate multifunctional crosslinker is specified in this example; grafting, rubber gel content and final SAN fraction remain distinct variables. The blending stage is not an additional step claimed as part of Example 1.

sections.overview: Acrylonitrile–styrene–acrylate copolymer (ASA) is an impact-modified thermoplastic that combines a styrene–acrylonitrile phase with acrylic-rubber particles. In a documented core–shell route, the acrylic phase is grafted and then melt blended with SAN, illustrating the material's multiphase character.
sections.history: BASF introduced ASA as Luran S in 1967 to offer an ABS-like material with improved weathering behavior. Replacing the vulnerable rubber chemistry with an acrylic elastomer was central to that development. The material grew into outdoor automotive trim, construction profiles, housings and other products requiring a durable appearance. INEOS’s 2023 account identifies that BASF lineage within its later Styrolution business. The history is thus tied to a specific technical need—outdoor durability—and subsequent application engineering, rather than simply the synthesis of another styrene copolymer.
sections.nomenclature: ASA identifies the acrylonitrile, styrene, and acrylate-rubber material class. It is distinct from ABS at the impact-modifier level: the documented ASA system uses an acrylic-rubber core rather than a butadiene-rubber phase; a particular core–shell composition or SAN blend is a formulation within, not the definition of, ASA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: ASA is an impact-modified styrenic material in which an acrylic-rubber phase, commonly a poly(butyl acrylate) core, is combined with a styrene–acrylonitrile (SAN) phase. In the documented emulsion-graft route, a slightly crosslinked butyl-acrylate core was grafted with styrene and acrylonitrile, then melt blended with SAN. Rubber-core crosslinking, graft composition, and the SAN blend ratio determine a particular ASA morphology; the route should not be read as a universal ASA composition or as an ABS route with the rubber merely renamed.
sections.mechanicalProperties: ASA mechanics arise from a glassy SAN matrix together with dispersed acrylic-rubber particles, so particle architecture, interfacial adhesion, SAN composition, and the article-conversion route all matter. The core-shell study found that acrylonitrile content and particle-size distribution affected adhesion and impact response in its graft-copolymer/SAN blends. A separate FDM study measured 39.97–50.57 MPa tensile strength in ASTM D638 specimens printed from ASA filament at 5 mm/min; its best observed specimen was printed at 265 °C with 0.08 mm layer height, 100% infill, and 15° raster angle. This is a printed-part result, not a bulk-resin or all-ASA value.
sections.processing: ASA is melt-processable, including conventional compounding and material-extrusion printing. The emulsion-graft work separates production of acrylic core-shell particles from subsequent melt blending with SAN. In the FDM study, nozzle temperature was varied from 245 to 265 °C, layer height from 0.08 to 0.16 mm, and infill from 30 to 100%, while print speed was held at 60 mm/s and bed temperature at 90 °C. These are the operating factors of one filament/printer experiment; drying, residence time, and temperatures for another ASA grade require its own guidance.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ASA is an impact-modified styrenic material with an acrylate-rubber phase associated with a styrene–acrylonitrile matrix. Core–shell particle design and acrylonitrile content alter the morphology relevant to toughening.
sections.properties: ASA provides a balance of rigid-matrix behavior and impact modification. Its response depends on the matrix composition, rubber-particle architecture, additives, and the fabrication route.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. ASA is used for automotive exterior trim and housings, outdoor building components, garden equipment and appliance parts where appearance must persist outdoors.

Purchasing. Order an application-specific ASA grade; INEOS Styrolution’s Luran S portfolio separates molding, extrusion and reinforced options. ASA–polycarbonate blends have their own composition and should be specified separately.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual ASA purchased or consumed tonnage was established from the checked portfolio. Its product examples do not quantify the share of ASA used in construction versus automotive applications.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Repeated extrusion of LOTTE WX-9730LE ASA produced progressive discoloration and an increased carbonyl-to-nitrile infrared ratio, consistent with oxidation during reprocessing. The study does not directly identify a complete set of small-molecule products.

Timescales: The study used four total extrusion passes: initial extrusion followed by three recycling passes, with subsequent injection molding. This processing history cannot be converted to an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Changes in color, infrared spectra and rheology are not measurements of mineralization in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical re-extrusion, pelletizing and injection remolding were demonstrated for this ASA grade. The experiments retained useful mechanical performance while showing progressive color changes, making grade, intended appearance and processing history relevant to reuse.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: ASA molding and repeated extrusion need control of thermal history and processing fumes. HSE guidance provides the workplace framework: assess the complete resin formulation, maintain reliable temperature control and suitable ventilation, and plan purging and shutdown. Styrenic-family emission examples cannot be taken as a complete ASA analysis because its acrylate-rubber phase differs from the butadiene phase in ABS.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The core–shell report concerns particles of specified acrylonitrile content, and the printing study tests particular printing parameters; those results do not define all ASA compositions or manufactured parts.

synthesisRoutes.conditions: Core formation, shell grafting, and matrix blending are distinct stages.
synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Staged radical grafting builds a styrene/acrylonitrile shell on acrylic-rubber particles. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. Matrix formation and graft growth remain distinct parts of the staged preparation; this chain-growth description does not imply a uniform monomer sequence throughout the multiphase material.

steps.title: Prepare the reaction
steps.body: Prepare the slightly crosslinked acrylic-rubber latex.

steps.title: Propagate the radical chain
steps.body: Successive monomer additions convert alkene π bonds into backbone σ bonds while regenerating the radical growth site. The cited initiator, feed composition and reaction medium determine the particular preparation; transfer, grafting and termination control architecture alongside propagation.

steps.title: Form and recover the product

sections.overview: Methacrylate–butadiene–styrene copolymer is a multiphase impact-modifier copolymer family incorporating methacrylate, butadiene-rubber, and styrene components. It is used as an impact modifier in PVC formulations.
sections.history: MBS developed as an impact-modification technology for plastics. Kaneka records the development and marketing of KANEACE B in 1964, followed in 1973 by a Japanese polymer-science award for its manufacturing technology and completion of a Belgian plant. Later production in Malaysia extended that industrial network. PVC films, sheets, bottles, pipes and fittings became applications for MBS grades balancing toughness and transparency. These milestones trace international manufacture of a modifier used within other plastics; they do not describe MBS replacing all of those host resins as a stand-alone bulk material.
sections.nomenclature: MBS abbreviates methacrylate–butadiene–styrene copolymer. The name describes the component chemistry of the impact-modifier family and should not be conflated with ABS or with generic styrene–butadiene rubber.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Methacrylate–butadiene–styrene copolymer (MBS) generally denotes a staged core–shell graft particle rather than a single random terpolymer. The elastomeric core is commonly polybutadiene or styrene–butadiene rubber, sometimes lightly crosslinked; a harder shell containing methyl methacrylate, optionally with styrene, is grafted onto that rubber latex. A detailed process patent performs the first butadiene-rich emulsion-polymerization stage under free-radical initiation, then feeds a methacrylate and/or vinyl-aromatic monomer mixture to build the outer stage. An independent patent likewise identifies MBS as a core–shell resin produced by grafting methacrylate and optional styrene shell components onto crosslinked butadiene or styrene–butadiene rubber. Core composition, graft level, shell sequence, and particle-size management are route-specific controls, not universal composition limits.
sections.mechanicalProperties: MBS is principally a core–shell rubber impact modifier, so its mechanical significance is usually the response of the host polymer rather than a standalone family tensile value. A butadiene-rich rubber core dissipates impact energy, while the methyl-methacrylate/styrene graft shell promotes adhesion and refractive-index matching with PVC. Modifier loading, core crosslinking, shell composition, particle size and dispersion, matrix compatibility, test temperature, and moulding morphology govern toughening. For a bounded PVC/wood-composite example, an open Thai research report found that 16.7 wt% MBS increased Izod impact strength from 2 to about 7 kJ/m². This is a composite-and-loading result, not MBS itself or a neat-PVC constant. Independent Kaneka documentation identifies the rubber-core/graft-shell architecture and PVC applications; it supports the mechanism but supplies no standalone MBS endpoint.
sections.processing: MBS is generally supplied as a core–shell impact-modifier powder or dispersion and is compounded into a host resin rather than shaped as an isolated neat polymer. Commercial guidance places MBS-modified PVC in extrusion, calendering, film, pipe, blow-molding, and injection-molding operations; engineering-resin MBS grades likewise require selection of a compatible matrix and conversion method. A bounded PVC/MBS formulation patent illustrates the resulting grade dependence: high-speed mixing for 12 min to about 95 ± 2 °C, cooling below 45 °C, twin-screw compounding with zones of about 150/165/175/175 °C and a 170 °C die at 200 rpm, pellet drying at 80 ± 2 °C for 4 h, and injection at 165–175 °C into a mold cooled near 40 °C. Those settings belong to the disclosed PVC formulation, screw, and specimen conditioning, not to all MBS products.
sections.structureAndMorphology: MBS impact modifiers use a rubbery butadiene-containing core with methacrylate/styrene-associated outer phases.
sections.properties: Impact modification depends on particle architecture, PVC matrix compatibility, and formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. MBS is used as an impact modifier in PVC containers, molded parts, films, sheet and pipe. In this documented role it is an ingredient in another polymer formulation, serving packaging and building-product converters.

Purchasing. Palmer Holland lists Kaneka Kane Ace B-58A in 25 kg polyethylene bags and 500 kg semi-bulk bags. Select an MBS modifier grade for the required clarity and impact behavior, rather than a finished PVC compound.

Scale and evidence limits. The documented delivery units span tens to hundreds of kilograms: 750 kg per pallet for the 25 kg bags and 1,000 kg per pallet for semi-bulk bags. These are packaging quantities, not a worldwide consumption estimate; no separate annual market tonnage was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For CLEARSTRENGTH 350 MBS modifier, Arkema lists acrylates, carbon oxides and other organic compounds among products of thermal decomposition. This formulation-specific list does not identify every molecule formed during weathering.

Timescales: The SDS does not provide a transferable degradation time for the MBS polymer.

Environmental persistence: The SDS reports biodegradation data for a proprietary component separately; those data cannot establish biodegradability of the whole MBS modifier. Polymer-specific environmental mineralization remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The accessible commercial evidence concerns MBS as an ingredient used to improve recycled compounds: Brenntag lists MBS impact modifiers in its portfolio for post-consumer and post-industrial recyclate production, alongside stabilizers and other compounding additives. This is an established supply-chain role in restoring the usefulness of a host resin. It does not demonstrate separate recovery of MBS from an existing blend, monomer recovery, or a recycling yield for the modifier itself; those are still distinct evidence needs.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Arkema’s CLEARSTRENGTH 350 MBS powder SDS identifies combustible-dust potential and irritation from processing vapors. It calls for preventing dust clouds and deposits, controlling ignition and static discharge during powder transfer, and suitable ventilation and eye/skin protection. These are handling precautions for the named impact-modifier product; the host resin and other ingredients add their own processing hazards.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Supplier claims and PVC studies concern named MBS grades and PVC compounds, not all MBS compositions.

sections.overview: Styrene–maleic anhydride copolymer contains styrene and reactive maleic-anhydride units. Its anhydride functionality distinguishes it from polystyrene and enables compatibility or reaction with suitably functionalized formulations.
sections.history: Styrene–maleic anhydride copolymer chemistry was documented in Arthur Voss and Ewald Dickhauser’s IG Farben patent, with German priority in 1930 and a U.S. grant in 1936. The patent already connected the copolymers to coatings, varnishes, impregnation and shaped articles. Its importance was the combination of a styrenic chain with reactive anhydride functionality, which allowed further formulation and chemical modification. This early record establishes a named research and industrial lineage, while later molding resins and functional additives represent developments of that platform rather than one unchanged commercial material.
sections.nomenclature: SMA abbreviates styrene–maleic anhydride copolymer. The term names a composition-variable copolymer family, not a blend of separate polystyrene and maleic anhydride materials.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–maleic anhydride copolymer (SMA) is formed by free-radical copolymerization of styrene with maleic anhydride. The strong tendency of the two monomers to cross-propagate permits nearly alternating, approximately equimolar SMA when the feed is near 1:1, whereas styrene-rich feeds and controlled maleic-anhydride addition give lower-anhydride random copolymers or, in some processes, blends containing polystyrene. Routes include solution or precipitation polymerization, bulk polymerization, and combined mass–suspension manufacture. In one industrially scoped process, maleic anhydride or its styrene solution is fed gradually into polymerizing excess styrene during a mass stage, with an optional radical initiator and chain-transfer agent; the partially converted mass is then dispersed in pH-controlled water and polymerization is completed with a free-radical initiator to form beads. Maleic-anhydride hydrolysis during the aqueous stage can be reversed by later dehydration. A distinct historical route dissolves approximately equimolar styrene and maleic anhydride with a radical generator in a medium that dissolves the monomers but precipitates and chain-terminates the copolymer, providing a low-molar-mass route variant. Monomer ratio and feed profile control composition and sequence distribution, while initiator, chain transfer, temperature, solvent, and conversion regulate molar mass and residual homopolymer. Hydrolysis, esterification, imidization, or other reaction of the anhydride groups is post-polymerization modification rather than formation of unmodified SMA.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SMA is an amorphous engineering thermoplastic whose stiffness, strength, and fracture response depend strongly on maleic-anhydride content, molecular mass, glass-fibre reinforcement, weldlines, and the injection-moulding/reprocessing history. In a 2026 open study, unfilled XIRAN SM200 retained similar tensile modulus through five reprocessing cycles while its tensile strength and strain at break changed; a 30 wt% glass-fibre SMA grade showed response governed by fibre volume and fibre-length loss, and weldlines reduced strength and fracture toughness. A separate full patent reports that preparation route, residual polystyrene, and anhydride fraction can also change the properties of commercial and experimental SMA. As one deliberately narrow endpoint, first-processed injection-moulded XIRAN SM200 in the recycling study had tensile strength 27.0 ± 0.3 MPa and strain at break 18.8% under DIN EN ISO 527 type 1A testing (modulus captured at 1 mm/min and the test continued at 5 mm/min). Those values describe that unfilled commercial grade and specimen protocol only, not reinforced or compositionally different SMA grades.
sections.processing:
Styrene–maleic anhydride (SMA) is an amorphous thermoplastic that can be converted by injection molding, melt extrusion, and melt spinning, and it is frequently melt compounded with impact modifiers, other thermoplastics, fibres, or particulate fillers before shaping. Pellet or powder feed uniformity, pre-drying where required by the grade, melt temperature, shear and residence time, filler dispersion, mold or die temperature, weld-line placement, cooling, and regrind history all affect flow and the finished article. The anhydride groups can react with suitable co-reactants, so moisture, contamination, and intentionally reactive blend partners should be controlled rather than treating SMA as an inert styrenic resin. Reprocessing can change melt flow, while injection shear can shorten reinforcing fibres; those effects depend on composition and cannot be inferred from the neat copolymer name alone. Copolymerization and deliberate derivatization belong in Synthesis; compounding, molding, extrusion, spinning, cooling, and clean production-scrap reprocessing belong here.

A Corning patent demonstrates article-conversion routes with commercial XIRAN SMA and describes melt spinning, twin-screw extrusion, and injection molding. Its bounded 250 g SMA–magnetite trials dry-blended the components, allowed melting for about 2 min in a Brabender mixer held at 250 °C, mixed for 5 min at 50 rpm, and cooled the discharged blend on foil; these settings apply only to those 10–40 wt% magnetite batches. In a distinct study, Taha, Schach, and Stricker pre-dried the commercial XIRAN SM200 and 30 wt% glass-fibre XIRAN SGH60 materials at 80 °C for 3 h to measured moisture contents of 0.046–0.078%, injection-molded them on a DEMAG 420 machine, and air-cooled the specimens at 23 °C. For SGH60, their two mold configurations used 240–265 °C barrel zones, a 260 °C nozzle, an 80 °C mold, and 20 s residual cooling, with different maximum injection and holding pressures for the film- and pinpoint-gated tools. The authors state that both commercial materials were SMA/ABS blends of undisclosed composition, so these numbers are not a family window for neat SMA.
sections.structureAndMorphology: SMA contains styrene and reactive maleic-anhydride units.
sections.properties: Composition and anhydride content control compatibility, hydrolysis sensitivity, and thermal response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. SMA is used in polymer modification and automotive compounds, including instrument-panel structures and trim. Chemically modified or dissolved SMA products also serve pigment dispersions, inks, coatings, adhesives and paper sizing.

Purchasing. The Xiran product range is sold as resins, formulated compounds and solution products through specialist suppliers. Select the molecular-weight and functionality grade, and distinguish unmodified SMA resin from chemically modified solution derivatives.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed SMA tonnage was established. The documented supply forms and application examples do not establish world market volume or an end-use mass split.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The cited SMA-composite recovery experiment dissolves an SMA-containing polymer phase; it does not identify chemical degradation products or demonstrate chain mineralization.

Timescales: A glass-fiber composite prepared from an SMA/styrene/maleic-anhydride formulation was extracted with acetone for 24 h. This is a dissolution/recovery timescale.

Environmental persistence: Dissolution separates material but does not demonstrate biodegradation. Environmental mineralization time remains unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A patent example recovers polymer mixture by solvent extraction and filtration from the specified SMA-containing composite. The result is a laboratory recovery demonstration, not monomer recovery or established general SMA recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: SMA-containing compounds require assessment of the full composition during hot processing. HSE identifies actual temperature, residence time and additives as key determinants of plastics fumes, and recommends ventilation and controlled purging/shutdown. Its PS examples are useful styrenic-family context, but the copolymer’s comonomer chemistry means they are not a complete emission inventory for this material.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Recycling studies report specified SMA materials and histories.

sections.overview: Styrene–methyl methacrylate copolymer is a transparent thermoplastic copolymer containing styrene and methyl-methacrylate units. Composition allows properties to be tuned between polystyrene-like and acrylic-like behavior.
sections.history: SMMA developed as a transparent styrenic alternative for articles where optical appearance and molding behavior both mattered. The NAS commercial lineage, documented in INEOS Styrolution’s portfolio, serves water-filter housings, food boxes, displays, writing instruments and medical-device components. INEOS’s 2023 account also distinguishes unmodified SMMA from rubber-containing blends, an important boundary in understanding its development. The sources used here document an established industrial material and its application directions, but do not establish a defensible first-synthesis or first-commercialization date. A date attached to NAS ownership or a particular grade should not be substituted for the invention of the whole copolymer class.
sections.nomenclature: SMMA abbreviates styrene–methyl methacrylate copolymer; MS is also used in product contexts. The name denotes a copolymer and should not be treated as a synonym for either polystyrene or PMMA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–methyl methacrylate copolymer (SMMA) is made by free-radical copolymerization of styrene and methyl methacrylate (MMA). Bulk and solution processes yield a homogeneous resin stream that is devolatilized after reaction, while suspension processes disperse the monomer phase in water and recover solid beads. In a cited solution process, a styrene/MMA mixture is polymerized homogeneously with methanol as solvent; a soluble peroxide or azo initiator can generate radicals, and n-dodecyl mercaptan, n-octyl mercaptan, or an alpha-methylstyrene dimer can serve as a chain-transfer agent. A distinct suspension patent charges styrene and MMA into water stabilized with tricalcium phosphate and an extender such as potassium persulfate or sodium alkylbenzene sulfonate; agitation and stabilizer level control bead size, while lower temperature and a larger water fraction manage the heat release of MMA-rich recipes. Other documented variants include continuous bulk or solution reactors followed by removal and recycle of residual monomers and solvent. Because styrene and MMA do not incorporate at identical rates, starting ratio, staged feed, residence time, and conversion determine composition drift and residual-monomer burden. Initiator concentration, temperature, solvent or aqueous-phase recipe, chain transfer, and reactor sequence control conversion and molar mass. SMMA denotes the binary copolymer; rubber grafting or adding acrylonitrile produces a different material family.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SMMA is an amorphous, transparent styrene/MMA copolymer used in optical and injection-moulded parts. Its mechanical response is consequently grade- and molding-history-dependent: the available manufacturer material identifies low residual stress in molded parts and low water uptake as useful attributes, while datasheet results also vary with grade, thickness, test speed, temperature, and conditioning. Neither source establishes a composition-independent family range or a directional/oriented-film response. As one tightly bounded current example, Resirene CET 116, an injection-molding SMMA grade, is reported at 5 mm/min under ASTM D638 with 55 MPa tensile strength at break, 2.5% break elongation, and 2.90 GPa tensile modulus; its 3.175 mm notched Izod value is 16 J/m under ASTM D256. These are average laboratory values for CET 116, with specimen conditioning and geometry beyond the named standard not supplied, rather than values for all SMMA compositions or forms.
sections.processing:
Styrene–methyl methacrylate (SMMA, or MS resin) is supplied in compositions and grades for injection molding and extrusion, including transparent molded articles and extruded optical sheet or light-guide panels. Melt compounding followed by injection or compression molding is also possible for blends. Feed cleanliness, optional pre-drying, melt and tool temperature, shear, residence time, weld-line placement, cooling rate, and post-forming stress relaxation matter because contamination, bubbles, flow orientation, or residual stress can compromise an otherwise transparent article. Extruded strands and sheet can retain flow-induced orientation, while slower hot pressing and cooling can relax it; the magnitude depends on composition, blend partner, thickness, and thermal history. Polymer manufacture belongs in Synthesis; pellet drying, melt mixing, extrusion, molding, cooling, and orientation control belong here.

Denka identifies TX-100S as an injection-molding MS grade and TX-800LF and TX-820 as extrusion grades. Its grade sheet gives a bounded setup for TX-100S: pre-dry at 70–80 °C for 3–4 h, use 190–240 °C cylinder and 220–240 °C nozzle temperatures, and hold the mold at 40–70 °C. Those supplier settings are for TX-100S, not all styrene/MMA ratios or optical products. In a distinct study, Yamaoka and Kimura extruded SBS/MS blends and then injection- or compression-molded the extrudates. They observed strong extensional-flow orientation after die exit and substantially more relaxation after compression molding and slow cooling. That morphology result belongs to their 10–40 wt% MS blends and shows why cooling and forming history should accompany any reported SMMA property or optical result.
sections.structureAndMorphology: SMMA is a styrene/methyl-methacrylate copolymer with composition-dependent amorphous morphology.
sections.properties: Transparency and stiffness depend on monomer ratio, molecular weight, and additives.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. SMMA is used in transparent water filters, displays, food-contact products, medical devices and cosmetic packaging. INEOS Styrolution’s NAS 90 is a specific commercial example.

Purchasing. Purchase a named SMMA grade through the resin supplier or its ordering channel. Confirm the composition: transparent impact-modified blends sold nearby in a supplier portfolio are not necessarily SMMA alone.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed SMMA tonnage was established. The NAS 90 page documents applications and commercial grade information without a market-wide volume or order-size statistic.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Ultrasonic stress cleaves styrene–methyl methacrylate copolymer chains into smaller polymer fragments. Block, random and alternating sequences show different limiting molecular masses and degradation rates.

Timescales: The reported time dependence concerns sonicated dilute solutions, not weathering of solid articles.

Environmental persistence: Mechanical chain scission is not mineralization; environmental product identities and transferable disappearance times remain unresolved.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The sonication study demonstrates molecular-mass reduction, not monomer recovery or an established recycling process. A material-specific reclamation route is an evidence gap.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: SMMA molding resins require assessment of the full composition during hot processing. HSE identifies actual temperature, residence time and additives as key determinants of plastics fumes, and recommends ventilation and controlled purging/shutdown. Its PS examples are useful styrenic-family context, but the copolymer’s comonomer chemistry means they are not a complete emission inventory for this material.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Supplier technical data describe individual grades.
