sections.overview: Poly(ether sulfone) is an aromatic thermoplastic whose backbone contains ether and sulfone linkages. It belongs to the high-temperature polysulfone-family materials while retaining a chemistry distinct from polysulfone and polyphenylsulfone.
sections.history: ICI introduced polyethersulfone in the United Kingdom and then the United States in 1972–1973 under the Victrex name. It joined the emerging range of high-temperature engineering thermoplastics, while retaining a chemical identity distinct from bisphenol-A polysulfone. Later commercial portfolios, including BASF’s Ultrason E, developed applications in heat-resistant molded components and filtration membranes. Household and catering equipment, electrical parts and automotive components became important application areas for this sulfone-resin technology. The ICI dates document commercial introduction; they should not be treated as a single invention date for every aromatic polysulfone.
sections.nomenclature: PESU is an unambiguous abbreviation for poly(ether sulfone); PES is also used but can be ambiguous. The name should not be used as a synonym for all sulfone-containing polymers.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ether sulfone) (PES) is a linear aromatic poly(aryl ether sulfone) commonly produced by nucleophilic polycondensation of 4,4′-dihydroxydiphenyl sulfone (bisphenol S) with 4,4′-dichlorodiphenyl sulfone. Base first forms the phenolate; an inert, dry polar-aprotic system then supports displacement of chloride and step-growth chain extension. Sulfolane, N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone, dimethylacetamide, or dimethyl sulfone are documented process media, with carbonate or hydroxide base and deliberate water removal used to control phenolate formation and molecular mass. High solids, monomer equivalence, dryness, and optional end-capping are synthesis variables that affect oligomer content and molar-mass distribution. This account covers the resin backbone and recovery by precipitation/washing; membrane casting, other fabrication, and post-synthesis modification are excluded.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PESU is an amorphous high-temperature thermoplastic; grade molar mass, moisture uptake/conditioning, thermal history, mold orientation, and glass or mineral reinforcement affect its measured mechanics. Studies of oriented polymer films including poly(ether sulfone)s emphasize that optical and mechanical anisotropy depend on chain orientation, so membrane, coating, and injection-molded values are not interchangeable.

A bounded unreinforced injection-molding grade endpoint is BASF Ultrason® E 6020 P, measured on specimens prepared from granules: at 23 °C it lists ISO 527 tensile modulus 2,650 MPa, yield stress 85 MPa, and yield strain 6.9%, with moisture absorption reported as 1% at 23 °C/50% RH. These are typical, uncoloured-grade values rather than universal PESU behavior; moisture state, specimen preparation, and reinforcement can change them.
sections.processing:
Poly(ether sulfone) (PESU) is an amorphous high-temperature thermoplastic converted by injection molding and extrusion, while solution grades are cast or coated and used to form membranes. Pellets or flakes absorb moisture quickly, so closed handling and drying are important to prevent splay, bubbles, and surface defects. Melt equipment needs high-temperature capability, smooth flow paths, effective venting, and controlled residence time; excessive melt temperature, shear heating, or stagnation can discolor and degrade the resin. High mold temperature reduces frozen-in stress, while extrusion generally demands a lower residual-moisture target than injection molding. Solution routes require solvent, solids, filtration, casting or coating, and solvent-removal conditions to be qualified separately from melt conversion.

For a bounded handling example, BASF's Ultrason E 6020 P PESU flakes, intended for membrane and coating uses, are to be dried at least 4 h at 130-150 °C in vacuum or dry air and kept below the supplier's 390 °C upper processing limit. A separate Veradel PESU molding bulletin starts injection-molding barrel zones at 343-354 °C, requires the measured melt to remain at or below 385 °C, and limits uninterrupted idle time to 30 min; its purge-frequency table shortens the interval to 15 min at 374-385 °C. Those conditions belong to the named Ultrason and Veradel materials and must not be generalized to every PESU molecular weight, filler package, solution grade, or machine.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(ether sulfone) is a rigid aromatic polymer with ether and sulfone linkages in the main chain. The backbone is predominantly amorphous, with chain rigidity and strong dipolar sulfone groups contributing to a high glass-transition region.
sections.properties: PESU provides high heat resistance, dimensional stability, hydrolytic resistance, electrical insulation, and resistance to many aqueous and chemical environments. Its optical, barrier, and solvent response depend on molecular mass, residual stress, additives, and processing history.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PESU serves membrane filtration, healthcare, electrical/electronic and automotive components, coatings and food-contact equipment; the selected grade determines the applicable use.

Purchasing. Syensqo offers Veradel PESU powders and unreinforced or reinforced compounds in several melt viscosities, including healthcare grades. Specify powder versus molding compound and intended service when using the supplier product finder or requesting a quote.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked sources do not report a separate annual purchase tonnage or end-use mass split for this material. Supplier availability establishes a commercial route, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hydroxylation of PESU cleaves aryl–oxygen bonds and recovers bisphenol S.

Timescales: PESU pellets treated with three equivalents of CsOH monohydrate for 4 h under the study’s 150 °C DMI conditions gave 92% bisphenol-S yield.

Environmental persistence: The cited chemical-recovery experiments do not measure environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine disappearance time is established here.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Chemical recovery is demonstrated in that laboratory experiment. The supplier design guide also describes controlled drying and regrind handling for its sulfone molding resins, a polymer-preserving route whose applicability depends on grade and contamination.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: BASF’s Ultrason guide includes PESU and warns that excessive temperature or residence time can generate decomposition gases and pressure in a blocked barrel. Hot equipment/melt, fume extraction and controlled shutdown are specific handling concerns. EU food-contact context, checked 8 September 2026: BASF’s March 2026 notice identifies its PESU food-contact applications for requalification under the bisphenol restrictions in Regulation (EU) 2024/3190. The actual chemistry, article category, transitions and derogations need current assessment; this does not prohibit all PESU uses.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PESU requires elevated processing temperatures and can be sensitive to notch geometry, residual stress, solvents, and prolonged thermal exposure. Grade, filler, drying, orientation, annealing, and chemical environment must accompany comparisons; membrane behavior is not equivalent to bulk molded resin.

sections.overview: Polyphenylsulfone (PPSU) is an aromatic polysulfone made by nucleophilic polycondensation of 4,4′-dihydroxybiphenyl with 4,4′-dichlorodiphenyl sulfone. The documented resin is an engineering thermoplastic whose composition and molecular weight are set during polymerization and end capping.
sections.history: PPSU grew from aromatic polyether-sulfone chemistry developed at Union Carbide by Robert N. Johnson and Alford G. Farnham; their patent lineage began in 1963 and a 1978 patent was later cited as a preparation route for the biphenyl-containing polymer. This establishes a research antecedent, not a definitive first-invention date. Commercial development continued through Amoco’s Radel R business. Selvaraj Savariar’s 2000 BP Amoco patent addressed low-molecular-weight material and melt flow, identifying medical trays, cookware, aircraft and plumbing parts as applications. Sterilizable surgical-instrument handles and trays became prominent markets, alongside hot-water fittings and food-service components. In 2025, Syensqo marked 35 years of its Radel PPSU product lineage and introduced a white medical grade; that anniversary should not be mistaken for the beginning of the underlying chemistry. Later product development also extended PPSU into filaments for additive manufacturing.
sections.nomenclature: PPSU identifies polyphenylsulfone, a specific member of the broader polysulfone family. It is distinct from bisphenol-A polysulfone (PSU) and polyethersulfone (PESU); a laser-sintered part, a fiber composite, or a filled grade must retain its added material and processing qualifiers.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyphenylsulfone (PPSU, also called polybiphenyl ether sulfone) is made by nucleophilic aromatic polycondensation of 4,4′-dihydroxybiphenyl with 4,4′-dichlorodiphenyl sulfone. An alkali carbonate converts the biphenol to phenoxide, which displaces chloride from the activated aryl sulfone to form the aryl-ether backbone. The reaction is conducted under dry inert conditions in a high-boiling polar aprotic medium such as N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone or sulfolane; water generated during salt formation is removed, often azeotropically. Near-equimolar monomer balance builds molar mass, while a deliberate small excess and monofunctional end cap control terminal groups. Salt is filtered away and polymer is recovered by precipitation, washing, and drying. One cited patent provides the canonical NMP/potassium-carbonate route and methyl-chloride end capping. A distinct patent demonstrates a sulfolane route with precipitation and repeated washing. Functionalized and block-polymer examples are variants and do not redefine ordinary PPSU.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyphenylsulfone (PPSU) is an amorphous high-temperature thermoplastic whose tensile and impact response depends on molecular mass, moisture/conditioning, temperature and rate, molding or extrusion history, annealing, and porous-membrane or additively manufactured architecture. A Radel R-5500 data sheet reports 3.18 mm ASTM specimens with 2,340 MPa tensile modulus, 69.6 MPa tensile strength, 7.2% yield strain and 60–120% break strain; these are typical values for that grade/form. Independent SLS work demonstrates how incomplete interlayer consolidation changes the endpoint: tested multilayer PPSU specimens produced at 13–20 W and stated scan speeds gave only 2.28–9.26 MPa UTS, so such porous sintered coupons are not injection-molded PPSU values.
sections.processing:
Polyphenylsulfone (PPSU) is an amorphous high-temperature thermoplastic converted by injection molding, profile/film/fiber extrusion, and blow molding. Pellets are hygroscopic and must be desiccant dried, conveyed with dry air, and protected from reabsorption; wet feed can produce splay, bubbles, viscosity loss, and degraded properties at the unusually high melt temperature. Color concentrate, filled feed, and clean regrind require the same moisture control and should be checked for thermal compatibility. Melt processing needs a machine capable of stable high barrel and nozzle or die temperatures, sufficient torque, controlled shear, and streamlined flow paths without dead spots. Shot-to-cylinder sizing, screw recovery, back pressure, short residence, filling and packing, venting, mold temperature, and balanced cooling govern weld lines, sink, frozen stress, shrinkage, warpage, and surface quality. Extrusion additionally depends on pressure stability, screen and die condition, restrained drawdown, filament or profile calibration, and uniform quench or roll cooling; blow molding requires a grade and parison program with adequate melt strength. Because PPSU is amorphous, cooling history mainly freezes orientation and residual stress rather than setting a crystalline fraction, and later heat exposure can reveal poorly controlled stress. Overheating or long residence causes discoloration and degradation, so interruptions require prompt purging under the supplier procedure. Polymer synthesis remains outside this section; drying, melt shaping, cooling, and post-forming conditioning are Processing.

Solvay's Radel guide gives named-grade starting guidance rather than a universal PPSU window. Its minimum drying examples are 2.5 h at 177 °C, 4 h at 150 °C, or 4.5 h at 135 °C, with target moisture below 500 ppm for injection molding and 100 ppm for extrusion. For Radel R-5000/R-5100 it lists a 365–393 °C melt and 150–163 °C mold, advises against injection melt temperatures above 395 °C, and limits residence to the guide's approximately 10–20 min range at the listed melt temperatures to avoid discoloration and degradation. A distinct experiment using Radel R-5500-NT dried pellets at 150 °C for 2 h and extruded a 1 wt% multiwall-carbon-nanotube PPSU yarn through barrel zones rising from 330 to 390 °C before a 350 °C die. That filled-yarn profile belongs only to the reported formulation, extruder, and yarn process.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyphenylsulfone (PPSU) is an aromatic polysulfone made from biphenol and dichlorodiphenyl sulfone; molecular weight and end capping are set during polycondensation.
sections.properties: Multilayer laser-sintered PPSU tensile results depend on energy density and interlayer consolidation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PPSU is used in sterilizable instrument trays, surgical handles and implant trial components, plumbing fittings and valves, food-service equipment, aircraft and wire insulation. Implant trials are distinct from permanent implant materials.

Purchasing. Syensqo lists Radel PPSU resins by flow level and transparent or opaque color; RG-5010 is a glass-filled example. Purchase the specified resin grade through technical sales, or specify it to a component converter.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked sources do not report a separate annual purchase tonnage or end-use mass split for this material. Supplier availability establishes a commercial route, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The hydroxylation study recovers bisphenol S and 4,4′-dihydroxybiphenyl from PPSU powder by selective ether cleavage.

Timescales: Reaction times under strong-base, hot-solvent treatment are process-specific; the cited experiments do not establish an ambient half-life.

Environmental persistence: The cited chemical-recovery experiments do not measure environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine disappearance time is established here.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Laboratory hydroxylation and thiolation recover aromatic feedstocks; thiolation was also applied to pieces of a PPSU baby bottle. The supplier guide separately documents clean regrind handling for its PPSU grades.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: BASF’s Ultrason guide includes PPSU and warns that excessive temperature or residence time can generate decomposition gases and pressure in a blocked barrel. Hot equipment/melt, fume extraction and controlled shutdown are specific handling concerns. For EU food-contact uses, BASF’s March 2026 notice identifies specified Ultrason P PPSU grades as alternatives for requalification of bisphenol-affected articles. This is supplier documentation for those grades; it does not establish universal approval of every PPSU formulation or use condition.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Supplier data and SLS tests concern specific grades and build parameters; polymer molecular weight, powder condition, scan settings, consolidation, and specimen direction limit transferability.

sections.overview: Poly(phenylene sulfide) (PPS) is an aromatic sulfur-containing polymer produced by polycondensation of p-dichlorobenzene with alkaline-metal sulfide or hydrosulfide chemistry. Its preparation uses a polar reaction medium and controlled dehydration before the polycondensation stage.
sections.history: Phillips Petroleum researchers James T. Edmonds Jr. and Harold W. Hill Jr. documented a practical aromatic-sulfide polymerization route in a patent filed in 1963 and granted in 1967. Phillips brought PPS to market as Ryton in the early 1970s. Its engineering uses expanded through reinforced and other specialized compounds. Toray’s 2006 business account illustrates that later breadth: automotive ignition and headlamp components, copier parts, pumps and valves, as well as insulating films and industrial filtration fibers. PPS history therefore includes the original manufacturing breakthrough and subsequent control of polymer form, compounding and fabrication for particular products.
sections.nomenclature: PPS identifies the poly(phenylene sulfide) polymer, not a PPS-filled composite, reinforced grade, or finished printed article. Additives, reinforcement, molecular mass, and crystallization history are material-specific descriptors that must be retained alongside the base polymer name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(phenylene sulfide) (PPS) is commonly the para-linked aromatic sulfide polymer produced by high-temperature nucleophilic aromatic-substitution polycondensation of a sulfide nucleophile with 1,4-dichlorobenzene. Commercially relevant routes use sodium sulfide or sodium hydrosulfide chemistry in a polar solvent such as N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), with controlled dehydration important before the high-temperature coupling stage. One patent prepares the reactive sulfide system from alkali metal hydroxide/hydrosulfide, removes excess water, and polycondenses with p-dichlorobenzene in NMP. A distinct fibre-grade route uses sodium hydrosulfide, p-dichlorobenzene, NMP, and a C5–C6 sodium-carboxylate additive. These are route-specific reagent packages: the additive and purification sequence are not universal PPS features, and post-polymer processing into fibre is outside this synthesis evidence.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PPS is a semicrystalline engineering thermoplastic whose stiffness and failure behavior depend on crystallinity and thermal history, molar mass, filler or fiber reinforcement, void content, orientation, and test temperature and rate. In printed or molded structures, layer direction, raster gap, extrusion mass, outline overlap, and cooling can change interlayer bonding and residual crystallization; moisture and chemical exposure should likewise remain part of the test context. One open study lists an unfilled commercial PPS grade (DIC DSP B-100-C) with ultimate tensile strength 110 MPa, Young's modulus 3.7 GPa, and 0.2% yield strength 100 MPa. Those values describe the named initial material in that composite study, not all PPS grades or forms. A separate open FDM study reports that infill angle, number of outlines, and layer thickness changed tensile, bending, and impact response of PPS printed at 1 mm min−1 tensile speed under ISO 527; it identifies filament alignment and interlayer microlattice slip as key form-specific variables.
sections.processing:
Poly(phenylene sulfide) (PPS) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic most commonly converted as neat, mineral-filled, or fiber-reinforced molding compounds by injection molding; extrusion and melt-fed additive manufacturing are also possible with suitable grades. Because crystallization continues during cooling, mold or chamber temperature and cooling uniformity strongly affect shrinkage, warpage, surface finish, and final crystallinity. PPS is processed at high melt temperature, so feed drying, short and reproducible residence time, effective mold venting, and corrosion- and abrasion-resistant screws, barrels, and tooling are important. Stagnant melt or abnormal residence can produce gas, discoloration, deposits, or viscosity change.

Toray's TORELINA guidance provides a supplier-bound injection-molding reference rather than a family specification: it recommends predrying its PPS materials at 130 °C for 3–4 h, resin temperature of 315–345 °C, mold temperature of 130–150 °C, and injection pressure of 40–100 MPa, while emphasizing venting and avoiding abnormal residence. For a distinct FDM example, Geng and co-workers printed PPS specimens in the Z direction at 285 °C through a 0.4 mm nozzle at 1500 mm/min with a forced-air system near the nozzle. Their design varied extrusion multiplier from 0.8 to 1.2, raster gap from −0.2 to 0.2 mm, outline overlap from 0 to 100%, and layer thickness from 0.1 to 0.4 mm. More deposited melt reduced internal voids and improved tensile and bending strength but excessive extrusion reduced impact performance and dimensional accuracy; filament alignment also made strength direction-dependent. These observations are limited to that PPS feedstock, printer, and specimen design.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PPS is a semicrystalline aromatic sulfide polymer.
sections.properties: Crystallinity, reinforcement, and processing control its high-temperature performance.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PPS serves molded heating-system components such as pumps, heat meters and manifolds. Other grades supply coatings and extrusion or compounding applications.

Purchasing. Syensqo’s Ryton V-1 is a documented powder resin; reinforced finished compounds are a different purchase from this base polymer. Specify the grade, reinforcement and conversion route through the supplier.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked product and heating guides provide no annual PPS purchased mass or end-use shares. Powder-resin and filled-compound tonnages would need their different polymer contents retained.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Iron-photocatalyzed cleavage of PPS produces 1,4-dichlorobenzene, with sulfur, sulfur dioxide and sulfate detected in mechanistic work. Chloroacetic acid arises from the 1,2-dichloroethane co-reagent, not solely from PPS.

Timescales: The study follows irradiation-driven breakdown over hours at room temperature. Added catalyst, oxygen, light and chlorinated co-reagent distinguish this from natural weathering.

Environmental persistence: No environmental half-life or mineralization time is established by this deliberately driven process.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The laboratory study converts commercial resins and selected post-consumer PPS composites, including gram-scale demonstrations. It is a chemical-recovery proof of concept; industrial collection and deployment are not established by the paper.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PPS processing and reprocessing require control of the actual melt temperature, residence time and formulation. HSE’s general plastics guidance calls for suitable ventilation and trained purging/shutdown, because overheated polymers and additives can produce irritating fumes. The high-temperature capability of a finished PPS part is not an occupational exposure assessment for extrusion, molding or thermal cleanup.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: FDM and carbon-fiber results are material-form and process-specific.

sections.overview: Poly(aryl ether ketones) are the PAEK family of aromatic polymers containing aryl ether and aryl ketone linkages. Linkage sequence, position, comonomers, and architecture distinguish members such as PEEK and PEK, and both nucleophilic and electrophilic formation routes are documented.
sections.history: Poly(aryl ether ketone)s comprise several related high-performance polymers with distinct development histories. PEKK research associated with the Apollo era preceded the ICI PEEK program whose first documented batch was made in November 1978 and commercialized in 1981. Later industrial development involved companies including Victrex and Arkema, with applications in aerospace composites, demanding mechanical components and medical devices. New product forms included films, fibers, pipes and additive-manufacturing feedstocks. These are family milestones: a PEEK date should not be treated as the invention date for every arrangement of ether and ketone groups within PAEK.
sections.nomenclature: PAEK is the abbreviation used for the poly(aryl ether ketone) family. It is a family-level record that includes narrower polymers such as PEEK and PEK; one member, processing grade, blend, or reinforced article is not an alias for all PAEKs.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(aryl ether ketones) (PAEKs) are a family whose aryl ether and aryl ketone sequence, linkage positions, and comonomers distinguish members such as PEEK or PEK; no one route defines every member. Two complementary polymer-forming approaches are documented. In nucleophilic aromatic-substitution polycondensation, activated aryl halide/aryl ketone building blocks react with phenoxide functionality to form aryl ether links. A reported poly(ether ether ketone) example uses potassium carbonate in DMAc/toluene and removes water azeotropically; its dendritic, hyperbranched, and linear products demonstrate that monomer functionality controls architecture. In an electrophilic (Friedel–Crafts) route, a carboxylic acid or acid derivative provides the ketone linkage by reaction with an activated aromatic C–H partner; an EP patent identifies aluminum chloride and chlorinated/nitro solvent media as examples. These route-specific catalyst and medium choices are not downstream cure schedules and should not be transferred indiscriminately across the PAEK family.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(aryl ether ketone) (PAEK) is a semicrystalline high-temperature thermoplastic family; ether/ketone sequence, molecular weight, crystallinity and cooling history, reinforcement, voids, orientation, temperature, and test rate all affect mechanics. A Victrex PEEK-based LMPAEK grade specifically cautions that tensile strain varies with molding conditions. As a bounded unfilled powder-grade endpoint, LMPAEK 103 PWD reports at 23 °C ISO 527 tensile modulus 3800 MPa, yield stress 91 MPa, and break strain 62%, plus ISO 180/1A notched Izod 7.6 kJ/m². Independently, an open PAEK resin study reports that modifying the aryl architecture changes tensile strength/modulus. Filled laminates and fiber-reinforced PAEK must not be compared directly with the unfilled grade.
sections.processing:
Poly(aryl ether ketone)s are high-temperature thermoplastics converted by injection and compression molding, profile/sheet/film and wire-coating extrusion, melt spinning and drawing, powder or dispersion coating, machining of molded stock, and material-extrusion or powder-bed additive manufacturing. Family members differ in ether-to-ketone ratio, melting behavior, crystallization rate, and viscosity, so drying, melt and tool temperature, pressure, shear, residence time, cooling, annealing, and orientation must be qualified for the selected PEEK, PEKK, PEK, or related grade. Hot flow paths should be streamlined to avoid stagnant degradation or gel formation, and controlled mold or build-chamber temperature is needed to manage crystallinity, shrinkage, residual stress, warpage, and interlayer bonding.

Victrex provides a bounded compression-molding sequence for its 450PF PEEK powder: dry for 3 h at 150 °C or overnight at 120 °C, pre-dry the mold near 150 °C, compact at 350-700 bar, back pressure off to about 140 bar, heat to 390-400 °C, hold pressure for 15 min per 25 mm section, and cool under pressure at about 40 °C/h to below 150 °C before ejection. The same guide separately covers injection molding, sheet and monofilament extrusion, wire coating, and powder coating. These settings belong to the named Victrex PEEK material and process, not to the entire PAEK family; higher-ketone and amorphous-modified materials can require materially different thermal histories.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PAEKs are aromatic thermoplastics containing ether and ketone linkages; members differ in repeat-unit sequence and crystallinity.
sections.properties: Heat resistance and mechanical response vary among PEEK, PEKK, and other PAEKs and with processing.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PAEK materials serve transport, electronics, energy/industrial equipment and medical devices. Commercial products include resin and converted stock shapes, compounds and finished parts.

Purchasing. Victrex describes direct application sales and value-added resellers that convert its PEEK/PAEK materials into compounds and stock shapes. Specify the actual PAEK chemistry, grade and product form rather than ordering the entire family interchangeably.

Scale and evidence limits. Victrex reported 4,164 tonnes of worldwide group sales in the year ending 30 September 2025, an order of 10³ tonnes per year. This is one supplier’s PEEK/PAEK business, not global family consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A directly studied family example is PEEK: Cs2CO3-assisted ethanol/water treatment yields phenol and dibenzofuran. Other PAEKs are not assigned the same product distribution.

Timescales: For the studied PEEK system, decomposition was achieved at 623 K within 30 min. This is a pressurized-solvent recovery test, not a family degradation lifetime.

Environmental persistence: No family-wide environmental mineralization time is established. PEEK reactor results do not determine PEKK or other PAEK persistence.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The PEEK example demonstrates matrix destruction to release carbon fibers and recover chemical products. Applicability to other ketone/ether sequences needs separate evidence.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Poly(aryl ether ketone) family operations require particular attention to material changeover and purging. Victrex’s PEEK guide warns that purge polymers can partially decompose at the temperatures used for PEEK, so suitable fume controls and the purge material’s own safety data are needed. This is a PEEK-based example for the wider PAEK family; it does not prescribe identical temperatures for PEKK or every PAEK grade. Hot tooling and resin also require protection appropriate to the actual process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Supplier and blend data apply to named grades and not to the entire PAEK family.

sections.overview: Poly(ether ether ketone) is a high-performance aromatic poly(aryl ether ketone) thermoplastic. Its backbone contains ether and ketone linkages, and it is used in demanding medical and engineering applications.
sections.history: ICI manufactured the first batch in the commercial PEEK lineage on November 19, 1978, and introduced VICTREX PEEK three years later, including glass- and carbon-filled grades. Development subsequently moved beyond resin supply to engineering applications and distinct product forms. Victrex’s 2018 retrospective describes gears, seals, films, pipes and fibers, together with automotive, industrial, electronics and implantable-medical uses. This progression depended on matching a demanding thermoplastic to suitable fabrication and component designs. Later low-melting PAEK composites and other PAEK grades belong to related developments and should not automatically be described as the original PEEK composition.
sections.nomenclature: PEEK abbreviates poly(ether ether ketone). It is a specific member of the broader poly(aryl ether ketone) family and is not interchangeable with PEKK or other related polymers.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ether ether ketone) (PEEK) is a linear aromatic step-growth poly(aryl ether ketone), commonly made by nucleophilic aromatic substitution between hydroquinone-derived phenolate and 4,4′-difluorobenzophenone. Carbonate base generates the phenolate; high-boiling polar media such as diphenyl sulfone or sulfolane and inert conditions permit the step-growth reaction and removal of water/by-product salt. Published process examples use the near-stoichiometric monomer balance and optional monofunctional end-capping to manage chain ends and molecular-mass distribution. These conditions describe resin manufacture, not melt shaping, annealing, or any later article-processing schedule.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(ether ether ketone) is a semicrystalline, high-temperature engineering thermoplastic. Unfilled, well-consolidated material can combine gigapascal-scale stiffness and high yield strength with appreciable post-yield deformation, but it remains viscoelastic: modulus, strength, creep, fatigue, and fracture behavior depend on loading time and temperature. The amorphous phase softens strongly near the glass-transition region, while crystals continue to carry load, so elevated-temperature properties cannot be inferred from room-temperature tensile data. Molecular weight and entanglement density, crystallinity and crystal morphology, cooling and annealing history, residual stress, specimen thickness and notch acuity, and strain rate all matter. Fiber or particulate reinforcement can greatly raise stiffness but introduces composition, interface, orientation, and anisotropy effects; machined, molded, and additively manufactured parts may also differ because of voids, weld lines, raster direction, and interlayer bonding.

A bounded commercial reference is natural, unfilled VICTREX 450G, a standard-flow general-purpose grade for injection molding and extrusion. Victrex lists typical values at 23 °C of 4.00 GPa tensile modulus by ISO 527-1, 98 MPa tensile yield stress and 25% strain at break by ISO 527-2, and 8.0 kJ/m² notched Izod impact strength by ISO 180/A. The public grade page identifies the methods and temperature but not specimen molding history, dimensions, conditioning, or test rate, so these figures are grade-screening values rather than a complete reproducible test record or PEEK-family constants. An independent open review likewise emphasizes that unfilled PEEK is distinct from carbon-fiber, hydroxyapatite, porous, and other PEEK composites, and that temperature above the glass transition materially reduces mechanical performance.
sections.processing:
Poly(ether ether ketone) (PEEK) is melt converted on high-temperature thermoplastic equipment by injection and compression molding, profile, sheet, film, tube, monofilament and wire-coating extrusion, fiber or composite-tape impregnation, powder coating, and material-extrusion or powder-bed additive manufacturing. Granules, coarse powder, fine powder, film, and filament serve different routes. Feed should be kept clean and dry; barrel, nozzle, runner, die, and tool must tolerate roughly 400 °C operation without stagnant pockets. Melt temperature, shear and residence time govern degradation, while mold or chamber temperature, cooling rate, annealing, pressure, and orientation govern crystallinity, shrinkage, warpage, residual stress, weld quality, and interlayer bonding. Filled and different-viscosity grades need their own settings.

Victrex's processing guide supplies route-specific equipment and handling coverage rather than one family-wide window. As an independent bounded experiment, Zhu and co-workers dried Jiangsu Junhua Type 7500G PEEK powder at 100 °C under vacuum for 24 h, injection molded it at 390 °C and 10 MPa into a room-temperature mold, and then held the molded specimens at 220 °C for 2 h to complete crystallization. Their subsequent pressure-induced-flow shaping preheated the specimen and die for 15 min and pressed for 5 min, including experiments at 280 °C. These settings describe that powder, specimen geometry, injection setup, and solid-state post-forming study, not all PEEK grades or production molds.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PEEK is a linear aromatic engineering polymer with repeating ether–ether–ketone linkages. Its rigid aromatic backbone forms a semicrystalline morphology with crystalline lamellae and an amorphous phase whose fraction depends on cooling and annealing.
sections.properties: PEEK offers high-temperature capability, chemical resistance, low moisture uptake, electrical insulation, and retention of useful properties over a broad service range. Crystallinity and orientation affect dimensional stability, wear, creep, and optical appearance.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PEEK is used for semiconductor polishing rings, acoustic films, transport components and energy equipment; medical applications require dedicated material and device qualification.

Purchasing. Buy specified resin or obtain compounds and stock shapes from a converter. Victrex identifies value-added resellers as an important route to market.

Scale and evidence limits. For context, Victrex’s worldwide PEEK/PAEK group sold 4,164 tonnes in FY2025; its end-market table reports 1,012 tonnes for transport and 186 for medical. These are supplier portfolio figures, not pure-PEEK global purchases or universal end-use shares.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cs2CO3-assisted ethanol/water decomposition gives phenol and dibenzofuran; this identifies high-temperature treatment products.

Timescales: The laboratory process achieved decomposition at 623 K within 30 min.

Environmental persistence: A separate artificial-seawater study measured absorption, crystallinity and wear changes under hydrostatic pressures up to 40 MPa. Those changes establish material deterioration, not mineralization or disappearance in the ocean.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Pressurized-solvent treatment releases carbon fibers from PEEK composites. This is a laboratory composite-reclamation route; fiber recovery and matrix conversion should be distinguished from recovery of intact PEEK.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Poly(ether ether ketone) operations require particular attention to material changeover and purging. Victrex’s PEEK guide warns that purge polymers can partially decompose at the temperatures used for PEEK, so suitable fume controls and the purge material’s own safety data are needed. This is a PEEK-based example for the wider PAEK family; it does not prescribe identical temperatures for PEKK or every PAEK grade. Hot tooling and resin also require protection appropriate to the actual process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PEEK is expensive and requires high melt temperatures and careful thermal control. Crystallinity, grade viscosity, filler, weld lines, annealing, moisture, and residence time affect performance; data from a reinforced or additively manufactured grade should not be generalized to neat PEEK.

sections.overview: Poly(ether ketone ketone) is an aromatic high-performance thermoplastic in the poly(aryl ether ketone) family. The ordering of ether and ketone linkages differentiates its repeat-unit chemistry from PEEK.
sections.history: Arkema traces PEKK’s origins to research for the Apollo program in the 1960s. Commercial development required much later work on a difficult and capital-intensive manufacturing process. Following its acquisition of Oxford Performance Materials in 2009, Arkema developed the Kepstan business and collaborated with PCAS to establish industrial production in France. Aerospace and offshore oil-and-gas components became important target markets, while carbon-fiber composites and additive manufacturing broadened the application range. This history separates early polymer research from later scale-up and illustrates why PEKK’s commercial trajectory differs from that of PEEK, despite their shared PAEK family.
sections.nomenclature: PEKK abbreviates poly(ether ketone ketone). It names a distinct polymer within the poly(aryl ether ketone) family rather than an alternative spelling of PEEK.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ether ketone ketone) (PEKK) is a linear aromatic poly(aryl ether ketone), not a cured resin network. A documented electrophilic route uses diphenyl ether and aromatic diacyl chlorides under a Lewis acid, commonly aluminium chloride, in an aprotic chlorinated-aromatic or related solvent. Terephthaloyl chloride can first form the bis(phenoxybenzoyl)benzene intermediate (often called EKKE); reaction of that intermediate with terephthaloyl and/or isophthaloyl chloride then produces the polymer–Lewis-acid complex, which is decomplexed to recover PEKK. The relative terephthaloyl/isophthaloyl content is a compositional control that changes the para/meta sequence, so it should be reported for a particular resin rather than assumed for all PEKK. Solvent choice, acyl-chloride hydrolysis control, catalyst complexation, and quench/decomplexation belong to resin synthesis; subsequent melt consolidation is excluded.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PEKK is a high-performance poly(aryl ether ketone) whose mechanics are sensitive to crystallinity, molecular architecture, thermal history, print or molding orientation, void content, and temperature. Open additive-manufacturing work reports that the printed-part response differs from filament vendor data and emphasizes anisotropy; this makes generic PAEK, PEEK, or fiber-filled PEKK values unsuitable substitutes for a specified PEKK form.

A bounded material-extrusion example is miniFactory PEKK-A: ASTM D638 Type I specimens tested at 0.2 in/min gave tensile modulus 3,140 MPa and break strain 9% in the XY orientation, versus 2,970 MPa and 2.9% in the ZX orientation. These are printed-orientation values for one PEKK-A filament/process and do not characterize isotropic molded or crystallized PEKK.
sections.processing:
Poly(ether ketone ketone) (PEKK) is a high-temperature PAEK thermoplastic available in compositions whose terephthaloyl/isophthaloyl ratio changes melting and crystallization behavior. Commercial grades are converted by injection molding, extrusion and filament fabrication, laser sintering, powder coating, rotational molding, and fiber-tape impregnation. Drying, melt temperature, viscosity and shear, residence time, tool or chamber temperature, layer temperature, cooling, and any anneal must be selected for the particular copolymer ratio and feed form. Slow-crystallizing grades can reduce printing warpage and retain an amorphous part, whereas annealing or slower cooling can create crystallinity, shrinkage, voids, distortion, and different properties.

A bounded Karlsruhe Institute of Technology study printed Kimya PEKK-A based on Kepstan 6000 with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 375 °C extruder temperature, 30 mm/s speed, 100% infill at 45°, and 0.1 mm layers. Its staged anneal heated at 1 °C/min to 150 °C, held 30 min, heated to 200 °C, held 60 min, then cooled slowly; the treatment caused pronounced warpage in that unconstrained specimen. Separately, miniFactory's 2019 PEKK-A sheet specifies 120 °C for 24 h pre-drying, 25 mm/s, 0.25 mm layers, and 100% infill at ±45° for its own Ultra-printer data. These windows are tied to those PEKK-A feedstocks, printers, geometries, and objectives.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PEKK is a linear aromatic ketone polymer with alternating ether and ketone linkages and a higher ketone fraction than PEEK. Its rigid chains can crystallize into different polymorphs depending on terephthalate/isophthalate sequence and thermal history.
sections.properties: PEKK combines high-temperature stability, chemical resistance, low flammability potential, and a tunable crystallization rate with melt processability. The balance of amorphous and crystalline regions controls modulus, dimensional stability, transparency, and thermal response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PEKK is used in continuous-fiber structural composites, industrial and aeronautical extrusion, and filament additive manufacturing. Arkema’s 7000 series offers grades with differing flow and crystallization behavior.

Purchasing. Arkema documents Kepstan pellets, flakes and powders. Standard packaging is 20 kg boxes for pellets, 40 kg drums for flakes and 10 kg boxes for powders; specify form, particle size or melt-flow grade to match the converter.

Scale and evidence limits. These are documented tens-of-kilograms supply packages, not annual purchase volumes. The sheet does not establish global PEKK demand or an end-use mass split.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermogravimetry of Kimya PEKK-A filament shows two stages of thermal mass loss and a carbonaceous residue. The experiment does not collect or identify the evolved molecules; its discussion of possible molecular products draws on other work.

Timescales: The stated filament reaches 5% mass loss at 557 °C during a 10 °C/min ramp in dry synthetic air containing 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen. This temperature-ramp endpoint is not an isothermal service life or an environmental degradation time.

Environmental persistence: Neither this thermal experiment nor composite reprocessing establishes soil, freshwater or marine mineralization. No ambient disappearance time is assigned.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A conference study mechanically recycles 60 wt% carbon-fiber/PEKK laminate material by shredding and compression molding. Adding shaped laminate cutouts improves the tested bracket geometry. This demonstrates reuse of a specified composite stream, not depolymerization or indefinite retention of fiber length and properties.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Poly(ether ketone ketone) operations require particular attention to material changeover and purging. Victrex’s PEEK guide warns that purge polymers can partially decompose at the temperatures used for PEEK, so suitable fume controls and the purge material’s own safety data are needed. This is a PEEK-based example for the wider PAEK family; it does not prescribe identical temperatures for PEKK or every PAEK grade. Hot tooling and resin also require protection appropriate to the actual process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PEKK needs high-temperature equipment and careful control of crystallization, annealing, and cooling. Isomer ratio, molecular mass, filler, porosity, deposition history, and thermal residence alter properties; a printed or reinforced part does not define the neat-polymer family.

sections.overview: Polyetherimide is a high-performance aromatic thermoplastic containing ether and imide linkages. Its rigid backbone supports high-temperature engineering applications and additive-manufacturing feedstocks.
sections.history: General Electric’s Ultem polyetherimide entered the market in 1982. Heat-resistant headlamp reflectors were an early automotive application, and later development expanded the material into electrical and electronic components. The business subsequently continued under SABIC, whose portfolio documents reinforced PEI for connectors and structural brackets, as well as specialized blends for medical devices, aerospace interiors and additive manufacturing. This development history reflects both the base polyetherimide and later grade design. The Ultem launch identifies a major commercial milestone, while individual reinforced, blended and siloxane-containing products have their own later development histories.
sections.nomenclature: PEI abbreviates polyetherimide. This abbreviation is ambiguous because it is also used for polyethyleneimine; the full name should be retained where both materials are in scope.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyetherimides (PEIs) are condensation polyimides whose aromatic backbone also contains ether linkages. A representative commercial-family chemistry reacts a bisphenol-A-derived aromatic dianhydride (BPA-DA) with an aromatic diamine such as m-phenylenediamine. Initial amic-acid/amide formation and cyclodehydration create imide rings while water is removed; a monoanhydride or monoamine can cap chains and control molar mass. One production patent describes BPA-DA and m-phenylenediamine in o-dichlorobenzene with water evolution and end capping. A distinct high-temperature solution route uses BPA-DA and p-phenylenediamine in halogenated aromatic solvent while continuously removing water. Diamine and dianhydride identity define the specific PEI; these route examples do not make all polyimides polyetherimides. Fiber, film, and molding operations occur after polymer formation.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyetherimide (PEI) is an amorphous high-temperature thermoplastic; its strength and stiffness depend on molecular grade, moisture/drying and thermal history, specimen form, porosity and interlayer bonding in FFF parts, raster orientation, annealing, fillers, and test temperature/rate. Literature values for dense PEI cited in an FFF study were 102.5–105.2 MPa tensile strength, 2.93–3.01 GPa modulus, and 18% maximum deformation, while printed specimens were weaker because of voids and orientation. A separate FDM study found 2.16 ± 0.09 GPa mean Young’s modulus for its ULTEM specimens; this is print-configuration-specific, not a neat-resin value.
sections.processing:
Polyetherimide (PEI) is a high-temperature amorphous thermoplastic available in grades for injection and compression molding, film and profile extrusion, extrusion blow molding, foam extrusion, compounding, and additive manufacture. Feed must be thoroughly dried and protected from renewed moisture uptake because the required melt temperatures make hydrolytic and cosmetic defects consequential. Stable barrel control, adequate venting, a shot size that avoids excessive hot residence, and prompt purging after interruptions help limit discoloration and degradation. High mold, die, bed, or build-chamber temperatures are often required to maintain flow and interlayer welding, but cooling must still be uniform to control residual stress and warpage. Fused-filament parts are sensitive to raster angle, air gaps, layer height, chamber temperature, and filament orientation, so printed properties remain direction- and machine-dependent.

SABIC's values are guidance for unfilled ULTEM 1000, not all PEI formulations. Its injection data specify drying at 150 °C for 4–6 h to at most 0.02% moisture, a 350–410 °C melt, and a 135–180 °C mold; its extrusion-blow-molding table instead gives 140–150 °C drying for 4–6 h, 0.01–0.02% maximum moisture, and a 320–355 °C parison melt. As a distinct additive-manufacturing example, Salazar-Martín and co-workers printed ULTEM 9085 on a Stratasys Fortus 400mc in a temperature-controlled chamber using a 390 °C model-material nozzle, 195 °C oven and bed, 28 mm/s print speed, 0.254 mm layers, 0.508 mm rasters, zero raster air gap, 45° raster angle, and solid infill. These settings belong to the named grade, machine, specimen, and slicer strategy rather than defining a general PEI window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyetherimide is an amorphous aromatic imide polymer containing ether linkages and imide groups in the main chain. Rigid aromatic units provide chain stiffness while ether segments introduce some flexibility and processability.
sections.properties: PEI provides high glass-transition temperature, flame resistance, dimensional stability, electrical insulation, and useful chemical and hydrolytic resistance. Optical clarity and toughness depend on molecular mass, residual stress, additives, and thermal history.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PEI resins serve high-heat electrical and electronic components. SABIC’s current portfolio highlights semiconductor-process films, LED headlight components, consumer electronics and electric-vehicle battery-pack applications.

Purchasing. SABIC offers ULTEM resin in transparent, opaque-color and glass-filled grades with a product selector and sales inquiry route. Specify PEI grade and reinforcement; copolymer products within the same trade portfolio need their own composition identification.

Scale and evidence limits. The product catalog does not quantify annual PEI purchases or the mass used by each industry. A count of listed grades is not a measure of demand.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The thiolation study cleaves aryl–oxygen bonds of PEI pellets, yielding bisphenol A and a dithiofunctionalized phenylene-bisphthalimide. It does not establish an ambient degradation-product inventory.

Timescales: The reaction is an imposed hot-solvent catalytic treatment; its kinetics cannot be used as an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The cited chemical-recovery experiments do not measure environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine disappearance time is established here.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Thiol-assisted backbone cleavage is an experimentally demonstrated chemical-conversion route for the studied PEI. Recovery performance for filled, contaminated or differently formulated PEI needs its own qualification; no commercial status is inferred.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PEI hot processing needs temperature/residence-time control and ventilation appropriate to the formulation, including at purging and shutdown, under HSE plastics guidance. EU food-contact context, checked 8 September 2026: BASF’s March 2026 notice includes PEI among materials for which food-contact applications may need requalification under Regulation (EU) 2024/3190. Assess the actual bisphenol-based chemistry, article and current transitional provisions; this does not describe a prohibition on all industrial PEI uses.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PEI needs high melt temperatures and careful drying and can be sensitive to stress cracking, notches, and solvents. Grade chemistry, filler, colorant, orientation, weld lines, annealing, and processing residence must accompany performance comparisons.

sections.overview: Polyamide-imide is an aromatic polymer containing both amide and imide linkages. It can be prepared through precursor-resin routes and converted to high-temperature engineering materials.
sections.history: Polyamide-imides developed as heat-resistant materials combining amide and imide chemistry. Amoco brought Torlon to market in 1973, establishing an important engineering-resin lineage. Related Standard Oil research by Robert B. Hanson and James R. Stephens, filed in 1973 and patented in 1974, developed film-forming PAI for electrical wire enamels, insulating coatings and shaped articles. Their work illustrates the importance of controlling precursor formation and subsequent conversion during fabrication. These documented commercialization and application milestones do not establish the first synthesis of every PAI composition; wire-coating systems and molded engineering grades should retain their own formulation histories.
sections.nomenclature: PAI abbreviates polyamide-imide. The name identifies the mixed amide/imide polymer chemistry and should not be treated as a synonym for either generic polyamide or generic polyimide.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyamide-imides (PAIs) are step-growth polymers that incorporate both amide and imide linkages. A widely documented route reacts trimellitic anhydride or trimellitic acid with aromatic diisocyanates in a polar aprotic solvent; carbon dioxide is evolved as amide/imide-forming reactions advance. Other routes first condense trimellitic anhydride with a primary diamine to an acid-terminated prepolymer and then react that prepolymer with a diisocyanate. A cited historical patent demonstrates the staged diamine/prepolymer route, while a later example directly polymerizes trimellitic anhydride with aromatic diisocyanates in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone. Monomer identity, functionality balance, solvent, and staged imidization control molecular mass and architecture. Subsequent wire coating, drying, or article cure schedules are processing rather than family-level polymer synthesis.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyamide-imide (PAI) mechanics depend on molecular architecture and final cure, as well as filler package, stock shape or film form, extrusion/fiber orientation, moisture state, temperature, and loading mode. A thermal cure is consequential because it raises molecular weight and advances imide/crosslinking reactions; an uncured green material therefore cannot be compared directly with a fully cured PAI. For a bounded grade example, Duratron T4203 PAI dry specimens machined parallel to the extrusion direction from extruded stock shape were reported at 23 °C with ISO 527-1/-2 tensile strength 150 MPa, tensile modulus 4200 MPa, and break strain 20%. These are indicative T4203 product-data values under the stated specimen/test conditions, not family-wide PAI values.
sections.processing: Polyamide-imide (PAI) is converted by high-temperature injection molding and, for solution grades, by solution spinning or membrane formation. Solvay's Torlon quick-molding guide requires drying before molding, recommends controlling residence time and screw velocity, and gives a starting point for the named Torlon family of approximately 149 °C for 8 h drying, 360–382 °C melt temperature, 177–232 °C mold temperature, and a forced-air post-cure; its standard 17-day cycle is limited to parts no thicker than 7.6 mm. A separate open PAI hollow-fiber study dried Torlon 4000 TF at 100 °C for 24 h, prepared a 15 wt% PAI/16 wt% ethylene glycol/69 wt% NMP dope, degassed it for 24 h, and dry-jet wet-spun fibers through a spinneret into a coagulation bath. These examples span a named injection-molding grade and a solution-membrane route; their temperatures, compositions, and schedules are not universal across PAI grades or geometries.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyamide-imide is an aromatic polymer combining amide and imide units in the main chain. Rigid aromatic segments and hydrogen-bonding amides produce an amorphous, high-temperature engineering morphology whose chain structure depends on the anhydride, diamine, or diisocyanate route.
sections.properties: PAI provides high heat resistance, dimensional stability, wear resistance, electrical insulation, and resistance to many chemicals. Its glassy matrix can be tough relative to many high-temperature resins, while moisture, orientation, filler, and cure or annealing history affect response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PAI serves aerospace, automotive and semiconductor equipment in bearings, bushings, thrust washers, seal rings and electrical insulators. Coating and adhesive precursor powders are a separate supply form from molded parts.

Purchasing. Syensqo offers Torlon PAI unfilled, fiber-reinforced and wear-resistant compounds. It identifies Mitsubishi Chemical Group, Drake Plastics and Ensinger as suppliers of plaques, rods and tubes for machining. Buyers can therefore specify resin to a molder or purchase stock shapes for machining.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked sources do not report a separate annual purchase tonnage or end-use mass split for this material. Supplier availability establishes a commercial route, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermal ageing of PAI enamel on copper wire first involves additional crosslinking, followed by decomposition attributed to amide and then imide groups. The study reports copper migration into the enamel and accelerated degradation; it does not identify individual evolved molecules.

Timescales: The wire study uses cyclic ageing at 260, 270, 280, 290 and 300 °C, with failure determined by a 900 V, 2 s electrical proof test. This endpoint concerns the specified wire insulation, not a universal PAI degradation duration.

Environmental persistence: Electrical failure under severe thermal ageing does not demonstrate environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine lifetime is established.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The Torlon guide permits clean sprues and runners to be reground before post-curing; post-cured material cannot be reprocessed by that route. Torlon 4203L tests show increasing melt viscosity and declining elongation with repeated processing. These results concern specified manufacturing scrap and do not establish recycling of all cured PAI articles.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PAI thermal curing and prolonged high-temperature exposure change the polymer; the cited enamel study observed further crosslinking followed by degradation during accelerated aging. For hot processing or removal, HSE’s plastics guidance supports controlling thermal history and fumes. A finished PAI enamel, a molding compound and a solvent-containing coating formulation require separate assessments of their actual ingredients and operations.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PAI requires high-temperature drying and processing and can be notch-sensitive or difficult to mold. Molecular architecture, residual solvent, moisture, filler, post-cure, orientation, and thermal history must accompany comparisons; a filled commercial grade is not representative of neat PAI.

sections.overview: Polyimides are polymers containing imide linkages, commonly prepared by imidization of polyamic-acid precursors. Their aromatic variants are prominent high-temperature film, fiber, coating, and electronic-material families.
sections.history: Polyimide chemistry has early-twentieth-century antecedents, but useful aromatic engineering polyimides emerged from a much later development period. William M. Edwards and I. M. Robinson’s DuPont patent, granted in 1955, documents pyromellitic-acid polyimides and their preparation. DuPont’s subsequent commercial aromatic-polyimide development helped establish heat-resistant films and electrical-insulation applications. Aerospace, microelectronics, membranes and composite matrices became major fields of use. Research later diversified substantially: work since 2010 on porous and crosslinked polyimides explored gas separation, catalysis and energy storage. The broad PI class has multiple monomer systems and architectures, so it has no single commercial introduction applicable to every member.
sections.nomenclature: PI abbreviates polyimide. The canonical record is family-level: narrower records such as polyetherimide, polyamide-imide and thermosetting polyimide keep their own names, and PI is not a synonym for any of them or for a particular commercial polyimide formulation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Many high-molar-mass polyimides are prepared from an approximately stoichiometric aromatic tetracarboxylic dianhydride and diamine. In the common two-step route, ring-opening polyaddition in a dry polar aprotic medium produces a soluble poly(amic acid), which is then dehydratively cyclized to the imide by heat or by chemical imidization. Monomer identity sets backbone rigidity and functionality, while purity, exclusion of moisture, stoichiometric balance, and optional monofunctional end caps control chain growth and end groups. The cited laboratory example reacts 6FDA with sulfur- and carboxyl-containing diamines in DMAc, then uses acetic anhydride and triethylamine for chemical imidization before precipitation, washing, and drying. A distinct patent demonstrates a one-pot solution variant in which dianhydride and diamine form poly(amic acid) in refluxing low-boiling solvent and water is removed as imidization proceeds. These examples represent aromatic solution routes; other polyimide families can use preformed amic-acid derivatives or direct high-temperature pathways.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyimides span aromatic, semi-alicyclic, thermoplastic, and thermosetting materials, commonly as films, coatings, laminates, fibers, or filled molded parts; no single tensile value represents this family. Consequential variables include dianhydride/diamine chemistry and chain rigidity, molecular weight and imidization/thermal history, aggregation/orientation, moisture uptake, filler content, film thickness, and test temperature/rate. In one thin-film series containing pyridine and phenyl pendant groups, PI-2 had tensile strength 105 ± 2.8 MPa, tensile modulus 2.3 ± 0.3 GPa, and break elongation 8.8 ± 1.4%. Independent copolyimide-film work reports that composition changes altered strength, modulus, and ductility. These PI-2 film values are composition- and specimen-specific, not family-wide properties.
sections.processing:
A principal article-conversion route for conventional aromatic polyimides is to cast, blade-coat, or otherwise deposit a poly(amic acid) precursor solution, remove solvent in gradual stages, and thermally imidize or cure the supported film before controlled cooling and release. The same sequence can form coatings and dielectric layers or be integrated with metal-foil lamination. Precursor solids content and viscosity, substrate cleanliness, blade gap and wet-film uniformity, trapped air, solvent-removal rate, oven atmosphere, ramp rate, hold schedule, vacuum or inerting, final cure temperature, cooldown, and release method govern bubbles, skinning, thickness, residual solvent, stress, adhesion, and dimensional stability. The chemistry that creates the precursor and imide linkage belongs in Synthesis; the coating, staged baking, cure operation, equipment settings, cooling, and film release are Processing. Melt molding applies only to polyimide formulations specifically designed for thermoplastic conversion and should not be inferred from these cast-film examples.

Yao and co-workers cast their 15 wt% 6FDA-based poly(amic acid) solutions on glass, dried them in an air oven at 60 °C for 2 h, 80 °C for 2 h, 100 °C for 1 h, and 120 °C for 1 h, then imidized under vacuum at 200 °C for 1 h, 250 °C for 0.5 h, and 300 °C for 0.5 h. After cooling, the films were released by soaking the plates in distilled water. Yu and co-workers used a distinct ODA/DAPBI/BTDA precursor series: a 300 micrometer blade set the wet layer on clean, dry glass; programmed drying progressed from 50 to 180 °C, and the PI-0 film was vacuum-cured at 200 °C for 1 h, 250 °C for 1 h, 300 °C for 0.5 h, and 360 °C for 0.5 h at a 5 °C/min heating rate, followed by cooling at 3 °C/min to give an approximately 30 micrometer film. Both schedules are formulation- and apparatus-specific, not universal polyimide cures.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyimides are polymers containing imide rings in the main chain, commonly made from aromatic dianhydrides and diamines through polyamic-acid intermediates followed by imidization. Rigid aromatic, semi-aromatic, aliphatic, thermoplastic, and thermosetting architectures give the family broad morphologies.
sections.properties: Polyimides are valued for high thermal stability, electrical insulation, chemical resistance, dimensional stability, and low flammability. Glass transition, toughness, optical behavior, dielectric response, and processability vary with backbone flexibility, imide content, molecular mass, and cure or annealing.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polyimide materials include flexible-circuit dielectric films and cover-coat inks, as well as thermoplastic grades for semiconductor machinery, electrical parts and transport components. Film-forming and melt-processable architectures are distinct.

Purchasing. Kaneka supplies PIXEO/APICAL film and cover-coat products; Mitsui offers AURUM thermoplastic resin in neat and reinforced grades. Purchase by architecture and product form, rather than treating all polyimides as an interchangeable resin.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked portfolios do not report a consistent worldwide polyimide purchase tonnage or industry mass split. Film area, precursor-solution mass and molded-compound mass require different accounting.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In the studied PMDA/ODA film, ethanolamine breaks imide rings and releases 4,4′-oxydianiline; subsequent hydrolysis and ring reconstruction yields a hydroxyethyl-substituted pyromellitic diimide. These are deliberately generated recovery products.

Timescales: The reported film experiment used a 3 h aminolysis stage at 120 °C, followed by a separate hydrolysis stage. It is not a total environmental decay time.

Environmental persistence: The cited chemical-recovery experiments do not measure environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine disappearance time is established here.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The study demonstrates aminolysis followed by hydrolysis and product isolation, with separate treatment of crosslinked formulations. Results from the PMDA/ODA film cannot define the recovery chemistry of every aromatic, aliphatic or network polyimide.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For polyimide manufacture and rework, health assessment depends on whether the material is a precursor solution, a cured film or a melt-processable grade. HSE plastics guidance provides general controls for heated polymer operations: reliable temperature control, appropriate fume extraction and planned cleanup/shutdown. A cured-film degradation experiment does not determine exposure to the solvent and reactive ingredients of a precursor formulation, which require their own safety documentation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Many polyimides are difficult to melt process and require solution casting, chemical imidization, or high-temperature curing. Moisture, residual solvent, imidization degree, thermal history, backbone chemistry, orientation, filler, and network state must accompany comparisons across this broad family.
