sections.overview: Tetrafluoroethylene–hexafluoropropylene–vinylidene fluoride terpolymer is the fluoropolymer terpolymer commonly called THV, made by aqueous free-radical polymerization of TFE, HFP, and VDF. Its fluorinated composition supports flexible, melt-processable material forms, while exact behavior varies with composition and grade.
sections.history: The commercial history of the TFE–HFP–VDF terpolymer is closely associated with THV and the collaboration between Hoechst and 3M. In its company history, 3M describes the formation of the Dyneon joint venture in 1996 and development of THV applications using Hoechst’s manufacturing capability and 3M’s market experience. Documented uses included automotive fuel-filler tube linings, greenhouse films and fiber-optic tubing. 3M bought Hoechst’s interest at the end of 1999. These are commercialization and application-development milestones; the account does not establish that the terpolymer was first synthesized when the joint venture was formed.
sections.nomenclature: THV is the common abbreviation for the TFE/HFP/VDF terpolymer. The name requires all three comonomer families in this record's scope; PVDF, TFE–HFP copolymers, and other fluoropolymer grades are related materials rather than aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Tetrafluoroethylene–hexafluoropropylene–vinylidene fluoride terpolymer is made by free-radical copolymerization of the three fluoromonomers TFE, HFP, and VDF. Commercial thermoplastic members are commonly called THV. Aqueous emulsion polymerization is an established route: deoxygenated water, a fluorinated emulsifier or alternative dispersing system, buffer, and a water-soluble radical source are charged to a pressure reactor, an initial monomer mixture establishes pressure, and TFE/HFP/VDF feeds are metered during batch, semibatch, or continuous reaction. Persulfate or persulfate/redox systems are useful initiators; a chain-transfer agent can regulate molar mass and end groups. One cited example maintains composition and pressure by feeding all three gaseous monomers to an aqueous reactor and then coagulates, washes, and dries the dispersion. A distinct patent uses ammonium persulfate in an aqueous fluorosurfactant medium and documents a TFE/HFP/VDF feed as one fluoro-copolymerization example. Monomer-feed ratios and conversion must be controlled because the three monomers have different incorporation behavior. Composition and sequence distribution determine whether the isolated material is semicrystalline and melt-processable or amorphous and elastomeric; a route example for an amorphous composition is therefore not a family-wide THV grade specification. Initiator, surfactant, chain transfer, pressure, temperature, and feed profile control particle nucleation, molar mass, composition, and residual monomer. The latex is coagulated or spray-isolated, washed as required, stabilized, and dried.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
TFE–HFP–VDF terpolymers, commonly encountered in commercial THV fluorothermoplastics, combine melt processability with a soft, highly extensible response. They are uncrosslinked thermoplastics rather than conventional cured fluoroelastomers: low-modulus grades can shear-yield, neck and draw to several times their original length, while still providing fluoropolymer chemical and thermal stability. Because commercial grades span glass transitions near room temperature and widely different melting points, the same material can feel elastomeric under one temperature/rate condition yet become substantially stiffer or more time-dependent under another. Tensile strength, elongation, flexural stiffness, impact response, creep and stress relaxation must therefore be associated with a particular grade and temperature.

The TFE/VDF/HFP ratio, sequence distribution and molar mass set chain mobility and intermolecular packing. Bulky HFP units disrupt crystallization; in one 52/36/12 mol% VDF/TFE/HFP statistical terpolymer they produced a low-crystallinity lamellar material whose crystals combined VDF- and TFE-like features. Crystal fraction and lamellar morphology then change with melt history, quench or anneal, drawing temperature and draw ratio, producing orientation-dependent film response. Grade additives, pigments, reinforcing or particulate fillers, blending and multilayer interfaces can further alter ductility and modulus. Extrusion or molding flow, film thickness and orientation, welds, residual stress, service temperature, loading rate and duration, and prior thermal or chemical exposure are consequential test variables. Neat THV is hydrophobic and usually is not dried like a hygroscopic engineering resin, but surface moisture after high-humidity storage and test conditioning should still be reported.

As a bounded commercial-grade example, 3M's product-comparison guide reports nominal, non-specification values for THV 500GZ pellets. At 23 °C and 50 mm/min under DIN EN ISO 12086, tensile strength is 26 MPa and elongation at break is 520%. The guide also reports a 23 °C ASTM D790 flexural modulus of 210 MPa on injection-molded bars measuring 127 × 12.7 × 3.2 mm. A separate THV 500GZ sheet identifies the tensile result as a film measurement, but neither document supplies tensile-film thickness or conditioning details. These values describe this grade and the stated test forms; they are not a family range and should not be transferred to other TFE/HFP/VDF ratios, filled compounds, oriented films, low-temperature service or long-duration loading.
sections.processing:
Tetrafluoroethylene–hexafluoropropylene–vinylidene fluoride terpolymers (often called THV fluorothermoplastics) are melt processable by extrusion and injection molding. Directly documented article routes include film, tube and profile extrusion, wire coating, injection molding, and multilayer coextrusion or coprocessing with compatible nonfluorinated polymers. Grade melt flow and melting point must be matched to the route and adjoining layers. Pellet cleanliness and surface moisture, feed-throat cooling, screw and die temperature, screen-pack filtration, melt pressure, shear and residence time, line speed, die dimensions, quench temperature, and take-up govern feed stability, gels, surface quality, crystallinity, clarity, dimensions, and interlayer bonding. Hydrophobic pellets may not normally require drying, but surface moisture after humid storage should be addressed. Corrosion-resistant equipment and local exhaust are important, and overheating or burn-off cleaning must be avoided because excessively hot fluoropolymer can release hazardous vapors. Terpolymer manufacture belongs in Synthesis; melting, shaping, cooling, and any post-shaping radiation crosslinking operation belong here.

3M's guidance is explicitly for Dyneon THV 500GZ, not a family-wide window. It gives an extrusion starting profile with the feed throat held at 30–70 °C, zones at 180, 220, and 260 °C, die and tooling near 260 °C, and a 1000/500/200 µm screen pack; for injection molding it lists a 260–280 °C nozzle and a 50–100 °C mold. A distinct Saint-Gobain patent supplies an actual terpolymer-tube example: a TFE/HFP/VDF terpolymer was extruded at a 590–610 °F (about 310–321 °C) melt temperature and 230–255 ft/min line speed into 1.58 mm outside-diameter tube, quenched in a 60–80 °F (about 16–27 °C) tank, and then electron-beam crosslinked at 75 Mrad. Those unusually hot, fast, fine-tube conditions and radiation dose apply only to the disclosed clarity-oriented experiment; the patent separately reports that melt temperature and quench affected crystallite size and transparency.
sections.structureAndMorphology: THV is a statistical TFE/HFP/VDF terpolymer with low crystallinity and composition-dependent lamellar morphology.
sections.properties: Commercial THV grades balance flexibility, tensile response, and low modulus, but values vary across grade composition.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. The historical THV 500GZ terpolymer grade was offered for molded parts, extruded film, tubes, profiles and wire coatings requiring flexibility. These are documented commercial uses, not proof of continued manufacture.

Purchasing. The 2016 3M sheet specifies pellets in 25 kg bags. However, 3M states that it completed its PFAS manufacturing exit at the end of 2025. Treat that sheet as historical: current inventory or alternative suppliers require direct verification before specifying a new purchase.

Scale and evidence limits. The historical package is tens of kilograms. Neither remaining stock nor current annual THV purchases is quantified by the checked documents; a legacy product sheet cannot establish 2026 production.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The THV 500GZ supplier identifies hydrogen fluoride and perfluoroisobutylene among possible products under extreme overheating, with carbon oxides and other fumes. This product-specific hazard list is not an ambient fate inventory.

Timescales: The SDS does not provide a transferable degradation time. Formation under equipment failure or severe heat is distinct from environmental aging.

Environmental persistence: Environmental mineralization time is not established for the specified terpolymer grade.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The SDS provides disposal guidance but no demonstrated THV material-reclamation process; a polymer-specific recycling route remains an evidence gap.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The 3M Dyneon THV 500GZ SDS revised 10 October 2025 identifies polymer fume fever from thermal-decomposition fumes and burns from hot material as handling concerns. These warnings apply to the named THV grade and its processing conditions. Prevent overheating, control processing emissions and use protection appropriate to molten resin; filled, modified or dispersion formulations need their own safety assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Grade tables and one 52/36/12 mol% study are not universal; comonomer ratio, quench, orientation, and specimen form must remain stated.

sections.overview: Poly(p-xylylene) is a family of vapor-deposited polymers formed when pyrolysis-generated xylylene diradicals deposit and polymerize on a surface. This deposition chemistry makes the family important as thin, conformal coating materials.
sections.history: Michael Szwarc discovered vapor-deposited poly(p-xylylene) during high-temperature studies of para-xylene at Manchester in 1947. His deposit prompted industrial investigation by ICI, DuPont, Kellogg and Polaroid. William Franklin Gorham at Union Carbide subsequently developed a more practical deposition route using the cyclic dimer; Donald Cram’s laboratory contributed a dimer synthesis in 1951. Union Carbide announced the commercial Parylene coating system on 17 February 1965. The principal historical product was therefore a deposited protective coating, with polymer chemistry and application method developed together. Nova Tran licensed the technology in 1971; the later Specialty Coating Systems business continued its commercialization.
sections.nomenclature: PPX and poly-para-xylylene identify the unsubstituted family boundary. Substituted parylene materials are related family members whose precursor substitution must be stated; a deposited film is an article form of a named PPX material, not a separate polymer synonym.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The poly(p-xylylene) family is commonly made by vapour-phase polymerization of a [2.2]paracyclophane precursor. Heating cleaves the dimer to reactive p-xylylene diradicals, which are transported under reduced pressure and condense/polymerize on the receiving surface without a conventional solution initiator or catalyst. The precursor substitution pattern is a family-level control: unsubstituted [2.2]paracyclophane gives poly(p-xylylene), while substituted cyclophanes furnish correspondingly substituted parylene members. These references describe polymer formation rather than downstream coating-use conditions.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(p-xylylene) materials are normally vapor-deposited films or conformal coatings, so mechanics depend on the substitution variant (for example PPX-N versus chloro-substituted PPX-C), deposition conditions and film thickness, substrate constraint, microstructure, test mode and loading rate, and thermal, humid, oxidative, or long-term aging exposure. A coating or thin-film indentation result is therefore not directly comparable with a free foil tensile test. In one open tensile study of five Parylene C foils, the measured Young's modulus was 2.81 ± 0.06 GPa, yield strength 42.5 ± 1.1 MPa, and yield strain 2.58 ± 0.17%. Those results are specific to the deposited Parylene C foils and the study's tensile protocol, not the entire PPX family. A separate open aging study of deposited Parylene C measured 3.56 GPa by nanoindentation initially and 3.93 GPa after approximately five years of non-accelerated aging; it explicitly notes that indentation values on thin films can differ from tensile measurements because of substrate influence.
sections.processing:
Poly(p-xylylene) family materials are unusual article-conversion polymers because the important route is conformal vapor deposition rather than melt extrusion or injection molding. In the commercial Parylene process, a solid dimer feed is vaporized and cracked upstream, and the reactive vapor reaches room-temperature articles in a low-pressure chamber, where a continuous poly(p-xylylene) coating grows on exposed surfaces and into small gaps. The precursor-to-polymer chemistry belongs in Synthesis; for Processing, the controlling operations are article cleaning and masking, fixture design, adhesion promotion where needed, chamber pressure and deposition rate, thickness monitoring, and post-deposition inspection. Surface contamination, shadowing, difficult cable or elastomer interfaces, and inadequate adhesion preparation can defeat an otherwise conformal coating.

Kohler and co-workers provide a bounded Parylene C encapsulation example for piezoelectric implant actuators. They used a Labcoater 300, treated the article with oxygen plasma at 300 W for 5 min, applied Silane A-174 adhesion promoter, and deposited at 2.0–4.0 Pa to obtain an 11.9 micrometre coating. Their separate free-film specimens omitted plasma and promoter and instead used a release layer on a silicon wafer, illustrating that surface preparation depends on whether adhesion or release is wanted. These settings and the reported coating thickness belong to that Parylene C experiment and its equipment; they are not a universal window for every poly(p-xylylene) derivative or article geometry.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Parylenes are linear p-xylylene polymers deposited as conformal vapor-phase films.
sections.properties: Barrier and mechanical behavior vary with parylene chemistry, film thickness, and aging.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Poly(p-xylylene) coatings protect components in electronics, automotive, aerospace and medical-device supply chains. Parylene variants differ in chemistry and must be selected for the application.

Purchasing. Buy a coating service for finished components, or buy the appropriate dimer precursor for an in-house deposition system. SCS lists N, C and D dimers and offers Parylene HT through its coating services; the precursor is not a melt-processing polymer pellet.

Scale and evidence limits. The supplier page does not disclose annual dimer or deposited-polymer tonnage. Coated-part counts and dimer purchases cannot be equated without coating thickness, surface area and deposition yield.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For unsubstituted poly(p-xylylene), vacuum pyrolysis principally yielded larger fragments rather than monomer. Halogenated parylene grades require separate evidence.

Timescales: The original small-sample experiment found 93.3% volatilization after 80 min at 430 °C in vacuum.

Environmental persistence: Vacuum volatilization is not an ambient mineralization endpoint; coating lifetime also depends on the specific parylene and substrate.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For parylene-coated electronics, practical reclamation often targets the valuable device: SCS describes microabrasion to remove local coating or expose an entire board for rework, with vacuum collection of coating and abrasive waste. Laser ablation offers precise local removal, while thermal and chemical methods have substrate, residue and solvent limitations. These are commercial repair/rework methods that can enable component reuse; they do not recover parylene monomer or establish a closed polymer-recycling loop.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Parylene-coated devices can be reworked by microabrasion, which creates removed coating and abrasive particles; SCS describes vacuum collection at the operation. Thermal removal and laser ablation introduce different heat and residue considerations, and chemical methods require assessment of the actual solvent. These process exposures are distinct from contact with an intact coating; a coating’s barrier function is not a substitute for controls during its removal.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Parylene C aging and foil studies do not represent all parylene families.

sections.overview: Epoxy resin is a family of reactive epoxide-containing resin precursors and formulations. Common members such as bisphenol-A/epichlorohydrin-derived resins are converted with a selected curing agent into crosslinked networks, so the family spans diverse uncured chemistries and cured material states.
sections.history: Modern epoxy-resin development involved several inventors and commercial routes. Pierre Castan’s patent, claiming Swiss priority in 1938 and issued in the United States in 1943, describes curing polyphenol–epichlorohydrin products with acid anhydrides. It proposed cast and molded articles, electrical components and varnishes. Independently, Sylvan Owen Greenlee at Devoe & Raynolds developed epoxy-derived drying compositions for coatings, documented in his 1948 patent. The Araldite brand dates its epoxy technology to 1946 and subsequently served industrial and household bonding. These early molding, coating and adhesive routes explain why the epoxy family developed as a platform of resins and curing systems rather than one fixed polymer.
sections.nomenclature: EP is the abbreviation used for the broad epoxy-resin family. The canonical record is a family boundary, not one molecular structure or one cured network: narrower novolac, cycloaliphatic, and other epoxy-resin subfamilies remain distinct records, and a hardener-cured formulation is not an alias for the resin precursor.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The epoxy resin family comprises oligomeric or polymeric precursors bearing epoxide groups; a central commercial member is bisphenol-A diglycidyl ether (DGEBA/BADGE). Conventional DGEBA manufacture reacts bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin to form chlorohydrin ether intermediates, then uses sodium hydroxide to dehydrohalogenate them to glycidyl ends. The Canadian assessment identifies direct bisphenol A/epichlorohydrin preparation, DGEBA advancement or homopolymerization, and DGEBA/bisphenol A reaction as routes to resin mixtures with different oligomer distributions. A recent source-specific alternative uses a quaternary-ammonium catalyst to form BADGE in epichlorohydrin without the conventional sodium hydroxide cascade. These are precursor-synthesis routes, not general curing instructions for finished networks.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Epoxy resins become covalently cross-linked networks on cure, so their mechanical response is not a property of the uncured resin alone. Many conventional, fully cured, unmodified epoxy thermosets are stiff and glassy at room temperature, with useful tensile and compressive strength and dimensional stability but limited strain to failure, notch sensitivity, and comparatively low impact or fracture toughness. Their response becomes increasingly viscoelastic as temperature approaches the glass transition, and sustained or cyclic loading can produce creep, stress relaxation, fatigue damage, or interfacial debonding. Consequential variables include epoxy functionality and backbone rigidity, curing-agent chemistry and stoichiometry, conversion and cure or post-cure history, cross-link density, dangling chains and other network defects, nanoscale heterogeneity and free volume, service temperature relative to glass transition, strain rate, moisture uptake and hydrothermal aging, physical aging, porosity, specimen geometry and notches, and the amount, morphology, dispersion, and interface quality of rubber tougheners, thermoplastics, particles, fibers, or other fillers. Increasing cross-link density commonly raises glass-transition temperature and rubbery modulus, but changes in network architecture can trade ductility and fracture resistance against stiffness or heat resistance; incomplete cure and moisture plasticization can shift those balances. As one bounded conventional formulation example, Nabipour and co-workers mixed a commercial diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A prepolymer with 4,4'-diaminodiphenylmethane at a 1:1 N-H-to-epoxy-group molar ratio, degassed it for 24 h at 70 °C and 24 h at 90 °C, then cured it for 2 h at each of 120, 140, 160, and 180 °C. Tensile testing on an Instron 5966 to ASTM D3039-08 at 2.0 mm/min gave 51.8 MPa tensile strength, 4.8% elongation at break, and 2.5 GPa Young's modulus; DMA gave 1,620.7 MPa storage modulus at 30 °C and a 143 °C glass transition. The article does not report tensile specimen dimensions or pre-test conditioning, and ASTM D3039 is primarily a polymer-matrix composite tensile method, so this single neat DGEBA/DDM network is an illustrative formulation result rather than a range for the epoxy family. Finished laminates, adhesives, coatings, and castings additionally depend on reinforcement architecture, adherend or substrate preparation, bond-line thickness, residual cure stress, defects, and the service environment.
sections.processing:
Epoxy resins are converted as formulation-specific reactive systems rather than by one family-wide cycle. Liquid or heat-softened resin and hardener are accurately metered and mixed, then used for adhesive bonding, coating, casting or encapsulation, fiber wet-out and laminating, or filled molding before cure. Surface cleanliness, mix stoichiometry, filler addition, viscosity, air removal, wet-out, film or section thickness, and cure temperature all affect the article. Mixed mass and container geometry also matter because the exotherm can shorten working time and cause overheating; spreading a batch into a thin layer or using smaller batches improves heat removal. A post-cure may be used when the named system and service temperature require it.

A bounded research example mixed commercial DGEBA with 4,4′-diaminodiphenylmethane at a 1:1 N–H-to-epoxy-group molar ratio. The formulation was degassed for 24 h at 70 °C and another 24 h at 90 °C, then cured sequentially for 2 h each at 120, 140, 160, and 180 °C. That unusually long laboratory schedule belongs to the reported DGEBA/DDM formulation and specimen preparation; WEST SYSTEM mixing ratios, working times, and application guidance likewise apply only to its named resin/hardener products, not to the epoxy family as universal settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Epoxy resins are reactive oligomer and polymer families bearing epoxide groups that form crosslinked networks upon curing with compatible hardeners.
sections.properties: The resulting thermosets span broad mechanical, thermal, electrical, and chemical-resistance behavior because network topology and formulation vary.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Epoxy systems serve bonding, coating and boat repair, as well as high-performance aerospace composite matrices.

Purchasing. Purchases range from matched liquid resin/hardener repair kits to specialized resin components for industrial formulators; compatibility and grade determine the system.

Scale and evidence limits. A WEST SYSTEM repair pack contains 250 g of 105 resin and 50 g hardener, while Huntsman lists MY721 resin drums of 145–500 lb. These documented examples span sub-kilogram kits to hundreds-of-kilograms supply units, not a global purchase/consumption total.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A bisphenol-A epoxy example undergoing hydrothermal liquefaction yielded bisphenol A in the oil and phenols in water; these are reactor products, not an ambient-weathering inventory.

Timescales: Milled commercial bisphenol-A epoxy was treated in water, with or without potassium hydroxide, in a sealed batch reactor at 350 °C for 20 minutes. This is a conversion experiment, not a natural lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Hydrothermal liquefaction is a laboratory chemical-recovery route for the tested epoxy. Product purification and hardener compatibility remain necessary before resin-to-resin recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Uncured epoxy systems can irritate skin and cause sensitization; hardeners have their own hazards. WEST SYSTEM warns that contact risks persist during partial cure and that sanding incompletely cured material creates hazardous dust. Avoid skin and eye contact and control dust and vapors. Large masses of mixed resin can self-heat rapidly during cure and ignite nearby combustible material.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The network review makes clear that performance belongs to the selected cured network. Results from a particular DGEBA or bio-based thermoset cannot be used as family-wide epoxy values.

sections.overview: Bisphenol A diglycidyl ether epoxy is the DGEBA-based subfamily of epoxy resins prepared by glycidylating bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin. The epoxide-functional resin becomes an article material after reaction with a compatible hardener to form a crosslinked network.
sections.history: Bisphenol A–epichlorohydrin chemistry was present in Castan’s foundational epoxy patent, with Swiss priority in 1938 and United States publication in 1943. Its examples prepare the resin and cure it with phthalic or adipic anhydride, while the proposed uses include molded electrical articles and varnish. This chemistry became a central branch of the commercial epoxy industry. Araldite’s history dates its epoxy-technology launch to 1946 and records subsequent industrial and domestic adhesive markets. The invention and commercialization milestones concern resin systems and hardeners; they do not imply that all present liquid, solid or formulated DGEBA grades originated in the same year.
sections.nomenclature: DGEBA identifies bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and is narrower than the general term epoxy resin. A DGEBA/hardener network is not the uncured resin alone: hardener chemistry, stoichiometry, and cure state define the finished thermoset and should remain part of its material name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: DGEBA is a difunctional epoxy precursor made by reacting bisphenol A with epichlorohydrin under basic conditions; the finished article is a formulation-specific network after reaction with an amine, anhydride, catalyst, or other hardener. The DGEBA molecular-mass distribution and epoxy equivalent weight affect viscosity and network functionality, while hardener stoichiometry determines conversion and crosslink density. An open DGEBA/DDS post-cure study distinguishes primary amine addition from etherification and dehydration reactions that can become important during extended high-temperature treatment. Those secondary reactions explain why a DGEBA network's final constitution depends on both resin/hardener chemistry and thermal history; they do not turn a post-cure schedule into a synthesis recipe for the uncured precursor.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured DGEBA networks range from stiff and glassy to toughened or rubber-modified systems; modulus, yield/fracture response, and ductility vary with resin length, stoichiometry, crosslink density, toughener, cure conversion, and temperature. In an open molecular-modeling study of DGEBA/DDS networks, etherification produced modest strength increases in stoichiometric models and larger increases in excess-epoxide models. Subsequent modeled dehydration generally reduced strength relative to the etherified state, except in the long-chain stoichiometric model, where stiffness and strength increased; the response is specific to those model chemistries and very high simulated strain rates. The existing open DGEBA blend study supplies a separate tensile comparison for neat cured resin and bio-oil-containing formulations. Together these sources support a formulation-bounded measured/mechanistic account, not a universal DGEBA strength or modulus.
sections.processing:
DGEBA resin is mixed with the selected hardener and any diluent, filler, or reinforcement, degassed while warm enough to lower viscosity, cast/impregnated or molded, and cured followed by optional post-cure. The open DGEBA/DDS study treats post-curing as an extended exposure at or above the cure temperature intended to raise strength and glass transition while reducing residual stress and outgassing; it also identifies etherification and dehydration as possible high-temperature reactions. This is a processing constraint rather than a portable schedule: pot life, exotherm, section thickness, hardener stoichiometry, and allowable post-cure temperature must be established for each DGEBA formulation.

One experimental example used acetone-conditioned walnut-hull bio-oil/DGEBA (WH 600 1:4), TEPA hardener, and silicone molds: 50 °C for 8 h followed by 65 °C for 12 h. This schedule belongs to the specified blend and laboratory preparation; it is not general DGEBA cure guidance.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Bisphenol A diglycidyl ether epoxies are based on a difunctional aromatic epoxide precursor that reacts with a curing agent to form a crosslinked network. Network topology depends on the hardener, stoichiometry, and cure schedule.
sections.properties: DGEBA-based networks can show a broad range of thermal and mechanical response because the cure chemistry, crosslink density, modifiers, and reinforcement are formulation variables.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Bisphenol-A epoxies are formulation ingredients for composite and adhesive systems, including aerospace grades.

Purchasing. Huntsman lists liquid ARALDITE LY 556 and distilled TACTIX 123; specify the exact precursor grade and intended hardener.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A bisphenol-A epoxy example undergoing hydrothermal liquefaction yielded bisphenol A in the oil and phenols in water; these are reactor products, not an ambient-weathering inventory.

Timescales: Milled commercial bisphenol-A epoxy was treated in water, with or without potassium hydroxide, in a sealed batch reactor at 350 °C for 20 minutes. This is a conversion experiment, not a natural lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Hydrothermal liquefaction is a laboratory chemical-recovery route for the tested epoxy. Product purification and hardener compatibility remain necessary before resin-to-resin recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For bisphenol-A epoxy formulations, distinguish the reactive resin/hardener mixture from the fully cured article. WEST SYSTEM handling guidance identifies skin irritation and sensitization during mixing and partial cure, dust exposure during sanding, and strong heat release from large curing batches. Gloves appropriate to the formulation, eye protection, ventilation and controlled batch size address these fabrication hazards.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Primary amine + epoxide → secondary β-hydroxyamine. Secondary amine + another epoxide → tertiary amine junction + another hydroxyl. sections.overview: Bisphenol F diglycidyl ether epoxy is the DGEBF-based subfamily of epoxy resins, in which bisphenol F is glycidylated to give an epoxide-functional precursor. A compatible amine or anhydride hardener converts the precursor into the crosslinked material used in a given application.
sections.history: Bisphenol F epoxy developed as a distinct branch of glycidyl-ether resin technology. By 1968, John Pfann and Adam Kopacki’s Stauffer Chemical patent already listed bisphenol F glycidyl ethers among commercial epoxy resins, so that date is a documented lower bound on established use rather than an invention claim. Later formulation work sought advantages in demanding coatings: a 1993 flooring patent identifies Shell’s EPON DPL-862 bisphenol F resin and develops hardener and aggregate combinations for impact and chemical resistance. This history illustrates how supplier resin development and application-specific formulation advanced the material after its initial introduction.
sections.nomenclature: DGEBF denotes diglycidyl ether of bisphenol F and is distinct from the bisphenol A DGEBA subfamily. The uncured DGEBF resin and a named DGEBF/hardener network are different material states; hardener identity, stoichiometry, and cure conversion belong to the description of the finished thermoset.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: DGEBF is a bisphenol-F-derived difunctional epoxy precursor. In the cited thermoset studies it is combined with an aromatic amine such as DETDA or with an anhydride-based hardener system. DETDA opens the epoxide rings in two sequential additions to form hydroxyl-bearing tertiary-amine crosslinks. An open DGEBF/DETDA study validated this network chemistry experimentally and varied crosslink density from uncured through fully crosslinked states in its process model, while a separate anhydride study shows that reactive-diluent selection is formulation-specific. Resin grade, stoichiometry, catalyst/hardener, diluent, and conversion are therefore part of the material scope.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured DGEBF networks are generally stiff and glassy, but modulus, yield strength, fracture response, and ductility vary with resin composition, hardener, crosslink density, diluent, temperature, and strain rate. In an open DGEBF/DETDA study, fully cured ASTM D638 Type I specimens prepared at a 100:26.4 resin/hardener mass ratio had an experimentally measured Young's modulus of 2.392 GPa and 0.2%-offset yield strength of 36.96 MPa at an estimated strain rate of 1.95 × 10−4 s−1. The paper's simulations separately show how stiffness and yield response evolve with crosslink density. These are bounded DGEBF/DETDA values, not universal DGEBF properties. The existing anhydride/diluent study provides a separate formulation comparison rather than a basis for merging disparate results into a family range.
sections.processing: DGEBF is mixed with its selected amine or anhydride, warmed to lower viscosity, degassed, cast or impregnated, and thermally cured; post-cure may be used to reach conversion and target Tg. In the open DGEBF/DETDA experiment, stoichiometric components were hand-mixed for 2 min, heated to 80 °C for 20 min to reduce viscosity, degassed for a further 20 min, and molded into ASTM D638 Type I tensile specimens. Gel-point and shrinkage measurements were run isothermally at 150 and 170 °C, and the reported experimental post-gelation volumetric shrinkage was 2.36 ± 0.08%. These are bounded laboratory conditions for one resin/hardener ratio; section thickness, exotherm, pot life, regioisomer composition, and post-cure require formulation-specific validation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Bisphenol F diglycidyl ether epoxies are difunctional aromatic epoxide systems cured with hardeners into crosslinked networks. Their network topology depends on hardener selection, stoichiometry, diluents, and cure conditions.
sections.properties: DGEBF-based epoxies exhibit formulation-dependent rheological and mechanical behavior because the cured network, diluent package, and cure schedule determine the finished material.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Bisphenol-F epoxy serves chemical-resistant flooring, conductive adhesives, encapsulants and composite prepregs.

Purchasing. EPALLOY 8220 is a liquid, undiluted supplier example available through quotation or sample requests. Its listed uses concern formulated cured systems.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The patent tests methyl-tetrahydrophthalic-anhydride-cured bisphenol-F epoxy. Solvothermal ester cleavage gives small molecules and oligomers while retaining much of the bisphenol-F backbone; amine-cured grades need separate evidence.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The demonstrated patent route uses solvent pre-swelling, amine-mediated treatment, precipitation and solvent recovery. This is a disclosed recovery experiment, not evidence of established municipal or commercial collection.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When working with uncured bisphenol-F epoxy systems, prevent skin contact with both resin and hardener. HSE identifies epoxy systems as occupational dermatitis hazards and recommends application tools and gloves suited to the chemicals involved. Handling controls apply to the complete formulation; curing changes the exposure scenario.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited simulation treats a specified DGEBF/DETDA hardening system, and the diluent study concerns epoxy/anhydride formulations. Neither provides a property value applicable to all DGEBF grades or cured networks.

sections.overview: Epoxy novolac resin is a family of epoxy-functional resins derived from phenol/formaldehyde novolac structures and epoxidation, commonly with epichlorohydrin. The family is a reactive precursor class rather than one single polymer structure.
sections.history: Epoxy novolacs combined established phenolic-resin chemistry with the expanding epoxy industry. Theodore Bradley and Herbert Newey at Shell Development filed a patent in 1952, issued in 1955, on epoxy resins made from alkylphenol novolacs. It documents an early route to resins with multiple reactive sites, rather than proving the first invention of every epoxy-novolac subtype. By 1968 Stauffer Chemical’s curing-agent patent listed epoxidized novolacs among commercial epoxy materials. Their history therefore includes both precursor synthesis and curing-system development, with coating and thermoset formulation work exploiting the additional functionality.
sections.nomenclature: Epoxy novolac (EPN) is used here for the novolac-derived epoxy-resin family. The name does not mean uncured phenol/formaldehyde novolac alone, a generic non-novolac epoxy resin, or one particular hardener-cured network; those scopes remain distinct even when related in a formulation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Epoxy novolac resins are multifunctional glycidyl-ether precursors made by epoxidizing a phenolic novolac. The novolac is first formed by acid-catalyzed condensation of phenol or substituted phenols with formaldehyde, producing a distribution of phenolic oligomers joined principally through ortho/para methylene bridges. Epichlorohydrin then converts accessible phenolic hydroxyl groups to glycidyl ethers under alkaline conditions. In a source-specific example, a phenol/cresol novolac is combined with epichlorohydrin and butanol, followed by controlled aqueous sodium hydroxide addition at 50 °C. This describes precursor formation; crosslinking of the resulting epoxy functionality is deliberately outside this section.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Epoxy novolac is a multifunctional epoxy-resin family, including phenol- and cresol-novolac epoxies, whose cured mechanical response depends on epoxide functionality/equivalent weight, curing-agent stoichiometry and schedule, network density, plasticizer or rubber toughener, and test temperature. The dense aromatic networks are often selected for high-temperature rigidity but can be brittle; open work on epoxy–novolac adhesive reports that reactive nitrile-rubber modification decreases Young’s modulus while raising failure strain and, at its optimum, tensile strength. Composite and filled molding-compound values must remain separate from neat cured-resin values.

A bounded unmodified epoxy–novolac adhesive example from Han and co-workers is the 0 wt% GNBR formulation: at room temperature its tensile strength was 68.1 MPa, Young’s modulus 2.27 GPa, and failure strain 2.88%; at 233 K the same formulation gave 78.7 MPa, 3.91 GPa, and 1.93%, respectively. The reported values are for that cured adhesive formulation, and the article’s table does not identify a tensile standard or specimen geometry. A separate cured epoxy cresol novolac example is Epon 164 with Epikure W: after 90 °C for 4 h plus 180 °C for 2 h, its storage modulus at 25 °C was 2.3 ± 0.3 GPa by DMA. That dynamic modulus is not interchangeable with tensile modulus and applies only to the named resin/amine cure.
sections.processing:
Epoxy novolac resins are converted as reactive thermosets by melting or dissolving the multifunctional prepolymer, mixing it with a hardener and catalyst, introducing filler or reinforcement where required, degassing, casting, coating, impregnation, or transfer into a mold, and then completing a formulation-specific cure and post-cure. High functionality and, for some commercial grades, a solid or high-viscosity feed can make wetting and homogeneous mixing harder than with lower-functionality liquid epoxies. Mix temperature, stoichiometry, catalyst level, degassing, part thickness, and staged heating must be coordinated to limit voids and cure exotherm.

Stanzione and co-workers provide a bounded commercial epoxy-cresol-novolac example: Epon 164 and Epikure W were mixed for 10 min at 2000 rpm in a centrifugal mixer, defoamed for 5 min at 2200 rpm, transferred to aluminum pans, vacuum-degassed for 15 min and held under oven vacuum for another 15 min, then cured for 4 h at 90 °C and post-cured for 2 h at 180 °C. A separate novolac/anhydride comparison cast its formulation in aluminum molds and used 3 h at 80 °C, 1 h at 120 °C, 3 h at 180 °C, and 10 min at 250 °C to control thermal gradients and runaway; its authors state that this laboratory schedule was longer than typical and not industrial. Both cycles are formulation-specific examples, not family windows.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Epoxy novolacs are multifunctional epoxy prepolymers derived from novolac structures and form high-crosslink-density networks on cure.
sections.properties: Their thermal, adhesive, and mechanical response depends on novolac architecture, epoxide functionality, hardener, cure schedule, and modifiers.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Epoxy novolacs upgrade high-temperature adhesives, laminates, electrical materials and composites.

Purchasing. The portfolio includes semi-solid ARALDITE EPN 1138 and solid cresol-novolac grades; choose functionality and formulation rather than buying by family name alone.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For the patent’s phenol-formaldehyde polyglycidyl-ether networks, thermogravimetry in air shows mass loss and a carbonaceous residue; added cardanol-derived flexibilizers alter char yield. Identified low-molecular-weight products and ambient fate remain gaps.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A separate patent includes epoxy novolacs in ground epoxy/fiber material compounded into polyolefins. This recovers composite material as a blend ingredient; it does not regenerate epoxy monomer and the broad claim is not a novolac-specific industrial validation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When working with uncured epoxy-novolac systems, prevent skin contact with both resin and hardener. HSE identifies epoxy systems as occupational dermatitis hazards and recommends application tools and gloves suited to the chemicals involved. Handling controls apply to the complete formulation; curing changes the exposure scenario.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited articles evaluate low-molecular-weight or rubber-modified epoxy novolacs; their results describe particular resin structures and cure formulations rather than the full epoxy-novolac family.

sections.overview: Glycidyl amine epoxy resins are multifunctional epoxy precursors made by converting aromatic amines to polyglycidyl amines with epichlorohydrin and base. They form useful thermoset materials only after reaction with a selected curing agent.
sections.history: Glycidyl amine epoxies illustrate the conversion of known small-molecule chemistry into engineering resins. Norman Reinking’s Union Carbide patent, filed in 1956 and issued in 1960, explicitly states that aromatic glycidyl amines had previously been prepared for biological investigation, but that their resin potential had not been appreciated. His work improved synthesis of products with high epoxy content and described formulations combining workable uncured resins with high heat-distortion resistance after cure. Thus 1960 is an identifiable resin-development milestone, not the first preparation of all glycidyl amines. The historical advance was the practical use of multifunctional aromatic amines as epoxy precursors.
sections.nomenclature: Glycidyl amine describes an epoxy-resin subfamily defined by amine-derived glycidyl functionality, not every epoxy resin or a finished network. A particular tetrafunctional resin, hardener mixture, and cure schedule identify a narrower material state and should not be collapsed into the subfamily name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Glycidyl amine epoxy resins are multifunctional epoxides made by glycidylating an amine precursor; they are resin precursors, not the already-cured epoxy network. A widely documented route first adds epichlorohydrin to primary aromatic amine sites to form a chlorohydrin amine intermediate, then uses alkali to dehydrochlorinate and close glycidyl rings. The amine identity and epichlorohydrin excess determine the resulting N-glycidyl functionality and molecular distribution. Newer examples likewise describe direct epichlorohydrin reaction with diamines or m-xylylenediamine, followed by base-promoted ring closure. Solvent, catalyst, base concentration, and purification are particular process choices, not family constants. Formulation with curing agent and the subsequent thermal cure create a network and are excluded from this resin-manufacture description.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Glycidyl-amine epoxies are multifunctional epoxy precursors that become highly cross-linked, glassy networks after cure; the resulting neat resins can be stiff and retain modulus at elevated temperature, but their cross-linked structure also makes unmodified matrices susceptible to brittle crack initiation and propagation. Mechanical response depends strongly on epoxy functionality, cure chemistry and stoichiometry, cure and post-cure schedule, conversion and network heterogeneity, test temperature relative to the network glass transition, and any reinforcing fibre or toughening phase. Thermoplastic and core-shell-rubber modifiers can trade some stiffness for crack-energy dissipation; their phase separation and dispersion are therefore consequential, rather than generic family properties.

As one bounded neat-network example, Van Velthem and co-workers cured tetrafunctional TGDDM (Araldite MY721) with DDS using 80 °C for 2 h, 100 °C for 1 h, 150 °C for 4 h, then 200 °C for 7 h. On 20 × 4 × 1 mm specimens, tensile-mode DMTA at 1 Hz gave a storage modulus of 2820 ± 120 MPa at 35 °C and 1960 ± 96 MPa at 160 °C (three specimens). These are viscoelastic storage moduli for that dry, fully specified network, not universal tensile moduli. In the same system, 5 wt% phenoxy plus 5 wt% core-shell-rubber masterbatch increased critical fracture energy by about 260% relative to the neat epoxy in ASTM D5045 single-edge-notched bending at 1 mm/min; the result is modifier- and morphology-specific. As an independent grade-specific reference, Huntsman lists 8.7 ksi tensile strength and 14.9 ksi flexural strength for ARALDITE MY 721, but does not give the cured formulation, specimen geometry, conditioning, or mechanical-test rate on the public product page, so those values are not comparable family constants.
sections.processing: Glycidyl amine epoxy resins are converted as reactive liquids or prepolymers: they are blended with a selected hardener and modifiers, degassed, impregnated or cast into a tool, and thermally cured to form the article's cross-linked matrix. In a TGDDM (Araldite MY721)/DDS study, phenoxy and core-shell-rubber additions were mixed into the resin at 115 °C, DDS was incorporated with continued stirring, and the mixtures were degassed under vacuum at 120 °C for 20 min. The reported cure cycle was 80 °C for 2 h, 100 °C for 1 h, 150 °C for 4 h, followed by a 200 °C post-cure for 7 h; the same formulation was used for carbon-fiber prepreg and autoclave laminates at 7 bar. Huntsman identifies MY721 as a tetrafunctional resin for filament-wound high-temperature composites with ARADUR 5200 and a long pot life at processing temperature. Hardener stoichiometry, viscosity, fiber architecture, pressure, and cure schedule are system-specific and must not be generalized to all glycidyl amine resins.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Glycidyl amine epoxy resins contain epoxy groups attached to an aromatic amine-derived core, often with more than two glycidyl functionalities. The uncured resin is a reactive molecular or oligomeric component; reaction with an amine, anhydride, or other hardener builds the crosslinked epoxy network.
sections.properties: The multifunctional aromatic structure can provide high glass-transition potential, stiffness, thermal stability, and chemical resistance after cure. Resin viscosity, epoxy functionality, cure conversion, network density, and toughener or filler content control the final properties rather than the glycidyl-amine label alone.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Glycidyl-amine epoxies supply high-temperature aerospace and industrial composites. MY 721 with ARADUR 5200 is a documented filament-winding system.

Purchasing. Huntsman supplies liquid MY 721 by quotation, with samples on request.

Scale and evidence limits. The product page lists 145, 450 and 500 lb drums, about 66–227 kg: tens to hundreds of kilograms per pack. These are packaging units, not annual purchases; no separate family consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A degradable-hardener patent explicitly includes glycidylamine epoxy resins. Acid treatment of these specially designed networks produces soluble resin fragments and separates reinforcement. This depends on the curing agent; it does not establish degradability or a major-product inventory for conventional glycidylamine epoxy networks.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Acid/solvent disassembly followed by separation of reinforcement and precipitation of resin-derived material is a patented recovery approach for deliberately cleavable epoxy formulations. Ordinary cured material and each reinforcement/filler combination require separate validation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Huntsman’s ARALDITE MY 721 safety sheet identifies skin sensitization for the tetraglycidyl-methylenedianiline resin and advises avoiding skin contact and inhalation of vapor or mist. It also identifies aquatic toxicity, making spill containment important. These findings describe the uncured commercial glycidyl-amine component; the hardener and finished composite require separate assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Highly functional glycidyl amine resins can have high uncured viscosity, short working life, cure exotherm, and brittle highly crosslinked networks. Moisture, hardener stoichiometry, cure schedule, toughener, filler, and post-cure materially change the result; cured-system data cannot be generalized to the neat resin.

sections.overview: Cycloaliphatic epoxy resin is a reactive epoxy-resin subfamily made by epoxidizing cycloalkene-containing precursors. It is handled as an uncured resin or formulation; curing converts a selected formulation into an epoxy network, so cured-network behavior is not a single family constant.
sections.history: Cycloaliphatic epoxies developed along a route distinct from bisphenol glycidyl ethers. Union Carbide’s 1972 patent traces relevant diepoxide monomers to Benjamin Phillips and colleagues’ patents of 1956 and 1959. The 1972 work addressed a practical limitation of liquid cycloaliphatic epoxides by making solid, curable intermediates. It targeted molding, coatings and laminates, emphasizing electrical applications after cure. These documents establish a sequence from postwar monomer chemistry to handling and formulation improvements. They support a history of several related monomers and resin systems, rather than one invention date for the entire cycloaliphatic epoxy category.
sections.nomenclature: CE is the abbreviation used here for cycloaliphatic epoxy resin. The name identifies an epoxy-resin subfamily by its cycloaliphatic precursor chemistry, not a particular hardener-cured network; glycidyl-ether epoxy families and their cured formulations are not aliases for this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cycloaliphatic epoxy resin is a reactive resin class made by epoxidizing cycloalkene-containing precursor molecules; it should not be conflated with a glycidyl-ether epoxy merely because both cure to epoxy networks. A documented route uses a dicycloalkene ester precursor and peracetic-acid epoxidation to form a diepoxy cycloaliphatic ester. An alternative two-step patent first esterifies a cycloalkene carboxylic acid with an alcohol or polyol (or a cycloalkene alcohol with a carboxylic acid), then oxidizes the cycloalkene-terminated ester with hydrogen peroxide in the presence of base, stabilizer, and acetonitrile. The epoxide functionality is then available for formulation-specific network formation, for example by anhydride or cationic curing chemistry; the cure recipe and any article-shaping schedule are not universal properties of the resin family.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cycloaliphatic epoxy becomes a mechanical material only after the reactive resin is formulated and cured. Tensile, flexural, fracture, and viscoelastic response depend on the particular epoxide, anhydride or other hardener, catalyst, filler and toughener content, stoichiometry, and cure/post-cure; values for a cured electrical-casting compound are not properties of the uncured resin or of all cycloaliphatic epoxies.

A bounded manufacturer example used TTA21P cycloaliphatic epoxy with methylhexahydrophthalic anhydride (130 parts per 100 parts resin) and AO-4 accelerator (2 parts), cured 2 h at 100 °C, 2 h at 140 °C, and 1 h at 180 °C. The reported cured system had tensile strength 57 MPa, tensile modulus 3205 MPa, elongation at break 2.8%, impact strength 5.95 kJ/m², and KIC 0.45 MPa·m½. These figures apply only to that formulation and schedule.

In an independent comparison cured with methyl nadic anhydride and 1-methylimidazole, the cycloaliphatic ECy-MNA network had a 253 °C Tg and 13.2 MPa rubbery plateau storage modulus under the study's torsional thermomechanical protocol. Its contrast with the novolac and BADGE networks illustrates why hardener, catalyst, cure protocol, and the measurement temperature must accompany any mechanical value.
sections.processing:
Cycloaliphatic epoxy formulations are commonly handled as low-viscosity reactive liquids for casting, coating, impregnation, or composite lay-up and then converted by a formulation-specific thermal or cationic-radiation cure. Anhydride-cured systems can offer long flow windows for wetting and filling, but mix stoichiometry, catalyst level, part thickness, and heat removal govern gelation and exotherm. A comparative laboratory study poured a cycloaliphatic epoxy/methyl-nadic-anhydride/1-methylimidazole formulation into aluminum molds and used a staged oven cycle specifically designed to limit thermal gradients and runaway before completing the cure.

The reported laboratory cycle was 3 h at 80 °C, 1 h at 120 °C, 3 h at 180 °C, and 10 min at 250 °C; the authors explicitly describe it as longer than a typical process cycle and not an industrial profile. A distinct one-component UV-curable grade, EPV 3408CO, illustrates another route: the supplier reports a 0.5 mm layer cured for 30 s at 395 nm and 0.5 W/cm², with the stated exposure suitable for layers up to 4 mm in aluminum molds. That grade is stored at 2–8 °C in closed, light-protective containers. Neither schedule is a universal family cure window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cycloaliphatic epoxies are reactive epoxide prepolymers containing cycloaliphatic structures; curing with anhydrides or other hardeners creates covalent thermoset networks.
sections.properties: Their thermal and mechanical response depends on epoxy functionality, anhydride or hardener selection, stoichiometry, and cure schedule.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Cycloaliphatic epoxy resins serve LED and optical-device encapsulants; TTA21 also functions as a reactive diluent in epoxy formulations.

Purchasing. Tetra lists TTA21S/L/P as clear liquid grades; formulate with a selected curing system and, where required, other epoxy resins.

Scale and evidence limits. A November 2022 supplier article reports 9,500 tons/year annual capacity at its Shandong base in the context of TTA21 expansion. This is roughly 10,000 tons/year plant capacity, not actual production, purchases or the complete cycloaliphatic-epoxy market.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A degradable-hardener patent explicitly includes cycloaliphatic epoxy resins. Acid treatment of these specially designed networks produces soluble resin fragments and separates reinforcement. This depends on the curing agent; it does not establish degradability or a major-product inventory for conventional cycloaliphatic epoxy networks.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Acid/solvent disassembly followed by separation of reinforcement and precipitation of resin-derived material is a patented recovery approach for deliberately cleavable epoxy formulations. Ordinary cured material and each reinforcement/filler combination require separate validation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The 2019 US safety sheet for ARALDITE CY 179 identifies skin sensitization, suspected mutagenicity and repeated-exposure organ toxicity for the supplied cycloaliphatic diepoxide component. It recommends avoiding skin and eye contact and inhalation of vapor or mist, with suitable contact protection. These warnings concern the reactive resin formulation and are not a classification of all fully cured cycloaliphatic epoxy articles.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The comparison study tests specified prepolymers and anhydride-cured formulations, so its structure–property results are not universal to every cycloaliphatic epoxy grade.

sections.overview: Unsaturated polyester resins are polyester prepolymers containing carbon–carbon unsaturation, commonly made by melt polycondensation of unsaturated acids or anhydrides with diols. A reactive vinyl diluent and radical initiator then convert the resin into a crosslinked thermoset during cure.
sections.history: Carleton Ellis developed the modern unsaturated-polyester concept in the 1930s: unsaturated polyester could be cured with a peroxide, and reactive monomers such as styrene made the system easier to use. His patent work dates from 1936. Early glass-reinforced applications included aircraft ducting, followed by civilian boat hulls. Pultrusion and filament winding widened use to rods, electrical insulation, pipes and storage vessels. The important historical transition was from polyester chemistry to resin systems that could wet reinforcement and cure into shaped composites; later orthophthalic, isophthalic and modified grades represent diversification within that platform.
sections.nomenclature: UPR and UP are abbreviations for unsaturated polyester resin. The family covers unsaturated polyester precursors and their cured networks; saturated thermoplastic polyesters, vinyl ester resins, and one filled or cured formulation are related materials rather than aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Unsaturated polyester resins (UPRs) are made in two chemically distinct stages. First, a difunctional alcohol such as propylene glycol, ethylene glycol, diethylene glycol, or neopentyl glycol is step-growth condensed with an unsaturated diacid or anhydride—classically maleic anhydride or fumaric acid and, in bio-based variants, itaconic acid—often together with a saturated aromatic or aliphatic diacid that adjusts rigidity and spacing of cure sites. Water is removed as ester bonds form, and the prepolymer is stopped at a target acid value. Nitrogen, a radical inhibitor such as hydroquinone, and controlled heating limit discoloration and premature reaction of the carbon–carbon double bonds; zinc acetate, organotin compounds, or acid catalysts are bounded catalyst examples. The unsaturated polyester is then dissolved in a copolymerizable reactive diluent. Styrene is conventional, while methyl methacrylate, dimethyl itaconate, and other multifunctional or bio-derived monomers are route variants. A peroxide, redox pair, or photoinitiator generates radicals that copolymerize the diluent with unsaturation in the polyester backbone, creating the thermoset network. One cited open study condenses itaconic and succinic acids with 1,2-propanediol using zinc acetate, toluene-assisted water removal, and hydroquinone, then crosslinks solutions in dimethyl itaconate/methyl methacrylate with methyl ethyl ketone peroxide. A distinct recycling route glycolyzes post-consumer PET with diethylene glycol using dibutyltin oxide, condenses the glycolysate with itaconic acid, and uses methacrylate or itaconate reactive diluent and a redox cure system. Diacid/diol balance, unsaturation spacing, acid value, inhibitor, reactive-diluent identity and fraction, initiator/promoter, and oxygen or moisture govern viscosity, gelation, network density, and residual monomer. Article-shaping cure schedules belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cured unsaturated polyester resin is a covalently crosslinked, usually glassy thermoset matrix. Neat castings characteristically sustain a relatively steep initial elastic response but fail at modest strain, so brittle cracking, notch sensitivity, and limited impact energy are recurring constraints. In reinforced parts, the measured response is no longer a resin-only property: fiber or fabric type, volume fraction, orientation, wet-out, interface quality, voids, laminate sequence, and loading direction can dominate stiffness, strength, fatigue, and fracture.

The network is highly formulation- and cure-dependent. Polyester backbone composition and spacing of unsaturation, reactive-diluent identity and loading, comonomer reactivity, and residual monomer govern crosslink density, segment mobility, microgel heterogeneity, and glass-transition behavior. Cure initiation, peak exotherm, conversion, post-cure, oxygen inhibition, shrinkage stress, and entrained pores can therefore alter both stiffness and failure. One open study of itaconate/MMA diluents found brittle tensile curves throughout its formulation set; changing diluent ratio shifted glassy storage modulus and tensile properties, while more volatile MMA was associated with cure-generated micro-/nanopores. Flexible backbone segments or diluents may raise failure strain or impact response but can reduce modulus or strength. Temperature approaching the formulation's glass transition, moisture or chemical exposure, fillers and tougheners, and test rate, geometry, and conditioning must also be reported.

A bounded example illustrates scale rather than a family specification. Rubeš and co-workers tested a 60 wt% solid UPET1 formulation made from glycolyzed post-consumer PET and itaconic acid with 40 wt% styrene (UPET1-STY40). After room-temperature cure overnight and sequential 1 h post-cures at 50, 70, and 90 °C, 2 mm dog-bone specimens tested at 5 mm min−1 gave ultimate tensile strength 82.4 ± 2.1 MPa, tensile modulus 2.71 ± 0.28 GPa, and elongation at failure 5.3 ± 0.4%. The same study showed large composition sensitivity in impact and bending: the corresponding UPET1-DMI40 formulation reached 140.4 ± 4.5 MPa ultimate flexural strength but only 4.9 ± 0.4% outer-face strain at failure, with 50 × 6 × 3 mm specimens in three-point bending over a 40 mm span at 1 mm min−1. These values apply only to those resin recipes, cure schedule, specimen forms, and test conditions; they are not general UPR design allowables.
sections.processing:
Unsaturated polyester resins are commonly supplied as low-viscosity reactive liquids that are shaped and cured in one operation. Important conversion routes include gel coating, casting, hand lay-up and spray-up, resin-transfer molding and vacuum-assisted infusion, filament winding, centrifugal casting, pultrusion, continuous lamination, and compression pressing of sheet- or bulk-molding compounds. Processing begins with controlled addition and dispersion of fillers, pigments, thixotropes, reinforcement, promoter and initiator appropriate to the supplied resin; mixing order, resin temperature, viscosity, pot life, and batch size govern whether the material can wet fibers and fill the tool before gelation. Molds require cleaning and release preparation, open laminates require complete wet-out and roller deaeration, and closed molds require balanced flow and venting. Cure exotherm, shrinkage, styrene or other reactive-diluent loss, entrained air, laminate thickness, and post-cure all require control. Preparation of the polyester prepolymer belongs in Synthesis; lay-up, molding, cure, and post-cure schedules belong here.

Aurer and Kasper describe the family-level conversion sequence and the major open- and closed-mold routes; their hand-lay-up procedure applies release agent and optional gelcoat, places and saturates cut glass mat, removes bubbles with serrated rollers, then cures at room temperature before demolding and finishing. A distinct experiment by Krishnan and co-workers gives a bounded schedule for Scott Bader Crystic 2-406PA, a preaccelerated UP resin containing 35–40 wt% styrene and 0.2 wt% cobalt octoate. They hand-stirred that resin with 2 wt% Catalyst M for about 5 min, cast it into 5 cm-diameter, 3 mm-deep molds, cured it at room temperature for 24 h, and post-cured it at 80 °C for 6 h. Their glass composite used eight individually impregnated 300 × 300 mm woven-E-glass layers, vacuum bagging, and the same resin-specific cure; these are experimental conditions, not universal UPR settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Unsaturated polyester resins are prepolymers with unsaturation that crosslinks through reactive diluent into thermoset networks.
sections.properties: Cured response depends on polyester feedstocks, diluent, initiator, conversion, and recycled-PET route.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Unsaturated polyesters bind reinforcement in boat structures, building panels, sanitaryware and vehicle panels. Chemical-containment service requires a suitable resin grade.

Purchasing. Suppliers sell application-specific liquid laminating or closed-mold resins; Crystic 703PA is a DCPD-modified example.

Scale and evidence limits. For that example, Scott Bader lists 25 kg, 225 kg and 1.1 tonne containers plus tanker delivery, spanning tens of kilograms to tonnes. This is supply format, not family consumption or use-share statistics.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Polyester-composite hydrolysis generates soluble organic mixtures and frees reinforcement. Product identities depend on resin chemistry.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: EURECOMP demonstrated water solvolysis and fiber reuse at laboratory and prototype scale. Separation of individual organic products remained difficult; this was not demonstrated as an established closed-loop resin process.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For styrene-containing unsaturated polyester formulations, open molding can expose workers to irritating styrene vapor, which can also cause headache or drowsiness. HSE recommends reducing exposed resin area and capturing emissions with ventilation. These hazards concern the liquid formulation and its application process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Mechanical data belong to named resin/diluent/cure systems, not the whole UPR family.

sections.overview: Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester resin is an unsaturated polyester-resin subfamily based on orthophthalic acid or anhydride-derived units. It is commonly supplied as a reactive resin and cured into a crosslinked thermoset.
sections.history: Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester belongs to the resin technology developed around Carleton Ellis’s 1930s work on unsaturated polyesters and reactive monomers. His 1941 patent includes phthalic-anhydride-containing formulations, documenting that this chemistry was already part of the early development period. The subsequent glass-reinforced polyester industry grew through aircraft ducting, boat hulls and other molded products. The parent-family history is better documented than a separate first-invention date for the orthophthalic grade category. Its historical significance lies in adapting an accessible aromatic acid component to practical reactive composite-resin formulations.
sections.nomenclature: Ortho-UPR abbreviates orthophthalic unsaturated polyester resin. “Orthophthalic” specifies a compositional subfamily and should not be used as a synonym for all unsaturated polyester resins.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester resin is an unsaturated-polyester subfamily distinguished by use of orthophthalic feedstock, conventionally phthalic anhydride or phthalic acid, as its saturated aromatic acid component. It is produced by polyesterification with one or more glycols and an unsaturated diacid or anhydride, commonly maleic anhydride, so the oligomer backbone retains carbon–carbon unsaturation. Published compositions specifically describe phthalic anhydride, propylene glycol, and maleic anhydride. The unsaturation may later participate in radical network formation with a vinyl reactive diluent such as styrene. The feedstock proportions, glycol package, inhibitor choice, and network formulation are grade- and source-specific, so the cited examples do not prescribe one universal orthophthalic resin or cure schedule.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester is a resin family whose measured mechanics belong to a specified formulation and cured article, not to the liquid resin alone. Styrene content, promoter/initiator package, cure and post-cure schedule, specimen quality/voids, and any fiber or mineral reinforcement can all change the response; laminate or filled-composite data should therefore not be substituted for neat casting data. Two publicly available technical sheets illustrate the need for this boundary by reporting different values and cure descriptions for different commercial ortho-UPR formulations.

As one bounded example, a Polynt Norsodyne® H 13212 TAE orthophthalic resin supplied through Resin Library is reported for cured, unreinforced resin after 16 h at 40 °C (and a separate 2 h at 120 °C step for HDT): ISO 527 tensile strength 57 MPa, tensile modulus 3,715 MPa, and break elongation 2.3%. These supplier values are not a family-wide range and omit specimen geometry, conditioning, cure initiator amount, and replicate statistics. An independent LRF sheet instead gives 40–60 MPa tensile strength, 2,500–3,500 MPa tensile modulus, and 1.5–2% elongation for a typical non-reinforced casting, tested to ISO 527/ASTM D638 but without a stated completed cure schedule.
sections.processing: Orthophthalic unsaturated polyester resin is supplied as a liquid reactive resin and converted by catalyst/accelerator mixing followed by casting or composite molding, gelation, and cure; section thickness, initiator level, reinforcement, and exotherm control make the cycle formulation-specific. The Polynt/Resin Library Norsodyne H 13212 TAE sheet reports cured unreinforced resin prepared with a 16 h at 40 °C curing cycle and gives the resulting ISO 527 tensile test context. A separate Laffan technical sheet gives a non-reinforced orthophthalic-resin casting example and its cure recommendation, with ISO 527/ASTM D638 test scope. These documents establish liquid-resin casting and bounded cure guidance for named products; they do not support treating either cycle as a universal orthophthalic-family window or as a laminate/RTM specification for every formulation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Orthophthalic UPR is an unsaturated polyester based on orthophthalic units, supplied as a reactive resin and cured into a network.
sections.properties: Viscosity, gel behavior, and cured properties depend on resin formulation, reactive diluent, initiator, and reinforcement.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Orthophthalic UPR grades serve general-purpose, noncritical composite moldings; suitability for marine or chemical service must be established for the grade.

Purchasing. The checked Resin Library sheet describes a pre-accelerated, thixotropic liquid resin in styrene for hand lay-up or spraying. Package quantities require a supplier quotation.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Subcritical-water treatment of the tested orthophthalic polyester recovered phthalic acid; glycols underwent secondary conversion.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: EURECOMP demonstrated water solvolysis and fiber reuse at laboratory and prototype scale. Separation of individual organic products remained difficult; this was not demonstrated as an established closed-loop resin process.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For styrene-containing orthophthalic polyester formulations, open molding can expose workers to irritating styrene vapor, which can also cause headache or drowsiness. HSE recommends reducing exposed resin area and capturing emissions with ventilation. These hazards concern the liquid formulation and its application process.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Technical sheets describe named commercial resins and specified cure conditions.
