sections.overview: Phenol–resorcinol–formaldehyde resin is a phenolic co-condensation-resin family containing phenol, resorcinol, and formaldehyde-derived units. It is formulated as a curing adhesive resin for wood bonding.
sections.history: Phenol–resorcinol–formaldehyde adhesives developed as a compromise between the room-temperature curing and durability of resorcinol adhesives and the lower cost of phenol. Myron Dietrich’s Koppers patent, filed in 1964 and issued in 1967, describes that rationale explicitly and presents sulfite-catalyzed resins with improved storage and dilution behavior. The patent treats modified phenolic adhesives as an existing commercial technology, so it is a development milestone rather than an invention date for the whole family. Historically, progress depended as much on usable shelf life, hardener addition and glue consistency as on producing the cured network.
sections.nomenclature: PRF abbreviates phenol–resorcinol–formaldehyde resin. It is distinct from phenol–formaldehyde resin because resorcinol is a specified co-reactant, and it is not an alternate name for generic wood adhesive.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Phenol–resorcinol–formaldehyde (PRF) resin is a co-condensation precursor that combines phenol, resorcinol, and formaldehyde; it should not be conflated with phenol–formaldehyde or resorcinol–formaldehyde resin alone. One documented route first forms a phenol–formaldehyde intermediate under controlled aqueous pH and then adds resorcinol for further copolymerization. Another uses alkaline phenol/formaldehyde reaction with alkali-metal sulfite, followed by resorcinol addition and reflux to a controlled-viscosity resin. Feed ratios, pH, catalyst, and staged addition determine storage stability and reactive functionality in each route. A separate added formaldehyde source can form the final network, but its cure chemistry is not a universal component of PRF precursor manufacture and is excluded here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Phenol–resorcinol–formaldehyde (PRF) is normally evaluated as a cured wood-adhesive bondline rather than as a free bulk resin. Its shear response depends on hardener level and cure, wood species/extractives, adhesive penetration and bondline geometry, moisture conditioning, and test treatment. In an open PRF study, chestnut-water extraction increased tensile-shear strength by 14% (A1) and 28% (A4) relative to the unextracted chestnut assemblies; the authors connect this to less acid-extract interference with curing/crosslinking. A separate beech study used Prefere 4040 PRF with 20% hardener, pressed at room temperature for 120 min and 1.5 MPa, conditioned 7 d at 20 °C/65% RH, then tested dry or after 4 d water soaking by EN 302-1. These joint-specific results show why neither a wood-joint value nor humidity response is a family-wide PRF modulus or strength.
sections.processing: Phenol–resorcinol–formaldehyde (PRF) is most often converted as a water-containing, reactive wood adhesive: the resin/hardener formulation is mixed, spread onto prepared wood, allowed a controlled closed-assembly period, and then consolidated by cold or heated pressing before conditioning. Pot life, spread rate, press pressure/time, wood moisture, temperature, and extractives are formulation and substrate variables, so an adhesive schedule should not be generalized to every PRF product. In a bounded Aerodux 185/HRP 150 example, resin and hardener were combined at 5:1 by mass; about 1 g of adhesive was manually mixed for 40 s, spread at 450 g m−2 on wood, held closed for 60 min, and pressed at 1 N mm−2 for 240 min at 20 °C/65% RH before seven days of conditioning. A separate beech-bonding study provides an independent PRF formulation, pressing, conditioning, and EN 302-1 wet/dry bond-testing route. Acidic wood extracts can alter cure rate, so closed assembly and press conditions require validation for the particular wood and adhesive. Phenol/resorcinol/formaldehyde condensation and resin manufacture belong in Synthesis; PRF mixing, application, pressing, and cure are the processing scope here.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PRF is a phenolic co-condensation resin whose cure creates an adhesive network containing phenol and resorcinol units.
sections.properties: Curing and bond performance depend on resin formulation, wood species, extractives, and pressing conditions.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PRF adhesives bond load-bearing wood structures and selected heat-resistant assemblies such as fire doors.

Purchasing. Aerodux 185 is listed as a retail two-part kit of liquid phenol-resorcinol resin and powdered hardener. Stock and exact kit size require confirmation from the distributor.

Scale and evidence limits. A retail kit listing establishes a purchasing channel, but no supported annual PRF purchase or consumption tonnage, or market-share split by use, was found.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Evolved-gas and pyrolysis analyses of cured Aerodux 185/HRP 150 show thermally released and decomposed organic fractions. Cure and wood extractives affect the resulting network; the paper does not establish a complete environmental product inventory.

Timescales: The analytical heating ramp spans 50–600 °C at 10 °C/min; it measures thermal release and decomposition, not a field degradation lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: AERODUX 185 instructions separate liquid adhesive residues and contaminated wash water from cured glue. Uncured spills are collected in closed containers for reclamation or licensed disposal, while cured adhesive is insoluble and must be mechanically removed from equipment. This supports segregation and controlled waste handling, rather than recovery of the original polymer from a bonded timber product.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The supplier’s AERODUX 185 safety sheet identifies free phenol, resorcinol and ethanol in the supplied phenol–resorcinol–formaldehyde adhesive. It warns of skin and eye burns and toxicity through skin contact or swallowing, and requires ventilation and contact protection during handling. This historical formulation illustrates why uncured adhesive must be assessed separately from the cured bond line.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Wood-adhesion studies are substrate- and adhesive-formulation-specific.

sections.overview: Urea–formaldehyde resin is an amino-resin family formed by staged reaction of urea with formaldehyde: methylolation is followed by acid-catalyzed condensation to methylene and methylene-ether linkages. Subsequent curing produces a thermoset network whose composition and residual formaldehyde depend on the formulation.
sections.history: Urea–formaldehyde developed commercially through several interwar investigations rather than one isolated invention. The Plastics Historical Society records F. Pollak’s Vienna group and its 1920–1924 patents, followed by industrial work on practical molding materials. Compared with early filled phenolics, these resins allowed pale, translucent and brightly colored articles. Early outlets included electrical fittings, telephone and radio housings, lampshades, decorative boxes and tableware. Melamine subsequently displaced UF in many tableware applications. The history illustrates both the importance of controlling condensation and the role of color and appearance in extending synthetic plastics into consumer products.
sections.nomenclature: UF is the abbreviation for urea–formaldehyde resin, also called urea–methanal resin. The record covers urea/formaldehyde condensation resins and their cured formulations; melamine–formaldehyde resin, a particular adhesive or coating formulation, and free urea/formaldehyde are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Urea–formaldehyde (UF) resin is made from urea and aqueous formaldehyde by staged addition and condensation reactions. In the conventional alkaline-first route, formaldehyde adds to the urea nitrogens to form mono- and polymethylolureas. The mixture is then acidified so methylol species condense into oligomers containing methylene and methylene-ether bridges, with water released during part of the condensation sequence. Resin advancement is monitored by viscosity or water tolerance and is stopped by cooling and returning the mixture to neutral or alkaline pH before storage. A cited open laboratory preparation splits the urea charge: the first portion undergoes alkaline methylolation, the batch is acidified with formic acid for condensation to a target viscosity, the pH is raised to stop rapid molecular-weight growth, and a second urea portion is added. Such staged urea addition adjusts the final formaldehyde/urea ratio and reduces unbound formaldehyde while changing the distribution of methylol and chain-end groups. A complementary mechanistic study distinguishes formation of methylene bridges, methylene-ether bridges, and cyclic uron structures and shows that pH and formaldehyde/urea ratio alter their competition. The storage-stable syrup is later converted to an infusible network by renewed acid catalysis; ammonium salts such as ammonium chloride are useful latent hardeners because they acidify the resin during cure. Formaldehyde/urea ratio, order of addition, pH trajectory, temperature, condensation endpoint, free formaldehyde, and hardener level control oligomer distribution, shelf stability, cure rate, and network structure. Article-shaping press schedules and substrate moisture belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Fully cured urea–formaldehyde is a hard, highly crosslinked aminoplast with restricted molecular mobility and characteristically brittle fracture. It can provide a strong, rigid bond to lignocellulosic substrates, yet neat or unmodified adhesive layers have little capacity to relax cure shrinkage; cracks may form during cure and pre-damage the adjacent wood interphase before service loading. Measurements on molded compounds, impregnated paper, particleboard, plywood, or wood joints combine resin behavior with filler or substrate stiffness, grain direction, density, porosity, bond-line geometry, and interface quality and are not neat-resin properties.

The formaldehyde/urea ratio, methylolation and condensation structure, hydrogen bonding and any crystalline domains, solids content, acid catalyst, pH history, cure temperature/time, conversion, and post-condensation all affect network density, shrinkage stress, hardness, and fracture. Flexible amines, polyols or polymeric tougheners, melamine or phenol co-condensation, mineral/cellulosic fillers, and plasticizers can reduce cracking or alter stress transfer but create chemically distinct formulations. Wood moisture at bonding, press conditions, adhesive spread and penetration, bond-line thickness, and adherend orientation govern joint results. In service, water can plasticize the network temporarily, but hot moisture and repeated wood swelling/shrinkage can hydrolyze susceptible linkages, erode crack faces, widen defects, and sharply reduce joint strength. Temperature, humidity history, loading mode and rate, and whether failure occurs cohesively in resin, at the interface, or in wood must therefore accompany any value.

A public-domain Forest Products Laboratory study provides a bounded joint-level example. It used contoured wood double-cantilever specimens for cleavage and reduced-size compression-block specimens for shear, bonded with laboratory and commercial unmodified UF controls or separately identified modified adhesives. Across all unaged UF formulations in that experiment, joint shear strength was 16–26 MPa; after ten vacuum–pressure–soak–dry cycles, the two unmodified UF joints lost 40% and 80% of their initial shear strength, and after 40 days at 70 °C and 80% relative humidity they lost 78% and 83%. Microscopy linked the unmodified systems to smooth brittle cure-shrinkage cracks and damage in the wood interphase. Those figures describe the particular bonded-joint preparations and ageing protocols, not bulk UF strength. A focused search did not locate an anonymously readable neat-cured-UF tensile or modulus result with adequate resin formulation, cure, specimen, and test detail, so no family-level bulk number is asserted here.
sections.processing:
Urea–formaldehyde resin is most often converted as a water-borne wood adhesive: liquid resin is mixed with a hardener and any flour, wax, filler, or functional additive, then spread on veneers or sprayed onto particles or fibers before assembly, prepressing, and hot pressing. Adhesive solids and viscosity, furnish or veneer moisture, coating uniformity, open time, mat density, press temperature, pressure, time, panel thickness, and heat transfer to the core govern flow and cure. Cold prepressing gives the assembly enough integrity for transfer; during hot pressing, controlled pressure release can vent steam and other volatiles and reduce blistering. After pressing, cooling and conditioning allow moisture and internal stresses to equilibrate. Resin manufacture and condensation chemistry belong in Synthesis; adhesive preparation, application, press schedule, venting, and conditioning belong here.

Two open studies provide bounded examples rather than a universal UF window. Silva and co-workers dried eucalyptus particles at 103 ± 2 °C to 3% moisture, sprayed a 65%-solids UF adhesive at 10% of particle mass in the face layers and 8% in the core, formed a 40 × 40 cm three-layer mat, and cold-prepressed it for 300 s at 0.3 MPa. Their approximately 13 mm boards were then hot-pressed for 600 s at 4 MPa and either 150 or 180 °C, with two 30 s pressure releases. In Gao and co-workers' plywood experiment, UF was mechanically mixed with flour at 25% of resin mass and a selected curing agent, spread manually on both sides of eucalyptus veneer at 280 ± 10 g/m², prepressed for 1 h at 0.8 MPa at room temperature, then hot-pressed at 120–125 °C and 1.2 MPa for 60 s per millimeter. Each schedule applies only to the reported furnish, adhesive formulation, panel construction, and equipment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: UF resin forms through alkaline methylolation followed by acid condensation, yielding methylene, methylene-ether, and related network linkages.
sections.properties: Pure UF coatings are hard and brittle, and moisture or cure shrinkage affects joint performance.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Urea–formaldehyde adhesives serve wood-panel lamination and veneering in furniture and woodworking.

Purchasing. The checked Prefere 4156 sheet lists liquid resin with separate liquid hardeners.

Scale and evidence limits. The resin is listed in 3, 5, 10 and 25 kg jerricans, 250 kg drums and 1000 kg IBCs: kilogram to tonne supply units. These are historical distributor pack formats, not annual consumption; current availability requires confirmation.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The cited process uses steam hydrolysis to break urea-formaldehyde binder in coated HDF. It does not provide a complete molecular inventory of that separated binder fraction.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Steam-assisted binder removal can reclaim wood fibers and expose the melamine-coated fraction for further treatment. This is substrate reclamation; it is not demonstrated regeneration of pure urea-formaldehyde resin.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: UF-bonded pressed-wood products can emit formaldehyde into indoor air. EPA identifies eye, throat and respiratory irritation as exposure concerns and recommends ventilation, moderate temperature and humidity control to reduce exposure. Emissions depend on the finished panel and indoor conditions, so the presence of UF adhesive does not establish a universal exposure level.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: pH, formaldehyde/urea ratio, hardener, cure, moisture cycle, and joint geometry limit property transfer.

sections.overview: Melamine–formaldehyde resin is a thermosetting amino-resin family formed from melamine and formaldehyde. Condensation and curing convert methylolated precursors into a crosslinked material.
sections.history: Melamine–formaldehyde resin became industrially practical during the 1930s, when melamine manufacture and resin condensation were developed together. Yuan Wang’s Waikato history identifies Henkel’s resin production and patenting around 1935 and Ciba’s contemporaneous commercially feasible melamine route. The resin’s combination of hard surfaces and resistance to water and heat helped establish molding, decorative laminates and protective-surface applications. Wang’s 2012 investigation, undertaken for Momentive Specialty Chemicals, represents a later stage: quantitative NMR was used to follow resin formation up to an industrial production endpoint. Thus the history runs from feedstock availability to consumer and industrial surfaces and continuing control of resin manufacture.
sections.nomenclature: MF abbreviates melamine–formaldehyde resin. The name identifies the melamine/formaldehyde resin family, not melamine itself or all formaldehyde-based resins.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Melamine–formaldehyde (MF) resin begins with melamine and formaldehyde. Hydroxymethylation of melamine amino groups forms a distribution of methylolmelamine intermediates; subsequent condensation connects melamine units through methylene and methylene-ether linkages. A kinetic study treats methylolation as the first stage of amino-resin formation and reports an apparent melamine functionality of six in its model. An independent open study varied melamine/formaldehyde ratio, pH, and temperature while preparing MF prepolymers and likewise identifies condensation of hydroxymethyl intermediates as the resin-forming step. This entry concerns the formation and advancing of MF resin; application-specific acid-catalyzed press cure schedules are not supplied.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured MF is a hard, highly cross-linked thermoset with limited ductility and impact tolerance. Its response depends on formaldehyde-to-melamine ratio, condensation and cure schedule, retained moisture and porosity, fillers or paper/wood substrate, and temperature. Values from impregnated paper or modified coatings are not intrinsic neat-MF constants. A public compilation for cellulose-filled MF molding material reports tensile modulus 7590–9660 MPa, tensile strength 35–90 MPa, elongation about 1%, and notched Izod impact 0.1–0.2 J/cm under listed ASTM methods. Grade, filler loading, molding cycle, and conditioning are absent, so these only illustrate a filled-molding-compound example. Independently, an open study of Diels–Alder-functional MF coating films used nanoindentation microhardness and dynamic-load thermomechanics through healing cycles, showing that reversible modification and thermal history change coating mechanics rather than defining a general MF value.
sections.processing: Melamine–formaldehyde (MF) is a thermosetting resin commonly converted as a filled molding compound by compression or transfer molding; laminate and coating formulations use related impregnation, drying, and hot-pressing operations. An open industrial-polymers text gives representative MF molding temperatures of 145–165 °C and pressures of 30–60 MPa, but these are formulation and tool dependent. A public patent gives a broader bounded window for a particular MF molding composition: compression molding at 120–180 °C (preferably 140–170 °C), 150–800 bar (preferably 200–500 bar), with a 30 s–5 min cycle. Separately, an open cure study on spray-dried Kauramin 773 MF (F/M 1.6) followed a 30–200 °C ramp at 2 °C/min and observed staged cure behavior; that schedule belongs to the named commercial formulation and analytical specimen, not to every MF grade. Cure time, filler loading, moisture, and section thickness must therefore be matched to the compound and article.
sections.structureAndMorphology: MF resins cure from methylolated melamine precursors to crosslinked amino-resin networks.
sections.properties: Hardness, heat response, and moisture behavior depend on melamine/formaldehyde ratio, cure, fillers, and formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Melamine–formaldehyde molding compounds make tableware, handles, buttons and electrical insulating components.

Purchasing. Landun lists filled powder grades for compression molding and granular grades for compression or injection molding.

Scale and evidence limits. Its A5 compound is listed in 20 kg bags. This is a filled compound’s package mass, not neat MF polymer mass or annual demand. No separate reliable consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Patented aqueous sulfite-based digestion breaks the melamine resin matrix into methylolmelamine-containing and sulfur-modified products that can be separated. Product chemistry depends on the chosen reagent.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The process recovers melamine-derived solids for resin synthesis, formaldehyde scavenging or hardening. It is patent-stage evidence for sorted wood-panel and laminate wastes, not proof that all melamine articles are routinely recycled.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Melamine-resin tableware can contain residual melamine capable of migrating into food, with migration increasing for hot, highly acidic food. FDA advises against heating food or drinks on melamine-based dinnerware in a microwave. This is product-use guidance for tableware, rather than a blanket restriction on every melamine–formaldehyde material or a finished-product compliance determination.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited sources cover specific molded and self-healing formulations, not a universal MF network.

sections.overview: Melamine–urea–formaldehyde resin is an amino-resin family incorporating melamine, urea, and formaldehyde-derived condensation products. It is commonly formulated and cured as a wood-bonding adhesive resin.
sections.history: Melamine–urea–formaldehyde belongs to the development of mixed amino-resin adhesives from the established UF and MF chemistries. Its history is application-driven: adding melamine sought improved resistance to moisture while retaining the economic advantages of urea-rich formulations. By 2013, Jun Zhang, Xiaodong Wang, Shifeng Zhang, Qiang Gao and Jianzhang Li were investigating how the stage of melamine addition altered resin performance and curing. This is a documented research milestone in wood-adhesive development, not evidence for a first invention in 2013. The resulting family encompasses different addition sequences and compositions, so no single launch date can represent all MUF adhesives.
sections.nomenclature: MUF abbreviates melamine–urea–formaldehyde resin. It is a co-condensed resin family distinct from urea–formaldehyde resin and from melamine–formaldehyde resin, rather than an alternate name for either binary resin.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Melamine–urea–formaldehyde (MUF) resin is a co-condensation system, not merely a physical blend of MF and urea–formaldehyde resins. Melamine, urea, and formaldehyde first form hydroxymethylated amino intermediates, which then undergo controlled condensation to methylene and methylene-ether-linked species. A conventional laboratory route is staged alkaline–acidic–alkaline: alkaline methylolation, acid-promoted condensation to a target resin state, then neutralization and final amino-reactant adjustment. Melamine may be charged at different stages, so its incorporation and the final co-condensed distribution are route-dependent. This describes resin synthesis and network-capable precursor formation only; cure schedules for wood panels or other articles are outside this record.
sections.mechanicalProperties: MUF is normally evaluated as a cured adhesive bond or wood-resin composite, rather than as a universal neat-polymer tensile material. Cure chemistry and melamine proportion, catalyst and press schedule, glue spread, wood species, density, moisture, grain orientation, and wet aging control the observed response. A wood-joint shear result must not be read as bulk MUF shear strength. In a bounded hybrid-glulam study, commercial MUF PREFERE 4535 with hardener 5046 at 100:30 mass ratio bonded five-lamella spruce/beech beams. EN 14080 shear testing found every glue line met the 6 MPa minimum average requirement with 100% wood failure; that is a joint-and-substrate result. An independent open review of MUF/UF plywood bonding likewise identifies tensile-shear strength and wood failure as adhesion outcomes dependent on formulation, spread, pressing, and wood construction.
sections.processing: Melamine–urea–formaldehyde (MUF) is typically converted as a formulated wood adhesive: the liquid resin is mixed with its cure system, applied to veneer or boards, assembled, and cold- or hot-pressed. Press temperature, pressure, glue spread, veneer moisture, and cure time vary with melamine content, catalyst, filler, and panel thickness. A public wood-adhesion study/review reports a representative MUF veneer route using about 170 g/m² adhesive, 0.78 MPa cold pressing for 20 min, then 120 °C and 0.78 MPa hot pressing for 4 min; this is a study-specific assembly schedule. A separate patent gives a bounded formulation/process example: dilute to 55% solids, add 1% ammonium salt, keep veneer moisture below 8%, coat 130 g/m², age 15 min, and hot-press at 120 °C and 1.0–1.2 MPa for 1.2 min/mm. These settings apply to the named adhesive and veneer construction; they are not synthesis conditions or a universal MUF recipe.
sections.structureAndMorphology: MUF is a co-condensed amino-resin network containing melamine- and urea-derived segments.
sections.properties: Cure and adhesion behavior depend on melamine content, formaldehyde chemistry, additives, and hot-press conditions.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. MUF adhesives serve glued laminated timber, finger joints and other structural wood bonds in construction.

Purchasing. Scott+Sargeant lists liquid Prefere4535 resin with separate Prefere5035 hardener through its woodworking-supplies store.

Scale and evidence limits. The listed resin sales unit is 25 kg. This is formulation/package mass rather than annual MUF consumption; no reliable separate total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Waste MUF-bonded boards can be mechanically disintegrated into adhesive-containing wood particles. Residual formaldehyde is a relevant recovered-material constituent; the study does not resolve complete MUF breakdown into specific molecular products.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical size reduction and recovery of wood particles for further board manufacture were studied directly for MUF-bonded waste. This recovers the wood fraction while retaining adhesive residues; it is not closed-loop recovery of melamine, urea and formaldehyde.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For uncured melamine–urea–formaldehyde formulations, HSE identifies formaldehyde resins and releasers as occupational contact-sensitization concerns. Prevent skin contamination and assess the actual formulation; this does not classify every cured article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited studies test particular adhesive formulations and wood substrates, not all MUF resins.

sections.overview: Phenol–urea–formaldehyde resin is a co-condensed formaldehyde-resin family combining phenolic and urea-derived components. It is used as a curing adhesive resin in wood-composite applications.
sections.history: Phenol–urea–formaldehyde combinations were already the subject of Pierre Cuvier’s patent issued in 1943, with a 1940 priority date. This is an early documented synthesis milestone, rather than a universal invention date for mixed phenolic/amino resins. Subsequent industrial work refined the balance between phenolic modification and UF processing. Frederick Schwartzenburg Jr. and Donald Griffin at Reichhold patented a controlled phenol-modified UF process in 1970, evaluating adhesive working life, storage behavior and plywood bonding. The development history therefore includes both mixed-resin chemistry and the practical demands of wood-panel manufacture.
sections.nomenclature: PUF abbreviates phenol–urea–formaldehyde resin. The name identifies a mixed phenol/urea/formaldehyde resin family and should not be used interchangeably with either phenol–formaldehyde or urea–formaldehyde resin.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Phenol–urea–formaldehyde (PUF) resin is a mixed condensation resin made from phenol, urea, and formaldehyde. It is distinct from an uncoupled blend of PF and UF resins: documented routes form a partially condensed phenol–formaldehyde component and combine it with a neutralized urea–formaldehyde component before further condensation, or carry out urea/formaldehyde condensation followed by phenolic addition under controlled pH. Formaldehyde-to-urea/phenol ratio, alkaline versus acid stage, catalyst, solvent, and reaction endpoint control the precursor resin’s molecular growth and free-formaldehyde content. Final hardening or molding is a later network-forming operation and is excluded from this synthesis-only account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Phenol–urea–formaldehyde (PUF) is a cured wood-adhesive resin system; mechanical outcomes are governed by phenol/urea/formaldehyde ratio, catalyst and cure, resin solids/spread, wood species and geometry, pressing history, and moisture exposure. An open PUF/PRUF plywood study reports that the adhesive and plywood performance were tested, with resorcinol used as an accelerator; its results belong to the formulated plywood adhesive rather than a neat PUF solid. Independently, an oriented-strandboard study bonded with PUF reports that mechanical strength decreased as urea addition increased, while dimensional stability increased. This pass found no directly comparable, openly readable tensile or flexural endpoint for a neat cured PUF specimen; the two sources instead support the qualitative formulation and wood-panel limitations, which should not be converted into a resin-family strength range.
sections.processing: Phenol–urea–formaldehyde (PUF) is processed mainly as a thermosetting wood-panel adhesive. Resin is blended with the selected filler or accelerator, spread onto veneer or strands, given a controlled assembly time, and hot-pressed; cure temperature/time and resin-solids loading must be matched to the PUF/PRUF formulation, wood furnish, panel thickness, and press. In an open plywood study, PUF or resorcinol-accelerated PUF adhesives were mixed with 20% wheat-flour filler, applied at 316 g m−2 by double gluing, and hot-pressed at 135 °C and 1 MPa for either 243 s (54 s mm−1) or 405 s (90 s mm−1), followed by 24 h ambient storage. Those settings are bounded examples for three-ply poplar plywood, not a family-wide cure window. An independent oriented-strandboard study varies urea addition (14% and 24%) and resin solids (3.5% and 4.5%) during PUF-bonded board fabrication, illustrating that formulation changes both processing and dimensional response. PUF/PRUF condensation chemistry and staged resin manufacture belong in Synthesis; adhesive preparation, furnish coating, pressing, and post-press conditioning belong here.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PUF is a co-condensed phenol/urea/formaldehyde adhesive network.
sections.properties: Cure, water response, and board performance depend on composition, catalyst, wood substrate, and pressing.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PUF cocondensed resins have documented plywood-bonding applications in wood-products research.

Purchasing. The checked study prepares PUF in the laboratory from chemical/reactive-resin inputs and compares it with commercial UF and PF resins. It does not establish a current ready-made PUF product or supplier.

Scale and evidence limits. No separate commercial purchase or consumption total was established. The 1995 plywood experiments support a demonstrated application, not a claim of widespread industrial adoption or present-day availability.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hot-water ageing of a commercial mineral-wool PUF binder releases soluble phenol/urea/formaldehyde-derived fragments. Ether-like bridges are more hydrolysis-sensitive than methylene bridges; mass spectra also indicate cleavage of urea units to amino-terminated fragments. Cure history changes resistance.

Timescales: The study tested 125–250 µm binder powders, cured at 200 °C for 15 or 60 minutes, in 80 °C water for 3 hours; mineral-wool products were also aged for 7 days at 70 °C and 91% relative humidity. These are chemical and surface-ageing endpoints, not complete mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Moisture can detach binder from mineral fibers and release soluble organic fragments. The study provides no transferable lifetime in soil, freshwater, seawater or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For MICROLITE AA uncured glass-fiber insulation containing PUF binder, Johns Manville calls for mechanical collection of waste without raising dust and disposal at an approved facility. This addresses management of the supplied binder–fiber composite. The safety sheet does not describe separation or chemical recovery of PUF resin from cured insulation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Johns Manville’s MICROLITE AA uncured aerospace insulation provides a formulation-specific example: glass fibers carry a phenol–urea–formaldehyde binder and residual formaldehyde. Its 2021 US/Canadian safety sheet identifies skin sensitization and carcinogenicity hazards for the supplied composite and calls for control of dust, fume and skin contact. These warnings describe the uncured binder-containing insulation, not an intrinsic classification of every cured PUF resin.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Cited plywood and board studies concern particular resin formulations and panel constructions.

sections.overview: Benzoguanamine–formaldehyde resin is an amino-resin material formed from benzoguanamine and formaldehyde and subsequently hardened into a thermoset network. It is used in resin formulations and cured laminates or molding compositions rather than as a single fixed linear polymer.
sections.history: Benzoguanamine–formaldehyde resin was an established amino-resin development platform by the 1950s. Richard Lindenfelser and Martha Kilthau’s American Cyanamid patent, filed in 1954 and issued in 1958, combined the resin with nitrile rubber to improve molding compositions. It documents a formulation advance aimed at overcoming limitations of the unmodified cured resin. Later coating work used benzoguanamine resins as crosslinking components, reflecting a shift between bulk molding and film-forming systems. The 1958 patent establishes a dated commercial research lineage; it does not establish the first synthesis of benzoguanamine or every benzoguanamine–formaldehyde resin.
sections.nomenclature: The name identifies the benzoguanamine/formaldehyde condensation-resin system; BF is used as its abbreviation in this record. A cured network, a paper-impregnated laminate, or a filler- or melamine-containing molding composition is a specified formulation made from that resin system, not an interchangeable name for every benzoguanamine–formaldehyde resin.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Benzoguanamine–formaldehyde (BF) is an amino-resin system made by methylolating benzoguanamine with formaldehyde and advancing the methylol species by condensation; the record is a resin family/network boundary, not one discrete repeat or one cured formulation. Co-condensation with melamine, etherification with an alcohol, or incorporation into a rubber- or paper-containing formulation produces a named variant rather than a synonym for binary BF. A historical filled-molding patent provides a concrete control example: benzoguanamine was first reacted with formaldehyde at about pH 9 and 200 °F for about 5 min to form a water-soluble methylol intermediate, after which melamine was added, magnesium bromide was introduced as a latent catalyst, and phthalic anhydride was added later during milling. The example illustrates pH, aminotriazine/formaldehyde ratio, staged addition, and latent-catalyst control; it is not a present-day specification for every BF resin.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured BF networks are hard, crosslinked amino resins, but their mechanical response is controlled by methylol/etherification state, co-resin content, filler or paper reinforcement, catalyst, moisture, and cure schedule. In a directly measured open study, cellulose paper impregnated with MF in which 10 mol% of the melamine charge was replaced by benzoguanamine gave 1.82 MPa tensile strength, compared with 1.18 MPa for paper impregnated with unmodified MF; the impregnated papers were tested at 1 mm min−1. The study's later high-pressure laminates used a combined PVA/BG-modified MF formulation, so neither result is a neat binary BF-network property. A separate historical patent already mapped to this record reports cured-hardness comparisons for rubber-modified BF molding formulations. These bounded formulation examples support the qualitative hardness/flexibility trade-off but do not establish a transferable tensile or flexural value for binary BF.
sections.processing: BF resin is converted as an aqueous or alcohol-modified syrup, coating/crosslinker, impregnating resin, or filled molding powder. In the historical filled-molding route, a methylol syrup was mixed with alpha-cellulose pulp, dried in a continuous hot-air oven at about 220 °F to below 10% volatile content, advanced to an intermediate state, ball-milled with catalyst and additives, densified, and granulated before molding. A separate open paper-laminate study impregnated cellulose paper with BG-modified MF resin and hot-pressed the laminate after drying. These are bounded examples for filled or paper-reinforced aminoplasts; drying, press temperature/time, catalyst latency, volatile removal, and final cure must be set for the selected BF formulation and article geometry. Network chemistry remains in Synthesis, while syrup handling, impregnation, drying, pressing, and cure belong here.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Benzoguanamine–formaldehyde resins are amino-resin networks derived from benzoguanamine and formaldehyde. Their crosslink density and network structure depend on monomer ratios, cure conditions, and any co-reacted amino resins.
sections.properties: These resins provide hard, crosslinkable thermoset behavior. Thermal and flame-related response depends on formulation, including whether melamine or other components are incorporated.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Alkylated benzoguanamine–formaldehyde derivatives crosslink can/container coatings, electrodeposition coatings and industrial primers.

Purchasing. CYMEL 1123 is a commercial clear-liquid example; its methylated/ethylated formulation is a coating crosslinker rather than an unmodified bulk molding resin.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Benzoguanamine-formaldehyde crosslinkers in coatings can undergo hydrolytic breakdown and migrant release. The thesis distinguishes crosslinker chemistry and curing-dependent release; coating results do not define bulk molded-resin fate.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For unused CYMEL 1123 coating resin, Allnex encourages reuse or recycling where feasible and recommends treatment at an approved thermal-treatment or incineration facility when those options are unavailable. Contaminated packaging is managed with the product, and releases to drains or soil are avoided. This is documented management of resin waste; the safety sheet does not demonstrate recovery of benzoguanamine resin from a cured coating.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The 2023 European safety sheet for CYMEL 1123, a modified benzoguanamine–formaldehyde coating resin, identifies skin sensitization and carcinogenicity hazards for the supplied product, which contains residual formaldehyde. It calls for prevention of skin and eye contact and enclosure or local extraction during spraying and hot curing. These classifications concern the uncured commercial formulation rather than all cured benzoguanamine coatings.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The laminate paper study is a melamine–benzoguanamine–formaldehyde formulation, while the patent concerns a rubber-containing molding composition. Neither establishes universal properties for the binary benzoguanamine–formaldehyde resin family.

sections.overview: Thermoset polyurethane is a crosslinked polyurethane network formed by polyaddition of polyols with di- or polyisocyanates; multifunctional reactants provide the network junctions. Formulation may include water or catalysts, but the cured network—not a single recipe—is the family boundary.
sections.history: Thermoset polyurethanes grew from Otto Bayer and colleagues’ discovery of polyurethane chemistry in 1937. Commercial development required further work on isocyanates, polyols and formulation. Covestro’s historical chronology records flexible polyester-based foam in 1952, protective coatings in 1958, refrigerator insulation in 1962 and metal-faced building panels in 1970. Furniture, vehicle seating and thermal insulation became major outlets, while later developments included integral foams and reinforced composites. These dates describe important products in the Bayer/Covestro lineage; the broad thermoset category includes many networks and should not be assigned a single formulation or commercialization date.
sections.nomenclature: Thermoset PU denotes crosslinked polyurethane materials and distinguishes them from the linear, melt-processable TPU family. The record excludes thermoplastic polyurethane, a particular foam or coating formulation, and an uncured two-component mixture treated as if it were a finished network.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Thermoset polyurethanes are covalent networks formed principally by addition of isocyanate groups to hydroxyl groups. The feedstocks are a di- or polyisocyanate such as methylene diphenyl diisocyanate (MDI) and a polyether, polyester, or other polyol; functionality above two in either component supplies branch points and ultimately gelation. The cited open network study combines an oligoether diol, an oligoether triol, and MDI, with the triol explicitly providing crosslinks. It mixes the alcohol components and then adds a stoichiometric quantity of isocyanate under very dry conditions. Moisture control is important because isocyanate reacts with water to form amine-derived urea linkages and carbon dioxide; that reaction is intentionally exploited in water-blown foams but creates gas and changes network chemistry when a dense casting is intended. A complementary study prepares chemically distinct rigid and soft networks from multifunctional polyester- or polyether-rich polyols and isocyanates and uses dibutyltin dilaurate as a urethane-exchange and network-forming catalyst. One-shot formulations combine the principal reactants together, while prepolymer routes first make an isocyanate-terminated oligomer and then add a multifunctional polyol or chain extender. Tertiary amines and organotin compounds are useful catalyst classes. Polyol backbone, average functionality, NCO/OH index, catalyst, water or physical blowing agent, and any chain extender control segment chemistry, crosslink density, cell formation, and residual groups. This entry concerns the reactants and network-forming chemistry; article-shaping cure schedules and equipment settings belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Thermoset polyurethane spans permanently crosslinked, dense resins and elastomers as well as cellular foams, so it does not have one family-wide stress–strain response. A dense network can be glassy and stiff with low failure strain, or rubbery and highly extensible, depending on whether the test temperature lies below or above its glass-transition and on its segmental architecture. In segmented materials, mobile polyol-derived soft segments supply compliance, while urethane- or urea-rich hydrogen bonding, aromatic units, hard-domain organization, and covalent junctions provide reinforcement and limit creep or permanent set. Foam response additionally depends on cell-wall bending or buckling, a compressive plateau, and densification; density, open- versus closed-cell content, cell anisotropy, skin, and rise direction therefore matter as much as the polymer network. Adhesive and coating results also depend on substrate constraint and interfacial failure.

Consequential formulation variables include polyether versus polyester polyol chemistry, polyol molecular mass and functionality, isocyanate structure and functionality, NCO/OH index, chain extenders and crosslinkers, hard-segment fraction, catalyst level, fillers or fibers, and the resulting crosslink density and phase morphology. Cure temperature, time, post-cure, conversion, mixing, degassing, and void content can change measured response. Water present during cure can consume isocyanate, form urea linkages and carbon dioxide, and alter both network chemistry and porosity; absorbed water later can plasticize polar segments, disrupt hydrogen bonding, and promote chemical ageing. Temperature relative to glass transition, humidity and immersion history, loading rate, cyclic history, specimen orientation, density, and test mode must therefore accompany comparisons. Polyester-rich networks can also be especially sensitive to hydrolytic history.

A composition- and process-bounded illustration comes from Swartz and co-workers' crosslinked polyurethane films. Their rigid network used a multifunctional polyester polyol, 4,4′-methylenediphenyl diisocyanate, and dibutyltin dilaurate at 1.5 mol% relative to carbamate groups; the dried formulation was cast and cured at 90 °C for two days, demolded, and held under vacuum at 90 °C for another two days. For this film the authors reported a glass transition of 64.3 °C, tensile stress of 40 ± 4 MPa, strain at break of 3.6 ± 0.9%, and Young's modulus of 1.6 ± 0.1 GPa. In the same study, a soft crosslinked polyether-polyurethane film had a 10.7 °C glass transition, tensile stress of 2.0 ± 0.1 MPa, strain at break of 430 ± 40%, and Young's modulus of 2.0 ± 0.1 MPa. These two laboratory formulations demonstrate architecture-dependent breadth; the anonymously readable manuscript's summarized tensile comparison does not specify all specimen-geometry and test-rate details, so the values are not family ranges or design allowables.

Moisture sensitivity is likewise network- and protocol-specific. Possart and Zimmer studied a free-standing, amorphous crosslinked polyether polyurethane made from an oligoether diol/triol mixture and MDI, cured for seven days near room temperature and post-cured for seven days at 60 °C. During ageing at 60 °C under controlled relative humidity, absorbed water lowered glass transition by about 17 K at saturation; the saturated network's viscoelastic modulus was approximately half its dry juvenile value, and measured fracture parameters fell by roughly 50% early in exposure. Those results belong to that PU9010 network and its ageing protocol, but they show why moisture content, exposure time, and temperature cannot be omitted from thermoset-polyurethane mechanical data.
sections.processing:
Thermoset polyurethane articles are generally formed by accurately metering and rapidly mixing liquid polyol and isocyanate-side components, then filling or wetting the article before the reacting mixture gels. Important routes include reaction injection molding, open or closed casting and potting, spray application and coating, and formulation-specific foam molding. Component temperature and viscosity, NCO/OH ratio, catalyst and blowing package, mixing intensity, shot size, mold temperature, venting, fill time, pot life, exotherm, and demolding schedule are coupled. Moisture control is especially important because water reacting with isocyanate produces carbon dioxide and urea; unintended gas can create bubbles or disrupt stoichiometry, while controlled gas generation is part of foam processing. Degassing helps dense castings, and thick sections may require staged cure or thermal management. The network-forming chemistry belongs in Synthesis; metering, mixing, mold or substrate delivery, foaming, cure and post-cure schedules, and demolding belong here.

Possart and Zimmer provide a bounded dense-casting example for their PU9010 oligoether network. They stored and prepared the hygroscopic reactants in dry air at 23 °C and 0.07% relative humidity, stirred the diol/triol mixture for 15 min, vacuum-degassed it for 10 min, slowly added stoichiometric MDI while stirring, homogenized for another 15 min, and vacuum-degassed for 15 min to remove dispersed air and traces of carbon dioxide. The batch was cast immediately into PTFE molds, cured for seven days at 23–25 °C, and post-cured for seven days at 60 °C. Those long schedules and dry-glove-box conditions belong to PU9010 and its research objective; fast RIM, sprayed coatings, and foams use different formulations and equipment windows.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Thermoset PU is a covalently crosslinked polyurethane network whose triol function, OH/NCO stoichiometry, and side reactions determine architecture.
sections.properties: Rigid and soft PU networks have formulation-dependent tensile and fracture behavior, including humidity-ageing effects.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Thermoset polyurethane foams cushion furniture, mattresses and vehicle seats; rigid foams insulate buildings and appliances. Cast elastomers also serve mold-making for concrete, gypsum, wax and resin objects.

Purchasing. Manufacturers use matched polyol/isocyanate formulations; finished foams and molded parts are separate product purchases. Smooth-On EZ-Mix40 illustrates a commercial two-liquid mold-rubber system selected by grade.

Scale and evidence limits. The industry association reports approximately 90% of flexible PU foam use in bedding, upholstery and automotive. Its page gives neither reference year nor geographic denominator, so this is qualitative end-use context, not a current tonnage estimate or a share of all thermoset polyurethane. No reliable thermoset-only consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The studied rigid polyurethane foam can be chemically cleaved by glycolysis to a hydroxyl-containing liquid suitable as recycled polyol. This chemical treatment is distinct from environmental biodegradation.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The paper demonstrates catalyst-assisted glycolysis of rigid foam and characterization of recycled polyols. Applicability to a particular crosslinked elastomer or coating requires testing its own network and additives.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: During thermoset polyurethane manufacture or application, unreacted isocyanate ingredients can irritate skin, eyes and airways and cause sensitization or occupational asthma. NIOSH emphasizes enclosure and ventilation to control vapor or aerosol exposure and protection against skin contact. These ingredient hazards concern reactive formulations and cannot be assigned unchanged to a fully cured article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Network studies apply to named polyol/MDI formulations, water control, cure, and ageing state.

sections.overview: Polyisocyanurate (PIR) is a family of isocyanurate-containing materials formed by catalytic cyclotrimerization of isocyanate groups. The trimerized isocyanurate structures can be incorporated into crosslinked foam or resin networks.
sections.history: Polyisocyanurate foams developed within the industrial chemistry of polyisocyanates as manufacturers sought cellular materials with useful thermal and fire behavior. By 1980, Upjohn’s patent literature described PIR foams as already widely used and cited a substantial earlier patent lineage. The 1980 development used esterified residues from dimethyl terephthalate manufacture as a formulation component and addressed the recurring tradeoff between brittleness and combustion behavior. It records an important stage in the engineering of rigid foams, rather than the invention of the isocyanurate group. The source does not establish one first-commercialization date for the entire PIR family.
sections.nomenclature: PIR is a family designation for materials containing isocyanurate structures, not the name of one monomeric isocyanurate or one foam formulation. A polyurethane/polyisocyanurate foam is a specified mixed network in which polyol content, isocyanate index, catalyst, and blowing formulation must remain explicit.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyisocyanurate networks form when organic isocyanates undergo catalyst-promoted cyclotrimerization: three isocyanate groups close into an isocyanurate ring, and di- or higher-functional polyisocyanates connect many rings into a crosslinked network. Rigid PIR foams commonly use MDI-rich polyisocyanates at a high isocyanate index together with a lesser polyol component, so urethane links coexist with the isocyanurate-rich network; blowing agents, water, and surfactants support cellular manufacture but do not define the PIR linkage. Trimerization catalysts include alkali-metal carboxylates, quaternary-ammonium salts, tertiary amines, and related cocatalyst systems. One cited patent prepares isocyanurate polyisocyanates using a quaternary-ammonium salt plus imidazole cocatalyst. A distinct foam patent reacts polyisocyanate with polyol using an alkali-metal or quaternary-ammonium carboxylate trimerization catalyst. These are catalyst and manufacturing examples only; detailed rise, mold, or cure schedules belong to processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyisocyanurate (PIR) mechanics are generally reported for thermoset foams, where apparent density, closed-cell morphology and cell-rise orientation, isocyanate index/trimerization, polyol/blowing-agent formulation, reinforcement, temperature, strain rate, and conditioning control compression response. A 35 kg m−3 closed-cell PIR plate tested as 50 mm cubes at 25 °C and 10 mm min−1 under ASTM D1621-00 showed strong orientation dependence: in its out-of-plane direction, compression modulus was 10.42 MPa, yield stress 0.32 MPa, and plateau stress 0.28 MPa, versus 2.88 MPa, 0.12 MPa, and 0.15 MPa in one in-plane direction. These data describe that foam density, cell structure, direction, and quasi-static compression test—not PIR resin generally.
sections.processing:
Polyisocyanurate (PIR) articles are most often shaped while a reactive foam formulation is being mixed, dispensed, expanded, and cured. Directly documented routes include continuous slabstock blocks, continuously laminated boardstock between facers, free-rise foam, and discontinuous open- or closed-mold molding. A production line meters separate isocyanate, polyol/additive, and blowing-agent streams; conditions them before a high-speed mixing head; lays the foamable mixture onto a moving facer or into a mold; constrains the rise with side belts, an upper facer, a double conveyor, or mold surfaces; and then cures, defaces, cross-cuts, skins, or mills the foam to size. Component temperature, metering ratio, mix energy and duration, cream/rise/gel/tack-free times, laydown uniformity, facer adhesion, conveyor gap and pressure, ventilation, and post-cure govern cell size, closed-cell content, anisotropy, density, surface quality, and dimensional stability. The chemistry that creates the isocyanurate network belongs in Synthesis; component conditioning, mixing, dispensing, rise control, molding, conveyor cure, and post-cure settings belong in Processing.

The Kingspan patent describes one particular continuous PIR-capable slabstock line, not a general PIR window: its polyol-side stream is conditioned to 19–21 °C, its blowing agent to 13–15 °C, the mixing-head blades run at 3,000–7,000 rpm with 5,500 rpm identified as suitable, and the lower and side conveyors travel at about 3–4 m/min. The mixture is deposited on a moving lower facer, rises under an upper facer and weighted mats or pans, cures between conveyors, and is then defaced and sawn. As a distinct laboratory example, Borowicz and co-workers mixed the stated mustard-oil-modified rigid PU/PIR component A and Purocyn B for 10 s at 1,800 rpm, poured the mixture into a 25 × 25 × 30 cm open mold for free rise, and after demolding conditioned the foam for 4 h at 120 °C in a forced-circulation dryer. These values apply only to those disclosed formulations, line, and mold.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyisocyanurate (PIR) materials contain isocyanurate rings created by catalytic cyclotrimerization of isocyanate groups and are commonly realized as crosslinked networks.
sections.properties: Closed-cell PIR foam compression response is anisotropic and varies with foam density, polyol, blowing agent, isocyanate index, trimerization, and catalyst selection.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PIR foam serves building thermal insulation; Celotex CW4000FF is a foil-faced board specifically for cavity walls.

Purchasing. Buyers order finished insulation boards by product, thickness and pack/pallet size, rather than uncured neat polymer.

Scale and evidence limits. For the 90 mm CW4000FF board the checked sheet lists 6 boards/pack (3.2 m²) and 96/pallet (51.4 m²). These are product-area supply units, not resin mass or annual PIR demand; no separate consumption tonnage was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The patent discloses glycolysis of rigid polyurethane/polyisocyanurate foam to polyol-containing mixtures, with unwanted primary aromatic amines requiring subsequent treatment. These are chemical-recycling products; ambient decomposition products remain unresolved.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Patented glycolysis followed by organic-acid treatment makes recovered polyols for new rigid foams. The disclosed route does not establish complete cleavage of every isocyanurate-rich formulation or commercial adoption.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Polyisocyanurate insulation foam remains a combustible cellular-plastic product even when formulated for improved fire performance. HSE’s cellular-plastics guidance emphasizes ignition control, separation of storage from heat-producing operations, and management of smoke and rapid fire spread. These precautions concern storage and fabrication of cellular-plastic products.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Compression data from a 35 kg m−3 foam and formulation-screening studies are not general PIR values; foam direction, density, formulation, and test standard must accompany them.

sections.overview: Polyureas are a family of urea-linkage polymers formed by reacting isocyanate-functional components with amines. The same addition chemistry can produce linear materials or elastomeric networks, depending on the functionality of the reactants and chain extenders.
sections.history: The modern spray-polyurea industry is associated with rapid-reaction elastomer formulation and spray equipment, rather than the first observation of a urea-forming reaction. Dudley Primeaux II’s patent lineage, with priority in 1989 and a United States patent issued in 1996, documents aliphatic spray polyureas developed through Texaco Chemical and Huntsman. This work combined amine-containing components with isocyanates to make sprayed elastomeric materials. Primeaux’s later technical account describes the movement from laboratory development into commercial coating and lining applications. These milestones refer to spray elastomers; other polyurea architectures have separate histories.
sections.nomenclature: PUA is used here for the polyurea family, not for polyurethane or one commercial spray system. A polyurea network made from a quasi-prepolymer, polyoxyalkylene amines, and chain extenders is a defined formulation whose isocyanate and amine components must remain identified.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyureas are formed when isocyanate groups react with primary or secondary amines to create urea linkages. Equimolar diisocyanate and diamine can produce linear thermoplastic chains, while polyisocyanates, polyamines with functionality above two, or branched amine-terminated prepolymers form elastomeric networks. The amine–isocyanate addition is rapid and releases no condensation byproduct, so stoichiometry, component functionality, mixing, and the reactivity of aliphatic versus aromatic partners are central architecture controls. One cited historical patent demonstrates interfacial polyaddition of a lysine-derived diisocyanate in an organic phase with aliphatic or aromatic diamines in an aqueous phase, followed by washing and drying of linear polymer. A distinct spray-elastomer patent uses an aliphatic isocyanate or isocyanate quasi-prepolymer as one component and amine-terminated polyoxyalkylenes plus low-molar-mass polyamine chain extenders as the other. Isocyanate-terminated prepolymers can moderate viscosity and distribute soft segments before final urea network formation. Diisocyanate–water chemistry and diamine–urea condensation are additional family routes, but polyurethane–ureas containing substantial urethane segments should be identified separately. Article-shaping spray settings and cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Engineering polyureas are commonly segmented, crosslinked elastomers with compliant polyether-rich soft domains and strongly hydrogen-bonded urea-rich hard domains. The hard domains act as reinforcing physical crosslinks within the covalent network, so the characteristic response can combine large recoverable deformation, nonlinear viscoelasticity, hysteretic energy dissipation, and strain hardening. It is also strongly time–temperature dependent: raising strain rate or lowering temperature can shift a formulation from rubber-like toward glass-like response, often increasing modulus and stress while reducing failure strain. Quasi-static values alone therefore do not describe blast or impact performance. Hard/soft-segment ratio, isocyanate and amine functionality, hard-domain size and ordering, hydrogen bonding, stoichiometry and conversion, cure time and temperature, mixing or spray-ratio accuracy, moisture-generated defects, fillers or fibers, plasticizers and pigments, coating thickness and substrate constraint, temperature, loading rate, cyclic history, and environmental ageing all matter. Aromatic and aliphatic spray systems, neat elastomers, reinforced formulations, and polyurethane–polyurea hybrids should not be treated as mechanically equivalent.

One bounded commercial example illustrates that formulation specificity. Acharya and co-workers cut approximately 5 mm-thick ASTM D638 die-type-I coupons from sheets of an unreinforced commercial Aro-Struct polyurea (their material S1) and loaded them at 5.08 mm/min. The reported averages were 27.7 MPa 0.2%-offset yield strength, 1903 MPa initial stress–strain slope, 43.4 MPa rupture strength, and 4.09% strain at rupture. Other commercial polyureas in the same study ranged from stiff, low-elongation responses to very compliant, highly extensible responses, and glass-fiber addition increased strength while reducing ductility. The S1 numbers describe that sheet, specimen, and monotonic test—not spray polyurea generally—and dynamic response requires rate-appropriate data.
sections.processing:
Spray polyurea coatings and liners are article-converted by conditioning two reactive components, accurately metering them through heated plural-component airless equipment, impingement-mixing at the spray gun, and building the film in controlled passes while it rapidly gels and cures. Substrates must be sound, clean, dry, profiled, and primed when the product system requires it; substrate temperature relative to dew point, ambient moisture, wind, and contamination govern adhesion, pinholes, and blistering. The component ratio, separate agitation of any filled side, drum and hose temperatures, pressure balance, recirculation and start-up checks, gun chamber condition, spray distance and traverse, pass thickness and overlap, recoat interval, and total film thickness control atomization, mixing, sag, holidays, intercoat adhesion, exotherm, and final cure. Long interruptions require the product's flush, shutdown, and gun-cleaning procedure so partially reacted material does not block the mix chamber. Repair and recoating must respect the stated surface preparation and recoat window, and the coating should not be loaded or exposed until its formulation-specific cure permits it. Network-forming chemistry and raw-component manufacture belong in Synthesis; the metering, spray application, build, and cure schedule that form the installed article belong in Processing.

The numerical settings are product and equipment specific. Fosroc Polyurea WPE110 is a 100%-solids two-component spray system whose guide calls for heated high-pressure plural-component equipment, at least 2000 psi spray pressure, and 55–65 °C material temperature. PPG Versaflex 291 separately specifies 1:1 base-to-hardener metering, agitation of the B side, drum conditioning around 21–38 °C, heated hose and preheater settings around 71–77 °C, and 2000–2500 psi nozzle pressure. Neither window should be generalized to hand-mixed polyurea, another formulation, or a different proportioner and gun.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyureas contain urea linkages from reaction of isocyanate-functional components with amines and may form microphase-separated hard and soft segments or fully crosslinked networks.
sections.properties: Polyurea strength, rate sensitivity, and impact-energy dissipation depend on hard/soft-segment chemistry, reinforcement, and test temperature and strain rate.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polyurea coatings serve concrete/steel waterproofing, wastewater-tank lining, roof protection, marine structures and secondary containment.

Purchasing. Fosroc WPE110 is a two-component spray system supplied through construction-chemicals channels for specialist applicators.

Scale and evidence limits. Its July 2025 Supply table lists Part A in 22.5/225 kg packs and Part B in 21/212 kg packs: tens to hundreds of kilograms per component. The separate Yield table uses inconsistent Part B masses, so confirm the current paired pack; no annual polyurea consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Acetic-anhydride/sulfuric-acid activation followed by alkaline hydrolysis cleaves urea bonds in tested MDI-based linear and crosslinked polyureas. Recovered products include the original polyether or silicone amines and methylenedianiline; these are deliberate chemical-treatment products.

Timescales: Cut LPU-PDMS film (4.5 g) was activated in DMAc with acetic anhydride and sulfuric acid by microwave heating at 100 °C for 20 minutes, followed by aqueous 1 M NaOH/ethanol treatment at 80 °C for 2 hours. This recovery schedule is not an environmental degradation time.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A laboratory process recovers amine monomers and repolymerizes them into polyureas. Both linear and crosslinked formulations were demonstrated, including gram-scale recovery; this does not establish commercial collection or recycling capacity.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: During polyurea manufacture or application, unreacted isocyanate ingredients can irritate skin, eyes and airways and cause sensitization or occupational asthma. NIOSH emphasizes enclosure and ventilation to control vapor or aerosol exposure and protection against skin contact. These ingredient hazards concern reactive formulations and cannot be assigned unchanged to a fully cured article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Commercial and reinforced tensile results are not family constants: isocyanate, amine, prepolymer, reinforcement, cure, geometry, and loading rate must remain identified.

sections.overview: Alkyd resins are oil-modified polyester resin families made from polyols, polybasic acids or anhydrides, and fatty-acid or triglyceride feedstocks. They are commonly used as coating binders, where unsaturated oil segments can support oxidative film drying.
sections.history: Alkyd resins became important coating binders during the interwar expansion of synthetic-resin chemistry. Roy Kienle and Lester Ferguson’s patent application of January 1927, issued in 1930, already used the term alkyd and addressed stable, pigmented coating compositions. It is a concrete early industrial milestone rather than a claim to every precursor polyester reaction. Oil-derived fatty components became central to alkyd paints and varnishes. Later development broadened feedstock choices and sought lower-solvent and more renewable coating systems; the 2023 review by C. Dizman and E. Cerrahoğlu Kaçakgil documents that continuation of an older coating platform.
sections.nomenclature: Alkyd is a family term, not the name of one polyester composition or cured coating. Oil length, oil source, polyol, acid component, and drying or baking formulation distinguish individual alkyd products; a pigment- and additive-containing coating is a formulation made with an alkyd binder, not a synonym for the resin family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Alkyds are oil-modified polyester resin families made from polyols, polybasic acids or anhydrides, and fatty acids or triglyceride oils. Glycerol or pentaerythritol, phthalic anhydride, and drying or semidrying oils are common examples, but their proportions establish distinct short-, medium-, and long-oil resins. Two established route families are alcoholysis/polyesterification through a monoglyceride intermediate and one-pot fatty-acid esterification; in the latter, fatty acid, dibasic acid, and polyol are esterified together at elevated temperature. PET-derived polyols and other bio-based substitutions are route variants, not a definition of all alkyds.
sections.mechanicalProperties: For alkyds, useful mechanical response is normally that of the cured coating film—hardness, adhesion, flexibility, abrasion resistance, and durability—rather than a universal bulk tensile value. Oil length, unsaturation, functionality, molecular mass, pigment/additive package, substrate, and cure all matter. As a bounded formulation example summarized in the bio-based-alkyd review, tung-oil/phthalic-anhydride alkyds containing 0–30 wt% isobornyl acrylate gave reported breaking tensile strengths of 6.13–10.89 MPa and pencil hardness from H to 3H. Those values concern those acrylated, cured coating formulations and cannot rank all alkyd resins.
sections.processing: Alkyds are formulated into coatings and converted by application, solvent or water removal, and oxidative or baking cure. Oil chemistry determines whether air drying is feasible: the review distinguishes oil-length classes and reports that unsaturation changes drying behavior. After resin manufacture, a particular coating's solids, drier package, substrate, film thickness, and cure schedule set film formation. These downstream variables are distinct from the elevated-temperature polyesterification used to make the binder and must be reported for the named formulation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Alkyd resins are branched polyesters derived from polyols, polyacids or anhydrides, and fatty-acid or oil components. Oil length and functionality influence branching and oxidative-curing behavior.
sections.properties: Alkyd resins are film-forming coating binders whose viscosity, drying, hardness, and durability depend on oil type, oil length, formulation, and curing environment.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Alkyds are paint binders; the short-oil ISALKYD SO 203 X-60 example serves industrial, fast-drying and hammer-finish coatings.

Purchasing. Isatis offers the resin through quotation in steel drums of 180 or 190 kg net.

Scale and evidence limits. The grade is listed at 60 ± 1 wt% solids, so drum mass includes solvent. The documented supply unit is hundreds of kilograms of resin solution; no independent annual alkyd consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A patented process hydrolyzes ester crosslinks in selected infusible alkyds to a mixture of acid/alcohol-terminated oligomers and monomers. The examples concern glycerol–maleate material; they do not define the product mixture from every oil-modified coating.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Water-assisted reactive extrusion followed by water removal and recondensation is a patented route to reshape selected alkyd networks. General applicability to oxidatively crosslinked paints, additives and mixed coating waste remains to be demonstrated.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Alkyd manufacture requires assessment of reactive feedstocks separately from the cured coating. A review identifies phthalic anhydride, a common alkyd monomer, as an eye, skin and respiratory irritant during occupational exposure; maleic anhydride also presents contact and eye hazards. These starting-material concerns are not intrinsic hazard classifications of the completed alkyd film.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited review surveys vegetable-oil-derived alkyd formulations, while the PET-recycling review treats particular synthesis routes; composition and curing differences prevent generalizing one reported coating response to all alkyd resins.
