sections.overview: Silicone resins are organopolysiloxane resin families that cure into crosslinked networks. Their siloxane backbone distinguishes them from carbon-backbone thermosetting resins, while organosilicon substituents and functionality control cure and properties.
sections.history: Silicone resins emerged from early-twentieth-century organosilicon work by F. S. Kipping and the industrial precursor chemistry independently developed by Eugene Rochow and Richard Müller in 1940. A documented resin-production lineage is Wacker’s: its first silicone pilot plant and development of fluids and resins date to 1950. The company subsequently expanded into protective treatments and introduced combination resins for coatings in 1960. These are milestones for the resin branch of silicone technology; silicone rubber and silicone fluids followed related but distinct application paths.
sections.nomenclature: Silicone resin and polysiloxane resin are broad family descriptors. “SI resin” is an informal shortened label; particular silicone-elastomer and silicone-fluid materials are not automatically synonyms for this crosslinkable resin family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Silicone resins are branched or network-forming organopolysiloxanes prepared by hydrolysis and condensation of hydrolyzable silanes. Multifunctional feeds such as methyl- or phenyltrichlorosilane and trialkoxysilanes create T units; silicon tetrachloride or tetraalkyl silicates can supply Q units, while difunctional diorganosilanes introduce D units and monofunctional species can cap the structure. Water converts Si–Cl or Si–OR groups to silanols, releasing hydrogen chloride or alcohol, and silanol condensation then forms Si–O–Si bonds with water loss. Organic-group identity, average organic-group-to-silicon ratio, T/D/Q proportions, water availability, pH, catalyst, and extent of precondensation control branching, residual silanol or alkoxy functionality, solubility, and gelation. One cited patent co-hydrolyzes methyl/phenyl di- and trichlorosilanes and regulates further condensation to a selected hydroxyl content. A distinct patent hydrolyzes trialkoxysilanes and stabilizes the partially condensed resin with a weak organic base before final thermosetting condensation. The isolated soluble partial condensate is the resin precursor; subsequent condensation completes the network. Coating-specific bake profiles and shaping conditions remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cured silicone resins are crosslinked polysiloxane networks, mechanically distinct from lightly crosslinked silicone rubbers. Depending on the proportions and arrangement of linear, cyclic, branched, and cage-like siloxane units, they can range from flexible coating films to hard, glass-like and brittle networks. A controlled hydrosilylation study of cyclic, linear, and tetrakis siloxane formulations showed that cyclic-rich, highly crosslinked networks were rigid and inherently brittle, whereas longer linear segments increased chain mobility and flexibility; the most flexible formulations were too soft for that study's three-point-bend DMA specimens. Thus “silicone resin” does not imply one modulus or toughness.

Important variables include methyl-versus-phenyl substitution, M/D/T/Q-unit architecture, reactive-group functionality and stoichiometry, molecular weight between junctions, degree and uniformity of cure, and the cure catalyst, temperature, and time. Pigments, mineral or fiber reinforcement, plasticizing linear siloxane, residual solvent, coating thickness, substrate adhesion, defects, service temperature, and thermal or moisture exposure can dominate a finished article's hardness, bending, impact, and crack response. As one tightly bounded coating example, Momentive's methylphenyl TSR117 solution was applied as a 30–40 µm film to SPC-1 steel and cured for 1 h: increasing cure temperature from 150 to 250 °C changed the reported Sward-rocker hardness from 34 to 50 and the Erichsen indication from 2 to 8 mm. Under the bulletin's 300 g, 0.5-inch-diameter drop-weight impact from 40 cm, the 150 °C film cracked while the 250 °C film showed no change; both passed bending over a 3 mm mandrel. Those values describe that named resin, film/substrate construction, and cure schedule, not neat bulk silicone resin or the family as a whole.
sections.processing:
The directly documented article-conversion routes in this pass are solvent-borne coating and electrical impregnation. A silicone-resin varnish or filled coating is first brought to a uniform, application-ready state, then applied by immersion, brush, roller, or spray as permitted by the named formulation. Substrate cleanliness, coating viscosity, filler or pigment redispersion, entrained air, wet-film control, drainage, flash-off, ventilation, recoating interval, and the ramp into a thermal cure all affect coverage and defect formation. Oil, dirt, oxide, or residual moisture can impair adhesion; thick or rapidly heated films can retain solvent or evolve gas during cure. Filled products therefore require thorough remixing without unnecessary air incorporation, while solvent-bearing systems require ventilation and enough air set or flash time before heating. Coated parts are held and cooled according to the selected product procedure before handling or service. The precursor reactions that create a silicone resin belong in Synthesis; surface preparation, formulation remixing or catalyst addition, application, solvent removal, article cure, and cooling belong in Processing. These documents do not establish a universal silicone-resin molding or casting window.

Momentive's TSR117 electrical-insulation example is a named methylphenyl silicone varnish procedure, not a family-wide schedule. It removes dust and oil, pre-bakes the substrate for several hours at 80–150 °C, cools it to 50 °C or below before immersion, drains excess varnish, air-dries for several hours, and gradually bakes at 80–120 °C for several hours before a second immersion and bake. The same bulletin also reports cured test films only 30–40 µm thick, illustrating why its coating and cure conditions should remain tied to TSR117, the stated substrate, and the specified film preparation.

Aremco's CP4000-S1 sheet gives a separate filled, pigmented high-temperature coating workflow. It calls for removing oil, dirt, and oxide, abrasive blasting where appropriate, and thorough mixing to redisperse settled filler and pigment. Brush, roller, or spray application is permitted; the sheet limits dry thickness to about 2–3 mil using two coats and gives, for spray application, a 40–50 mil nozzle, 40–50 psi atomizing pressure, and an 8–10 inch stand-off. For this product family, the stated application range is 50–120 °F, dry-to-touch time is 1–2 h, handling time is 2–4 h, and recoating is allowed after 1–24 h. CP4000 uses at least a one-hour air set followed by 480 °F for 0.75 h. The CP4000-S1-HT variant instead has a product-specific sequence of 200 °F for 0.25 h, 480 °F for 0.25 h, and 1200 °F for 0.25 h. The sheet warns of outgassing during cure, reinforcing the need for ventilation and controlled heating. All dimensions, pressures, times, and temperatures here are supplier guidance for the cited formulations rather than a general silicone-resin window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Silicone resins are crosslinkable organopolysiloxane networks with variable functionality.
sections.properties: Network structure and substituents determine thermal, electrical, and coating behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Silicone resins bind protective coatings for boilers, exhausts, kilns, heat exchangers and process vessels; filled molding compounds also serve electrical components.

Purchasing. Aremco supplies single-part, heat-curable solvent-based Corr-Paint coatings. Sumitomo Bakelite lists reinforced silicone molding compounds, a distinct purchased product form.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked sources document formulated industrial products but no separately verified silicone-resin purchase or consumption tonnage. Coating/compound mass would include solvent or fillers and cannot be counted directly as neat resin.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Silicone resins are explicitly within a patent’s catalytic-depolymerization scope, producing cyclic siloxanes and residue. This broad disclosure does not establish yields for every T/Q-rich resin.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The disclosed process combines catalytic heating, volatile-siloxane recovery and residue processing. Its patent scope is broader than the demonstrated feedstocks; commercial applicability requires formulation-specific qualification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Aremco’s CP4000-S1 silicone-resin coating instructions call for ventilation during application and curing because the coating outgasses. Handling therefore needs to consider the complete coating formulation and its cure emissions, alongside the eventual silicone network. The supplier’s instruction concerns this solvent-borne protective-coating system and is not a hazard classification for all silicone resins.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Supplier coating data concern specific resin products.

sections.overview: Bismaleimide (BMI) resins are high-temperature thermoset resin families based on molecules bearing two maleimide groups. They cure by reactions of the maleimide unsaturation to produce crosslinked networks; modifiers are often used to tune brittleness and flow.
sections.history: Bismaleimide thermosets were developed during the 1960s search for heat-resistant addition-cured polymers. Friedrich Grundschober and Joerg Sambeth’s patent for Rhodiaceta, claiming Swiss priority in 1964 and issued in 1968, describes crosslinked materials made from bis-imides, including maleimides. The work demonstrates curing of low-molecular precursors into insoluble polymers and represents an early industrial foundation for BMI resin technology. Its importance was the combination of imide chemistry with an addition-curing route. The patent documents a particular research lineage; it does not establish the first synthesis of every bismaleimide monomer or the launch of every later composite grade.
sections.nomenclature: BMI is a family name, not the name of one dimaleimide monomer or one cured network. A diamine-, allyl-, filler-, or reinforcement-modified BMI is a distinct formulation whose modifier and cure state must be named rather than treated as neat BMI.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Bismaleimide (BMI) denotes a family of thermoset resin formulations built from difunctional maleimides, commonly 4,4′-bismaleimidodiphenylmethane (BDM), optionally combined with allyl-bisphenol-A, diamines, or other modifiers. Maleimide double bonds undergo addition/self-polymerization and co-reaction to form a network without the small-molecule by-product characteristic of condensation cure. In an open BDM/modified-BMI study, BDM and an allyl bisphenol-A component were blended at 130 °C to form a prepolymer before final cure; in a separate diamine-modified study, BMI was preheated at 80 °C and reacted with a diamine by Michael addition. These examples show that monomer architecture, modifier ratio, prepolymerization, and cure schedule are part of the specific BMI formulation, not universal family settings.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured BMI networks are generally stiff and heat-resistant but can be brittle because of high crosslink density. A branched-diamine study measured flexural strength of 83.9 MPa for its unmodified BMI control and 189.9 MPa for the ODA-modified system; specimens were 100 × 10 × 5 mm and tested at 10 mm min−1, so the values are bounded to those formulations and test conditions. A separate BDM/DABPA/BMIX/SiC study reported 109.52 MPa flexural strength before high-temperature treatment for its maximum-performing composite, which contained 27.5 vol% resin and was molded to 2.31 g cm−3; its three-point-bend specimens were 30 × 6 × 6 mm and loaded at 0.05 mm s−1. Flexible bridges, allyl co-reactants, and fillers can change crack dissipation and stiffness, but these results must not be combined into a single BMI-family property range.
sections.processing: BMI formulations are commonly preblended or melt-mixed, degassed or dried as needed, shaped by compression, transfer, or composite molding, and cured in stages as viscosity and conversion evolve. One open diamine-modified BMI study used 80 °C preheating and then a four-stage cure of 150 °C for 1 h, 180 °C for 2 h, 200 °C for 2 h, and 220 °C for 1 h. A BDM/allyl/modified-BMI/SiC composite route prepolymerized at 130 °C, cooled, dried, crushed, sieved, mixed with SiC and wetting agent, then cold-pressed and cured. These schedules are formulation- and equipment-specific; the cure profile must be validated against resin flow, exotherm, filler loading, void content, and the target glass transition.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Bismaleimide resins cure from multifunctional maleimide monomers into crosslinked thermoset networks. Branching and monomer architecture determine network density and the balance of thermal, electrical, and mechanical behavior.
sections.properties: BMI resins are high-temperature thermosets with property profiles that depend on the bismaleimide structure, cure schedule, reinforcement, and other formulation components.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Bismaleimides serve advanced composite structures and high-performance structural adhesives.

Purchasing. Huntsman lists solid MATRIMID 5292 A, with 5292 B as a formulation partner. This is a resin-component purchase, not a ready-made composite.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Specially designed disulfide-containing bismaleimide networks can be disassembled by thiol exchange into soluble fragments, with a polyaryletherketone additive recovered as a solid. This is evidence for a modified BMI formulation, not the degradation-product inventory of conventional BMI.

Timescales: For 120–130 mg blocks of the four modified resins, disappearance took 14–22 minutes in 10 mL DMF/beta-mercaptoethanol (2:1 by volume) at 120 °C with stirring. Disappearance into solution is not mineralization.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent demonstrates hot pressing of crushed dynamic BMI resin and chemical disassembly using DMF/beta-mercaptoethanol. These are formulation-specific patented laboratory methods; ordinary permanently crosslinked BMI requires separate evidence.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The MATRIMID 5292 A-2 bismaleimide component is supplied as a powder. Huntsman’s safety sheet identifies inhalation toxicity and combustible-dust hazards and notes that airborne powder can irritate eyes, skin and airways. Avoid dust accumulation, ignition sources and inhalation during handling. These precautions concern the uncured diphenylmethane-bismaleimide component rather than a completed composite.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited work compares BMI resins with different branched structures, so measured responses apply to those specified networks and curing conditions rather than all BMI formulations.

sections.overview: Cyanate ester resin is a thermosetting resin family based on cyanate ester monomers that cure into crosslinked networks. Network structure and cure conditions are important determinants of the resulting material properties.
sections.history: An important precursor to cyanate-ester resin technology was Grigat and Pütter’s 1963 preparation of cyanate esters from phenols, as summarized in the later manufacturing patent. Subsequent development converted these reactive precursors into thermoset systems. By 1990, Jack Boyd, Hermann Sitt, Hong-Son Ryang and Theodore Biermann’s BASF patent targeted radar-transparent structures using cyanate-containing matrices, adhesives and foams. That application illustrates why electrical behavior as well as temperature resistance shaped the family’s development. Later manufacturing work sought more controlled resin composition. These milestones distinguish monomer synthesis, formulated composite uses and production improvements.
sections.nomenclature: “Cyanate ester resin” refers to the resin family and its cured-network materials, while a cyanate ester monomer is a precursor rather than the same material state. “CE resin” is ambiguous in polymer contexts and should be used only with the full name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cyanate ester resins are thermoset precursors whose reactive groups are aryl cyanate ester (–OCN) functionalities. Polyfunctional phenolic feedstocks—including bisphenols, dihydroxy aromatics, phenol novolacs, and cresol-derived novolacs—can be converted to di- or polycyanate esters with cyanogen chloride or cyanogen bromide. These cyanate-functional monomers may be partly advanced to prepolymers with heat, with or without a catalyst. During network formation, polyfunctional cyanate esters cyclotrimerize to sym-triazine links; catalyst choice and monomer functionality affect the network, but an article-shaping cure schedule is outside this synthesis account. A continuous patent example uses a phenolic organic compound, triethylamine, and cyanogen halide in an inert solvent at low temperature, followed by quench; it specifically names novolac phenolic resin as a feedstock. A separate patent establishes the broader phenolic/cyanogen-halide precursor family and phenol/cresol novolacs as suitable starting structures.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cyanate ester resins cure by cyclotrimerization of cyanate groups to triazine-linked three-dimensional networks. Mechanical response therefore depends strongly on monomer architecture, prepolymer state, catalyst and cure/post-cure schedule, crosslink-network regularity, and any toughener or reinforcement; blend and laminate values should not be substituted for a neat homopolymer. An open BADCy (bisphenol-A dicyanate) study found that adding reactive BADCy microparticles altered the network and increased tensile, flexural, compressive, and impact values relative to its neat cured matrix, directly illustrating this formulation dependence.

A bounded neat-resin example from that study is the cured BADCy matrix: tensile strength 32.4 MPa and modulus 2.7 GPa; flexural strength 70.3 MPa and modulus 2.9 GPa; compressive strength 124.6 MPa and modulus 2.6 GPa; and impact strength 7.41 kJ m−2. Specimens were tested on an Instron 1121 according to GB/T 2567–2008 after a 180 °C/2 h + 200 °C/2 h + 220 °C/2 h cure. These values are for that bisphenol-A dicyanate formulation and schedule, not cyanate esters generally. As a separate commercial homopolymer comparison, Mitsubishi Gas Chemical lists CYTESTER TA flexural strength 136 MPa and flexural modulus 2.8 GPa by ASTM D790 after 150 °C/3 h + 180 °C/5 h + 250 °C/3 h; the manufacturer explicitly marks the data typical and not guaranteed.
sections.processing:
Cyanate-ester matrices are converted as neat resins, adhesives, or fiber prepregs. Depending on the formulated system and part, composite consolidation may use an autoclave, heated press or pressclave, or an oven/vacuum-bag cycle; automated fiber placement can lay narrow prepreg tapes before consolidation. Moisture control before cure is important: Toray's BTCy guidance calls for sealed frozen storage below −12 °C, warming in the sealed bag before opening to avoid condensation, clean lay-up, and drying moisture-bearing core materials before assembly. It also warns that vacuum-bag/oven processing can leave voids that darken during post-cure, so pressure-assisted consolidation is preferred where optimum laminate quality is required.

A bounded research example used a phenol-novolac cyanate ester toughened with 15 phr polyethersulfone in 0.06 mm T800S carbon-fiber prepreg. Tapes were placed by automated fiber placement and autoclave-cured by heating at 2 °C/min to 120 °C for 2 h under 5 bar, then at 2 °C/min to 180 °C for 2 h, cooling at 1 °C/min, and finally post-curing in an oven at 260 °C for 2 h. That schedule belongs to the reported CE–PES prepreg and is not a universal cyanate-ester cure cycle; formulation, laminate thickness, tooling, and exotherm control require their own qualified cycle.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cyanate ester resins are cyanate-functional precursors that cure to triazine-linked thermoset networks; monomer functionality and prepolymer advancement define a particular resin system.
sections.properties: Mechanical and thermal response belongs to the specified cured network and can change with microparticles, thermoplastic modifiers, reinforcement, and cure schedule.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Cyanate esters serve high-frequency printed wiring boards, thermally conductive materials, structural FRP and adhesives.

Purchasing. MGC offers CYTESTER TA as a standard solid grade and identifies prepolymer and liquid variants as R&D grades; supplier inquiry determines availability and quantities.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cured cyanate esters first undergo chain scission and further crosslinking on strong heating, followed by breakdown of cyanurate rings. Pyrolysis experiments found cyanate-containing volatiles, substituted benzenes, phenols, methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide, together with nitrogen/oxygen-containing char. Substituents change the product distribution.

Timescales: For nine cured polycyanurates, nitrogen TGA at 10 °C/min showed major mass loss near 450 °C. This heating-rate-dependent decomposition endpoint is not an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The experiment establishes high-temperature breakdown and a substantial carbonaceous residue. It does not establish complete biodegradation or a soil, marine or landfill mineralization time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Chemical recycling has been demonstrated for cured cyanate-ester networks. Dreyer and coworkers decomposed bisphenol-A, bisphenol-E and novolac polycyanurates with reactive liquid agents, producing phenolic and triazine-containing material. Resin composition, agent and temperature strongly affected dissolution; this is controlled chemical treatment, not environmental degradation. The recovered hydroxyl-containing mixture was incorporated into new polyurethane foams and solid thermosets. Tests on reinforcement fibers found comparatively small effects on carbon and glass fibers, while aramid and flax compatibility depended on the treatment. The study establishes laboratory recovery and reuse options rather than a universal process for every cyanate-ester composite.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Huntsman’s AROCY L 10 safety sheet describes a bisphenol-E dicyanate precursor that is harmful if inhaled or swallowed and can seriously damage eyes. It also warns of organ effects after repeated exposure and aquatic toxicity. Control vapor or mist, protect against splashes and contain spills. These precursor hazards must be distinguished from those of a cured polycyanurate composite.

sections.overview: Polybenzoxazines are thermosetting polymer families obtained by ring-opening polymerization of benzoxazine monomers. Monomer structure and curing conditions govern the resulting crosslinked network.
sections.history: Polybenzoxazines developed from benzoxazine monomer chemistry into a practical thermoset platform through work on synthesis and ring-opening cure. Hatsuo Ishida’s solventless synthesis patent, filed in 1994 and issued in 1996 through Edison Polymer Innovation, is an important documented milestone. It sought a practical route from phenols, amines and formaldehyde-containing reactants. Anthony Gallo’s later Henkel Loctite patent, filed in 1999 and issued in 2002, addressed preparation and cure of polybenzoxazine molding and coating compositions. This sequence records the movement toward usable resin systems; it should not be taken as the date of the earliest small-molecule benzoxazine synthesis.
sections.nomenclature: PBZ is used for polybenzoxazine, while benzoxazine resin commonly refers to the precursor or cured resin system. The abbreviation can be ambiguous, so the full name is preferred where other polymer abbreviations are present.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polybenzoxazines are thermosetting networks formed by ring-opening polymerization of benzoxazine monomers. The monomers are commonly prepared by Mannich-type condensation of a phenolic compound, a primary amine, and formaldehyde; using a bisphenol or multifunctional amine creates more than one benzoxazine ring and enables network formation. Heating can open the oxazine rings without release of a volatile condensation byproduct, while acids or cationic initiators can lower or alter the polymerization pathway. One cited patent prepares monomers from phenol or bisphenol A, formaldehyde, and aniline/methylamine and uses a heterocyclic dicarboxylic-acid catalyst for thermal ring opening. A distinct patent compares conventional thermal polymerization with cationically initiated ring-opening routes for bisphenol-A/aniline benzoxazine. The monomer structure and functionality set network architecture; article-specific cure schedules and molding operations remain processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polybenzoxazine denotes thermally ring-opened benzoxazine networks, not a single neat thermoplastic. Cured networks are commonly stiff and low-elongation, but their strength, modulus, fracture/impact behavior, and stress relaxation depend on phenol/amine monomer structure, functionality and cross-link density, cure schedule and post-cure, flexible segments or reactive diluents, tougheners, fillers/fibers, residual porosity, moisture, and temperature relative to the network transition. Thus a cured casting, adhesive, composite laminate, and reprocessable vitrimer must be kept distinct. In one bio-based cross-linked main-chain benzoxazine series, the composition poly(Dz-0.3d600-1.4f) gave 54.7 ± 5.1 MPa tensile strength, 1,620 ± 32 MPa Young modulus, and 3.9 ± 0.5% tensile strain, while increasing furan-derived crosslinking points raised storage modulus and reduced tensile strain. The article does not report tensile specimen geometry, loading rate, or conditioning in the cited table, so these are composition- and cure-specific network results. An independent monobenzoxazine study shows that aromatic substitution can shift 25 °C storage modulus from 1.67 to 3.41 GPa and change calculated cross-link density substantially; those DMA values are not direct tensile moduli but support the network-structure dependence.
sections.processing: Polybenzoxazine is converted as a thermoset resin: a benzoxazine formulation is degassed or cast, heated through ring-opening and network formation, and optionally post-cured. In an open bio-based polybenzoxazine study, the liquid formulations remained relatively low-viscosity from 100–150 °C but gelled rapidly above 150 °C; composition-dependent gelation temperatures were 167–176 °C, isothermal gel points at 150 °C were 12.8–37.6 min, and a 200 °C, 2 h treatment removed the residual curing exotherm for the cited formulation. A separate open study thermally treated substituted monobenzoxazines under vacuum for 5 h and found polymerization-onset temperatures spanning about 226–271 °C across substituent structures. These values belong to the named molecular formulations and heating programs; viscosity, catalyst or substituent effects, degassing, mold geometry, and cure exotherm must be re-established for each benzoxazine resin.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polybenzoxazines are thermoset networks formed by ring-opening polymerization of benzoxazine monomers. The monomer's phenolic, amine, and benzoxazine structures generate phenolic and amine-rich crosslinked networks without requiring a separate curing agent in many formulations.
sections.properties: Cured polybenzoxazines can provide high glass-transition temperature, low water uptake, low cure shrinkage, flame resistance, and useful chemical and dielectric stability. Network structure and substituent choice tune toughness, thermal expansion, and cure behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Benzoxazine systems have documented aerospace prepreg/tooling, automotive composite, oil-and-gas vessel and printed-wiring-board laminate applications.

Purchasing. Huntsman’s historical product announcement identifies XU 35610 and XU 35910 formulated resins and XU 35500 reactive diluent. Current grades and availability require supplier confirmation.

Scale and evidence limits. The announcement reports an intended manufacturing expansion but supplies no tonnage. No reliable separate annual production, consumption or purchasing volume was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A sulfur-modified polybenzoxazine example undergoes sulfur–sulfur bond cleavage and reformation on heating. Spectroscopy retained the main network components after recycling, while mechanical changes indicated altered crosslinking; this is network rearrangement, not monomer recovery.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Chopping and thermal remolding was demonstrated for a specific 40/40/20 wt% poly(propylene oxide)-benzoxazine/diallylbenzoxazine/sulfur formulation. Repeated cycles changed toughness. This laboratory strategy depends on deliberately installed dynamic bonds and cannot be assumed for conventional polybenzoxazines.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Heated polybenzoxazine processing calls for control of fume and adherence to formulation-specific temperature and dwell-time guidance. HSE recommends ventilation and assessment of additives and degradation products. This process guidance does not assign a universal toxicity classification to the polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polybenzoxazine precursors can be viscous solids or liquids and often require elevated cure temperatures. Monomer substitution, catalyst, blend, filler, cure schedule, post-cure, voids, and network conversion strongly affect properties; a cured formulation is not a universal family representative.

sections.overview: Phthalonitrile resin is a high-performance thermosetting-resin family derived from phthalonitrile monomers or oligomers. Thermal curing produces crosslinked networks, and monomer architecture strongly affects the resulting resin.
sections.history: Phthalonitrile thermoset development has a prominent United States Naval Research Laboratory lineage. A documented commercialization milestone came in May 2015, when NRL announced licenses for its second-generation PEEK-like phthalonitrile compositions. Teddy Keller, Matthew Laskoski and Andrew Saab were the inventors of the licensed technology. The intended uses included high-temperature, flame-resistant composites for military and civilian equipment. The announcement describes a later generation of an existing resin technology, not its first synthesis. It shows how government materials research moved toward commercial manufacture while addressing the practical combination of heat resistance, moisture behavior and composite processing.
sections.nomenclature: Phthalonitrile resin describes the cured-resin family; “PN resin” is a shortened label that should be expanded where ambiguity is possible. The term does not identify any single phthalonitrile monomer or formulation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis:
Phthalonitrile resin systems begin with aromatic phthalonitrile monomers or oligomers bearing reactive nitrile termini, frequently prepared by nucleophilic aromatic substitution of a bisphenolic or aromatic-ether precursor with nitro- or halophthalonitrile. The uncured oligomer/prepolymer is not yet the crosslinked high-temperature network. A documented aryl-ether route first reacts a bisdihydroxyaryl compound with dihalobenzophenone or a related dihalide under base, then end-caps the oligomer with nitro- or halophthalonitrile. Another source describes low-melting oligomeric phthalonitriles and curing additives that react through the cyano groups. Amine, metal-salt, acid, and other nucleophilic additives can initiate network formation, but particular cure cycles and composite fabrication conditions are deliberately omitted.

Cure mechanism: Precursor synthesis and nitrile-network formation are separate chemical stages. In a mechanistic study of the amino-functional phthalonitrile 4-APN, Sheng and coworkers proposed initial amine addition to a nitrile followed by cyclization involving a neighboring nitrile, generating isoindole/imine intermediates that can react further. The cured material contains several nitrogen-containing ring environments, rather than a single uniform repeat unit. Their evolved-gas measurements detected ammonia during 4-APN cure; the proposed mechanism includes ammonia-forming pathways alongside nitrile addition and cyclization. Thus a gas-free cure should not be assumed for every amino-promoted phthalonitrile formulation. Their comparison with 1,3-diiminoisoindoline demonstrates that the catalyst changes cure behavior and void formation; it does not establish one universal pathway or cure schedule for all phthalonitrile resins.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Phthalonitrile resins are high-temperature crosslinked networks whose stiffness, strength, and brittleness depend strongly on monomer/cure-agent chemistry, modifier content, cure/post-cure schedule, oxygen exposure, and whether the test is neat resin or fiber composite. A recent open review describes multistep cures typically spanning about 180–375 °C, with heating rate and post-cure determining the final network; results from different formulations must therefore not be pooled. A bounded neat-thermoset example is a phosphate-bridged phthalonitrile series: PN10 (10% phosphate-containing monomer) had flexural strength 141.8 ± 0.8 MPa and modulus 4.3 ± 0.1 GPa, while the related PN50 formulation had 140.0 ± 4.4 MPa and 4.7 ± 0.1 GPa. After 200 h oxidative aging at 300 °C, the reported PN10 strength was 121.6 ± 7.6 MPa; this is a formulation- and aging-specific flexural result, not a universal phthalonitrile value.
sections.processing: Phthalonitrile resins are high-temperature thermoset precursors: low-melting oligomer or monomer formulations are compounded with any cure promoter, degassed, impregnated into fiber preforms or otherwise shaped, and then cured in staged heating cycles. Resin viscosity, melt point, catalyst/additive package, fiber architecture, and tooling determine whether casting, compression molding, prepreg, resin-transfer molding, or vacuum-assisted infusion is practical. The usual constraint is a slow, multi-step cure that preserves flow and avoids voids before the high-temperature network-forming stage; post-cure is often needed to reach the target thermal state. A recent furan-derived study explicitly frames low-melting phthalonitrile resins as a processability strategy and evaluates their curing into high-performance thermosets; its temperatures and cure behavior apply to the named diimine-linked formulations. A separate review describes the common commercial pattern of an initial tooling cure around 180–200 °C followed by a higher-temperature 280–375 °C cure/post-cure, with slow heating used to limit softening, distortion, and trapped volatiles. These are formulation-specific thermoset schedules, not a universal phthalonitrile window. Monomer synthesis and oligomer preparation belong in Synthesis; this section covers resin handling, shaping, degassing, impregnation, cure, and post-cure.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Phthalonitrile resins cure from nitrile-functional monomers or oligomers into highly crosslinked aromatic networks.
sections.properties: Thermal-oxidative stability and mechanics depend on monomer structure, cure additives, and cure schedule.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Supplier-documented phthalonitrile applications include near-engine aerospace parts, thermal-protection structures, marine components and heat-resistant sandwich panels.

Purchasing. Azista lists a one-part infusion/RTM resin, hot-melt prepregs and towpregs, and a foam-core grade. These are distinct formulated product forms.

Scale and evidence limits. The supplier documents proposed/specified application fields, but not installed fleet quantities or sales tonnage. No reliable separate annual PN purchase or consumption figure was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The resorcinol-based phthalonitrile example undergoes high-temperature oxidative mass loss; alumina addition changes its thermal stability. The experiment does not identify a complete inventory of environmental breakdown molecules.

Timescales: The paper uses a 10 °C/min thermogravimetric ramp in air; a ramp-decomposition temperature is not an environmental residence time.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: A study of 4-APN phthalonitrile chemistry identified ammonia during thermal cure and precursor volatilization in heated, high-vacuum measurements. Cure-emission assessment therefore needs to consider the catalyst and processing conditions; the results are not a gas inventory for every phthalonitrile resin. HSE plastics-processing guidance supports ventilation to control hot-process emissions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited reviews compare specific bio-based and phosphate-bridged resins, not all phthalonitrile networks.

sections.overview: Poly(furfuryl alcohol) resin is a furan-based thermosetting resin formed by acid-catalyzed polymerization of furfuryl alcohol. Polymerization involves a complex mixture of ring-opening and coupling reactions rather than one simple linear repeat structure.
sections.history: Poly(furfuryl alcohol) resin was an established industrial research subject by the early 1950s. Quaker Oats’ patent filed in 1950 and issued in 1952 describes furfuryl-alcohol resin production, linking the material to the company’s industrial furan-chemicals business. The work concerns controlled resinification and useful resin products rather than discovery of the alcohol monomer. It illustrates the practical difficulty that shaped the field: controlling a readily polymerizing feedstock so that it could be manufactured and handled before final cure. The patent provides a dated production milestone, while the earliest resin observations and the full sequence of foundry-market introductions remain outside this account.
sections.nomenclature: PFA is sometimes used for poly(furfuryl alcohol), but it is ambiguous because PFA also denotes perfluoroalkoxy polymer. “Poly(furfuryl alcohol) resin” or “furfuryl resin” makes the intended material scope clearer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(furfuryl alcohol) (PFA) resin is produced by acid-catalyzed conversion of furfuryl alcohol, a furanic alcohol commonly obtained from biomass-derived furfural. It is a heterogeneous thermosetting resin chemistry rather than a single, perfectly defined linear repeat polymer: early condensation can produce methylene-linked furanic structures, while furan-ring opening, conjugation, and interchain Diels–Alder-type reactions can contribute to branching and network formation. A spectroscopic study prepared a cured PFA sample by adding sulfuric acid to furfuryl alcohol at room temperature, then heating the solid to complete the reported conversion. A separate acidic-resin study reports that acid identity/strength, acid concentration, temperature, and reaction time alter conversion, molar-mass development, and exotherm; its low-temperature route is one bounded example, not a universal cure schedule. The structural mixture and network density must therefore be tied to the catalyst history and extent of acid-driven conversion rather than inferred solely from the name PFA.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cured poly(furfuryl alcohol) is a crosslinked furan thermoset whose typically brittle response is controlled by acid catalyst and cure schedule, ring-opening and network structure, residual water and other volatile-driven porosity, and any fiber, filler, or toughener. Temperature relative to the cured network's transition region and specimen moisture or cure state must also be retained when comparing results. In one open study, neat furan resin made with an improved curing protocol had flexural modulus 3.2 ± 0.2 GPa, flexural strength 110.5 ± 17.3 MPa, and failure strain 4.1 ± 0.8%. These are flexural results for that specified neat, cured resin protocol—not tensile data and not a general PFA-resin range. A separate open prepreg-resin study shows why cure history matters: a 120 min B-stage at 60 °C reduced subsequent cured-resin porosity to below 3%, whereas direct curing produced a macrovoided, foam-like morphology; that work identifies porosity and network formation as likely influences on later stiffness, strength, and fracture behavior but does not provide a transferable mechanical endpoint.
sections.processing:
Poly(furfuryl alcohol) (PFA) resins are shaped as cast resin articles, foundry binders, impregnated wood or porous substrates, and matrices for fiber-reinforced laminates made by resin infusion, prepreg lay-up, and compression molding. Article conversion typically includes catalyst and additive mixing, degassing, reinforcement impregnation, optional B-staging to establish tack and drape, lay-up or casting, consolidation, venting or vacuum assistance, and a staged thermal cure. Water already in the resin and water evolved while the resin advances can form steam and voids; heating rate, open vent paths, pressure timing, and gel time therefore have to be coordinated. Acid catalyst strength and contact time also matter for acid-sensitive natural fibers.

Two formulation-specific studies illustrate those controls. Budelmann and Fiedler degassed their p-toluenesulfonic-acid-catalyzed PFA resin for 5 min, found about 50 °C suitable for impregnation/prepregging before premature gelation, B-staged it for 120 min at 60 °C, and then used three 30 min cure dwells at 90, 120, and 150 °C with 5 K/min ramps; this neat-resin experiment produced cured samples with less than 3% porosity. In a separate Furolite 120621/hemp-prepreg study, solvent water was first removed for 4 min at 100 °C, then four-layer laminates were compression molded at 155 °C and 15 bar for 20 min while alternative early mold-opening times were tested for steam release. Those schedules belong to the stated catalysts, resin grades, and test geometries; they are not universal PFA cure cycles.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(furfuryl alcohol) resin is an acid-cured furanic thermoset formed from furfuryl alcohol or related furan precursors. The curing reaction creates a crosslinked, aromatic heterocyclic network whose porosity and residual monomer depend on water, catalyst, and cure history.
sections.properties: Cured PFA resin is rigid, thermally stable, chemically resistant, and char-forming, with useful resistance to many acids and solvents. It is often dark and can be brittle; shrinkage, exotherm, porosity, and network density affect thermal and barrier behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Furfuryl-alcohol resins serve foundry binders, composite impregnation, chemical-resistant mortars and well-sand consolidation in metal casting, construction and oilfield service.

Purchasing. DynaChem offers custom FURALLOY liquid resin systems; its 1330, 170 and 175 examples are modified furfuryl-alcohol homopolymers with residual monomer or other ingredients.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Controlled pyrolysis of poly(furfuryl alcohol) forms carbonaceous residue; subsequent atmosphere and heat treatment determine activated, glassy or graphitic carbon structures. This thermal conversion does not identify its ambient weathering products.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Carbonization is an established patented use of furfuryl-alcohol resin as a carbon precursor. The cited process starts from deliberately prepared formulations; it does not demonstrate recovery of monomers or an operating recycling system for contaminated waste resin.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Acid-catalyzed furfuryl-alcohol polymerization can release heat rapidly. Coimbra and coworkers found that some hotter trial reactions became difficult to control, and used gradual acid addition with external temperature control to moderate the exotherm. This establishes a manufacturing runaway-reaction concern and the need for controlled addition and heat removal, rather than a hazard classification for a cured poly(furfuryl alcohol) article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Acid catalysis can produce substantial exotherm, shrinkage, porosity, and cure gradients, especially in thick sections. Furfuryl alcohol content, catalyst, water, filler or fiber, staging, post-cure, and storage age strongly affect gelation and final performance.

sections.overview: Poly(diallyl phthalate) is a diallyl-phthalate-based thermosetting polymer family typically supplied through prepolymer or molding-compound stages and cured into crosslinked materials.
sections.history: Diallyl-phthalate thermosets developed through techniques for stopping polymerization at a useful prepolymer stage and completing cure after shaping. Charles Heiberger and James Thomas’s 1954 application, issued in 1958, describes solid prepolymers; subsequent FMC work produced a further preparation patent in 1968. These documents treat diallyl-phthalate polymerization as already known and focus on practical yield, isolation and handling. The resulting prepolymer route supported molding-resin technology rather than requiring the final article to be made directly from neat monomer. These are documented manufacturing advances, not a first-invention claim for the whole polymer.
sections.nomenclature: PDAP abbreviates poly(diallyl phthalate), while DAP resin is a customary shortened descriptor. These names refer to diallyl-phthalate-based resin materials, not to phthalate plasticizers generally.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(diallyl phthalate) is normally made through a deliberately staged radical process from diallyl phthalate, rather than by treating a fully cured article as the starting material. In the first stage, thermal or peroxide-initiated partial polymerization is stopped before gelation to make a soluble, fusible prepolymer containing residual allyl unsaturation. One documented manufacturing route then removes unreacted monomer from the prepolymer by short-residence, high-vacuum thin-film distillation; another describes partial polymerization followed by monomer removal to obtain a solid prepolymer. The remaining unsaturation permits a subsequent heat- and initiator-assisted crosslinking step to form the insoluble network. The prepolymer and final network are distinct material states, so filler compounding, molding, and article-specific cure cycles are not treated here as the synthesis of the polymer family.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Diallyl-phthalate materials develop their useful mechanical response after cure into a crosslinked thermoset network; commercial molding compounds are commonly mineral- or fiber-filled, so crosslink state, phthalate isomer, reinforcement, flame-retardant package, voids, post-bake, moisture exposure, temperature, and compression versus transfer molding all control the finished article. A government report on DAP compounds found that increasing preheat increased the mechanical strength of its compression-molded specimens and that its compression-molded specimens were stronger than transfer-molded ones, illustrating the process sensitivity of compound data. For a bounded open numerical example, Sumitomo Bakelite 52-40-40-P is a coarse-flake, long-glass-fiber-reinforced DAP molding compound: its typical compression-molded ASTM specimens are reported at 125 MPa flexural strength and 13.8 GPa flexural modulus (ASTM D790), 52 J/m notched Izod impact (ASTM D256A), and 187 MPa compressive strength (ASTM D695). The sheet does not state cure cycle, fiber content/orientation, specimen dimensions, rate, or conditioning; these are therefore values for that reinforced, molded compound rather than for unfilled cured poly(diallyl phthalate).
sections.processing:
Poly(diallyl phthalate) article manufacture normally starts from a soluble, fusible prepolymer compounded with initiator, mineral or glass reinforcement, pigments, and release additives, then uses heat and pressure to shape and cure the charge. Compression and transfer molding are the established routes for filled electrical and dimensional-stability parts; charge form, preform consolidation, radio-frequency or oven preheat, spiral flow, mold venting, pressure, cure time, and any post-bake must be qualified together because advancing the charge before molding improves handling but consumes flow life. Sumitomo Bakelite's long-glass-filled 52-40-40-P sheet identifies both compression- and transfer-molding grades and reports properties on compression-molded specimens, while directing users to obtain grade-specific post-bake recommendations.

A bounded government study used a particular glass-filled diallyl-phthalate molding compound in two schedules: compression molding at 149 °C and 44.1 MPa for 15 min, or transfer molding at 149 °C and 58.4 MPa for 15 min. Its optional B-stage was 30 min at 121 °C, and maximum radio-frequency preheat was 20 s at a 200 mA setting; increasing preheat changed spiral flow and the molded response, and the transfer-molded specimens were weaker than the compression-molded specimens in that experiment. These are formulation- and apparatus-specific schedules, not universal cure conditions for every diallyl-phthalate compound.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(diallyl phthalate) is a crosslinkable allyl-ester polymer made from diallyl phthalate. The material is commonly handled as a partially polymerized prepolymer and then converted to a three-dimensional network through residual allyl unsaturation.
sections.properties: The cured resin is a rigid thermoset with electrical insulating ability, dimensional stability, and resistance to many solvents. Network density, residual monomer, filler, and cure history control hardness, shrinkage, thermal response, and dielectric behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Diallyl-phthalate molding compounds serve electrical connectors, terminal bases, circuit breakers and related insulating parts.

Purchasing. Sumitomo Bakelite offers compounds reinforced with glass or other fillers through its materials-sales inquiry channel; specify the compound and molding method.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A microwave-prepared poly(diallyl phthalate) example shows thermal mass loss on heating. The cited characterization does not identify the evolved molecules; a full breakdown-product inventory for the cured network remains unresolved.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A patent lists diallyl phthalate resin among carbon-fiber matrices suitable for heated drawing and fiber recovery. This route seeks to soften the matrix while limiting decomposition; listed scope is not a DAP-specific demonstration or proof of commercial recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Buehler’s 2024 European safety sheet for its mineral-filled diallyl-phthalate mounting compound warns of respirable dust and classifies the mixture as a reproductive toxicant, identifying vinyltris(methoxyethoxy)silane on its hazard label. Avoid dust inhalation and direct contact. These warnings apply to the specified filled formulation and should not be assigned to neat cured poly(diallyl phthalate).
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Cure exotherm, incomplete conversion, brittleness, residual stress, and difficult rework can limit the resin. Performance varies with prepolymer stage, catalyst, filler, mold cycle, post-cure, and network density; a filled molding is not equivalent to neat resin.

sections.overview: Thermosetting polyimide is a polyimide resin or oligomer that is converted into an insoluble network by curing reactive end groups, including phenylethynyl or related addition-cure functionalities. The uncured imide oligomer and its cure schedule are formulation-specific, while the network is the material boundary.
sections.history: Thermosetting polyimides became important in high-temperature aerospace composites. NASA’s account traces polymerization-of-monomeric-reactants, or PMR, addition-polyimide technology to Lewis Research Center in the 1970s. PMR-15 became a widely used first-generation material for demanding composite components. Later NASA work by Kathy Chuang and Raymond Vannucci developed DMBZ-15, replacing the diamine used in PMR-15 while seeking improved high-temperature performance. This is the history of an influential thermosetting-polyimide lineage, not all polyimide chemistry. It shows the movement from laboratory resin design into aircraft-engine applications and subsequent reformulation of an established aerospace matrix.
sections.nomenclature: Thermosetting polyimide is also abbreviated TSPI in materials literature. This record covers imide resins designed to crosslink on cure, including PMR and end-capped oligomer routes; thermoplastic polyimide and a cured composite containing the resin are related but distinct scopes. Bismaleimide resins, whose maleimide double bonds polymerize into insoluble, infusible networks that keep the imide rings, were described from the outset as reticulated polyimides and are recorded as a narrower entry of this class.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Thermosetting polyimides are usually prepared as finite-molar-mass imide or imide-precursor oligomers whose reactive end groups subsequently form an infusible network. Aromatic diamines and aromatic tetracarboxylic dianhydrides, or ester derivatives of those dianhydrides, build the imide-containing backbone; a calculated stoichiometric excess of a monofunctional reactive end cap limits oligomer length and supplies cure sites. In a cited phenylethynyl route, biphenyl tetracarboxylic dianhydride is converted to a diethyl ester in dry ethanol and reacted with an aromatic oxydianiline and a monoester derived from 4-phenylethynylphthalic anhydride. This produces phenylethynyl-endcapped poly(amic ester) solutions of controlled calculated molar mass. Heating removes solvent and converts the amic-ester precursor to imide rings; at higher conversion temperature the phenylethynyl termini undergo addition reactions that create the thermoset network without requiring a stoichiometric volatile coproduct from the crosslinking step. Low-molar-mass phenylethynyl-endcapped oligomers can act as reactive diluents and co-cure into that network. A historically important complementary route is PMR: the dimethyl ester of benzophenonetetracarboxylic acid and an aromatic diamine such as methylenedianiline are combined in methanol with a monoester of nadic acid as the end cap. Removal of solvent, imidization, and addition reaction of the norbornene-type termini yield a crosslinked polyimide. Diamine/dianhydride identity, end-cap chemistry and amount, target oligomer molar mass, solvent, imidization completeness, and cure-site conversion control flow before gelation and final network density. This entry excludes linear thermoplastic polyimides; article-shaping pressure and thermal schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Thermosetting polyimides form permanently crosslinked, usually aromatic networks whose room-temperature response is generally glassy: they can combine gigapascal-scale tensile stiffness and useful strength with only modest strain to failure. Their value is the ability to retain load-bearing stiffness at temperatures that soften many other organic matrices, but the same rigid backbones and network constraints can make neat resins notch- and flaw-sensitive. This is a broad chemistry class rather than one material specification; PMR, phenylethynyl-terminated, bismaleimide-like and other addition-cured imide systems should not be assigned one family-wide strength or modulus.

Consequential variables include backbone rigidity and symmetry, end-cap chemistry, formulated oligomer molecular mass, reactive-diluent or toughener content, crosslink density, cure and post-cure schedule, residual solvent or cure volatiles and the voids they create, oxidation and physical aging at temperature, moisture conditioning, reinforcement and fiber interface, specimen thickness and defects, and test temperature, rate and loading mode. A historical NASA PMR report independently illustrates why formulation and thermal history matter: it compared neat-resin tensile behavior at four formulated molecular-weight levels and before versus after post-cure, while treating fiber composites separately. Those composite results are not neat-resin properties.

One bounded neat-resin example comes from a phenylethynyl-endcapped thermosetting blend study. Its TMR-50/RDm-a-5 formulation combined the named TMR and reactive-diluent oligomers at 50/50 by mass, was B-staged, pressure molded through a 300–380 °C cycle, and held at 380 °C for 2 h. At 25 °C, 5 mm-wide specimens tested at 1 mm min⁻¹ to GB/T 1040-2006, with at least seven runs averaged, gave tensile strength 84.0 ± 4.36 MPa, tensile modulus 2.4 ± 0.10 GPa and elongation at break 4.1 ± 0.50%. Across that paper's formulation series, increasing calculated TMR oligomer molecular mass from 1500 to 5000 g mol⁻¹ raised tensile strength and elongation before the response largely plateaued. These values describe those cured formulations and protocol, not thermosetting polyimides generally.
sections.processing:
Thermosetting polyimide matrix resins are shaped while they remain soluble, fusible, or both, and are then imidized and/or addition-cured under a controlled pressure and temperature history. Solution impregnation and coating produce fiber prepreg; solvent removal and B-staging set a manageable volatile content before lay-up and autoclave or press consolidation. Neat molding powder can be compression molded, while appropriate low-viscosity formulations can impregnate reinforcement before cure. The critical window is bounded by solvent evolution, imidization by-products, oligomer melt viscosity, gelation, and crosslinking: pressure applied too early can trap volatiles, while pressure applied after the resin loses flow leaves porosity or poor fiber wet-out. Staged heating, vent paths, pressure timing, residence at cure temperature, cooling under pressure, and optional post-cure determine void content and residual stress. Oligomer and end-cap manufacture belongs in Synthesis; prepreg preparation, B-staging, consolidation, cure, post-cure, and cooling belong here.

Zhang and co-workers report one schedule for their TMR-50/RDm-a-5 phenylethynyl-terminated blend, not for all thermosetting polyimides. Neat powder in a stainless-steel die was held at 300 °C for 0.5 h under contact pressure, brought to 350 °C under 1.5 MPa, ramped from 350 to 380 °C at 5 °C/min while pressure was increased to 2 MPa, held at 380 °C for 2 h, and cooled to 100 °C before pressure release. For T700 prepreg made with the same matrix family, their solution-coated tape was dried for 24 h at 30 °C while retaining 10–15 wt% volatiles; autoclave holds at 120, 240, and 320 °C for 1 h each under contact pressure expelled volatiles, followed by a 3 °C/min ramp to 380 °C under 2 MPa and a 2 h hold. Pressure was maintained to 250 °C, and one variant was post-cured for 1 h at 420 °C. The historical NASA PMR report independently illustrates the same need to stage solvent removal and imidization before full-pressure molding; altered pressure/temperature sequences produced blisters or surface depressions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Thermosetting polyimides use reactive end-capped poly(amic ester) or PMR oligomers that imidize and addition-cure into networks.
sections.properties: Tensile and flexural data depend on end cap, molecular weight, reactive diluent, molding, and post-cure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Thermosetting polyimide systems serve aerospace engine/vehicle structures; PMR-15-derived composites also make wear liners and bushings for steel and aluminum mills.

Purchasing. NASA documented commercial liquid and powder RP46 resin sales in 2001 and fabricated PMR-derived composite components in 1997. These historical forms require present-day supplier verification.

Scale and evidence limits. NASA’s 2001 RP46 report describes a Unitech reactor capable of small-production quantities up to two tons/month. This historical single-reactor capability is not actual sales, present capacity or family-wide consumption; no current separate total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Aminolysis followed by acid hydrolysis of the studied phenylethynyl-end-capped polyimide (PETI) breaks imide/amide bonds. Recovered products include the original diamines TFMB and 1,3-bis(4-aminophenoxy)benzene and hydroxyl-bearing aromatic oligomers retaining some imide structure.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Laboratory aminolysis-coupled hydrolysis recovers diamines and converts remaining PETI fragments into a flame-retardant component for polyester synthesis. This is demonstrated for the reported PETI chemistry, with incomplete diamine recovery, rather than a universal route for every thermoset polyimide.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The PMR-15 thermosetting-polyimide system illustrates precursor-specific health concerns: NASA identifies its methylenedianiline starting material as a liver toxin and describes special handling to limit exposure during fabrication and waste management. Development of alternative diamines was motivated partly by this issue. The finding applies to MDA-containing PMR formulations and should not be generalized to all thermosetting polyimides.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Neat PMR and phenylethynyl blend results must remain formulation- and cure-specific.

sections.overview: Natural rubber is a biologically produced cis-1,4-polyisoprene material obtained as latex from rubber-producing plants. Its biosynthetic origin and naturally occurring non-rubber components distinguish it from synthetic polyisoprene materials.
sections.history: Natural rubber has no single inventor. Indigenous Mesoamerican communities processed plant latex into useful rubber by about 1600 BCE; archaeological and experimental work by Dorothy Hosler, Sandra Burkett and Michael Tarkanian documents balls, figurines and tool bindings. Industrial development was a much later history. Charles Goodyear’s sulfur-vulcanization discovery in 1839 helped make rubber goods usable across seasonal temperatures. Pneumatic tires then greatly expanded demand: Dunlop’s bicycle work and Michelin’s removable and automobile tires were influential late-nineteenth-century developments. Plantation research, improved latex harvesting and later block-rubber production changed the supply industry. Michelin’s radial-tire development further reinforced the importance of natural rubber alongside synthetic elastomers.
sections.nomenclature: NR abbreviates natural rubber. The canonical name denotes plant-derived natural-rubber material and is not an alternate name for every polyisoprene elastomer or for synthetic isoprene rubber.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Natural rubber is principally cis-1,4-polyisoprene biosynthesized in latex-producing organisms, especially Hevea brasiliensis. Biosynthesis occurs at the surface of rubber particles in laticifer latex, where cis-prenyltransferase-associated machinery elongates isoprenoid chains; it is therefore distinct from synthetic isoprene rubber made by chemical polymerization. Harvested Hevea latex can be collected by tapping and the rubber fraction recovered by acid coagulation followed by concentration, or latex can be purified/concentrated by centrifugation, membrane separation, and washing. A recovery patent gives examples of solvent separation or coagulation followed by selective removal of non-rubber extractables. These recovery choices alter latex purity and physical form but are not sulfur-vulcanization instructions, which are excluded here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Natural rubber develops its characteristic high extensibility, strength, fatigue resistance, and strain-induced crystallization only in a particular compounded and vulcanized form; raw latex, dried gum, and filled vulcanizates must not be conflated. Crosslink system and density, protein/non-rubber content, carbon black or silica reinforcement, temperature, strain rate, and aging all change tensile, tear, and hysteretic response. One open study reports for its D0 sulfur-vulcanized natural-rubber compound at room temperature: tensile strength 26.3 ± 0.7 MPa, elongation at break 584 ± 28%, 100% modulus 3.1 ± 0.2 MPa, Shore A 66, and tear strength 49 ± 5 kN/m. The test specimen, formulation, and cure details in that study govern these values; they are not raw-NR properties. A separate open study identifies naturally occurring network, protein and nonisoprene changes as variables affecting vulcanized-NR mechanics.
sections.processing: Natural rubber is converted either as stabilized latex or as dried raw rubber. Field latex is preserved and concentrated by routes such as centrifuging, creaming, or evaporation, then compounded or prevulcanized for dipped goods; dry rubber is masticated and compounded before operations such as calendering, extrusion, molding, and vulcanization. The open IntechOpen chapter covers field-latex handling, concentration, compounding/prevulcanization, and dipping, and emphasizes that latex stability must be maintained during mixing, pumping, and dipping. It reports a mechanical-stability-time test run at 14,000 rpm, with more than 650 s used as a standard criterion; short stability can cause coagulum and thickening during processing, while excessive stabilization can make deaeration and gelling on the former difficult. A separate processing review discusses mastication and compounding of natural rubber and the need to control raw-rubber conditioning, mastication temperature, and time. These constraints apply to the stated latex or rubber form and formulation, not to every natural-rubber article cycle.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Natural rubber is cis-1,4-polyisoprene latex containing non-rubber components and naturally occurring network features.
sections.properties: Properties depend on botanical source, maturation, molecular weight, non-rubber components, and vulcanization.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Tires account for a majority of natural-rubber consumption according to ANRPC; additional uses span aerospace, construction and healthcare.

Purchasing. Natural rubber is traded by grade, including technically specified rubber such as STR20/SMR20, ribbed smoked sheets such as RSS3/RSS4, and concentrated latex. Producer/exporter sourcing and specification differ between these forms.

Scale and evidence limits. CATAS’s June 2025 report, citing ANRPC, reports 2024 world production of 14.824 million tonnes and consumption of 15.364 million tonnes: an order of 10 million tonnes/year. These are reported supply/use estimates, not buyer orders, and are subject to statistical revision.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Purified latex-clearing protein cleaves cis-polyisoprene into oligomers with aldehyde and ketone ends. This establishes a biochemical pathway for natural rubber, not the fate of all compounded rubber articles.

Timescales: Products were isolated after 20 hours at 30 °C from latex in pH-7 buffer with purified enzyme; the endpoint was oligomer formation, not mineralization.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Sulfur-cured natural rubber is included in patented thermochemical devulcanization followed by reuse in rubber compounds. Enzyme cleavage is a laboratory route; vulcanization, fillers and additives complicate recovery.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Proteins carried by natural rubber latex can cause allergic reactions ranging from skin symptoms to severe systemic reactions. Processing chemicals can separately cause contact rashes. NIOSH distinguishes these protein allergens from synthetic rubber latex, which does not supply the same natural proteins. Exposure depends on the product and contact route, so material selection must consider users with known latex allergy.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Reported vulcanizate properties are compound- and cure-specific and cannot represent all natural rubber latexes.
