sections.overview: Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is the synthetic rubber form of polyisoprene whose backbone is predominantly formed by cis-1,4 addition of isoprene. Coordination catalysts such as neodymium or titanium/aluminum systems are used to obtain high-cis material; vulcanization is a separate formulation step.
sections.history: Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene became practical when stereoselective catalysts of the 1950s allowed chemists to approach natural rubber’s chain configuration. Shell commercialized lithium-catalyzed isoprene rubber in 1960; Goodyear introduced its more highly cis-rich Natsyn material in 1962, followed by Goodrich-Gulf. Applications included tires, molded mechanical goods, footwear, rubber bands and nipples. Zeon began isoprene-rubber production in 1971 alongside its own isoprene-extraction technology, illustrating how monomer supply and polymer manufacture developed together. Later research continued to refine stereochemical control and processing; Goodyear’s 2004 neodymium-catalyst patent records one such manufacturing advance. Earlier rubberlike isoprene polymers should not automatically be identified as this highly cis-selective material.
sections.nomenclature: Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is also abbreviated cis-PI or IR in rubber contexts. The record is limited to the synthetic high-cis 1,4 polymer; natural rubber, trans-1,4-polyisoprene, and a particular sulfur-vulcanized compound are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is produced by stereoselective coordination polymerization of purified isoprene. The monomer and hydrocarbon medium must be kept dry and oxygen-free because the coordination catalysts are readily poisoned. A long-established solution route uses a Ziegler-type catalyst made from titanium tetrachloride and a trialkylaluminum compound; catalyst ratio, preparation history, temperature, solvent, and conversion control activity, molar mass, gel formation, and cis-1,4 content. A distinct high-cis route uses a neodymium catalyst assembled from a neodymium carboxylate, organoaluminum compound, and dialkylaluminum chloride, with isoprene present during catalyst aging. Polymerization is stopped by deactivating the catalyst, antioxidant is added, and the rubber is recovered by coagulation or steam/solvent removal and dried. Latex grades can instead be made by emulsifying a solution-polymerized high-cis rubber and removing the organic solvent. The uncured polymer is not the final load-bearing network. A documented sulfur system combines cis-polyisoprene with sulfur, zinc oxide, stearic acid, and an accelerator such as TBBS; sulfur bridges formed between chains convert it into a vulcanizate. Peroxide and other cure systems are route variants, but their network structures are not interchangeable. Article shaping and time–temperature cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Synthetic high-cis-1,4-polyisoprene is a soft elastomer whose useful engineering response normally comes from a cured network: it sustains large, nonlinear recoverable strains, but the measured stress response and set depend on loading history and test conditions. Its stereoregular chains can undergo strain-induced crystallization (SIC) at sufficiently large extension. The resulting oriented crystallites produce a stress upturn (strain hardening) and reinforce highly strained regions, including material near a crack tip; they disappear again as the sample is released. This response is therefore not represented by one small-strain modulus or strength value.

Principal controls include cis-1,4 stereoregularity, network crosslink density and distribution, sulfur/cure-package chemistry and cure state. Fillers can change tensile stress and hardness through loading, particle structure and surface area, rubber–filler interaction, coupling treatment, and dispersion or agglomeration; oils and other compounding ingredients also shift stiffness and extensibility. Mixing and curing history, ageing, specimen geometry and orientation, temperature, strain rate, cyclic preconditioning, and deformation mode must accompany comparisons. In particular, planar or biaxial extension orients chains differently from uniaxial extension and can move the apparent onset of SIC and strain hardening. Moisture is generally a secondary direct variable for the hydrocarbon network, but conditioning can matter when water-sensitive fillers or interfaces are present.

One bounded unfilled example was a laboratory sulfur-cured synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene compound containing, per 100 phr rubber, 5 phr ZnO, 2 phr stearic acid, 1 phr sulfur, 2 phr TBBS and 2 phr PEG. It was Banbury/two-roll mixed, press-cured as an approximately 2 mm sheet at 150 °C to its 9.5 min T90, conditioned overnight, and tested at 500 mm min−1. The authors used ASTM D412 procedures but explicitly substituted a smaller 25 × 4 mm dumbbell for the standard Die C specimen. Under that specific protocol the compound gave 1.2 MPa stress at 300% strain, 4.7 MPa at 600%, 19.0 MPa ultimate tensile strength, and Shore A hardness 35.7; these values should not be generalized to other grades, cure systems, or specimens. As a complementary mode-dependence example, a separately reported IR2200 sulfur vulcanizate (initial Young's modulus 1.42 MPa) tested at 25 °C in a custom thin-centre specimen at about 7 × 10−3 s−1 showed strain-hardening/SIC onset stretches of 4.7 in planar extension and 5.7 in uniaxial extension. Those onset stretches describe that formulation and protocol, rather than universal thresholds for synthetic polyisoprene.
sections.processing:
Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is commonly converted as a compounded elastomer: the gum is mixed with fillers, oils, antioxidants, activators, accelerators, and a vulcanizing package in an internal mixer or on rolls; curatives are often added in a later, cooler mill stage to preserve scorch safety; the stock is then sheeted, calendered, extruded, molded, or built into an article and vulcanized. Latex- and solution-dip molding are additional routes for thin films, gloves, and balloons, using controlled solution or latex viscosity, degassing, form preparation, withdrawal, repeated dip/dry cycles, residual-solvent removal or leaching, cure, cooling, rinsing, powdering, and stripping. Filler drying and dispersion, mixing sequence, rotor or roll shear, compound temperature, residence time, sheet gauge, green-stock tack, scorch time, and rheometer-derived optimum cure time are consequential. Polymerization and chemical modification of the polymer belong in Synthesis; compounding, article shaping, and the vulcanization equipment and schedule belong here.

Wang and co-workers provide a bounded dry-mixing and press-cure example for SKI-5 PM cis-1,4-polyisoprene (reported Mw 272,100). Fumed silica was dried at 150 °C for 2 h; IR, silica, TESPT, ZnO, stearic acid, and BHT were blended in a Banbury mixer, after which TBBS and sulfur were added on a two-roll mill and approximately 2.5 mm sheets were formed. The named formulation used, per 100 parts rubber, 30 parts silica, 3 TESPT, 5 ZnO, 2 stearic acid, 2 BHT, 1 TBBS, and 1.5 sulfur, and was press-cured at 145 °C and 15 MPa for its measured t90. Those settings apply to that laboratory composite. In a distinct dip-molding example, McGlothlin and Schmid dissolved 40 g NATSYN 2200 and 1.2 g dicumyl peroxide in 1,000 g tetrahydrofuran, allowed bubbles to dissipate, built a catheter balloon film through nine dip/dry repetitions, oven-dried the coated mandrel for 2 h, and cured it for 4 min in a 180 °C molten-salt bath before cooling and rinsing. That solvent/peroxide schedule is specific to the disclosed NATSYN 2200 balloon process, not a universal polyisoprene cure window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is an isoprene elastomer whose high-cis microstructure is set by coordination catalyst chemistry.
sections.properties: Its crystallization and tensile response depend on extension mode, filler, sulfur network, and cure recipe.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Synthetic isoprene rubber serves vehicle, bicycle and aircraft tires, conveyor/V-belts, seals and footwear.

Purchasing. Zeon lists Nipol IR 2200 and 2200L compounding grades through its rubber-materials inquiry channel.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese IR capacity of 40,000 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Synthetic cis-polyisoprene is cleaved by purified latex-clearing protein into carbonyl-terminated oligomers.

Timescales: Purified synthetic-rubber granules in pH-7 buffer were incubated for five days with daily enzyme addition; this does not define outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Sulfur-cured isoprene rubber is within the patent’s devulcanization scope. Recovery aims at reusable chains rather than pure isoprene; the cited enzyme study is laboratory proof of depolymerization.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene is compounded, bag opening and ingredient weighing can release dust. HSE recommends dust-reduced or preweighed additives and local extraction. Ingredient-dependent skin allergy and dermatitis require contact control. This guidance concerns the uncured compound and its additives, rather than establishing a hazard classification for the base polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: IR2200 and named sulfur-network data are formulation- and test-specific.

sections.overview: Trans-1,4-polyisoprene is the stereoregular polyisoprene material whose isoprene units are predominantly linked in the trans-1,4 configuration. Coordination catalysts based on supported titanium or vanadium systems are documented routes; sulfur vulcanization is a separate downstream network step.
sections.history: Trans-1,4-polyisoprene has both a natural-material history and a later synthetic-polymer history. Gutta-percha was used in Southeast Asia for tool handles before its nineteenth-century introduction to European industry. William Montgomerie promoted medical uses in 1843; Werner Siemens’s cable-coating machinery helped make it central to submarine telegraph insulation. Golf balls and dental root fillings were other important uses of the natural material. Synthetic trans-polyisoprene was subsequently developed by producers including Polysar and Kuraray. Jack Lasky’s United States Rubber patent, issued in 1963, documents a stereoselective catalyst route. The nineteenth-century dates therefore concern natural gutta-percha and its processing, rather than invention of synthetic trans-polyisoprene.
sections.nomenclature: Trans-1,4-polyisoprene is commonly abbreviated TPI. This record is the synthetic high-trans 1,4 polyisoprene boundary; synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene, natural rubber, and a particular vulcanized compound are distinct scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Synthetic trans-1,4-polyisoprene is made by stereoselective coordination polymerization of purified isoprene, with the catalyst directing successive monomer additions predominantly into the trans-1,4 configuration. One industrial patent uses bulk precipitation polymerization with a supported titanium tetrachloride/magnesium chloride catalyst activated by a trialkylaluminum. In that route inhibitor and high-boiling impurities are removed from polymer-grade isoprene, the monomer is dried, low-temperature prepolymerization forms catalyst-centered particles, and a second polymerization stage grows them while hydrogen is used in a bounded range as a molecular-weight regulator. Unreacted monomer is recovered during vacuum devolatilization and drying, and antioxidant is added before product recovery. A distinct historical catalyst system combines finely divided vanadium trichloride, an aluminum trihydrocarbyl, and a tetrahydrocarbyl titanate in an inert hydrocarbon solvent; catalyst-component ratios, solvent, dilution, and temperature control activity and trans selectivity. Moisture, oxygen, inhibitors, and polar impurities deactivate these coordination catalysts, so monomer purification and inert handling are central controls. Uncrosslinked high-trans material can be semicrystalline. Where a rubber network is required, a cited formulation compounds trans-polyisoprene with sulfur, zinc oxide, stearic acid, and accelerator; sulfur amount controls the balance between covalent network formation and crystallization. That vulcanization route is a downstream chemical modification rather than part of the stereoselective chain-growth step, and not every trans-polyisoprene product is vulcanized. Article-shaping cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Trans-1,4-polyisoprene differs mechanically from the rubbery cis isomer because its regular trans chains can crystallize substantially near room temperature. Crystals can act as a stiff reinforcing and shape-fixing phase, so a high-trans material may behave as a hard, semicrystalline plastomer below its melting interval and soften markedly when those crystals melt. With an appropriate permanent network, recrystallization and melting can instead provide the reversible switching phase for thermally activated shape memory. It is therefore misleading to assign one elastomer-like strength or hardness to all trans-polyisoprene.

The response depends on trans content, molecular mass, crystal fraction and polymorph, cooling and annealing history, strain-induced orientation, chemical crosslink density and cure system, filler loading and dispersion, polymer–filler adhesion, plasticizer or blend components, oxidation and aging, temperature relative to melting, strain rate, cyclic history, specimen geometry and test mode. In one controlled sulfur series, Kuraray TP-301 (number-average molecular mass 7.0 × 10⁴ g mol⁻¹ and reported trans content above 98%) was compounded per 100 phr polymer with 5 phr ZnO, 2 phr stearic acid, 1 phr accelerator and 1–4 phr sulfur, mixed on a 60 °C two-roll mill, held 24 h, and compression cured at 150 °C and 15 MPa to t90. Raising sulfur from 1 to 4 phr reduced tensile strength from 23.5 to 10.8 MPa, tear strength from 60.3 to 17.3 kN m⁻¹, 100% modulus from 11.3 to 3.3 MPa, elongation at break from 360% to 237%, and Shore A hardness from 96.2 to 71.5. The authors linked the change to suppression of crystallinity as crosslinking increased. Results were means of three specimens, but the paper does not state the Chinese standard number, specimen geometry or test speed, so the values are bounded to that formulation series rather than treated as transferable specifications.

An independent study provides a second formulation-scale check. Its unfilled Qingdao Dipai TPI control contained, per 100 phr TPI, 2 phr stearic acid, 4 phr ZnO, 2 phr antioxidant, 1.2 phr NOBS accelerator and 1.5 phr sulfur; it was milled at 70 °C for 15 min, rested 24 h, and hot-pressed at 150 °C and 5 MPa for 10 min into 2 mm sheets. The reported room-temperature tensile strength was 17.7 MPa, elongation at break 380.5%, and Young's modulus 0.052 GPa. Because that article omits the tensile standard, specimen geometry and crosshead rate, these numbers are only a bounded control for its carbon-nanotube study. Its filled series further shows that nanoparticle dispersion and interfacial modification can change strength and stiffness without defining neat trans-polyisoprene behavior.
sections.processing:
Trans-1,4-polyisoprene can be mixed and shaped while warm, then used as a crystalline thermoplastic, a lightly crosslinked shape-memory material, or a more fully vulcanized elastomer depending on formulation. Reported article conversion uses two-roll or open-mill compounding followed by compression molding or vacuum hot pressing and sulfur cure. Fillers, zinc oxide, stearic acid, antioxidant, accelerator, and sulfur must be distributed without scorching; mill-roll temperature, mixing time and order, compound maturation, cure-meter endpoint, mold pressure, cure temperature, and sheet thickness all affect the result. Cooling and storage history are unusually important because crystallization near ambient conditions continues after molding and competes with crosslinking. For shape-memory articles, deformation above the crystalline transition, cooling under constraint, and reheating form an additional orientation and recovery operation. Polymerization and sulfur-network chemistry belong in Synthesis; mixing, molding, vulcanization schedule, cooling, crystallization conditioning, and shape programming belong here.

Fu and co-workers compounded Kuraray TP-301 (more than 98% trans structure) on an XK-160 two-roll mill at 60 °C with, per 100 phr TPI, 5 phr zinc oxide, 2 phr stearic acid, 1 phr accelerator, and 1–4 phr sulfur. After 24 h, the compounds were compression molded at 150 °C and 15 MPa for the rheometer-derived tc90; the reported tc90 values ranged from 470 to 550 s across that sulfur series. Zhang and co-workers provide an independent schedule: TPI and 0–3 phr polydopamine-modified nanotube were open-mill blended at 70 °C for 15 min with 2 phr stearic acid, 4 phr zinc oxide, 2 phr antioxidant 4010NA, 1.2 phr NOBS accelerator, and 1.5 phr sulfur, rested 24 h, and vacuum hot pressed at 150 °C and 5 MPa for 10 min into 2 mm sheets. Both windows belong to the stated recipes, and changing sulfur or filler changes crystallinity, cure response, and shape-memory behavior.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Trans-1,4-polyisoprene is a high-trans isoprene elastomer whose crystallinity competes with sulfur-network formation.
sections.properties: Crystallinity, melting, resilience, DMA, and tensile response change with sulfur level and CNT-filled formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Trans-1,4-polyisoprene is the polymer basis of gutta-percha; formulated gutta-percha points remain a dental root-canal material. Golf balls and submarine-cable insulation are historical uses, not evidence of today’s main market.

Purchasing. Material suppliers offer trans-polyisoprene pellets for laboratory work; Sigma-Aldrich lists a 50 g unit. Dental practices instead buy formulated points selected for size and taper; Dentsply Sirona lists a 60-point pack. Such points are not neat polymer pellets.

Scale and evidence limits. These examples establish tens-of-grams research packages and tens-of-points dental packages. No annual global trans-polyisoprene purchase tonnage is established; natural-rubber statistics primarily concern the cis material.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The tested trans-polyisoprene resisted the latex-clearing protein that cleaved cis-polyisoprene. No positive major-product inventory for environmental degradation was established.

Timescales: No cleavage was detected in the reported five-day, pH-7 enzyme-incubation experiment; this is not evidence for indefinite persistence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: No trans-polyisoprene-specific reclamation process was established by this enzyme experiment; cis-rubber devulcanization should not be assumed equivalent.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: In compounded trans-1,4-polyisoprene products, heating and conversion can generate rubber fume. HSE identifies dermatitis and skin-allergy risks from such process emissions and recommends ventilation that carries rising fume away from workers. This manufacturing guidance does not assign natural-latex protein allergy to every polyisoprene source or stereoisomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Results depend on high-trans grade, cure recipe, filler, and test conditions.

sections.overview: Polybutadiene rubber is an elastomer produced by polymerizing butadiene. Its cis/trans and vinyl microstructure depend on the catalyst and influence rubber performance, including tire-compound behavior.
sections.history: Polybutadiene rubber’s industrial development includes successive generations of stereoselective catalyst technology. A documented Japanese production milestone is Zeon’s start of butadiene-rubber manufacture at Tokuyama in November 1965. Later, Thomas Knauf and Akhtar Osman’s Polysar patent, issued in 1995, sought a more active rare-earth catalyst system for producing high-cis polybutadiene. This illustrates continued refinement of a material already established commercially, rather than its original invention. Tire compounds have been a major outlet; Arlanxeo’s account also identifies plastic modification and golf balls as applications. The family encompasses different chain microstructures, so the launch of a particular high-cis grade is not a universal date for all polybutadiene.
sections.nomenclature: BR abbreviates polybutadiene rubber. The name denotes butadiene homopolymer rubber and is distinct from styrene–butadiene rubber or nitrile butadiene rubber copolymers.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polybutadiene rubber is made by chain-growth polymerization of 1,3-butadiene. Coordination catalysts are important because they control whether the chain is rich in cis-1,4, trans-1,4, or 1,2-vinyl units; polybutadiene is therefore a family of microstructures rather than one stereochemically uniform material. High-cis solution routes commonly use a rare-earth catalyst assembled from a neodymium carboxylate, an organoaluminum component, and a halogen-containing activator in a dry hydrocarbon solvent under inert atmosphere. One cited process uses neodymium carboxylate, alkylaluminum chloride, and dialkylaluminum hydride; another uses a monomeric neodymium carboxylate with halogen and organometallic cocatalysts. Catalyst ratios, aging order, solvent, temperature, and termination set activity, molar mass, and cis content. These examples do not imply that all polybutadiene is high-cis; lithium-anionic and other transition-metal systems can give different architectures.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polybutadiene rubber (BR) develops its useful elastic, rebound, abrasion, flex, and tensile response only after compounding and vulcanization; raw gum, a filled tire compound, and BR used as an impact-modifier phase are not mechanically equivalent materials. The cis/trans/vinyl microstructure, molecular mass and branching, crosslink type and density, carbon black or silica and coupling-agent package, oil/plasticizer, blend partner, cure temperature/time, strain amplitude/rate, temperature, and aging control stiffness, hysteresis, crack growth, and failure. High-cis BR may strain-crystallize and can give low heat build-up and high resilience, whereas higher trans or vinyl content changes modulus, hardness, transition behavior, and cure response. A deliberately bounded historical tire-tread example—not an intrinsic BR value—is an SBR/BR vulcanizate containing 25 parts Buton 500 polybutadiene and about 64–65 parts ISAF carbon black, with sulfur, zinc oxide, stearic acid, antioxidant, and accelerators: the UNIDO table reports 3,250–3,290 psi tensile strength (about 22.4–22.7 MPa), 660–685% elongation, 1,000–1,101 psi 300% modulus, and Shore A 62. Test temperature and procedure are not reported, and the SBR-rich reinforced blend cannot be assigned to neat or any single BR grade. Independent high-cis BR vulcanization work specifically attributes variation to stereopurity and cure recipe/temperature/time, while noting extension crystallization as a mechanism for strong high-cis vulcanizates.
sections.processing: Polybutadiene rubber is compounded with reinforcing fillers, oils or processing aids, and sulfur or peroxide curatives, then mixed, sheeted or extruded, shaped, and vulcanized. The high-cis polybutadiene vulcanization study discusses how cure ingredients, temperature, and time affect unfilled vulcanizates. A separate open study used high-cis Buna CB24 with 30 phr silanized silica and 1 phr dicumyl peroxide; the compound's cure properties were measured at 160 °C and its t95 was 32.31 min. These examples show the importance of filler dispersion and cure kinetics, but the peroxide formulation and 160 °C result are specific to that silica-filled compound; sulfur systems, cis content, branching, oil extension, and article geometry require separate rheometric and molding conditions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polybutadiene rubber is a diene elastomer whose cis-1,4, trans-1,4, and 1,2-vinyl repeat contents depend on catalyst and polymerization route. Unsaturation remains along the backbone and enables sulfur, peroxide, or other crosslinking chemistries.
sections.properties: Polybutadiene provides low glass-transition temperature, high resilience, abrasion resistance, and useful low-temperature flexibility. Modulus, hysteresis, crack growth, and wear depend on microstructure, molecular mass, branching, filler, and vulcanization.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polybutadiene rubber serves tire compounds, belts, seals, footwear and coated fabrics in transportation and industrial goods.

Purchasing. Zeon lists distinct Nipol BR grades, including BR1220 and low-cis BR1250H, through supplier inquiry; the grade and intended compound must be specified.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese BR capacity of 65,000 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Air oxidation produces epoxide, peroxide and carbonyl-bearing structures. A primary study of 1,4- and 1,2-polybutadiene films identified epoxide-rich oxidized chains; subsequent hot-air analysis detected alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and acids, including 2-butenal, 2-butanone and acetic acid.

Timescales: The films were aged at 100 °C over hours; the 1,2 material became insoluble after 8 h. Volatile-product analysis covered 130–400 °C at a 10 °C/min ramp, a separate thermal protocol.

Environmental persistence: Insolubility and oxidation do not demonstrate mineralization. These accelerated results supply no environmental disappearance time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes controlled devulcanization and reincorporation into rubber compounds. Listed applicability alone does not prove performance for every cure system; peroxide- and sulfur-cured materials need separate qualification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When polybutadiene rubber is compounded, bag opening and ingredient weighing can release dust. HSE recommends dust-reduced or preweighed additives and local extraction. Ingredient-dependent skin allergy and dermatitis require contact control. This guidance concerns the uncured compound and its additives, rather than establishing a hazard classification for the base polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The unsaturated backbone is vulnerable to oxidation, ozone, and heat unless protected by formulation. Microstructure, cis content, branching, filler, blend, cure package, temperature, and dynamic strain make a vulcanized compound's results unsuitable as a universal polybutadiene range.

sections.overview: Styrene–butadiene rubbers are synthetic elastomer families made from styrene and butadiene. Polymerization route, styrene content, and diene microstructure create grades with different compounding and tire-material behavior.
sections.history: The styrene–butadiene rubber family grew from German Buna-S research and became a strategic mass-production material during the Second World War. When access to Southeast Asian natural rubber was cut off, the United States government coordinated a GR-S program involving Firestone, B. F. Goodrich, Goodyear, Standard Oil of New Jersey, United States Rubber and academic laboratories. Commercial wartime plants began operating in 1942. The collaborative effort turned a laboratory and pilot-scale technology into a large industrial supply of general-purpose rubber for tires and other essential equipment. Postwar production and research continued, and later emulsion and solution processes developed into distinct branches with different product and manufacturing histories.
sections.nomenclature: SBR abbreviates styrene–butadiene rubber. The canonical record is family-level: emulsion SBR, solution SBR, and functionalized SBR are narrower related materials rather than uniform aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–butadiene rubber (SBR) is a family of random copolymer rubbers made from styrene and 1,3-butadiene. Emulsion SBR is produced by free-radical copolymerization in water with soap or another emulsifier. Hot recipes use thermal radical sources, whereas cold recipes use low-temperature redox initiation; mercaptans serve as chain-transfer agents to limit molar mass. Polymerization is stopped at a selected conversion, residual monomers are removed, and the latex is coagulated, washed, stabilized, and dried. One cited patent documents a conventional peroxide or peroxydisulfate emulsion recipe and mercaptan control. Solution SBR instead uses an organolithium initiator in a dry hydrocarbon solvent; polar modifiers or mixed-metal additives regulate random styrene placement and the butadiene 1,2/1,4 microstructure, while living ends permit coupling or functionalization. A distinct patent demonstrates amine-modified anionic initiation, end-group reaction, and solvent recovery. The uncured copolymer becomes an elastic network through vulcanization, most commonly sulfur crosslinking with zinc oxide, fatty acid, and accelerator; a third cited patent gives an SBR-specific sulfur-cure formulation. Polymerization and crosslink chemistry belong here, while compound shaping and article cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Styrene–butadiene rubbers are generally amorphous, non-strain-crystallizing elastomers. A vulcanized gum network can undergo large, nonlinear deformation, but unfilled SBR is comparatively weak; practical compounds obtain much of their tensile, tear, abrasion, and stiffness performance from carbon black, silica, or other reinforcement. Their response is viscoelastic and hysteretic rather than a single elastic constant: stress depends on strain amplitude, loading rate or frequency, temperature, and prior cycles, and filler networks add pronounced strain-dependent dynamic stiffness and energy dissipation.

Emulsion SBR (ESBR) and solution SBR (SSBR) are processing and molecular-design families, not grades with one inherent strength ranking. Emulsion free-radical routes commonly give broader molecular and sequence distributions, whereas solution carbanionic routes can more closely control molar mass, dispersity, styrene distribution, butadiene 1,2-vinyl versus cis/trans-1,4 microstructure, branching, and chain-end functionality. Increasing bound styrene or 1,2-vinyl content generally raises the glass-transition region, tending to increase hardness and stiffness at a fixed temperature near that transition while reducing low-temperature flexibility; the actual balance also depends on sequence distribution and molar mass. Functional SSBR chain ends can strengthen interaction with polar silica, but any comparison must retain the filler and cure formulation.

Consequential compound variables include filler loading, particle surface area and aggregate structure, silica or carbon-black surface chemistry, macrodispersion, mixing history, bound-rubber interphase, and silane or polymer-end coupling. Crosslink chemistry, density and spatial distribution, accelerator/sulfur ratio, and cure state change modulus, set, strength, and extensibility; fillers can also alter cure kinetics. Process oil, plasticizer, tackifying resin, and oil extension change compound viscosity, glass-transition/damping behavior, and effective network and filler volume fractions, while antioxidants and antiozonants affect retention of properties. Higher loading rates or lower temperatures normally give a stiffer response and can suppress extensibility, whereas higher temperatures or longer times promote softening, creep, and stress relaxation. Thermal-oxidative or ozone ageing can cause both additional crosslinking and chain scission, often changing hardness and reducing ultimate elongation; fatigue, abrasion, crack geometry, specimen direction, and conditioning therefore matter. Moisture is usually a weaker direct variable for the hydrocarbon matrix, but it can affect silica surfaces, coupling, interfaces, and wet-friction or abrasion tests.

One bounded specification example is SIBUR SBR-1502, a cold-emulsion copolymer described as 23.5% styrene and 76.5% butadiene, with bound styrene specified at 23.5 ± 1.0 wt%. For grades B and C compounded using the ASTM D3185 Method A standard recipe, cured at 145 °C for 35 min, and tested by ASTM D412, the technical sheet sets minimum requirements of 13.0 MPa tensile stress at 300% elongation, 22.5 MPa tensile strength, and 420% elongation at break. These are quality-control limits for that named grade in the referenced standard compound—not measured properties of raw SBR, a typical family range, or finished-product design values; the sheet does not independently restate specimen geometry, conditioning, or test speed.
sections.processing:
Styrene–butadiene rubber (SBR) articles are made by compounding the gum with process oil, reinforcing filler, activators, antioxidants, and a cure package, shaping the uncured compound, and vulcanizing it. General rubber operations directly applicable to SBR compounds include internal or Banbury mixing, two-roll milling, extrusion, calendering, cloth coating, fabrication, compression or transfer molding, continuous vulcanization, press cure, and autoclave cure. Mixing order, fill factor, rotor and roll shear, filler moisture and agglomeration, silane distribution, dump temperature, cooling before curatives, sheet gauge, scorch safety, residence time, mold pressure, and a formulation-specific rheometer cure time are important. Curative chemistry and network formation belong in Synthesis; mixing, article shaping, and the cure equipment and schedule belong here.

The UK Health and Safety Executive's rubber-process flow maps rubber, oil, carbon black, bulk filler, and rubber chemicals through internal mixing and/or two-roll milling to extrusion, coating, calendering, fabrication, molding presses, continuous vulcanization, or autoclaving. A distinct bounded experiment by Staropoli and co-workers used an 80 phr SBR/20 phr polybutadiene compound: the rubbers were blended in an 85 cm³ internal mixer at 80 °C and 40 rpm, oil, activators, antioxidant, silane, and 80 phr silica were mixed for 10 min, and the compound received six roll-mill passes at 50 °C with a 5 mm gap before one hour of cooling. Sulfur and accelerators were then mixed at 60 °C and 40 rpm for 2 min, followed by six more mill passes and hot-press cure at 170 °C and 150 bar for 10 min. Those settings belong to that filled SBR/PBD formulation and laboratory equipment, not to every SBR compound.
sections.structureAndMorphology: SBR is a styrene/butadiene elastomer family varying in styrene content and diene microstructure.
sections.properties: Compound and vulcanizate response depend on polymer route, filler, and cure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. SBR grades serve tires, footwear, sports flooring, refrigerator gaskets and other mechanical rubber goods. Solution grades are also tailored to tire compounds.

Purchasing. Suppliers sell non-oil-extended and oil-extended emulsion grades and separate solution grades; buyers specify grade and compound requirements.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon’s undated corporate page, checked September 2026, lists 70,000 tons/year capacity for its Singapore S-SBR subgroup plant. This is one supplier’s stated capacity, not measured output, purchases or global demand; the page supplies no statistical reference year.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For sulfur-cured SBR, the patent uses chloramines to disrupt crosslinks and produce reclaimable rubber rather than purified styrene and butadiene.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Grinding and reuse in rubber-containing products provide material recovery. Chloramine treatment followed by revulcanization is a patented chemical alternative; commercial scale and grade-specific performance remain unestablished.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Mixing styrene–butadiene rubber family compounds can generate dust and expose skin to sensitizing additives. HSE recommends enclosed or extracted mixing, maintained seals and dust-suppressed ingredient forms. The formulation’s safety sheets determine chemical hazards; the polymer name alone does not identify the risk of a finished rubber article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Emulsion and solution SBR are distinct process-derived subfamilies.

sections.overview: Emulsion styrene–butadiene rubber is the emulsion-polymerized SBR copolymer material made from styrene and butadiene in an aqueous latex process. It is a rubber-grade copolymer whose final behavior depends on compounding and vulcanization as well as polymer composition.
sections.history: Emulsion SBR began with I. G. Farben’s Buna-S work in the 1930s. The United States wartime program began commercial production in 1942, initially using the hot-polymerization process. Development of cold-polymerized SBR in 1947 improved the practical rubber platform; government plants were subsequently sold or closed as the industry moved into private ownership. Tires remained an important driver of research. Howard Colvin and Michael Senyek’s 1999 Goodyear patent application sought emulsion-SBR tread formulations combining traction, rolling-resistance and wear objectives. These later formulation developments built on the original emulsion platform and should not be mistaken for its invention.
sections.nomenclature: E-SBR is the abbreviation used for emulsion styrene–butadiene rubber. The record is limited to styrene–butadiene copolymers made by the emulsion route; solution-polymerized SBR, block copolymers, and a particular filled or vulcanized compound are not alternate names for this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Emulsion styrene–butadiene rubber (ESBR) is the aqueous-latex route to a copolymer of styrene and 1,3-butadiene, rather than solution SBR. The aqueous polymerization medium contains water, soap/emulsifier, the two monomers, and a free-radical source; the resulting latex can be coagulated, washed, and dried to recover rubber. A Goodyear patent records a historical GR-S recipe with butadiene, styrene, soap, potassium peroxydisulfate, water, and a mercaptan modifier, followed by brine/acid coagulation. In a separate Bridgestone example, water, electrolyte, soap, reductant, styrene, butadiene, and a peroxide-containing feed were used for redox emulsion polymerization. These feed compositions and reaction controls are source-specific examples, not a universal ESBR specification.
sections.mechanicalProperties: E-SBR is a non-strain-crystallizing diene elastomer whose useful strength and wear resistance normally arise from vulcanization and reinforcing fillers rather than from the raw gum alone. Cured compounds show large, nonlinear, time- and temperature-dependent deformation, with hysteresis, stress softening after the first loading cycles, creep or stress relaxation under sustained load, and a strong change in stiffness and damping as the glass-transition region is approached. Mechanical performance depends on bound-styrene content and butadiene microstructure, molecular mass and dispersity, oil extension, filler type, loading, aggregate structure and dispersion, polymer-filler interaction, sulfur and accelerator system, total cross-link density and sulfide structure, mixing history, cure state, test rate and temperature, and thermal, oxidative, or fatigue aging. Carbon black generally increases small- and large-strain stiffness, tensile and tear strength, and abrasion resistance, but also changes heat build-up and hysteresis; its surface area, aggregate morphology, surface chemistry, and the bound-rubber interphase are consequential. Hwang and co-workers provide one bounded E-SBR compound example. Their laboratory emulsion polymer contained 23.5 wt% styrene, 20.7% vinyl within the butadiene units, weight-average molecular mass about 540,000, and dispersity 4.1. An E60 compound contained, per 100 phr E-SBR, 60 phr N330 carbon black, 3 phr ZnO, 1 phr stearic acid, 1.8 phr sulfur, and 1 phr TBBS and was press-cured at its t90 at 160 °C. ASTM D412 dumbbells (100 x 25 x 2 mm) gave stresses of 26 kgf/cm2 at 100% strain (about 2.55 MPa) and 138 kgf/cm2 at 300% strain (about 13.5 MPa), elongation at break of 470%, and DIN 53516 abrasion loss of 58 mg. The paper does not report tensile crosshead speed or specimen conditioning, and this synthesized, carbon-black-filled cure is not a family-wide E-SBR range. In finished products, geometry, reinforcement, residual strain, notches, multiaxial loading, and temperature history further govern fatigue, tear, and service life.
sections.processing:
E-SBR is converted through rubber compounding, shaping, and vulcanization. The polymer is mixed with reinforcing filler or mineral filler, oil or other process aid, zinc oxide and stearic acid, antidegradants, and a formulation-specific accelerator/sulfur cure package; ingredients whose early addition could shorten scorch safety are commonly staged. The compound can then be calendered, extruded, or molded, assembled with reinforcement where needed, and cured under pressure or by a continuous heating route. Mixing energy and temperature control are important because filler dispersion and polymer–filler interaction affect performance, while excessive thermal history can promote premature crosslinking or, for functionalized variants, gelation.

Kumho's public SBR grade table gives one supplier-bounded reference compound—100 phr SBR, 50 phr HAF carbon black, 3 phr ZnO, 1 phr stearic acid, 1 phr TBBS, and 1.75 phr sulfur—press-vulcanized for 35 min at 145 °C; it is a test formulation, not a production recipe for every E-SBR grade. In a separate GMA-functional E-SBR/silica study, a wet-masterbatch route was used to improve silica dispersion and avoid the high compounding temperature that caused gelation in the functional polymer; final compounds were press-cured at 160 °C for their measured t90. That constraint applies to the reported GMA-E-SBR formulation, not ordinary E-SBR as a whole.
sections.structureAndMorphology: E-SBR is a styrene–butadiene copolymer produced in emulsion, with composition and microstructure affected by emulsion recipe and polymerization control.
sections.properties: Its vulcanized response depends on styrene content, molecular structure, carbon black or silica filler, curatives, and compound design.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Emulsion SBR serves tire carcasses, treads, footwear, sports flooring and mechanical rubber goods.

Purchasing. Zeon’s non-oil-extended Nipol 1502 and oil-extended 1723/1739 illustrate distinct raw-rubber grades available through supplier inquiry.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese E-SBR capacity of 80,000 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The patent explicitly describes emulsion-polymerized SBR and subsequent sulfur vulcanization. Chloramine treatment targets the sulfur-linked matrix.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Grinding and reuse in rubber-containing products provide material recovery. Chloramine treatment followed by revulcanization is a patented chemical alternative; commercial scale and grade-specific performance remain unestablished.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When emulsion styrene–butadiene rubber is compounded, bag opening and ingredient weighing can release dust. HSE recommends dust-reduced or preweighed additives and local extraction. Ingredient-dependent skin allergy and dermatitis require contact control. This guidance concerns the uncured compound and its additives, rather than establishing a hazard classification for the base polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited studies evaluate carbon-black-filled RAFT E-SBR or modified silica masterbatches; such compound-specific results cannot be assigned to all emulsion SBR grades.

sections.overview: Solution styrene–butadiene rubber is styrene–butadiene rubber produced by solution polymerization, commonly using organolithium initiation. The process route enables control of microstructure and functionalization relevant to compounded-rubber performance.
sections.history: Solution SBR developed as a distinct way to control styrene–butadiene rubber architecture through organometallic polymerization. Ralph Farrar’s Phillips Petroleum patent, filed in 1977 and issued in 1979, documents coupling-agent addition during organolithium polymerization, including styrene–butadiene examples. It targeted processable rubbers for tires, hose, belting and related goods and treated solution polymerization as an established technology. Zeon began solution-SBR production at Tokuyama in 1986 and later opened production in Singapore in 2014. These milestones show continued process development and geographic expansion; they do not establish the first synthesis of the entire solution-SBR class.
sections.nomenclature: S-SBR abbreviates solution styrene–butadiene rubber. It is a process-defined SBR subfamily and is distinct from emulsion SBR; it does not name every styrene–butadiene rubber material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Solution styrene–butadiene rubber (S-SBR) is made by copolymerizing styrene and 1,3-butadiene in a dry hydrocarbon solvent, usually by anionic polymerization with an organolithium initiator such as n- or sec-butyllithium. Water, oxygen, and other protic impurities terminate the living chains and are therefore excluded. Because styrene and butadiene have different propagation behavior, a polar randomizer or an alkali-metal alkoxide can promote statistical styrene placement and also alter the fraction of 1,2- versus 1,4-butadiene units. One cited patent combines organolithium with an alkali-metal alkoxide in an alkane solvent to prepare random rubber at controlled styrene content. A distinct patent uses n-butyllithium, tetrahydrofuran or potassium tert-amyloxide as randomizer, and silicon tetrachloride or tetraethyl orthosilicate as a coupling agent. Monomer feed profile, randomizer level, temperature, initiator concentration, and hydrogen-free chain transfer or termination determine composition, vinyl content, molar mass, and sequence distribution. Living ends may be coupled into branched architectures or reacted with functional end-group modifiers before antioxidant addition, solvent removal, and drying. Sulfur crosslinking with an accelerator and activator package subsequently creates the elastomer network; article cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Solution styrene–butadiene rubber is an amorphous random diene copolymer whose useful mechanical response normally refers to a compounded and vulcanized network, not the uncured polymer gum. Above its formulation-dependent glass transition, a cured S-SBR compound can undergo large, substantially recoverable tensile deformation with pronounced rate-, temperature-, and strain-amplitude-dependent hysteresis. Unfilled S-SBR does not provide the strain-crystallization reinforcement of natural rubber, so tensile strength, tear, abrasion, fatigue, hardness, and modulus are commonly governed by sulfur crosslinks and by carbon-black or silica reinforcement. Tire-tread formulations deliberately balance wet traction, rolling-loss hysteresis, heat buildup, wear, and crack resistance rather than maximizing one static endpoint.

Styrene fraction and sequence, 1,2-vinyl versus cis/trans 1,4-butadiene microstructure, molar mass and distribution, branching and chain-end or backbone functionalization set glass transition, chain mobility, and filler affinity. Oil extension and plasticizer, S-SBR/BR or other rubber blending, silica or carbon-black loading, surface area and dispersion, silane type and dosage, mixing temperature and silanization, sulfur/accelerator chemistry, crosslink density and sulfur rank, cure time and temperature, antidegradants, moisture on silica, oxidative aging, test temperature, loading rate and strain history all change the observed response. Reinforcing filler can raise modulus and wear resistance, while too much filler networking or crosslinking can reduce extension and strength; polymer–silica coupling and functionalization can reduce filler–filler hysteresis while improving load transfer.

A bounded tread-compound example used oil-extended Trinseo SLR4630 S-SBR (25 wt% styrene, 63% vinyl within the butadiene fraction, and 37.5 phr oil), 60 phr Ultrasil 7000GR silica, 4.8 phr TESPT silane, and 0.9 phr sulfur with the reported activator/accelerator package. The silica–silane mix was held for 3 minutes at 145 °C, the sheet was press-vulcanized at 160 °C for 1.2 times its measured t90, and ASTM D412 tension was run at 500 mm/min. That formulation gave Shore A 57, stress at 100% and 300% elongation of 1.7 and 7.3 MPa, tensile strength 14.6 MPa, and elongation at break 460%. Raising sulfur alone to 1.5 phr in the same 60-phr-silica system raised Shore A to 61 and M300 to 10.1 MPa but reduced tensile strength to 13.5 MPa and break elongation to 370%. These are compound-specific results, not properties of neat S-SBR, other microstructures, carbon-black compounds, blends, or commercial tire treads.
sections.processing: Solution-SBR (SSBR) is converted as a compounded elastomer: plasticize the rubber, incorporate filler and coupling/activating chemicals under controlled shear and temperature, sheet the intermediate, add sulfur and accelerators in a cooler finishing stage, and then press-mold or otherwise shape and vulcanize the compound. In an open silica-filled S-SBR tire-tread study, the rubber was premixed for 30 s at 15 rpm; silica, silane, zinc oxide, and stearic acid were added during the first stage, silanization was held for 3 min at 145 °C, and the batch was dumped at 145 °C. After sheeting, sulfur and accelerators were added in stage 2 and the compound was dumped below 100 °C; 60/80 phr silica and 0.9–1.5 phr sulfur formulations had 160 °C rheometer t90 values of 14.7–18.2 min, and hydraulic-press vulcanizates used 160 °C for 1.2×t90. An independent silica-filled SSBR/BR study used a 70 rpm initial rotor speed and 160 °C cure testing for 30 min, with tensile specimens cured for 30 min. These are filler-, sulfur-package-, and machine-specific examples; keeping curatives out of the hot silanization stage limits scorch risk, and SSBR manufacture in solution is outside this Processing section.
sections.structureAndMorphology: S-SBR is solution-polymerized styrene–butadiene rubber with tunable microstructure and end functionalization.
sections.properties: Filler interaction and vulcanizate response depend on polymer design and compound formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Solution SBR grades serve tire compounds designed for rolling-resistance and grip requirements.

Purchasing. ENEOS lists SL grades for carbon-black formulations and HPR grades for silica or carbon-black formulations, with technical and supply inquiries handled by the producer.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon’s undated corporate page, checked September 2026, lists 70,000 tons/year capacity for its Singapore S-SBR plant. This is one supplier’s stated capacity, not measured output, purchases or global demand; the page supplies no statistical reference year.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Family-level SBR evidence supports chloramine-assisted crosslink disruption. The cited patent does not separately validate a solution-SBR grade or its particular microstructure.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Grinding and reuse in rubber-containing products provide material recovery. Chloramine treatment followed by revulcanization is a patented chemical alternative; commercial scale and grade-specific performance remain unestablished.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When solution styrene–butadiene rubber is compounded, bag opening and ingredient weighing can release dust. HSE recommends dust-reduced or preweighed additives and local extraction. Ingredient-dependent skin allergy and dermatitis require contact control. This guidance concerns the uncured compound and its additives, rather than establishing a hazard classification for the base polymer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Sulfur-variation results apply to stated silica-filled formulations.

sections.overview: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber is a carboxyl-functional styrene–butadiene copolymer material, commonly supplied as a latex or compounded rubber. The carboxyl functionality distinguishes it from unmodified styrene–butadiene rubber.
sections.history: Carboxylated SBR belongs to the development of functional latex binders, where small amounts of acid functionality broadened the usefulness of styrene–butadiene copolymers. Paul Steinwand’s Union Oil patent, filed in 1989 and issued in 1991, describes carboxylated copolymer binders intended to improve wet strength in nonwoven fabrics. The application context included wipes, disposable medical products, carpet backings and durable textile goods. The patent’s subsequent assignment history runs through Rohm and Haas and Mallard Creek Polymers. This is a documented formulation and ownership lineage within an already developed latex field, rather than evidence that carboxylated SBR was first invented in 1991.
sections.nomenclature: XSBR denotes carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber. The name describes a functionalized styrene–butadiene copolymer family rather than one fixed styrene, butadiene, or carboxyl-group composition; it does not make ordinary SBR an alias for this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber is made by aqueous free-radical emulsion copolymerization of styrene and butadiene with an ethylenically unsaturated carboxylic-acid comonomer. The acid component can be selected from acrylic, methacrylic, itaconic, maleic, or fumaric acid; its identity, proportion, and any crosslinking comonomer define the particular latex rather than a single universal composition. One patent example starts an itaconic-acid, surfactant, and seed-latex aqueous charge with persulfate, then feeds styrene and butadiene; tertiary-dodecyl mercaptan is included during the feed as a chain-transfer control. A separate staged patent route uses batch and continuous emulsion-polymerization charges of styrene, butadiene, acrylic and itaconic acids, anionic emulsifier, and persulfate/redox initiation; it specifically uses the chain-transfer agent and the late acid-monomer addition to control gel content. These are route-specific latex examples, not a general formulation for every carboxylated SBR.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Mechanical response in the accessible evidence is formulation- and material-state-dependent: an unvulcanized latex film, a filled film, and a sulfur-cured tire compound are not interchangeable XSBR states. Visakh and co-workers used an XSBR latex containing 59% styrene (47% dry-rubber content) as an unvulcanized control and as the matrix for cast films with 4.1–9.0 wt% crab-chitin whiskers. In nanoindentation creep at 23 °C (Berkovich tip, 0.05 mN maximum load, 200 s hold; 20 tests per sample), their fitted Burgers-model constants for the unannealed neat XSBR control were K1 = 48.664 N/m and K2 = 80.901 N/m. Those surface-creep fit parameters are not a bulk Young’s modulus; the authors also found that annealing neat XSBR at 100 °C for 90 min did not show the increased indentation resistance observed for the higher-chitin films. In a separate sulfur-cured tire-compound example, 50 phr of a named carboxylated SBR was combined with 50 phr E-SBR, 127 phr N330 carbon black, 95 phr paraffinic oil, zinc oxide, sulfur, and accelerator. The reported compound had tensile strength 8.7 MPa, elongation at break 673%, 300% ring modulus 3.32 MPa, and Shore A hardness 61 at 23 °C; stress–strain data were obtained on a Zwick 1445 tester. This is a filled, oil-extended, sulfur-cured blend—not a neat-XSBR property—and the document does not give tensile specimen geometry, test speed, or statistical basis. These bounded examples should therefore not be combined into family-wide ranges.
sections.processing: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber (XSBR) can be compounded and vulcanized as solid rubber, or used as a waterborne latex for sprayed and dried coatings. Formulation, filler loading, and final cure are article-specific. In a laboratory ENR/XSBR experiment, latex blending preceded coagulation; recovered rubber was mixed with ZnO, stearic acid, CBS, and sulfur, sheeted on a cold two-roll mill, and compression molded at 130 °C for its measured t90. Those conditions apply to that ENR-30/XSBR blend, not all XSBR compounds. A separate carpet-backing patent demonstrates wax-modified XSBR latex sprayed onto wet, skinned foam then dried at 130 °C for 12 min; its 10% solids coating and 60 g/m² dry application rate are example-specific, and heavier coatings can crack on bending and lengthen drying.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber (XSBR) is a styrene/butadiene latex copolymer containing an acid comonomer; finished materials are commonly filled and vulcanized rubber networks.
sections.properties: Its response depends on the carboxylated-latex composition and on compounding, cure, and filler choices rather than on an intrinsic XSBR value.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Carboxylated SBR is supplied within industrial latex portfolios serving paper coatings, carpet backing, foam and fiber-to-rubber adhesives.

Purchasing. ENEOS identifies SBL0696, 0533 and several other grades specifically as carboxy-modified aqueous emulsions. Buyers select solids content and grade through supplier inquiry.

Scale and evidence limits. Listed carboxy-modified latex examples contain approximately 48–54% total solids. This characterizes purchased dispersion, not annual tonnage; no separate XSBR consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Specially formulated carboxylated SBR carpet adhesive can detach from fibers under shear in alkaline surfactant solution while the adhesive remains insoluble. This is physical separation of an adhesive-containing fraction, not molecular depolymerization. A complete environmental product inventory remains unresolved.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A patented process combines size reduction, wet granulation and hydrocyclone separation to reclaim carpet face fibers. Performance depends on the acid-comonomer formulation: the conventional XSB comparator was not removed under the same treatment.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Mixing carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber compounds can generate dust and expose skin to sensitizing additives. HSE recommends enclosed or extracted mixing, maintained seals and dust-suppressed ingredient forms. The formulation’s safety sheets determine chemical hazards; the polymer name alone does not identify the risk of a finished rubber article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Published creep, tensile, and dynamic results describe named chitin-filled, tire-tread, or coating formulations and their stated test methods; they do not define all XSBR grades.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical terpolymerization introduces carboxyl sites into SBR latex. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

sections.overview: Nitrile butadiene rubber is an elastomeric copolymer of butadiene and acrylonitrile. Its bound acrylonitrile content is a central compositional variable in NBR production and material behavior.
sections.history: Nitrile rubber emerged from the interwar search for useful synthetic elastomers. Erich Konrad and Eduard Tschunkur’s I. G. Farben patent, with 1930 German priority and a United States grant in 1934, describes rubberlike copolymers made from butadiene and polymerizable nitriles. It provides a firm early milestone for the family. Zeon began Japan’s first domestic nitrile-rubber production in 1959 and subsequently expanded its rubber and feedstock technology. Industrial development produced a range of specialty grades: Arlanxeo’s Krynac products, for example, serve adhesives, sealants and plastics modification. Later hydrogenated and carboxylated derivatives developed their own application histories rather than simply inheriting the original polymer’s invention date.
sections.nomenclature: NBR abbreviates nitrile butadiene rubber. The name identifies the acrylonitrile–butadiene rubber family and should not be treated as a synonym for butadiene rubber without nitrile comonomer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is the synthetic copolymer of acrylonitrile and 1,3-butadiene. Commercially relevant routes use aqueous free-radical emulsion polymerization with emulsifier, initiator, and often a molecular-weight regulator, followed by coagulation and recovery of the latex polymer. Acrylonitrile feed and staged butadiene addition influence bound acrylonitrile content and the copolymer’s composition; they are not universal values for all NBR grades. One continuous patent describes incremental butadiene feeds during free-radical emulsion polymerization, while another identifies the binary aqueous-emulsion route and a carboxylated-NBR terpolymer variant. Hydrogenation of NBR produces HNBR, a different material, and finished-article vulcanization is excluded from this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is a cured acrylonitrile--butadiene elastomer, so tensile, modulus, tear, and compression response are compound rather than raw-polymer constants.  Acrylonitrile content and polymer Mooney viscosity, carbon-black or mineral reinforcement, plasticizer, sulfur/peroxide cure system, cure time and temperature, specimen geometry, temperature, strain rate, and ageing environment can all change a reported result.  Two 34%-acrylonitrile supplier compounds demonstrate the required limits.  Astlett NBR B6240 (34% bound acrylonitrile, ML1+4 42 at 100 °C) is tested in ASTM D3187 compound with 40 phr HAF black, 3 phr zinc oxide, 0.7 phr TBBS, and 1.5 phr sulfur; after 35 min at 145 °C, it reports ASTM D412 tensile strength 285 kgf/cm², elongation 600%, and 300% modulus 120 kgf/cm².  Separately, Kumho KNB 35L has 34 ± 2% bound acrylonitrile and a stated ASTM D3187/D412 test compound cured at 150 °C for 40 min in a press with carbon-black IRB #7; it lists tensile strength at least 220 kgf/cm², elongation at least 420%, and 300% modulus 150 ± 30 kgf/cm².  These are deliberately non-interchangeable compound-and-cure examples, not an NBR family range.
sections.processing: Nitrile butadiene rubber is normally converted as a compounded elastomer: the gum is mixed with reinforcing filler, zinc oxide, stearic acid, sulfur, and an accelerator, then shaped by extrusion, calendering, or molding and vulcanized. The Astlett B6240 sheet identifies that grade as suitable for extrusion and calendering and gives an ASTM D3187 compound of 100 parts B6240 NBR, 40 parts HAF carbon black, 3 parts zinc oxide, 1 part stearic acid, 0.7 part TBBS, and 1.5 parts sulfur; its stated cure example is 35 min at 145 °C. A separate Kumho KNB 35L sheet gives a different bound-acrylonitrile grade and an IRB #7 carbon-black compound press-cured at 150 °C for 40 min. The formulations and cure cycles are named-grade test recipes, so they should not be generalized across NBR grades, acrylonitrile levels, filler systems, or article thicknesses.
sections.structureAndMorphology: NBR is an acrylonitrile–butadiene elastomer whose nitrile content sets a central composition variable.
sections.properties: Oil resistance, low-temperature response, and mechanics depend on bound acrylonitrile, molecular weight, filler, and cure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. NBR serves oil-contact hoses, seals, membranes, belts and roll covers in vehicles and industrial machinery; selected grades also serve adhesives and footwear.

Purchasing. Suppliers offer grade-specific raw rubber. Zeon lists bale, liquid and powder forms; these are distinct products for compounding rather than interchangeable forms of one specification.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese NBR capacity of 60,000 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: NBR O-ring pyrolysis produces butadiene and acrylonitrile, with additional nitriles such as benzonitrile and aromatic fragments. Separately, an 80 °C ageing study finds increased crosslinking; its ketone/aldehyde mechanism is supported by molecular simulations rather than direct product collection.

Timescales: The O-ring analysis flash-pyrolyzed 100–200 µg portions at 700 °C in helium. The ageing experiment used 10 mm cylinders compressed 30%, sampled over 19–228 h at 80 °C. Neither is a natural mineralization test.

Environmental persistence: These heat-driven endpoints do not establish disappearance in soil, freshwater or seawater. The ageing formulation was proprietary, further limiting transfer to other NBR grades.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes controlled devulcanization and reincorporation into rubber compounds. Listed applicability alone does not prove performance for every cure system; peroxide- and sulfur-cured materials need separate qualification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Mixing nitrile butadiene rubber compounds can generate dust and expose skin to sensitizing additives. HSE recommends enclosed or extracted mixing, maintained seals and dust-suppressed ingredient forms. The formulation’s safety sheets determine chemical hazards; the polymer name alone does not identify the risk of a finished rubber article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Technical data apply to named NBR grades; they cannot be generalized across acrylonitrile content or compounds.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical emulsion copolymerization produces nitrile rubber. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

sections.overview: Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is the modified nitrile-rubber material obtained by selective hydrogenation of NBR's diene-derived unsaturation. The nitrile-containing copolymer backbone remains the starting material boundary while catalyst and hydrogenation conditions control the modification.
sections.history: Hydrogenated nitrile rubber developed as a heat- and oil-resistant extension of nitrile-rubber technology. A clear commercialization milestone is Zeon’s introduction of Zetpol in 1984. Its account identifies automotive timing belts as an important application, alongside other demanding mechanical rubber goods. The advance lay in producing a durable specialty elastomer from an existing nitrile-polymer platform; the much earlier invention of NBR is therefore not the invention date of HNBR. Zeon’s continued emphasis on controlled specialty-elastomer manufacture and automotive performance shows how hydrogenation created a commercially distinct branch of the nitrile family.
sections.nomenclature: HNBR is not a synonym for unmodified nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR): it specifically denotes hydrogenated NBR. Residual unsaturation, acrylonitrile content, and a subsequent vulcanized network are separate grade or formulation descriptors that should accompany any particular HNBR material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is a chemically modified nitrile-butadiene rubber, made by selectively hydrogenating the residual carbon–carbon unsaturation in NBR rather than by a new acrylonitrile/butadiene copolymerization. NBR itself is the acrylonitrile–butadiene copolymer precursor. Documented solution-hydrogenation routes contact dissolved NBR with hydrogen and noble-metal catalysts, including rhodium, ruthenium, or palladium systems; catalyst and ligand choice, solvent, hydrogen pressure, and conversion determine the degree and selectivity of hydrogenation. A heterogeneous palladium/rhodium catalyst patent and an open-access report on metathesis/hydrogenation provide complementary examples. Hydrogenation of nitrile groups is a different, more extensive modification and should not be assumed for conventional HNBR. Vulcanization of the finished rubber is a separate formulation step and is not included here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is used as a cured elastomer; its tensile and recovery response is governed by acrylonitrile content, residual unsaturation and crosslink density/cure, reinforcement and plasticizer package, temperature, and ageing history.  An open study of sulfur-vulcanized HNBRs containing 34 or 36 wt% acrylonitrile and varied crosslink density reports an amorphous room-temperature state without strain-induced crystallization; stretching instead orients amorphous segments, with the orientation influencing tensile strength, strain hardening, toughness, and recovery.  A bounded compound example is M-Seals HNBR-F/101, a black nominal 75-Shore-A material: the supplier's standard-test-specimen record gives 71 Shore A hardness, 22.70 MPa tensile strength and 346% ultimate elongation by ASTM D412/C, plus 21% compression set after 22 h at 150 °C by ASTM D395/B.  The data sheet expressly cautions that standard specimen results are not directly comparable with finished parts.
sections.processing:
Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is converted as a compounded elastomer: the polymer is masticated and mixed with carbon black or other fillers, plasticizer/process aids, antioxidants, metal oxide, coagent, and a sulfur, sulfur-donor, or peroxide cure package. Internal mixers and two-roll mills are used; staged addition of curatives and strong cooling are important because HNBR compounds build heat and premature scorch would reduce processing safety. Shaped compounds can be extruded, injection-, transfer-, or compression-molded, then vulcanized and, where specified, post-cured. Cure choice and temperature are formulation- and peroxide-specific; oxygen exposure can cause surface reversion in pressureless peroxide cures.

A supplier guide describes a common two-pass internal-mixer sequence: masterbatch discharge near 140 °C, then addition of cure chemicals and second discharge near 100–110 °C, followed by cooled milling. In an independent HNBR-4307 hose-compound study, rubber was thin-pass plasticized on a two-roll mill, ingredients were added in stages, the compound was press-vulcanized at 170 °C for its measured T90, and samples were secondarily cured at 165 °C for 4 h. Those conditions apply to that carbon-black/plasticizer/DCP/TAIC formulation and recycled-powder variants, not to every HNBR grade. Selective hydrogenation of NBR is upstream Synthesis; compounding, shaping, and crosslinking the article belong here.
sections.structureAndMorphology: HNBR is made by selective hydrogenation of nitrile–butadiene rubber, converting much of the residual carbon–carbon unsaturation while retaining polar nitrile groups. The resulting elastomer has a saturated backbone with composition-dependent residual unsaturation and acrylonitrile content.
sections.properties: Hydrogenation improves resistance to heat, ozone, and oxidative aging relative to conventional NBR while the nitrile groups retain useful resistance to oils and fuels. Cure response, hardness, compression set, swelling, and low-temperature flexibility vary with hydrogenation level, acrylonitrile content, filler, and crosslink system.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. HNBR serves automotive timing belts, seals, hoses and axle boots, oilfield packers and drilling seals, and industrial paper-machine rolls.

Purchasing. Zeon supplies Zetpol grades distinguished by acrylonitrile content and hydrogenation, plus named latex variants; specialist inquiries can request samples and application guidance.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese HNBR capacity of 4,500 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermo-oxidative ageing of peroxide-cured HNBR involves both chain scission and additional crosslinking; the balance changes with ageing. Broken load-bearing chains and network changes explain loss of elastic recovery. The experiment does not identify a complete small-molecule product inventory.

Timescales: A commercial peroxide-cured HNBR containing 36 wt% acrylonitrile was studied as O-ring segments and 2 mm sheets in circulating air at 125 °C for 2 hours to 31 days. Compression relaxation and compression set measured network damage, not mass disappearance or mineralization.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Used HNBR vulcanizate can be mechanically reduced to powder and incorporated into fresh HNBR compounds. A laboratory study froze and roll-ground the scrap, then modified its surface with 5 wt% trans-polyoctenamer before compounding it into HNBR-4307 hose-lining formulations. The modified powder performed better than unmodified powder at the same loading, although increasing powder content generally reduced tensile and tear properties and increased compression set. This route retains crosslinked particles in a new peroxide-cured rubber matrix; it does not recover HNBR monomer or establish unrestricted replacement of virgin rubber.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Freshly molded HNBR rubber articles can remain an exposure source while cooling. HSE recommends extraction at cooling racks, avoiding skin contamination, and gloves suitable for chemical and heat exposure. These are process controls for formulated rubber articles; the cure package and other ingredients determine additional chemical hazards.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: HNBR is not equally resistant to every fluid: polar solvents, strong acids or bases, steam, and extreme low temperatures can remain limiting. Residual unsaturation, acrylonitrile level, cure package, filler, post-cure, temperature, pressure, and compression history must be retained when comparing grades.
