sections.overview: Carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber (XNBR) is a nitrile-rubber-derived copolymer/terpolymer that incorporates an unsaturated carboxylic-acid comonomer alongside butadiene and acrylonitrile. The carboxyl functionality enables ionic as well as covalent network formation in formulated latex or rubber articles.
sections.history: Carboxylated nitrile rubber developed as a functional extension of the nitrile-latex platform. By 1999, Pascale Francine Jeanne Muller’s Goodyear patent application described it as widely used for gloves, nonwoven fabrics, masking tapes, seals and coating or binding applications. The proposed advance was emulsifier-free latex manufacture, aimed at reducing residual emulsifier in products and wash water. This is a useful dated stage in a longer development history: it demonstrates that XNBR was already established and that research had moved toward product cleanliness and manufacturing improvements. The document does not establish a first invention or launch date for all carboxylated nitrile rubbers.
sections.nomenclature: XNBR identifies carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber and is not interchangeable with unmodified nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR). Acid-comonomer level, latex grade, crosslinker, and any filler define narrower materials; a dipped or vulcanized XNBR article is a formulation-specific network rather than the base copolymer alone.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber (XNBR) is an acrylonitrile–butadiene rubber modified by incorporation of an unsaturated carboxylic-acid comonomer, such as methacrylic or acrylic acid, through free-radical aqueous emulsion terpolymerization. In one publicly described emulsifier-free latex route, 1,3-butadiene, acrylonitrile, and methacrylic acid are initiated with potassium persulfate plus an acid-active co-initiator in an aqueous reactor, giving a seed latex before a delayed feed of butadiene, acrylonitrile, and additional initiator. That patent reports 25–80 °C for the polymerization and, for its preferred embodiment, an initial charge of 20–40 wt% acrylonitrile, 5–9 wt% methacrylic acid, and 51–75 wt% butadiene; these are route-specific composition and operating ranges, not a definition of all XNBR grades. It also notes that differing monomer reactivities can make bound-unit composition depart from the charge. Chain-transfer agent, conversion/solids target, neutralization, and stabilizer choice are therefore manufacturing controls. The separate phase-transfer study provides a second, independently published context for carboxylated-nitrile-rubber preparation rather than evidence for one universal recipe.
sections.mechanicalProperties: XNBR mechanical response is governed by the carboxyl groups’ ability to form ionic as well as covalent networks, so cure system, crosslink density, filler, latex grade, and film history must remain attached to any reported value. In an XNBR-latex glove-material study conditioned at 21 ± 3 °C and 50 ± 5% relative humidity, unfilled films crosslinked with 1.5 phr sulfur had tear resistance of 2.7 ± 0.4 N, whereas films crosslinked with 2.0, 4.0, and 8.0 phr magnesium oxide gave 6.3 ± 1.1, 7.5 ± 0.6, and 9.8 ± 2.1 N, respectively, in the reported EN 388 testing. The same formulations had puncture resistance from 42 to 63 N and 2000 abrasion cycles, emphasizing that a change in ionic/covalent cure balance shifts endpoints differently. Those are thin, conditioned glove-film results, not a tensile or tear range for every XNBR compound. A separate open XNBR study compared ZnO ionic, sulfur covalent, and hybrid networks using ASTM D412 tensile specimens; it found that ionic crosslinks dominate room-temperature stiffness at low covalent-crosslink density while extra covalent crosslinking increases modulus at elevated temperature. Its AFM-derived values describe phase-scale modulus, not a bulk-grade specification. Together, the sources support the qualitative cure–mechanics relationship and bounded examples, while leaving grade-to-grade tensile comparability unresolved.
sections.processing: XNBR is commonly converted from an aqueous latex after compounding into dipped or coagulated films, coatings, binders, and related rubber articles; it is then dried and crosslinked. In one bounded flat-film glove-material procedure, a mold was dipped in either 35 wt% calcium nitrate or 20 wt% calcium chloride in methanol, dried at 30–50 °C, dipped into a sulfur- or magnesium-oxide-formulated XNBR latex, dried at 55–60 °C, and crosslinked at 100–115 °C for 180 min. Those laboratory conditions show why coagulant/dip history, cure system, and formulation cannot be treated as interchangeable family settings. For a different laboratory XNBR formulation, an open study measured cure behavior at 160 °C for 30 min by ASTM D5289 rheometry before preparing tensile specimens; that is a formulation-specific cure-screening condition, not a general production schedule. Upstream latex manufacture imposes separate controls—aqueous-phase solids, initiator/feed sequence, pH adjustment, and stabilization in the documented emulsifier-free route. Article processing should therefore specify the named latex/compound and conversion route; the sources do not establish one universal oven cycle, coagulant recipe, or cure window for XNBR.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber is an acrylonitrile–butadiene elastomer containing carboxyl-functional comonomer units. The functional groups alter interfacial interactions and cure behavior relative to unmodified NBR.
sections.properties: XNBR is a composition- and cure-dependent elastomer; nitrile level, carboxyl content, latex formulation, crosslinking, and fillers influence mechanical and barrier-related response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. XNBR serves abrasion-resistant linings and belts and modifies epoxy adhesives for aircraft structures, printed circuit boards and electronics.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO offers Krynac X grades; Zeon separately lists Nipol NX775 as carboxylated rubber in bale form. Formulation and grade selection precede a supply inquiry.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For sulfur-cured carboxylated nitrile rubber, a patent proposes preferential cleavage of sulfur crosslinks at crumb surfaces while retaining a cured core and much of the backbone. This scope does not cover every ionic or peroxide-cured XNBR formulation; ambient products remain unresolved.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Patented options include surface devulcanization and blending ground waste XNBR into PVC, with optional graft modification. These sources demonstrate or propose material recovery, not recovery of pure acrylonitrile/butadiene monomers or verified commercial throughput.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Mixing carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber compounds can generate dust and expose skin to sensitizing additives. HSE recommends enclosed or extracted mixing, maintained seals and dust-suppressed ingredient forms. The formulation’s safety sheets determine chemical hazards; the polymer name alone does not identify the risk of a finished rubber article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The glove study evaluates specific XNBR-latex composite formulations, and the phase-transfer study compares a selected catalyst route. Their outcomes should not be generalized to all XNBR latexes or finished vulcanizates.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical terpolymerization places acid functionality in nitrile-rubber chains. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

sections.overview: Butyl rubber (IIR) is the low-unsaturation copolymer of isobutylene with a small amount of isoprene. Its polyisobutylene-rich backbone gives low gas permeability, while the isoprene-derived unsaturation permits vulcanization.
sections.history: William Sparks and Robert Thomas developed butyl rubber at Standard Oil of New Jersey in 1937 while investigating isobutylene-based materials. The Second World War created an urgent demand for synthetic rubber and drove the transition toward large-scale supply. Butyl’s air-retention behavior made it particularly useful in tire inner tubes, while subsequent uses included protective coatings, tapes and other industrial rubber goods. ExxonMobil’s company history preserves this Standard Oil research lineage. Later chlorination and bromination produced separate halobutyl branches for improved curing and tire construction; those modifications are later developments, rather than part of the original 1937 formulation.
sections.nomenclature: IIR and isobutylene–isoprene rubber identify the same copolymer boundary in this record. Halobutyl rubbers are chemically modified derivatives made after IIR production and are not synonyms for unmodified butyl rubber; a filled and vulcanized compound is likewise a separate formulation state.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Butyl rubber (IIR) is a low-unsaturation random copolymer of isobutylene with approximately 0.5–2.5 mol% isoprene, produced by carbocationic polymerization at low temperature. The isoprene fraction supplies isolated unsaturation for sulfur, resin, or other cure chemistry, while the polyisobutylene-rich sequence gives the family its dense, low-permeability backbone. Open industrial and manufacturing accounts describe catalyst/initiator choice, chlorinated-solvent or slurry/solution phase, temperature, monomer ratio, and molecular-mass control before the rubber is isolated and compounded. Postpolymerization halogenation or other functionalization produces a modified IIR rather than redefining the unmodified family.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Unvulcanized IIR is soft and tacky; vulcanization and compounding create the useful elastomeric tensile, damping, fatigue, and compression response. In an open phyllosilicate/IIR study, Butyl 206 containing about 2.3 mol% unsaturation was compounded on a two-roll mill and vulcanized at 160 °C under 150–180 bar for 30 min. At a tensile-test speed of 500 mm min−1, the unfilled vulcanizate gave 2.5 ± 0.0 MPa tensile strength and 590 ± 57% elongation at break, while the filled formulations spanned 5.3–13.4 MPa and 1260–1289%, depending on the silica/phyllosilicate package. These are filler-specific compound examples, not neat-IIR constants. Molecular mass, isoprene level, filler dispersion, cure system, crosslink density, temperature, and strain history must accompany comparisons.
sections.processing: IIR is plasticized and compounded with zinc oxide, stearic acid, accelerators, sulfur, carbon black or mineral fillers, then sheeted/extruded, molded, and vulcanized. The open IIR composite study mixed the rubber and ingredients on a two-roll mill at 30–35 °C for 5–8 min, then compression-vulcanized filled plaques at 160 °C, 150–180 bar, and 30 min; cure kinetics were measured by MDR at 160 °C under ASTM D5289-17. This bounded example illustrates the need to manage filler incorporation, scorch/cure time, pressure, and heat transfer; actual innerliner, tube, sealant, or TPV processing depends on grade and formulation. Dynamic vulcanization or postpolymerization functionalization should not be folded into the base IIR process description.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Butyl rubber is an isobutylene–isoprene copolymer with an isobutylene-rich backbone and low unsaturation from isoprene. The small unsaturated fraction permits vulcanization while the backbone structure contributes to low gas permeability.
sections.properties: IIR is an elastomer known for low gas permeability and damping-related behavior, but response depends on isoprene content, molecular architecture, filler, cure state, and compound formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Regular butyl rubber serves tire inner tubes, curing bladders, protective clothing and adhesive tapes; designated food grades serve chewing gum.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO lists X_Butyl RB100, RB301 and RB402 in bales, with RB101-3 separately designated food grade.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Butyl rubber is explicitly listed in a thermochemical devulcanization patent. The intended breakdown is crosslink cleavage yielding reusable rubber chains; excessive heating can also damage the backbone. A complete ambient degradation-product inventory remains a gap.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes controlled devulcanization and reincorporation into rubber compounds. Listed applicability alone does not prove performance for every cure system; peroxide- and sulfur-cured materials need separate qualification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When butyl rubber compounds are processed on two-roll mills, HSE recommends extraction for dust and hot-process fume. Capture should cover the mill’s emission sources and remain effective during operation. Skin-contact controls and suitable cleaning methods address dermatitis risks from the compound and its additives; these are manufacturing exposure controls.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The industrial sources cover manufacturing and rubber-family behavior rather than one standardized compound. Finished-property claims must specify the particular IIR grade, curing system, and filled or unfilled formulation.

sections.overview: Bromobutyl rubber (BIIR) is a modified butyl rubber made by brominating the residual unsaturation in isobutylene–isoprene rubber. The modification adds cure reactivity while retaining the low gas permeability associated with the butyl-rubber backbone.
sections.history: Bromobutyl belongs to the halogenated-butyl technologies developed during the 1950s to overcome ordinary butyl rubber’s slow curing. This is later chemistry than the parent butyl material’s 1930s origins. Eric George Kent and John Walker’s Polysar patent, with priority in 1972 and issued in 1976, documents continued work on peroxide-containing cure systems for bromobutyl. Tire air-retention applications became a principal outlet for halobutyl materials. A later industrial account by JSR researcher Takuo Sone identifies Japan Butyl, the JSR–ExxonMobil venture, as a producer of both brominated and chlorinated grades. These milestones trace development and manufacture without assigning a single first-commercialization date to every bromobutyl grade.
sections.nomenclature: BIIR identifies brominated butyl rubber, not unmodified butyl rubber (IIR) or the separately halogenated chlorobutyl material. Bromine content and starting-IIR microstructure remain grade-defining variables, while a vulcanized BIIR compound is a formulation-specific network rather than the base modified polymer alone.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Bromobutyl rubber (BIIR) is made by brominating residual isoprene-derived unsaturation in IIR after low-temperature cationic copolymerization of isobutylene and a small isoprene fraction. In an open industrial account, unreacted monomers are first removed, the IIR is redissolved in a hydrocarbon solvent such as heptane or hexane, and liquid bromine is contacted with the polymer solution at about 40–60 °C before solvent recovery and finishing. A separate current technical sheet independently describes commercial BIIR as a butyl-rubber derivative reacted with bromine in a continuous process. These sources distinguish upstream halogenation from later compounding and vulcanization; bromine content and starting-IIR composition remain grade qualifiers rather than a unique repeat-unit definition.
sections.mechanicalProperties: BIIR retains the low gas permeability and elastomeric flexibility associated with IIR while bromination increases cure reactivity and compatibility with other unsaturated rubbers. In ISO 37 tests on 2 mm S2 specimens at 500 mm min−1, an open study of carbon-black-filled 50/50 natural-rubber/BIIR vulcanizates found that adding 3 phr of a bismaleimide co-curative to the conventional accelerated-sulfur formulation increased tensile strength by 60% and the modulus at 100% elongation by about 97% relative to the study's CV-only blend. The result is a filled/blended vulcanizate, not intrinsic BIIR. The existing industrial account separately reports faster cure and improved co-vulcanization after halogenation. Compound hardness, filler, sulfur/accelerator ratio, co-rubber, and cure state must accompany any numeric BIIR claim.
sections.processing: BIIR is compounded on an internal mixer or two-roll mill with fillers, activators, sulfur or peroxide curatives, and blend partners, then shaped and vulcanized. In the open BIIR/NR study, the rubbers were masticated in an internal mixer at 50 °C and 50 rpm, combined with zinc oxide, stearic acid, 25 phr carbon black, sulfur/CBS, and selected bismaleimide and dicumyl-peroxide additions, homogenized on a two-roll mill, and compression-molded at 170 °C using rheometer-derived cure times. Varying bismaleimide and DCP changed cure, tensile, and compression-set response; the work does not provide a universal tire-innerliner schedule. Mixing sequence, stock temperature, scorch safety, filler dispersion, vulcanization time, and section thickness should be established for the selected bromine grade and compound.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Bromobutyl rubber is a brominated derivative of butyl rubber, retaining an isobutylene-rich backbone with a low level of reactive halogenated unsaturation. Curing converts the compounded material to a formulation-specific network.
sections.properties: Bromobutyl combines low gas permeability associated with butyl rubber and reactivity introduced by bromination. Final properties depend on bromine content, grade, curatives, filler, and vulcanization conditions.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Bromobutyl serves tire and non-tire compounds, including pharmaceutical closures and sealants.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO lists X_Butyl BB2030, BB2040 and BBX2 raw rubber in bales; the grade is selected before compounding and curing.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.

sections.overview: Chlorobutyl rubber is a chlorinated derivative of butyl rubber, an isobutylene–isoprene elastomer. Its halogen functionality distinguishes it from the unhalogenated parent rubber.
sections.history: Chlorobutyl emerged from the 1950s modification of butyl rubber to improve curing and compatibility in rubber assemblies. Francis Baldwin and Robert Thomas’s Standard Oil research lineage is documented in a patent issued in 1960. It describes controlled chlorination and applications in tubeless-tire inner linings, bonding layers and tire-curing bags. Those examples show why the modification mattered commercially: air retention had to be combined with workable cure and adhesion behavior. Later producers included Japan Butyl, the JSR–ExxonMobil venture. The 1960 patent is a dated technical milestone in chlorobutyl development, rather than a claim that all halobutyl materials were invented at that moment.
sections.nomenclature: CIIR is the customary abbreviation for chlorobutyl rubber. It is distinct from unhalogenated butyl rubber (IIR) and from bromobutyl rubber; those related elastomers are not synonyms for this chlorine-functionalized material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chlorobutyl rubber is a chemically modified butyl rubber. Its parent elastomer is an isobutylene–isoprene copolymer made by low-temperature copolymerization; an NPTEL course example describes methyl chloride as the polymerization medium and 1–3% isoprene in the feed description. Chlorination is then a separate post-polymerization reaction: the parent rubber is dissolved in an inert hydrocarbon, commonly hexane, and contacted with chlorine. The cited industrial patent makes clear that hydrogen chloride accompanies chlorine incorporation, so chlorine charge and removal or neutralization are route controls. Vulcanization belongs to subsequent rubber compounding and is not part of the synthesis claim here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Chlorobutyl rubber (CIIR) is an elastomeric butyl-rubber derivative whose tensile, compression-set, stiffness, and damping response are compound properties rather than family constants. Open experimental work describes CIIR as a comparatively high-damping rubber, but its dynamic response varies with temperature and excitation frequency; reinforcing filler, oil or resin additions, crosslink system, and blending with other rubbers further change the result. In particular, a CIIR reference compound had a loss-factor peak at subzero temperature and substantially lower damping above 0 °C, while CIIR/NBR/CPE blends changed both tensile response and temperature-dependent damping.

A bounded tensile example is the reference CIIR compound reported by Roshan-Tabari and co-workers: 100 phr CIIR, 30 phr carbon black, 20 phr paraffinic oil, 3.5 phr coumarone resin, 2 phr sulfur, 5 phr zinc oxide, 1 phr stearic acid, and 3 phr accelerators. Before ageing, it had tensile strength at break of 7.0 ± 0.9 MPa and elongation at break of 762 ± 91% by ISO 37; after 168 h at 70 °C, the corresponding values were 8.1 ± 0.7 MPa and 720 ± 51%. The paper does not report the ISO 37 specimen geometry or tensile-test temperature. These values describe that filled and cured reference compound, not unfilled CIIR or a universal chlorobutyl-rubber range.

A commercial lining sheet further illustrates formulation specificity: Polycorp 1055 is explicitly a blended chlorobutyl lining with a soft natural-rubber tie gum. Its press-cured ASTM D3182 sample-sheet data specify a minimum ASTM D412 tensile strength of 900 psi and minimum elongation of 400%, with face hardness 55 ± 5 Shore A. Those minimum values do not define the CIIR family or a neat chlorobutyl grade.
sections.processing: Chlorobutyl is converted as a compounded, vulcanizable elastomer into hose, tire-inner-liner or sidewall, belt, sheet, roofing, and wire-insulation articles. Fillers, plasticizers/softeners, tackifiers, stabilizers, pigments, and cure ingredients should be mixed to homogeneity before shaping. In a filled chlorobutyl hose example, an 1100 cm³ Banbury mixed compound and cure ingredients for 4–6 min; approximately 2.3 mm sheet was applied to a steel mandrel and steam-autoclave cured at about 150 °C for 40 or 60 min. This is a formulation/article example, not a universal schedule. A separate carbon-black/ZnO/stearic-acid compound was vulcanized at 160 °C for 30 min, illustrating compound-dependent cure conditions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Chlorobutyl rubber is butyl rubber whose residual isoprene-derived unsaturation has been chlorinated, yielding a modified isobutylene/isoprene elastomer.
sections.properties: Its reported tensile and damping behavior belongs to specified vulcanized compounds and changes with temperature, frequency, fillers, and cure formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Chlorobutyl serves tire and non-tire compounds, including pharmaceutical closures and sealants.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO’s portfolio identifies X_Butyl CB1240 as chlorobutyl supplied in bales; closure or tire suitability depends on the formulated compound.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Chlorobutyl rubber is explicitly listed in a thermochemical devulcanization patent. The intended breakdown is crosslink cleavage yielding reusable rubber chains; excessive heating can also damage the backbone. A complete ambient degradation-product inventory remains a gap.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes controlled devulcanization and reincorporation into rubber compounds. Listed applicability alone does not prove performance for every cure system; peroxide- and sulfur-cured materials need separate qualification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When chlorobutyl rubber compounds are processed on two-roll mills, HSE recommends extraction for dust and hot-process fume. Capture should cover the mill’s emission sources and remain effective during operation. Skin-contact controls and suitable cleaning methods address dermatitis risks from the compound and its additives; these are manufacturing exposure controls.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited results are for named blends or filled vulcanizates and specified test conditions; chlorine content, parent-IIR grade, compound formulation, and cure prevent family-wide property values.

sections.overview: Polychloroprene rubber is an elastomer made by polymerization of chloroprene. Its chlorine-bearing diene-polymer backbone distinguishes it from polybutadiene and supports use in specialty rubber compounds.
sections.history: Polychloroprene’s development is closely associated with DuPont’s Wallace Carothers laboratory. In April 1930 Arnold Collins isolated chloroprene and observed its polymerization; Elmer Bolton encouraged the company to develop the material commercially. The resulting Neoprene became an important early synthetic rubber, with an industrial introduction in 1931. Its history subsequently extended beyond that original DuPont lineage into multiple producers and specialty grades. Industrial applications included footwear, adhesives and technical rubber goods. The discovery therefore involved a team and subsequent process development, rather than Carothers alone.
sections.nomenclature: CR abbreviates polychloroprene rubber, and chloroprene rubber is an equivalent common name. “Neoprene” is a commercial name and should not be used as the canonical family name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polychloroprene is produced by free-radical polymerization of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene), most commonly in alkaline aqueous emulsion. Water, emulsifier, radical initiator, and a chain-transfer or sulfur-based modifier are used to manage latex stability, conversion, molar mass, branching, and crystallization behavior. A historical example uses an azo initiator and an alkane thiol in aqueous dispersion. A separate sulfur-free route uses a persulfate/dithionite initiator and a combination of xanthogen disulfide and bis(acylaminophenyl) polysulfide transfer agents, then stops polymerization, removes residual monomer, and isolates the polymer. These are formulation-specific examples; not all polychloroprene uses the same transfer package. Copolymerized chloroprene grades should retain their comonomer limitation, and vulcanization is network formation after polymer manufacture rather than the chloroprene-polymerization step.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Polychloroprene is normally used as a formulated and crosslinked elastomer, so the mechanics of an uncured gum, a dense vulcanizate, an adhesive film, and an open- or closed-cell foam should not be combined. A dense cured compound can undergo large, nonlinear, substantially recoverable deformation with hysteresis and rate-dependent stiffness. Chain regularity and crystallization can add green strength or time- and temperature-dependent stiffening, while the crosslink network controls low-strain modulus, set, strength, tear, and fatigue. Grade modification and molar mass, crystallization rate, metal-oxide and accelerator cure chemistry, cure time and temperature, crosslink density, carbon-black or mineral reinforcement, plasticizer and antioxidant loading, foam density and cell structure, fabric reinforcement and orientation, specimen thickness and notch, temperature, strain rate, cyclic history, oil or water exposure, and ozone or thermal aging are all consequential. Oxidative aging can continue crosslinking and raise stiffness while reducing extensibility before chain scission or cracking dominates.

A bounded compound example is Denka DCR-30, a mercaptan-modified, very-slow-crystallizing polychloroprene grade. Denka's one-sheet test formulation contains 100 parts DCR-30, 1 part antioxidant, 4 parts calcined magnesia, 5 parts zinc oxide, and 0.35 part 2-mercaptoimidazoline, cured at 141 °C for 25 minutes. For that formulation the supplier lists 500% modulus of 1.0–4.0 MPa, tensile strength of at least 14.0 MPa, and elongation at break of at least 750%. These are descriptive formulation-control values, not neat-polymer constants or universal design allowables; specimen geometry, tensile rate, conditioning, and scatter are absent from the sheet. Independently, compression and dynamic-mechanical tests on a commercial black, 5 mm polychloroprene sheet showed increasing stress with rising strain rate or falling temperature, a largely rubbery response down to about −40 °C, and a sharp transition toward glassy behavior below that range. That study's filled commercial sheet and compression geometry are separate from the DCR-30 tensile formulation and should not be numerically merged.
sections.processing: Polychloroprene (CR, neoprene) is processed as a compounded elastomer by mastication, internal or two-roll mixing, calendering, extrusion, compression/transfer/injection molding, and subsequent vulcanization. Cure packages commonly use metal oxides and accelerators; scorch safety, compound viscosity, mold venting, section thickness, and heat removal control the balance between flow and premature cure. Denka's DCR-30 grade sheet gives a bounded test formulation containing 100 parts DCR-30 with 4 parts calcined magnesia and a 141 °C × 25 min cure; the values are for that mercaptan-modified, very-slow-crystallizing grade and formulation. A separate polychloroprene vulcanization patent describes conventional kneaders, rolls, internal mixers, and mixing extruders, a 16 min example mixing sequence, and vulcanization preferably at 140–210 °C under optional pressure, while emphasizing that the exact temperature/time pair depends on formulation, mold, and thickness. Chloroprene emulsion polymerization belongs in Synthesis; this section covers compounding, shaping, vulcanization, and post-cure conditioning.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polychloroprene is a chlorinated diene elastomer made by polymerizing chloroprene. Its backbone retains controlled unsaturation and chlorine-containing repeat units, and crystallization or crosslinking can develop during storage, stretching, or vulcanization.
sections.properties: Polychloroprene offers useful ozone, weathering, oil, flame, and abrasion resistance together with elastomeric flexibility. Crystallization, molecular architecture, filler, plasticizer, and cure system affect modulus, resilience, compression set, and low-temperature behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polychloroprene serves hoses, belt and roll covers in transport, machinery and marine/mining equipment, and contact adhesives in footwear and construction.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO offers Baypren grades for rubber-goods compounding and separate adhesive grades, with product selection and purchasing through its sales channel.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Polychloroprene is explicitly listed in a thermochemical devulcanization patent. The intended breakdown is crosslink cleavage yielding reusable rubber chains; excessive heating can also damage the backbone. A complete ambient degradation-product inventory remains a gap.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes controlled devulcanization and reincorporation into rubber compounds. Listed applicability alone does not prove performance for every cure system; peroxide- and sulfur-cured materials need separate qualification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: When polychloroprene rubber compounds are processed on two-roll mills, HSE recommends extraction for dust and hot-process fume. sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polychloroprene can crystallize during storage or strain and can show limited resistance to some fuels, aromatic solvents, strong oxidants, or high temperatures. Grade type, crystallization state, cure package, filler, aging, and test temperature must accompany service comparisons.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical polymerization produces polychloroprene. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another. For the diene component, addition leaves residual unsaturation whose position depends on the addition microstructure.

sections.overview: Ethylene–propylene rubber is the binary EPM/EPR copolymer of ethylene and propylene. It is a saturated elastomeric copolymer whose compound properties depend on molecular composition, fillers, oils, and the selected crosslinking formulation.
sections.history: Ethylene–propylene rubber arose from the 1950s expansion of coordination-catalyst chemistry. Giulio Natta, Giorgio Mazzanti and Giorgio Boschi’s Montecatini patent lineage claims Italian priority in December 1955 for amorphous elastomeric ethylene–propylene copolymers. The Natta archive records a Ferrara plant milestone in 1958. These saturated copolymers provided an alternative rubber platform with subsequent uses in electrical insulation and industrial rubber products. Later addition of a diene produced the related EPDM branch, with different curing possibilities. The research dates, plant milestone and later applications describe distinct stages; they should not be collapsed into a single invention date for all ethylene–propylene elastomers.
sections.nomenclature: EPM is the abbreviation used for ethylene–propylene rubber; EPR is also used in the cited literature for the binary copolymer. The record excludes EPDM, which adds a diene, as well as a particular vulcanized compound or an ethylene/propylene copolymer with a different modifier scope.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–propylene rubber (EPR, also called EPM) is the binary coordination copolymer of ethylene and propylene; it is distinct from EPDM because no diene feedstock is used. Conventional solution routes use a vanadium compound with an alkylaluminum cocatalyst, whereas metallocene catalyst systems offer an alternative documented route. One patent describes passing the two monomer gases into dry n-hexane containing vanadium oxychloride and an alkylaluminum catalyst, followed by catalyst removal and solvent flashing. A later patent describes metallocene catalysts for EPR production and contrasts them with vanadium-based production. Catalyst selection, monomer ratio, solvent, and process conditions are route-dependent; sulfur or peroxide vulcanization of a finished rubber article is not part of binary EPR synthesis.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–propylene rubber (EPM) is a saturated elastomer whose useful mechanical response is established after compounding and crosslinking, rather than being a single resin constant. Ethylene content and Mooney viscosity vary across commercial ethylene–propylene grades; in filled vulcanizates, filler/oil loading, cure chemistry, crosslink density and crosslink type, and specimen history govern strength, modulus, extensibility, compression set, and dynamic response. A peroxide network favors thermally robust carbon–carbon links, whereas the cited hybrid sulfur–peroxide study found that a mixed network can change the stiffness–extensibility balance; those findings are formulation-specific.

A bounded research example is Dutral CO 38 EPM (72 wt% ethylene; Mooney 60 MU) compounded with 70 phr N550 carbon black and 10 phr paraffinic oil. Its EPM6 formulation also contained 3 phr ZnO, 1 phr stearic acid, 1 phr sulfur, and 5 phr peroxide. Dumbbells punched from 2 mm compression-molded sheets gave a mean tensile strength of 15.7 MPa when tested at ambient temperature by ASTM D412 at 500 mm/min. This is a result for that cured, filled compound and test protocol—not a general EPM specification.
sections.processing:
EPM/EPR is normally compounded with fillers, oils, and a selected cure package before extrusion or molding; processing behavior varies with ethylene content, Mooney viscosity, oil extension, and filler loading. ENEOS lists EPM/EPDM grades with distinct processability choices: some have excellent extrusion characteristics, some high-speed vulcanization or unplasticized compounds, and others retain extrusion performance at high filler loading. These product-line descriptors support grade selection but do not define one family-wide extrusion or cure schedule.

A bounded high-ethylene EPM/EPDM cable-coating example used an ASTM D2230 tube extrusion test with a 50-mm device, 70 °C screw temperature, 90 °C head temperature, and 20 rpm; the reported samples were subsequently vulcanized at 160 °C for 20 min. The patent treats EPM and EPDM together, so the extrusion and cure settings are an equipment-, compound-, and specimen-specific example rather than a universal EPM recipe.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EPM is a saturated ethylene–propylene copolymer elastomer; it lacks the diene cure sites of EPDM and therefore requires curing approaches suitable for its saturated backbone.
sections.properties: EPM provides weather- and heat-resistant elastomer behavior, but molecular composition, filler, crosslinking, and compound design determine the finished response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. EPM serves automotive rubber goods, cables, appliances, masterbatch binders and polymer modification.

Purchasing. Versalis supplies Dutral CO054 as polyethylene-wrapped bales for downstream compounding.

Scale and evidence limits. The November 2022 sheet specifies a typical 25 kg bale and a 750 kg box containing 30 bales: tens-of-kilograms units consolidated toward a tonne. These are package sizes, not annual EPM demand.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Ethylene-propylene rubber is explicitly listed in a thermochemical devulcanization patent. The intended breakdown is crosslink cleavage yielding reusable rubber chains; excessive heating can also damage the backbone. A complete ambient degradation-product inventory remains a gap.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes controlled devulcanization and reincorporation into rubber compounds. Listed applicability alone does not prove performance for every cure system; peroxide- and sulfur-cured materials need separate qualification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Press curing of ethylene–propylene rubber compounds can release rubber fume, especially when a mold opens. HSE recommends source extraction around presses and control of skin contact with process residues. Assessment should use the complete compound formulation because curatives, fillers and processing aids contribute to exposure alongside the elastomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited crosslink study treats a designed composite, while product information groups EPM and EPDM offerings. Its values or application details must not be transferred between the two rubber classes.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Coordination copolymerization forms the binary EPR chain. Olefin first coordinates to an active metal site and then inserts into the metal–carbon bond of the growing chain. sections.overview: Ethylene–propylene–diene rubber is the EPDM terpolymer of ethylene, propylene, and a nonconjugated diene such as ethylidene norbornene, dicyclopentadiene, or vinyl norbornene. The diene-derived unsaturation supports subsequent vulcanization of formulated rubber articles.
sections.history: EPDM developed from ethylene–propylene rubber by incorporating a diene to provide additional curing chemistry. The Society of Polymer Science, Japan’s chronology records DuPont and Montecatini production in 1963, followed by other manufacturers. DSM’s Keltan production at Geleen began in 1967; the later Arlanxeo site chronology documents additional lines in 1973 and 2003 and adoption of its ACE catalyst on the third line in 2013. Major application areas have included automotive seals and hoses, building membranes and electrical products. This sequence shows the progression from a new terpolymer platform to large-scale manufacture and later catalyst improvements, with supplier milestones distinguished from the earliest ethylene–propylene research.
sections.nomenclature: EPDM is the abbreviation for ethylene–propylene–diene rubber. The diene comonomer is the defining boundary: binary EPM/EPR is excluded, and a cured EPDM compound, reclaimed rubber, or reinforced membrane is a formulation/article state rather than a separate synonym for the terpolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–propylene–diene rubber (EPDM) is produced by coordination terpolymerization of ethylene, propylene, and a diene, commonly a nonconjugated diene such as ethylidene norbornene (ENB), dicyclopentadiene, or vinyl norbornene. An open review describes the family as catalytic coordination terpolymerization and surveys Group IV catalyst systems; a separate patent identifies solution or slurry Ziegler–Natta manufacture using vanadium compounds such as VOCl3, V(acac)3, or VCl4 with aluminum cocatalysts. A specific historical solution example charges a diene feedstock before ethylene and propylene in a vanadium/organaluminum-catalyzed solution. Diene selection, catalyst chemistry, and monomer conversion govern the product architecture. The retained unsaturation may subsequently support formulation-specific vulcanization, but cure-agent packages and curing schedules do not define EPDM synthesis and are excluded here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–propylene–diene rubber (EPDM) is a vulcanizable terpolymer, so its tensile, tear, hardness, elastic recovery, and aging response are properties of a particular cured compound and construction. Relevant variables include ethylene/propylene balance, diene type and content, cure system and crosslink network, carbon-black/filler and oil loading, reclaimed-rubber fraction, and thermal or weathering exposure. An open study of a Keltan 8550 ECO sealing compound found that replacing virgin polymer with devulcanized EPDM changed network structure: increasing reclaimed content raised Shore A hardness but reduced tensile strength and elongation; reducing the accompanying carbon black and softener partially changed that response. This trend should not be read as a general EPDM value.

A bounded product example is FlexWhite EPDM roofing membrane. The 60 mil membrane, listed at 1.549 mm actual thickness, reported 9.2 MPa tensile strength and 420% ultimate elongation by ASTM D412, Die C; the corresponding 90 mil product reported 11.0 MPa and 495%. These are specific reinforced membrane constructions, not properties of unfilled EPDM resin or every EPDM compound.
sections.processing:
EPDM articles are made from compounded rubber by internal or two-roll mixing, extrusion or calendering, and heat/pressure vulcanization; the cure schedule must be matched to the diene, curative package, section thickness, and target article. A public GenFlex reinforced-membrane process flow lists mixer → extrusion → calendering (with optional scrim) → curing with heat/steam and pressure → trimming and packaging. This is a membrane manufacturing route, not a universal requirement for every EPDM product.

A laboratory EPDM formulation study illustrates bounded feed and cure handling. EPDM, zinc oxide, stearic acid, carbon black, and naphthenic oil were charged sequentially to an internal mixer at 90 °C and 60 rpm; sulfur and accelerator were added in a second stage at 50 °C. After more than 16 h storage, the compound was press-vulcanized at 170 °C under 15–20 MPa. Those temperatures, pressure, dwell history, and formulation apply to the tested vulcanizates; other extrusion profiles, peroxide cures, and thick sections require separate rheometry and heat-transfer validation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EPDM is an ethylene–propylene elastomer containing a low level of diene-derived unsaturation that enables sulfur or peroxide crosslinking. The selected diene and cure system affect network structure.
sections.properties: EPDM is valued for weathering and thermal-oxidative resistance, but vulcanizate behavior depends on diene content, filler, curatives, reclaimed-rubber content, and aging exposure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. EPDM serves vehicle weatherseals and coolant hoses, roof and pond membranes, building gaskets, wire/cable and appliance seals.

Purchasing. ARLANXEO supplies Keltan raw-rubber grades through its product and technical-sales channels; formulation, curing system and end-use requirements guide selection.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: EPDM is explicitly listed in a thermochemical devulcanization patent. The intended breakdown is crosslink cleavage yielding reusable rubber chains; excessive heating can also damage the backbone. A complete ambient degradation-product inventory remains a gap.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes controlled devulcanization and reincorporation into rubber compounds. Listed applicability alone does not prove performance for every cure system; peroxide- and sulfur-cured materials need separate qualification.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Press curing of ethylene–propylene–diene rubber compounds can release rubber fume, especially when a mold opens. HSE recommends source extraction around presses and control of skin contact with process residues. Assessment should use the complete compound formulation because curatives, fillers and processing aids contribute to exposure alongside the elastomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The membrane declaration concerns a specific reinforced roofing product, and aging studies concern formulated vulcanizates. Their values and aging results are not general EPDM-family properties.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Coordination terpolymerization retains diene-derived sites for later cure. Olefin first coordinates to an active metal site and then inserts into the metal–carbon bond of the growing chain. The longer metal-bound chain can coordinate and insert another monomer; catalyst environment and feed selection govern the resulting sequence and stereochemistry. The selected nonconjugated diene provides residual unsaturation for a later vulcanization step.

steps.body: Follow repeated olefin coordination and insertion at the activated catalyst. Each insertion adds carbon atoms to the chain and regenerates a metal-bound growth site. Apply the catalyst and comonomer choices of this route when interpreting branching or stereoregularity.

steps.body: Control monomer incorporation during terpolymerization; diene identity determines the residual cure-site motif.

sections.overview: Acrylic rubber is the ACM family of alkyl-acrylate copolymer elastomers. Its cure-site comonomer and selected cure system are formulation variables, so a finished vulcanized network is not a single, composition-invariant ACM material.
sections.history: Acrylic rubber was already the subject of dedicated United States government research during the 1940s. W. C. Mast and C. H. Fisher’s December 1948 report describes the Eastern Regional Research Laboratory’s Lactoprene elastomers, pilot-scale work and B. F. Goodrich’s commercial production. This establishes activity and manufacture by 1948 without claiming a unique first synthesis. Heat- and oil-resistant automotive seals, gaskets and hoses became important uses. Manabu Sugiyama’s 2016 Zeon account describes later demand from hotter engine compartments and identifies Zeon and Unimatec as major producers at that time. Across this history, incorporation of cure sites and development of reliable curing systems were recurring routes to useful acrylic elastomers.
sections.nomenclature: ACM is used here for acrylic rubber as a family name, rather than for one specified alkyl-acrylate copolymer or cured compound. Cure-site chemistry and the resulting crosslinked network remain part of the particular grade or formulation, not alternate names for the family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Acrylic rubber (ACM) is a family of alkyl-acrylate copolymer elastomers, generally made by emulsion free-radical copolymerization. Alkyl-acrylate selection establishes the base elastomer, while a small cure-site comonomer is incorporated so that the chosen cure system can subsequently form the finished network. The industrial emulsion route and cure-site/cure-agent pairing therefore describe family chemistry, not one invariant ACM recipe. The resulting gum is later compounded with a grade-matched cure system to form the finished network.
sections.mechanicalProperties: ACM is used when an elastomeric response is needed alongside oil and heat resistance, but tensile behavior depends on acrylate composition, cure-site chemistry, crosslink density, fillers, and any blend phase. The sliding-graft study likewise shows that vulcanization and formulated additions alter ACM-composite damping and mechanical response. As a bounded neighboring formulation example, an NBR/ACM 90:10 dual-vulcanized seal compound reported tensile strength 21.15 MPa, elongation at break 276%, and 100% modulus 6.35 MPa; these are values for that NBR-rich, filled covulcanizate, not ACM-family constants.
sections.processing: ACM is normally compounded and shaped while uncured, then vulcanized with a cure package selected for its cure-site comonomer. Two-roll-mill mixing, molding, and thermal cure are therefore meaningful conversion steps, but the settings belong to the named compound. In the NBR/ACM 90:10 study, ingredients were mixed on a two-roll mill and vulcanized in a flat press at 165 °C before an oven stage at 160 °C; that procedure cannot be transferred unchanged to another ACM grade, cure chemistry, or part geometry. Supplier or compound-specific guidance remains necessary for mixing, mold filling, and cure time.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Acrylic rubber is an alkyl-acrylate copolymer elastomer. A small cure-site comonomer is incorporated into the polymer, and vulcanization converts the formulated rubber into a network whose structure depends on the cure system.
sections.properties: ACM is valued as an elastomer with heat- and oil-resistant behavior, but its final response is governed by acrylate composition, cure-site chemistry, crosslink density, fillers, and other compounding ingredients.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. ACM serves automotive and industrial oil seals and hoses.

Purchasing. Zeon lists Nipol AR71 and AR72LS oil-seal grades and AR22 hose grades, with specialized heat/cold variants; purchase by raw-rubber grade through supplier inquiry.

Scale and evidence limits. Zeon reported Japanese ACM capacity of 8,500 t/year in May 2015. This historical company capacity is neither current capacity nor measured production, purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A hydrothermal-devulcanization patent explicitly lists acrylic rubber and targets sulfur crosslinks while seeking to preserve the backbone. This is proposed network breakdown for applicable cure systems; the source does not identify ambient acrylic-rubber degradation products.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Hot, pressurized-water devulcanization followed by recompounding is a patented route explicitly including acrylic rubber. Its sulfur-bond mechanism must not be generalized to every ACM cure chemistry; an ACM-specific recovery yield and commercial implementation are not established.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Press curing of acrylic rubber compounds can release rubber fume, especially when a mold opens. HSE recommends source extraction around presses and control of skin contact with process residues. Assessment should use the complete compound formulation because curatives, fillers and processing aids contribute to exposure alongside the elastomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Reported ACM properties cannot be treated as neat-family constants: the industrial source distinguishes cure-site and cure-system choices, while the cited composite study concerns a separately formulated, chemically crosslinked ACM composite.

sections.overview: Ethylene–acrylic elastomer is the AEM rubber family based on ethylene and alkyl-acrylate comonomers, with cure-site chemistry used in suitable grades. It is an elastomeric copolymer material whose final network and properties depend on the cure formulation.
sections.history: Ethylene–acrylic elastomers became commercial materials when DuPont introduced Vamac in 1975. Their development sought to combine resistance to oils and oxidation with useful low-temperature flexibility. Anestis Logothetis’s DuPont patent, with a 1971 application lineage and issued in 1975, documents ethylene/alkyl-acrylate copolymers incorporating cure-site monomers. Automotive sealing became an important application, including cylinder-head-cover gaskets. Later grades and formulations developed both terpolymer and dipolymer branches with different cure systems. The early patent records a particular polymerization approach; it is evidence of the development effort, not proof that every commercial AEM grade uses that exact route.
sections.nomenclature: AEM is the abbreviation used for ethylene–acrylic elastomer. The record covers ethylene/alkyl-acrylate elastomer copolymers, including specified cure-site variants; it excludes the thermoplastic ethylene–acrylic acid copolymer (EAA), ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymer (EMAA), and a particular cured compound as synonyms.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–acrylic elastomer (AEM) is an ethylene–alkyl-acrylate copolymer family, not the acid copolymer EAA. A manufacturer reference identifies a common AEM composition as ethylene, methyl acrylate, and a small amount of a carboxylic-acid-containing cure-site monomer. A historical DuPont patent supplies one bounded polymerization example: ethylene, a C1–C8 alkyl acrylate, and an optional cure-site monomer react in an inert solvent with boron trifluoride and a free-radical initiator. The cure-site is relevant only for formulations intended to be subsequently crosslinked; it should not be treated as mandatory for every ethylene–acrylate copolymer, and cure schedules are outside this synthesis record.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–acrylic elastomer (AEM) is an ethylene/acrylate rubber, commonly with a small cure-site comonomer, whose mechanical behavior is determined after vulcanization. Ethylene-to-acrylate balance controls low-temperature behavior, while cure-site chemistry, crosslink density, filler, plasticizer, hardness, and heat or fluid ageing control tensile, tear, damping, and compression-set results. An openly available AEM technical chapter notes that most commercial AEM materials include a third cure-site monomer enabling diamine crosslinking, so base-polymer composition alone does not define finished-part mechanics.

A bounded AEM technical-sheet example describes an ethylene/methyl-acrylate AEM family with 8–40% methyl acrylate and reports, for its stated test material, 100% tensile stress 6.00 MPa, tensile strength 16.0–16.4 MPa, elongation at break 260–280%, Shore A hardness 63–64, and compression set 16% after 70 h at 150 °C. Tensile values are labeled ASTM D412, hardness ASTM D2240, and compression set ASTM D395. These are supplier test-sheet values for that material, not a universal AEM range. A separate compound supplier reports 60- and 70-Shore-A AEM compounds at 13.8 MPa tensile strength with 450% and 400% elongation, respectively, further showing the formulation and hardness dependence.
sections.processing:
Ethylene–acrylic elastomer is converted as a compounded and vulcanized rubber. The selected AEM grade is mixed with filler, plasticizer or process aid, antioxidant, and its compatible cure package in an internal mixer or on an open mill, sheeted or pelletized, then extruded, calendered, compression-, transfer-, or injection-molded and cured. Cure chemistry is grade-dependent: acid-cure-site terpolymers commonly use diamine systems and may require post-cure, whereas ethylene/methyl-acrylate dipolymers can use peroxide/coagent systems. Ingredient compatibility, stock temperature, dispersion, scorch safety, venting, oxygen inhibition, article thickness, and post-cure requirements must therefore be qualified together.

DuPont's bounded Vamac DP examples were mixed in a small laboratory internal mixer, sheeted on a roll mill, and press-cured for 10 min at 177 °C. The same guide describes extrusion-head temperatures around 70 °C for its dipolymer compounds, pressure of at least 0.41–0.55 MPa during autoclave cure to avoid sponging, nitrogen purging because oxygen inhibits peroxide cure, and 160–190 °C molds. These values apply to the cited Vamac dipolymer compounds and equipment; diamine-cured AEM terpolymers use different packages and usually different cure/post-cure schedules.
sections.structureAndMorphology: AEM is an ethylene/alkyl-acrylate elastomer that may include a cure-site comonomer. The final vulcanizate structure depends on the particular dipolymer or terpolymer and cure system.
sections.properties: AEM balances elastomeric flexibility with heat and oil resistance, but its response depends on composition, crosslinking, fillers, and compound formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. AEM serves automotive fluid-contact seals and gaskets, extruded hoses and wire/cable compounds.

Purchasing. The documented Vamac Ultra DX product is a raw-rubber bale grade intended for compounding and peroxide cure. The historical DuPont bulletin establishes product form; current supplier and availability require confirmation.

Scale and evidence limits. The bulletin gives nominal bale dimensions but no order mass or annual purchasing/consumption figure. No independent AEM-specific tonnage was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The manufacturer lists alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, esters and organic acids among the possible thermal decomposition products of VAMAC Ultra EV. Named examples include acetaldehyde, formaldehyde, acrolein, acrylic acid and maleic anhydride; carbon oxides and phosphorus-containing products are also listed. These are formulation-specific thermal products, not a measured inventory from neat AEM weathering.

Timescales: The SDS states that thermal decomposition accelerates above 282 °C and depends on both temperature and time at temperature. This is not a measured complete-decomposition duration or an environmental rate.

Environmental persistence: The supplied grade is water-insoluble and stable under normal handling. The SDS supplies no persistence or degradability data; these physical characteristics do not establish a soil, water or landfill lifetime.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For VAMAC Ultra EV as supplied, Celanese lists recycling, energy-recovery incineration and landfill as disposal options, emphasizing the material’s fuel value when recycling is unavailable. These are grade-specific waste-management options, with treatment subject to local requirements. The safety sheet does not establish a devulcanization process or recovery of AEM from a cured automotive part.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Celanese’s VAMAC Ultra EV safety sheet distinguishes the supplied AEM bales from hot processing conditions: heated material can emit irritating fumes, while contact with hot material can burn skin. It recommends local exhaust during hot processing, eye protection and gloves. These handling findings describe the specified commercial grade and its formulation, rather than every ethylene–acrylic elastomer compound.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Manufacturer and handbook guidance differentiate AEM grades and cure systems. Values in a named seal or Vamac compound cannot be extended to all AEM materials.

sections.overview: Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber is the CO elastomer made by polymerizing epichlorohydrin (chloromethyloxirane). It is a synthetic rubber material whose formulation and vulcanization determine the properties of a finished article.
sections.history: The useful rubber form of polyepichlorohydrin must be distinguished from earlier crystalline polymer. Pruitt and Baggett at Dow prepared semicrystalline material in 1954; Edwin Vandenberg at Hercules developed amorphous polyepichlorohydrin in 1957. In his oral history, Vandenberg describes discovering the importance of water-modified organoaluminum catalysts and the subsequent licensing arrangement with B. F. Goodrich. Hercules and Goodrich commercialized epichlorohydrin elastomers under Herclor and Hydrin names. The oil-resistant rubber platform supported hoses, seals and air ducts, while later research explored membranes and electrolytes. Those later applications include copolymers and modified materials, and should not all be assigned to the unmodified homopolymer.
sections.nomenclature: CO is the abbreviation for the epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber record; poly(chloromethyloxirane) is an alternate chemical name. The homopolymer boundary excludes ECO, the epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide copolymer, and does not equate a cured compound with the uncured polymer record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber (CO, polyepichlorohydrin) is the ring-opening polymerization product of epichlorohydrin; the resulting repeat units retain chloromethyl side groups. A historical assessment identifies high-molecular-weight CO as a distinct elastomer made from the single epichlorohydrin feedstock. In one modern, source-specific activated-monomer route, epichlorohydrin is added in a controlled manner to a boron trifluoride diethyl etherate/water initiating system in toluene; the report describes operation at 20–40 °C and polymer isolation after conversion. These are polymer-formation examples, not a recommendation of a universal catalyst system or an article cure schedule.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber (CO) is a cured elastomer, so its tensile, elongation, hardness, rebound, and compression-set response belong to a specified vulcanizate rather than to the uncured gum alone. The chlorine-rich CO homopolymer is described as having good oil resistance and low-temperature flexibility but poorer rebound than the ethylene-oxide copolymer. Cure chemistry and crosslink density, carbon-black reinforcement, plasticizer, hardness target, and ageing environment all materially change the measured response; the public EPA report specifically notes carbon black as a tensile-strength improver and plasticizer as a low-temperature-flexibility aid.

A bounded published vulcanizate comparison in that EPA report gives the ECH homopolymer 15.9 MPa tensile strength, 230% ultimate elongation, 82 Shore A hardness, −18 °C low-temperature brittleness, and Lupke rebound 26% at 23 °C and 75% at 100 °C. The report does not identify the complete formulation or the tensile test standard, so these are comparative vulcanizate values, not neat-gum properties or a family range. A separate rubber-compound supplier illustrates the formulation issue: its 50-Shore-A CO/ECO compound 571AG lists 9.7 MPa tensile strength and 400% elongation; because it does not distinguish CO from ECO or disclose a full cure package, it is contextual compound evidence only.
sections.processing:
Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber is converted by conventional elastomer compounding, shaping, and vulcanization. Fillers, plasticizers, process aids, antidegradants, metal oxides, and the selected cure package are incorporated on a mill or internal mixer before extrusion, calendering, or molding. Because many CO cure systems release or generate acidic species, the Vanderbilt handbook emphasizes acid acceptors and pH control; magnesium oxide, calcium carbonate, or calcium oxide may be used in formulation-specific roles to bind hydrogen chloride and support the cure. Mixing sequence and temperature must preserve scorch safety and dispersion, and the chosen press, injection, steam, hot-air, infrared, or microwave cure must be qualified for the compound and article thickness.

A bounded Osaka Soda patent example mixed a stated epichlorohydrin-rubber formulation for 15 min on rolls held at 80 °C, sheeted it, and pressure-molded it at 160 °C and 7.8 MPa for 20 min. The patent also gives a much broader 100–200 °C and 0.5–60 min cure envelope across its examples and cure systems. Neither the roll/mold schedule nor that broad patent envelope is a universal CO production window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: CO is a polyepichlorohydrin elastomer with chloromethyl-bearing repeat units; compounding and curing form a finished rubber network.
sections.properties: Its fuel-, oil-, and gas-resistant elastomer behavior depends on molecular characteristics, cure system, filler, and compound design.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber serves automotive fuel/oil hoses, diaphragms and gaskets.

Purchasing. Zeon explicitly identifies Hydrin H75 as the homopolymer and supplies it in bales for compounding; it is distinct from ECO copolymers and GECO terpolymers.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber is explicitly included in a heat-stabilization patent describing hydrogen chloride release during curing or severe heating. A complete inventory of environmental breakdown products remains unresolved.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The cited chlorine-containing elastomers resist weathering and ozone. This resistance is not a measured mineralization lifetime; stabilizers and cure chemistry influence the finished compound.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Laboratory chlorine reclamation has been demonstrated using commercial polyepichlorohydrin (PECH; reported Mw about 700,000). Liu and colleagues reacted this polymer with 7,8-benzoquinoline using Cu/Pd catalysts and sodium nitrate in DMSO under 3 bar oxygen at 140 °C for 15 h, producing 10-chlorobenzoquinoline. This chemical-reclamation route transfers chlorine into a new product; it does not recover intact rubber or epichlorohydrin monomer. The study used purchased pure polymer, so its result does not establish recovery of compounded, vulcanized CO service parts or commercial operation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber articles, trimming and finishing are distinct exposure-generating operations. HSE recommends local extraction for finishing emissions, appropriate protection against skin contamination and cleaning without dispersing dust. These controls address fabricated rubber compounds; any additional chemical hazards must be assessed from the grade’s curatives, fillers and processing conditions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The EPA assessment and compound guide cover industrial elastomer uses and specified vulcanizates; they do not establish generic properties for every CO grade or cured compound.

sections.overview: Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber is the ECO elastomeric copolymer of epichlorohydrin and ethylene oxide. The comonomer-containing backbone distinguishes it from the epichlorohydrin homopolymer CO; finished performance still depends on formulation and cure.
sections.history: Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber emerged from Edwin Vandenberg’s Hercules research into high-molecular-weight polyethers. Adding ethylene oxide developed the amorphous epichlorohydrin platform into a distinct copolymer rubber. Vandenberg’s 1976 technical account identifies both Hercules and B. F. Goodrich as substantial producers, under the Herclor and Hydrin names, and explains the appeal of combining oil resistance with useful rubber and environmental behavior. The Hydrin business subsequently became associated with Zeon. Automotive fuel-system parts were an important outlet, and later grades also served conductive printer and copier components. These are milestones for the copolymer branch, rather than an independent discovery date inferred from the first epichlorohydrin homopolymer.
sections.nomenclature: ECO is the abbreviation used for the epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide copolymer rubber. This copolymer record excludes CO homopolymer and other epichlorohydrin copolymers with different comonomer scopes; a vulcanized ECO compound is a formulation state, not a separate synonym for the base copolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber (ECO) is a copolyether elastomer made by ring-opening copolymerization of epichlorohydrin and ethylene oxide. The historical assessment distinguishes ECO from CO and describes trialkylaluminum/water catalyst systems, with acetylacetone as a catalyst-promoting additive, for epichlorohydrin elastomer manufacture; it also notes that ethylene oxide reacts more rapidly than epichlorohydrin in a cited copolymer operation. An independent patent example instead polymerizes the two epoxides in ether/toluene using an organomagnesium/resorcinol catalyst system, then precipitates and purifies the copolymer. These route examples establish feedstocks and polymer-formation chemistry only; downstream vulcanization is not included here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber (ECO) is a vulcanized copolyether elastomer whose physical response varies with epichlorohydrin/ethylene-oxide composition, polymer molecular weight, cure chemistry and density, reinforcement and plasticizer loading, hardness target, and ageing medium. Relative to the epichlorohydrin homopolymer, the ethylene-oxide-containing copolymer is described in a public comparison as having better low-temperature flexibility and rebound but lower oil resistance. Zeon likewise presents tensile, elongation, and compression set as values of a ‘typical Hydrin compound’ and a broad compound range, rather than ECO constants.

A bounded vulcanizate example in the EPA comparison reports ECH–ethylene oxide copolymer tensile strength 15.0 MPa, ultimate elongation 320%, Shore A hardness 74, low-temperature brittleness −40 °C, and Lupke rebound 67% at 23 °C and 63% at 100 °C. The source does not give full formulation or tensile-method details, so these are comparative cured-compound values only. Zeon’s current ECO page lists, for a typical Hydrin compound, tensile at break 14 MPa, elongation at break 450%, and compression set 15% after 22 h at 100 °C; the listed across-compound ranges are 8–18 MPa, 150–600%, and 10–25%, respectively. These supplier figures are illustrative formulation ranges, not specifications for every ECO grade.
sections.processing:
Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber is processed by compounding the gum with reinforcing or mineral filler, plasticizer and process aid, antidegradant, metal oxides or other acid acceptors, and a cure system, followed by extrusion, calendering, injection molding, or compression molding and vulcanization. The Vanderbilt handbook notes that ECO is compounded broadly like other elastomers but that cure-package acidity and compound pH deserve particular control: acid acceptors such as magnesium oxide, calcium carbonate, or calcium oxide can bind hydrogen chloride and influence cure behavior. Mixing order and stock temperature should therefore be set to obtain dispersion without consuming scorch safety, and cure time must be adjusted for the formulation and article thickness.

A patent example covering an epichlorohydrin/ethylene-oxide copolymer mixed the specified compound for 15 min on 80 °C rolls, formed a sheet, and pressure-molded it at 160 °C and 7.8 MPa for 20 min. The same patent lists press and injection molding plus steam, hot-air, infrared, and microwave heating as possible cure routes and gives a broad 100–200 °C, 0.5–60 min range across its formulations. Those conditions are examples from that cure chemistry, not universal ECO settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ECO is a copolyether elastomer containing epichlorohydrin- and ethylene-oxide-derived units. Cure chemistry converts the formulated polymer to a network.
sections.properties: Ethylene-oxide incorporation changes low-temperature and fuel-related elastomer behavior, while final properties remain compound- and cure-dependent.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber serves automotive fuel/oil hoses, diaphragms and gaskets.

Purchasing. Zeon lists Hydrin C2000L and C2000 specifically as copolymer bales. Buyers specify the ECO grade rather than assuming every Hydrin product has this composition.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable, separately reported purchase or consumption tonnage for this material was established in the checked open sources. The listed grades document availability and uses, not market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber is explicitly included in a heat-stabilization patent describing hydrogen chloride release during curing or severe heating. A complete inventory of environmental breakdown products remains unresolved.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The cited chlorine-containing elastomers resist weathering and ozone. This resistance is not a measured mineralization lifetime; stabilizers and cure chemistry influence the finished compound.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Laboratory chlorine reclamation has been demonstrated using commercial poly(epichlorohydrin-co-ethylene oxide) containing 64–69 wt% epichlorohydrin. Liu and colleagues reacted this polymer with 7,8-benzoquinoline using Cu/Pd catalysts and sodium nitrate in DMSO under 3 bar oxygen at 140 °C for 15 h, producing 10-chlorobenzoquinoline. This chemical-reclamation route transfers chlorine into a new product; it does not recover intact rubber or epichlorohydrin monomer. The study used purchased pure polymer, so its result does not establish recovery of compounded, vulcanized ECO service parts or commercial operation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber articles, trimming and finishing are distinct exposure-generating operations. HSE recommends local extraction for finishing emissions, appropriate protection against skin contamination and cleaning without dispersing dust. These controls address fabricated rubber compounds; any additional chemical hazards must be assessed from the grade’s curatives, fillers and processing conditions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The product information describes named Hydrin materials and the EPA report covers industrial elastomer categories; neither should be read as a universal ECO formulation or performance envelope.
