sections.overview: Modacrylic fiber polymers are acrylic-type copolymers designed for conversion into synthetic fibers. Their comonomer composition differentiates them from conventional acrylic fiber polymers and can be tailored for flame-resistant fiber performance.
sections.history: Modacrylic fibers are a group of acrylonitrile copolymers with several commercial histories. A well-documented example is Kaneka’s Kanekalon/Kanecaron, manufactured at Takasago and marketed from 1957. Hairlike texture, colorability and flame resistance supported wigs, hairpieces, artificial fur, curtains, bedding and stuffed toys. In its 2014 annual report, Kaneka described an additional Malaysian manufacturing facility intended to supply hair-extension markets in Africa. This illustrates how development moved from introducing a new synthetic textile fiber to tailoring large-scale production to specific consumer uses. The 1957 date belongs to Kaneka’s product line, not a universal invention date for all modacrylic compositions.
sections.nomenclature: Modacrylic is a fiber-polymer family term, not the name of one fixed copolymer composition. It should not be used as an unqualified synonym for acrylic fiber polymer, because the comonomer scope differs.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Modacrylic fiber polymers are acrylonitrile-containing copolymers in the modacrylic composition range, commonly incorporating vinyl chloride or vinylidene chloride and optional ionic or vinyl-ester comonomers. The polymer family is defined by the copolymer composition and is distinct from the wet- or dry-spinning operation that turns a solution into fiber. Documented examples use acrylonitrile, vinylidene chloride, vinyl acetate, and an ionic comonomer, while another route uses acrylonitrile with vinyl chloride or vinylidene chloride and a sulfo-containing vinyl monomer. Emulsion and solution polymerization are both reported; feed composition, monomer-addition timing, initiator/redox system, and conversion control the copolymer architecture. The cited monomer ratios are particular flame-resistant or color-control examples, not a universal modacrylic formulation.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Modacrylic is supplied chiefly as drawn staple or filament fibre, so tenacity and elongation apply to a defined fibre grade, linear density, orientation, and conditioning rather than an isotropic bulk polymer. Acrylonitrile/comonomer composition, draw and heat-setting history, denier, crimp, moisture, and blend construction control textile response; flame-retardant comonomers and finishing can alter strength and elongation. Protex® regular FR modacrylic grades are reported at less than 3.3 dtex with tenacity 2.6–2.8 cN/dtex and elongation 27–29%; these reference values are grade- and fibre-size-specific, with no test rate or conditioning stated. Independently, a modacrylic/polyacrylate/lyocell yarn study reports its specified 1.0 and 1.7 dtex modacrylic staple fibres at 3.13 and 3.17 cN/dtex, respectively, with about 36% breaking elongation; those fibre data do not establish intrinsic bulk-modacrylic properties or a general textile-fabric value.
sections.processing: Modacrylics are generally converted to fiber by solution spinning because the acrylonitrile-based copolymer family is not normally melt-spun. Wet spinning extrudes a polymer dope through a spinneret into a water/solvent coagulation bath, followed by washing, drawing, drying, and sometimes heat setting; dry spinning instead removes solvent in a heated gas stream. An open study of poly(acrylonitrile-co-vinyl chloride) used a 20 wt% DMSO dope, a 100-hole spinneret with 0.07 mm holes, and coagulation baths containing 20, 35, or 50 wt% DMSO at 60 °C; coagulation and draw ratio changed voids, orientation, and fiber performance. A separate high-retraction modacrylic patent gives a bounded sequence for its particular copolymer composition: draw 2× in an 80 °C bath, dry in air at 110–120 °C with 25–30% free contraction, then draw 2× in air at 70–80 °C. It warns that air-drawing above 100 °C can deteriorate characteristics and below 50 °C can cause filament breakage. These dope, bath, draw, and thermal settings are formulation- and line-specific, not family-wide spinning specifications.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Modacrylic fibers are acrylonitrile-based copolymer fibers containing substantial comonomer content.
sections.properties: Flame resistance, shrinkage, and fiber mechanics vary with comonomer composition, spinning, and blend construction.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Modacrylic grades serve protective clothing, mattress fire barriers, upholstery, curtains and nonwoven filters. Kaneka also lists automotive uses, paint rollers and battery reinforcement for particular grades.

Purchasing. Kaneka Protex offers staple grades selected by linear density, cut length, color and blend compatibility, plus uncrimped tow for short-cut battery use. Textile and nonwoven buyers source specified fiber grades through the producer.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found in the checked open sources; supplier offerings establish availability, not sales volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Chlorine-containing modacrylic fibers can release hydrogen chloride during burning and leave a carbonaceous residue. Products depend on the acrylonitrile/comonomer composition and additives.

Timescales: The cited technical proceedings describe fire behavior but provide no condition-qualified environmental degradation time.

Environmental persistence: Self-extinguishing behavior is a fire property; it does not demonstrate biological mineralization or specify the lifetime of shed fibers.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The Cellusuede modacrylic-fiber sheet recommends reclaiming spilled material for processing when possible. Its disposal discussion concerns the named acrylonitrile–vinylidene-chloride fiber and requires compliance with applicable waste rules. This supports recovery of suitable clean production material, rather than demonstrating closed-loop recycling of blended, dyed or contaminated textiles.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For Cellusuede’s acrylonitrile–vinylidene-chloride modacrylic fiber, the safety sheet treats eye, skin and inhalation exposure as fiber-dust concerns. The specified copolymer composition matters: guidance for this product should not be generalized to every modacrylic blend or finish. Handling should limit dust and follow the actual fiber formulation’s fire precautions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited study tests a particular modacrylic/polyacrylate/lyocell blend; it does not define all modacrylic fibers.

sections.overview: Vinyon is a generic manufactured-fiber family whose long-chain synthetic polymer contains at least 85 wt% vinyl chloride units. Historical members include vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate copolymers and afterchlorinated variants, which are spun into fibers and may be used as binder fibers.
sections.history: Vinyon’s development belongs to the early industrial use of vinyl-chloride-rich resins as textile fibers. A concrete postwar milestone is Theophilus A. Feild Jr.’s Union Carbide and Carbon patent, filed in 1946 and published in 1951, for coloring vinyl-resin yarns without losing their useful physical properties. It builds on existing vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate fiber technology and addresses the difficulty of applying ordinary textile dyeing methods to these water-resistant fibers. By 1970, the U.S. National Bureau of Standards described vinyon principally as a bonding fiber for nonwoven fabrics, as well as in embossed carpets, pressed felts and waterproof clothing. These sources document established fiber technology and its uses rather than prove a unique first-invention date.
sections.nomenclature: Vinyon is a fiber generic name, not one fixed polymer composition or one trade grade. The record covers the regulatory vinyl-chloride-unit boundary and its established copolymer or afterchlorinated lineages; ordinary PVC resin, other vinyl fibers, and a finished textile construction are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Vinyon is a regulated fiber-family name rather than one unique resin recipe. Under the cited U.S. generic-name definition, the fiber-forming long-chain polymer contains at least 85 wt% vinyl chloride units. The principal chain-forming step is therefore free-radical polymerization of vinyl chloride, either as the homopolymer or with a limited amount of a compatible comonomer. Historically important fiber resins include vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate copolymers; vinyl acetate disrupts the PVC sequence and can lower softening temperature or improve solution handling, but enough vinyl chloride must remain to meet the vinyon compositional boundary. A cited historical patent uses aqueous suspension polymerization with partially hydrolyzed poly(vinyl acetate) as protective colloid and diisopropyl peroxydicarbonate as initiator. Vinyl chloride is polymerized first, then a small vinyl acetate charge is introduced and polymerization continues at a higher temperature before residual monomer is vented and the copolymer is centrifuged, washed, and dried. Afterchlorination is an optional historical modification, not a requirement for every vinyon: the same patent suspends the vinyl chloride copolymer in an inert medium, introduces chlorine under oxygen-excluding conditions, follows hydrogen chloride evolution, removes residual chlorine and medium, and isolates the more highly chlorinated polymer. A second historical patent confirms textile use of both conjointly polymerized vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate resin and its afterchlorinated variant. Monomer ratio and addition sequence, initiator, polymerization temperature, degree of polymerization, residual monomer removal, and optional chlorine content control resin solubility, softening behavior, and suitability for a fiber route. Solution preparation, spinning, drawing, and textile finishing belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Vinyon is a historical fiber-family label rather than a single invariant formulation; the original commercial fibers were predominantly vinyl chloride copolymers, especially vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate compositions, while later similarly named variants used different comonomers and should not have their measurements pooled. At family level, vinyon is described as a soft, flexible, low-strength and highly extensible thermoplastic fiber. Its low moisture affinity helps preserve broadly similar wet and dry behavior, but its low strain-release and softening temperatures make shrinkage and loss of orientation under heat central mechanical limitations. These traits made it more useful as a heat-activated binder in nonwovens, felts, and carpets than as a load-bearing spun yarn; in those bonded structures, web architecture, vinyon fraction, contact area, and bonding temperature, time, and pressure govern strength, tear resistance, drape, and dimensional stability.

Composition and molecular weight, comonomer content, after-chlorination, plasticizer and stabilizer package, solvent-spinning history, filament fineness, draw ratio and draw temperature, molecular orientation, heat setting, residual strain, and subsequent thermal or solvent exposure all affect the measured response. Temperature is especially consequential: a National Bureau of Standards guide reports shrinkage above 150 °F (about 66 °C), tackiness at 185–215 °F (about 85–102 °C), and melting near 260 °F (about 127 °C), values intended as historical fiber guidance rather than universal transition temperatures. As one bounded numerical example, U.S. Patent 2,577,846 reports a 100-denier, initially unoriented yarn made from an after-chlorinated vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate copolymer containing about 60% chlorine. The starting yarn had wet tenacity below 1.0 g/denier and elongation above 100%; after dye application and 510% drawing through a 181 °C radiant heater, the 16-denier yarn had wet tenacity 2.59 g/denier and elongation 16.2%. This is a process-specific patent example—not a family range—and the document does not report a modern tensile standard, conditioning protocol, specimen count, or uncertainty. Those omissions, and the broad chemistry hidden by the vinyon name, should remain explicit when comparing grades or products.
sections.processing:
Vinyon compositions are converted primarily as fibers, but the spinning route depends on whether the material is a vinyl-chloride homopolymer, a vinyl chloride copolymer, or an after-chlorinated composition. Historical practice includes wet or dry solution spinning followed by solvent removal, while suitably stabilized formulations can be melt compounded and melt spun. Important operations are resin/additive mixing, filtration or gel homogenization, metering through a spinneret, take-up, drawing and orientation, heat relaxation or setting, dyeing where required, and winding or cutting. Vinyl-chloride polymers have a narrow heat-processing margin: heterogeneous fusion can leave particles that break filaments, while excessive melt temperature, pressure, shear, or residence time promotes yellowing and decomposition. Solvent-spun routes additionally require controlled coagulation or evaporation and solvent recovery. Finished fibers may also be used as heat-activated binder fibers, so subsequent web temperature must be high enough to tack or bond yet controlled against excessive shrinkage or melting. Polymerization and after-chlorination belong in Synthesis; compound preparation, spinning, drawing, dyeing, heat setting, and binder activation belong here.

Kaneka's patent provides a bounded melt-spinning example for its PVC/CPVC/EVA/stabilizer/lubricant compositions, not a universal vinyon window. Four kilograms of vinyl-chloride resin mixture and additives were mixed in a 20 L Henschel mixer until the compound reached 115 °C, then jacket-cooled with continued mixing to 75 °C. The resulting powder was spun on a 40 mm, 24:1 single-screw extruder through 120 spinneret holes of 0.063 mm²; cylinder zones were 155–170 °C, the adapter 175 °C, and turn-head and nozzle 180 °C, followed by drawing and relaxation atmospheres at 110 °C. The patent warns that spinning above 195 °C caused marked yellowing and ties drawing temperature and ratio to strength, feel, and filament breakage. A separate historical example in Feild's patent treated a 100-denier after-chlorinated vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate yarn at 25 °C in a dye bath and drew it to 510% of its original length through a 181 °C radiant heater; that combined dye-fixing/drawing operation is specific to the stated yarn and apparatus.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Vinyon is a manufactured-fiber family whose long-chain synthetic polymer contains at least 85 wt% vinyl chloride units; documented lineages include vinyl chloride/vinyl acetate copolymers and afterchlorinated variants.
sections.properties: Vinyon fibers have qualitative strength and extensibility and exhibit heat-induced shrinkage, tackiness, and melting behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. The historical NBS account identifies vinyon mainly as a binder for nonwoven fabrics, pressed felts and embossed carpets, with additional coated-textile uses. These are documented historical applications.

Purchasing. The cited account names historical vinyon fiber products but is not a current sales catalog. A buyer needs a specialist vinyl-chloride-fiber supplier to verify composition and bonding behavior; current orderable grades were not established.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable current annual vinyon production or consumption statistic was found. Bulk PVC resin volumes cannot be assigned to this narrower textile-fiber family.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Vinyl-chloride-rich fibers are vulnerable to thermal decomposition during melt spinning; the patent studies stabilizer-containing formulations that suppress processing damage. Molecular environmental products remain an evidence gap.

Timescales: Processing stability depends on formulation and time at temperature; no outdoor or biological degradation time is established by these experiments.

Environmental persistence: The melt-spinning experiments do not establish biodegradability or mineralization of discarded vinyon fibers.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: PVC-family recycling provides context for vinyl-chloride-rich vinyon: segregated material can undergo mechanical size reduction and reprocessing, while dissolution and chlorine/additive separation are investigated recovery routes. The cited review addresses PVC waste generally; it does not validate a dedicated process for every vinyon copolymer fiber, textile blend or finish.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Vinyon is a vinyl-chloride-rich fiber family, so PVC fume guidance is relevant when its formulations overheat: HSE identifies hydrogen chloride as a possible decomposition constituent and recommends controlling temperature, residence time and extraction. Stabilizers, comonomers and finishes vary; a finished textile cannot be evaluated solely from the hazards of its starting monomer.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Fiber response depends on resin lineage, afterchlorination, draw ratio, denier, and heat history; historical yarn data are not all-vinyon constants.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Staged radical copolymerization forms a vinyl-chloride-rich fiber resin. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

sections.overview: Elastane (spandex) is a family of segmented polyurethane and polyurethane-urea elastomers formed into elastic fibers. Exact chemistry varies with the macrodiol, diisocyanate, and chain extender, so the family is not one fixed polyurethane composition.
sections.history: Elastane grew from the effort to replace heavy rubber threads in foundation garments with fine synthetic elastic fibers. Joseph Shivers developed the DuPont material that became Lycra during the 1950s; the National Inventors Hall of Fame identifies his work on segmented synthetic elastomers as the central breakthrough. The material spread from underwear into sportswear, fashion and other stretch textiles, with additional applications in healthcare, furnishings and automotive products. DuPont’s 2004 sale of its Invista synthetic-fibers business to Koch Industries transferred the Lycra business as part of a larger industrial reorganization. Lycra is one commercial lineage within the broader elastane or spandex family.
sections.nomenclature: Elastane and spandex are the names used for this family, which is not one fixed polyurethane composition. The record covers segmented polyurethane/polyurethane-urea elastic-fiber materials and excludes treating every polyurethane, or a finished textile construction, as an elastane polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Elastane (spandex) is a family of segmented polyurethane and polyurethane-urea elastomers. A common polyether polyurethane-urea route first caps a macrodiol, such as poly(tetramethylene ether) glycol, with excess diisocyanate (often MDI) to make an isocyanate-terminated prepolymer; diamine chain extension then forms the polyurethane-urea hard segments. Polyester, polyether, and polycarbonate glycols are all documented macrodiol families, so no single soft-segment composition defines all elastane. In one patent example, the prepolymer and ethylenediamine/diethylamine chain-extension mixture are handled in dimethylacetamide; another documented route uses ethylenediamine and 1,2-diaminopropane as a specified chain-extender mixture. These feedstock, NCO/OH ratio, chain-extension, and chain-termination choices set segmented-polymer architecture. Dry, wet, reaction, and melt spinning are fiber-forming operations applied after or during polymer formation; they are conversion routes, not evidence that a single spinning method defines the elastane family.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Elastane fibers are segmented polyurethane or polyurethane-urea elastomers designed for very large, substantially recoverable extension. Their soft segments supply low-temperature chain mobility and entropic elasticity, while hydrogen-bonded hard-segment domains act as reinforcing physical cross-links; deformation and rearrangement of those domains produce stress softening, hysteresis, delayed recovery, and fatigue sensitivity. Mechanical response varies with soft-segment chemistry and molecular mass, hard-segment fraction and sequence, hydrogen-bond cohesion and phase separation, chain-extension chemistry, spinning and draw-induced orientation, filament bundle structure, test temperature and rate, imposed prestrain, hold and recovery time, and cyclic history. Yoshihara and Ishihara found that room-temperature instantaneous and delayed unrecovered strain in model segmented polyurethane-urea fibers passed through a minimum near a PTMG soft-segment molecular mass of about 2000. At low temperature, higher-molecular-mass PTMG could undergo strain-induced crystallization that persisted after unloading and impaired recovery; copolymerizing dissimilar soft segments suppressed this fixed crystallization and broadened the useful recovery range. A separate bounded measurement on the commercially available spandex fiber used by Zhang and co-workers gives a numerical example: in room-temperature uniaxial tests at 5 mm/s, the multifilament fiber had an initial modulus of 1.38 MPa, maximum stretch ratio 7.0 (about six times its initial length added before fracture), and work of fracture 71.1 MJ/m3. The same material showed substantial cyclic hysteresis attributed to hard-segment plastic deformation. The paper does not identify a commercial grade, linear density, conditioning humidity, or a detailed cross-sectional-area protocol for the porous multifilament bundle, so these results are illustrative for that tested fiber only and are not a specification or family range. Fabric-level stretch, tear, and recovery additionally depend on elastane fraction, yarn covering, knit or weave geometry, and interaction with companion fibers and must not be inferred directly from single-fiber values.
sections.processing:
Elastane is converted primarily as continuous filament by solution dry spinning or wet spinning; reaction spinning and melt spinning are also documented for suitable chemistries. In dry spinning, a filtered polymer solution is metered through a spinneret into a heated, usually inert-gas shaft, the solvent is removed, elementary filaments are combined, a finish is applied to control sticking and friction, and the yarn is wound. Wet spinning instead extrudes solution into a nonsolvent coagulation bath, then washes, draws where required, dries or heat-sets, finishes, and winds the filament. Solution viscosity, spinneret pressure, solvent removal or bath mass transfer, filament coalescence, draw, and residual solvent therefore belong to the qualified spinning process rather than to the family as fixed settings.

A bounded Bayer wet-spinning example used a 30 wt% polyurethane-urea solution whose viscosity was 18 Pa·s at 50 °C after a specified 140 °C pretreatment. It was extruded through 397 holes of 0.08 mm diameter into an 85 °C bath containing 20% dimethylacetamide in water, followed by the patent's washing, drying, setting, finishing, and winding sequence. Those settings apply to that polymer solution and spinning line; they do not define a universal elastane wet-spinning window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Elastane fibers are segmented polyurethane or polyurethane–urea elastomers with soft segments and hard-segment domains that create a physically crosslinked fiber morphology.
sections.properties: High extensibility and elastic recovery depend on soft-segment chemistry, molecular weight, hard-segment content, spinning, and thermal history.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Elastane supplies stretch and recovery in underwear, jeans, hosiery, swimwear and activewear, generally as a constituent of a textile blend.

Purchasing. Mills purchase specified spandex/elastane fibers; clothing producers purchase fabrics containing them. LYCRA is one commercial fiber portfolio, and a LYCRA-containing fabric is not pure elastane.

Scale and evidence limits. Textile Exchange reports just under 1.5 million tonnes of global elastane fiber production in 2024, order 10^6 tonnes/year. This is fiber output, not total garment mass or purchases by one apparel segment.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Solvent treatment can chemically alter the tested MDI-derived elastane: NMR detected methylenedianiline-containing species as well as carbamate structures. This is treatment chemistry, not an inventory of environmental degradation products.

Timescales: Dissolution and thermal-analysis experiments establish processing behavior; a condition-qualified environmental mineralization time remains unavailable.

Environmental persistence: The studied polyester/elastane and polyamide/elastane blends do not establish the lifetime of shed elastane fibers in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Selective dissolution removes elastane from mixed textile waste using solvents such as tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol or γ-valerolactone. Laboratory validation and life-cycle modeling support further scale-up, but solvent-driven polymer changes limit assuming recovery of virgin-equivalent elastane.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Elastane separation and recycling can involve DMF or DMAc and therefore requires solvent-specific exposure and emission controls. A study of selective dissolution compares these established solvents with alternatives using health, safety and environmental criteria. These are process-solvent concerns, distinct from the biological response to a washed, finished elastane-containing textile.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited work links recovery to specified soft-segment structures, and production documents concern dry- or wet-spun fibers; a commercial spandex fiber is not a composition-invariant family material.

sections.overview: Novoloid fiber polymers are crosslinked phenolic fibers produced from novolac-type precursor resins. The crosslinked phenolic chemistry differentiates this fiber family from melt-spun thermoplastic fibers.
sections.history: Novoloid fiber’s commercial history is closely tied to Kynol. The Museum of Fine Arts conservation reference attributes its development in 1968 to Carborundum, followed by licensing to Nippon Kynol and American Kynol. The manufacturer’s history places this work in U.S. space-technology development and dates full-scale industrial production to 1982. Flame-resistant clothing and spacecraft were early application areas. Later product development included carbon fibers and activated carbon fibers derived from the phenolic precursor, extending use into filtration and adsorption. These dates concern the Kynol novoloid-fiber lineage; phenol-formaldehyde resins themselves have a substantially earlier history.
sections.nomenclature: Novoloid is a family name for phenolic fiber materials and is not synonymous with uncured novolac resin. Commercial fiber names may identify particular products but do not replace the canonical family name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Novoloid denotes a family of infusible, cross-linked phenolic fibers whose precursor is a novolac, rather than a separate linear fiber polymer. The cited routes prepare the thermoplastic novolac by acid-catalyzed condensation of a phenolic feedstock, commonly phenol, with formaldehyde under phenol-rich conditions. Network formation then converts the novolac precursor to novoloid: documented cross-linking agents include hexamethylenetetramine, paraformaldehyde, trioxane, or tetraoxymethylene, with an acid catalyst or acidic environment used to promote formation of the phenolic methylene-bridge network. Phenol–formaldehyde is the common example, while substituted phenols can also be precursors. These sources establish precursor and cross-link chemistry only; fiber-forming equipment and individual cure schedules are not generalized here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Novoloid fibers are cured, amorphous, cross-linked novolak networks rather than meltable linear-fiber grades. Their tensile response therefore depends on fiber diameter/linear density, curing profile and the resulting cross-link gradient, and—when used as reinforcement—fiber length, loading, dispersion, and fiber–matrix bonding. A published friction-material study describes the fibers as modest in strength but comparatively extensible, and reports that their reinforcing effect in phenolic composites is strongly formulation- and interface-dependent; those composite observations are not intrinsic-fiber properties.

A bounded virgin-fiber reference is Kynol's 15–33 µm (2.2–11 dtex) novoloid-fiber range: the supplier lists tensile strength of 12–16 cN/tex, elongation of 10–50%, and modulus of 260–350 cN/tex. These are typical supplier values that explicitly vary with diameter; specimen conditioning, gauge length, test rate, and statistical basis are not supplied, so they should not be treated as universal novoloid-fiber specifications.
sections.processing: Novoloid fiber is made by converting a novolac precursor into a fiber before infusibilization: the precursor is melt-spun through a conventional spinnerette and then treated with formaldehyde or a formaldehyde-generating system to produce an amorphous, three-dimensional crosslinked network. Once cured, the fiber is infusible and insoluble, so downstream conversion is cutting, blending, or forming it into fiber-filled friction and sealing materials rather than remelting it. Hayes' open article directly describes melt spinning followed by formaldehyde curing and discusses novoloid fiber in friction and sealing formulations. A separate Toray patent describes melt-spun curable phenol-formaldehyde fibers, acid-catalyzed curing chemistry, crosslinking agents, and subsequent heat treatment. Exact spinning, curing, and heat-treatment conditions depend on precursor molecular mass, fiber diameter, catalyst, and crosslinker; the cited sources do not establish a universal cycle.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Novoloid fibers are crosslinked phenolic fibers derived from novolac precursors.
sections.properties: Their flame and thermal behavior depend on precursor chemistry, cure, and fiber construction.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Novoloid fiber serves heat-protective textiles including aircraft fireblocking layers. It is also a precursor for carbon and activated-carbon fibers; those converted materials have distinct adsorption and thermal uses.

Purchasing. Gun Ei supplies Kynol fibers, while partner factories convert yarn, felt and activated-carbon products. The supplier offers small samples on inquiry but publishes no sample mass or standard commercial order size.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found in the checked open sources; supplier offerings establish availability, not sales volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The supplier identifies char, water vapor and carbon dioxide as principal flame-exposure products of its cured phenolic novoloid fibers, with carbon monoxide possible under oxygen limitation.

Timescales: The fiber chars without melting during flame exposure. No condition-qualified environmental mineralization time is provided.

Environmental persistence: Flame resistance and char formation cannot establish degradation rates in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The supplier markets novoloid fibers and textiles as precursors for activated carbon. This is a demonstrated material-conversion application; the bulletin does not establish a post-consumer fiber collection or closed-loop monomer-recycling system.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Kynol novoloid chars rather than melting, but flame resistance does not mean smoke is harmless. The supplier reports carbon monoxide when oxygen is limited, alongside char, water and carbon dioxide. These are fire-exposure considerations for the supplier’s phenolic fiber, and should remain separate from the behavior of coatings, blends and additives.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Published friction and sealing performance concerns particular commercial fibers and formulations.

sections.overview: Regenerated cellulose is cellulose dissolved and re-formed into fibers, films, or other materials. Regeneration changes the material morphology while retaining the cellulose chemical backbone.
sections.history: Regenerated cellulose developed through multiple ways of dissolving and re-forming plant cellulose. Charles Frederick Cross, Edward John Bevan and Clayton Beadle’s 1892 viscose patent became a foundation for the rayon and cellophane industries. Subsequent fiber development improved wet performance and changed solvent systems. Lenzing dates its first high-wet-modulus fiber to 1965 and large-scale lyocell production at Heiligenkreuz to 1997; it acquired the Tencel business in 2004. Textile fibers remained central, while regenerated films provided a separate use of the same underlying cellulose chemistry. These dates distinguish a particular viscose process from later regenerated-cellulose technologies rather than assigning the whole class one invention date.
sections.nomenclature: Regenerated cellulose is a process-defined cellulose subfamily. Rayon and viscose cellulose are common names for particular regenerated-cellulose fiber routes and should not be treated as names for every regenerated-cellulose material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Regenerated cellulose starts with purified native cellulose, commonly dissolving-grade wood pulp or cotton linters; the cellulose backbone is dissolved or temporarily derivatized and then precipitated back as cellulose rather than polymerized from a small-molecule monomer. In the viscose route, pulp is steeped in sodium hydroxide to form alkali cellulose, pressed, shredded, and aged to adjust degree of polymerization. Reaction with carbon disulfide gives soluble cellulose xanthate, which is dissolved in dilute sodium hydroxide, filtered, and deaerated. Contact with an acidic salt bath coagulates the solution and decomposes the xanthate, regenerating cellulose that is washed to remove sulfur compounds, acid, and salts. One cited patent documents this full viscose sequence. A distinct lyocell patent directly dissolves pulp in aqueous N-methylmorpholine N-oxide by controlled water removal, filters the dope, regenerates cellulose in an aqueous bath, washes out the amine oxide, and recovers solvent. Pulp purity and degree of polymerization, solution filtration, solvent/water balance, and coagulation chemistry control the regenerated material. Fiber drawing and article-specific spinning settings remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Regenerated cellulose covers viscose/rayon, modal and high-wet-modulus viscose, lyocell, cupro, and laboratory solvent-spun cellulose-II products, so fiber, film, sponge, membrane, yarn, fabric, and composite results must remain separate. In a drawn filament the hydrogen-bonded cellulose-II network gives a strongly anisotropic response: axial stiffness and tenacity rise as long chains, crystallites, and amorphous tie material become aligned, while transverse cohesion, bending, fibrillation, knot or loop strength, and fatigue can be limiting. Lyocell commonly retains more dry and wet strength and has higher modulus but lower extension than ordinary viscose because its direct-solution dry-jet wet-spinning route can preserve greater degree of polymerization, crystallinity, and axial orientation. Water penetrates amorphous regions, swells and plasticizes the hydrogen-bonded structure, generally lowering modulus and strength and increasing deformation; the loss is especially consequential for ordinary viscose, whereas modal/high-wet-modulus and lyocell variants are designed for better wet retention.

Mechanical response depends on pulp degree of polymerization and purity, hemicellulose content and prior chain degradation, solvent and regeneration chemistry, dope concentration and entanglement, spinneret and air-gap geometry, extrusion and take-up speed or draw ratio, coagulation-bath composition and mass transfer, washing and drying tension, crystallinity and crystal orientation, skin–core and void morphology, filament diameter and defects, fibrillation, crosslinking and finishes, moisture history, temperature, aging, gauge length, strain rate, and whether a single filament, yarn, nonwoven, woven fabric, film, or composite is tested. A bounded laboratory example used bamboo pulp of viscosity-average molecular mass 1.2 × 10^5 g/mol (reported DP 760) at 5 wt% in tetrabutylammonium acetate/DMSO, wet-spun through a 0.355 mm needle into ethanol at 20 °C. The resulting cellulose-II fiber table reports dry tenacity 3.85 cN/dtex, wet tenacity 3.21 cN/dtex, and 11.9% elongation at break. Dried filaments were tested over a 20 mm gauge length with 30 replicates, but the paper does not report tensile rate, scatter, final filament diameter, or the wet-conditioning/test protocol. The endpoint therefore applies only to that bamboo-pulp solvent/spinning experiment and is not a specification for commercial viscose, modal, lyocell, films, or regenerated cellulose generally.
sections.processing:
Regenerated cellulose is converted from a cellulose solution or dope into fibers, films, membranes, powders, or related articles by regeneration rather than melt processing. In conventional wet spinning, a filtered and deaerated dope is metered through a spinneret into an aqueous or acidic coagulation bath; solvent exchange and precipitation form a gel filament, which is withdrawn, washed (often first with hot water and then with distilled water), and dried. Dry-jet wet spinning adds a controlled air gap before coagulation, while dry spinning and related solution-spinning variants use solvent removal or a different nonsolvent path. Take-up speed, air-gap or bath conditions, spinneret geometry, dope viscosity and concentration, and draw ratio control filament diameter, orientation, skin–core structure, voids, and fibrillation. Drawing may occur during take-up or in subsequent wet/dry zones; it increases axial orientation but must be matched to the gel strength and coagulation state. Commercial route names such as viscose, lyocell, and cupro therefore denote different solution/coagulation and post-treatment windows rather than one universal spinning schedule.

Casting is used for regenerated-cellulose films and membranes: a solution layer is spread on a plate or support, immersed in or contacted with a coagulation bath, washed to remove solvent and soluble reagents, and dried under controlled tension, humidity, temperature, or relaxation conditions. Coagulant identity and miscibility, bath temperature, layer thickness, and mass-transfer rate affect regeneration kinetics, shrinkage, porosity, crystallinity, and the final film surface; drying can compact or collapse the wet gel and alter morphology, so film and fiber settings are not interchangeable.

A bounded film example from Nguyen et al. dissolved 20 wt% cellulose in 50 wt% aqueous tetrabutylphosphonium hydroxide at 23 °C for 30 min, cast the clear solution as an approximately 500 µm layer on glass, and rapidly immersed it in propylene carbonate. Coagulation occurred within seconds in that formulation; the regenerated film was washed with distilled water and dried at 80 °C. These conditions are an experiment-specific example for that solvent, cellulose concentration, layer thickness, and coagulant, not a family-wide operating window. The general spinning and post-treatment sequence likewise varies with pulp degree of polymerization, solvent system, dope rheology, spinneret, bath composition, draw history, washing endpoint, and drying tension.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Regenerated cellulose retains the cellulose backbone but has morphology set by dissolution and re-formation.
sections.properties: Fiber properties depend on solvent route, draw, crystallinity, and source pulp.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Regenerated cellulose fibers supply apparel, home and technical textiles, nonwovens and hygiene products. Viscose, modal and lyocell are commercially distinct fiber routes within this family.

Purchasing. Textile and nonwoven manufacturers buy specified fiber grades from producers such as Lenzing; later buyers obtain yarns, fabrics and finished goods. Dissolving pulp is a precursor purchase rather than a regenerated-fiber product.

Scale and evidence limits. Lenzing reported worldwide fiber sales of 962,000 tonnes in 2024, order 10^6 tonnes/year for one producer. These are company sales across its cellulosic fiber portfolio, not the global market or a single viscose grade.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Regenerated cellulose is biologically attacked, but visible loss of textile fibers and conversion to carbon dioxide are different endpoints.

Timescales: The cited California seawater study observed disintegration of its regenerated-cellulose textiles in approximately 35 days; this cannot specify the lifetime of thick, coated or blended articles.

Environmental persistence: The study separately measured carbon dioxide evolution in closed 30 °C bioreactors; that test must not be treated as the rate of mineralization in the open sea.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Mechanical textile recycling opens and shreds fibers for reuse, but the resulting shorter fibers may need stronger carrier fibers for spinning. Lenzing’s 2025 report describes commercial REFIBRA recycling of cotton or regenerated-cellulose textile waste, blended with virgin pulp to produce new fibers; its ECOVERO viscose example contains at least 20% recycled material. This is a defined manufacturer route rather than a guarantee that every blended garment is accepted.

A laboratory Ioncell study directly redissolved white, black and blue Danufil viscose and white Lenzing modal in the ionic liquid [DBNH][OAc], then regenerated lyocell-type fibers by dry-jet wet spinning. The fibers were made into yarn and knitted demonstrators. This demonstrates reuse of these low-degree-of-polymerization regenerated fibers; mixed textile waste and dye removal remained further development work.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Regenerated cellulose articles can generate cellulose dust during cutting or abrasion. NIOSH identifies eye, skin and respiratory irritation and treats cellulose as a combustible solid. Its powder-handling guidance concerns airborne particles; it does not imply the same exposure from an intact fiber, film or paper article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Viscose and Lyocell-type materials are distinct regenerated-cellulose routes.

sections.overview: Cellulose acetate is an acetate ester derivative of cellulose. It is used as a thermoplastic or solution-processable cellulosic material, with properties governed in part by acetyl substitution and plasticization.
sections.history: Cellulose acetate was developed by Paul Schützenberger in 1865, decades before it became an important commercial plastic and fiber. The Museum of Fine Arts account identifies Eastman Kodak’s introduction of acetate safety film in 1908 and Dreyfus production by 1910 as early industrial milestones. British production of acetate textile fibers followed in 1919 under the Celanese name. Film, lacquers and transparent sheeting were joined by textile, eyewear, tool-handle and cigarette-filter applications. Its history therefore spans chemical discovery, film-base manufacture and fiber commercialization, with different dates for each rather than one date applicable to every acetate grade.
sections.nomenclature: CA is a common abbreviation for cellulose acetate. This record covers cellulose acetate generally; cellulose triacetate is a more highly acetylated cellulose-acetate material and is maintained as a distinct record rather than a synonym.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cellulose acetate is a cellulose-ester subfamily whose degree of acetyl substitution distinguishes materials such as highly acetylated triacetate and lower-substituted secondary acetates. It is made from cellulose feedstock, including dissolving pulp, cotton linters, or purified plant cellulose, by acetylating hydroxyl groups. A conventional acetic-acid process first produces highly acetylated material with excess acetic anhydride in acetic acid and an acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid; controlled partial hydrolysis can then lower the substitution level. A laboratory example first isolated cellulose from Agave sisalana, then treated it with acetic acid, sulfuric acid, and acetic anhydride before water precipitation and drying. That plant source and laboratory sequence are a bounded example, not evidence that all cellulose acetate is made from Agave or under identical conditions.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cellulose acetate mechanics depend on molecular-chain length and distribution, degree and distribution of substitution, feedstock, and article form; values for cast films, fibers, plasticized compounds, and membrane structures are therefore not interchangeable. In an early film study, cellulose-acetate fractions with degree of polymerization (DP) 30 could not form coherent films; properties increased rapidly with chain length above that point, while further improvement was slight above DP 150. That study also found ultimate elongation and folding endurance more sensitive than tensile strength to chain length and its distribution. A later cast-film study illustrates a bounded tensile endpoint: cellulose acetate made by homogeneous acetylation of tunicate-cellulose material (TCM; DS 2.66) was cast from 1 wt% dichloromethane solution onto polyethylene, air-dried for one week (mean thickness 29 µm), and pulled at 5 mm/min. It gave a Young’s modulus of 6.6 GPa and tensile strength of 58.9 MPa. Within that experiment, films obtained by heterogeneous acetylation or from powdered-tunicate and cotton celluloses were lower in modulus and strength, consistent with the authors’ reported molecular-mass and reaction-route differences. The article does not report specimen geometry, test temperature/humidity, or replicate statistics, so these values describe that cast-film preparation rather than a cellulose-acetate family range.
sections.processing: Cellulose acetate (CA) can be solvent-cast or solution-blown into films and melt-compounded, extruded, and injection molded when the formulation provides adequate flow. Because CA is moisture-sensitive and its melt-processing window can be constrained by thermal sensitivity, drying, plasticizer level, shear, and residence history must be set for the particular grade/formulation. Erdmann and co-workers dried CA before twin-screw compounding and again before injection molding; their 15–40 wt% plasticizer formulations used lower injection-unit temperatures for more highly plasticized materials, illustrating that plasticizer content changes the usable settings. Eastman’s cellulosic-plastics drying guidance gives moisture limits only as supplier operating guidance; it notes that permissible moisture depends on the individual extrusion operation. These moisture observations and experimental settings are not universal CA-family specifications.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cellulose acetate is a cellulose ester whose substitution level distinguishes primary acetate from lower-substituted secondary acetate.
sections.properties: Film strength, elongation, and folding response vary with chain length, degree of substitution, plasticizer, and moisture history.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Cellulose acetate is used in acetate filter tow and plastic articles. Daicel’s CAFBLO compounds target molded daily goods and furniture parts, packaging sheets, profiles and additive manufacturing.

Purchasing. Producers supply application-specific cellulose acetate compounds and fibers. CAFBLO has named molding/extrusion and 3D-printing grades and a sample/technical-sales channel; formulation and acetylation grade matter.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found in the checked open sources; supplier offerings establish availability, not sales volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Ester substitution can inhibit cellulase attack; acetyl content matters.

Timescales: The tested highly substituted film showed no visible degradation over 12 weeks in pilot compost reaching 70.7 °C.

Environmental persistence: That negative result applies to this film and compost trial, not every acetate grade or environment.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Laboratory recovery from cigarette filters uses washing, dissolution in acetone, filtration and recasting. This recovers polymer; it does not establish an operating collection system or mineralization.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For cellulose acetate photographic film, the archival term “safety film” distinguishes it from nitrate film, while acidic deterioration remains possible. NARA recommends identifying vinegar syndrome and using controlled cold storage to slow it. The guidance concerns film preservation rather than a general toxicological assessment of every cellulose-ester formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Reported film and melt-processing data apply to the specified acetate grade and plasticizer loading; they cannot be generalized across cellulose-acetate substitution levels or article forms.

sections.overview: Cellulose triacetate is a highly acetylated cellulose ester, typically associated with acetyl substitution near the triacetate level. Its scope is distinct from more broadly substituted cellulose acetate.
sections.history: Cellulose triacetate’s photographic history followed earlier, less highly acetylated cellulose films. The Canadian Conservation Institute dates production to 1948, when it offered a more stable base than earlier acetates. By about 1950, many film manufacturers were making triacetate roll film. Motion-picture use persisted partly because acetate can break when a projector jams and can be spliced readily. This is the history of commercial film-base development, not a claim that the triacetate chemical structure was first synthesized in 1948.
sections.nomenclature: CTA abbreviates cellulose triacetate, and “triacetate” is a common shortened name. It is not interchangeable with the broader cellulose acetate record, because the degree of acetylation defines an important material boundary.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cellulose triacetate (CTA) is the highly acetylated cellulose ester obtained by converting essentially all three hydroxyl groups per anhydroglucose unit; it is a modified natural polymer, not a polymerization of acetate monomer. Purified cellulose can be obtained from wood pulp, cotton linters, or other cellulose-rich biomass before acetylation. A date-palm-cellulose study describes heterogeneous reaction with acetic anhydride and acid catalysts and reports CTA at degree of substitution 2.9; it also distinguishes subsequent partial hydrolysis used to make lower-substitution cellulose acetates. As a different route example, mild-acid-pretreated sugarcane bagasse was dissolved in an EmimOAc/DMSO medium and acetylated homogeneously with isopropenyl acetate, then reprecipitated to separate a cellulose-triacetate-rich fraction from lignin acetate. That one-pot biomass conversion is a source-specific alternative to direct acetylation of isolated cellulose.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cellulose triacetate mechanical response is sensitive to article form and sorbed liquid: fiber viscoelasticity, a dense membrane, and a filled film should not be treated as equivalent materials. Okiyama and co-workers report that the dry triacetate fiber they studied had a glass-transition temperature of 193 °C, but during drying of a wet fiber a mechanical-loss-tangent peak occurred at room temperature; polar and nonpolar organic solvents also induced a room-temperature glass transition. Their comparison with regenerated cellulose fibers found a lower loss-tangent maximum for the triacetate fiber, which they interpreted qualitatively as a smaller water-affected moving unit. A focused membrane example gives a bounded strength endpoint: Nakanishi and co-workers prepared dense membranes under 35 °C and 70% relative humidity and reported, for their commercial cellulose-triacetate control membrane, Young’s modulus of 0.74 GPa and maximum stress of 46.3 MPa. The same study found its sugarcane-bagasse-derived triacetate membranes too fragile to handle for modulus measurement, whereas its lower-acetylated diacetate materials formed mechanically measurable membranes. The commercial-control values are therefore condition- and membrane-specific; the report does not give specimen geometry, loading rate, or replicate statistics, and they are not a cellulose-triacetate family range.
sections.processing: CTA is commonly converted as film or membrane by solution casting: prepare a homogeneous dope, cast from a die or blade onto a support, evaporate solvent until self-supporting, peel, then dry, cool, and wind as needed. A CTA-film patent describes this route and, for its tear- and fold-endurance process, uses a principal methylene-chloride solvent with 13–25 wt% poor solvent and a support below 10 °C; those conditions are process-specific. A distinct CTA/CDA mixed-matrix membrane experiment vacuum-dried powder at 120 °C overnight, dissolved an 80/20 (wt.%) CTA/CDA blend in NMP with stirring at 40 °C overnight, sonicated the filler suspension before mixing, blade-cast on glass, evaporated at 100 °C overnight, peeled, and vacuum-dried at 120 °C for at least 24 h. That is a formulation-specific membrane route, not a general CTA window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cellulose triacetate (CTA) is the highly acetylated cellulose-ester subfamily, commonly described at degree of substitution about 2.7–3.
sections.properties: CTA fiber and membrane behavior is sensitive to solvent or water exposure, source, and membrane morphology.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Cellulose triacetate films serve display polarizers in LCD and OLED electronics; photographic film bases are an established historical use. Optical-film performance is grade and film-design specific.

Purchasing. Industrial film manufacturers source optical TAC resin; Daicel documents supplying TAC to Fujifilm for film manufacture. Display assemblers then purchase converted optical films or polarizer components.

Scale and evidence limits. The June 2026 supplier announcement confirms an established industrial supply chain but gives no resin sales or consumption tonnage. No reliable separate annual TAC purchase statistic was found.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Acid hydrolysis can remove acetyl substituents from triacetate; subsequent cellulose-chain degradation depends on the treatment.

Timescales: No condition-qualified environmental mineralization time was verified.

Environmental persistence: The industrial hydrolysis sources do not establish biodegradation of triacetate films in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A recycling patent includes triacetate in its feedstock scope for acid treatment and recovery of an acid-containing stream. The broad claim is not proof of a commercial triacetate recycling loop.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For cellulose triacetate photographic film, the archival term “safety film” distinguishes it from nitrate film, while acidic deterioration remains possible. NARA recommends identifying vinegar syndrome and using controlled cold storage to slow it. The guidance concerns film preservation rather than a general toxicological assessment of every cellulose-ester formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited response belongs to specified triacetate fiber or membrane preparations; feedstock, degree of substitution, solvent, humidity, and filler or plasticizer must remain stated.

sections.overview: Cellulose is a linear beta-(1→4)-glucan and a principal structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls. Its chains assemble into fibrous, semicrystalline structures in natural cellulosic materials.
sections.history: Cellulose is a natural material, so its history begins with human use and scientific identification rather than invention. Anselme Payen isolated and characterized the plant substance in work reported in 1838; the name cellulose entered the literature in 1839. Paper, textiles and construction materials made it an industrial raw material long before modern structural analysis. Nishikawa and Ono obtained cellulose-fiber X-ray diffraction patterns in 1913. Later milestones included VanderHart and Atalla’s 1984 recognition of two native cellulose allomorphs and diffraction studies resolving their structures. This scientific progression supported a broader understanding of the material used for fibers, paper and chemical derivatives.
sections.nomenclature: Cellulose names the polymer itself. “Cellulosic” is a broader material descriptor and can include derivatives or composite materials, so it is not a synonym for the canonical cellulose record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cellulose is a natural polymer family produced by plants, algae, selected bacteria, and some other organisms. In biological synthesis, membrane-associated cellulose synthase uses UDP-glucose to form beta-(1→4)-glucan chains, which are assembled into microfibrils; this biosynthetic route is distinct from industrial isolation. Technical cellulose fiber is commonly isolated from lignocellulosic feedstocks by pulping that removes much of the lignin rather than by creating the glucan chain anew. The kraft example uses wood chips and aqueous sodium hydroxide/sodium sulfide cooking liquor in a batch or continuous digester, followed by washing and chemical recovery. Feedstock species, biological origin, and pulp-isolation route therefore need to remain explicit when describing a particular cellulose material.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cellulose mechanics are hierarchical and strongly anisotropic rather than describable by one family-wide modulus or strength. Linear glucan chains assemble into partly crystalline microfibrils that carry load principally along their axes. Crystallinity, cellulose allomorph, microfibril size and orientation, and interactions with neighboring cellulose and matrix polymers therefore govern stiffness, strength, and extensibility. Native plant walls, purified pulp fibers, regenerated fibers, films, and nano- or microfibrillar materials are mechanically different forms. In plant material, the more hydrated and disordered primary wall is comparatively flexible, whereas the more oriented cellulose arrangement and lignified matrix of secondary walls produce greater rigidity. Source species, noncellulosic constituents, moisture, defects introduced during pulping, drawing or other processing, and test direction must consequently remain attached to reported results.

A single-fiber study by Zizek, Czibula, and Hirn illustrates loading-rate sensitivity under bounded conditions. The authors tested chemi-thermomechanical softwood pulp, bleached chemical softwood pulp, unbleached softwood kraft pulp, and regenerated viscose fibers after water swelling, drying for 1 h at 95 °C, and conditioning for five days at 25 °C and 50% relative humidity. Fibers mounted across a 0.8 mm gap were cycled in longitudinal tension at ten strain rates from 0.113 to 800% s⁻¹ while maximum displacement was limited to 15 µm. Across the tested materials, longitudinal modulus increased approximately log-linearly with rate; per tenfold rate increase, the reported increase was 5–7% for the bleached chemical-pulp fibers and 11–18% for the viscose fibers, depending on the loading protocol. The pulp results showed substantial fiber-to-fiber scatter, and the authors judged some CTMP and unbleached-kraft comparisons statistically uncertain. These rate effects apply to the particular conditioned single-fiber forms and protocol, not to bulk cellulose, films, crystals, or a universal cellulose modulus.
sections.processing: Native cellulose is normally shaped after dissolution or as fibers/pulp rather than by ordinary melt molding. Regenerated-fiber routes include viscose wet spinning, Lyocell air-gap spinning, and ionic-liquid wet or dry-jet-wet spinning; all-cellulose composites and solution-cast materials are further options. Solvent, pulp molecular mass, dope concentration/rheology, coagulation, draw, and orientation materially affect spinnability and final structure. Hermanutz and co-workers describe viscose and Lyocell as established fiber routes and note the need to stabilize an NMMO spinning dope against side reactions. In the Ioncell experiment by Ma and co-workers, dissolving pulps with intrinsic viscosity 360–820 mL/g and cellulose dope concentration 11–15 wt% produced fibers; these narrow feed-window values are for the stated Ioncell system, not a generic cellulose-processing range.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cellulose is a family of β-1,4-glucan microfibrillar materials with crystalline and less ordered regions; native cellulose occurs in multiple allomorphs and interacts with other plant-wall polysaccharides.
sections.properties: Crystallinity, microfibril organization, moisture, molecular mass, and orientation govern the behavior of a cellulose article.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Cellulose-containing pulps support paper and paperboard and regenerated textile fibers. Purified microcrystalline cellulose supplies pharmaceutical tablet binders/fillers; specialty cellulose particles serve as removable pore formers in technical ceramics.

Purchasing. Buy the form required: pulp for paper or regenerated fibers, pharmaceutical microcrystalline-cellulose powder, or technical fiber/particle grades. JRS offers twelve VIVAPUR excipient grades, differentiated by particle size and bulk density, with a supplier sample channel.

Scale and evidence limits. FAO reports global wood-pulp production of 193 million tonnes and trade of 71 million tonnes in 2023, establishing order 10^8-tonne production context. Wood pulp contains other constituents and covers many grades: these totals are not chemically pure cellulose purchases or pharmaceutical-cellulose consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cellulases hydrolyze cellulose to soluble reducing sugars; accessibility and crystalline form influence conversion.

Timescales: The cited laboratory enzyme study uses 50 °C and 30 FPU per gram; its accelerated hydrolysis does not provide a soil or marine lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Results for microcrystalline cellulose and regenerated hydrogel cannot be assigned unchanged to lignified, coated or composite articles.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Established paper recycling reclaims cellulose-rich fibers by repulping sheets in water, screening and cleaning contaminants, and forming new paper. For coated fine papers, Sappi describes flotation deinking, further washing and bleaching, and blending recovered fibers with virgin fiber and mill broke. Fiber damage and contamination affect the resulting paper quality; repulping recovers fibers rather than purified glucose monomer.

Cellulosic textiles also enter dissolution-and-regeneration routes. Lenzing reports commercial REFIBRA use of pre- and post-consumer cotton or regenerated-cellulose textile waste together with virgin pulp to make new fibers. Mechanical textile shredding is another route, although fiber shortening can require blending with carrier fibers before spinning. These paper and textile processes apply to selected cellulose-rich waste streams; they do not establish equivalent recyclability for every coated or composite cellulose article.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Cellulose powder presents an occupational dust exposure. NIOSH identifies eye, skin and respiratory irritation and treats cellulose as a combustible solid. Its powder-handling guidance concerns airborne particles; it does not imply the same exposure from an intact fiber, film or paper article.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Native source, pulp quality, solvent route, draw, and orientation limit transferability between cellulose fibers, films, pulps, and natural tissues.

sections.overview: Cellulose acetate butyrate is a mixed cellulose ester bearing acetate and butyrate substituents. It is a cellulosic thermoplastic whose material behavior depends on composition and formulation.
sections.history: Cellulose acetate butyrate emerged from efforts to improve the durability of early cellulose-acetate materials. The Canadian Conservation Institute dates its photographic development to 1936, while the Museum of Fine Arts records commercial availability in 1938. It served as a film base, including X-ray film, and as a varnish and molding resin. Kodak’s work on mixed cellulose esters belongs to this photographic development; Eastman subsequently maintained CAB for uses beyond photographic negatives. The different development and commercialization dates concern stages of industrial adoption rather than competing dates for a single event.
sections.nomenclature: CAB abbreviates cellulose acetate butyrate. The name identifies a mixed ester of one cellulose backbone, not a physical blend of separate cellulose acetate and cellulose butyrate polymers.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cellulose acetate butyrate (CAB) is a mixed cellulose ester: acetyl and butyryl groups replace some of the hydroxyl groups on an existing cellulose backbone, rather than being formed by chain-growth polymerization. Thus purified cellulose, including microcrystalline cellulose or refined cotton linters, is the precursor. In one reported laboratory preparation, microcrystalline cellulose was dispersed in acetic acid with sulfuric acid, then treated with acetic and butyric anhydrides; water precipitation, washing, and drying isolated the CAB. The reported mixed-ester identity and composition depend on substitution by both acyl groups. A separate patent example activates cotton linters in acetic and butyric acids, uses sulfuric acid during esterification with acetic anhydride, then applies an aqueous butyric-acid hydrolysis step before neutralization, precipitation, washing, and drying. That sequence is a particular patent route, not a universal CAB recipe.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cellulose acetate butyrate (CAB) does not have a context-free mechanical-property set. In thin-film tests of CABs with 17, 35, and 52 wt% butyryl contents, the higher-butyryl materials had lower modulus and greater flexibility; film preparation and ageing also changed the response. Commercial CAB formulations likewise show a plasticizer trade-off: Eastman’s 3–23% plasticizer selector chart reports declining tensile and flexural stiffness with increasing plasticizer content, alongside increasing notched Izod impact strength. These comparisons describe the named substitution levels and formulations, rather than a CAB family range.

A bounded primary-film result was reported for a virgin CAB-35 material supplied with 35–39 wt% butyryl content. Buják and co-workers solvent-cast rectangular films from a 10 wt% CAB/acetone solution; specimens were approximately 0.2 mm thick and were tested by ISO 527 at 10 mm/min. Before UV ageing, CAB-35 had stress at break 9.8 ± 1.6 MPa, Young’s modulus 1010.6 ± 60.1 MPa, and strain at break 1.02 ± 0.18%. The material supplier, casting route, thin-film geometry, and test protocol limit this result; it is not a value for molded, plasticized, reinforced, or otherwise formulated CAB.

For a commercial formulation comparison under stated conditions, Eastman’s Tenite CAB selector chart lists at 23 °C and 50% relative humidity a 3%-plasticizer formula with ASTM D638 tensile yield stress of 45.5 MPa and ASTM D790 flexural modulus of 1862 MPa, versus 17.2 MPa and 827 MPa, respectively, for its 23%-plasticizer formula. Eastman identifies these as typical average-lot values rather than shipment specifications.
sections.processing: Cellulose acetate butyrate (CAB) is a thermoplastic cellulose ester used for injection molding, extrusion, and solution-cast films; its grade, plasticizer/solvent package, moisture level, residence time, and tool temperature should be selected for the intended article. Eastman’s Tenite cellulosics injection-molding guide identifies drying, melt and mold temperature, pressure, and injection speed as variables that affect molded article quality; its values are supplier guidance for its named cellulose-ester products rather than a generic CAB window. A separate CAB-containing fiber patent supplies a bounded melt-spinning route: CAB/DMSO-2 or CAB/CA/DMSO-2 solids were compounded and melt-spun, then the as-spun fiber was drawn/washed under tension to remove solvent. Its compounding, spinning, wash, and take-up ranges are formulation-specific; retaining tension during the hot-water wash was part of that reported operation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cellulose acetate butyrate (CAB) is a mixed cellulose ester bearing both acetyl and butyryl substituents; the substitution pattern defines a particular CAB grade.
sections.properties: Butyryl content and ultraviolet ageing affect the measured behavior of CAB films, while plasticizer level changes commercial CAB mechanical data.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. CAB grades modify coatings for automotive manufacture and refinishing, protective finishes and personal-care formulations. CAB-381-0.5 is a documented low-viscosity coating additive.

Purchasing. Eastman supplies CAB-381-0.5 as dry, free-flowing powder through its sales and authorized distributor channels. Butyryl content and viscosity grade distinguish purchasing specifications.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found in the checked open sources; supplier offerings establish availability, not sales volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Acid treatment of CAB waste is demonstrated in a hydrolysis/recovery patent; a complete environmental product inventory is unavailable.

Timescales: No ambient degradation time was verified.

Environmental persistence: Reactor hydrolysis does not establish environmental mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent tests CAB waste in an acid reactor to recover useful acid streams. This is a patented experimental route, not documented commercial collection and closed-loop recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Eastman CAB-321-0.1 powder can form combustible dust concentrations in air; the supplier calls for ignition and static-control precautions. Molten material can cause serious thermal burns. These process hazards apply to the named cellulose acetate butyrate grade and are distinct from the additional solvent, pigment or plasticizer hazards of a formulated coating.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Film and commercial-grade properties remain limited by butyryl/acetyl substitution, plasticizer, ageing exposure, and test specimen; they are not universal CAB values.

sections.overview: Cellulose acetate propionate is a mixed cellulose ester bearing acetate and propionate substituents. It is used as a melt-processable cellulosic plastic, with formulation and substitution level affecting the resulting material.
sections.history: Cellulose acetate propionate was developed in Kodak’s search for cellulose esters with improved film-base behavior. The Canadian Conservation Institute dates development to 1927 and records Kodak roll-film use from 1927 to approximately 1949. This was one branch of mixed-ester development alongside cellulose acetate butyrate. Its early photographic history should be distinguished from later molded-plastic grades and from cellulose acetate’s nineteenth-century discovery.
sections.nomenclature: CAP is the standard abbreviation for cellulose acetate propionate. The name denotes a mixed ester of cellulose rather than a physical blend of separate cellulose acetate and cellulose propionate materials.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cellulose acetate propionate (CAP) is a mixed ester made by acylating the hydroxyl groups of a cellulose precursor with acetyl and propionyl groups. A Daicel patent illustrates the chemistry with cellulose slurried in acetic and propionic acids, followed by cooled additions of acetic and propionic anhydrides with sulfuric acid; excess anhydrides are hydrolyzed, then the acid catalyst is neutralized before the ester is separated, washed, and dried. Its examples show that the acetic/propionic acylating balance can give different acetyl and propionyl substitution levels. A later patent describes a distinct, catalyst-specific example: propionic-acid activation of cellulose followed by propionic and acetic anhydrides with a sulfate-modified zirconia–iron oxide solid acid and beta zeolite, then acetic-acid hydrolysis and isolation. These are bounded preparation examples, not a claim that one catalyst or substitution pattern defines all CAP.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cellulose acetate propionate (CAP) is a thermoplastic cellulose ester whose tensile, flexural, hardness, and impact responses vary substantially with ester composition, molecular mass, plasticizer level, filler or blend formulation, and the molded or film specimen. Plasticization generally trades stiffness and strength for ductility and impact response; values for a commercial compounded grade or a membrane/composite are therefore not intrinsic CAP-family constants.

A bounded molded-grade example is Eastman Tenite™ Propionate 377-12 (clear, transparent; 12% plasticizer). Its technical data sheet reports ASTM D638 tensile stress at yield and break of 31.7 and 33.1 MPa, respectively, with 45% elongation at break; ASTM D790 flexural modulus is 1448 MPa. The same datasheet reports ASTM D256 notched Izod impact strength of 416 J/m at 23 °C and 107 J/m at −40 °C. These are typical results for that named, plasticized grade and the stated test methods, not a general CAP specification.

An injection-molded CAP482-20 composite study likewise measured tensile, flexural, and notched-Izod responses after drying, plasticization, melt blending, and addition of treated natural fiber or biofiller. Its results reinforce that plasticizer and modifier chemistry, filler loading and interface quality, and article preparation can change the balance of stiffness, strength, and elongation; comparisons require the exact formulation and test specimen.
sections.processing: CAP is supplied as a thermoplastic molding/extrusion compound, with injection molding a directly documented route. Eastman states that its propionate materials are generally easier to mold than cellulose acetate because of lower melt viscosity; keep regrind clean, separate from incompatible plastics, and blend it with virgin material. Moisture can cause roughness and bubbles, while incomplete cavity fill before chilling can leave marks and strain. For Eastman Tenite CAP, the supplier lists 2 h drying after storage below one month and 3 h after more than five months in an efficient dryer at 70 °C or above; its named M-to-H4 CAP flows span 195–245 °C cylinder and 40–75 °C mold settings. These are supplier-flow settings, not a universal CAP window. ARBURG's guide, which covers CA, CAB, CAP, and CP together, advises about 3 h at 80 °C if water absorption exceeds 0.2%, warns against excessive drying because of plasticizer migration/decomposition, and calls for slow cooling to limit strain.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cellulose acetate propionate (CAP) is a mixed cellulose ester with acetyl and propionyl substitution; feedstock activation and esterification conditions set that substitution.
sections.properties: Commercial CAP data are tied to the named grade and its plasticizer content, while biofiller composites show further formulation-dependent changes.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. CAP supplies film-forming functionality in printing inks, clear overprint varnishes and nail topcoats. Blends of CAP viscosity grades allow formulators to adjust their products.

Purchasing. Eastman CAP-482-0.5 is supplied as low-odor, free-flowing powder via regional sales and authorized distributors. Specify propionyl content and viscosity grade, rather than purchasing an unspecified cellulose ester.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found in the checked open sources; supplier offerings establish availability, not sales volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Acid treatment of CAP waste is demonstrated in a hydrolysis/recovery patent; a complete environmental product inventory is unavailable.

Timescales: No ambient degradation time was verified.

Environmental persistence: Reactor hydrolysis does not establish environmental mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent tests CAP waste in an acid reactor to recover useful acid streams. Scale and operating commercial adoption are not established.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The supplier sheet for Eastman CAP-482-0.5 identifies combustible dust as a processing hazard. It calls for control of ignition sources and static discharge and for approved waste handling. These considerations apply to the supplied resin; solvents, plasticizers and colorants in a finished cellulose acetate propionate article require their own assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Properties and molding behavior depend on acetyl/propionyl substitution, plasticizer, filler, drying, melt flow, and grade; a filled CAP composite is not representative of all CAP.
