sections.overview: Cellulose nitrate is the nitrate ester derivative of cellulose, formed when some cellulose hydroxyl groups are nitrated. Its composition varies with the extent of nitration and the starting cellulose material.
sections.history: Cellulose nitrate became an important nineteenth-century route from plant material to manufactured plastics. Alexander Parkes established the Parkesine Company in 1866 to commercialize a material he had demonstrated through objects ranging from jewelry to cutlery. John Wesley Hyatt’s Celluloid followed around 1870 and spread into articles such as combs and motion-picture film. By 1890, Hilaire de Chardonnet was marketing cellulose-nitrate-based artificial silk. These are milestones in plastic and fiber manufacture, distinct from the earlier preparation of nitrated cellulose. The Museum of Fine Arts also records a substantial later role in lacquers, aircraft fabric coatings, adhesives and glossy paints.
sections.nomenclature: Cellulose nitrate is commonly called nitrocellulose; both names refer to nitrate-ester derivatives of cellulose, not inorganic nitrate salts. The record covers the substitution-variable material family rather than a single nitrogen-content grade.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Cellulose nitrate is the nitrate-ester derivative produced by nitrating hydroxyl groups on cellulose; it is not a vinyl-polymerization product. The cellulose feedstock can be purified plant cellulose such as cotton, wood, or flax material, and published work also investigates bacterial or synthetic cellulose precursors. A review of cellulose modification identifies nitric acid/sulfuric acid mixtures and nitric acid/acetic acid/acetic anhydride systems as nitrating routes. One 2025 study is a deliberately narrow alternative-feedstock example: cellulose first obtained by electropolymerization of aqueous glucose with a tungsten–vanadium heteropolyacid catalyst was dried, nitrated in mixed sulfuric–nitric acids, then filtered, cold-water washed, and stabilized by sequential water, dilute sodium bicarbonate, and water treatments. The paper presents that as a synthetic-cellulose route, not as conventional cellulose-nitrate manufacture.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Cellulose nitrate does not have a single mechanical response across lacquer, membrane, molded-plastic, and energetic-binder forms. Nitrate substitution removes cellulose hydroxyl groups and disrupts part of the parent hydrogen-bonded order; the cellulose source, degree of nitration, chain length or solution-viscosity grade, and retained morphology consequently influence cohesion and strength. Solvent history, residual solvent, porosity, orientation, moisture, and aging further distinguish a dense cast film from a porous diagnostic membrane. Unmodified films can be comparatively brittle, while camphor, nitrate-ester liquids, cyclic-ester polymers, oils, resins, and other formulation components plasticize or reinforce the nitrate-cellulose phase and change the balance among tensile strength, extensibility, hardness, and impact response. Values from such compounds must remain attached to their composition and article form.

A Union Carbide patent provides a bounded unmodified-film comparison within a plasticizer study. Its control used an SS one-half-second nitrocellulose grade containing about 11 wt% nitrogen. A solution containing 20 wt% of that nitrocellulose with ethyl acetate, 2-nitropropane, and isopropanol was cast on glass and air-dried, then tested in tension on an Instron instrument. The control row reports 4,980 psi ultimate tensile stress (about 34.3 MPa) and 9% elongation; the table note says values are averages of at least two tests. The digitized patent renders the ASTM procedure number ambiguously and does not state film thickness, final conditioning, test speed, or direction. The result therefore describes that historical low-nitrogen solution grade and cast-film protocol, not a cellulose-nitrate family constant or the response of plasticized celluloid, porous membranes, or propellant binders.
sections.processing: Cellulose nitrate is documented as a solution-converted material: collodion can be poured or coated onto a support and dried to a film, while camphor-plasticized celluloid has been cast as flexible sheet. The Canadian Conservation Institute records historical casting on large glass tables and cutting, heating, and pressing nitrate sheet between metal plates; these sources support casting, coating, drying, and pressing rather than a generic melt window. In a Neves et al. reference-film experiment, a 4% (w/v) methanolic cellulose-nitrate solution was dissolved overnight at 20 °C, poured onto porcelain, dried over silica gel for 3 h, and peeled as an approximately 150 µm transparent film. Their celluloid reference used 70/30 cellulose nitrate/camphor by mass. This is a research-film protocol; material instability and combustion/degradation hazards remain relevant handling constraints.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cellulose nitrate is a nitrate ester of cellulose; degree of nitration and residual formulation components determine the particular material.
sections.properties: Its film behavior and stability depend on nitration level, solvent state, and plasticizer formulation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Industrial cellulose nitrate supplies wood, leather and metal finishes, printing inks, nail polish and specialized analytical or medical membranes. These applications use qualified industrial grades.

Purchasing. Synthesia offers Type E nitrocellulose in specified viscosity grades, wetted with water or alcohols. The listed alcohol-wetted products contain 30% or 35% wetting agent, so delivered product mass differs from dry polymer mass.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found for these industrial grades. The supplier’s wetting percentages describe formulation composition, not market size or a purchase lot.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Light-induced nitrate-group loss can release nitrogen dioxide radicals; oxidation and cleavage of glycosidic links produce carbonyl-containing structures, including a proposed gluconolactone product. Yellowing and embrittlement accompany chemical change.

Timescales: Thin laboratory films were photoaged at 40 °C with a xenon source, wavelengths at least 280 nm and 800 W/m², for up to 150 hours. These accelerated optical/chemical aging results are not a mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: The study of historical and artificial film aging does not quantify soil or aquatic persistence. Formulation and prior storage history alter the observed condition.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For historic cellulose nitrate film, specialist duplication preserves the image rather than recovering the polymer. NARA recommends transfer to an institution able to store nitrate safely; where controlled storage is unavailable, its U.S. guidance directs disposal under the applicable regulations. Ordinary paper or plastic recycling is not the preservation route described.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Cellulose nitrate photographic film can become unstable as it ages and presents a serious fire hazard under unsuitable storage. NARA recommends separating it from other collections and using specialized storage and trained handlers. These precautions concern nitrate film; nitrogen content and formulation also distinguish other cellulose nitrate materials.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Nitration degree and camphor or other formulation components limit comparison of cellulose-nitrate films; the reported cast-film evidence is not transferable to every nitrate grade.

sections.overview: Methyl cellulose is a cellulose ether in which some cellulose hydroxyl groups are methylated. The extent of etherification governs its composition-dependent solubility and material behavior.
sections.history: Methyl cellulose belongs to the early industrial cellulose ethers. BeMiller’s historical review dates Dow’s commercial methylcellulose production to 1938. It became a useful substitute for natural gum and adhesive systems, with applications in paper sizing and textile and paper conservation. Dow’s Methocel, Hoechst’s Tylose and ICI’s Methofas illustrate several commercial development lines. Conservators also used methyl cellulose in cleaning poultices and as an adhesive. These milestones concern commercialization and adoption of the material; the 1938 date is specific to Dow’s production and does not identify the first laboratory preparation.
sections.nomenclature: MC is a common abbreviation for methyl cellulose. The name identifies a methylated cellulose derivative, not unmodified cellulose or cellulose ethers generally.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Methyl cellulose is a semisynthetic cellulose ether made by partial etherification of the hydroxyl groups on the cellulose anhydroglucose units, not by making a new carbohydrate backbone. In the usual heterogeneous route, cellulose is first alkalized with sodium hydroxide to form alkali cellulose, then reacted with a methylating agent such as chloromethane; methyl substitution level and its distribution along the chains are important route outcomes. A patent example uses cotton linters or high-alpha wood cellulose, aqueous sodium hydroxide activation, and methyl chloride under pressure, with the alkali concentration and alkali-to-cellulose ratio identified as controls on substitution uniformity. These examples apply to methyl-cellulose manufacture; hydroxyalkyl methylcellulose variants and final-use gelation are not treated as the same material or as synthesis requirements here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Methyl cellulose (MC) can present two very different mechanical regimes. A dry, self-supporting MC film is an amorphous cellulose-ether solid whose tensile response can range from stiff and relatively brittle to ductile after plasticization; in water, MC forms viscous solutions and, on heating, thermoreversible physical gels whose fibrillar network has a much lower shear or tensile modulus. These forms are not interchangeable. Degree and pattern of methyl substitution, residual hydroxyl content, molar mass and distribution, polymer concentration, grade viscosity, water content and relative humidity control chain association and mobility. Drying rate, film thickness, thermal history and orientation affect film density and residual stress. Water, glycerol, polyethylene glycol and other small molecules generally plasticize a dry film, often reducing modulus and strength while increasing elongation, but phase separation or plasticizer migration can reverse simple trends. In aqueous systems, salt identity and concentration, MC concentration, temperature and heating rate set the sol-gel transition and network density; test frequency, strain amplitude, pre-shear or stress during gelation, and time at temperature affect the measured modulus and failure response. Chemical cross-linking improves wet stability and stiffness but may suppress thermoreversibility. Nanocellulose or other fillers can reinforce films and gels when well dispersed, whereas aggregation creates defects. Moisture sorption, dissolution, cyclic humidity, creep and stress relaxation therefore require form- and service-specific testing. Paunonen's open review treats freestanding MC films and documents the importance of water, plasticizer, blend composition, filler dispersion and film preparation rather than presenting a universal family range. Bonetti and co-workers provide a bounded wet-hydrogel example. They prepared an 8% w/v Sigma M0512 MC suspension in 0.05 M sodium sulfate, held it at 4 °C for 24 h, cast and dried it at 50 °C for 24 h, and used the non-chemically-cross-linked material as the control. After 24 h in distilled water at 37 °C to reach swelling equilibrium, three specimens were tested in tension by DMA with a 0.001 N preload and a strain ramp of 0.3 min^-1; Young's modulus from the 0-5% strain slope was 5.53 ± 1.00 kPa. A medium citric-acid-cross-linked formulation containing 3 wt% acid relative to MC and cured at 177.5 °C for 8 min reached 67.83 ± 6.03 kPa under the same hydrated test, whereas heavier cross-linking produced still higher stiffness but lost the desired thermoresponsive behavior. These numbers characterize hydrated, sodium-sulfate-prepared laboratory hydrogels near 37 °C, not dry MC film, powder, coating, tablet binder or other MC grades.
sections.processing: Methyl cellulose is commonly converted from aqueous solution or dispersion by coating, casting, and evaporative drying; concentration, molecular mass, substitution, plasticizer, and drying history strongly affect viscosity and film formation. The open cellulose-derivative film review describes methylcellulose film preparation, plasticizer/additive dispersion, casting, drying, and the difficulty of comparing films made under different conditions. A bounded laboratory example used an 8% w/v methyl-cellulose formulation in 0.05 M sodium sulfate, held at 4 °C for 24 h, cast and dried at 50 °C for 24 h; a citric-acid-containing version was then cured at 177.5 °C for 8 min. That hydrogel/film protocol is formulation-specific and includes a post-cure chemistry not intrinsic to every methyl-cellulose grade; it should not be generalized to ordinary aqueous coatings or to upstream etherification.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Methyl cellulose is a partially methylated cellulose ether whose substitution controls chain association and solubility.
sections.properties: Its film, gel, and water-response behavior depends on substitution, molecular weight, additives, and crosslinking.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Methylcellulose grades provide thermal gel structure in plant-based burgers and cheese. Pharmaceutical methylcellulose excipients also support controlled-release drug matrices.

Purchasing. Food formulators can request Benecel grades through ingredient sales; pharmaceutical portfolios documented in 2024 include METHOCEL. Choose the required viscosity and food or pharmaceutical specification.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found in the checked open sources; supplier offerings establish availability, not sales volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cellulase susceptibility falls with substitution; the tested MC had degree of substitution 1.7.

Timescales: Its film completely disintegrated visually after 10 weeks in pilot compost peaking at 70.7 °C.

Environmental persistence: Visible disappearance does not measure mineralization or predict cold-water persistence.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Pilot composting demonstrates an organic-treatment route for that film; acceptance of a formulated article requires separate evidence.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: EFSA’s 2018 EU assessment of methylcellulose (E461) found no safety concern at reported food uses and levels and no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake. This conclusion concerns specified food additives, not all industrial or medical applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited studies examine specified films and citric-acid-crosslinked hydrogels, not every MC grade.

sections.overview: Ethyl cellulose is a semisynthetic cellulose-ether subfamily in which cellulose hydroxyl groups are substituted with ethyl groups. Degree of substitution controls solubility and material behavior across grades.
sections.history: Ethyl cellulose was the product with which Dow entered the plastics business in 1935, under the Ethocel name. Dow’s history describes substantial wartime use in telephone components, goggles, control knobs, aircraft parts and canteens. Its later uses included protective paper and textile coatings, inks and hot-melt adhesives. Pharmaceutical formulation offered another direction: a 1993 Sterling Drug patent by Steven Frisbee, Gregg Stetsko and Margaret Lawton used ethylcellulose-containing coatings to control drug release. These milestones trace the transition from molded cellulose plastic to a functional coating polymer, without treating Dow’s launch as the first synthesis of ethyl cellulose.
sections.nomenclature: EC is the abbreviation used for ethyl cellulose. The name covers cellulose with ethoxy substitution across a range of degrees of substitution, not native cellulose, cellulose acetate, or one particular molecular-mass/solution grade; cast films and other formulated products are downstream material forms.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethyl cellulose is a semisynthetic cellulose ether rather than a polymer made from ethylene. Cellulose feedstock can be isolated from paper or supplied as purified pulp, then converted to alkali cellulose before an ethylating reaction replaces some hydroxyl hydrogen atoms with ethoxy groups. In one research-scale example, paper-derived cellulose was de-inked with aqueous sodium hydroxide, reacted with ethyl chloride in acetone, neutralized with acetic acid, washed, and then sonicated only to make nanosized particles. A Hercules patent gives a distinct staged process example: cotton linters, aqueous sodium hydroxide, and liquid ethyl chloride form an alkali-cellulose slurry; additional alkali and successive etherification stages increase substitution, followed by water washing and drying. Those reagent ratios, temperatures, and substitution targets are source-specific process examples, not universal requirements for every grade.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Ethyl cellulose is a film-forming thermoplastic cellulose ether. Commercial film grades can form strong, adherent, comparatively hydrophobic coatings, but the observed response ranges from stiff or brittle to flexible and tough because ethyl cellulose is commonly tested as a cast film, coating, fiber, gel, blend, or plasticized formulation rather than as one standardized bulk material. Below its glass-transition region, unplasticized films show an initially elastic response followed by limited or formulation-dependent plastic deformation; softening and viscoelastic deformation increase with temperature. Molecular mass and chain-length distribution, ethoxy content and degree of substitution, residual hydroxyl groups, plasticizer identity and loading, solvent quality, polymer concentration, blend or filler content, particle coalescence, residual solvent, casting and drying rate, film thickness, porosity, orientation, humidity or water uptake, aging, strain rate, and test temperature all affect strength, modulus, elongation, and toughness. Higher molecular mass generally increases film strength until entanglement-related gains level off, while added plasticizer commonly lowers stiffness and strength but increases flexibility and elongation. Solvent and drying history can change packing and morphology enough to shift tensile results even without a plasticizer. Horvat and co-workers give one bounded example using a Sigma-Aldrich ethyl cellulose with 48.7 wt% ethoxyl content, degree of substitution 2.5, and stated solution viscosity of 57 mPa s. A 10 wt% solution in ethanol was prepared at 70 °C, cooled and dried at 6 °C without plasticizer, producing a 0.19 mm film. For 30 x 4 mm strips tested at 100 mm/min, the reported tensile strength was 14.2 MPa and elastic modulus was 576.5 MPa. A 10 wt% ethanol film from the same material dried at room temperature was 0.48 mm thick and gave 28.9 MPa tensile strength and 913.0 MPa modulus under the same reported tensile procedure, illustrating the importance of film-formation history. The paper does not identify a tensile standard, gauge length, test temperature or humidity, pre-test conditioning, or uncertainty for the tabulated values, so these are preparation-specific film results rather than grade specifications or family-wide ranges. In coated articles and composites, substrate constraint, adhesion, coat continuity, defects, residual stress, and loading direction further control cracking, peeling, fatigue, and apparent durability.
sections.processing:
Ethyl cellulose is commonly converted from solution or dispersion into films, coatings, binders, matrices, and encapsulating layers; suitable thermoplastic grades can also be hot-melt processed. Solvent or carrier choice, polymer molecular mass and ethoxy substitution, solids content, plasticizer, mixing temperature, coating or casting thickness, and evaporation or drying history control solution viscosity, coalescence, residual solvent, and film integrity. Polymer and plasticizer should be dissolved or dispersed uniformly and entrained bubbles controlled before casting or coating. Because a solvent and drying schedule can change packing and porosity, a temperature taken from one film experiment is not a universal grade window.

Horvat and co-workers provide a bounded solvent-casting example for an ethyl-cellulose grade containing 48.7 wt% ethoxyl groups and having degree of substitution 2.5. They prepared 10 wt% solutions in ethanol at 70 °C, cooled them, cast them without plasticizer, and compared drying at 6 °C with room-temperature drying. The low-temperature route produced a reported 0.19 mm transparent film, whereas the room-temperature route produced a 0.48 mm film with different tensile response. These solution concentration, mixing and drying conditions apply to that grade, solvent, and casting geometry.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Ethyl cellulose is a cellulose ether in which hydroxyl groups are partially ethylated. Substitution level and molecular weight control chain interactions, solubility, and film formation.
sections.properties: EC is hydrophobic relative to cellulose and can form transparent films; barrier and mechanical behavior depend on substitution, plasticizer, solvent, and processing.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Ethyl cellulose serves pharmaceutical multiparticulate coatings for modified release and taste masking. Research applications include controlled-release microcapsules and drug-delivery fibers.

Purchasing. Commercial pharmaceutical EC includes ETHOCEL grades; a research example is Sigma-Aldrich 247499, specified by ethoxyl content and solution viscosity, in 100 g and 500 g packs.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked catalog establishes order 10^2-gram research packs, not typical industrial orders. No reliable separate annual EC consumption or purchase tonnage was found.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Ethyl-cellulose film tests show thermal mass loss; the source does not identify a complete molecular product inventory.

Timescales: Programmed heating experiments are thermal stability measurements, not a duration for environmental degradation.

Environmental persistence: No condition-qualified soil, marine or freshwater mineralization time was established in the cited work.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A 1977 EPA research report demonstrated solvent removal of ethyl-cellulose textile size and partial recovery of both size and solvent by distillation for reuse. The laboratory work also identified brittleness after thermal recovery as a limitation. This is a historical process demonstration, not evidence of modern commercial adoption or an endorsement of its chlorinated solvents.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: EFSA’s 2018 EU assessment of ethylcellulose (E462) found no safety concern at reported food uses and levels and no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake. This conclusion concerns specified food additives, not all industrial or medical applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The film study reports a particular one-pot preparation, and pharmaceutical architectures depend on grade and formulation. Those results do not define all ethyl-cellulose materials.

sections.overview: Hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC) is a cellulose-ether subfamily produced by reacting alkali cellulose with ethylene oxide. The amount of hydroxyethyl substitution is a controlled compositional variable in its manufacture.
sections.history: Hydroxyethyl cellulose entered industrial use during the early development of water-soluble cellulose ethers; the Museum of Fine Arts places it in the 1930s. Thickeners, emulsifiers and film formers for coatings, cosmetics and other formulations became major roles, with Cellosize, Natrosol and Tylose H among commercial lines. A documented manufacturing advance was Rayonier’s patent filed in 1959 by Reid Logan Mitchell, Arthur Albohn and Stig Palmgren. Published in 1962, it described continuous contact between alkali cellulose and ethylene oxide using a vibrating conveyor. This was a process-engineering contribution to an existing polymer, not its first synthesis.
sections.nomenclature: HEC identifies hydroxyethyl-substituted cellulose, not unmodified cellulose or every cellulose ether. Molar substitution and any later crosslinking or blending define narrower HEC materials; a cast film or composite is a formulation based on HEC rather than a synonym for the base derivative.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC) is a cellulose ether produced by etherifying cellulose hydroxyl groups with ethylene oxide after alkali activation of the cellulose. A conventional route first converts cellulose to alkali cellulose using aqueous sodium hydroxide, then reacts it with ethylene oxide in a water-containing slurry or other controlled medium. Water and caustic levels affect competing ethylene-oxide hydration and the attainable or uniform molar substitution, so they are important process controls rather than incidental details. A staged slurry patent uses partial neutralization between ethylene-oxide charges to control substitution; a separate continuous process contacts fibrous alkali cellulose with ethylene-oxide gas. These are specific manufacturing examples, not a prescription for all HEC grades. Dissolution, film casting, and other use-stage processing are excluded.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC) mechanical measurements are form-dependent: the open studies below concern dry, solution-cast films, not hydrated solutions or bulk cellulose.  In those film systems, formulation additives, crosslinking, and the casting/drying protocol change tensile response.  A bounded neat-film example was prepared from 1 g HEC in 20 mL water, cast on Teflon and dried at 45 °C: the reported HEC film had tensile strength 2.10 MPa, elongation at break 147.69%, and Young's modulus 2.98 MPa, measured by ASTM D638 at 5 mm/min from five specimens.  In that study, 2.5--10 wt% mangiferin was a formulation variable.  Independently, a crosslinked HEC/PVA/epsilon-polylysine food-packaging-film study found its maximum reported tensile strength (95.9 ± 4.1 MPa) and elongation at break (148.8 ± 2.6%) for the 40% PVA formulation; those values belong to that multicomponent film and must not be generalized to HEC.
sections.processing:
Hydroxyethyl cellulose (HEC) is commonly converted from aqueous solution into coatings, films, and other cast articles rather than treated as a conventional melt-molding resin. A typical sequence is dissolution with controlled agitation, incorporation of a plasticizer, filler, or crosslinker, degassing or sonication as needed, casting or coating onto a support, and drying to constant mass. Water content and drying rate strongly affect film uniformity, porosity, flexibility, and residual moisture; formulation additives and crosslinking can change the usable rheology. The following conditions are bounded solution-film examples, not universal HEC processing settings.

Tohamy and co-workers dissolved 1 g HEC in 20 mL water, ultrasonicated the solution with 2.5–10% mangiferin, poured it onto Teflon, and dried at 45 °C to constant weight. In a distinct HEC/PVA/epsilon-polylysine study, 1 g HEC was dissolved in 25 mL of 0.25 M NaOH, mixed with a PVA solution, crosslinked with epichlorohydrin at 50 °C for 6 h, stirred with epsilon-polylysine at 50 °C for 1 h, poured into dishes, and dried at room temperature. These examples establish aqueous casting and formulation-specific crosslinking; the etherification manufacture of HEC belongs in Synthesis.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Hydroxyethyl cellulose is a cellulose ether in which some anhydroglucose hydroxyl groups carry hydroxyethyl substituents. The cellulose backbone remains a polysaccharide chain, while substitution disrupts native crystal packing and provides water-compatible, hydrophilic segments.
sections.properties: HEC is a nonionic, water-soluble or water-dispersible thickener and film former whose viscosity depends on molecular mass, substitution, concentration, temperature, and shear history. It can stabilize aqueous formulations and modify rheology without the ionic sensitivity characteristic of many charged cellulose derivatives.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. HEC acts as a water-soluble thickener, binder, protective colloid and suspension stabilizer for aqueous formulations. Purchasing is driven by the formulation’s required rheology and stability.

Purchasing. A documented research supply is Sigma-Aldrich 434973, average viscosity molecular weight about 720,000, sold in 250 g and 1 kg packs. Specify grade and solution-viscosity requirements for formulation work.

Scale and evidence limits. These catalog packs span order 10^2–10^3 grams. They do not measure industrial HEC demand; no reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Endoglucanase-mediated cleavage of internal β-1,4 links in hydroxyethyl cellulose lowers viscosity and creates additional reducing ends; this does not demonstrate removal of every hydroxyethyl substituent.

Timescales: The patent establishes an enzyme-activity substrate and reaction mechanism, not an environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: Susceptibility in a cellulase assay cannot establish complete biodegradation of every HEC grade in soil or water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For Natrosol 250HX PHARM HEC spills, the supplier recommends collecting the powder without generating dust and keeping it in closed containers for disposal. This is controlled waste handling, not polymer reclamation. The same sheet’s poor ready-biodegradability result cautions against assuming that dissolved HEC waste will rapidly disappear in treatment.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Ashland’s Natrosol 250HX PHARM HEC powder may irritate eyes, skin and airways and can form combustible dust–air mixtures. The supplier recommends ventilation, grounded transfer equipment and removal of accumulated dust. Pharmaceutical-grade identity does not remove powder-handling hazards or establish every finished formulation’s suitability for a particular medical route.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: HEC performance varies with degree and uniformity of substitution, molecular-weight distribution, hydration procedure, salts, surfactants, pH, temperature, and shear. Enzymes, strong oxidants, and prolonged heat can reduce chain length or viscosity; a solution-grade result should not be generalized to dry powder or another formulation.

sections.overview: Hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) is a cellulose-ether subfamily produced by etherifying alkali cellulose with propylene oxide. Its hydroxypropyl substitution is controlled through the activation and etherification conditions.
sections.history: Hydroxypropyl cellulose became an industrial cellulose ether through Hercules development associated with Eugene D. Klug. BeMiller dates its commercialization to 1966. A Klug patent filed in 1963 and published in 1966 documents process improvements in which propylene oxide served as both reagent and diluent. The commercial Klucel line subsequently supported thickening and film-forming uses in formulations, as well as paper sizing and leather consolidation in conservation. These developments link manufacturing control to a polymer soluble in selected aqueous and organic media; they should not be conflated with the invention of cellulose ethers as a whole.
sections.nomenclature: HPC denotes hydroxypropyl-substituted cellulose, not cellulose itself or the separate hydroxyethyl and hydroxypropyl-methyl cellulose derivatives. Molar substitution and molecular mass identify individual HPC grades, while a crosslinked film or fiber is a formulation-specific material state.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) is made by converting cellulose to alkali cellulose and etherifying it with propylene oxide. Sodium-hydroxide and water contents during activation, the propylene-oxide charge, diluent choice, and reaction staging control the hydroxypropyl molar substitution and byproduct formation. One patent describes a two-stage propylene-oxide reaction of alkali cellulose in an inert diluent and warns that excessive alkali or water favors polypropylene-glycol byproduct; another describes a pressable alkali-cellulose route followed by etherification with propylene oxide in heptane. These are manufacturing examples and do not make their exact substitution level or solvent universal. Neutralization, washing, and drying are recovery operations after etherification, not evidence for article-level processing guidance.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
HPC can form flexible, transparent films and fibres, but its solid-state mechanics are strongly moisture-, morphology-, and process-dependent. Residual water plasticizes the cellulose-ether network, while molecular weight, hydroxypropyl substitution, solvent-casting history, crystallinity or liquid-crystalline order, and crosslinking alter stiffness and deformation. In fibre form, shear-induced chain alignment can raise stiffness and strength relative to a solution-cast film; elevated humidity substantially softens the material.

As a bounded example, Guivier and Weder studied HPC of weight-average molecular weight 370,000 g/mol. For solvent-cast films conditioned at 0% relative humidity, room-temperature tensile testing at 10 mm/min gave Young's modulus 657 ± 44 MPa, tensile strength 19 ± 1 MPa, and strain at break 27 ± 2%. Wet-spun fibres from aqueous HPC/CaCl2 processing gave 1346 ± 148 MPa, 36 ± 6 MPa, and 4 ± 1%, respectively, under the same dry condition; at 60% relative humidity the corresponding fibre values fell to 258 ± 76 MPa and 8 ± 1 MPa while break strain rose to 19 ± 5%. These film/fibre and humidity-specific results are not a general HPC specification. A separate USDA study of solvent-cast films found multiple dynamic-mechanical relaxations associated with amorphous and more ordered phases, and reported that diisocyanate crosslinking shifted the primary relaxations upward, supporting the importance of morphology and crosslink density to service-temperature response.
sections.processing:
Hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) is readily converted from aqueous or other solution dope into solvent-cast films and wet-spun fibers. Processing generally requires complete dissolution and filtration, controlled dope concentration and viscosity, and either casting followed by solvent evaporation or extrusion through a spinneret into a nonsolvent coagulation bath. Bath composition and temperature, take-up/draw, washing, drying, and humidity conditioning govern coagulation, shrinkage, orientation, and residual solvent or salt; HPC grade molecular mass and substitution alter these settings.

A recent wet-spinning study varied HPC dope concentration from 5–20 wt% and used water, aqueous CaCl2/NaCl, acidic, alcohol, acetone, or DMAc/water baths at 25–80 °C. Its bounded film protocol cast 15 wt% aqueous HPC in PTFE dishes, evaporated solvent under ambient conditions for 72 h, then oven-dried at 50 °C for 48 h. Separately, the USDA-hosted Rials–Glasser report characterizes solvent-cast HPC films and notes a residual-diluent relaxation; this supports solvent casting but not a universal solvent or drying schedule. The alkali-cellulose/propylene-oxide etherification route is upstream Synthesis, not article processing.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Hydroxypropyl cellulose is a cellulose ether with hydroxypropyl substituents on the anhydroglucose backbone. Substitution reduces native cellulose crystallinity and allows hydrated chains to form viscous solutions; sufficiently concentrated solutions can also display ordered or liquid-crystalline behavior.
sections.properties: HPC is water-soluble over a useful formulation range and acts as a film former, binder, and rheology modifier. Its hydration, viscosity, optical response, and thermal behavior depend on substitution, molecular mass, concentration, solvent composition, and temperature.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. HPC is used in pharmaceutical binder and drug-delivery formulations. Food grades include whipping agents for nondairy toppings and vegetable creams.

Purchasing. Food formulators can request Aerowhip HPC through ingredient suppliers. Sigma-Aldrich 191884 provides a research example: nominal molecular weight about 100,000, powder, with a 100 g catalog pack.

Scale and evidence limits. The 100 g pack documents research-scale supply only. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed HPC tonnage was found.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Dissolution in cold water and precipitation on heating can leave HPC recoverable as polymer. These reversible changes are not backbone degradation; a verified environmental product inventory remains a gap.

Timescales: A precipitation/recovery operation does not supply a chemical degradation time.

Environmental persistence: Water dispersal must not be equated with mineralization; soil and aquatic persistence remain unquantified here.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A textile-sizing patent demonstrates cold-water removal, heating to precipitate HPC, separation and reuse as warp size, with comparable reported yarn performance. This is a specific reclamation process, not proof of universal post-consumer recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: EFSA’s 2018 EU assessment of hydroxypropyl cellulose (E463) found no safety concern at reported food uses and levels and no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake. This conclusion concerns specified food additives, not all industrial or medical applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: HPC can lose viscosity through chain scission, oxidation, enzymes, or prolonged thermal and shear exposure. Solubility and phase behavior change with temperature, salts, solvent composition, substitution, and concentration, so a product's solution window and film behavior cannot be transferred to every HPC grade.

sections.overview: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) is a mixed cellulose ether made by etherifying alkali cellulose with methyl chloride and propylene oxide. Its methyl and hydroxypropyl substitution targets are controlled during manufacture.
sections.history: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose developed through the tailoring of mixed cellulose ethers to different solvents and applications. A 1974 Dow patent by George Greminger Jr., Carl Strange, Karl Krumel and James Hudson Jr. describes earlier commercial HPMC as a thickener for water-based paints and coatings. Their advance increased hydroxypropyl substitution to obtain grades soluble in anhydrous alcohol, addressing pharmaceutical-coating applications where water or chlorinated solvent mixtures were undesirable. Tablet coatings and water-soluble films therefore accompanied the established coatings-thickener role. The patent documents a particular grade-development milestone, not a first invention date for all HPMC.
sections.nomenclature: HPMC identifies the mixed methyl/hydroxypropyl cellulose derivative, not unmodified cellulose, hydroxypropyl cellulose, or methylcellulose alone. Substitution levels and any plasticizer, reinforcement, or crosslinking formulation describe particular HPMC materials rather than alternate names for the derivative.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) is a mixed cellulose ether made by first forming alkali cellulose and then methylating and hydroxypropylating cellulose hydroxyl groups with methyl chloride and propylene oxide. It is distinct from methylcellulose or hydroxypropyl cellulose because both substituent classes are intentionally installed. The feed ratio and addition sequence of methyl chloride and propylene oxide, the alkali-cellulose composition, reaction medium, and temperature determine methoxyl degree of substitution and hydroxypropoxyl molar substitution. A historical patent describes concurrent methyl-chloride/propylene-oxide etherification of alkali cellulose; a later process documents controlled feed ratios with dimethyl ether as an inert medium. These are grade-specific examples. Recovery, drying, and final use as a thickener or film former are outside this synthesis-only account.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
HPMC is commonly used as a water-soluble film-former or coating, and the mechanics of a dried HPMC film depend on substitution and molecular-weight grade, residual moisture, casting and drying history, thickness, and the identity and loading of plasticizers, pigments, oils, or reinforcing particles. Strong intermolecular interactions make unplasticized films relatively stiff and low-elongation; small-molecule plasticizers increase segmental mobility and elongation while reducing tensile strength and modulus. The material's hydrophilicity means humidity and water exposure remain consequential to any measured film response.

In a bounded solvent-cast-film study, Owusu-Ware and co-workers tested HPMC containing 0, 6, 8, 11, or 17 wt% PEG 400. Films were pulled between texture-analyzer grips at 0.2 mm/s (0.1 N trigger force) to break or a 300 mm travel limit. The unplasticized formulation gave tensile strength 31 ± 2 MPa, elongation 4 ± 1%, and elastic modulus 1271 ± 105 MPa; at 17 wt% PEG the corresponding values were 21 ± 2 MPa, 23 ± 1%, and 565 ± 54 MPa. Film dimensions, conditioning humidity, and HPMC substitution grade are not specified in the summarized report, so these results demonstrate a particular cast-film/plasticizer trend rather than a family range. An independent open review likewise identifies casting formulation and additive type, loading, moisture sensitivity, and filler dispersion as central controls on HPMC-film strength, modulus, and flexibility.
sections.processing:
Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) is most often converted as a water- or mixed-solvent solution into films, coatings, capsules, and other cast articles. The usual sequence is controlled dissolution and hydration, addition and dispersion of plasticizer, oil, active ingredient, or reinforcement, casting or coating, and drying under controlled humidity. HPMC grade viscosity, methoxyl/hydroxypropoxyl substitution, solids content, plasticizer level, and drying history determine solution rheology, gelation, film coalescence, flexibility, and residual moisture. These sources support solution casting and additive-sensitive film processing; they do not establish a general HPMC melt-processing window.

Owusu-Ware and co-workers provide a bounded example in which HPMC/PEG 400 formulations were prepared as solvent-cast films and mechanically tested; PEG level was a formulation variable rather than a family-wide prescription. A separate open review surveys HPMC film/coating preparation and shows that plasticizers, oils, cellulose reinforcement, and humidity alter drying behavior and tensile flexibility. Accordingly, plasticizer choice, drying atmosphere, and film thickness should be optimized for the named formulation. Methylation/hydroxypropylation of alkali cellulose belongs in Synthesis, not this article-conversion account.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Hydroxypropyl methylcellulose is a mixed cellulose ether bearing methoxy and hydroxypropoxy substituents on a cellulose backbone. The two substituent types tune hydration, chain association, gelation, and film formation relative to unmodified cellulose.
sections.properties: HPMC is a nonionic water-soluble polymer used for viscosity control, film formation, suspension stabilization, and thermally reversible gelation in aqueous systems. Viscosity, gel temperature, surface activity, and film behavior vary with substitution pattern, molecular mass, concentration, and salts or additives.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. HPMC supports gluten-free bakery structure and pharmaceutical controlled-release matrices. Food and pharmaceutical specifications serve different manufacturing needs.

Purchasing. Ingredient suppliers offer application-specific HPMC grades, including Benecel for foods and the METHOCEL pharmaceutical portfolio documented in 2024. Buyers specify viscosity, substitution grade and relevant quality requirements.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual purchased or consumed tonnage was found in the checked open sources; supplier offerings establish availability, not sales volume.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Cavitation can cleave HPMC chains mechanically. Added hydrogen peroxide causes oxidation as well, giving carbonyl-containing chains; formic acid and other small oxidation products were tentatively assigned spectroscopically.

Timescales: For K4M HPMC initially about 335 kg/mol, hydrodynamic cavitation with peroxide at 60 °C reduced weight-average molar mass to about 4 kg/mol in 30 minutes. This is chain shortening, not mineralization.

Environmental persistence: These controlled dilute-solution treatments do not establish a soil, freshwater or seawater half-life.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Cavitation is a laboratory method for obtaining shorter-chain HPMC and a possible treatment approach. The study does not establish recovery of equivalent high-molar-mass polymer or commercial post-consumer recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: EFSA’s 2018 EU assessment of hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (E464) found no safety concern at reported food uses and levels and no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake. This conclusion concerns specified food additives, not all industrial or medical applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: HPMC grades differ substantially in substitution, viscosity, particle form, and gelation temperature. Hydration order, temperature, electrolyte level, pH, shear, and interacting ingredients can cause lumping, precipitation, or a large viscosity shift; formulation data should remain tied to the named grade.

sections.overview: Carboxymethyl cellulose is a cellulose ether in which some cellulose hydroxyl groups carry carboxymethyl substituents. It is widely used in aqueous formulations and film-forming systems, while its behavior depends on substitution and counterion form.
sections.history: Carboxymethyl cellulose’s early history includes a German preparation patent issued in 1918. Hercules began commercial U.S. production in 1943, according to BeMiller’s historical review. Initially developed as a replacement for natural gums, it expanded into applications that used its ability to alter solution behavior. This chronology distinguishes the early patent from later industrial scale-up and explains why CMC belongs to the history of formulated products as much as to the history of plastics.
sections.nomenclature: CMC is the customary abbreviation for carboxymethyl cellulose; sodium carboxymethyl cellulose is a salt form within that material family. The name does not cover cellulose ethers generally, nor does it identify unmodified cellulose.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Carboxymethyl cellulose is a chemically modified cellulose subfamily: carboxymethyl ether groups replace some of the hydroxyl hydrogens on a cellulose backbone. Plant-derived cellulose is a common feedstock, with alternative cellulosic residues also reported. A conventional heterogeneous route first alkalizes cellulose with sodium hydroxide, then etherifies the activated material using monochloroacetic acid or sodium monochloroacetate. Degree of substitution is route- and feedstock-dependent; the available studies identify alkali concentration, carboxymethylating-agent concentration, solvent system, temperature, and time as important controls. In one laboratory example, microcrystalline cellulose was alkalized in mixed alcohol solvent before sodium monochloroacetate addition, followed by neutralization, washing, and drying. That example demonstrates a particular preparation and should not be read as a family-wide manufacturing recipe.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) can form free-standing films and can act as a structural or reinforcing component in films and paper-like composites. Its tensile response is not a family constant: the review literature reports that moisture lowers the mechanical properties of CMC-containing films, while the degree of substitution, added fillers or cross-linking, and plasticizer content alter the strength–stiffness–ductility balance. In the surveyed film literature, well-dispersed fillers commonly increased tensile strength and elastic modulus while reducing strain at break; increasing glycerol typically increased ductility while reducing tensile strength and modulus.

One bounded neat-film example comes from a sodium CMC (USP-grade) control film. Zhang and co-workers cast 25 g of their CMC film-forming solution in a 5.5 cm PTFE mold and dried it at 40 °C for 48 h; the reported film thickness was 0.126 ± 0.015 mm. In tensile strips 4.0 × 1.0 cm tested at a crosshead speed of 0.2 cm/min, the film had tensile strength 13.57 ± 0.47 MPa, elongation at break 44.41 ± 0.61%, and Young’s modulus 30.84 ± 0.96 MPa. The article does not report a test standard or conditioning protocol. These values describe that cast, dried sodium-CMC film, not all CMC grades, film preparations, or hydrated formulations.
sections.processing: Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) is commonly converted from aqueous solution by casting, coating, spraying, or electrospinning; thermo-mechanical extrusion and compression molding are reported chiefly for suitably plasticized CMC or blends. For cast films, CMC is dissolved in water with plasticizer and any functional additive, spread into a mold, then dried; its hydrophilicity means that moisture response and water resistance remain formulation-dependent, often motivating blends, ionic/covalent crosslinking, or fillers. In Basu and co-workers’ CMC/PEG wound-film experiment, material was formed by solution casting; this is a laboratory route for that CMC/PEG system rather than a general CMC melt-processing window. The packaging review likewise emphasizes that degree of substitution, molecular mass, additive selection, and processing conditions limit direct comparison among CMC films.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) is an anionic cellulose ether whose carboxymethyl degree of substitution is controlled during etherification.
sections.properties: CMC can form films, but water sensitivity and film response change with degree of substitution, molecular weight, plasticizer, filler, blending, and crosslinking.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. CMC, commonly supplied as its sodium salt, supports food, textile, detergent and pharmaceutical formulations. Research and materials applications include particle stabilization and electrode binders.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich 419311 illustrates a specified sodium CMC powder: average molecular weight about 250,000 and degree of substitution about 0.7, in 100 g and 1 kg packs. Salt form and substitution grade should be explicit.

Scale and evidence limits. Catalog packs span order 10^2–10^3 grams and establish a research purchasing route. No reliable separate annual CMC purchase or consumption tonnage was found.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Enzymatic cleavage yields soluble reducing carbohydrate fragments; dissolution can also remove visible material.

Timescales: Aluminum-crosslinked CMC film visually disappeared after two weeks in pilot compost peaking at 70.7 °C.

Environmental persistence: Disintegration of this formulation does not establish complete CMC mineralization in environmental water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Pilot composting supports a formulation-specific organic-treatment route; polymer reclamation was not demonstrated.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: EFSA’s 2018 EU assessment of sodium carboxymethylcellulose (E466) found no safety concern at reported food uses and levels and no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake. This conclusion concerns specified food additives, not all industrial or medical applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Film data and barrier behavior are formulation-specific: moisture, substitution level, and additives must be retained when comparing CMC materials.

sections.overview: Starch is a natural polysaccharide reserve material composed primarily of glucose-based amylose and amylopectin components. Its botanical source, amylose/amylopectin ratio, water content, and processing strongly affect material behavior.
sections.history: Starch is a natural plant material with a long history as food and adhesive. FAO’s historical account connects wheat-starch preparation with ancient Egyptian papyrus manufacture and identifies Kirchhoff’s 1811 conversion of starch to sugar by acid hydrolysis as an important chemical milestone. Later industries used starch in paper and textile sizing, coatings, adhesives and glucose manufacture as well as food. Wartime loss of tapioca supplies helped drive American Maize Products and National Starch Products to commercialize waxy maize starch in 1942. High-amylose maize followed commercially in 1958, extending the range available for formulated foods. These dates concern extraction, conversion and crop development rather than invention of starch.
sections.nomenclature: Starch is a family-level material name, not one uniform polymer. “Starch polymer” is descriptive, while amylose and amylopectin are constituent molecular fractions rather than interchangeable synonyms for the whole material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Starch is a plant-produced polysaccharide stored as semicrystalline granules composed chiefly of amylose and branched amylopectin. Commercial material is isolated from biological feedstocks rather than synthesized from glucose in a reactor. Major sources include cereal endosperm, especially maize, and roots or tubers such as cassava, potato, and wheat-derived fractions. In corn wet milling, cleaned kernels are steeped to soften the protein matrix, coarsely milled, and separated from germ. Further milling releases granules; screening and countercurrent washing remove fiber, while centrifuges or hydrocyclones separate starch from gluten and repeatedly wash the starch-rich stream before dewatering and drying. One cited patent documents the integrated corn sequence of germ separation, fiber washing, starch–gluten separation, and starch washing. A distinct cassava patent washes and peels fresh roots, disrupts tuber cells, washes and separates liberated granules from fiber, and removes soluble matter and residual fiber from the slurry. Botanical source, granule integrity, steeping chemistry, milling severity, and washing efficiency affect the isolated fraction. Chemical derivatization, gelatinization, and thermoplastic-starch formulation are separate modification or processing routes.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Native starch is a semicrystalline particulate material composed principally of linear amylose and highly branched amylopectin, so a single bulk tensile property is not meaningful for the family. Mechanical response depends first on material form. Intact granules behave as a powder; hydrated dispersions and gelatinized pastes are viscoelastic soft matter; dried, gelatinized films form hydrogen-bonded glassy networks that can be stiff but brittle when dry; and foams, fiber-filled articles, coatings, and blends introduce their own cellular or interfacial failure modes. Melt-plasticized thermoplastic starch is treated separately in this encyclopedia and should not inherit a cast-film value.

In a dried starch film, intermolecular hydrogen bonding and chain entanglement provide cohesion, while water and polyol plasticizers lower the effective glass transition and increase segmental mobility. Increasing water or compatible plasticizer therefore commonly lowers modulus and tensile strength while increasing elongation, but the balance is unstable: loss of water at low relative humidity can embrittle a film, whereas sorption at high humidity can soften it and sharply reduce load bearing. Amylose-to-amylopectin ratio and molar-mass distribution, botanical source and minor lipid/protein/phosphate components, native granule and crystal structure, degree of gelatinization and molecular degradation, drying temperature and rate, film thickness, plasticizer identity/loading/compatibility or migration, storage time and retrogradation, chemical modification or crosslinking, blend and filler content/dispersion/orientation, porosity, specimen conditioning, test temperature, strain rate, and notch or defect population are all consequential. Greater effective amylose network formation often raises film strength and stiffness and reduces extensibility, but that trend is conditional on preparation, moisture, and recrystallization and is not a family-wide numerical rule.

One bounded cast-film comparison used commercial hydroxypropyl cornstarch reported as degree of substitution 0.4%, moisture 13 wt%, and molar mass 130,000. Ten grams of dry starch was gelatinized with water at 98 °C for 1 hour, cast, and dried at 35 °C for 10–12 hours. After conditioning at 40% relative humidity, ASTM D882 tension at 25 °C and 5 mm/min (seven specimens) gave the water-only St-W film, about 156 ± 4 µm thick, a modulus of 1152 ± 119 MPa, tensile strength of 57.3 ± 2.9 MPa, and elongation of 3.6 ± 0.7%. In the otherwise analogous St-WG-4 casting formulation containing 3 parts glycerol per 10 parts starch (30 parts glycerol per 100 parts dry starch), the approximately 181 ± 9 µm film gave 933 ± 86 MPa, 49.4 ± 5.6 MPa, and 8.6 ± 0.6%, respectively. These values demonstrate the plasticizer tradeoff within one modified-corn-starch film system; they are not properties of native starch granules, unmodified starch from other plants, gels, foams, thermoplastic starch, or commercial starch composites.
sections.processing:
Starch is converted into articles after water and/or a plasticizer disrupts the native granular structure and produces a continuous thermoplastic-starch phase. Important routes include aqueous solvent casting and tape casting, hot extrusion followed by film blowing or thermocompression, and formulation-dependent injection molding, compression molding, foaming, and melt, wet, or electrospinning. Feed-water level, botanical source and amylose/amylopectin balance, plasticizer type and loading, mixing order, gelatinization, screw shear, die pressure, drying rate, and conditioning humidity all matter. Insufficient heat or shear can leave ungelatinized granules or uneven plasticizer distribution, whereas excessive moisture loss, later water uptake, plasticizer migration, and retrogradation can change dimensions and embrittle or soften the article after conversion. Starch extraction and chemical modification belong in Synthesis; gelatinization, melt mixing, shaping, drying, and conditioning belong here.

Muñoz-Gimena and co-workers' open review identifies casting, extrusion/thermocompression, and blow molding as the three main starch-film routes and describes injection molding, compression molding, foaming, and spinning as additional options. Its literature-typical casting sequence mixes starch and plasticizer in water, heats the suspension at 80–95 °C for 10–15 min, casts it on a plate, and oven-dries at 40–75 °C for about 24 h; those aggregated values are review guidance, not a universal starch schedule. In a distinct bounded experiment, Niu and co-workers dispersed potato starch in 100 mL distilled water and stirred for 30 min at 80 °C until gelatinized, added glycerol and gelatin sequentially, ultrasonically degassed for another 30 min, cast the solution on a plate, and dried it at 40 °C for 36 h. That schedule belongs to their potato-starch/glycerol/gelatin films.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Starch granules contain amylose and amylopectin fractions with source-dependent organization.
sections.properties: Water, plasticizer, and processing determine gelatinization, retrogradation, and film properties.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Starch ingredients serve food manufacture and animal feed; nonfood uses prominently include corrugating and papermaking. Native starch, modified starch and starch-derived sweeteners are separate commercial categories.

Purchasing. Processors supply crop- and function-specific native or modified starch ingredients to food and industrial manufacturers. Buyers must distinguish starch polymer from downstream sweeteners when comparing volumes.

Scale and evidence limits. Starch Europe reports 9.8 million tonnes of EU starch and derivative production in 2024. Its accompanying overview gives 7.2 million tonnes EU consumption, split 54% food, 2% feed and 44% nonfood. These order 10^7-tonne aggregates include sweeteners and modified products, not pure native starch alone.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Enzymatic cleavage converts starch to smaller carbohydrates. In the cited experiment, a bacterial neopullulanase preferentially converted its amylose fraction to maltose while leaving much of the amylopectin.

Timescales: Rates depend on enzyme specificity and starch architecture; the cited experiment supplies no environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The laboratory result does not establish a soil, freshwater or marine mineralization time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Enzyme-assisted saccharification recovers soluble carbohydrates. The cited process demonstrates selective conversion of starch fractions, rather than recycling of contaminated post-consumer starch plastics.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Starch powder involves dust exposure. NIOSH identifies irritation of the eyes, skin and respiratory tract and an explosion hazard when starch dust disperses in air. This guidance addresses starch powder, rather than establishing the toxicology of every isolated fraction or finished blend.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Packaging properties are formulation- and plasticizer-specific.

sections.overview: Amylose is the mostly linear alpha-(1→4)-glucan component of plant starch. Its ability to reassociate after gelatinization is important to the structure and behavior of amylose-containing starch articles.
sections.history: Amylose was identified through research on natural starch, rather than invented as a synthetic polymer. Thomas J. Schoch’s separation work in the 1940s established the distinction between its comparatively linear chains and branched amylopectin. In 1958, Bear Hybrids Corn Company, American Maize Products and National Starch and Chemical commercialized a high-amylose maize hybrid. Such crop development made amylose-rich ingredients accessible to industry. Research by Hizukuri and colleagues in 1981 subsequently demonstrated limited branching in amylose, refining the earlier structural picture.
sections.nomenclature: Amylose denotes the linear starch polysaccharide, not starch as a whole; amylopectin is the distinct branched component. High-amylose starch is a compositionally enriched starch material rather than a synonym for isolated amylose, so its film and extrusion evidence remains formulation-specific.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Amylose is the mostly linear alpha-(1→4)-glucan fraction of plant starch. It is sourced from botanical starch; high-amylose maize is an enriched starch source, not identical to purified amylose. Isolation history, residual amylopectin, molecular mass, and subsequent chemical treatment all delimit a particular material. Heating starch in water mobilizes chains after granule disruption and cooling enables reassociation, but these article-preparation steps are distinct from biosynthesis or extraction of amylose.
sections.mechanicalProperties: The mostly linear architecture can promote chain alignment and hydrogen-bonded reassociation in starch films, often yielding a stronger but potentially more brittle matrix than amylopectin-rich systems. The 70% high-amylose corn-starch extrusion study reported 10.03 MPa tensile strength and 40% elongation at break for its 2% NaOH-treated film; those values are for an alkali-treated, composition-variable starch film, not pure amylose. In a separate glycerol-plasticized, 6 wt% montmorillonite film series spanning waxy starch through nominally 100% amylose, regular corn starch gave the highest tensile strength, elongation decreased as amylose increased, and neither endpoint changed significantly above 50% amylose. That second result is composite- and process-specific and does not define an intrinsic amylose property.
sections.processing: Amylose-containing starch articles can be produced by gelatinization/casting or by thermomechanical extrusion with controlled water and plasticizer. In a laboratory starch–clay study, dry starch, 15 wt% glycerol, 0–21 wt% clay, and 19 wt% water were processed at 200 rpm in an 18 mm twin-screw extruder with an 85–90–95–100–110–120 °C barrel profile; ground extrudate was then dispersed in water, heated at 95 °C for 10 min, cooled, cast, and dried. The authors cautioned that the 120 °C maximum might be insufficient for extensive gelatinization of the high-amylose samples. These conditions produced nanocomposite granulate followed by cast films and are not a melt-processing window for isolated amylose.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Amylose is the predominantly linear glucose-polymer fraction of starch. Its chain association and complexation behavior differ from the highly branched amylopectin fraction.
sections.properties: Amylose content affects starch-film organization, water response, and mechanical behavior, but those properties also depend on botanical source, treatment, and added plasticizer.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Isolated amylose is a laboratory reagent for starch chemistry and amylase substrate studies. High-amylose crop starch is a different, mixed-polysaccharide industrial product.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich offers potato amylose powder described as essentially free of amylopectin, in 250 mg, 1 g, 5 g and 25 g catalog packs. Botanical source and purity distinguish this purchase from bulk starch.

Scale and evidence limits. The documented packs span roughly 10^-1–10^1 grams. No reliable annual isolated-amylose purchase or consumption statistic was found; starch-industry tonnage cannot be assigned to purified amylose.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Bacterial neopullulanase hydrolyzed amylose, producing mainly maltose.

Timescales: This is an enzyme-treatment result; it supplies no environmental disappearance time.

Environmental persistence: The laboratory result does not establish a soil, freshwater or marine mineralization time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Selective enzymatic conversion of amylose to maltose is demonstrated. Application to recovered waste requires its own feedstock and process validation.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Amylose is a constituent of starch; general starch-powder handling involves dust exposure. NIOSH identifies irritation of the eyes, skin and respiratory tract and an explosion hazard when starch dust disperses in air. This guidance addresses starch powder, rather than establishing the toxicology of every isolated fraction or finished blend.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited film work evaluates alkali-treated high-amylose corn starch rather than every amylose source or fraction. Its reported structural and property changes are therefore treatment- and formulation-specific.

sections.overview: Amylopectin is the highly branched glucan component of native starch. Its branch architecture contributes to starch gelatinization and retrogradation behavior, and amylopectin-rich waxy starches are important material sources.
sections.history: Amylopectin’s history combines starch fractionation with development of waxy crop starches. Schoch’s work in the 1940s established its branched character. Waxy maize starch entered use during that decade to provide thickening with reduced gel formation. Later structural advances included the amylopectin cluster models proposed independently by Z. Nikuni in 1969 and Dexter French in 1971, followed by refinements from Robin and colleagues and Hizukuri. These were discoveries about a naturally produced polymer; commercialization concerned amylopectin-rich starch ingredients rather than a newly invented molecule.
sections.nomenclature: Amylopectin names the branched starch polysaccharide, not starch as a whole; ordinary starch also contains amylose. Waxy starch is amylopectin-rich rather than automatically purified amylopectin, so composition-specific starch-film or thermoplastic-starch results should retain that distinction.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Amylopectin is the highly branched glucan fraction of botanical starch, not a commodity polymer made by a separate monomer process. Its practical feedstock is plant starch, while botanical source, branch-chain distribution, and the amylose/amylopectin ratio remain material-defining. Waxy corn starch is amylopectin-rich rather than automatically purified amylopectin. To form articles, starch is commonly gelatinized in water or thermomechanically processed with controlled water/plasticizer; those operations disrupt granules and are conversion steps, not synthesis of the polysaccharide.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Amylopectin-rich starch matrices are generally more flexible and less dominated by the dense reassociation associated with high-amylose formulations, but moisture, plasticizer, botanical source, crystallinity, filler, and retrogradation can dominate the observed response. In one bounded composition study, films made from glycerol-plasticized starch and 6 wt% montmorillonite compared waxy corn starch (approximately 0% amylose), regular corn starch, high-amylose starches, and nominally 100% amylose. Regular corn starch gave the highest tensile strength, elongation decreased as amylose content increased, and neither tensile strength nor elongation changed significantly above 50% amylose. These are results for starch–clay nanocomposite films; waxy starch was an amylopectin-rich endpoint, not isolated amylopectin, and the series does not yield an intrinsic amylopectin property.
sections.processing: Amylopectin-containing starch is converted either by aqueous gelatinization followed by casting/drying or by thermomechanical extrusion with controlled water and/or plasticizer. In a laboratory starch–clay study that included waxy corn starch, dry starch, 15 wt% glycerol, 0–21 wt% clay, and 19 wt% water were processed at 200 rpm in an 18 mm twin-screw extruder with an 85–90–95–100–110–120 °C barrel profile. Ground extrudate was then dispersed at 4 wt% in water, held at 95 °C for 10 min, cooled to 65 °C, cast, and dried at 23 °C and 50% relative humidity for 24 h. These are study-specific nanocomposite-granulate and casting conditions; waxy corn starch was one composition and not purified amylopectin.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Amylopectin is the highly branched glucose-polymer fraction of starch. Its branched chain clusters contribute to starch granule organization and influence gelatinization and retrogradation behavior.
sections.properties: Amylopectin-rich starch materials show water-sensitive thermal and mechanical behavior that depends on botanical source, branching characteristics, plasticizer content, and processing.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Isolated amylopectin supplies laboratory studies of starch structure and behavior. Waxy starch ingredients are related commercial materials, but are not identical to a purified amylopectin reagent.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich A8515 is sold as potato-starch amylopectin powder in a 25 g catalog pack. Specify botanical source and product composition for research.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked product establishes order 10^1-gram reagent supply. No separate annual isolated-amylopectin purchased or consumed tonnage was found; total starch volumes include other constituents and derivatives.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Amylopectin response is enzyme-specific: the cited neopullulanase caused limited molecular-weight reduction, whereas other amylolytic enzymes had different substrate preferences.

Timescales: Resistance to one enzyme is not evidence of permanent persistence. No environmental lifetime is assigned.

Environmental persistence: The laboratory result does not establish a soil, freshwater or marine mineralization time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Enzymatic processing is a route to carbohydrate products. Selectivity demonstrated for amylose cannot be assumed to recover an equal yield from branched amylopectin.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Amylopectin is a constituent of starch; general starch-powder handling involves dust exposure. NIOSH identifies irritation of the eyes, skin and respiratory tract and an explosion hazard when starch dust disperses in air. This guidance addresses starch powder, rather than establishing the toxicology of every isolated fraction or finished blend.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The packaging reviews address starch systems that contain both amylose and amylopectin and frequently include plasticizers or modification. Those results cannot be assigned to isolated amylopectin without specifying composition and formulation.
