sections.overview: Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is a processable starch material made by destructuring native starch under heat and shear in the presence of water or another plasticizer. It is a converted polysaccharide material rather than a newly polymerized synthetic backbone, and its behavior depends strongly on moisture and plasticizer content.
sections.history: Thermoplastic starch developed through efforts to turn starch into material processable with plastics equipment. A Novamont patent published in 1992 by Catia Bastioli, Vittorio Bellotti and Alessandro Montino documents one route: plasticized starch combined with synthetic thermoplastic polymers. This was part of a broader development field, not the invention date of every thermoplastic-starch grade. Novamont, established in 1990 from the Montedison research tradition, records a Mater-Bi biodegradable bag in 1992 and later packaging, foam and food-service applications. Mater-Bi illustrates the commercial history of starch-containing blends; its formulations should not be equated with pure plasticized starch.
sections.nomenclature: TPS is the abbreviation for thermoplastic starch. The record covers plasticized, thermomechanically destructured starch containing amylose and amylopectin; native granular starch, chemically modified starches, and a particular starch blend or film are not alternate names for the base material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is produced by destructuring native starch granules in the presence of plasticizer rather than by polymerizing new glucose chains. The biological feedstock may be maize, potato, cassava, wheat, or another purified starch; amylose/amylopectin ratio and granule structure remain consequential. Water and low-molar-mass hydrogen-bonding plasticizers such as glycerol, sorbitol, urea, or compatible mixtures penetrate the granules. Heat and intensive shear then disrupt native crystallites and the inter- and intramolecular hydrogen-bond network, producing a continuous thermoplastic phase in which amylose and amylopectin chains can flow. The cited open review describes plasticizer selection, water content, melt mixing, extrusion, and optional blending or compatibilization across TPS formulations. A distinct laboratory study prepares water-plasticized potato TPS by equilibrating starch with water, thermomechanically destructuring it in an extruder, and recovering a homogeneous amorphous material before later sheet formation. Feedstock moisture, plasticizer identity and ratio, temperature, shear and residence time must be balanced: insufficient treatment leaves residual granules, while excessive heat or mechanical energy causes chain scission. Drying or conditioning after conversion sets the retained water content, and storage can permit retrogradation. Chemical esterification, etherification, oxidation, grafting, or limited crosslinking can be used as modification variants, but they are not required for TPS identity. Article geometry and shaping conditions belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Thermoplastic starch (TPS) is produced when native starch granules are destructured and plasticized under heat and shear so that the material can be shaped by melt-processing equipment. Its solid response is not a fixed property of botanical starch: it ranges from glassy and brittle below its moisture- and formulation-dependent glass transition to yielding/ductile or soft-rubbery above that transition. TPS is viscoelastic and strongly rate dependent; creep, stress relaxation, hysteresis, and fracture can change with service time and water exchange. Neat TPS usually lacks the moisture stability and toughness of commodity polyolefins, while commercial “starch plastics” may be TPS/polyester or TPS/polyolefin blends whose mechanics are controlled by phase morphology and compatibilization rather than starch alone.

Water is both a processing aid and a powerful solid-state plasticizer. Increasing equilibrated moisture or compatible polyol content generally lowers glass transition, modulus, and strength while increasing deformability, but low plasticizer levels can show antiplasticization and excess or migrating plasticizer can phase-separate. Botanical source, amylose/amylopectin ratio and molar-mass distribution, residual granules and degree of destructuring, extrusion temperature/shear/specific mechanical energy and molecular scission, water and glycerol/sorbitol/urea/ionic-liquid content, moisture gradients, conditioning relative humidity and duration, storage-driven retrogradation and physical aging, chemical modification or crosslinking, filler and fiber dispersion/orientation, blend ratio and interfacial adhesion, processing orientation, porosity and weld lines, specimen thickness, loading rate, temperature, and strain history all affect the result. Reported tensile values must therefore carry both conditioning and test environment; temperature and relative humidity can move the same formulation across its glass transition.

A bounded demonstration used Roquette potato starch with a 23/77 amylose/amylopectin mass ratio and water as the only stated plasticizer. Feed was adjusted to 35 wt% water on a dry-starch basis, equilibrated, single-screw extruded at a 110 °C die temperature and 25 rpm (about 170 kJ/kg specific mechanical energy), rehydrated, and compression molded at 120 °C and 180 bar into 1 mm sheets. At 80 °C, dumbbells cut from those sheets (20 mm by 5 mm, initial strain rate 10−2 s−1, at least three tests) changed from a glassy-side response at 30% RH—12 wt% water, Young's modulus 80 ± 10 MPa, break stress 4 ± 1 MPa, and break strain 15 ± 4%—to a rubbery response at 90% RH—20 wt% water, modulus 0.4 ± 0.1 MPa, break stress 0.3 ± 0.2 MPa, and break strain 240 ± 80%. This is one amorphous, water-plasticized potato-TPS sheet tested hot under controlled humidity; it is not a room-temperature family range or a value for glycerol-plasticized, retrograded, reinforced, blended, foamed, injection-molded, or commercial TPS grades.
sections.processing:
Thermoplastic starch is converted by combining feed conditioning with heat and shear, then shaping the destructured, plasticized material before moisture redistributes. Twin- or single-screw extrusion is widely used for plasticization, compounding, pellet production, sheet or cast-film extrusion, and film blowing; injection molding, compression molding, and thermoforming are also suitable for formulation-dependent articles. Water and polyols govern both flow and the later glass transition, so starch source, amylose/amylopectin balance, initial moisture, plasticizer loading, mixing order, screw shear, specific mechanical energy, residence time, and die temperature must be controlled together. Too little treatment leaves granules or an inhomogeneous melt, whereas excessive heat or shear can reduce molar mass. Drying and humidity conditioning after shaping are part of the process because moisture gradients, plasticizer migration, physical aging, and retrogradation can change dimensions and embrittle or soften the article. Chemical derivatization of starch belongs in Synthesis; destructuring, compounding, shaping, cooling, and conditioning belong here.

Leroy and co-workers provide a bounded example for their water-plasticized Roquette potato starch, not a universal TPS window. They adjusted the feed to 35 wt% water on a dry-starch basis, equilibrated it for two days at 5 °C, and used a single-screw extruder at 25 rpm with a 110 °C die temperature and about 170 kJ/kg specific mechanical energy. Extruded rods were conditioned for at least one week at 20 °C and 58% relative humidity, then rehydrated overnight at 20 °C and 89% relative humidity before compression molding into 1 mm sheets at 120 °C and 180 bar. The sheets were subsequently conditioned for at least three days at the selected humidity. This sequence illustrates why feed equilibration and post-forming humidity history must accompany any reported TPS temperature or pressure.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Thermoplastic starch is destructured starch plasticized with water and/or polyols; amylose/amylopectin composition and retrogradation influence its amorphous and reassociated states.
sections.properties: Temperature, humidity, plasticizer, storage, fillers, and blends strongly alter modulus, stress, and strain.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Plasticized starch is used in starch-containing packaging compounds, including loose-fill protective packaging. Commercial compound portfolios also serve films, bags, coated substrates, trays and molded articles.

Purchasing. Compounders supply process-specific starch-containing resins; Novamont’s MATER-BI provides an industrial example. Its formulations can contain other polymers, so specify the starch fraction and blend rather than assuming the product is neat TPS.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable separate annual neat-TPS purchase or consumption figure was established. Commercial starch-blend output and all starch-derived ingredients are broader categories and cannot be assigned entirely to TPS.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Melt reprocessing can alter the molecular structure and properties of thermoplastic starch formulations. The cited experiment concerns commercial Mater-Bi EI51N0 and its almond-shell composite, not pure starch.

Timescales: Repeated processing cycles are the measured exposure; they cannot be converted to a biodegradation time.

Environmental persistence: Biodegradation of a starch-containing product must include its other polymers and additives. The recycling experiment does not measure environmental mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical grinding and reinjection were tested on the specified commercial starch-based material and its composite. This supports controlled reuse of production scrap; the effects of repeated processing and filler content must be retained when selecting an application.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Raw starch feeding and mixing in thermoplastic-starch manufacture involves dust exposure. NIOSH identifies irritation of the eyes, skin and respiratory tract and an explosion hazard when starch dust disperses in air. This guidance addresses starch powder, rather than establishing the toxicology of every isolated fraction or finished blend.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Potato-starch specimens conditioned at stated humidity are not universal TPS evidence.

sections.overview: Chitin is a natural linear polysaccharide of N-acetylglucosamine and is a structural component of arthropod exoskeletons and fungal cell walls. Its natural crystalline forms and limited solubility motivate processing as nanofibers, derivatives, or composites.
sections.history: Chitin is naturally produced, so its chronology begins with scientific isolation. Henri Braconnot isolated material from mushrooms in 1811 and called it fungine; Odier introduced the name chitin in 1823. Later industrial recovery relied heavily on shrimp and crab shell wastes. Research broadened toward food, paper, textile and biomedical materials, while fungal fermentation offered an alternative to seasonal marine feedstocks. The 2019 review by Abo Elsoud and El Kady describes this transition from extraction of natural waste to controlled biological production. Chitin and its deacetylated derivative chitosan have connected but distinct histories.
sections.nomenclature: Chitin names the acetylated polysaccharide; alpha-, beta-, and gamma-chitin identify different naturally occurring structural arrangements rather than unrelated polymers. Chitosan, the deacetylated derivative, is outside this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chitin is a natural structural polysaccharide biosynthesized by organisms rather than a material normally made by synthetic polymerization. Commercial recovery therefore begins with chitin-containing biomass, commonly crustacean shell/cuticle residues such as shrimp or crab, where the polymer is associated with proteins and calcium carbonate; fungal, insect, molluscan, and squid sources also have distinct feedstock contexts. Conventional chemical recovery separates the native polymer by acid demineralization (often hydrochloric acid) and alkaline deproteinization (often sodium hydroxide); the order can vary, and decolorization may be added when pigments remain. These are extraction and purification operations, not a conversion of chitin into chitosan. Reviews also describe biological alternatives such as fermentation or enzyme-assisted protein removal, and newer ionic-liquid or deep-eutectic-solvent approaches; their use and purification performance depend on the source material and route.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Chitin mechanics depend strongly on the material form and hierarchy. Native cuticle and shell structures contain protein and, in some cases, mineral phases; their measured response cannot be assigned to chitin alone. For purified chitin and nanochitin films, allomorph (α, β, or γ), acetylation state, molecular mass, crystallinity, fibril diameter and aspect ratio, alignment, packing, moisture, and film-forming route all change stiffness, strength, and strain to failure. Open review evidence reports that smaller and higher-aspect-ratio chitin nanofibers can give stronger films, while crystallinity and surface modification can strengthen or weaken a network depending on the resulting fibrillation and interfibrillar bonding. Consequently, results for a nanofiber film, nanowhisker film, regenerated material, or biological composite should not be treated as a chitin-family constant.

One bounded measurement comes from α-chitin nanofiber films prepared from sea-crab-shell chitin (initial degree of N-acetylation 92%). Zhang and co-workers partially deacetylated one nanofiber feedstock to 70% N-acetylation, dispersed it in acidified water, cast the dispersion on plates, and dried the films at 40 °C; their chitin nanofiber films averaged 0.025 mm thick. Tensile strips with a 20 mm initial grip separation were tested at 1 mm/min. The partially deacetylated, TEMPO-oxidized, and oppositely charged composite α-chitin nanofiber films each had tensile strengths of approximately 90 MPa. The paper does not provide a test standard, conditioning protocol, modulus, or a single-value uncertainty for that approximate strength, and the value applies only to those dried, modified nano-fiber-film preparations—not bulk chitin, natural exoskeletons, or other chitin allomorphs and forms.
sections.processing: Chitin's high crystallinity and limited solubility make solution or dispersion route selection central. Public sources describe top-down fibrillation of aqueous chitin dispersions for moldable/cast nanofiber films, and bottom-up processing in which depolymerized chitin is dissolved for electrospinning; HFIP, imidazolium ionic liquids, and dry-jet wet spinning from acetate-salt solutions are documented routes. Muzzarelli reports 5% chitin in 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium bromide at 100 °C for 48 h and reports chitin/cellulose films cast on glass, soaked in water, and dried. These are reported ionic-liquid and film experiments, not universal chitin conditions; the RSC review emphasizes that untreated chitin is poorly soluble in water and most organic solvents, while nanofiber dispersions improve handling and molding.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Chitin is a crystalline amino-polysaccharide that occurs in multiple allomorphs and hierarchical microfibrillar structures.
sections.properties: Chitin is difficult to dissolve, and its film behavior depends on source, extraction, dissolution or fibrillation route, and final morphology.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Chitin serves as a precursor for chitosan and glucosamine and as a substrate in chitinase analysis. The latter is a laboratory biotechnology use, not evidence of a mass-market chitin article.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich C7170 provides a shrimp-shell chitin practical-grade powder in a 100 g catalog pack. Source organism and purification grade distinguish research purchases.

Scale and evidence limits. This documents order 10^2-gram reagent supply. No reliable annual isolated-chitin purchase or consumption statistic was found; shell waste mass is not equivalent to purified chitin output.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Chitinases yield N-acetylglucosamine oligomers, including chitobiose; oxidative enzymes can additionally form oxidized chitin products. Product analysis distinguishes hydrolysis from oxidative cleavage.

Timescales: Enzyme assays have defined reaction times; those times are not environmental decomposition rates.

Environmental persistence: Crystallinity and enzyme accessibility matter. The cited analytical protocols do not establish disappearance of an intact chitin article in soil or sea.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Enzymatic depolymerization can recover N-acetylglucosamine-containing carbohydrates. The cited work supplies analytical procedures for these conversions, not evidence of industrial recycling of mixed chitin-containing wastes.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Chitin particles can stimulate innate and adaptive immunity. The reviewed animal and cell studies show that particle size, purity, acetylation and exposure route alter whether inflammatory or immunomodulatory responses predominate. Results for purified particles, intact biological structures and chitosan are consequently different evidence categories; natural origin does not imply immune inertness.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Results depend on allomorph, biological source, extraction, nanofibrillation or dissolution route, and final article morphology, so they should not be promoted to a single chitin property.

sections.overview: Chitosan is a partially deacetylated derivative of chitin, commonly prepared from chitin-containing biological feedstocks. Its amine-bearing backbone gives it composition- and pH-dependent behavior that supports use in films, membranes, and biomedical formulations.
sections.history: Rouget described chitosan formation in 1859, and Hoppe-Seyler proposed its name in 1894. Most manufactured chitosan has been obtained by deacetylating chitin from crustacean shells. A separate biological route developed when Araki and Ito described chitin-deacetylase activity in Mucor rouxii in 1974; White and colleagues advanced fungal-mycelium extraction in 1979. Subsequent research extended applications from industrial formulations toward wound dressings, drug-delivery systems and tissue-engineering supports. These uses include research-stage materials as well as commercial products; they do not imply that every proposed biomedical use was adopted clinically.
sections.nomenclature: Chitosan is not simply an alternate name for chitin: it denotes the deacetylated chitin-derived material family. Degree of deacetylation and molecular characteristics vary among chitosans, so the canonical name does not identify one fixed composition.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chitosan is a family of partially deacetylated chitin rather than a vinyl-type synthetic polymer. Chitin feedstock is recovered from chitin-bearing biomass, especially crustacean-shell side streams; fungal and insect sources are alternatives. For crustacean material, isolation commonly removes minerals, proteins, and pigments before conversion. In a conventional chemical route, concentrated alkali (commonly sodium or potassium hydroxide) hydrolyses N-acetyl groups on chitin to give a copolymer containing glucosamine and residual N-acetylglucosamine units. Degree of deacetylation and chain degradation are coupled process outcomes: base concentration, temperature, time, and starting-chitin characteristics affect both. Enzymatic deacetylases and less conventional extraction/deacetylation approaches are reported alternatives, but should not be treated as equivalent commercial routes.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Chitosan mechanics are article- and composition-dependent rather than intrinsic to one material grade. For cast films, molecular mass, degree of deacetylation, acid solvent, polymer and plasticizer content, drying/neutralization history, and test humidity change tensile strength and elongation; hydrated gels have a different compression and rheological response and should not be compared directly with dry films.

A bounded cast-film example comes from a study using 500 kDa chitosan with 85–90% deacetylation. Films were made from 0.5–2.0% (w/v) chitosan in 1.0% acetic acid with 10 wt% glycerin, dried at 45 °C for 12 h, then conditioned for at least 72 h at 25 ± 1 °C and 52 ± 1% relative humidity. In ASTM D882 tensile tests, unneutralized film tensile strength increased from 37.6 ± 0.9 to 60.5 ± 3.1 MPa across that film-forming-solution concentration series. Those values describe the stated glycerol-plasticized, cast and conditioned films, not a chitosan-family strength.

An independent review of chitosan films similarly reports limited extensibility in many unplasticized film formulations and identifies molecular mass, deacetylation, solvent, and test humidity as decisive comparability limits. For example, it compiles 1% chitosan/1% acetic-acid films tested at 25 °C and 20% relative humidity with tensile strength/elongation-at-break values of 61.8 MPa/4.59% for a high-molecular-mass sample and 55.8 MPa/4.58% for a low-molecular-mass sample. Plasticizers and blends may markedly change this balance of strength and ductility.
sections.processing: Chitosan is widely converted from acid-solubilized solution into films, membranes, and coatings by solution casting; layer-by-layer assembly and silanization are additional coating routes. The solution needs to be homogeneous and free of undissolved material; degassing or centrifugation before casting helps control inhomogeneity. Molecular mass affects solution viscosity, and dried acid-cast membranes may need neutralization to become water-insoluble. Lieder et al. used 1% (w/w) chitosan in water with 50 mM acetic acid, centrifuged for 1 h at 5,000 rpm, cast 0.1 mL/cm², dried overnight at 37 °C, then neutralized with 0.1 M NaOH. A separate Foods study used 0.5–2.0% (w/v) chitosan in 1% acetic acid with 10% glycerin, cast in 10 × 10 cm dishes and dried at 45 °C for 12 h; its neutralized films received 5% NaOH and washing before redrying. These are protocol-specific examples, not universal settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Chitosan is the partially deacetylated derivative of chitin, with molecular mass and degree of deacetylation defining a particular material.
sections.properties: Chitosan films are solution-formed materials whose tensile response changes with molecular mass, deacetylation, solvent, humidity, plasticizer, and film preparation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Chitosan supports water treatment, chromatography, cosmetic formulations, antimicrobial textiles and films. Biomedical research also uses it in controlled-release and implant materials; reagent availability does not establish clinical approval.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich C3646 illustrates shrimp-shell chitosan with at least 75% deacetylation, in a 100 g pack. Deacetylation, molecular size and application-specific quality requirements matter.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked pack is order 10^2 grams. No reliable separate annual chitosan purchased or consumed tonnage was found.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A GH46 chitosanase cleaves chitosan into chitooligosaccharides. Degree of deacetylation and enzyme specificity affect the products.

Timescales: The source optimizes an enzyme reaction; it supplies no universal environmental degradation time.

Environmental persistence: Activity of an isolated marine-derived enzyme is not equivalent to mineralization of a chitosan article in seawater.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The recombinant chitosanase produced chitooligosaccharides in a laboratory process. This is a potential carbohydrate-recovery route; industrial performance on contaminated waste and closed-loop chitosan regeneration were not demonstrated.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Chitosan’s immune effects depend on molecular weight, degree of deacetylation, physical form and biological setting. Residual endotoxins and other impurities can confound apparent pro- or anti-inflammatory effects. Purified material and the complete formulation therefore require evaluation for the intended exposure; natural origin alone does not establish compatibility with tissue.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A film result depends on the specified chitosan grade, acid solution, neutralization, conditioning, and additives; it is not a property of all chitosan derivatives or crosslinked networks.

sections.overview: Alginate is a family of anionic polysaccharides sourced chiefly from brown algae and also produced by some bacteria. Its mannuronic- and guluronic-acid sequence distribution governs how a particular alginate responds to ionic crosslinking.
sections.history: E. C. C. Stanford’s 1881 discovery of alginic acid began the scientific and industrial history of this natural seaweed polymer. Early ventures included binders for anthracite dust and, by 1927, can-sealing materials in San Diego. The business was reorganized as Kelco in 1929. Production expanded in Britain during 1934–1939 and in Norway after the Second World War. Alginate subsequently became important in textile-printing pastes, paper products and food thickening and gelling. Stanford, F. C. Thornley and later Kelco developers helped move it from crude seaweed extract into controlled industrial ingredients. Propylene glycol alginate, developed through later esterification work, is a derivative rather than the original polymer.
sections.nomenclature: Alginate is the family-level term used for alginic-acid salts and related source-dependent materials, not for one fixed molecular composition. A calcium- or otherwise crosslinked alginate hydrogel is a network made from a specified alginate and crosslinking system, rather than a synonym for the uncrosslinked family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Alginate is a family of anionic polysaccharides obtained principally from brown algae and, in some cases, produced by bacteria. The biological source, extraction, molecular mass, and mannuronate/guluronate block distribution remain material-defining variables. Manufacture therefore starts with recovery or purification of an alginate salt, followed when needed by ionic, covalent, or hybrid network formation rather than monomer polymerization. Calcium-mediated crosslinking is a network-forming route, not a synonym for alginate itself.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Calcium and other divalent ions create ionically associated alginate hydrogels whose stiffness and brittleness depend on M/G sequence, molecular mass, concentration, ion delivery, and hydration. G-rich material is often reported as forming stronger, more brittle ionically crosslinked networks, whereas M-rich regions contribute flexibility. As a bounded measured example, sodium-alginate gels crosslinked with 1 M CaCl2 and tested by 1 mm indentation showed instantaneous elastic moduli of 33.36 ± 2.25 kPa for 1% alginate and 166.43 ± 23.15 kPa for 5% alginate in the dry test condition (n = 3); wet-condition values were lower. These are measurements of one CaCl2 hydrogel protocol, not family-wide moduli.
sections.processing: Aqueous alginate solutions can be shaped under mild conditions by external or internal multivalent-ion gelation, including casting, droplets, microfluidics, and extrusion printing. In the cited bioprinting experiment, 1–5% sodium alginate was crosslinked with 1 M CaCl2; 5% produced smooth continuous deposited filaments while concentrations above 5% became difficult to control because of high extrusion pressure and clogging. The study used a 22-gauge (410 μm) needle. These concentration-specific observations supplement, rather than replace, broader advice that viscosity, M/G composition, ion delivery, and intended geometry must be set for the particular alginate.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Alginate is an anionic polysaccharide composed of mannuronate and guluronate residues. Divalent-ion crosslinking creates ionically associated hydrogel networks whose junction structure depends on sequence composition and ion availability.
sections.properties: Alginate readily forms hydrated ionic gels; gel strength, swelling, and transport behavior depend on molecular weight, M/G composition, ionic environment, and crosslinking conditions.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Alginates supply textile-printing thickeners, food texture agents and pharmaceutical or medical materials, including dental impressions and wound-dressing products. Sodium alginate is a common soluble purchasing form.

Purchasing. Industrial suppliers such as KIMICA offer sodium alginate grades distinguished by solution viscosity. Buyers specify application grade and salt form; finished dressings and alginate blends are separate products.

Scale and evidence limits. FAO’s historical estimate for the worldwide 2001 alginate market is 30,000 tonnes: 20,000 technical and 10,000 food/pharmaceutical. This establishes order 10^4-tonne historical use, not current demand or isolated alginic-acid sales.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The tested Bacteroides ovatus isolate degraded alginate using activities toward mannuronate and guluronate sequences, yielding smaller uronate-containing carbohydrates.

Timescales: The experiment uses anaerobic bacterial culture at 37 °C; it supplies no environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Gut-culture utilization cannot be transferred to seawater or soil. Dissolution of an ionically crosslinked gel also differs from chain degradation.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Calcium-alginate microgel printing supports were recovered by rehydration and ion exchange using sodium and calcium salts. This is a laboratory reuse route for a controlled formulation, not general monomer recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Alginate implant responses depend on purification and formulation. The review identifies endotoxins, proteins, polyphenols and heavy metals as potential contaminants that can complicate interpretation of inflammatory responses. Results for highly purified alginate should therefore remain distinct from technical-grade material and from modified or cell-containing gels.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Alginate is composition-variable by source, and the cited hydrogel literature evaluates particular crosslinking and modification conditions; resulting gel properties must be tied to that composition and medium.

sections.overview: Agarose is a natural, neutral galactan polysaccharide obtained from red algae. In water it forms a thermoreversible physical gel on cooling, a trait that underlies its use as a gel matrix and separation medium.
sections.history: Agarose’s history concerns the separation and characterization of a natural agar component. Alfred Polson’s patent account credits C. Araki’s 1937 work with distinguishing agarose from agaropectin and cites subsequent structural studies, including Hjertén’s 1962 work. Polson’s process, filed in the United States in 1964 and patented in 1967 for the South African Inventions Development Corporation, used polyethylene glycol to fractionate agar. Purification supported electrophoresis, gel filtration, bacterial culture and virus-plaque work by reducing interfering components. This is a documented purification advance; agarose itself was not invented in 1967, and the older history of edible agar is not the same as that of purified laboratory agarose.
sections.nomenclature: Agarose denotes the polysaccharide fraction, not agar as a whole: agar also contains agaropectin. Chemically modified, grafted, or compounded agarose materials remain derivatives or formulations whose substitution or added component should be named rather than treated as identical to native agarose.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Agarose is the neutral galactan fraction obtained from red-algal agar, rather than agar as a whole. Recovery and purification, algal source, molecular mass, and any chemical modification determine the particular material. Native agarose is not conventionally made by monomer polymerization; specialized low-melting and substituted grades are chemically modified derivatives and should be named as such. The hydrogel review and fluid-gel study both support retaining source and grade when describing an agarose material.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Cooling an agarose solution creates a physical three-dimensional network through helix association, so concentration, thermal history, and shear history govern gel mechanics. Under shear-driven gelation, the cited fluid-gel study found that storage and loss moduli increased across 0.5, 1, and 2 wt% agarose systems; these are microgel dispersions, not an intrinsic modulus for dry or quiescent agarose. Chemical modification can also reduce gel strength or alter gelation behavior. Any comparison therefore needs concentration, derivative, hydration state, and preparation history.
sections.processing: Agarose is commonly hot-dissolved and then physically gelled by cooling; casting, gel preparation, and shear-assisted fluid-gel production are all downstream conversion routes. In a defined fluid-gel preparation, 0.5, 1, or 2 wt% agarose was hydrated at 85 °C for about 20 min, then cooled from 85 to 25 °C at 1 °C/min under 400 s−1 shear and held for 15 min. That example makes clear that shear and cooling create a different particle morphology from a quiescent gel, so it is not a general preparation prescription for other agarose grades.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Agarose is a linear galactan that forms physical gels through temperature-dependent chain association and junction-zone formation. Gel morphology is controlled by concentration, molecular characteristics, cooling history, and the surrounding medium.
sections.properties: Agarose gels are water-rich, thermoreversible materials whose stiffness and transport behavior depend on agarose concentration and gel microstructure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Agarose provides gel matrices for molecular-biology separations, especially DNA and RNA electrophoresis, and related blotting or immunodiffusion methods.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich A9539 illustrates a low-electroendosmosis molecular-biology grade in a 100 g pack. Select gel strength, electroendosmosis and melting behavior for the assay.

Scale and evidence limits. This documents order 10^2-gram laboratory supply. No separate annual agarose consumption statistic was found; bulk agar statistics include other fractions and are not purified agarose volumes.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Agarase activity produces smaller agarose carbohydrates. The cited bacterial study identified beta-agarase activity during agarose utilization.

Timescales: Anaerobic cultures were incubated at 37 °C; their reaction time is not a marine decomposition time.

Environmental persistence: The laboratory result does not establish a soil, freshwater or marine mineralization time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Used electrophoresis agarose was washed to remove diffusible contaminants, dried, ground and recast. The documented laboratory procedure maintained separation performance through at least ten uses; contaminant removal is integral to the method.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Agarose hydrogels are studied as cell-supporting and drug-delivery materials, but heating during gel preparation can damage temperature-sensitive cargo. Chemically modified gels and composites introduce distinct components and biological responses. The reviewed biomedical examples support formulation-specific investigation rather than unrestricted suitability of laboratory electrophoresis agarose for implantation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The hydrogel review covers modified and biomedical agarose systems, and fluid-gel measurements are concentration- and processing-specific; neither warrants representing one gel formulation as an intrinsic agarose value.

sections.overview: Carrageenan is a family of sulfated galactan polysaccharides obtained from red seaweeds. Its composition-dependent gelling and film-forming behavior makes it important in food and other formulated materials.
sections.history: Carrageenan has roots in longstanding use of red seaweeds for jellies, milk puddings and adhesives. Stanford named the extracted material carrageenin in 1862; Bourgade’s 1871 process used alcohol precipitation to recover it. Twentieth-century development broadened both feedstocks and uses, including stabilization of chocolate milk. The introduction of Eucheuma farming in the Philippines in 1971 expanded supplies beyond traditional Irish-moss harvesting. Air-freshener gels became another significant application in the early 1970s. This chronology describes extraction and industrial development of a naturally occurring polysaccharide family, whose different seaweed sources yield different carrageenan structures.
sections.nomenclature: Carrageenan is a family name, not the name of one uniform polymer. Terms such as kappa-, iota-, and lambda-carrageenan identify structurally distinct members, so they should not be silently treated as interchangeable names.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Carrageenan is a family of sulfated polysaccharides obtained from the cell walls of red algae rather than a polymer normally made by monomer polymerization. Commercial feedstocks include cultivated Kappaphycus and Eucheuma species; the available sources distinguish kappa-, iota-, and lambda-rich materials by algal source and structure. Refined carrageenan can be produced by washing seaweed, extracting in hot alkaline solution, separating insoluble matrix material, then precipitating the dissolved polymer with alcohol or, for kappa material, by potassium-chloride gel pressing. Semi-refined material instead retains more of the treated seaweed matrix. An alkaline, ultrasound-assisted experiment on Chondracantus canaliculatus is a source- and method-specific extraction variant; it illustrates that heat and ultrasound can alter extraction yield and should not be generalized to every carrageenan source.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Carrageenan’s mechanical response is strongly dependent on carrageenan type and material state. In aqueous gels, κ-carrageenan is comparatively stiff and prone to brittle yielding, whereas ι-carrageenan gives softer, more deformable gels; carrageenan concentration, counter-ion identity and concentration, and thermal/gelation history all alter the network and its measured response. These hydrogel results should not be treated as properties of a dry film or of every commercial carrageenan product.

A bounded small-amplitude oscillatory-shear example illustrates this variation. Hilliou prepared 2 wt% commercial κ- and ι-carrageenan gels in 0.1 M NaCl (and a selected κ2 material in 0.1 M KCl), equilibrated them at 20 °C for 3 h, and measured with serrated parallel plates at 0.1% strain. The reported linear/storage moduli were about 24 kPa for κ, 0.3 kPa for ι, and 4.4 kPa for the selected κ2 gel. The values are specific to those samples, salts, concentration, temperature, and oscillatory test conditions, not a family-wide modulus range.

For cast films, tensile strength and elongation at break are common endpoints, but the film literature likewise distinguishes κ, ι, blends, and filled or plasticized formulations. A review characterizes neat κ films as relatively strong but brittle and reports that composition and drying conditions affect film tensile response; film values should therefore be compared only with their documented formulation and conditioning.
sections.processing: Carrageenan is commonly shaped from aqueous film-forming systems by solution casting and coating; electrospinning and formulated extrusion are additional routes, although extrusion must be assessed for heat sensitivity and formulation compatibility. The κ, ι, and λ forms do not behave interchangeably: κ is associated with firmer ion-responsive gels, ι with more elastic gels, and λ is principally a non-gelling thickener, so salt, plasticizer, blend, and drying choices are article-specific. In Kristó and co-workers’ κ-carrageenan/glycerine buccal-film study, heating was used to make the casting solution and process temperature was deliberately optimized because over-heating adversely affected the film. The study is a bounded drug-film example, not a universal carrageenan casting schedule. More generally, humidity and drying can affect cast-film thickness and moisture-sensitive performance.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Carrageenan is a family of sulfated galactan polysaccharides; κ-, ι-, and λ-type materials have different substitution patterns and gel-forming behavior.
sections.properties: κ- and ι-carrageenan form composition- and ion-dependent gels, while carrageenan films show type- and formulation-dependent strength and elongation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Carrageenan controls texture in dairy and plant-based alternatives, confectionery, meat products and gels. Technical uses include toothpaste.

Purchasing. Cargill offers refined thickening grades as Satiagum, refined gelling grades as Satiagel, and refined/semi-refined options as Aubygel. Food manufacturers source a grade matched to the formulation through ingredient-sales channels.

Scale and evidence limits. FAO estimated the worldwide 2001 market at 33,000 tonnes, order 10^4 tonnes: dairy accounted for 11,000 tonnes, meat/poultry and water gels 5,000 each. The total includes 8,000 tonnes of PES food grade and is historical, not a current purchase forecast.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Carrageenase activity cleaves carrageenan-related glycosidic links. The cited experiment directly examines kappa-carrageenan oligosaccharides, so it cannot establish complete breakdown of all carrageenan types.

Timescales: The anaerobic 37 °C culture experiment supplies no environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: Evidence from oligosaccharides must not be equated with disappearance of an intact carrageenan gel or composite.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A palladium catalyst supported on iota-carrageenan xerogel was separated and reused in laboratory oxidation reactions. This is reuse of a specific functional composite, not an established recycling stream for carrageenan packaging.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Carrageenan safety assessment requires distinguishing food-grade carrageenan from deliberately degraded, lower-molecular-weight poligeenan. EFSA’s 2018 EU assessment did not identify genotoxicity or carcinogenicity concerns for the evaluated food additives, but retained uncertainties and a temporary group ADI pending better data. This historical assessment is neither a blanket safety finding for every carrageenan preparation nor a current-use authorization for poligeenan.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Gel and film observations depend on carrageenan type, concentration, counterion, plasticizer, additive loading, and thermal history; a κ-film result is not a carrageenan-family constant.

sections.overview: Lignin is a family of complex, branched aromatic biopolymers associated with plant cell walls. Its structure is strongly affected by botanical source and by isolation: technical lignins recovered by pulping or fractionation differ from lignin in the native biomass matrix.
sections.history: Lignin is a natural component of wood, and its industrial history grew from separating cellulose during pulping. Borregaard provides one documented example of turning the resulting liquor into products: it began making vanillin from lignin in 1962 and, according to Norsk Industri’s historical account, commercial lignosulfonate production in spring 1968. During 1972–1983 it invested in recovering the lignin stream as chemicals following pressure to reduce river discharges. Concrete admixtures, gypsum-board additives, dye dispersants and feed binders became important outlets. This history concerns technical lignins and lignosulfonates recovered or modified during pulping, not the invention of native lignin.
sections.nomenclature: Lignin is a family-level name, not a single uniform polymer or a synonym for one isolated technical product. Kraft, organosolv, and other named lignins should retain their extraction route and source because those terms identify chemically different technical materials rather than interchangeable aliases for native lignin.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Lignin is a naturally biosynthesized, heterogeneous aromatic polymer of plant lignocellulosic cell walls, not a material made by one standardized monomer polymerization. Material called technical lignin is recovered from biomass and is therefore defined both by botanical feedstock and by its separation history. Kraft, sulfite, and soda pulping give distinct technical lignins; organosolv processing extracts lignin with an organic solvent or solvent/water system and can yield a relatively sulfur-free fraction. Extraction can substantially change linkage distribution and condensation relative to native lignin. Post-isolation fractionation is also used to narrow material distributions: for example, solvent systems can separate technical lignin into fractions with different solubility and molecular-weight-related composition. Accordingly, a lignin feedstock description should name the source biomass and isolation or fractionation method rather than imply a uniform polymer identity.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Lignin is not a single uniform engineering resin. In plant cell walls, the highly branched, amorphous aromatic network occupies a hydrated composite with cellulose and hemicellulose; after isolation, kraft, lignosulfonate, soda, organosolv and near-native preparations differ substantially in chain scission, condensation, sulfur content, hydroxyl functionality and molar-mass distribution. Dry, unmodified technical lignins are commonly glassy, rigid and brittle, so they may crack rather than form useful self-supporting tensile articles. Heating or adding moisture increases segmental mobility and promotes stress relaxation and flow near the glass-transition region, but prolonged or excessive heat can drive irreversible condensation, cross-linking and degradation. Consequently, mechanical response depends strongly on botanical source and syringyl/guaiacyl/hydroxyphenyl composition; isolation and drying route; molar mass and branching; hydroxyl content and hydrogen bonding; residual carbohydrate, ash and solvent; moisture and humidity; temperature, pressure, rate and thermal history; and the degree of chemical modification or enzymatic polymerization. Plasticizers can lower stiffness and glass-transition temperature while increasing deformability, but their polarity, molecular mass, loading, migration and water uptake control the result. When lignin is a filler, binder or macromonomer, particle size and aggregation, dispersion, matrix compatibility, interfacial adhesion, lignin fraction, cross-link density and porosity dominate composite strength, toughness and creep; values for wood, paper, rubber, polyurethane or another matrix are not intrinsic lignin properties. Börcsök and Pásztory show why moisture and temperature must be retained in any mechanical interpretation: lignin's glass transition varies with molecular structure, cross-linking, molecular mass, isolation and thermal history, and water disrupts hydrogen bonding and lowers the transition until saturation. Their survey concerns lignin in wood rather than isolated test bars and therefore supports the family behavior, not a tensile range for neat lignin. A focused search found an open, bounded formulation example summarized by Fabbri and co-workers: dried laccase-polymerized lignosulfonate was described as highly brittle without plasticizer, while a PEG-600-plasticized lignosulfonate material reached 74 MPa tensile strength and a separate glycerol-plasticized formulation reached 111% elongation at break. These endpoints belong to enzymatically polymerized, plasticized lignosulfonate formulations, not native lignin or unmodified kraft lignin. The open review does not retain the specimen geometry, conditioning, test rate, plasticizer loading attached to those two maxima, replicate count or uncertainty from the underlying experiment, so the numbers are illustrative only; no adequately contextualized open numerical endpoint for an unmodified, self-supporting lignin specimen was found in this focused pass.
sections.processing:
Isolated lignin is not a single plug-compatible thermoplastic: source, isolation history, molecular architecture, moisture, ash, and prior heating determine whether a technical lignin softens, crosslinks, chars, or can be carried in a printable blend. Open literature demonstrates conversion through melt-compounded filaments for fused-deposition or fused-filament printing, direct-ink writing of formulated pastes or hydrogels, vat photopolymerization of reactive lignin-containing resins, and powder-bed routes. For extrusion-based printing, drying, particle dispersion, carrier-polymer compatibility, filament stiffness, shear thinning, thermal stability, nozzle pressure, layer cooling, and interlayer adhesion must be qualified together; raising temperature to lower viscosity can instead accelerate lignin degradation or crosslinking.

Nguyen and co-workers provide a bounded melt-extrusion example rather than a neat-lignin window. They formulated solvent-free composites containing 40-60 wt% fractionated hardwood organosolv lignin with NBR/ABS or nylon 12 and, in selected nylon blends, 4-16 wt% chopped carbon fiber. Rheology at 230 °C was used to identify a roughly 70-500 Pa·s printability region, and the authors tied successful filament feeding and deposition to composition, shear rate, viscosity, thermal stability, and reinforcement. Their melt-stable hardwood lignin lowered nylon-blend viscosity, whereas a kraft softwood lignin had a higher softening point and viscosity. Those findings are specific to the named lignins and matrices and should not be generalized to kraft, lignosulfonate, soda, or other technical-lignin streams.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Lignin is a heterogeneous, branched aromatic biopolymer associated with cellulose and hemicellulose in plant cell walls. Its phenylpropanoid-derived units, ether and carbon–carbon linkages, branching, and condensation state vary with botanical source and isolation route.
sections.properties: Lignin commonly provides aromaticity, UV absorption, antioxidant activity, rigidity, and thermal softening behavior, while its hydroxyl groups enable hydrogen bonding and chemical modification. These properties vary strongly between native, kraft, sulfite, soda, organosolv, and fractionated lignins.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Kraft lignin can replace part of the phenol in wood-panel and impregnating-paper resins and serves in polymers, asphalt formulations and dispersants. Lignosulfonate grades are chemically different purchasing products.

Purchasing. Stora Enso’s Lineo page lists industrial big bags and samples by inquiry. Buyers should verify current supply and grade: the company separately announced closure of its Sunila lignin plant in 2023.

Scale and evidence limits. Sunila, Finland, had stated lignin capacity of 50,000 tonnes/year, order 10^4, when its permanent closure was announced in September 2023. This is historical closed-site capacity, not current available supply, sales or worldwide lignin consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Alkaline-peroxide depolymerization of the tested lignin produced aromatic compounds including vanillin, vanillic acid, syringaldehyde, acetosyringone and syringic acid. These are controlled oxidation products; lignin composition changes their distribution.

Timescales: Reaction time under chemical oxidation cannot be converted to a natural decomposition lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The source does not establish mineralization or disappearance rates in soils, where lignin chemistry and association with other biomass matter.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The study combined chemical depolymerization with engineered microbial conversion to muconic acid and pyrogallol. This is laboratory valorization of lignin, not evidence of a commercial closed-loop lignin-recycling system.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Biomedical lignin studies concern selected purified lignins, derivatives or nanoparticles. Cytotoxicity can change with lignin source, isolation chemistry, particle size, concentration and surface functionality. A favorable cell assay for one preparation does not establish the safety of technical lignin mixtures or a finished drug-delivery formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Lignin is not a uniform commodity polymer: source biomass, pulping or fractionation chemistry, sulfur and ash, molar-mass distribution, moisture, and condensation control solubility, color, softening, and reactivity. Thermal processing can cause irreversible condensation or degradation, and results from one technical lignin should not be generalized to another.

sections.overview: Collagen is a family of fibrous structural proteins whose molecules assemble into hierarchical fibrillar or networked biological materials. Its biocompatible, degradable protein basis makes it important in tissue-derived and biomedical material systems.
sections.history: Collagen is an animal structural protein, not a human invention. Its modern molecular history includes competing models by Astbury and Bell in 1940 and Pauling and Corey in 1951. Ramachandran and Kartha proposed the essential triple-helix arrangement in 1954; Rich and Crick and North’s group refined it in 1955. Synthetic collagen-related peptides became structural probes from the late 1960s, and Berman’s group reported a high-resolution model-peptide crystal structure in 1994. Later research used this understanding to design collagen-like assemblies and tissue-supporting biomaterials. These advances concern molecular understanding and engineered collagen materials, distinct from the much older use of animal tissues.
sections.nomenclature: Collagen is a family-level name rather than a single molecular species; named collagen types, such as type I, have more specific biological and materials scopes. Gelatin and collagen hydrolysates are derived materials, not interchangeable names for collagen.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Collagen is a family of natural structural proteins biosynthesized by animals, rather than a synthetic-polymer product. Commercial or laboratory collagen is therefore recovered from collagen-rich tissue such as mammalian hides and tendons or fish skin, with the source, collagen type, and pretreatment affecting the recovered material. Reviews describe a recovery sequence of cold washing and tissue preparation, controlled acid or alkali pretreatment, extraction, and purification. Acid-soluble collagen can be extracted with acetic acid under cold conditions, then separated by filtration or centrifugation, salt precipitation, redissolution, and dialysis. Enzymatic pretreatment or extraction, especially with pepsin, is used for more extensively cross-linked tissues and can increase solubility by cleaving telopeptide regions; it can also change the recovered collagen relative to acid-only extraction. These are source- and method-dependent isolation routes, not a universal procedure or a route to hydrolyzed collagen peptides.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Collagen is a family of hierarchical protein materials rather than a single mechanically uniform substance. Triple-helical molecules assemble into fibrils, fibers, networks, and tissues; load response therefore depends on collagen type and animal source, fibril diameter and alignment, cross-link density, hydration, mineral or matrix content, extraction and reconstitution history, porosity, and the length scale and loading direction of the test. Type I collagen is the best-characterized load-bearing member. Aligned fibrils carry high axial tension but are much softer in shear or transverse loading, and larger fiber or tissue structures commonly show a nonlinear toe region as crimp and network architecture straighten. Collagen is also viscoelastic: rate, hold time, cyclic history, and temperature affect stiffness, hysteresis, recovery, fatigue, and failure. Water plasticizes and swells the structure, generally lowering modulus while increasing mobility and extensibility; drying can embrittle it. Chemical or enzymatic cross-linking often increases stiffness and dimensional stability, but its effect on strength and toughness depends on cross-link chemistry, density, and hydration. As a bounded numerical example, Shen and co-workers tested 13 isolated type I collagen fibrils from sea-cucumber dermis, 150-470 nm in diameter, in uniaxial tension with a MEMS device at 31-60% relative humidity. For the partially hydrated fibrils they reported a low-strain modulus of 0.86 +/- 0.45 GPa (range 0.36-1.60 GPa, strain below 0.09), mean yield stress of 0.22 +/- 0.14 GPa, and mean yield strain of 0.21 +/- 0.13. Individual responses included linear behavior, yielding followed by softening or hardening, recoverable residual strain, accumulated cyclic damage, and dehydration-induced embrittlement. These single-fibril, type I values must not be treated as ranges for bulk collagen films, porous scaffolds, gelatin, or collagen-rich tissue, whose mechanics also reflect architecture, additives, conditioning, and specimen preparation.
sections.processing: Collagen can be reshaped as solutions, suspensions, membranes/films, porous sponges, threads, wet-spun fibers, electrospun nonwovens, molded articles, or bioinks. Mechanical disintegration, viscosity adjustment, shaping, stabilization/crosslinking, drying, packaging, and sterilization are process stages; crosslinking commonly follows shaping to fix the new form. The cited processing review reports that high-viscosity masses at 5–10% dry matter can be extrudable, whereas castable suspensions require about 1% or lower; those statements describe its collagen-material processing discussion, not all collagen grades. In electrospinning, solution concentration/viscosity/conductivity, voltage, collection distance and speed, temperature, humidity, and solvent affect fiber morphology. The cited chapter's collagen-type-I example reports sensitivity to temperature, pH, and solvent, supporting their control rather than a universal spinning setpoint.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Collagen is a family of hierarchical fibrillar proteins whose organization extends from molecular triple helices to fibrils, fibers, and tissue-scale structures.
sections.properties: Hydration, crosslinking, source tissue, extraction, engineered architecture, and time-dependent response govern collagen material behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Collagen biomaterials serve wound care and tissue-engineering applications. Laboratory collagen provides extracellular-matrix coatings that support cell attachment and culture; these grades are distinct from a qualified medical device.

Purchasing. A documented research product is rat-tail type I collagen C3867, supplied in acidic solution. Tissue source, collagen type, concentration and quality specifications distinguish products.

Scale and evidence limits. The C3867 datasheet gives approximately 100 mg protein per vial in 22–25 mL solution, order 10^-1 gram of collagen. No reliable separate annual intact-collagen purchase tonnage was established; gelatin and hydrolysate volumes are different categories.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Proteolysis breaks collagen peptide bonds, producing lower-molecular-weight peptides and amino acids. The distribution depends on protease and treatment conditions.

Timescales: The cited study follows porcine-skin hydrolysis over 24 hours under enzyme-specific controlled conditions; this is processing, not an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: No lifetime is assigned to environmental collagen articles; purified collagen, crosslinked biomaterials and tanned leather are not interchangeable substrates.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Hydrolysis of porcine by-products followed by ultrafiltration recovered peptide fractions. This is a laboratory valorization route using commercial proteases; it does not demonstrate treatment of every collagen-containing waste.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Collagen immune responses depend on molecular conformation, accessible telopeptides and source. For extracellular-matrix scaffolds, residual cellular DNA and other non-collagen constituents can also cause adverse responses after incomplete decellularization. Clinical suitability therefore depends on purification and the complete biomaterial, not simply on collagen being a natural component of human tissue.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Single-fibril, tissue, and engineered-collagen results are not directly comparable; source, extraction, hydration, crosslinking, porosity, and test scale must accompany a reported result.

sections.overview: Silk fibroin is the structural protein component of silk fibers. It can be recovered and regenerated into films, fibers, gels, and other biomaterial forms, whose properties depend on molecular weight and processing.
sections.history: Silk fibroin is a natural protein with a textile history extending into antiquity. The Metropolitan Museum preserves Chinese woven silk dated to the Warring States period, 475–221 BCE. Silk later supplied Byzantine court and ecclesiastical clothing, with state and private workshops developing elaborate woven fabrics. Modern research sought to recover fibroin for uses beyond textiles. A documented process advance came from Jen-Chang Yang and colleagues at Taipei Medical University: their patent, filed in 2010 and granted in 2012, used precipitation under shear to recover fibroin without conventional dialysis. It addressed a production bottleneck for regenerated material. The patent describes application directions including cell-culture supports, wound-dressing membranes and tissue-engineering materials. These developments concern processing a natural protein and proposed biomedical uses, not an invention of silk itself.
sections.nomenclature: Fibroin protein is a descriptive synonym for silk fibroin. The canonical name identifies the structural protein rather than whole silk fiber, which also contains other components such as sericin.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Silk fibroin is a natural structural protein obtained chiefly from the core filaments of domesticated Bombyx mori silkworm cocoons. Raw cocoon silk contains fibroin coated and cemented by sericin, so preparation begins with degumming rather than monomer polymerization. An alkaline, soap, hot-water, or enzymatic treatment removes sericin; the fibroin fibers are then thoroughly rinsed and dried. For regenerated fibroin solutions or powders, the hydrogen-bonded protein is dissolved in a concentrated salt or chaotropic medium, purified to remove salt and particulates, and recovered by dialysis, membrane filtration, antisolvent precipitation, or drying. One cited patent degums cocoons with pressurized hot water, dissolves the recovered fibroin in calcium chloride/ethanol/water, and uses a dialysis-free organosoluble recovery route. A distinct patent uses sodium-carbonate degumming, water washing, and choline-hydroxide ionic-liquid dissolution followed by antisolvent precipitation, centrifugation, washing, filtration, and drying. Degumming severity and dissolution conditions must balance sericin removal against fibroin-chain degradation. Regenerated films, fibers, gels, or scaffolds are later shaping choices and remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Native silkworm fibroin is a strong, tough, anisotropic protein fiber in which oriented β-sheet crystallites act as load-bearing junctions and less ordered chain regions supply extensibility and energy dissipation. Its tensile response depends on the intact hierarchical fiber structure rather than composition alone. Regenerated fibroin films, fibers, mats, foams, and hydrogels have lost or rebuilt different parts of that hierarchy and can range from stiff and brittle to soft and highly extensible; numerical results therefore must remain attached to species, material form, secondary structure, and processing history.

Principal variables include silkworm species and strain, reeling and fiber diameter measurement, residual sericin, degumming chemistry and severity, protein-chain molecular weight, dissolution and regeneration solvent, β-sheet content and crystallinity, porosity, defects, and molecular or fibril orientation from drawing, rolling, spinning, or pressing. Water is both a temporary plasticizer and a structural-processing agent: absorbed moisture can soften amorphous regions, whereas water treatment followed by drying can promote β-sheet reorganization and stiffening. Humidity, temperature and annealing, crosslinking, blends or plasticizers, test direction, gauge geometry, loading rate, and conditioning consequently alter modulus, strength, elongation, and toughness.

Two bounded examples illustrate this sensitivity. Feng and co-workers tested Grade 6A Bombyx mori 20/22-denier reeled single fibers after degumming for 60 min at 85 ± 2 °C in 3.0 g L⁻¹ papain at pH 6, drying at 60 °C, and conditioning for 24 h at 20 ± 2 °C and 65 ± 5% RH. For 20 specimens at 20 mm gauge length and 10 mm min⁻¹, they reported breaking stress (tenacity) 2.7 ± 0.2 cN dtex⁻¹, breaking strain 16.5 ± 2.2%, and specific Young's modulus 0.7 ± 0.1 cN dtex⁻¹; the harsher Na₂CO₃-degummed comparison was 1.5 ± 0.2 cN dtex⁻¹, 8.7 ± 2.2%, and 0.4 ± 0.1 cN dtex⁻¹, respectively. In a separate regenerated-film study, a formic-acid/CaCl₂-cast Mori fibroin film had reported elastic modulus 787.9 MPa and maximum elongation 19.0%; after 24 h water soaking and 72 h vacuum drying, the corresponding film reached 1.645 GPa modulus but only 1.97% elongation under the study's ambient ASTM D3039-type tensile protocol at 2 mm min⁻¹. Neither fiber nor film values define silk fibroin generally.
sections.processing:
Once an aqueous or solvent-based silk-fibroin dope is available, the directly documented article routes in this pass are solution casting of films and electrospinning of fibrous mats or tubes. A uniform dope is metered onto a casting surface or through an electrospinning needle, shaped, dried, and then annealed or otherwise post-treated to change water stability, orientation, and beta-sheet content. Concentration, fibroin molecular mass, blend ratio, pH and solvent, dope viscosity and entrained bubbles, applied flow and shear, humidity, electric field and collector geometry, casting thickness, drying rate, and annealing conditions can alter jet stability, film or mat morphology, shrinkage, and handling. Extraction and degumming of silk, fibroin dissolution chemistry, and any network-forming chemistry remain in Synthesis; metering, casting or electrospinning, drying, annealing, and final article handling belong in Processing.

In one casting study, aqueous, HFIP, and formic-acid silk-fibroin solutions were each adjusted to 5% (w/v); 2.5 mL was poured into a 35 mm Petri dish and dried overnight at 37 °C. The films were then exposed to water vapor, methanol vapor, or steam in the study's covered treatment arrangement at 37 °C for 24 h and air-dried. This schedule applies to those solvent systems, concentration, dish geometry, and annealing treatments rather than all silk-fibroin films.

An independent electrospinning study blended aqueous silk with PEO at 2 mL silk solution to 1–4 g PEO to raise dope viscosity, then used 0.7–2.0 mL/h flow, potentials up to 20 kV, and an 18 cm needle-to-collector gap. Its mats or tubular grafts were water-vapor annealed under vacuum overnight at 4, 24, 37, or 55 °C. Those settings are bounded to the reported fibroin/PEO blends, electrospinning apparatus, collector, and post-treatment; they are not a general spinning window, and they do not establish melt processability for silk fibroin.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Silk fibroin is a protein with beta-sheet-rich physical crosslinks in fibers and regenerated forms.
sections.properties: Mechanical response depends on molecular weight, processing, and secondary structure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Silk supplies textiles; isolated or regenerated silk fibroin also supplies tissue-engineering scaffolds and cell-culture research. A silk fiber or fabric is not the same purchasing product as purified fibroin solution.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich lists Bombyx mori fibroin solution at 50 mg/mL in a 20 mL pack, nominally 1 g fibroin by concentration × volume. This is a research-material supply route.

Scale and evidence limits. Textile Exchange reports 91,415 tonnes of worldwide raw silk production in 2024, order 10^5 tonnes/year. This broader textile statistic includes raw silk and does not measure isolated fibroin sales; the checked solution pack is gram scale.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Proteolysis of regenerated silk films releases peptide-rich soluble material and can release crystalline particles after susceptible connecting regions are cleaved. Morphology, not just beta-sheet fraction, controls the response.

Timescales: The study compared silk-fibroin film mass loss over hours to days in protease XIV/PBS at 37 °C and pH 7.4. Its methods and discussion report different enzyme concentrations, so a transferable numerical degradation rate is not assigned here.

Environmental persistence: Released crystalline fragments can remain after the film loses integrity; laboratory enzymatic degradation does not establish their environmental disappearance time.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Defective cocoons and silk production waste were degummed and dissolved to form regenerated fibroin films. This laboratory route recovers polymer from a defined silk waste stream; coatings, blends and contamination require separate assessment.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Silk fibroin responses depend on material format and processing. The review distinguishes fibroin from residual sericin and other processing-associated constituents, whose contributions to inflammation are not uniform across studies. Degumming and a favorable cell test do not by themselves establish the safety of a specific implanted silk device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Modification-strategy results are not intrinsic to native silk fibroin.

sections.overview: Polyhydroxyalkanoates are microbially produced polyesters composed of hydroxyalkanoate units. Monomer composition creates a broad family spanning materials with different crystallinity, mechanical behavior, and biodegradation profiles.
sections.history: PHA research grew from observations of bacterial storage granules. Maurice Lemoigne’s studies in the 1920s identified the polyester now called poly(3-hydroxybutyrate); subsequent work established a much broader family of microbial polyesters. Macrae and Wilkinson clarified the storage role in 1958, and W. R. Grace attempted commercial production from 1959. Later work varied microbial strains and monomer composition to expand material behavior. Packaging, agricultural products and biomedical materials became major development directions. This family history begins with discovery of natural polymers; individual PHA homopolymers and copolymers have separate commercialization histories.
sections.nomenclature: PHA abbreviates polyhydroxyalkanoate. The name is family-level; PHB and PHBV are particular members or copolymer compositions, not synonyms for all PHAs.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are intracellular polyesters biosynthesized by bacteria and other microorganisms from assimilable carbon sources rather than conventionally polymerized after isolating a monomer. Sugars, lipids, organic acids, and carbon-rich waste streams can feed the cells; organism, PHA-synthase pathway, substrate composition, and cultivation regime determine whether the accumulated material is a homopolymer or a copolymer containing hydroxyalkanoate units of different chain lengths. Recovery therefore follows cultivation: cells are separated, concentrated or dried, disrupted or digested, and the polymer is extracted and purified by solvent recovery, washing, and/or precipitation. One cited study fermented industrial-waste substrates with a Bacillus isolate, harvested biomass, and extracted intracellular PHA. A distinct patent route first acidogenically ferments a water-based waste feed into fatty acids, feeds that stream to PHA-producing bacteria, separates a PHA-rich cell paste, and extracts the polymer with a polar organic solvent. These are bounded production examples; strain, feed, and downstream recovery method remain route-specific.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are a compositionally broad family: short-chain-length P(3HB)-rich materials are commonly semicrystalline and stiff/brittle, whereas 4HB, 3HV, 3HHx, and medium-chain-length units can lower crystallinity and modulus while increasing extensibility and toughness. Molecular mass, monomer ratio and sequence, crystallinity/aging, thermal and moisture history, plasticizer/nucleant/fiber package, and processing into film, injection molding, fiber, or porous scaffold are therefore controlling variables. An open composition review reports P(3HB) values of 1.1–3.5 GPa modulus, 0.4–5% elongation, and 19–40 MPa tensile strength, versus a 3HB:3HV 80–90:10–20 mol% copolymer at 0.8–1.2 GPa, 50–100%, and 20–32 MPa. These literature summaries do not retain a common grade, method, or conditioning and are composition envelopes, not a PHA-wide specification. A second open review independently attributes the broad PHA response to monomer composition and highlights crystallinity as a key determinant of PHB mechanics.
sections.processing:
Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are compositionally diverse thermoplastic polyesters that can be shaped by solution casting and particulate leaching; compression or melt molding; extrusion, blown film, and injection molding; melt, dry, wet, and electrospinning; phase separation and freeze drying; gas foaming; and additive manufacture. Processability cannot be reduced to one family temperature window: PHB has a narrow margin between melting and damaging thermal exposure, whereas comonomers such as hydroxyvalerate, hydroxyhexanoate, or 4-hydroxybutyrate can lower melting temperature and crystallinity. Dry feed, short and controlled melt residence, low unnecessary shear, oxygen and moisture control, and appropriate plasticizers, nucleating agents, fillers, or blends can reduce chain scission and improve melt strength. Mold or chill-roll temperature and cooling rate control crystallization, skin-core orientation, shrinkage, brittleness, and cycle time; solution routes additionally require complete dissolution or dispersion, solvent control, and removal of residual solvent or porogen.

Puppi, Pecorini, and Chiellini review these melt- and solution-based article routes and explicitly warn that PHB's narrow melt-processing interval and slow or composition-dependent crystallization require formulation and process control. Vanheusden and co-workers provide a bounded melt example for Aonilex X151A PHBHHx containing 10.5 mol% 3-hydroxyhexanoate. They dried pellets for at least three days at 65 °C, twin-screw extruded them, immediately transferred the melt to a heated piston-injection cylinder, and optimized their test bars at a 145 °C processing temperature, 80 °C mold, 50 rpm screws, and 60 s mold cooling. Their study found that higher mold temperature allowed more chain relaxation and reduced oriented skin formation, while elevated temperature plus shear narrowed the practical interval through thermo-mechanical and thermo-oxidative degradation. Those values apply to that grade, specimen, and laboratory line, not to PHB, PHBV, P4HB, or every PHBHHx composition.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyhydroxyalkanoates are biologically produced aliphatic polyesters composed of hydroxyalkanoate repeat units with variable side-chain length and composition. Monomer composition controls crystallinity, lamellar structure, flexibility, and degradation behavior across the family.
sections.properties: PHAs are biodegradable or bioassimilable thermoplastics with tunable stiffness, flexibility, barrier behavior, and thermal processing windows. Molecular mass, comonomer distribution, crystallinity, residual biomass, and plasticizer or blend content strongly affect performance.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Commercial PHA grades include resins for straws, cutlery, coffee capsules, bags and films. The family also supplies biomedical research materials; uses depend on monomer composition and formulation.

Purchasing. Source a specified PHA chemistry and grade through producers, compounders or research catalogs. Kaneka Green Planet is a PHBH example; PHB research resin is separately sold in 10 g and 100 g catalog packs.

Scale and evidence limits. Kaneka’s 2022 announcement identified 5,000 tonnes/year existing PHBH capacity and an additional 15,000 tonnes/year planned at Takasago, Japan. These order 10^3–10^4-tonne capacities concern one PHA chemistry and announcement date, not worldwide PHA purchases or verified subsequent output.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For the PHB member, hydrolysis yields 3-hydroxybutyric acid; dehydration can instead yield crotonic acid. Other PHA monomer compositions require their own product inventories.

Timescales: No single degradation time applies to this chemically diverse family.

Environmental persistence: A controlled PHB recycling reaction establishes neither family-wide environmental biodegradation nor the lifetime of all PHA articles.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: PHB hydrolysis to recover hydroxy acid is an emerging laboratory route. Its success cannot be assigned to every short- or medium-chain-length PHA.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PHA intended for biomedical use requires control of impurities from microbial production, especially bacterial endotoxin released during recovery. The PHA review emphasizes purification and material-dependent host responses. Reported compatibility of selected films or scaffolds is evidence for those preparations, not authorization of every polymer grade or device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PHA properties and cost vary with microorganism, carbon feedstock, fermentation, recovery, monomer composition, and thermal history. Many grades have narrow processing windows, slow or complex crystallization, brittleness, and moisture or hydrolysis sensitivity; one PHB or PHBV study cannot represent the family.
