sections.overview: Poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) is PBSA, an aliphatic copolyester containing succinate and adipate residues with 1,4-butanediol. It is formed by condensation polymerization, and the relative diacid feed controls copolymer composition.
sections.history: PBSA developed alongside PBS as manufacturers varied aliphatic-polyester composition for flexible materials. Showa Highpolymer’s 1994 polyester-fiber patent includes succinate/adipate chemistry and describes turning such polymers into fibers and nonwoven products. More recent BioPBS literature from PTT MCC Biochem distinguishes PBSA grades from PBS and documents packaging-film, fiber and molded-product development using technology licensed from Mitsubishi Chemical. Biomedical exploration formed a separate branch: Simon Williams and colleagues at Tepha included PBSA among the PBS copolymers in a 2021 patent publication on implant materials. That patent represents an investigated application, not evidence of routine clinical adoption or a first synthesis date.
sections.nomenclature: PBSA is the abbreviation for poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate). The record denotes a covalent succinate/adipate copolymer, not a physical PBS/poly(butylene adipate) blend; PBS homopolymer, PBAT, and modified or filled formulations are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA) is an aliphatic copolyester in which both succinate and adipate residues are incorporated with 1,4-butanediol; it is not a physical blend of PBS and poly(butylene adipate). The cited syntheses charge succinic acid, adipic acid, and 1,4-butanediol to form a prepolymer and then perform condensation poly­merization. The relative diacid feed is a compositional control variable and can change the resulting copolyester, so no single ratio is implied for the entire PBSA name. Additional branching, cross-linking, or chain-extending reactants described in individual sources define modified PBSA variants and are not part of the base copolymer identity.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PBSA is a composition-sensitive aliphatic copolyester. The adipate fraction can lower crystallinity and melting behavior relative to PBS, while molecular weight, film orientation/draw ratio, annealing, filler loading, and environmental exposure further alter tensile response. Independent open studies accordingly describe PBSA as ductile but show that oriented and filled films can be substantially stiffer or less extensible than the neat material.

A bounded neat-PBSA film result from one five-replicate study is Young's modulus 0.29 ± 0.05 GPa, stress at break 21.10 ± 0.50 MPa, and break elongation 400 ± 53%; the same paper reports 32.1% crystallinity for that PBSA. These values are for its particular film and formulation, not for PBSA composites, blends, orientation states, or all succinate/adipate compositions.
sections.processing:
PBSA is a melt-processable aliphatic copolyester used in blown and cast film, extrusion and compounding, injection molding, sheet thermoforming, and blends or composites. Adipate content, molar mass, branching, and blend formulation govern crystallization and melt strength. Pellets and hygroscopic co-components should be dried; melt temperature, shear, residence time, die and chill-roll temperature, draw/blow ratio, cooling and winding must balance homogeneous dispersion against hydrolytic or thermal degradation. Too little melt strength destabilizes film, while repeated heat/shear histories and excessive temperature can lower molar mass.

A bounded cast-film study by Alfano and co-workers used BioPBS FD92PM PBSA in PHBV/PBSA blends. PBSA, PHBV, and compatibilizer were oven-dried at 60 °C for at least 12 h, manually premixed, and fed to an L/D 25 single-screw extruder with a flat die and calender. The profile was 175/175/165/165/165/165 °C at 40 rpm, producing about 500 micrometre sheets. These conditions were selected for those blend compositions and compatibilized films, not neat PBSA generally. The PBS/PBSA review identifies extrusion, injection, casting, and film blowing as established routes and emphasizes that molecular architecture, crystallization, and thermal stability select the suitable process.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PBSA is an aliphatic copolyester with succinate and adipate units that tune chain flexibility and crystallization.
sections.properties: Composition and processing control its mechanical response, hydrolysis, and biodegradation.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PBSA grades serve flexible packaging sealant films and fiber/nonwoven or molded applications. The adipate-containing grades are distinct from PBS homopolymer within commercial BioPBS portfolios.

Purchasing. PTT MCC’s brochure identifies PBSA grades and lists FD92 for extrusion film and FD72 for fibers/spunbond. Buyers specify the copolymer grade and end-use requirements through the producer.

Scale and evidence limits. The brochure states total BioPBS capacity of 20,000 tonnes/year at Rayong, Thailand, but gives no reporting year or separate PBSA allocation. This order 10^4-tonne portfolio capacity is not PBSA annual consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Alcoholysis with propylene glycol shortens PBSA chains and creates hydroxyl-terminated and glycol-ester-containing products. This treatment does not define ambient metabolites.

Timescales: The approximately 100 μm PBSA film showed no surface change after one month in nutrient-amended seawater at 23 °C.

Environmental persistence: A laboratory film result is not a universal environmental lifetime.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Microwave-assisted alcoholysis produces lower-molar-mass PBSA for aqueous coating dispersions. Coated paper was repulped experimentally; that demonstrates substrate reclamation and a potential PBSA conversion route, not closed-loop recovery of postconsumer PBSA.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The supplier sheet for BioPBS FD grades, including FD92PM and FD92PB PBSA, identifies hot-polymer burns, dust-related eye irritation and irritating processing fumes. It recommends ventilation, dust control and prevention of pellet release to waterways. The guidance addresses these industrial grades and does not replace evaluation of a finished food-contact or biomedical formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Carbon-chain and film studies apply to specified copolymer compositions and fillers.

sections.overview: Poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate) is an aromatic polyester built from ethylene glycol and 2,5-furandicarboxylate units. Its furan-containing diacid component distinguishes it from terephthalate polyesters.
sections.history: PEF’s recent development has centered on making its furan-based monomer available at industrial scale. Avantium records proof of its YXY conversion technology in 2006, an FDCA pilot plant and a first PEF bottle in 2011, and the formation of the Synvina venture with BASF in 2016. Avantium regained full ownership in 2019. Led technically by researchers including Gert-Jan Gruter, the program developed partnerships for bottles, films, packaging and textiles. The FDCA flagship plant was inaugurated in October 2024, when Releaf was introduced as the PEF brand. These are scale-up and commercialization milestones, distinct from the first laboratory synthesis of a furan polyester.
sections.nomenclature: PEF abbreviates poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate), often shortened to poly(ethylene furanoate). The canonical name specifies the 2,5-furandicarboxylate structure and is not a name for all furan-based polyesters.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate) (PEF) is the polyester from 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA), or a diester thereof, and ethylene glycol. FDCA is a furan dicarboxylic-acid feedstock; its use, rather than terephthalic acid, defines the furandicarboxylate repeat unit. Routes first esterify FDCA with ethylene glycol, or transesterify an FDCA diester, then polycondense the oligomer under reduced pressure while removing low-molar-mass products. Titanium alkoxide and antimony- or germanium-based catalysts occur in the cited examples, and solid-state polycondensation may be used for additional molecular-weight build-up. Those catalyst and finishing choices are source-specific, not a single mandatory PEF recipe.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PEF mechanics depend on molar mass, furan-polyester microstructure, crystallinity/polymorph, thermal history and annealing, strain orientation, and any comonomer or diethylene-glycol content. Open studies find that monomer route and intrinsic viscosity change crystallinity and elastic response, while biaxial stretching induces crystallinity and modifies rigidity; therefore amorphous plaques, annealed material, stretched film, and fibers cannot be pooled.

A bounded high-molecular-weight PEF example (Mn 83,000 g/mol, made by melt polymerization followed by solid-state post-condensation) reported Young's modulus 2,450 ± 220 MPa and maximum stress 35 ± 8 MPa. The paper also studied crystallinity effects with temperature, so these results are not a universal PEF datasheet value or directly transferable to lower-molar-mass, copolymer, or oriented PEF.
sections.processing:
Poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate) (PEF) can be converted by melt extrusion and extrusion casting, injection molding of preforms and other parts, stretch blow molding, thermoforming, and fiber spinning. Stretching and shear during these operations alter crystallization kinetics and morphology, so melt temperature, residence time, shear history, cooling, and subsequent uniaxial or biaxial orientation must be developed together. A recent open review also identifies high melt viscosity, shear sensitivity, and the proximity of useful melt processing to thermal degradation as practical reasons not to transfer a PET schedule unchanged to PEF.

For one bounded stretch-blow-molding approach, The Coca-Cola Company's EP 3 194 134 B1 discloses water-conditioning an already injection-molded PEF or PEF-copolymer preform, followed by removal of trapped and surface water and stretch blow molding. Claim 1 gives alternative conditioning ranges of room-temperature water for about 3 h to at least 48 h, water at about 80 °C for up to about 15 h, at least about 65% RH air above about 45 °C for about 0.25 h to at least 72 h, or at least about 85% RH air above about 35 °C for about 0.5 h to at least 44 h. The patent warns that excessive moisture together with heat can produce excessive crystallization. These are claimed options for the disclosed preform process, not a general PEF drying or blow-molding window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PEF is a polyester formed from ethylene glycol and 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid or its ester. The rigid furan-containing aromatic-like diacid unit produces a semicrystalline polyester whose packing and crystallization differ from PET.
sections.properties: PEF can provide high stiffness, useful thermal behavior, and strong barrier performance to oxygen and carbon dioxide relative to conventional polyester benchmarks. Crystallinity, chain orientation, molecular mass, and humidity affect permeability and dimensional response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PEF is being developed for beverage bottles, packaging film, fibers and textiles. Avantium’s 2026 examples include functional-beverage shot bottles, a PEF-containing cushion and sportswear fibers; these are commercialization partnerships and prototypes, not evidence of mature market-wide adoption.

Purchasing. Contact Avantium and its conversion partners for development supply and negotiated offtake. Its September 2026 Sukano agreement reserves future licensed-plant volumes for masterbatch-related uses; such reservations are distinct from a readily available commodity-resin shipment.

Scale and evidence limits. In August 2026, Avantium reported 15 capacity reservations covering more than 150 kilotonnes of future FDCA and PEF combined. This is prospective reservation volume, not PEF purchases or annual consumption. On 7 September 2026, first commercial deliveries under existing plant offtakes were still expected at end-2026, conditional on start-up and qualification.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Glycolysis converts PEF ester chains to bis(2-hydroxyethyl) furan-2,5-dicarboxylate (BHEF). This reactor product is distinct from a measured environmental-degradation inventory.

Timescales: The study examines heated catalyst-assisted depolymerization of thermocompressed films; it does not establish an environmental mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: Renewable feedstock origin alone does not establish biodegradability. Soil, freshwater and marine lifetimes remain unquantified here.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Organocatalytic glycolysis recovered BHEF and subsequent polymerization regenerated PEF with similar thermal properties. This demonstrates a laboratory closed loop for the tested films, rather than commercial collection or universal recovery from mixed packaging.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The U.S. food-contact assessment for Avantium’s PEF notification 2383 is explicitly use-limited: the July 2024 submission covers specified food-contact articles under room-temperature, refrigerated and frozen-storage conditions and excludes foods above 15% alcohol. It is evidence for that supplier’s notified use and conditions, not unrestricted permission for every PEF grade, hot-fill application or medical device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PEF remains sensitive to molecular mass, crystallization rate, hydrolysis, processing temperature, and residual catalyst or moisture. Much evidence is formulation- and process-specific, and PEF should not be treated as a drop-in equivalent for every PET conversion line or application.

Initial esterification releases water; subsequent ester exchange between hydroxyl-ended species extends the chains. Removal of volatile products favors further condensation, and chains grow through reactions among monomers and oligomers.

sections.overview: Poly(ethylene oxide) is a polyether made from ethylene oxide repeat units. Molecular weight strongly affects its physical form and use, from lower-molar-mass polyethylene glycols to higher-molar-mass PEO polymers.
sections.history: High-molecular-weight PEO advanced through manufacturing work on water-soluble polyethers during the 1950s. Frederick E. Bailey Jr. and John T. Fitzpatrick’s Union Carbide patent, filed in 1957 and granted in 1960, improved catalyst removal while retaining readily handled granular polymer. It describes established uses as thickeners, sizing agents and binders. Later development extended this solution behavior to medicines: Alan E. Royce’s 1993 Sandoz patent used PEO as a directly compressible tablet matrix to regulate drug release. These records document industrial purification and pharmaceutical formulation milestones, rather than the first preparation of the ethylene-oxide polymer family.
sections.nomenclature: PEO abbreviates poly(ethylene oxide); polyethylene glycol (PEG) is commonly used for chemically equivalent lower-molar-mass materials. The names should be qualified by molecular-weight scope rather than treated as universally interchangeable.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO), also called poly(oxyethylene) and often termed polyethylene glycol at lower molar mass, is the ring-opening polymerization product of ethylene oxide. Anionic routes combine ethylene oxide with a hydroxyl- or amine-functional initiator and a strongly basic catalyst such as potassium hydroxide; active-hydrogen initiators produce hydroxy-terminated chains or multiple arms according to initiator functionality. Metal-cyanide catalysts are a separately documented ethoxylation route. Thus initiator identity, catalyst system, and ethylene-oxide-to-initiator feed determine architecture and molar mass; they should not be inferred from the bare PEO family name.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
High-molecular-weight poly(ethylene oxide) is a semicrystalline, water-soluble thermoplastic. In a dry film at room temperature its amorphous phase is well above the glass-transition region and the crystals act as physical load-bearing domains, so the material can yield, neck or craze, and deform substantially rather than responding as a rigid glass. It is also strongly viscoelastic and susceptible to creep and rate-dependent fracture. Molecular weight and entanglement density, crystalline fraction and lamellar morphology, solvent-casting or melt history, cooling and annealing, orientation, physical aging, test rate and temperature, and specimen thickness affect modulus, yield, ductility, and wear. Water uptake is especially consequential because it changes crystallinity and chain mobility and can progress to swelling or dissolution; humidity and conditioning must therefore accompany useful PEO mechanical data. Salts, crosslinks, blend segments, and dispersed fillers create mechanically different PEO-based materials.

A bounded neat-film example used Sigma-Aldrich PEO with viscosity-average molecular mass 1,000,000 g/mol. A 4 wt% aqueous solution was cast in glass dishes and vacuum-dried at 80 °C for about 5 hours. The unfilled film had 82% crystallinity by the study's DSC convention. Ten dumbbells with a 2 mm by 20 mm narrow section were pulled at 20 cm/min, giving 760 ± 109 MPa Young's modulus, 14.2 ± 0.9 MPa yield strength, 12.8 ± 0.4 MPa stress at failure, and 86 ± 14% strain at failure. The paper does not report film thickness, tensile-test temperature, or humidity/conditioning, so the values remain specific to that molecular mass and aqueous-cast/dried specimen preparation and are not a general dry-PEO range. A separate NASA study of PEO sliding contacts found molecular-weight, sliding-speed, and load-dependent friction, surface melting, and crack formation, independently reinforcing that load history and molecular size matter without supplying a transferable tensile endpoint.
sections.processing:
Poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) is commonly converted from solution into cast or doctor-bladed films and coatings, electrospun fiber mats, and solution-derived feed for three-dimensional printing; the appropriate route depends strongly on molecular mass and formulation. For PEO-based solid polymer electrolytes, solution concentration and viscosity, salt or filler dispersion, coating thickness, solvent choice and evaporation rate, and the final vacuum-drying or heat-treatment step control film uniformity and crystallization. Electrospinning additionally requires coordinated control of solution viscosity and conductivity, feed, electric field, collector, and solvent removal. These routes and limitations apply to the cited PEO-containing formulations rather than defining a universal schedule for neat PEO.

As a bounded film-casting example, Xu and co-workers used PEO of viscosity-average molecular mass about 1,000,000 g/mol. They made a 4 wt% aqueous PEO solution, added aqueous cellulose-nanocrystal suspension or cellulose-nanofibril gel to obtain 0–10 wt% reinforcement on PEO solids, homogenized at 100 rpm for 5 min at room temperature, then magnetically stirred at about 100 rpm and 60 °C for 12 h. The mixtures were cast in glass Petri dishes and vacuum-oven dried at 80 °C for about 5 h. That mixing and drying sequence belongs to those PEO/cellulose nanocomposite films and should not be generalized to other molecular masses, solvents, or filled systems.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(ethylene oxide) is a flexible polyether with repeating –CH2CH2O– units. Depending on molecular mass, crystallinity, water content, and salt or polymer interactions, it can occur as a semicrystalline solid, hydrated chain phase, or entangled solution.
sections.properties: PEO is water-soluble, hydrophilic, film-forming, and capable of coordinating cations through ether oxygens. Molecular mass and crystallinity control viscosity, melting behavior, transport, and electrolyte conductivity; moisture and salt strongly alter the response.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. High-molecular-weight PEO supplies pharmaceutical osmotic-pump and mucoadhesive matrices. Research uses include drug-delivery hydrogels and polymer-electrolyte membranes.

Purchasing. Pharmaceutical portfolios documented in 2024 include POLYOX. Sigma-Aldrich 182028 is a research powder with nominal viscosity molecular weight 600,000, offered from 5 g to 2.5 kg; lower-molecular-weight PEG is a related but distinct grade category.

Scale and evidence limits. These catalog packs span grams to kilograms. No reliable separate annual high-molecular-weight PEO purchase or consumption total was found; all PEG or ethoxylate volumes cannot be assigned to PEO.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hydroxyl-ended PEG is oxidized from its ends, followed by chain shortening; oxidative chemical treatment can cleave internally.

Timescales: No environmental lifetime is assigned to high-molar-mass PEO from lower-molar-mass PEG experiments.

Environmental persistence: Molar mass and end-capping affect biological utilization; dissolution alone is not mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Chemical cleavage offers a research route to smaller glycol derivatives. US5254723A tested the low-molar-mass PEG member (nominal molecular weight 600): acetic anhydride and ferric chloride at 140 °C for 2 h gave ethylene glycol diacetate at 12% yield by gas chromatography. The corresponding zinc-chloride experiment gave less than 10%. This is a demonstrated, low-yield conversion to a chemical intermediate, rather than recovery of ethylene oxide or proof of an efficient recycling process for high-molecular-weight PEO articles. Molecular weight, contamination and product separation remain important boundaries when assessing this route.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Polyether immune recognition depends on chemical form and exposure. The PEG-immunity review discusses PEG, the lower-molecular-weight naming convention for the same ethylene-oxide backbone in antibody-recognition studies. This parenteral-carrier context warrants attention to formulation and molecular weight; it does not supply a universal occupational or oral safety threshold for the entire polymer family.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PEO can crystallize, absorb moisture, undergo oxidative chain scission, and lose viscosity under heat, radiation, or strong shear. Molecular mass, end groups, salt identity and concentration, humidity, crystallinity, and blend compatibility must accompany any application claim.

sections.overview: Poly(propylene oxide) is a polyether made by ring-opening polymerization of propylene oxide. Double-metal-cyanide and anionic catalyst systems can produce polyoxypropylene polyols with controlled chain growth and end groups.
sections.history: Poly(propylene oxide) development has been closely connected to polyether catalysts and polyurethane raw materials. Robert J. Herold at General Tire & Rubber filed a double-metal-cyanide catalyst patent in 1963, granted in 1966, that included propylene-oxide polymerization. Herold and Robert E. Bingham’s 1982 patent subsequently addressed catalyst-residue treatment in polypropylene-ether polyols. This helped make the products suitable for subsequent reactions and polyurethane manufacture, including foams and elastomeric materials. The dated advances concern catalyst and purification technology within an existing polyether field; hydroxyl-terminated PPO polyols, high-molecular-weight PPO and PPO-containing copolymers should not be treated as one commercial grade.
sections.nomenclature: PPO, PPG, and poly(propylene oxide) refer to the polyether record boundary here; in polyol contexts PPG emphasizes hydroxyl-terminated material. A crosslinked PPO elastomer or polyurethane soft segment is a network or copolymer formulation made from PPO, not a synonym for the base polyether.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(propylene oxide) (PPO, also poly(oxypropylene)) is the ring-opened polyether from propylene oxide. Anionic ring-opening polymerization with alkoxide/basic initiators is a principal route; common starter choices such as an alcohol, diol, triol, or polyol determine chain-end functionality and whether the product is a linear polyether or a multifunctional polyether polyol. A controlled study uses potassium initiators activated by crown ether in THF and shows that initiator identity affects regioselective ring opening, unsaturation, and molar mass. Double-metal-cyanide catalysts provide a different route for propylene-oxide polyether-polyol formation and can reduce/tune unsaturation and initiation behavior. These route examples do not make a polyurethane network or a CO2/PO copolymer into PPO; such subsequent reactions and carbonate-containing copolymers are separate materials.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PPO/PPG spans low-molar-mass polyether fluids, elastomer networks, and stereoregular solid forms, so it has no single useful bulk tensile value. Mechanical response depends on molar mass and end groups, tacticity/crystallizability, crosslink architecture, fillers or solvent, temperature and strain rate, and whether a sample is a free network, a blend, or a block copolymer. In one open study, an α,ω-diallyl PPO network (PPO Mn 16,500 g mol−1) was photochemically crosslinked with a tetrafunctional thiol and tested at 25 °C. The unfilled network had local tensile modulus 143 kPa at 100% strain and failed at about 170% elongation; treated-fumed-silica-filled networks extended beyond 500% in that study. These numbers describe the specified crosslinked dielectric-elastomer networks, not liquid PPG or uncrosslinked PPO. A second open catalyst study identifies tacticity as a key determinant of isotactic PPO mechanical properties, making stereoregularity and processing history additional scope limits. No open, form-appropriate tensile endpoint for an uncrosslinked commercial PPO/PPG fluid was identified in this focused pass.
sections.processing:
Poly(propylene oxide) (PPO) is commonly encountered as a soft, low-glass-transition polyether rather than a rigid molding resin. Useful articles are therefore often made by solution coating or casting PPO-containing blends, or by mixing a functional PPO with fillers and cure components, casting a thin film, and curing it in place. Molecular weight, end groups, blend partner, solvent removal, filler dispersion, humidity, film thickness, and cure depth must be controlled. The crosslink-forming reaction itself belongs in Synthesis, while formulation mixing, casting geometry, solvent removal, irradiation schedule, and demolding are Processing operations.

A 3M patent directly supports solution and solventless film conversion for PPO-containing adhesive articles: its specified PPO homopolymer or ethylene-oxide/propylene-oxide copolymer can be blended with polyurethane or polyester, dissolved for example in tetrahydrofuran or ethyl acetate, coated onto polyester or paper support, and dried, or the blend can be solventlessly melt cast. These are patent formulations and not neat-PPO molding instructions. For a separate bounded cured-film example, Goswami and co-workers combined 10 g of allyl-terminated Kaneka Silyl ACS003 PPO with 0.244 g tetrafunctional thiol and 0.192 g photoinitiator, mixed at 3500 rpm for 5 min, poured the mixture into an 8 × 10 cm steel mold over Parafilm-lined glass, ventilated it for 45–60 min, and irradiated it at 365 nm and 4.5 mW cm−2 for 45 min in air. Filled versions added fumed silica with 40–60 wt% toluene before mixing. Their films were 80–226 micrometres thick; the neat network was mechanically weak and silica improved handling, while filler choice had to account for UV absorption. The formulation and cure schedule are specific to that study.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PPO is a polyether whose tacticity and molecular weight depend on polymerization route.
sections.properties: It is often used as a flexible polyol; crosslinked systems have formulation-dependent mechanics.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Hydroxyl-terminated poly(propylene oxide), commonly sold as polypropylene glycol, is a reactive ingredient for polyurethane elastomers, adhesives, coatings and sealants. The checked P400 diol is used with other polyols in compact or foamed systems.

Purchasing. Dow lists VORANOL P400 through its product catalog and commercial inquiry route. Specify molecular weight, initiator, hydroxyl functionality and water content; not every commercial polyether polyol is a linear PPO homopolymer diol.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked grade page does not report annual PPO purchase tonnage or package mass. Polyurethane or total-polyol production is a broader category and cannot be assigned wholly to PPO.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hydroxyl-ended polypropylene glycol can undergo terminal oxidation followed by stepwise ether-chain shortening by selected bacteria.

Timescales: No transferable mineralization time was established.

Environmental persistence: Results for the tested PPG cannot be generalized to every molar mass or end-capped PPO grade.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Catalytic cracking has been demonstrated for polypropylene glycol, the hydroxyl-ended PPO polyether. Martinez and coworkers used mesoporous Y zeolites with PPG of number-average molecular weight 425 or 2000 Da. Their laboratory semi-batch tests used 450 °C, a 10-minute hold, nitrogen and a 1:1 polymer/catalyst mass ratio. Rapid product quenching and catalyst drying favored propionaldehyde; the optimized system gave about 95% selectivity and up to 86% yield. This converts the polyether to a chemical feedstock rather than returning propylene oxide. The work establishes catalyst/reactor requirements for these PPG feeds, not a validated collection and recycling system for contaminated PPO-based products.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Polyether immune recognition depends on chemical form and exposure. The PEG-immunity review discusses polypropylene glycol, a hydroxyl-terminated PPO form in antibody-recognition studies. This parenteral-carrier context warrants attention to formulation and molecular weight; it does not supply a universal occupational or oral safety threshold for the entire polymer family.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Crosslinked-elastomer results are not properties of neat PPO.

sections.overview: Poly(tetramethylene ether glycol) is a hydroxyl-terminated polyether diol made by ring-opening polymerization of tetrahydrofuran. It is supplied in molecular-weight grades and commonly serves as a soft-segment precursor in urethane and copolymer elastomers.
sections.history: PTMEG became an important intermediate for polyurethane and polyester manufacture before the late 1970s. Gerfried Pruckmayr and Robert H. Weir’s DuPont patent, filed in 1977 and granted in 1978, explicitly describes that established industrial position. Their advance used a separable polymeric acid catalyst to polymerize tetrahydrofuran, addressing catalyst recovery and disposal. BASF’s later PolyTHF materials illustrate the range of applications developed around this intermediate: spandex fibers, polyurethane hoses, films and cable sheathing, and elastomers for skate wheels. These are manufacturing and market milestones; the 1978 patent improved an existing material rather than marking PTMEG’s invention.
sections.nomenclature: PTMEG, PTMG, and PTHF are names used for this tetrahydrofuran-derived polyether glycol. The hydroxyl-terminated precursor is distinct from a polyurethane or other copolymer elastomer made from it; molecular-weight grade and end-group state should be retained for a specific material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(tetramethylene ether glycol) (PTMEG) is a hydroxyl-terminated polyether produced by cationic ring-opening polymerization of tetrahydrofuran (THF), followed by termination or hydrolysis that furnishes terminal hydroxyl groups. Strong-acid catalyst systems activate THF; water or 1,4-butanediol can act as chain terminators, so catalyst loading, water content, and terminator concentration help set molar mass and functionality. One cited route uses a reusable sulfonic-acid-functional polymeric catalyst with water or 1,4-butanediol. A distinct route uses fuming sulfuric acid together with a lithium halide, then quenches with water and hydrolyzes sulfuric-ester chain ends. These are catalyst-specific manufacturing examples rather than a universal PTMEG formulation, and THF copolymers containing other cyclic ethers are outside the homopolyether boundary unless separately identified.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PTMEG is commonly supplied as a low-molar-mass, hydroxyl-terminated polyether diol used as a soft segment, not as a finished load-bearing homopolymer article. The supplied material can be a waxy solid at room temperature and becomes a low-viscosity liquid near 38 °C; grade molar mass, moisture, temperature, and its conversion into a polyurethane, copolyester, polyamide elastomer, or spandex fiber therefore determine the useful mechanical response. The hard-segment chemistry, isocyanate:hydroxyl ratio, chain extender, crosslink density, cure, blend composition, and final geometry are consequential variables in such products. A public patent gives one deliberately bounded endpoint: an 80:20 PTMEG 2000/Polyol B mixture reacted with MDI to 6% free NCO, chain-extended with 1,4-butanediol, cast as a 1/4-inch plaque and heat-cured, reached 410% elongation in its ASTM D412 tensile test. This is a cured mixed-polyol polyurethane elastomer, not a value for unreacted PTMEG. No open, form-appropriate standalone tensile endpoint for a commercial PTMEG polyol was identified in this focused pass.
sections.processing:
Poly(tetramethylene ether glycol) (PTMEG) is normally a reactive polyol feed rather than a self-supporting article material. Its article-conversion relevance is chiefly in PTMEG-segmented polyurethane elastomers: liquid systems are metered, mixed without entrained air, vacuum-degassed where needed, cast, reaction-injection-molded, transfer-molded, or sprayed, then cured and post-cured; thermoplastic grades can be pelletized and extruded or injection molded into film, sheet, tubing, or elastomeric components. PTMEG molecular mass and phase state, moisture exclusion, polyol/prepolymer temperature and viscosity, stoichiometry, mixing energy, pot life, mold temperature, bubble removal, cure time, and demolding strength are formulation-specific controls. Urethane formation and network chemistry belong in Synthesis; metering, mixing, degassing, article shaping, and cure equipment or schedule belong here.

Sugita and co-workers provide one bounded rapid-cast formulation. Their Example 1 used a PTMEG-1000-containing curing side and an MDI-based prepolymer, vacuum-degassed the two liquids, mixed them for 1.5 min at NCO/OH 1.05 without entraining bubbles, cast a 2 mm sheet in a 60 °C mold, and demolded after 10 min; Example 2 used a low-pressure casting machine, a 50 °C sheet mold, and 2 kg/min discharge and demolded after 5 min. A separate Simula patent demonstrates that PTMEG-based urea-extended polyurethane can be cast, granulated or pelletized, and then extrusion-shaped; its PTMEG-1000 example first cast a 72 mil sheet, while the general process describes tubular structures and sheets and warns that moisture introduced with processing aids can cause hydrolysis and swelling. These schedules belong to the patents' exact isocyanate, chain-extender, catalyst, and stoichiometric systems, not to PTMEG generally.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PTMEG is a flexible polyether diol used as a soft-segment precursor.
sections.properties: Its molecular weight and end groups control polyurethane-elastomer behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PTMEG is purchased as a reactive soft-segment ingredient for spandex/elastane fibers, polyurethane elastomers and copolyester elastomers. Textile examples include sportswear, swimwear and underwear; other grades serve industrial elastomer, adhesive and coating formulations.

Purchasing. Obtain a specified molecular-weight polyol grade from a supplier, such as POLYMEG or PolyTHF, for incorporation into a downstream polymer. These polyols are distinct purchases from finished spandex yarn or elastomer compounds.

Scale and evidence limits. BASF’s November 2025 announcement targeted Ulsan closure in 2026 and stated a post-closure worldwide PolyTHF capacity of 250,000 metric tonnes/year across three sites, an order of 10⁵ tonnes/year. This is planned supplier capacity, not verified closure completion, actual purchases or global consumption.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Selected microorganisms utilize hydroxyl-ended PTMG; terminal oxidation and subsequent chain processing are implicated.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was verified.

Environmental persistence: End groups, molar mass and organism specificity matter; incorporation into polyurethane changes the material and requires separate evidence.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Acid-catalyzed ring-closing depolymerization can recover tetrahydrofuran from PTMEG manufacturing fractions. US6429321B1 describes β-zeolite treatment of off-specification PTMEG and its acetate-terminated intermediate, with THF removed through a condenser as it forms. Its PTMEG-650 example began at 130 °C and increased to 160 °C as production slowed; further examples included water and salt impurities. The recovered THF contained water, so downstream purification matters. This is a documented monomer-recovery route for the stated production streams. It does not demonstrate direct processing of an intact, crosslinked polyurethane article containing PTMEG soft segments.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Polyether immune recognition depends on chemical form and exposure. The PEG-immunity review discusses polytetramethylene ether glycol in antibody-recognition studies. This parenteral-carrier context warrants attention to formulation and molecular weight; it does not supply a universal occupational or oral safety threshold for the entire polymer family.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Technical information applies to named Polymeg grades and downstream formulations.

sections.overview: Poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) is PHEMA, the addition polymer of 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA). It is a hydrophilic acrylic polymer that can be prepared as a linear polymer or, with multifunctional crosslinker, as a water-swollen hydrogel network.
sections.history: PHEMA’s defining application history grew from Otto Wichterle’s work on water-swollen materials for eye implants in the 1950s. Wichterle and Drahoslav Lím’s hydrophilic-polymer patent, filed in 1960 and granted in 1965, documents crosslinked gels and biomedical articles. In 1961 Wichterle developed a spin-casting process for soft contact lenses using homemade equipment, turning a promising gel into reproducible optical shapes. Bausch & Lomb acquired manufacturing rights in 1966, providing a major commercial development route. These milestones concern PHEMA-based hydrogels and lens manufacture; the invention of the lens-making process is distinct from the initial polymer chemistry.
sections.nomenclature: PHEMA is the abbreviation used for poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate). The record denotes the HEMA homopolymer; HEMA copolymers, crosslinked PHEMA hydrogels, and a particular porous or biomedical formulation are related materials rather than aliases for the linear polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (PHEMA) is formed by addition polymerization of the vinyl group in 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA), usually by a radical route. A solution-polymerization example uses AIBN as thermal radical initiator in toluene under nitrogen, then removes residual solvent after polymerization. A different high-pressure-ramp study shows a bounded initiator-free bulk route: pressure first generates radical species from HEMA and rapid propagation follows on decompression. Linear PHEMA and a PHEMA hydrogel must be distinguished: multifunctional dimethacrylate crosslinkers or multifunctional initiator systems produce a network, whereas their amounts and cure conditions belong to the specific gel route rather than to PHEMA homopolymer synthesis generally.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PHEMA mechanics are most commonly reported for hydrated, cross-linked networks, where water content, cross-linker chemistry and concentration, polymerization solvent, network molecular weight, porosity, loading mode, and test timescale dominate the measured response. Open pHEMA-hydrogel studies show both cross-linker-dependent stiffening and time-dependent stress relaxation; nanoindentation and macroscale compression need not return the same modulus because hydration, equilibration, and geometry differ. Values for dried PHEMA, porous scaffolds, copolymers, and filled networks therefore are not directly comparable.

A bounded example is a porous, unfilled PHEMA scaffold tested in compression in one study: compressive modulus 88.7 ± 15.9 kPa and compressive strength 46.5 ± 4.9 kPa. The reported scaffold had 22% porosity and an 84 µm most-frequent pore diameter. These are wet porous-scaffold compression results, not tensile properties or generic values for bulk PHEMA hydrogel.
sections.processing:
PHEMA articles are commonly formed as hydrated or subsequently hydrated networks by casting in a mold, replica molding, particulate-leach casting, phase separation, freeze-drying, gas foaming, and electrospinning. The article-forming sequence has to control formulation homogeneity, mold wetting, cure exposure, porogen packing or surface-pattern replication, demolding, washing, and hydration. Because swelling changes dimensions and stiffness, the water content used during demolding and service is part of the processing specification. Thick or highly porous articles also need a washing schedule that removes residual soluble species without cracking the network.

Two open experiments illustrate bounded schedules. Zasońska and co-workers loaded a solution containing 3.1 g HEMA, 33 mg EDMA, and 24 mg AIBN in 1.7 mL dioxane into a 10 mL syringe packed with 6.75 g ammonium-oxalate needles, held the filled mold at 60 °C for 16 h, removed and trimmed the cylinder, immersed it in saturated NaCl for 24 h to avoid cracking, and water-washed it for 10 days to leach the porogen. In a separate ophthalmic-surface experiment, Krajňák and co-workers poured their H1 PHEMA formulation onto a nanopatterned silicon replica mold, exposed it for 10 min to a 365 nm, 36 W lamp at a 15 cm distance, then hydrated and rinsed the article and kept it in fresh water for two days. These are formulation- and geometry-specific casting/cure examples, not general PHEMA cure windows; the underlying monomer chemistry belongs in Synthesis.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PHEMA is a hydrophilic methacrylate polymer commonly crosslinked as a hydrogel.
sections.properties: Swelling and mechanics depend on crosslink density and hydration.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PHEMA-based hydrogels are established soft-contact-lens materials. Other applications include tissue-engineering scaffolds, drug-delivery research and sorbent systems; crosslinked article formulations differ from a catalog polymer.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich 192066 supplies a research PHEMA grade of nominal viscosity molecular weight 300,000 in 10 g or 25 g packs. These are raw research materials rather than finished contact lenses or qualified lens formulations.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked packs are order 10^1 grams. No reliable separate annual PHEMA resin purchase or consumption statistic was found; total contact-lens units include other polymer systems.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PHEMA hydrogels have a carbon-chain network that resists simple hydrolysis. The cited study measures thermal destruction of PHEMA-based composites; it does not identify complete environmental degradation products.

Timescales: Thermal-analysis heating is not an environmental lifetime, and no condition-qualified mineralization time is established.

Environmental persistence: Water uptake or release of an incorporated substance does not demonstrate decomposition of the PHEMA network.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For PHEMA-containing clinical materials, contamination and the complete article determine the disposal stream. WHO guidance separates infectious and chemical healthcare waste from ordinary refuse. This is a disposal framework for medical use, not demonstrated hydrogel recovery.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PHEMA is established in hydrogel contact-lens research and use, while the review distinguishes the polymer’s biological properties from those of the HEMA monomer. Water content, crosslinking and copolymer formulation affect oxygen transport and lens performance. Compatibility of a finished contact lens is consequently more specific than the polymer identity.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Reported scaffold properties belong to specified porous and magnetic formulations.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical addition consumes the methacrylate double bond. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

sections.overview: Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) is a thermoresponsive polymer made by radical polymerization of N-isopropylacrylamide. It is commonly converted into temperature-responsive hydrogel materials through physical or chemical crosslinking, where network composition controls the final response.
sections.history: A landmark in PNIPAM research was M. Heskins and J. E. Guillet’s 1968 investigation of its unusual aqueous phase behavior. Heating-induced changes in solubility and chain dimensions made it a model temperature-responsive polymer. Subsequent research pursued gel actuators, drug-delivery materials and tissue-engineering systems, with applications depending on polymer form and formulation. Molecular interpretation remained active: Patrick K. Quoika and colleagues’ 2023 simulation study examined how the water model changes predicted thermal behavior. This history concerns the recognition and development of responsiveness, rather than identifying 1968 as the first synthesis or implying that all proposed biomedical applications became commercial products.
sections.nomenclature: PNIPAM and PNIPAAm identify the N-isopropylacrylamide polymer. An uncrosslinked PNIPAM chain is distinct from a PNIPAM hydrogel, interpenetrating network, or composite: crosslinker, comonomer, and added polymer must remain stated rather than being absorbed into the base-polymer name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) is the linear radical-addition homopolymer of N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM). Conventional solution polymerization uses a thermally decomposing azo initiator after deoxygenation; monomer purity, solvent, initiator concentration, conversion, and chain transfer govern molecular mass and dispersity. Reversible addition–fragmentation chain-transfer (RAFT) polymerization offers a controlled route: NIPAM, an azo initiator, and a thiocarbonylthio chain-transfer agent are polymerized in a dry, oxygen-free solvent to give a chain-transfer-functional PNIPAM that can serve as a macro-CTA. Homopolymer synthesis should not be conflated with PNIPAM hydrogels, which deliberately add a difunctional crosslinker to form a network, or with later block-copolymer extension.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PNIPAM is commonly used as a thermoresponsive swollen network or microgel rather than as a dry bulk plastic. Its load response is controlled by covalent or physical cross-link density, polymer concentration and molecular mass, water content and ionic environment, temperature relative to the approximately 32 °C lower critical solution temperature, heating/cooling history, porosity, and any second network or particulate reinforcement. The volume transition changes both stiffness and deformation mode, so a value for a hydrated gel cannot be assigned to linear PNIPAM or to a dry film. In one open study, UV-cured gels made from 5 wt% NIPAM, 0.25 wt% methylene bisacrylamide, and 0.1 wt% photoinitiator in water (monomer:cross-linker 100:5 by mass), then swollen overnight in deionized water, gave a fully swollen compressive bulk modulus of 6.32 ± 1.43 kPa by calorimetry and 4.59 ± 0.52 kPa by osmotic compression. The latter equilibrated for one week against dextran solutions; these values are for that equilibrium, macroscopic gel, not a universal PNIPAM modulus. Independent PNIPAM/HPMC hydrogel work likewise finds that increasing covalent cross-linker raises differential modulus and strength but decreases extensibility, while HPMC association and microphase separation can substantially alter the response.
sections.processing:
PNIPAM articles are most often aqueous gels, microgels, coatings, fibers, or porous scaffolds rather than bulk melt shapes. Conversion routes include casting and curing in tubes or molds, physical or chemical crosslinking, interpenetrating-network formation, electrospinning, cryogelation or freeze-thaw structuring, and drying or lyophilization when a porous dry article is required. Mixing and degassing, filler dispersion, mold heat transfer, crosslink density, cure exposure, extraction of residual soluble material, drying path, hydration, pH, ionic strength, and temperature all affect homogeneity, pore structure, swelling, and dimensional response near the lower critical solution temperature.

For a bounded monolithic-gel example, the HPMC-intercalated PNIPAM study dissolved HPMC in water for 24 h, added NIPAM and bisacrylamide, cooled the mixture to 15 °C, purged with argon, added TEMED and APS, and transferred it into argon-purged 10 or 4 mm internal-diameter glass tubes. The sealed tubes were held for 24 h at 25 °C before demolding, and most specimens were then equilibrium-swollen to extract soluble material. The authors showed that crosslinker and HPMC contents affected phase separation, transparency, swelling, and demolding-state properties; slow air/vacuum drying preserved a nonporous morphology whereas freeze-drying would create porosity. This schedule is specific to those formulations and specimen sizes.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PNIPAM is a thermoresponsive polymer commonly crosslinked into water-swollen networks.
sections.properties: Its volume transition and mechanics depend on temperature, crosslinker, concentration, and medium.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PNIPAM supplies thermoresponsive hydrogel research and commercial cell-culture surfaces. Nunc UpCell plates use grafted PNIPAM to release adherent cells when cooled, supporting nonenzymatic cell harvesting for research.

Purchasing. Buy bulk research polymer, such as Sigma-Aldrich 535311 in a 10 g pack, or prepared PNIPAM-coated cultureware. The checked UpCell 96-well plate is individually packed with eight plates per case.

Scale and evidence limits. The evidence documents order 10^1-gram reagent packs and unit-count cultureware purchasing. It provides no annual PNIPAM tonnage or polymer loading per plate, so these cannot be converted to a market mass.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PNIPAM undergoes thermal mass loss; hydrogel breakup can instead be engineered by introducing cleavable polyester links, leaving PNIPAM-containing fragments. These modified networks are not evidence that ordinary PNIPAM mineralizes.

Timescales: The thermal study investigates programmed heating. The modified-hydrogel experiments use accelerated alkaline hydrolysis; neither supplies an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Collapse and reswelling at the thermal transition are physical changes. Environmental persistence of the remaining carbon-chain polymer is not quantified by those changes.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Reversible salting-out permits recovery of physically crosslinked PNIPAM printed objects: immersion in water dissolves the structure, and the collected polymer can be reprinted. The study demonstrated recovery with optional drying at 70 °C. This applies to the reported physical PNIPAM networks; calcium-crosslinked PNIPAM/alginate composites did not completely dissolve, and permanently crosslinked hydrogels require separate assessment.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: A study of prepared PNIPAM hydrogel surfaces found no cytotoxic or genotoxic effects in its tested 3T3-L1, HEK293 and A549 cell assays. This is evidence for those hydrogel surfaces and exposure conditions; it does not establish the safety of soluble polymer, unreacted NIPAM, injected particles or an implanted device.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Hydrogel measurements apply to defined crosslinker and hydration conditions.

synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Radical addition forms the linear PNIPAM chain. An initiating radical adds to a monomer carbon–carbon double bond, creating a new carbon-centered radical that adds further monomer. Combination or disproportionation removes active radical ends; chain transfer ends one growing segment and can start another.

sections.overview: Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) is a cationic polymer formed from diallyldimethylammonium chloride monomer. Its permanently charged ammonium groups make it a polyelectrolyte rather than an uncharged vinyl polymer.
sections.history: PDADMAC belongs to the water-soluble polycations developed through diallyl-monomer polymerization. George B. Butler’s patent for Peninsular ChemResearch, filed in 1962 and granted in 1966, documents high-molecular-weight diallyldimethylammonium chloride polymers and their preparation. The work described applications in water clarification, paper wet-strength improvement and textile treatment. Nalco subsequently advanced industrial preparation: Wood E. Hunter and Theodore P. Sieder’s 1979 patent addressed monomer purification and polymerization in salt-containing solutions. These records trace laboratory polymer development into water-treatment manufacturing; they document specific advances rather than establishing one universal invention date for all diallyl-ammonium polymers.
sections.nomenclature: PDADMAC and polyDADMAC are common names for poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride). The canonical name includes the chloride counterion and should not be shortened to a generic polyammonium label.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (polyDADMAC) is the chloride-salt cationic homopolymer obtained by free-radical cyclopolymerization of diallyldimethylammonium chloride (DADMAC) in water. DADMAC itself can be prepared from dimethylamine and allyl chloride under alkaline aqueous conditions. During chain growth, the two allyl functions give the characteristic cyclic quaternary-ammonium repeat structure rather than a simple pendant-diallyl vinyl polymer. Aqueous production examples use radical initiators such as persulfate, azo, or organic-peroxide systems under inert-gas control. Monomer purity, initiator concentration, reaction time and temperature, and added salts can change conversion, viscosity, and molecular mass; these are route controls rather than universal grade specifications. Copolymer and graft examples are outside the homopolymer boundary unless explicitly identified as polyDADMAC-containing materials.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PDADMAC is ordinarily handled as a water-soluble cationic polyelectrolyte, so a stand-alone bulk tensile value is not a useful family property. Mechanical response becomes meaningful for a dried film, a layer-by-layer coating, or an ionically complexed hydrogel/saloplastic, where counterion identity and concentration, water content and humidity, pH when the partner is weakly charged, charge stoichiometry, molecular mass, porosity, drying/annealing, temperature, and strain rate govern the ionic cross-link density and relaxation. In an open study of a PSS/PDADMA multilayer (a PDADMAC-containing polyelectrolyte complex film), the equilibrium shear modulus was 0.3 MPa in 1 M NaCl at room temperature; the same composition as a compact, water-rich complex at 37 °C was almost three orders of magnitude softer. This is a complex-film versus compact-complex comparison, not a value for dissolved or neat PDADMAC. A separate open study reports that cast PSS/PDDA complex films made from 2 g/L solutions at 2 M NaCl and dried after 60–70 °C pressing were tensile-tested as 0.5 cm × 4 cm × 2 mm specimens at 1 mm/s; it found PSS/PDDA about three times softer than a PAA/PAH complex and showed that water exposure, salt, and mixing ratio can markedly alter integrity. Its plotted tensile data do not provide a reliable tabulated endpoint for reuse here.
sections.processing:
Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDADMAC, also written PDADMA or PDDA) is normally handled in water rather than melt-shaped as a neat thermoplastic. Article-conversion routes include alternate adsorption with a polyanion to build layer-by-layer coatings and capsules, solution mixing followed by casting or pressing a wet polyelectrolyte complex, and salt-plasticized consolidation into bulk complex articles. Concentration, charge stoichiometry, pH, ionic strength, mixing order and time, substrate preparation, rinse steps, retained water, drying, and applied pressure control deposition, complex mobility, thickness, porosity, and dimensional stability. These routes make PDADMAC-containing complexes or multilayers; their windows must not be presented as neat-PDADMAC melt-processing data.

Two bounded examples show the practical range. Porcel and Schlenoff mixed 20 mL portions of 0.5 M repeat-unit PSS and PDADMAC solutions in 2.5 M NaCl, then centrifuged the precipitated complex at 188,000g for 4 h at 25 °C to form a transparent compact article; they found that more than about 2 M NaCl at room temperature was needed to reshape that PSS/PDADMAC system efficiently, followed by salt exchange to restore ionic cross-links. In a distinct casting study, Gai and co-workers mixed 2 g/L PSS and PDDA solutions containing 2 M NaCl, collected the wet complex, pressed it against a patterned PDMS mold while heating to 60-70 °C, and then dried before mold release. The salt levels, centrifugal field, heat, and pressure belong to those paired-polyelectrolyte experiments.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDADMAC) is a water-soluble cationic polymer formed from a diallyl quaternary-ammonium monomer. Its charged backbone and chloride counterions make it a polyelectrolyte whose conformation changes with ionic strength and interactions with oppositely charged species.
sections.properties: PDADMAC provides strong cationic charge, water compatibility, flocculation, charge neutralization, and film-forming or complex-forming behavior. Solution viscosity and association depend on molecular mass, concentration, counterion, salt, pH, and the presence of anionic polymers or particles.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PDADMAC supplies cationic coagulation chemistry for water and wastewater treatment. Research applications include functional coatings for sensor substrates and particle surfaces.

Purchasing. Industrial water-treatment suppliers such as SNF offer polyDADMAC coagulants. Sigma-Aldrich 409014 provides a research example as 20 wt% aqueous solution in 25 mL, 1 L and 4 L packs; active-polymer concentration must be specified.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked catalog spans tens of milliliters to liters of solution. No reliable separate annual PDADMAC purchased or consumed mass was found; supplier-wide water-soluble-polymer capacity is not PDADMAC tonnage.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: PolyDADMAC is resistant to ordinary hydrolytic and biological degradation. Ozonation can release small nitrogen-containing products, including N-nitrosodimethylamine; this treatment pathway is distinct from natural biodegradation.

Timescales: The Canadian assessment reports failed ready/inherent biodegradability tests, not a measured universal half-life.

Environmental persistence: For the assessed polyDADMAC polymers, the authority expects stability in water, soil and sediment and strong binding to negatively charged particles. Settling into sludge or sediment is removal from water, not mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Use as a flocculant transfers polymer into separated solids. The assessment does not establish recovery of intact polymer or closed-loop monomer recycling from this dilute, contaminated waste stream.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Canada’s August 2020 assessment included PDADMAC homopolymer and concluded low human-health risk for the assessed uses. Its ecological conclusion assumed significant treatment overdosing was avoided: free cationic polymer can affect aquatic organisms, while binding to anionic solids lowers availability. This is a use- and exposure-based assessment, not permission for uncontrolled discharge.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Ionic strength can screen charge and sharply change conformation, viscosity, adsorption, and complexation. Molecular mass, branching or microstructure, residual monomer, counterion, pH, and blend ratio must be retained; a PDADMAC–polyanion complex is not the same material as the neat polymer.

sections.overview: Polyethyleneimine is an amine-rich polymer typically made by aziridine polymerization and available in branched or linear architectures. Its high density of amine functionality gives it polyelectrolyte and reactive-formulation behavior.
sections.history: Polyethyleneimine developed as an industrial polyamine and later became a major research tool for nonviral gene delivery. BASF’s branched Lupasol materials illustrate established roles in adhesion promotion, lamination inks and improving dye acceptance. A distinct biomedical development line followed Boussif and colleagues’ 1995 DNA-complexation work. Thomas Kissel, Dagmar Fischer, Hans-Peter Elsässer and Thorsten Bieber subsequently developed lower-molecular-weight PEI for gene-transfer studies; their patent family claims priority from 1997 and was granted in Europe in 2006. This progression connects surface-binding chemistry with nucleic-acid delivery research, without assigning the gene-delivery date to PEI’s original synthesis or implying clinical adoption of every formulation.
sections.nomenclature: PEI abbreviates polyethyleneimine, also written poly(ethylene imine). This abbreviation is ambiguous with polyetherimide; branched and linear PEI are structural variants, not automatically the same material form.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyethyleneimine (PEI) exists in branched and linear architectures that arise from different routes. Acid-catalyzed cationic ring-opening polymerization of aziridine (ethyleneimine), often in water, gives a branched polymer because secondary amines in growing chains can also open monomer rings; monomer feed, acid, water, and temperature affect branching and molar mass. Linear PEI is commonly made indirectly: a 2-alkyl-2-oxazoline is polymerized cationically to a linear poly(2-oxazoline), then its amide side chains are hydrolyzed under acidic conditions without cleaving the C–N backbone. One cited patent gives aqueous HCl-catalyzed aziridine polymerization, while a distinct patent demonstrates hydrolysis of poly(2-phenyl-2-oxazoline) and poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) to linear PEI followed by neutralization and purification. Architecture must therefore be reported; branched and linear PEI are not interchangeable grades of one route.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyethyleneimine (PEI) is a highly amine-functional family whose mechanics depend first on architecture (branched versus linear), molecular mass, protonation/pH and water content, and then on whether it is a neat film, an ionically associated layer, a blend, or a covalently crosslinked hydrogel. Water and ionic state can plasticize or swell the amine-rich material, whereas crosslinking and reinforcing polysaccharide/mineral phases can greatly raise stiffness at the cost of extension. No useful open standalone neat-PEI tensile endpoint was found in this focused pass. As a bounded neighboring-formulation example, a 30 wt% PEI/PEG-diglycidyl-ether gel study reports Young modulus, break stress, and break strain as functions of amine:epoxy feed ratio and solvent; these are swollen covalent-network values, not linear or branched PEI resin values. Independent linear-PEI/starch and DDGS film data likewise show that even 3–10% PEI changes modulus, strength, and elongation in a matrix-dependent manner, so composite-film numbers cannot stand in for PEI itself.
sections.processing:
Polyethyleneimine is generally article-converted from aqueous or water-compatible solvent solutions as a thin coating, primer, adhesion-promoting layer, or component of a cast formulation rather than by ordinary thermoplastic melt shaping. Directly documented application operations include roll and reverse-gravure coating, spray coating, slot coating, meniscus coating, immersion or dip coating, and placement of an in-line coating before, between, or after film-drawing stages but before final heat setting. Solution concentration, molecular architecture and molar mass, pH, cosolvent and wetting aids, substrate cleaning or corona treatment, withdrawal or web speed, coating weight, and evaporation before stretching or winding govern coverage, adhesion, and defects. If polyethyleneimine is crosslinked into a network, the network-forming chemistry belongs in Synthesis; the coating, drying, drawing, and cure or heat-set schedule belong in Processing.

Rice and Rudd's patent provides a bounded in-line film example for commercial MICA A 131X polyethyleneimine: a Hostaphan 2400 polyester film was interdraw-coated by reverse gravure from a 1 wt% aqueous solution after a 2.5 kW/ft²/min corona treatment; the coated web was dried at about 80–100 °C, transversely drawn about 3.9:1, and heat-set at a maximum of about 230 °C. The patent's broader 0.1–25 wt% aqueous range and preferred 0.2–6 wt% range belong to that disclosed primer system. In a distinct dip-coating experiment, Gorejová and co-workers diluted branched polyethyleneimine of 60–100 kDa, supplied as 50% in water, to 5 wt% in 96 vol% ethanol; cleaned iron pellets were immersed for 90 min and dried at 37 °C for 12 h. These are substrate-, solution-, and equipment-specific examples rather than universal polyethyleneimine coating schedules.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyethyleneimine is a polyamine family with primary, secondary, and tertiary amine groups in branched or linear chain architectures. Protonation and hydrogen bonding make its conformation, charge density, and association strongly dependent on pH, counterion, and solvent.
sections.properties: PEI is strongly hydrophilic and cationic when protonated, with useful chelation, adsorption, charge-neutralization, and film-forming behavior. Molecular architecture and protonation control solubility, viscosity, adhesion, and interaction with anionic polymers or surfaces.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Branched PEI promotes adhesion between plastic films and polar substrates such as paper and serves in lamination inks. Research PEI also acts as a nonviral nucleic-acid delivery reagent.

Purchasing. BASF Lupasol supplies industrial branched-PEI grades. Sigma-Aldrich 408727 is a viscous research liquid with nominal Mw about 25,000, sold in 100 mL, 250 mL and 1 L packs. Specify branching, molecular size and concentration.

Scale and evidence limits. The research listing establishes order 10^-1–10^0-liter packages. No reliable separate annual PEI purchased or consumed tonnage was found; formulations and modified PEIs cannot be counted as identical neat polymer.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Supported PEI adsorbents can lose functionality by thermal and oxygen-induced degradation. The cited study quantifies deactivation rather than completely identifying the resulting molecular products.

Timescales: Deactivation was measured at 50–80 °C under nitrogen and air. These adsorbent-aging experiments provide no soil or water mineralization time.

Environmental persistence: Loss of carbon-dioxide capture capacity is not disappearance of the polymer or proof of biodegradability.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: PEI-containing carbon-dioxide sorbents can be regenerated by heating to desorb captured gas. Oxidative and thermal deactivation gradually reduce performance, so service regeneration and eventual polymer recovery are different questions. The cited study examines PEI adsorbent deactivation; it does not demonstrate depolymerization or recycling of mixed PEI waste.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PEI’s high cationic charge can disrupt cell membranes; cytotoxicity depends on molecular weight, branching, concentration and formulation. Biomedical work therefore modifies PEI or incorporates degradable and shielding components to balance delivery efficiency with tolerance. Favorable results for a selected carrier do not establish safety of unmodified bulk PEI at other doses or exposure routes.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PEI can be corrosive or cytotoxic in some formulations and is highly sensitive to pH, salt, concentration, molecular mass, and branching. Adsorption and complexation can be irreversible or difficult to reproduce; data from a crosslinked or low-molecular-mass grade do not define the family.

sections.overview: Poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) is the sodium-sulfonate polymer obtained by radical polymerization of sodium p-styrenesulfonate in water. Its charged repeat units make it a polyelectrolyte precursor for aqueous complexes, membranes, and networks.
sections.history: Sodium polystyrenesulfonate was among the water-soluble polymers explored during the expansion of industrial emulsion polymerization. John W. Vanderhoff and Ralph M. Wiley’s Dow Chemical patent, filed in 1959 and issued in 1966, includes its preparation as a water-in-oil latex. This records an early manufacturing route rather than establishing the polymer’s first synthesis. Later applications included aqueous pigment dispersion, textile finishing, antistatic treatment and water treatment. Shinji Ozoe, Kenichi Yamanoi and Hideaki Matsunaga at Tosoh Organic Chemical addressed monomer purity in a patent with 2012 priority, granted in 2016. Controlling iron and isomer impurities improved polymer color, an important consideration for adhesives and finishing products.
sections.nomenclature: PNaSS is the explicit abbreviation for the sodium 4-styrenesulfonate polymer; PSS is used in this record in that salt-qualified context. A PSS/PEI membrane or a crosslinked PNaSS hydrogel contains additional polymers or network chemistry and is not an alternate name for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) (PNaSS or PSSNa) is the anionic vinyl-addition polymer of sodium 4-styrenesulfonate. It can be prepared directly by aqueous or mixed-solvent radical polymerization of NaSS, including conventional persulfate/azo initiation or controlled radical (for example RAFT) routes when molar mass and end groups are deliberately targeted. A patent example feeds aqueous sodium p-styrenesulfonate with ammonium persulfate under nitrogen and describes initiator options; its purity/color-control steps are specific to that manufacturing route. Plasma initiation is a distinct supported-network route: a DBD study polymerizes NaSS inside filter paper with a difunctional crosslinker, giving a network rather than linear PNaSS. Sulfonation of preformed polystyrene can also furnish polystyrenesulfonate chemistry, but it is not interchangeable with direct NaSS homopolymerization, and crosslinked/grafted materials should not be described as unmodified linear PNaSS.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) (PSS) is a strong, water-soluble polyanion, so a dry or hydrated solid response is normally that of a cross-linked homopolymer, a polyelectrolyte complex, or a composite rather than an intrinsic value for the dissolved polymer. Ionic pairing with the oppositely charged component, counterion and salt concentration, molecular mass, pH where a weak partner is present, water content/swelling, cross-link density, casting/coagulation route, porosity, temperature, and loading rate therefore control stiffness, strength, creep, and fracture. In an explicitly bounded homopolymer example, an SS gel radical-polymerized in water at 70 °C with 2 mol% divinylbenzene sulfonate (total monomer/cross-linker ratio 50:1) was too soft and fragile for a reported compression-fracture strain and had an initial compression modulus below 1 kPa after water swelling; this is not a value for commercial PSS powder, solution, film, or a polyelectrolyte complex. In a separate PSS/PEI membrane route, changing the PSS:PEI ratio, PEI molecular mass, acetate-bath pH and concentration, and glutaraldehyde cross-linker determined whether cast films were brittle/cracked or mechanically stable, illustrating why those variables must accompany any membrane datum.
sections.processing:
Poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) (PSSNa) is water soluble, so it is most often converted from aqueous solution as a coating, cast film, hydrogel component, or membrane phase rather than melt molded as a durable neat article. Water-insoluble articles usually immobilize PSS chains by blending, polyelectrolyte complexation, or network formation. The chemistry that establishes ionic or covalent junctions belongs in Synthesis; Processing comprises solution preparation and mixing order, deaeration, coating or casting gap, substrate wetting, bath composition and temperature, immediate coagulation, washing, drying, and thickness control. Polymer concentration, counterion and salt level, pH, partner-polymer ratio, and shear history govern dope homogeneity, precipitation rate, porosity, brittleness, and dimensional stability.

Durmaz and co-workers demonstrate the general aqueous-phase-separation route by mixing PSSNa with poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) at high salinity and precipitating the polyelectrolyte complex in a lower-salinity coagulation bath; varying the PSS-to-polycation ratio from 1:0.8 to 1:1.2 altered membrane morphology, charge, and mechanical stability. Baig and co-workers provide a separate bounded casting example with PSSNa of about 1000 kDa and branched polyethyleneimine (PEI). They mixed 25 wt% aqueous PSS and PEI solutions at a 1:2 monomer ratio until homogeneous, cast the 25 wt% dope on glass with a 0.5 mm gap, and immediately immersed it in acetate buffer. At pH 4, 0.1–0.3 M baths produced brittle or cracked membranes, whereas 0.4–0.5 M baths produced mechanically stable membranes; at 0.5 M, pH 4.5–5 membranes were too brittle for further processing. Some trials placed 0.01 wt% glutaraldehyde in the bath. These concentrations and outcomes describe that PSS/PEI system, not neat PSSNa or other partner polymers.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PSSNa is an anionic polyelectrolyte with sodium sulfonate groups on a polystyrene backbone.
sections.properties: Hydration, ion exchange, and complexation control its swelling and transport behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Soluble sodium PSS supplies polyelectrolyte coatings and materials research, including coated graphitic particles and mixed electrode films. Crosslinked ion-exchange resins and PEDOT:PSS formulations are distinct products.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich 243051 offers powder/solid sodium PSS of nominal Mw about 70,000 in 5 g, 100 g and 500 g packs. Specify molecular size, salt form and soluble versus crosslinked structure.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked supply spans order 10^0–10^2 grams. No reliable separate annual soluble sodium PSS purchase or consumption statistic was found; broader sulfonated-polystyrene categories cannot be assigned entirely to this material.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Fenton oxidation cleaves PSS backbone C–C bonds and disrupts aromatic rings. Detected low-molar-mass products include organic sulfonic acids and hydrogen sulfite; the product mixture is not solely styrene sulfonate monomer.

Timescales: The cited experiments use iron/peroxide at room temperature. Lower molar mass is the measured endpoint, so no environmental half-life or complete mineralization time is assigned.

Environmental persistence: Water solubility and oxidative chain shortening do not establish complete biological mineralization; ambient persistence remains unquantified here.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Fenton chemistry is a laboratory oxidative-treatment route for aqueous PSS. It produces mixed fragments rather than demonstrating recovery of equivalent polymer or a purified monomer for closed-loop recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For the linear sodium polystyrenesulfonate reagent of average molecular weight 70,000, the supplier recommends avoiding airborne dust, skin and eye contact, and release into drains. Heating can yield sulfur and sodium oxides as well as carbon oxides. This research reagent is distinct from crosslinked medicinal ion-exchange resins.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Double-network and PEI-complex data concern specified multicomponent systems.
