sections.overview: Perfluorosulfonic acid ionomers are fluorocarbon ionomer families bearing sulfonic-acid functionality. Their hydrophobic fluoropolymer backbone and ionic groups enable ion-exchange membrane behavior.
sections.history: The PFSA ionomer family grew from DuPont’s fluoropolymer and ion-exchange research during the 1960s, associated particularly with Walther Grot and the Nafion product line. Chemours’ company history connects that development with chlorine production and fuel-cell membranes. Further work tuned membrane selectivity: Grot’s DuPont patent, filed in 1971 and granted in 1974, modified one surface of a sulfonyl-containing fluoropolymer film to a sulfonamide form. Such chemical differentiation addressed the competing demands of ion transport and selectivity. Chlor-alkali electrolysis remained a major industrial application, with later Nafion products marketed by Chemours. These milestones describe the Nafion development lineage within PFSA, whose members include differing side-chain structures and membrane formulations.
sections.nomenclature: PFSA abbreviates perfluorosulfonic acid. Here it labels the ionomer family, not a single fixed polymer; specific commercial ionomers are narrower material families rather than aliases for all PFSAs.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Perfluorosulfonic acid ionomers are perfluorinated ion-exchange copolymers, usually prepared first in a sulfonyl-fluoride precursor form. The characteristic route copolymerizes tetrafluoroethylene with a perfluorovinyl ether bearing a sulfonyl fluoride side-chain precursor; hydrolysis converts those pendant groups to sulfonate or sulfonic-acid functionality, and a subsequent ion-exchange step selects the counterion where needed. Side-chain length and ether content vary across the family, so monomer identity must be recorded rather than inferred from the family name alone. A documented aqueous-emulsion route charges water, emulsifier, sulfonyl-fluoride vinyl ether comonomers, tetrafluoroethylene, and a perfluorodiacyl peroxide initiator. This is a source-specific preparation example, not a fixed ionomer equivalent weight or membrane fabrication procedure.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PFSA ionomers are commonly used as thin, oriented membrane films rather than as a dry bulk resin; their tensile and creep response is therefore governed by membrane construction as well as polymer chemistry. Water uptake plasticizes and swells the ionic morphology, while temperature, relative humidity, counter-ion, equivalent weight/side-chain architecture, membrane thickness or reinforcement, strain rate, and machine versus transverse direction alter modulus, strength, relaxation, and rupture. In one Chemours product document, Nafion™ N115 film at 23 °C and 50% RH had ASTM D882 strength of 31 MPa in the machine direction and 27 MPa transverse, whereas N117 was 36 and 33 MPa, respectively; these are supplier-reported values for those defined commercial membranes, not a dry-resin or all-PFSA strength range. Open membrane experiments likewise show that hydration and membrane grade change the tensile curve and swelling response, so a number taken from a hydrated, oriented film should not be transferred to a dry PFSA resin, solution, reinforced membrane, or another ionomer grade.
sections.processing: Perfluorosulfonic acid (PFSA) ionomers are commonly converted from aqueous or alcohol-based dispersions into dense or reinforced membranes, thin coatings, and catalyst-layer binders by casting or coating, solvent evaporation, and thermal or hydrothermal conditioning. The usable window depends strongly on equivalent weight, side-chain architecture, dispersion solids, reinforcement, and membrane thickness; drying too quickly can leave voids or residual solvent, while hydration and swelling must be controlled before assembly. Ordinary melt-processing guidance should not be generalized across PFSA acid forms, dispersions, and membrane grades. In one bounded Nafion dispersion example, a 20 wt% Chemours D2021 dispersion was cast from 5.2 g in a glass Petri dish, evaporated at 60 °C for 6 h in a vacuum oven, then separated in water; the recast membrane was additionally annealed at 120 °C for 3 h. A CeO2-filled variant used 7 mg CeO2 per 5.2 g dispersion, ultrasonication at 70 °C for 30 min followed by stirring, and the same casting/annealing route. A separate Nafion 117 study (EW 1100 g eq−1, 180 μm) used DMSO-assisted annealing at 140 °C followed by long hydrothermal conditioning in water, illustrating that annealing schedules are formulation- and performance-target-specific rather than family-wide settings. Copolymerization, sulfonyl-fluoride hydrolysis, and ion exchange that manufacture the ionomer belong in Synthesis; this section covers membrane/coating conversion and post-casting conditioning.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PFSAs combine a fluoropolymer backbone with sulfonic-acid side groups that form hydrated ionic domains.
sections.properties: Membrane transport and mechanics depend on equivalent weight, hydration, morphology, additives, and annealing.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PFSA ionomers serve fuel cells, hydrogen-generating electrolyzers, energy-storage cells and other electrochemical equipment. The supplier tables distinguish membrane grades and uses rather than treating all ion-exchange membranes alike.

Purchasing. Chemours supplies Nafion sulfonic membranes in solution-cast and extrusion-cast grades, alongside dispersions and resin products. Specify ionomer chemistry, thickness, reinforcement and product form through technical sales; carboxylic chlor-alkali membranes are a separate portfolio category.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked catalogs do not disclose annual PFSA purchase tonnage or dry-ionomer end-use shares. Membrane area and dispersion mass cannot be converted into polymer demand without thickness, density and solids content.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In Nafion, side-chain cleavage can release fluorinated sulfonate fragments; extensive defluorination requires more severe treatment of the fluorocarbon backbone. Phosphate-assisted mechanochemistry yields recoverable inorganic fluoride.

Timescales: The cited work uses ball milling at room temperature and 30 Hz, with reaction progress followed over hours. Milling without an activator left the membrane largely intact. These are reactor times.

Environmental persistence: No environmental half-life is established. Polymer fragmentation and release of fluorinated products must not be called complete mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Phosphate-assisted milling demonstrates fluoride recovery in a laboratory process. Membrane reuse/redispersion and destructive recovery of fluorine are different aims; this study does not establish commercial throughput for mixed membrane-electrode wastes.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: For reinforced Nafion N-324 PFSA membrane, the supplier lists skin and eye irritation and advises ventilation and avoidance of dust. Thermal decomposition can release hydrogen fluoride and sulfur oxides. These are membrane-product handling hazards; flammable alcohol hazards in some ionomer dispersions belong to those solvent formulations and should be assessed separately.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Nafion brochures and hydrated-membrane studies concern named membranes and conditions, not all PFSAs.

sections.overview: Sulfonated poly(ether ether ketone) is PEEK chemically modified with sulfonic-acid groups. The ionic functionality gives SPEEK ion-exchange and membrane behavior that is distinct from unmodified PEEK.
sections.history: SPEEK developed as a functional derivative of PEEK for membrane applications. Martin James Peer’s PCI Membrane Systems patent application, published in 1989 with 1988 priority, describes blends of SPEEK with compatible polymers to make hydrophilic membranes for reverse osmosis, ultrafiltration and microfiltration. It also acknowledges earlier SPEEK membrane work, so the filing is an application-development milestone rather than a first synthesis claim. Later researchers investigated SPEEK as an aromatic alternative to perfluorinated proton-exchange membranes for fuel cells. Madhusmita Tripathy, P. B. Sunil Kumar and Abhijit P. Deshpande’s 2017 study at IIT Madras used molecular simulation to examine hydration, water-domain connectivity and transport, illustrating the shift from membrane fabrication toward understanding its conducting pathways.
sections.nomenclature: SPEEK abbreviates sulfonated poly(ether ether ketone). The name identifies a substitution-variable modified-PEEK family, not a single degree of sulfonation or a generic sulfonated aromatic polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Sulfonated poly(ether ether ketone) (SPEEK) is most commonly prepared by post-polymerization electrophilic sulfonation of PEEK rather than by constructing a new backbone from sulfonated monomers. Commercial PEEK powder or pellets are dried and dissolved or swollen in concentrated sulfuric acid; the acid is both reaction medium and sulfonating reagent, introducing sulfonic-acid groups mainly on the hydroquinone-derived aromatic rings of the PEEK repeat unit. Reaction time, temperature, acid strength, particle size, and mixing control the degree and distribution of sulfonation. The reaction mixture is then poured into water or ice water to precipitate the polymer and quench further sulfonation. Repeated washing, filtration, and sometimes dialysis remove sulfuric acid until the wash is near neutral, after which SPEEK is dried. One open study varies sulfonation temperature and time, then precipitates, washes, and dries the product before determining ion-exchange capacity; a distinct open study uses separate 40 and 50 °C sulfuric-acid reactions followed by ice-water precipitation, neutral washing, and drying. Excessive sulfonation can make the product water-soluble or mechanically unstable, so workup and target substitution are integral route controls. Alternative direct copolymerization of sulfonated and unsulfonated activated aromatic monomers exists, but post-sulfonation of preformed PEEK is the defining widely documented route. Counter-ion exchange, covalent crosslinking, blending, and membrane casting are subsequent modification or processing choices.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SPEEK membrane mechanics reflect a competition between the stiff aromatic PEEK backbone and hydrophilic sulfonate domains. Degree of sulfonation, acid/counter-ion state, hydration and swelling, casting solvent and solids content, dry-film thickness, drying conditions, crosslinking or inorganic additives, temperature, and tensile-test conditioning can therefore change modulus, yield, ductility, and dimensional stability. An open preparation study found that higher sulfonation temperature increased ion-exchange capacity, water uptake, and swelling, while membranes made above 70 °C were over-sulfonated and deteriorated or dissolved in water; casting conditions also influenced the formed membranes. As one tightly bounded example, solution-cast SPEEK films from a biomedical study made after 1.5 h sulfonation at 40 °C (SA-01, degree of sulfonation 61.6%) had Young’s modulus 88.1 ± 0.87 MPa, yield stress 20.73 ± 0.09 MPa, and 77% elongation, whereas its 50 °C counterpart (SA-02, 98.9% sulfonation) had 32.9 ± 1.21 MPa, 4.9 ± 0.1 MPa, and 17.44%, respectively. These are dry cast-membrane results for two explicitly prepared compositions, not values for hydrated, crosslinked, reinforced, or fuel-cell SPEEK membranes generally.
sections.processing:
Preformed sulfonated poly(ether ether ketone) is commonly converted into membranes and coatings by solution processing rather than by applying an unqualified PEEK melt-processing window. The polymer is dissolved in a compatible polar solvent, optionally blended with a drug, filler, second polymer, or crosslinking component, and then poured, blade-coated, or otherwise cast on a controlled substrate before staged ambient, heated, or vacuum drying. Degree of sulfonation and counter-ion state govern solvent and water solubility, while polymer concentration and solution viscosity govern wet-film leveling and dry thickness. Mixing completeness, filtration or deaeration where used, blade gap, substrate wetting, temperature, humidity, solvent-evaporation rate, residual solvent, and final hydration/conditioning all affect uniformity, swelling, mechanical integrity, and transport. Thick wet layers can pool, an overly dilute dope can yield fragile films, and highly sulfonated material may become water-soluble or unstable. Post-polymerization sulfonation, precipitation, and neutralization belong in Synthesis; dissolving the isolated SPEEK, casting or coating, drying, peeling, and conditioning the article belong here.

Yee, Zhang, and Ladewig doctor-blade-cast SPEEK/DMAc solutions on glass and found, for their method, that 15–25 wt% SPEEK produced even, flexible membranes and dry films around 30–50 µm were easiest to handle. They noted that ambient-pressure spreading made the dry film much thinner than the nominal wet gap, higher humidity lengthened solvent removal, and 50–60 °C drying gave reasonable morphology without excessive drying time. Those observations apply to their prepared SPEEK series and casting setup. In a distinct bounded example, Padinjarathil and co-workers dissolved 100 mg portions of their SA-01 or SA-02 SPEEK in 10–15 mL DMF, poured the solutions into 2 inch Petri plates, dried them at room temperature for one day, and then vacuum-dried at 60 °C for 4–6 h. Their resulting films were approximately 60–70 µm thick; drug-loaded versions used a 1:10 drug/polymer mass ratio and about 8 h reduced-pressure drying at 60 °C. These conditions are specific to the reported sulfonation states and formulations, not a universal SPEEK membrane schedule.
sections.structureAndMorphology: SPEEK is PEEK bearing sulfonic-acid groups that create ionic domains in hydrated membranes.
sections.properties: Transport, swelling, and mechanics depend on sulfonation degree, hydration, and processing.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. SPEEK is supplied as a proton-conducting material for membrane development, including fuel-cell and hydrogen-related research. A research catalog listing does not establish broad commercial adoption in these industries.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich lists product 941875 as powder, chunks or fibers with a specified degree of sulfonation. Select molecular weight and sulfonation level and confirm available quantities with the supplier; the checked public page does not expose a reliable pack-size table.

Scale and evidence limits. No annual SPEEK purchase tonnage or end-use mass split is disclosed. General PEEK and fuel-cell market figures have different scopes and cannot be used as SPEEK demand.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: SPEEK can lose sulfonic groups during heating and undergo backbone damage under oxidative attack. Higher sulfonation changes water uptake and chemical durability.

Timescales: The source compares Fenton-test damage across sulfonation degrees; those accelerated oxidizing conditions do not supply an environmental lifetime.

Environmental persistence: No natural-environment mineralization time is established, and dissolution or loss of a membrane does not prove complete biodegradation.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: A study sulfonated recovered PEEK granules to make an adsorbent-coating binder. This valorizes a PEEK feedstock into SPEEK; it does not demonstrate closed-loop recovery of used SPEEK membranes.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Biomedical surface-sulfonated PEEK studies emphasize removing residual sulfuric acid after treatment; incomplete removal can impair cellular responses. Sulfonation level, post-treatment and added antibacterial components change the interface. This evidence concerns modified PEEK implant surfaces and does not establish the biological suitability of bulk SPEEK fuel-cell membranes.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Preparation conditions and degree of sulfonation must be specified.

sections.overview: Poly(2-oxazoline)s are the POx family of pseudo-polypeptide-like polymers made from 2-substituted 2-oxazoline monomers by living or quasi-living cationic ring-opening polymerization. Monomer substituents tune side-chain chemistry and solution behavior across family members.
sections.history: Poly(2-oxazoline) synthesis emerged from independent ring-opening-polymerization studies in 1966–1967. The early groups included D. A. Tomalia and D. P. Sheetz; W. Seeliger and colleagues; T. Kagiya and colleagues; and T. G. Bassiri, A. Levy and M. Litt. Subsequent research varied the monomer side chains and refined controlled polymerization, creating a broad family with tunable thermal and solution behavior. Commercial and biomedical development followed different paths. Polymer Chemistry Innovations markets the poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) member as Aquazol for binding applications including ceramics, while academic researchers such as Richard Hoogenboom and collaborators have advanced systematic understanding of the family’s structures and properties and its potential in biomedical materials. Aquazol’s history applies to that particular member, rather than every poly(2-oxazoline).
sections.nomenclature: POx is the abbreviation used for the poly(2-oxazoline) family. It is a family boundary covering different 2-substituted monomers, architectures, and functional states; one homopolymer, block copolymer, or cationic derivative is not an alias for the entire family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(2-oxazoline)s (POx) are a family of pseudo-polypeptide-like polymers made from 2-substituted 2-oxazoline monomers by living or quasi-living cationic ring-opening polymerization (CROP). An electrophilic initiator, commonly an alkyl tosylate, triflate, or another alkylating agent, first produces an oxazolinium active center; sequential monomer attack opens the rings during propagation. Molecular mass and architecture can therefore be set by monomer-to-initiator ratio, monomer sequence, and deliberate termination with nucleophiles such as water, amines, or alcohols. Monomer substituents set the side-chain chemistry, so poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline), poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline), and block or gradient POx are members of the family rather than interchangeable materials. Adventitious nucleophiles can cause chain transfer or premature termination, making feed purity and functional-group compatibility route controls.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(2-oxazoline) (POx) is a broad side-chain-defined family, so no single modulus represents it. Published homopolymer work relates mechanical behavior to side-chain identity and length, glass transition, crystallinity, molar mass, and water uptake: for low-molar-mass poly(2-n-alkyl-2-oxazoline) films, increasing alkyl side-chain length from methyl to butyl lowers indentation modulus, while absorbed water plasticizes hygroscopic members such as PMeOx, PEtOx, and Pn-PrOx. The number of reports is limited because many low-molar-mass POx samples are brittle.

A bounded reference from the open review concerns low-molar-mass (degree of polymerization about 60) spin-coated homopolymer films measured by nanoindentation. Members with side chains longer than four carbons, tested above their respective glass transitions, gave moduli of about 0.8 GPa. This is an indentation result for a particular homopolymer subset and humidity/temperature state, not a tensile modulus or a general property of solution-phase, hydrogel, block-copolymer, or cross-linked POx materials.
sections.processing:
Poly(2-oxazoline)s can be converted from solution by electrospinning, casting, and coating, while suitably softening members and copolymers can be melt-extruded into filament or compounded for hot-melt extrusion, injection molding, and compression of drug-delivery articles. Processability is strongly side-chain-, molar-mass-, and composition-dependent: aqueous or fluorinated-solvent concentration controls fiber formation, and melt routes require a temperature high enough for flow but short enough residence and modest enough shear to avoid chain scission or other degradation. Drying before melt processing, homogeneous drug or additive distribution, stable feeding, nozzle pressure, cooling, and the thermal history from repeated extrusion must therefore be qualified for the exact polymer and formulation.

Wałach and co-workers electrospun selected PiPrOx materials from water at 16-20 kV or from hexafluoroisopropanol at 10-14 kV, using a 12 cm gap, a 27-gauge needle, and formulation-dependent flow rates of 0.5-1.5 mL/h. For melt-fed printing they vacuum-dried material at 25 °C and 50 mbar, then extruded selected iPrOx/nPrOx copolymers at 155-160 °C and PiPrOx homopolymer at 205 °C with 5 bar feed pressure and a 160 rpm auger; prolonged processing increased dispersity and indicated degradation. Separately, Samaro and co-workers processed particular drug-loaded poly(2-alkyl-2-oxazoline) mixtures by twin-screw hot-melt extrusion at 100 rpm and formulation-specific 110-160 °C settings, followed by injection molding at formulation-specific 130-200 °C, 800 bar for 10 s and 400 bar for 5 s. These are bounded experiments on named polymers and blends, not family-wide windows.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(2-oxazolines) are side-chain-tunable polyamides made by cationic ring-opening polymerization.
sections.properties: Water uptake and thermal behavior vary strongly with side-chain identity and molecular weight.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. A commercially established family member, poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline), serves adhesives, paints, films/coatings and water-technology formulations. Its commercial uses should not be generalized to every poly(2-oxazoline) chemistry.

Purchasing. Polymer Chemistry Innovations supplies Aquazol as 100%-active granules in four viscosity grades, with higher-purity/narrower-distribution options by inquiry. Specify the side-chain chemistry and grade.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked producer page gives grade availability but no pack mass, annual output or purchased tonnage. No reliable separately quantified poly(2-oxazoline) market mass was found.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Acid hydrolysis removes acyl side groups from poly(2-oxazoline)s, producing polyethyleneimine-containing chains and the corresponding carboxylic-acid products. Deacylation is not cleavage of the entire carbon–nitrogen backbone.

Timescales: The reported controlled reactions use strong aqueous acid and temperature-dependent reaction periods. No family-wide environmental mineralization time follows.

Environmental persistence: Side-chain chemistry strongly affects hydrolysis, and persistence of the residual PEI-containing polymer is a separate question.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Controlled hydrolysis and subsequent functionalization provide laboratory routes to reuse polymer backbones as new functional materials. The paper does not demonstrate a post-consumer collection or closed-loop monomer-recovery system.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Poly(2-oxazoline) is not uniformly invisible to the immune system. The PEG-immunity review describes complement activation by particular poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline)-coated nanoparticles in human serum. Polymer substitution, architecture and carrier surface matter; results for one PMOXA coating should not be extended to every polyoxazoline or administration route.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Family reviews compare many side-chain chemistries, so no one POx result is universal.

sections.overview: Poly(vinylpyrrolidone) is a water-soluble polymer formed from N-vinylpyrrolidone. Molecular weight and crosslinking distinguish soluble PVP grades from insoluble crosslinked PVP materials.
sections.history: PVP’s industrial history is associated with Walter Reppe’s development of its manufacturing process at BASF around 1940. BASF’s 2015 account marked 75 years since that work and separately recorded production of the vinylpyrrolidone precursor at Ludwigshafen from 1939. The polymer became a versatile formulation ingredient: pharmaceutical tablet excipients were marketed under Kollidon, hair-styling products under Luviskol, and detergent ingredients under Sokalan. Later uses included water-treatment and dialysis membranes and specialty adhesives in the Luvitec range. BASF’s 2015 announcement of planned capacity additions in Germany, the United States and China illustrates continuing industrial investment. Brand ranges include different compositions and grades, so their application histories do not establish identical behavior for every PVP material.
sections.nomenclature: PVP abbreviates poly(vinylpyrrolidone), also called poly(N-vinylpyrrolidone). The names identify the same polymer backbone; crosslinked PVP is a material form rather than a distinct monomer name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP) is the linear addition polymer of N-vinylpyrrolidone (NVP). Aqueous free-radical solution polymerization commonly uses hydrogen peroxide, another hydroperoxide, persulfate, or a redox system; water-soluble alcohol regulators can suppress molar-mass buildup and permit higher-solids solutions. Base-catalyzed NVP polymerization is also documented. The choice of initiator, regulator, monomer concentration, and heat removal governs exotherm, conversion, and the molecular-mass range of the resulting soluble PVP. This linear PVP scope excludes crosslinked PVP (crospovidone), which is deliberately made with a difunctional crosslinker or in-situ crosslinking conditions and is a distinct network material.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP) is water-soluble and commonly used as a dried film or a hydrated, cross-linked/blended network; its mechanical response consequently depends on molecular mass, residual water and humidity, plasticizer, cross-link type and density, co-polymer or filler, irradiation/curing history, swelling medium, film thickness, and loading rate. In PVP-based hydrogel dressings, increasing cross-linker content raised tensile strength but reduced elongation, while cross-linker molecular mass and swelling medium also altered the response. As one bounded cast-film example, a 0.30 ± 0.03 mm PVP film cast from a 2% PVP gel containing glycerol had tensile strength 0.71 ± 0.11 MPa, Young’s modulus 0.825 ± 0.23 MPa, and break elongation 812 ± 25%; these values are triplicate measurements of that plasticized wound-dressing film, not dry neat PVP or a cross-linked hydrogel value.
sections.processing:
Poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP) is normally article-formed from water, alcohol, or another compatible solvent rather than by conventional thermoplastic molding. Important routes include solution coating and casting of soluble films, plasticized gel casting, electrospinning of fiber mats, and casting followed by radiation, photo, or chemical curing when an insoluble hydrogel or dressing is required. Powder is added under agitation until fully dissolved, then the solution is compounded with plasticizer or active ingredients, filtered and deaerated as needed, deposited into a mold or through a needle/coater, and dried under controlled temperature, airflow, humidity, or vacuum. Molecular mass and concentration determine entanglement and viscosity; solvent volatility, moisture uptake, mixing and bubble control, coat or mat thickness, drying rate, and cure dose or time govern beading, skinning, residual solvent, tack, and dimensional stability. Network chemistry belongs in Synthesis, while casting, electrospinning, drying, and the cure operation or equipment schedule belong here.

Pérez-Garibay and co-workers give a bounded cast-film recipe for 360 kDa PVP: 1.2 g PVP was dissolved in 42 mL ethanol, 16 mL water, and 0.3 g glycerol; the homogeneous gel was poured into a 46 cm² silicone mold, covered with perforated aluminum foil, and dried at room temperature to a 0.30 ± 0.03 mm film. Their later radiation and grafting steps are formulation chemistry, not a general PVP cure. In a distinct electrospinning study, Zahra and co-workers stirred 10 or 55 kDa PVP in ethanol for 1 h at room temperature and found bead-free operating points strongly dependent on molecular mass. Their optimized 10 kDa case used 80 wt% PVP, 0.5 mL/h, 20 kV, a 14 cm gap, and a 25 G needle; the 55 kDa case used 50 wt% at the same flow, voltage, gap, and needle. Lower concentrations produced particles or beads, so these unusually concentrated solutions are experiment-specific rather than general spinning guidance.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PVP is a water-soluble vinyl polymer that can be crosslinked into hydrogels.
sections.properties: Hydration and mechanics depend on molecular weight and crosslink density.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PVP supplies soluble pharmaceutical binders and formulation aids; applications also extend to cosmetics and toiletries. Materials researchers use it to stabilize or cap metal nanoparticles.

Purchasing. BASF’s soluble Kollidon povidone grades provide a pharmaceutical sourcing route. Sigma-Aldrich 856568 is nominal Mw 55,000 research powder in 100 g and 500 g packs. Copovidone and insoluble crospovidone are different materials.

Scale and evidence limits. The checked research packages are order 10^2 grams. No reliable separate annual soluble-PVP purchase or consumption figure was established; a supplier’s entire Kollidon portfolio is broader than this homopolymer.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hypochlorite aging of PVP-containing membranes generated succinimide functionality and carboxyl-containing products associated with opening of pyrrolidone rings, and could remove PVP from the membrane.

Timescales: Accelerated chemical-cleaning exposure is not an environmental half-life. No condition-qualified natural mineralization time is provided.

Environmental persistence: Leaching of water-soluble PVP or its fragments transfers material to water; it does not by itself establish biodegradation.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: PVP-containing healthcare formulations require disposal according to their drug, chemical or infectious contents. WHO guidance classifies these waste hazards separately from ordinary refuse. This concerns the complete formulation; it does not establish a process for recovering PVP.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Water-soluble PVP can elicit immune recognition in some parenteral contexts. The review discusses antibodies following intramuscular administration of high-molecular-weight PVP and supporting animal studies. These results concern molecular weight and administration route; they are not evidence of the same response to all oral, topical or technical PVP uses.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Hydrogel values require the stated crosslinker and water content.

sections.overview: Poly(ethylene oxide)-block-poly(propylene oxide)-block-poly(ethylene oxide) is an ABA triblock-copolymer family with hydrophilic PEO end blocks and a PPO center block. These materials can self-assemble and undergo temperature- and composition-dependent gelation in water.
sections.history: The PEO–PPO–PEO triblock family emerged from industrial work on nonionic surfactants in the early 1950s. Lester G. Lundsted’s Wyandotte Chemicals patent, filed in 1953 and granted in 1954, describes adding ethylene oxide to polypropylene-oxide chains to tune water affinity and surface activity. Detergent and related formulation uses were central to that development. Irving R. Schmolka later explored concentrated aqueous gels at BASF Wyandotte; his patent, filed in 1966 and granted in 1973, described applications including pharmaceutical and cosmetic preparations. The progression from surface-active blocks to gel-forming formulations became an important part of poloxamer development. These patent dates distinguish early block-copolymer manufacturing from later application inventions.
sections.nomenclature: PEO–PPO–PEO describes the block sequence. Poloxamer is the customary family name, but particular poloxamers such as Poloxamer 407 are narrower grade/composition members rather than synonyms for the whole family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ethylene oxide)-block-poly(propylene oxide)-block-poly(ethylene oxide) is a sequence-defined ABA polyether, often called a poloxamer, not a random EO/PO copolymer. A common preparation starts with a difunctional diol initiator such as propylene glycol, adds propylene oxide by ring-opening polymerization to form the central poly(propylene oxide) block, then adds ethylene oxide so each living chain end forms a terminal poly(ethylene oxide) block. Sequential monomer addition is the key architectural control; changing the order produces different block arrangements, while simultaneous EO/PO feeding gives random segments rather than the same triblock. Catalyst and initiator examples are source-specific and do not prescribe a single molecular weight or EO/PO ratio.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PEO–PPO–PEO triblocks (poloxamers/Pluronics) are usually assessed as aqueous, micelle-associated physical gels rather than as dry structural plastics. Their small-strain stiffness and yielding therefore depend on PEO/PPO block lengths and total molar mass, polymer concentration, temperature history relative to the sol–gel transition, solvent and additives, and any terminal functionalization or covalent crosslinking. An open study of 30% w/v Poloxamer 407 (PEO100–PPO65–PEO100) hydrogels at 37 °C found linear-viscoelastic storage moduli of approximately 20 kPa for non-sterile material, 19 kPa after steam heating, and 14 kPa after dry heating. Those oscillatory-shear values are for that concentrated aqueous grade and sterilization protocol, not a tensile modulus or a family-wide value. A separate open study identifies the variable PEO and PPO block sizes across the PEO–PPO–PEO family and describes the use of terminal methacrylation and photochemical crosslinking to create mechanically more stable hydrogel constructs; physical and chemically crosslinked materials should not be interchanged.
sections.processing:
PEO–PPO–PEO poloxamers are commonly article-converted as aqueous thermoreversible formulations: a cool, mobile solution can be mixed with an active or filler, pumped, injected, coated, cast, or extruded for bioprinting and then gels as temperature rises. Grade identity, PEO/PPO ratio, concentration, dissolved salts, drugs, and other polymers all shift viscosity and the sol–gel transition, so low-temperature dissolution and dispensing conditions must be qualified for the complete formulation. In one review example, 20 wt% Poloxamer 407 in water changed from a clear solution at 25 °C to a gel near 37 °C; this is a P407 formulation example, not a transition temperature for every PEO–PPO–PEO copolymer.

A second open study gives a practical preparation and terminal-sterilization comparison for a 30% w/v Poloxamer 407 formulation of average molecular mass 12.6 kDa. The polymer was dissolved in Milli-Q water by manual stirring at 4 °C and held at 4 °C for 24 h to complete dissolution. Separate samples then received steam heat at 121 °C for 20 min, dry heat at 160 °C for 1 h, gamma irradiation at 25 kGy, or electron-beam irradiation at 15 or 25 kGy. Steam heat and electron-beam samples retained the non-sterile formulation's reported 22 °C gelling temperature, whereas dry heat shifted it to 21 °C and gamma irradiation to 24 °C; dry heat promoted water loss/oxidation, and gamma treatment produced an acidic, cytotoxic formulation in that experiment. These results bound handling and sterilization choices for this 30% P407 hydrogel only.
sections.structureAndMorphology: This poloxamer family has a central poly(propylene oxide) block flanked by two poly(ethylene oxide) blocks. The amphiphilic block architecture enables concentration- and temperature-dependent micellization, association, and reversible gel formation in water.
sections.properties: Poloxamers are nonionic surfactant-like polymers with tunable hydrophilic/lipophilic balance, aqueous solubility, interfacial activity, and thermoresponsive rheology. Block lengths, concentration, additives, and temperature determine micelle size, viscosity, and gelation behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Poloxamer grades act as nonionic surfactants, solubilizers and gel formers in pharmaceutical and oral-care formulations. Research uses include cell culture and reducing nonspecific adhesion in microfluidic devices.

Purchasing. Kolliphor supplies pharmaceutical poloxamer grades. Research Pluronic F-127, also called poloxamer 407, is sold as Sigma-Aldrich P2443 powder in 250 g and 1 kg packs. Block composition and grade determine the appropriate purchase.

Scale and evidence limits. The documented research packages span order 10^2–10^3 grams. No reliable separate annual PEO-PPO-PEO triblock purchase or consumption total was found; all ethylene-oxide/propylene-oxide products are a broader category.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Poloxamer 407 can suffer sterilization-induced molecular changes; degradation must be distinguished from reversible gel dissolution on cooling or dilution. The source does not establish a complete degradation-product inventory.

Timescales: The cited work examines defined sterilization treatments and subsequent functional properties; no environmental half-life is assigned.

Environmental persistence: Disappearance of a poloxamer gel does not show mineralization of its PEO and PPO blocks. Environmental fate depends on block size and formulation.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Temperature-controlled precipitation is a laboratory recovery option for selected poloxamer-containing systems. Zhu and coworkers found that unmodified Pluronic F-127 at 100 mg/mL in toluene was soluble at room temperature and precipitated at 4 °C; the same response was not observed at 10 mg/mL. They then demonstrated recovery and reuse of a covalently attached enzyme–F-127 conjugate by cycling between 4 and 40 °C, retaining more than 95% of the measured enzyme activity after ten cycles. This is recovery of a functional conjugate through reversible phase behavior, rather than depolymerization or a general process for reclaiming poloxamers from dilute, mixed pharmaceutical waste. Polymer concentration, attached species and solvent determine whether this separation works.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Poloxamer behavior depends on block lengths, formulation and route. The review reports generally favorable results for several nanoparticle coatings but also discusses complement activation and possible hypersensitivity associated with PEO-containing carriers. A low-toxicity cell result for one poloxamer formulation does not establish equivalent tolerance for every Pluronic grade or injection.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Gelation and solution stability are sensitive to block ratio, molecular mass, concentration, temperature, salts, active ingredients, and sterilization history. A poloxamer hydrogel or drug formulation is not interchangeable with the unmodified triblock polymer, and dilution can eliminate the desired network.

sections.overview: Poly(amidoamine) dendrimers are the PAMAM family of discrete, generation-defined, highly branched macromolecules rather than conventional linear chain polymers. Divergent synthesis repeats methyl-acrylate Michael addition and ethylenediamine amidation from an amine-containing core.
sections.history: PAMAM dendrimers originated in Donald Tomalia’s Dow Chemical research program. Tomalia and Jean Fréchet’s historical account dates discovery of the acrylate-based divergent synthesis to 1979 and its development to 1979–1985, with contributors including Jim Dewald, George Kallos and Jesse Roeck. Public disclosure began at a 1983 Gordon Research Conference, followed by fuller publications in 1984–1985. Stepwise construction made molecular size, branching and terminal groups systematic design variables. Commercial Starburst materials subsequently supplied research into host–guest chemistry and drug solubilization. Dendritic Nanotechnologies and other suppliers helped disseminate these research reagents. Investigations of encapsulated anticancer and anti-inflammatory compounds illustrate later biomedical exploration; they should not be read as proof of clinical adoption of the entire PAMAM family.
sections.nomenclature: PAMAM is the abbreviation for the poly(amidoamine) dendrimer family. Generation and terminal-group state are part of the architecture boundary; a single generation, hybrid dendrimer, hydrogel network, or other composite is not an alias for the whole PAMAM family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(amidoamine) (PAMAM) is a family of discrete, generation-defined dendrimers, not a conventional linear chain-growth polymer. In the canonical divergent construction, an ammonia or ethylenediamine core bearing amines undergoes Michael addition with methyl acrylate to form an ester-terminated half generation. Aminolysis/amidation of those esters with excess ethylenediamine then gives an amine-terminated full generation, whose peripheral amines become the sites for the next cycle. Core choice, number of completed cycles, terminal-group conversion, and purification therefore define generation and architecture. A hybrid-dendrimer report separately describes the same repeated two-reaction, outward-growth logic with methyl acrylate and ethylenediamine in methanol. Its particular hybrid core and workup are route-specific; they do not redefine all PAMAM as the hybrid material. Incomplete Michael addition, retro-Michael reaction, cyclization, and amidation-associated dimerization are documented sources of defective branches, so the ideal generation label should not be treated as an automatic guarantee of a defect-free population.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PAMAM is a family of discrete, generation-defined dendrimers rather than a single bulk engineering polymer. Its measured deformation therefore depends on generation, terminal-group chemistry and protonation, concentration and solvent or ionic conditions, adsorption surface, and whether a single dendrimer, an aggregate, or a covalently connected gel is being tested. An open review describes greater protonation under acidic conditions as making surface-bound PAMAM less deformable and more prone to aggregation; it also reports compression-AFM/Hertz-model values of about 700 MPa for an individual generation-5 PAMAM dendrimer and about 150 MPa for adsorbed aggregates. These are nanoscale, surface-adsorbed compression measurements—not a tensile or bulk modulus for PAMAM material. In a separate in-situ-forming PAMAM hydrogel study, network properties were tunable through dendrimer functionality and aza-Michael network formation, reinforcing that a gel measurement must retain its network and aqueous-test context. No family-level, form-appropriate open tensile endpoint was identified in this focused search.
sections.processing:
PAMAM dendrimers are molecular building blocks and modifiers rather than conventional melt-processing resins. Article conversion therefore centers on aqueous casting or injection of dendrimer-engineered hydrogels, micro- and nanogels, thin coatings, membranes, and composite films. Generation and surface functionality control viscosity, charge, crosslink density, gel time, and compatibility. Mixing order, concentration, pH and ionic strength, stoichiometry, entrained air, substrate wetting, cure or gelation time, washing/dialysis, drying or lyophilization, and hydration must be defined for the chosen dendrimer and partner polymer.

Wang and co-workers provide a bounded in-situ-gelling example using generation-5 PAMAM or partially acetylated G5. They prepared 5, 10, or 20 wt% dendrimer solutions in water or pH 7.4 PBS at 25 °C and added PEG diacrylate 575 at an equal molar ratio of acrylate groups to remaining primary surface amines. At 20 wt%, unmodified G5 solidified in about 1 min and the G5-Ac64 formulation in about 4 min, while more highly acetylated analogues required roughly 146-158 min; lower concentration could remain liquid over the observation window. For thin layers they placed 2.5 microlitres per well and held the plate for 24 h. These gel times are specific to the G5 surface state, concentration, stoichiometry, temperature, and test definition.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PAMAMs are branched dendritic polyamidoamine macromolecules organized by discrete generation.
sections.properties: Size, surface charge, deformability, and uptake vary with generation and terminal groups.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PAMAM dendrimers supply research in chelation, DNA compaction, biofunctional assay surfaces, contrast-agent materials and templated silica particles. These examples establish research uses rather than broad clinical deployment of the family.

Purchasing. Specify generation, core and terminal groups. Sigma-Aldrich 412449, manufactured by Dendritech, is generation 4 with amino surface groups, supplied as 10 wt% solution in methanol in listed 2.5 g and 10 g packs.

Scale and evidence limits. The packs describe solution mass, corresponding nominally to 0.25 g and 1 g dendrimer by the stated mass fraction. No reliable separate annual PAMAM purchased or consumed tonnage was found.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In a deliberately crosslinked PAMAM microgel, remaining amines cleave ester-containing links by aminolysis, releasing smaller dendrimer-containing species. This does not show destruction of ordinary PAMAM dendrimers.

Timescales: The modified microgels were followed for up to 72 hours in pH 5.3 or 7.4 buffer at 37 °C; behavior was pH dependent.

Environmental persistence: Network breakup and formation of nanoscale fragments are not mineralization. No environmental lifetime is established for the dendrimer family.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Functional reuse is demonstrated for a generation-zero PAMAM–palladium catalyst attached to magnetic iron oxide: magnetic separation allowed six Suzuki or Heck reaction cycles, with less than 1% total palladium leaching reported. This recovers a dendrimer-containing catalytic composite for repeated service; it is not monomer recovery from free PAMAM or mixed pharmaceutical waste.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PAMAM dendrimer cytotoxicity depends strongly on generation, concentration and terminal groups. Cationic amine-terminated dendrimers can disrupt cell membranes; neutralization, PEGylation and other surface modifications can change this response. Results for one modified dendrimer are therefore insufficient to classify the entire family as biocompatible.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Generation and surface chemistry must be retained when interpreting reported results.

sections.overview: Polydimethylsiloxane is a silicone polymer with repeating dimethylsiloxane units. It is commonly formulated and crosslinked into soft elastomers and is widely used in coatings, seals, and microfabricated devices.
sections.history: PDMS belongs to the methyl-silicone industry that developed around improved organosilicon chemistry and electrical insulation. In his oral history, Eugene G. Rochow describes methyl-silicone experiments at General Electric in 1938 and the direct-synthesis breakthrough in 1940 that enabled industrial preparation of its precursors. These are broader silicone milestones rather than a single invention date for every PDMS form. Commercial development produced silicone oils and curable rubbers, while later manufacturing work improved precursor hydrolysis and by-product recovery. A new research role expanded during the 1990s: Younan Xia and George Whitesides’ 1998 review documents PDMS elastomers, including Dow Corning materials, as stamps and molds for soft lithography. This connected an established silicone platform to microfabrication and analytical-device research.
sections.nomenclature: PDMS abbreviates polydimethylsiloxane, also written poly(dimethylsiloxane). The name identifies the dimethyl-substituted silicone backbone and is distinct from vinyl-containing silicone rubbers and other polysiloxanes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is built from dimethylsiloxane units. Industrial feedstock preparation commonly hydrolyzes dimethyldichlorosilane to a mixture of cyclic and linear siloxane oligomers while releasing hydrogen chloride; water ratio, acidity, temperature, and residence time control the cyclic/linear and hydroxy/chloro end-group distribution. Purified cyclics such as octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane (D4) can then undergo acid- or base-catalyzed ring-opening/equilibration polymerization, with a chain stopper determining molar mass and terminal groups. One patent documents continuous dimethyldichlorosilane hydrolysis and condensation intermediates. An open study provides a distinct photoinitiated cationic D4 ring-opening route using an iodonium salt, with benzophenone or pyrene sensitization and photogenerated protonic/silylium species. These are linear-polymer routes; multifunctional silanes and deliberate crosslinkers instead form silicone networks.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PDMS spans low-molar-mass fluids and cured silicone-elastomer networks; only the latter have a useful tensile modulus. Network response depends on base/curing-agent ratio, cure temperature/time, filler, film thickness, temperature, strain amplitude/rate, and cyclic preconditioning. A bounded Sylgard 186 pristine-network example reported 1.13 MPa Young’s modulus, 4.92 MPa ultimate strength, and 461% elongation in its initial tension test; these values do not describe PDMS fluid or carbon-fiber-filled networks. Cyclic loading can alter the apparent modulus even where monotonic modulus is thickness-insensitive.
sections.processing: Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is usually converted as a liquid one- or two-part silicone formulation by mixing, degassing, casting, spin coating, replica molding, or coating, followed by thermal or room-temperature crosslinking. Base-to-curing-agent ratio, viscosity, feature size, film thickness, vacuum history, cure temperature/time, and surface treatment control bubbles, incomplete cure, shrinkage, release, and final modulus. A review of Sylgard 184 describes the common 10:1 base:curing-agent workflow, vacuum degassing, casting over a master, and oven cure, with room-temperature cure for at least 48 h sometimes used for complex parts. A bounded open-film example mixed Sylgard 184 at 10:1, centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 1 min and vacuum-desiccated for 15 min, spin-coated the degassed liquid at 1700 rpm for 60 s, and cured on a hot plate at 95 °C for 10 min. These settings are specific to Sylgard 184 films or molds and must not be transferred to other PDMS viscosities or catalyst packages. Siloxane monomer manufacture and ring-opening polymerization belong in Synthesis; this section covers formulation, air removal, coating/casting, curing, and demolding.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PDMS is a silicone polymer with a flexible Si–O backbone and two methyl substituents on each silicon atom. Low rotational barriers and weak intermolecular interactions produce highly flexible chains; crosslinking converts liquid or gum precursors into elastomeric networks.
sections.properties: PDMS provides low-temperature flexibility, hydrophobicity, low surface energy, optical transparency in suitable grades, gas permeability, and resistance to weathering. Viscosity, modulus, permeability, and swelling depend on molecular mass, crosslink density, filler, and fluid exposure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. PDMS fluids and emulsions serve mold release and lubrication in rubber/plastics manufacturing, metal casting, wire/cable extrusion and printing. Low-volatility fluids also serve specialized damping and vacuum equipment; crosslinked PDMS products require separate formulations.

Purchasing. Gelest lists neat fluids by viscosity and volatility, plus water-dilutable emulsions and blends. Specify end groups, viscosity, volatiles and solids content when purchasing; a fluid, an emulsion and a cured silicone elastomer are different products.

Scale and evidence limits. No standalone annual PDMS purchase tonnage is disclosed in the checked catalogs. The 0.1–3.5% solids range cited for diluted release emulsions is a use-stage formulation range, not a market share or typical purity of neat PDMS.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Si–O bond cleavage can yield silanols, including dimethylsilanediol; this downstream product undergoes microbial conversion to carbon dioxide in the studied soils. Catalyzed recycling instead generates cyclic siloxanes such as D4–D6.

Timescales: The soil study measures dimethylsilanediol fate, not the overall PDMS lifetime. Rapid solvent/catalyst depolymerization is not an ambient-degradation timescale.

Environmental persistence: Polymer formulation, crosslinking, soil contact and cleavage to mobile silanols must be distinguished. Biodegradation of isolated dimethylsilanediol does not establish rapid disappearance of an intact silicone article.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Acid/base-catalyzed depolymerization and recovery of cyclics are chemical-recycling routes. A public patent demonstrates fluoride-catalyzed depolymerization in swelling solvents, quenching and repolymerizable cyclic recovery at laboratory scale; it also addresses separating silicone from mixed objects.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Cured PDMS can release uncrosslinked oligomers and absorb small hydrophobic molecules. A microfluidic study detected oligomers in channel liquid and showed reduced availability of estrogen to cultured cells. These observations concern the studied elastomer devices and culture conditions; curing alone does not establish biological inertness or preserve intended drug concentrations.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PDMS is permeable to gases and can swell in nonpolar solvents; uncrosslinked oligomers may migrate or extract. Cure ratio, catalyst, inhibitor, filler, surface treatment, temperature, humidity, and post-cure affect network properties, so one silicone formulation does not represent the polymer generally.

sections.overview: Polyacetylene is a conjugated polymer built from acetylene-derived repeat units. Its alternating backbone and sensitivity to doping made it a foundational conducting-polymer material.
sections.history:
Giulio Natta and colleagues reported high-molecular-weight polyacetylene powder in 1958. In the 1970s, Hideki Shirakawa’s group developed a film-forming synthesis, providing samples that could be studied as continuous material. Shirakawa’s 1975 meeting with Alan MacDiarmid led to collaboration with MacDiarmid and Alan Heeger at the University of Pennsylvania. Their 1976 work on doped films demonstrated a dramatic rise in conductivity; the three researchers received the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for conducting polymers.

Polyacetylene’s central historical role was as an experimental material that helped establish organic electronics. The subsequent field pursued batteries, transistors, antistatic materials and displays, but those applications should not all be attributed to polyacetylene itself. Heeger later founded UNIAX to develop polymer light-emitting diodes, illustrating how the research program moved toward other conjugated polymers.
sections.nomenclature: PAc and polyethyne are names used for polyacetylene. The name describes the acetylene-derived conjugated polymer and should not be confused with polyethylene, which has a saturated backbone.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyacetylene is the conjugated addition polymer of acetylene. A classic heterogeneous route contacts dry acetylene with a Ziegler–Natta catalyst dispersion made from an organoaluminum component and a transition-metal compound in an oxygen- and water-free organic medium. Catalyst composition, pretreatment, solvent, acetylene pressure, and polymerization temperature influence morphology and the cis/trans microstructure: low-temperature examples favor a more cis-rich product, while higher-temperature conditions increase trans content. A distinct catalyst-free route compresses acetylene to a high-pressure solid and polymerizes it in the solid state, avoiding catalyst and solvent residues. Iodine or other dopants change electronic properties after polymer formation and are excluded from the synthesis boundary here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyacetylene is a conjugated polymer whose mechanical response varies sharply with cis/trans microstructure, molecular orientation and draw history, crystallinity/packing, dopant or oxidation state, porosity and defects, molecular weight, and tensile temperature and rate. It is difficult to treat as a conventional melt-processed bulk thermoplastic because films are typically catalyst-derived and chemically sensitive; values for a drawn film should not be used for an unoriented, doped, aged, or substituted polyacetylene. A focused historical-film endpoint reported in an open stretchable-electronics paper is a tensile modulus of 50 GPa and ultimate tensile strength of 900 MPa for highly oriented polyacetylene film. The result is specifically orientation-enabled and is not an intrinsic, all-form polyacetylene value; a separate open review emphasizes that the identity and structural description of nominal polyacetylene material has itself required careful verification.
sections.processing:
Polyacetylene is insoluble, does not provide a practical stable melt-processing window, and readily undergoes interchain reaction and oxidation. It therefore cannot normally be remelted or solution-cast like a commodity thermoplastic. Macroscopic films and fibrillar articles are instead given their geometry while acetylene is polymerized on a catalyst-coated wall, sheet, fiber, or other substrate; the polymerization chemistry belongs in Synthesis, while substrate geometry, film removal or transfer, inert drying, mechanical drawing, rolling, tensioned heat treatment, and device assembly are the conversion operations. Drawing or rolling aligns the fibrillar structure and can be followed by controlled electrical doping, but atmosphere, residual catalyst, film thickness, draw uniformity, temperature, tension, oxygen exposure, and storage are critical because crosslinking or oxidation can destroy extensibility and conductivity.

Hudson's open review supplies the central handling constraint: polyacetylene is entirely insoluble, reactive with itself, conformationally disordered, subject to crosslinking, and difficult to obtain with macroscopic crystallinity; it also discusses stretched-film measurements and the need to exclude oxygen in oriented material. A separate AIST patent shows one bounded conversion sequence after a film had formed on the reactor wall. Its Example 1 dried a 0.05 mm film at room temperature under argon and then drew it to about six times its starting length at room temperature; Example 2 reached about 6.2 times. The chemical catalyst treatment, polymerization, and catalyst extraction remain Synthesis content, and the later dopant chemistry is not a general shaping prescription. The reported drawability belongs to those patent films and cannot be generalized to polyacetylene made by other catalysts, morphologies, or exposure histories.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyacetylene has a conjugated carbon backbone with cis/trans structure and doping-sensitive electronic behavior.
sections.properties: Conductivity and stability depend on morphology, doping, and environmental exposure.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polyacetylene is a conducting-polymer research material used to study electronic transport, doping and chiral polymer structures. The checked research account does not establish a major current consumer-product or industrial-resin market.

Purchasing. The documented route is laboratory preparation of the polymer from acetylene and reagents. The supplier-hosted article links reagents but does not offer an identified finished-polyacetylene grade or pack; no routine bulk-resin purchasing route was verified.

Scale and evidence limits. No annual purchase tonnage, commercial end-use split or defensible market-size estimate was found in this evidence. Quantities for other conducting polymers cannot be transferred to polyacetylene.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Air oxidation introduces hydroxyl and carbonyl groups into polyacetylene and destroys electrical conductivity. Oxygen uptake can increase specimen mass despite chemical degradation.

Timescales: The NBS report observed chemical change in films oxidized at 50 °C for 40 hours and continued oxidation during months at room temperature. These are oxidation and conductivity endpoints, not mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Loss of conjugation or conductivity does not prove the carbon has been biologically mineralized; soil and aquatic lifetimes remain an evidence gap.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Polyacetylene’s insolubility and tendency to crosslink limit ordinary solvent recovery; this is a recovery constraint inferred from the review’s material characterization. Its discussion does not establish repeated remelting or a closed-loop monomer recovery process. Doped films and residual synthesis chemicals must be distinguished from nominally undoped polymer waste.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Polyacetylene requires protection from oxygen to preserve its structure and conductivity; the open review also describes spontaneous crosslinking and the material’s intractability. Handling therefore depends on atmosphere, catalyst residues and whether the material is doped. These chemical-stability observations are not a toxicological clearance for laboratory films or human-contact applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Review conclusions distinguish different synthesis and doped-film forms.

sections.overview: Polyaniline is a conjugated nitrogen-containing polymer whose conductivity can be changed by oxidation state and protonic-acid doping. It is a foundational conducting polymer used in films, composites, and sensing-related materials.
sections.history:
The material lineage now called polyaniline reaches back to Ferdinand Runge’s oxidation experiments in 1834. Its early commercial importance was as aniline-black and related cotton dyes, introduced in the 1860s, long before the products were understood as polymers. Heinrich Rheineck’s 1872 work and subsequent investigations by Richard Willstätter, Arthur Green and Arthur Woodhead helped establish the relationships among its colored, oxidized and protonated forms.

Electrical applications became a separate development history. Alan MacDiarmid and colleagues reported protonic-acid doping in 1985. A 1987 application by Stuart Yaniger, MacDiarmid and Marie Angelopoulos, associated with Lockheed and the University of Pennsylvania, became US4806271 in 1989. It pursued alternative conducting forms and described battery, electrode, shielding and electronic-component uses. These documented development targets should be distinguished from the much earlier established dye industry and from evidence of large-scale adoption.
sections.nomenclature: PANI abbreviates polyaniline. The name identifies an aniline-derived polymer family with multiple oxidation/protonation states, rather than one invariant conductive form.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyaniline (PANI) is produced by oxidative polymerization of aniline, most commonly in aqueous acidic medium. A protonic acid both provides the acidic reaction environment and supplies counterions to the protonated emeraldine-salt form, while an oxidant such as ammonium persulfate generates the radical-cation chemistry that couples aniline units. Oxidant/monomer ratio, acid identity, temperature, addition rate, and optional seed or template influence molar mass, oxidation state, doping state, and particle morphology. One open study compares hydrochloric, acetic, and sulfuric acids while using ammonium persulfate; a distinct patent uses aniline/dianiline ratio as a molecular-mass control and documents conventional persulfate/HCl oxidative polymerization. Deprotonation produces emeraldine base after polymerization; electrochemical polymerization and template-assisted nanostructure routes are valid variants but should be identified rather than conflated with the conventional bulk route.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyaniline (PANI) mechanical response is especially form- and state-dependent: oxidation/protonation and dopant, molecular weight, casting or coating route, residual solvent/humidity, and any binder, plasticizer, fiber, or nanoparticle phase can dominate the result. Open PANI-film literature consequently reports blends and composites rather than a universal bulk-resin value. In one self-supported-film study, the reported neat PANI film had tensile strength 5.11 ± 0.42 MPa and elongation at break 0.018 ± 0.002%; adding 5 wt% hydroxypropyl methylcellulose (HPMC) gave 9.16 ± 0.08 MPa and 0.075 ± 0.003%. These values apply to those prepared PANI/HPMC films and should not be transferred to other doped PANI powders, coatings, fibers, or composites.
sections.processing: Polyaniline (PANI) is commonly converted as a dispersion or solution rather than as a conventional melt: it can be blended with a film-forming polymer, cast or coated, and dried into self-supported films, coatings, or composite membranes. An open RSC study overcame PANI's poor standalone processability by directly mixing aqueous PANI and hydroxypropyl-methylcellulose dispersions and drying the mixture into self-supported conducting films. A separate open review surveys PANI thin-film preparation, including solution-based film formation, blends, nanocomposites, and deposition routes. The aqueous-dispersion route is therefore a formulation-specific conversion method; solids content, dispersion stability, dopant state, drying rate, substrate, and post-treatment must be established for each PANI grade or composite, and the cited sources do not justify a universal melt-processing window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyaniline is a conjugated aromatic polymer with a nitrogen-containing backbone and oxidation states ranging from reduced leucoemeraldine through emeraldine to oxidized pernigraniline forms. Protonation of suitable oxidation states creates conducting domains whose morphology depends on dopant and processing.
sections.properties: PANI can combine environmental stability, redox activity, tunable electrical conductivity, optical absorption, and charge storage with film-forming behavior. Conductivity and swelling depend strongly on oxidation state, protonic dopant, humidity, morphology, and composite matrix.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Doped polyaniline is supplied as a conductive additive for polymer blends and dispersions used in charge dissipation, electromagnetic shielding, electrodes, batteries and sensor development. The catalog does not quantify commercial deployment of each proposed application.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich offers emeraldine-salt powder in 5 g and 25 g packages. Specify oxidation state, dopant and form; emeraldine salt and undoped emeraldine base are not interchangeable products.

Scale and evidence limits. The documented packages are grams to tens of grams. They establish a laboratory purchasing route, not annual polyaniline demand or industry market shares.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Oxidative degradation of PANI electrodes produces quinone-containing species, including p-benzoquinone; chain cleavage and hydrolysis differ from reversible doping/dedoping.

Timescales: The cited work follows chemical and electrochemical changes during cycling in aqueous zinc-sulfate electrolyte. Cycle stability is not a calendar time for environmental mineralization.

Environmental persistence: Electrolyte composition and operating potential affect electrode degradation; these results do not quantify persistence in soil or natural water.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For PANI-containing electronics, EPA guidance supports device reuse or collection through electronics-recycling programs. This addresses the complete article and recoverable components; it does not demonstrate PANI monomer recovery.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PANI tissue-engineering studies use selected dopants and material architectures; their host responses cannot be assigned to every aniline polymer preparation. The review’s experimental examples are not generic medical-device authorization.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Conductivity is highly sensitive to acid dopant, dedoping, humidity, thermal history, film morphology, and counterion mobility. PANI is often difficult to melt process and can lose conductivity or mechanical integrity during cycling; a doped film or composite is not equivalent to the undoped polymer.

sections.overview: Polypyrrole (PPy) is a pyrrole-derived conjugated polymer commonly prepared by chemical oxidative polymerization. Aqueous ferric-chloride synthesis produces a particulate polymer whose oxidant ratio and processing define the recovered material.
sections.history:
Polypyrrole’s origins include Angelo Angeli’s early-twentieth-century pyrrole-black work, documented in a 1916 report. Donald Weiss and collaborators investigated conducting polypyrrole in 1963. A further milestone was A. F. Diaz’s 1979 work on coherent conducting films made by anodic polymerization. These were successive advances in synthesis, electrical behavior and usable film formation.

Herbert Naarmann, Dieter Naegele and colleagues at BASF subsequently pursued mechanically useful films in the work published as US4401545 in 1983, targeting electrodes, batteries and antistatic finishes. A concrete commercial application followed in NEC’s 1994 NeoCapacitor, which used a conducting-polymer cathode. Philip Lessner’s technical history identifies the first material as polypyrrole and describes its early use in small consumer-electronics capacitors; NEC researchers independently date that product introduction. Later generations adopted different polymer formulations, so the brand does not identify polypyrrole throughout its history.
sections.nomenclature: PPy identifies the pyrrole polymer, not a particular counterion, composite film, or membrane. A carrageenan- or carbon-nanotube-containing PPy composite and a template-formed PPy membrane are distinct formulations or article forms that should retain their added component and morphology.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polypyrrole (PPy) is formed by oxidative coupling of pyrrole. In the common chemical route, pyrrole is dissolved or dispersed in water or an organic medium and contacted with an oxidant such as ferric chloride or a persulfate; the oxidized chain is isolated with counteranions that act as dopants. Oxidant identity and ratio, acid or electrolyte, temperature, addition rate, and surfactant or stabilizer influence oxidation state, conductivity, particle morphology, and dispersibility. One cited open study adds aqueous ferric chloride to pyrrole and cetyltrimethylammonium bromide, then filters, washes, and dries the resulting powder. A distinct patent prepares powder by contacting pyrrole with a strong oxidant in an aqueous or organic medium and identifies ferric, cupric, ceric, nitrosonium, and related oxidants. Electrochemical oxidation of pyrrole at an electrode is a separate established route for directly depositing doped PPy films; its applied potential, current, electrolyte, and counterion control film growth. Composite deposition and device fabrication are route-specific variants, not intrinsic requirements of the polymer family.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polypyrrole (PPy) is a conducting polymer whose mechanical response is strongly governed by dopant and oxidation state, morphology/porosity, counterion loss during washing, film-formation route, humidity or electrolyte exposure, and supporting-polymer, fiber, or nanotube reinforcement. Free-standing PPy can be brittle, so composite-film values must not be treated as intrinsic PPy properties. In one template-assisted interfacial-polymerization study, an as-prepared PPy membrane tested as dog-bone specimens at 1.0 mm min−1 had break stress 692.82 ± 79.60 kPa and break strain 4.13 ± 0.41%; after seven-day washing these became 376.90 ± 98.02 kPa and 2.78 ± 0.32%. Independent PPy composite-film work shows that the dopant and carbon-nanotube phase further change strength and modulus. These membrane values are therefore preparation- and washing-state-specific.
sections.processing:
The direct open conversion evidence located for polypyrrole (PPy) concerns its use as a particulate conductive additive in composite coatings and elastomers, rather than a single melt-processing window for neat PPy. Starting with a preformed, dried PPy powder or PPy-containing filler, the material can be redispersed into a liquid binder or mixed into a carrier polymer and then shaped as a coating or molded composite. Dispersion stability and agglomeration control matter because PPy particles can reaggregate; mixing must distribute the conductive phase without excessive shear heating. For coating, a clean and compatible substrate, controlled bath or coating-solids composition, deposition, solvent or water removal, and binder crosslinking determine thickness, adhesion, porosity, and handling durability. For rubber composites, mastication and staged filler/additive incorporation, roll milling, pressure molding, vulcanization, and cooling determine filler distribution, cure state, and the final pressure-sensitive article. Heat, moisture, counterion or oxidation state, and repeated thermal or mechanical history can change conductivity and composite morphology, so matrix, dopant, filler loading, and post-treatment remain part of the article description. Pyrrole polymerization, polymer workup, and direct electrodeposition that creates new PPy belong in Synthesis; this section concerns blending and shaping already prepared PPy-containing feed.

Contri and co-workers provide a bounded coating example. They dispersed prepared PPy particles into an epoxy-based waterborne electrocoat and deposited that dispersion on cleaned AA1200 aluminum panels. Their 0.4, 0.8, and 1.2 wt% PPy formulations used a bath at pH 5.7 and 15.2 wt% solids; panels were electrocoated at 150 V for 120 s at 28 °C and then vacuum-crosslinked at 180 °C for 30 min. This is an epoxy/e-coat/aluminum procedure, not a printable ink, neat-PPy coating, or free-standing-film recipe.

França and co-workers independently compounded prepared PPy-composite fillers into NBR at 5, 10, or 15 wt%. NBR was masticated for 2 min, mixed with filler at 150 °C and 70 rpm for 4 min, compounded with vulcanizing additives at 100 °C and 50 rpm, roll-milled, and hot-pressed at 160 °C for 10 min under 6 tons. That hot-press schedule applies only to the reported NBR/PPy filler, rubber matrix, equipment, specimen geometry, and cure package; it does not establish PPy thermal stability or a general molding temperature for unsupported PPy.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polypyrrole is a conjugated polymer formed by oxidative polymerization of pyrrole; oxidant and counterion choices influence the recovered polymer state.
sections.properties: Free-standing and composite PPy films show formulation- and washing-dependent strength and strain behavior.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Polypyrrole is supplied as a conductive additive for thermoplastics and thermosets and for electrochemical-materials research. Battery, fuel-cell-composite and sensor studies are distinct from evidence of a mass-market product.

Purchasing. Sigma-Aldrich lists doped solid polypyrrole in 5 g and 25 g units. Specify the dopant and form, since an in-situ-deposited film and a dispersible conductive powder require different purchasing or preparation routes.

Scale and evidence limits. The catalog demonstrates gram to tens-of-grams packages; it supplies no annual polypyrrole purchase tonnage or mass allocated to each use.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Overoxidation introduces hydroxy and carbonyl groups into PPy. Removal of chloride dopant by alkali is a separate dedoping process and does not demonstrate destruction of the backbone.

Timescales: The source documents overoxidation during strongly exothermic oxidative preparation; this is not an environmental degradation time.

Environmental persistence: The chemical characterization gives no condition-qualified soil or aquatic mineralization rate.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: For PPy-containing electronics, EPA guidance supports device reuse or collection through electronics-recycling programs. This addresses the complete article and recoverable components; it does not demonstrate PPy monomer recovery.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: PPy studies show that dopants, substrates and material preparation influence cellular response; the conjugated backbone alone does not determine implant suitability. The review’s experimental examples are not generic medical-device authorization.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Membrane and composite data are bounded by template, wash history, counterion, carrageenan or nanotube content, film preparation, and tensile method; they are not neat-PPy constants.
