sections.overview: Plasticized poly(vinyl chloride) is PVC compounded with plasticizers to produce a flexible material class. Its behavior depends on the PVC grade, plasticizer type and concentration, stabilizers, and processing history.
sections.history:
Plasticized PVC arose from making a previously stiff polymer flexible and shapeable. Waldo Semon joined B. F. Goodrich in Akron in 1926 to work on rubber-to-metal coatings. His experiments with PVC and high-boiling solvents led to elasticized, moldable materials. Lemelson-MIT identifies early applications in shoe soles and coatings for tool handles and wire, with commercial production by Goodrich in the 1930s.

PVC subsequently replaced scarce rubber in wartime wire insulation, and flexible formulations expanded into cables, flooring and medical devices. Semon’s contribution concerns plasticization and useful formulations rather than the first observation of PVC. Goodrich’s vinyl division became Geon in 1993, marking a later corporate transition in this development lineage. The history is therefore one of additives, processing and application development around an already known polymer.
sections.nomenclature: PVC-P denotes plasticized PVC, and flexible PVC is a customary material descriptor. This record is a formulated grade family rather than a separate vinyl-chloride polymer, and it is distinct from rigid, unplasticized PVC.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Plasticized poly(vinyl chloride) is a PVC composition, not a separately polymerized macromolecule. The PVC resin is first made by polymerizing vinyl chloride, commonly by suspension, emulsion, or bulk polymerization. A plasticizer is then incorporated into the PVC resin together with formulation-specific stabilizers, lubricants, pigments, fillers, or other additives when required. The plasticizer identity and loading are composition choices, not a new PVC repeat-unit chemistry; plasticized PVC also remains distinct from internally plasticized or covalently modified PVC. One source documents conventional vinyl-chloride suspension polymerization in water with suspending agent and initiator, and a second describes plasticizer preparations and additives for PVC made by those polymerization routes. Mixing, calendaring, extrusion, and article shaping are conversion operations and are not included here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Plasticized PVC (PVC-P) is a formulation family: plasticizer identity/loading, stabilizers and fillers, molecular weight, extrusion orientation, temperature/rate, plasticizer migration, and ageing determine its flexible mechanical response. A manufacturer comparison sheet explicitly notes that flexible PVC can stiffen at cold temperature and that plasticizer migration can cause stiffness changes. Its bounded flexible-PVC row reports specific gravity 1.32, tensile strength 1,400 psi, elongation 400%, tear strength 160 lb/in, hardness 64 Shore A, and compression set 56%, with ASTM D412/D638, D624 Die C, D2240, and D395 identified in the table; no plasticizer formulation is disclosed. Independently, a New York State DOT specification for virgin-resin, plasticizer-, and stabilizer-containing extruded PVC joint shapes/sheet requires ASTM D412 Die C tensile strength at least 1,400 psi and ultimate elongation at least 250%, with 65–88 Shore A hardness. These are product/specification limits, not a PVC-P family property range.
sections.processing: Plasticized PVC is converted as a compounded thermoplastic or plastisol by dry blending and fusion, extrusion, calendering, injection molding, coating, and compression/rotational molding where the formulation is designed for it. Plasticizer type and loading, PVC particle morphology, stabilizer package, filler, shear history, and temperature determine fusion, wall slip, viscosity, surface finish, and resistance to HCl-producing overheating; therefore a rigid-PVC setting or one flexible formulation should not be generalized. A bounded laboratory extrusion study covered ten flexible PVC tube formulations containing approximately 22.3–37.3% DOTP plasticizer, 43–67.6% PVC, and 0–28.8% calcium carbonate; its recommended barrel range was 155–165 °C, with steady extrudate collected after 2 min and screw-speed effects interpreted alongside wall slip. A separate open thesis varied plasticizer at 30, 50, and 70 phr and studied fusion in extrusion, a Brabender Plastograph, two-roll milling, and compression molding over roughly 150–200 °C. These examples show why fusion and rheology must be checked for the named compound; they are not a universal plasticized-PVC temperature window. Vinyl-chloride polymerization and resin manufacture belong in Synthesis; plasticizer compounding, fusion, shaping, cooling, and cure/gelation of a supplied compound belong here.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Plasticized PVC is a formulation of PVC resin with plasticizer and stabilizers, producing flexible amorphous material rather than a new repeat-unit polymer.
sections.properties: Flexibility, hardness, migration, and processability depend on plasticizer type and loading, PVC grade, stabilizers, and fusion history.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Plasticized PVC serves flexible sheet, pool liners, inflatables, roofing membranes, cable insulation and transparent medical products. These uses span building materials, wire/cable manufacture, healthcare and consumer products.

Purchasing. Buy the selected flexible compound, or a compatible PVC base resin plus a specified plasticizer/additive system for compounding. Vynova’s VynoKlear data sheet explicitly requires appropriate additives to produce flexible products; grade and formulation define the purchased material.

Scale and evidence limits. The broad PVC category is about 53 million tonnes of preliminary global fossil-based production in 2023 according to Plastics Europe. This combines rigid and flexible outlets and is resin production, not plasticized-compound purchases; no separate PVC-P annual consumption total was established.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The PVC backbone can lose hydrogen chloride, develop conjugated polyenes and undergo subsequent oxidation and chain breakdown. Plasticizer migration or release is a separate process from cleavage of the PVC backbone.

Timescales: Rates depend on stabilizers, temperature, light and product geometry; the cited lifecycle assessment does not establish one environmental lifetime for plasticized PVC.

Environmental persistence: Aged PVC and fragments can remain after loss of additives or mechanical integrity; these changes are not complete mineralization.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Sorted plasticized PVC can be mechanically recycled after size reduction and formulation control. The lifecycle literature also describes solvent separation and chlorine-management routes; additive composition and contamination constrain reuse.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Plasticized PVC processing must control overheating and excessive residence time because the backbone can eliminate hydrogen chloride. HSE treats PVC as heat-sensitive and emphasizes temperature control, effective ventilation and defined purging/shutdown procedures. Plasticizer migration is a separate exposure issue from backbone decomposition: the identity and concentration of the plasticizer, stabilizers and intended contact conditions must be evaluated for the finished formulation.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited extrusion and thesis work concern particular plasticized-PVC formulations and processing conditions.

sections.overview: Fluoroelastomer is an umbrella family of fluorinated rubbers; documented examples include FKM and FFKM compounds. Their cure chemistry, filler package, and storage or conversion conditions affect the behavior of a finished elastomer article.
sections.history:
Commercial fluoroelastomers expanded during the 1950s as aircraft and chemical equipment created demand for seals combining elasticity with resistance to heat and aggressive fluids. DuPont introduced Viton in 1957 for aerospace seals and gaskets. This is a major FKM milestone within the broader fluoroelastomer family, not an invention date for every fluorinated rubber.

Other manufacturers developed separate product lineages. Daikin records DAI-EL commercialization in 1970, while AGC’s chemical-company history records AFLAS manufacture beginning in 1975. These developments broadened the available chemistry and sealing options. Subsequent family members include distinct FKM, tetrafluoroethylene–propylene and perfluoroelastomer materials; their composition and service roles should not be collapsed into one brand history. Aerospace sealing and chemical-process equipment remain the principal historical application thread in the cited accounts.
sections.nomenclature: The canonical name is family-level and should not be used as a synonym for FKM, FFKM, or any one commercial compound. A cured and filled fluoroelastomer formulation is a specific networked material, so its elastomer class and formulation need to be retained in addition to the family name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Fluoroelastomer is a family-level label covering several fluorinated-elastomer backbones, so its synthesis must be described by monomer architecture rather than a single recipe. Representative aqueous routes copolymerize VDF with one or more other fluorinated monomers, optionally with a chain-transfer agent, to form a stable latex. A Solvay patent gives an aqueous-emulsion example using polycarboxylic acid or salt, free-radical initiator, VDF, and another fluorinated monomer while omitting added fluorinated surfactant. A Nippon Mektron example instead copolymerizes VDF with perfluoro(methoxypropyl vinyl ether), optionally TFE or another perfluoroalkyl vinyl ether, using water-soluble peroxide/redox initiation and an emulsifier. Some members incorporate cure-site monomers or bromine/iodine chain ends to enable subsequent crosslinking; those are deliberately optional architecture choices, not a cure schedule.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Fluoroelastomers are a family of cured elastomers rather than one material: FKM, perfluoroelastomer (FFKM), and tetrafluoroethylene–propylene elastomer (FEPM) differ in polymer chemistry and cure system. Their mechanical response is correspondingly set by polymer type, curative and crosslink density, filler package, post-cure, component geometry, and exposure history. An open FKM/FFKM study illustrates this processing-sensitive behavior: its uncured FKM and FFKM compound filaments had room-temperature DMA storage moduli of 3 and 2 MPa, respectively, rising to 36 and 17 MPa after cooling to −40 °C. Those figures describe the particular silica-filled curable filaments, not cured sealing parts.

A bounded cured-FKM example is Chemours Viton A-201C, a vinylidene-fluoride/hexafluoropropylene dipolymer compound with 30 phr N-990 carbon black, 3 phr MgO, and 6 phr calcium hydroxide. Slabs cured for 10 min at 177 °C and post-cured for 24 h at 232 °C gave 13.0 MPa tensile strength, 211% elongation at break, and 79 Shore A at 23 °C. The document specifies ASTM D412 at 8.5 mm/s for tensile testing; these are compound and cure results, not fluoroelastomer-family constants.
sections.processing: Fluoroelastomers are normally compounded with fillers and curatives, shaped while uncured by compression, transfer, or injection molding (and, for suitable compounds, extrusion), then vulcanized and sometimes post-cured. Cure chemistry and scorch behavior vary across FKM, FFKM, and FEPM grades. A low-temperature extrusion study mixed silica-filled FKM and FFKM compounds, extruded 1.75 mm filaments, and used modified FDM equipment with a constrained filament path and dry-ice precooling to prevent soft-filament buckling. The reported FKM and FFKM print trials used 130 °C and 150 °C, respectively, below their compound-specific cure completion temperatures; dry-ice cooling raised filament rigidity and enabled higher drive pressure. As a conventional molding example, Chemours Viton A-201C compound stock was monitored by rheometry and slab-cured at 177 °C for 10 min, followed by a 232 °C, 24 h post-cure. These examples are not portable across formulations because filler loading, curative, viscosity, mold geometry, and cure kinetics change the process window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Fluoroelastomer is an umbrella family of fluorinated rubber backbones, including FKM, FFKM, and FEPM architectures. Members are generally amorphous elastomeric chains that become three-dimensional networks after a formulation-specific cure.
sections.properties: Fluoroelastomers are valued for combinations of heat, fuel, oil, weathering, and chemical resistance that are difficult to obtain with nonfluorinated rubbers. Their electrical, barrier, low-temperature, and fluid-response properties vary substantially with backbone and cure chemistry.
sections.applications:
Products and industries. Fluoroelastomers serve demanding seals, gaskets and hoses in transport, chemical processing, oil/gas and semiconductor equipment.

Purchasing. Purchasing separates FKM gums/precompounds, FEPM grades and FFKM semiconductor grades; buyers select the actual polymer and compound through material suppliers or component fabricators.

Scale and evidence limits. No reliable combined purchase or consumption tonnage was established. The documented subfamilies serve different requirements; supplier portfolios are not a measure of market size.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: A VDF/HFP member of this family can be defluorinated to fluoride and carbonaceous residue in alkaline superheated water. Perfluoroelastomers and other comonomer systems are outside that demonstrated scope.

Timescales: No transferable environmental mineralization time was established by the cited evidence.

Environmental persistence: The reported treatment or ageing endpoint does not establish complete biodegradation in soil, freshwater, seawater, or landfill.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: The cited laboratory route recovers fluorine as calcium fluoride. It should not be read as a commercially universal fluoroelastomer recycling technology.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: Fluoroelastomer handling depends on material form and formulation. Chemours advises avoiding skin contact with Viton A-201C, which includes cure chemicals. For cured Gumlast perfluoroelastomer parts, the supplier emphasizes hazardous fumes from overheating or burning, including hydrogen fluoride. Thus uncured-compound exposure and severe-heat decomposition need separate controls; ordinary sealing performance does not establish a family-wide safety classification.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Fluoroelastomer behavior is highly formulation-dependent: backbone, fluorine content, cure system, filler, post-cure, crosslink density, and exposure history all matter. Some family members trade chemical resistance for low-temperature flexibility or cost, and uncured gum, cured compound, and finished seal data are not interchangeable.

sections.overview: The ethylene–propylene elastomer family covers rubbery polymers in which ethylene and propylene units are combined at random. It has two established members: the binary copolymers (EPM) and the terpolymers that also contain a small proportion of a non-conjugated diene (EPDM). Both have a saturated, chemically stable main chain built from the same monomers as polyethylene and polypropylene, and this backbone underlies their resistance to heat, oxygen, ozone and weathering. In EPDM the diene leaves reactive double bonds on side groups rather than in the backbone, so these sites are available for vulcanization and other chemical modification; EPM has no such sites. Members are produced over a wide range of compositions and molecular weights, so the family name does not identify one material or compound.
sections.history: The family grew out of the mid-1950s expansion of coordination-catalyst chemistry. A Montecatini patent family naming Giulio Natta, Giorgio Mazzanti and Giorgio Boschi claims Italian priority from December 1955 for amorphous, elastomeric ethylene–propylene copolymers, and the Natta archive places the first plant for these rubbers at Ferrara in 1958. Diene-containing terpolymers followed: a Japanese polymer-science chronology lists production of both EPM and EPDM by DuPont and Montecatini in 1963, with further producers entering in later years. Supplier records then document scale-up and process change, for example at Geleen in the Netherlands, where production began in 1967, further lines were added in 1973 and 2003, and a new catalyst technology was adopted in 2013. Uses spread across automotive parts, building products and electrical applications. These milestones belong to particular patents, companies and plants, and no single invention date applies to the whole family.
sections.nomenclature: The family name groups the two established member types and is not a synonym for either of them. EPM denotes the ethylene–propylene copolymer and EPDM the ethylene–propylene–diene terpolymer; in industry usage the trailing M of EPDM marks the saturated main chain and the D marks the diene. EPR also appears in the literature, sometimes for the binary copolymer and sometimes for ethylene–propylene rubbers generally, so it is not used here as a family abbreviation. Vulcanized compounds, thermoplastic vulcanizates and blends that contain these rubbers belong to formulation or article records, and ethylene copolymers built on other comonomers are outside the family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Both members are made by coordination polymerization of ethylene with propylene. EPDM adds a non-conjugated diene, commonly ethylidene norbornene, dicyclopentadiene or vinyl norbornene, as a third monomer, whereas EPM is made without any diene feed. Conventional manufacture uses vanadium-based Ziegler–Natta catalysts with organoaluminum cocatalysts in solution or slurry processes; one patent example passes the monomer gases into a dry hydrocarbon solvent containing such a catalyst and then removes catalyst residues and solvent. Metallocene and other Group IV single-site catalysts are documented alternatives for both the binary copolymers and the terpolymers. Catalyst type, monomer feed ratio and diene choice govern composition, sequence distribution and branching, while compounding and vulcanization of rubber articles are later steps outside polymer synthesis.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Ethylene and propylene units are combined randomly along a saturated backbone, and depending on composition and monomer arrangement the members range from amorphous to semicrystalline. In EPDM the diene is built in so that its remaining double bond sits on a side group; with ethylidene norbornene, the ring double bond is consumed during polymerization while the exocyclic ethylidene double bond is retained. Different dienes introduce different amounts of long-chain branching.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Ethylene content, molecular weight, crystallinity, diene identity and diene level all vary between grades, so a value measured on one grade or compound does not describe the family. Diene choice affects both branching and the speed and extent of cure. The behavior of finished articles also depends on fillers, plasticizing oils and the cure system, so property data need to stay tied to a named grade, compound and test.

polymers.canonicalName: Cyclic olefin polymer and copolymer family

sections.overview: The cyclic olefin polymer and copolymer family covers thermoplastics whose chains contain a substantial share of units derived from cyclic olefins such as norbornene or tetracyclododecene. Its two established branches are defined by polymerization route. Cyclic olefin copolymers (COC) are addition copolymers of a cyclic olefin with ethylene or another α-olefin, while cyclic olefin polymers (COP) are most commonly made by ring-opening metathesis polymerization of cyclic olefins followed by hydrogenation of the backbone double bonds. The literature discusses the two branches together because both give transparent materials with good heat resistance and very low moisture uptake, which suits them to optical parts, medical and diagnostic products and packaging. Monomer, composition and route differ between members, so properties cannot be transferred from one to another.
sections.history: The producers of the two branches document separate commercial histories. For the ring-opened, hydrogenated branch, Zeon completed a cyclo-olefin polymer plant at its Mizushima works in Japan in November 1990 and began selling a second COP product line in September 1998, with optical uses later joined by medical and industrial molded parts. For the addition-copolymer branch, the producer's account traces metallocene-based research at Hoechst during the 1990s and a commercial plant at Oberhausen, Germany, operating by 2000. After the Hoechst demerger the business sat with Celanese's Ticona unit until Daicel and Polyplastics acquired it in 2006, and its markets grew to include optical, diagnostic and packaging applications. These supplier milestones date particular product lines rather than the first laboratory preparation of cyclic olefin polymers, and other producers have separate histories.
sections.nomenclature: The family is an umbrella for two route-defined subclasses that the literature usually names as a pair, cyclic olefin copolymers (COCs) and cyclic olefin polymers (COPs), rather than under one abbreviation, so the family carries no abbreviation of its own. COC refers to addition copolymers of a cyclic olefin with ethylene or another α-olefin. COP refers to polymers made from cyclic olefins alone, chiefly by ring-opening metathesis polymerization with subsequent hydrogenation, and some authors also count cyclic olefin addition homopolymers as COP. The narrower record titled cyclo-olefin polymer covers only the COP branch; despite its general-sounding name it is not a synonym for this family and does not include COC. Supplier trade names identify particular commercial products and are not family names, and ethylene copolymers that contain a cyclic diene only as a minor cure-site comonomer fall outside the family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Both branches start from related cyclic olefin feedstocks, such as norbornene, tetracyclododecene and their derivatives, but use different polymerization chemistry. COC is made by coordination–insertion copolymerization of ethylene or another α-olefin with the cyclic olefin, typically over titanium- or zirconium-based molecular catalysts with an aluminoxane or borate activator; the ring double bond is consumed while the ring framework stays in the chain. COP is made by ring-opening metathesis polymerization, for example with a ruthenium catalyst, which opens the ring and leaves double bonds in the main chain; a separate hydrogenation over a homogeneous or heterogeneous catalyst then saturates the backbone. Addition homopolymerization of cyclic olefins is also described as a COP route. Catalyst, comonomer and feed ratio govern cyclic-unit content, glass transition and molecular weight, so individual process examples are not specifications for every grade.
sections.structureAndMorphology: In COC the cyclic units stay intact as rigid ring structures in a chain that also contains ethylene-derived segments. Addition homopolymers likewise keep the complete bicyclic ring in the backbone, whereas ring-opening metathesis converts each monomer into a backbone unit that keeps a smaller ring and, after hydrogenation, contains no main-chain double bonds. Higher cyclic-unit content and bulkier cyclic monomers raise the glass transition, so monomer choice and composition largely set heat resistance.

polymers.canonicalName: Ethylene–carboxylic acid copolymer and ionomer family

sections.overview: The ethylene–carboxylic acid copolymer and ionomer family covers ethylene-rich copolymers that carry acrylic or methacrylic acid units, sometimes with an additional comonomer, together with the ionomers formed when some of their acid groups are neutralized with metal cations. The un-neutralized acid copolymers keep a polyethylene-like, partly crystalline character, and their polar acid groups change how they behave compared with polyethylene. In the ionomers, the ionic groups gather into domains within the nonpolar matrix and act as reversible physical crosslinks at service temperature, yet the material can still be melt processed. Acid type and content, comonomers, neutralizing cation and degree of neutralization all vary, so the family name does not describe one material.
sections.history: Acid-functional ethylene copolymers and their ionomers developed together in the high-pressure polyethylene industry. DuPont commercialized carboxylate polyethylene ionomers in the 1960s, and its ionomer resin was being imported into Japan by 1964; partial domestic manufacture there began in autumn 1978, and full domestic production of both the ionomer and an ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymer followed in 1985. On the acid-copolymer side, a Dow patent by John Thomson and George Waples published in 1970 describes ethylene–acrylic acid copolymers and their adherent coatings, and by 1988 a General Electric patent treated DuPont's ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymer as an established commercial material. Uses grew to include coatings, adhesive layers, packaging films and seal layers, golf-ball covers and molded parts. These dates belong to particular companies and patents and do not fix a first synthesis date for the family.
sections.nomenclature: The family name groups the parent acid copolymers with their neutralized derivatives and is not a synonym for any one member. EAA and EMAA denote the un-neutralized ethylene–acrylic acid and ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymers, while ionomer denotes material in which part or all of the acid is present as metal carboxylate; some authors also describe the un-neutralized copolymer as the acid form of a polyethylene ionomer. Ethylene copolymers that carry only acrylate or methacrylate ester groups and no acid groups, such as ethylene–methyl methacrylate, are excluded. So are sulfonated, chlorosulfonated and perfluorinated ionomers. Supplier trade names for particular acid-copolymer or ionomer grades are not family names.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: All members share a main route in which ethylene is copolymerized with acrylic or methacrylic acid, optionally with an alkyl acrylate third monomer, by high-pressure free-radical polymerization in stirred autoclave or tubular reactors, much as low-density polyethylene is made. Ionomers are then made by converting a controlled fraction of the acid groups to carboxylate salts with a metal source such as sodium, zinc, lithium or magnesium. The neutralization can be carried out in solution, as a slurry or in the melt, including during melt blending of different parent acid copolymers. Less common documented routes include making an ethylene–acrylate ester copolymer with a late-transition-metal catalyst and then converting the ester groups to acid, as well as newer catalytic and post-functionalization routes to polyethylene ionomers. Acid level, molecular weight, cation and degree of neutralization depend on the chosen process, so patent examples are not family-wide specifications.
sections.structureAndMorphology: The ethylene-rich backbone can crystallize, but the randomly placed acid units reduce crystallinity and melting point relative to polyethylene. After neutralization, ion pairs separate from the nonpolar matrix into small aggregates, called multiplets, and at higher ion content into larger ion-rich clusters, which behave as thermally reversible physical crosslinks. Models of commercial ionomers describe crystalline polyethylene, amorphous polyethylene and ionic regions coexisting in the solid.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Because the acid units disrupt polyethylene crystallinity, both the acid copolymers and their ionomers melt and soften well below polyethylene, which limits their upper use temperature. Neutralization raises melt viscosity, so the low melt flow needed for good mechanical properties can make processing difficult. Properties therefore depend on acid level, molecular weight, cation and neutralization degree, and values from one grade or blend should not be generalized.

sections.overview: The amino–formaldehyde resin family covers thermosetting condensation resins obtained when formaldehyde reacts with compounds that carry amino or amido groups. Urea and melamine are the principal amino components, while benzoguanamine and related guanamines serve more specialized grades. The established members are urea–formaldehyde, melamine–formaldehyde, co-condensed melamine–urea–formaldehyde and benzoguanamine–formaldehyde resins. All of them are made and stored as reactive, partly condensed precursors and only later cured into insoluble crosslinked networks. The same chemistry supplies wood-bonding adhesives on one side and alkylated crosslinking agents for coatings on the other, so the family name does not fix one composition, form or property set.
sections.history: No single invention date applies to the family, because each member moved from laboratory chemistry to industry on its own timetable. Urea–formaldehyde came first: the Plastics Historical Society credits patents from Pollak's group in Vienna in the years after the First World War, followed by industrial work that turned the resin into molding materials for light-colored electrical and household goods. Melamine–formaldehyde became practical later in the interwar period, once melamine itself could be produced, and a Waikato thesis identifies Henkel's resin work and Ciba's melamine route as milestones. Benzoguanamine–formaldehyde resin was already a development platform when an application on rubber-modified molding compositions was filed in 1954, and later patents adopted benzoguanamine resins as aminoplast crosslinkers in protective coatings. Co-condensed melamine–urea–formaldehyde adhesives grew from combining the two established chemistries for wood bonding, and published research still examines how the timing of melamine addition changes resin behavior.
sections.nomenclature: Amino resin and aminoplast are the general class names, and a United States federal air-emission regulation defines an amino resin as a thermoset made from formaldehyde and amino-group compounds such as melamine and urea, with phenolic resins given a separate definition. Member names state the amino reactants and are abbreviated UF, MF, MUF and BF in this encyclopedia. MUF covers resins in which melamine and urea are condensed together with formaldehyde, from urea resins upgraded with a little melamine to melamine-rich exterior grades, and it is not a label for either binary resin. Etherified melamine and benzoguanamine crosslinkers used in coatings are variants inside this chemistry rather than a separate family. Phenol–formaldehyde resins form their own family. Phenol–urea–formaldehyde resins are linked as related rather than as members: an open review treats them as phenol–formaldehyde resins co-reacted with urea, whereas some patents call phenol-modified urea resins amino resins, and the single phenol–urea–formaldehyde record spans both.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Every member starts from formaldehyde and an amino compound whose nitrogen–hydrogen groups first add formaldehyde to give a distribution of methylol intermediates. These intermediates then condense, releasing water, into oligomers joined by methylene and methylene-ether bridges; in urea systems the pH and the formaldehyde-to-urea ratio decide how these bridges compete with cyclic uron structures. Common UF and MUF schedules use an alkaline addition step, acid-promoted condensation to a target resin state, and a return to neutral or alkaline conditions for storage, with renewed acid catalysis or heat later curing the resin into a network. Melamine and benzoguanamine are methylolated in the same way, and in MUF the stage at which melamine is charged changes how it enters the co-condensate. Resins intended as coating crosslinkers commonly have their methylol groups etherified with alcohols such as methanol or butanol. Reactant ratios, pH history, temperature, condensation endpoint and hardener are formulation choices, so no single recipe defines the family.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Cured members are networks in which amino-compound centres are joined through formaldehyde-derived methylene and methylene-ether bridges. Melamine and benzoguanamine supply triazine-ring centres, whereas urea supplies a carbonyl group flanked by two reactive nitrogens. Degree of substitution, bridge distribution and crosslink density are not fixed and follow composition and cure.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Properties belong to a particular resin formulation and cure rather than to the family, because the amino component, formaldehyde ratio, condensation endpoint, etherification and hardener all vary. Melamine level separates upgraded interior-grade urea resins from exterior-grade MUF adhesives, so the urea-rich and melamine-rich ends of the family should not share moisture-resistance claims. Performance measured on one adhesive, laminate or coating system should stay attached to that system.

polymers.canonicalName: Poly(vinyl ester), poly(vinyl alcohol), and poly(vinyl acetal) family

sections.overview: This family groups vinyl polymers linked by one derivation chain that starts from poly(vinyl acetate), rather than by a shared monomer. Poly(vinyl acetate) is the radical addition polymer of vinyl acetate, and poly(vinyl alcohol) is made from it by hydrolysis or alcoholysis of the acetate groups because vinyl alcohol is too unstable to be polymerized directly. The poly(vinyl acetal)s are then obtained by acid-catalysed reaction of poly(vinyl alcohol) with aldehydes, and poly(vinyl butyral) and poly(vinyl formal), from butyraldehyde and formaldehyde, are the commercially established acetal members. Each conversion is usually incomplete, so real products are statistical chains that combine acetate, hydroxyl and, where present, acetal units in grade-dependent proportions.
sections.history: The family's milestones belong to different members and companies, so no single date covers it. Wacker traces its poly(vinyl acetate) lineage to Herrmann's research in 1924 and its first production plant for the polymer to 1930. A recent review dates the first patent on making poly(vinyl alcohol) by saponifying a poly(vinyl ester) to 1924 as well. In Japan, Ichiro Sakurada's group produced a poly(vinyl alcohol) fibre precursor in 1939, and Kuraray commercialized its fibre in 1950 before starting merchant sales of the resin itself in 1958. Poly(vinyl butyral) gained its lasting role through a 1939 effort on safety-glass interlayers involving several American glass and chemical companies, while a surviving 1943 Australian sample of poly(vinyl formal) shows the formal already in wartime use as electrical-wire covering. These are discovery, commercialization and application milestones for particular members, not invention dates for the class.
sections.nomenclature: The family name joins the vinyl ester precursor polymers, the hydrolysed polymer and its acetals; the member abbreviations are PVAc for poly(vinyl acetate), PVA, PVOH or PVAL for poly(vinyl alcohol), PVB for poly(vinyl butyral) and PVFM for poly(vinyl formal). Poly(vinyl acetal) is the class name for the aldehyde-derived members, and each acetal is named after its aldehyde, so formal, acetaldehyde-derived and butyral resins are distinct materials rather than synonyms. Partially hydrolysed grades remain poly(vinyl alcohol) materials whose residual acetate content must be stated, not a separate polymer type. The family is unrelated to the thermosetting vinyl ester resins, which are epoxy-derived resins recorded as a separate family. Ethylene copolymers such as ethylene–vinyl acetate and ethylene–vinyl alcohol, and vinyl chloride–vinyl acetate fibre polymers, are also outside this family even though they contain vinyl acetate or vinyl alcohol units.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The chain begins with free-radical polymerization of vinyl acetate, carried out either in alcoholic solution or in aqueous emulsion stabilized by a protective colloid or emulsifier. Poly(vinyl acetate) in methanol is then converted to poly(vinyl alcohol) by alkali-catalysed alcoholysis or hydrolysis, and stopping this step early leaves partially hydrolysed grades that retain acetate units. Acetals are formed by treating poly(vinyl alcohol) with an aldehyde under acid catalysis, usually in water, where the product separates from solution as acetalization advances; butyraldehyde gives poly(vinyl butyral) and formaldehyde gives poly(vinyl formal). Formal resins have also been made by condensing formaldehyde directly with partially hydrolysed poly(vinyl acetate), which leaves both acetate and hydroxyl groups in the product. Monomer feed, initiator and colloid, extent of hydrolysis, choice and amount of aldehyde, acid, temperature and precipitation conditions are route variables, so each member's composition reflects its process history rather than one family recipe.
sections.structureAndMorphology: All members share a saturated carbon backbone in which alternate carbons carry the functional side group, and they differ in whether that group is an acetate ester, a hydroxyl or part of an acetal ring. In the acetals one aldehyde molecule bridges two neighbouring hydroxyl-bearing carbons, closing a six-membered cyclic acetal along the chain. Because hydrolysis and acetalization stop short of completion, commercial poly(vinyl alcohol), poly(vinyl butyral) and poly(vinyl formal) are statistical chains whose acetate, hydroxyl and acetal contents vary from grade to grade.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Degree of polymerization, degree of hydrolysis, residual acetate content and degree of acetalization are set by the producer, and each changes hydrogen bonding, solubility and processing behavior. A measured value therefore belongs to a named grade or formulation rather than to the family. Statements about one member should not be transferred to another merely because they share the same backbone and precursor.

sections.overview: The styrenic copolymer family groups polymers in which styrene is copolymerized with one or more other monomers, as distinct from polystyrene made from styrene alone. Comonomers such as acrylonitrile, butadiene, acrylic or methacrylic esters and maleic anhydride shift the balance of stiffness, toughness, chemical resistance, heat resistance and transparency away from that of polystyrene. Members range from single-phase thermoplastic copolymers, through rubber-toughened multiphase resins and impact modifiers, to synthetic rubbers and block-copolymer thermoplastic elastomers, so the family is defined by its chemistry rather than by one kind of material behavior. Rubber-modified polystyrene (HIPS) is treated with the related polystyrene record because its continuous matrix is styrene homopolymer, even though its rubber particles carry grafted polystyrene; some industry overviews list it alongside the styrene copolymers.
sections.history: Copolymerized styrene appears early in the patent record: an IG Farben patent with German priority in 1930 described styrene–maleic anhydride copolymers. Styrene–butadiene rubber grew out of German Buna-S research and was scaled up by a wartime United States program that joined government, industry and university laboratories. Several thermoplastic members arrived later as separate commercial product lines, including Kaneka's MBS impact modifier in 1964, Shell's styrenic block copolymers for footwear in 1964 after development work that supplier accounts date to either 1955 or 1961, and BASF's weather-resistant ASA in 1967. A later U.S. Environmental Protection Agency review listed several producers and trade names for SAN and ABS, showing both were by then established commercial materials. These milestones belong to individual members and companies, so the family has no single invention date.
sections.nomenclature: The family name is a grouping term with no abbreviation of its own, and the abbreviations SAN, ABS, ASA, MBS, SMA, SMMA, SBR and SBC stay with the member records. The family covers styrene–acrylonitrile, acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene, acrylonitrile–styrene–acrylate, methacrylate–butadiene–styrene, styrene–maleic anhydride and styrene–methyl methacrylate copolymers, together with the styrene–butadiene rubber and styrenic block copolymer families. The wider term styrenic polymers is often used to include general-purpose polystyrene, polystyrene foams and HIPS as well, but those materials belong to the related polystyrene record rather than to this family. Styrene-crosslinked unsaturated polyester resins and styrene–acrylate dispersion resins also contain copolymerized styrene but are not members here.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Members are made by chain-growth copolymerization of styrene with one or more comonomers, but the route depends on the intended architecture. Single-phase copolymers such as SAN, SMA and SMMA are made by free-radical copolymerization in bulk, solution, suspension or staged mass-to-suspension processes. In these processes the feed ratio and feed profile govern composition drift, while initiator, temperature and chain-transfer agent govern molar mass. Rubber-modified members are built in stages. For ABS, styrene and acrylonitrile are polymerized in the presence of a preformed butadiene rubber, either grafted onto a latex in emulsion or in a mass process where phase inversion leaves rubber particles in a SAN-rich matrix; ASA grafts styrene and acrylonitrile onto a butyl-acrylate rubber core before blending with SAN, and MBS grafts a methacrylate or vinyl-aromatic shell onto a butadiene-rich rubber latex. Emulsion styrene–butadiene rubber comes from aqueous free-radical copolymerization, whereas solution styrene–butadiene rubber and the styrenic block copolymers use organolithium-initiated anionic polymerization in hydrocarbon solvent, with sequential monomer addition or coupling building the block architectures.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Some members, notably SAN, SMA and SMMA, are single-phase copolymers whose behavior follows comonomer content and sequence. The rubber-modified members are multiphase. ABS disperses butadiene-rich rubber particles in a styrene–acrylonitrile-rich matrix, ASA uses an acrylate rubber phase instead, and MBS particles combine a butadiene-containing core with methacrylate- or styrene-associated outer material. Styrenic block copolymers microphase-separate, so polystyrene-rich domains act as physical junctions within a rubbery phase.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Comonomer identity, composition, sequence and phase structure vary widely across the family, from transparent single-phase copolymers to opaque rubber-toughened grades and their blends with engineering polymers, and elastomers. A property or processing value measured on one member or grade therefore cannot be transferred to the family. Even within one member, rubber content, grafting and particle morphology differ between grades and production routes.

sections.overview: The aliphatic polyester family groups polymers whose backbones are chains of carboxylic ester links joined by aliphatic, non-aromatic segments. One branch is built from hydroxy acids or their cyclic esters and includes polylactide, poly(glycolic acid), lactide–glycolide copolymers, polycaprolactone and the microbially produced polyhydroxyalkanoates. A second branch is built from diols condensed with aliphatic dicarboxylic acids and includes poly(butylene succinate) and its succinate–adipate copolymer. The hydrolysable ester bonds in the main chain are the shared feature behind the family's use as biodegradable or bioresorbable materials, although members degrade at very different rates. Stereochemistry, composition, crystallinity and molar mass vary within and between members, so the family name does not describe a single material.
sections.history: The members have separate histories rather than one founding date. Bacterial poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) was identified in microbial storage granules in the 1920s, while a DuPont patent on lactide resins issued in 1935 and a Union Carbide patent on caprolactone polymerization issued in 1962 document early synthetic work. Absorbable sutures drove the medical branch, with an American Cyanamid poly(glycolic acid) suture patent granted in 1967 and an Ethicon patent on lactide sutures containing glycolide issued in 1972. Diol–diacid members grew out of later biodegradable-plastics development, including a Showa Highpolymer patent on succinate and succinate–adipate polyester fibers granted in 1994, and a large polylactide plant was commissioned in 2002. These dates mark particular discoveries, patents and plants, not the first synthesis of each polymer.
sections.nomenclature: In this record, aliphatic polyester has its usual carboxylic-ester meaning, and the members are polylactide, poly(glycolic acid), poly(lactide-co-glycolide), polycaprolactone, the polyhydroxyalkanoates, poly(butylene succinate) and poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate). Copolyesters that build aromatic diacid units such as terephthalate into the chain, with poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) as the main example, are aliphatic–aromatic copolyesters and are excluded even when they biodegrade. Aliphatic polycarbonates such as poly(propylene carbonate) are joined by carbonate rather than carboxylic ester links and are usually treated as a separate class in the biodegradable-polymer literature. Because general textbooks sometimes count polycarbonates as a kind of polyester, poly(propylene carbonate) is linked as a related, overlapping class rather than listed as a member. Abbreviations such as PLA, PGA, PLGA, PCL, PHA, PBS and PBSA name individual members or subfamilies, not the family, and trade names are not family names.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Hydroxy-acid members can be made by direct polycondensation of the hydroxy acid, which usually limits molar mass, or by ring-opening polymerization of a cyclic ester such as lactide, glycolide or ε-caprolactone. Ring-opening polymerization with a metal or organic catalyst and an alcohol or other active-hydrogen initiator is the usual route to high molar mass, and lactide–glycolide copolymers come from ring-opening copolymerization of the two cyclic dimers. Poly(butylene succinate) and its adipate copolymer are made by esterifying 1,4-butanediol with succinic acid, or with succinic and adipic acids or their esters, and then polycondensing the oligomers with a catalyst under reduced pressure. Polyhydroxyalkanoates are instead accumulated inside bacteria fed sugars, lipids, organic acids or waste streams, and the polymer is recovered by separating the cells and extracting it with solvents. Catalyst, initiator, monomer stereochemistry, comonomer feed and recovery method are route-specific, so no single member recipe defines the family.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Every member has backbone ester groups separated by aliphatic segments, some of which carry side groups such as the methyl group of lactyl units or the variable side chain of hydroxyalkanoate units. Crystallinity ranges widely, from typically semicrystalline poly(glycolic acid), polycaprolactone, poly(butylene succinate) and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) to amorphous stereochemically mixed polylactide and some lactide–glycolide compositions. Stereochemistry, comonomer content and side-chain length therefore set chain packing and thermal transitions within each member.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Properties reported for one member, grade or composition do not transfer across the family, because stereochemistry, comonomer ratio, molar mass and crystallinity change stiffness, toughness and thermal behavior. Recognized weaknesses include the brittleness and limited thermal stability of polylactide, the brittleness and narrow melt-processing window of poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) and the low tensile strength of polycaprolactone. Many aliphatic polyesters are mechanically weaker than conventional non-degradable plastics, and aliphatic–aromatic copolyesters were developed partly to overcome that gap.

sections.overview: The thermoplastic elastomer family groups materials that behave like rubber in service but can be melted, shaped and reprocessed like thermoplastics. It is a material-behavior class rather than a chemical family: its members include olefinic, styrenic, urethane, copolyester and polyamide-based materials made by unrelated chemistries. In each of them a soft, rubbery phase provides elasticity while a hard phase restrains flow at service temperature and gives way on heating. The hard phase can be glassy or crystalline domains formed by segments of the same chain, or a separate thermoplastic polymer in a blend. Unlike conventionally vulcanized rubber, most members depend on physical association of hard domains rather than a permanent network, and in thermoplastic vulcanizates the crosslinked rubber stays dispersed in a meltable thermoplastic matrix.
sections.history: The family has no single origin, because its member classes were developed and commercialized separately. Lubrizol dates the commercial arrival of its Estane thermoplastic polyurethanes to 1959. Shell's styrenic block copolymers, whose development supplier accounts place in either 1955 or 1961, reached commercial footwear use in 1964. Copolyester elastomers became commercial products in the 1970s, with DuPont starting Hytrel production in 1972 and Toyobo beginning Pelprene sales in 1976. Thermoplastic vulcanizates grew from the earlier idea of curing a rubber while it is mixed with a molten thermoplastic, which preceded commercial polypropylene/EPDM grades such as Santoprene, and polyether block amides are represented by Arkema's long-running Pebax line. Later development included replacing metal car bumpers with elastomer-modified polypropylene of the kind now classed as thermoplastic polyolefin elastomers, and supplier work on renewable or recycled feedstocks.
sections.nomenclature: TPE is the family abbreviation, and the member records keep their own abbreviations. The family covers thermoplastic polyolefin elastomers, thermoplastic vulcanizates, thermoplastic polyurethanes, thermoplastic copolyester elastomers, polyether block amides and styrenic block copolymers. An open chapter that follows ISO 18064 nomenclature reports the classes TPA, TPC, TPU, TPO, TPS and TPV. It separates copolymer-based types, whose hard and soft segments share one chain, from blend-based types such as TPO and TPS compounds and the dynamically vulcanized TPV. An open review instead uses industry abbreviations such as SBC, PEBA and COPE alongside TPO, TPV and TPU, and also lists thermoplastic natural rubber blends, which have no record here. Conventionally vulcanized rubbers, thermoset polyurethanes and ordinary thermoplastics are outside the family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Because the family spans several chemistries, its members are made by unrelated routes whose common aim is to combine hard and soft phases. Styrenic block copolymers are built by living anionic polymerization with organolithium initiators in dry hydrocarbon solvent, either adding styrene and diene in sequence or coupling living arms. Thermoplastic polyurethanes form by step-growth polyaddition of a diisocyanate, a long-chain diol and a short-chain extender, in one-shot or prepolymer processes. Copolyester elastomers and polyether block amides form by melt polycondensation: one example is ester interchange of dimethyl terephthalate with butanediol and a polyether glycol, and another couples carboxyl-terminated polyamide blocks with polyether diols or diamines. Thermoplastic polyolefin elastomers are made either by melt blending polypropylene with an olefin rubber or by sequential reactor polymerization, and thermoplastic vulcanizates by dynamic vulcanization, in which the rubber phase is crosslinked during intensive mixing with molten polypropylene. In block and segmented members the hard and soft segments are covalently joined, whereas in blend-based members they are separate polymers whose morphology is set during compounding.
sections.structureAndMorphology: In copolymer-based members, hard blocks or segments gather into glassy or crystalline domains that act as thermally reversible physical crosslinks within a continuous soft phase. As a result these materials soften over a range of temperature rather than melting sharply. In blend-based members the rubber is dispersed in, or co-continuous with, a thermoplastic phase; in thermoplastic vulcanizates that rubber is covalently crosslinked during mixing while the thermoplastic matrix stays meltable. The hard/soft ratio, segment lengths and blend morphology therefore set the balance between elasticity and processability.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Members differ in chemistry, phase structure and formulation, so a property or processing value measured on one grade does not describe the family. Blend-based grades can vary in matrix and rubber type, phase ratio, oil, filler and compatibilizer, and in the degree of crosslinking for vulcanizates. An open chapter notes that this formulation freedom makes comparable flow data difficult to generate and publish.

sections.overview: The cellulose ether family covers semisynthetic derivatives in which some hydroxyl groups on the anhydroglucose units of cellulose are converted to ether groups, so alkyl, hydroxyalkyl or carboxyalkyl substituents sit on an otherwise intact cellulose backbone. The members recorded here are methyl, ethyl, hydroxyethyl and hydroxypropyl cellulose, the mixed methyl/hydroxypropyl ether, and the ionic carboxymethyl ether. Substituent type, degree of substitution, molar substitution of hydroxyalkyl groups and chain length govern solubility, thickening and film formation, so each member name covers a range of grades. These materials are chemically modified forms of cellulose; they are related to the unsubstituted cellulose record but are not members of it.
sections.history: Industrial cellulose ethers followed the earlier cellulose esters, and ether production methods reached industrial use from the 1920s. Individual members were commercialized at different times: Dow introduced ethyl cellulose resins in 1935, used them in molded wartime parts, and began methyl cellulose production in 1938. Hydroxyethyl cellulose entered industrial use in the 1930s, and Hercules began carboxymethyl cellulose production in the United States in 1943, partly as a replacement for natural gums. Hydroxypropyl cellulose was commercialized in 1966, and a 1974 Dow patent extended hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, already used as a paint thickener, to alcohol-soluble grades for pharmaceutical coatings. These dates describe commercialization of particular products, not first laboratory preparation.
sections.nomenclature: Cellulose ether is a class name for cellulose derivatives with ether-linked substituents, carrying either one substituent type or, in mixed ethers, more than one. Abbreviations such as MC, EC, HEC, HPC, HPMC and CMC name the substituent pattern rather than a fixed degree of substitution, and sodium carboxymethyl cellulose is a salt form within carboxymethyl cellulose. Unmodified and regenerated cellulose are outside the family, as are cellulose esters, whose hydroxyl groups carry acyl or nitrate groups instead of ether groups. Other ethers that fit the definition, such as cyanoethyl, hydroxyethyl methyl and ethyl hydroxyethyl cellulose, do not yet have member records.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Members are made by modifying purified cellulose, such as wood pulp or cotton linters, rather than by polymerizing a monomer. In the usual heterogeneous process the cellulose is activated with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give alkali cellulose, which is then etherified with an alkyl chloride, with ethylene or propylene oxide, or with a chloroacetate, alone or in combination for mixed ethers. Neutralization, washing and drying then recover the product. Alkali and water levels, reagent charge and order, diluent and temperature control the degree and uniformity of substitution and the extent of side reactions of the etherifying agent. Homogeneous etherification in cellulose-dissolving solvents can give more uniform and more regioselective substitution than the heterogeneous industrial process.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Ether substituents can sit on the C2, C3 and C6 hydroxyl positions of each anhydroglucose unit, and they disrupt the hydrogen bonding and crystal packing that make native cellulose insoluble. Degree of substitution counts substituted hydroxyl groups per anhydroglucose unit, while molar substitution counts added hydroxyalkyl groups, which can extend into short side chains.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Because commercial products are made mostly in heterogeneous systems, substitution is often unevenly distributed along and between chains, and product purity and uniformity depend on the process. Degree of substitution, molar substitution, molecular weight and counterion differ between grades, so solubility, viscosity and film behavior measured on one grade do not describe the whole family.

sections.overview: The cellulose ester family covers semisynthetic derivatives in which hydroxyl groups on the anhydroglucose units of cellulose are esterified, either with organic carboxylic acids or their derivatives or with an inorganic acid. The organic-acid members recorded here are cellulose acetate, the highly acetylated cellulose triacetate, and the mixed esters cellulose acetate propionate and cellulose acetate butyrate, while cellulose nitrate is the inorganic-acid member. Most members are thermoplastic or solution-processable materials used as films, fibers, coatings and molded articles, and their behavior depends on ester type and degree of substitution. These materials are chemically modified forms of cellulose; they are related to the unsubstituted cellulose record but are not members of it.
sections.history: Cellulose esters were among the earliest semisynthetic plastics and fibers, and cellulose nitrate is often described as the oldest plastic. Alexander Parkes founded a company to make cellulose nitrate goods in 1866, and John Wesley Hyatt's cellulose nitrate plastic followed around 1870. Cellulose acetate, first developed in 1865, became a safety-film base in 1908 and a British textile fiber in 1919. The mixed esters grew out of photographic-film work, with cellulose acetate propionate dated to 1927 and cellulose acetate butyrate developed in 1936 and commercially available by 1938, and triacetate film base followed in 1948. These dates belong to particular products and companies and do not mark a single origin for the family.
sections.nomenclature: Cellulose esters are divided by the acid that forms the ester: organic-acid esters such as acetates, propionates and butyrates, including mixed esters with two acyl types on one chain, and inorganic-acid esters, of which cellulose nitrate is the earliest and most important industrial example. Names such as cellulose acetate or cellulose acetate butyrate state which ester groups are present, not a fixed degree of substitution, and cellulose triacetate denotes acetate near full substitution of the three hydroxyl groups. Cellulose sulfate and cellulose phosphate fit the same definition but do not yet have member records. Cellulose ethers, which carry ether-linked substituents, and unmodified or regenerated cellulose are outside the family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: All members are made by esterifying purified cellulose, such as dissolving pulp, cotton linters or microcrystalline cellulose, rather than by polymerizing a monomer. Organic esters are usually formed with carboxylic anhydrides in the corresponding acid under sulfuric acid catalysis, and mixed anhydrides or acids introduce propionyl or butyryl groups alongside acetyl groups. Acetylation first gives nearly fully substituted material, and controlled partial hydrolysis can then lower the substitution level. Cellulose nitrate is made by nitrating cellulose with mixed nitric and sulfuric acids or with nitric acid, acetic acid and acetic anhydride, followed by washing and stabilization. Heterogeneous processes are the industrial norm, whereas homogeneous esterification in dissolved cellulose gives more uniform substitution, and acid ratios, catalyst, temperature and any hydrolysis step set the final ester composition.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Each anhydroglucose unit offers one primary hydroxyl group at C6 and two secondary hydroxyl groups at C2 and C3, so esterification can replace up to three hydroxyl groups per unit, and triacetate lies close to that limit. The kind of ester group, the degree of substitution and how substituents are distributed among positions and chains define particular grades of each member.

sections.overview: The methacrylate polymer family covers addition polymers of methacrylic acid esters. Every repeat unit carries a methyl group and an ester side group on the same backbone carbon, and the alcohol part of the ester largely decides how a member behaves. Poly(methyl methacrylate) is the most widely used member, a hard, transparent glassy plastic often used in place of glass. Poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) carries a hydroxyethyl ester that makes it hydrophilic, and it forms water-swollen hydrogels when crosslinked. Members are made as linear polymers, crosslinked networks and copolymers, so the family name does not identify one composition or property set.
sections.history: Methacrylate polymers entered use through separate member histories rather than a single family launch. Poly(methyl methacrylate) was first obtained in 1928, and Röhm's company registered PLEXIGLAS for its transparent sheet in 1933 before extending the material to molding compounds and to dental, automotive and coating uses. Transparent acrylic glazing then became important for enclosed aircraft cockpits, as a National Park Service account of early aircraft plastics describes. Poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) followed a biomedical path: Otto Wichterle's 1950s work on water-swollen gels led to a hydrophilic-polymer patent with Drahoslav Lím, a 1961 spin-casting method for soft contact lenses, and the purchase of manufacturing rights by Bausch & Lomb in 1966. These dates mark first preparation, commercial introduction and later application development for particular members, not an invention date for the class.
sections.nomenclature: Polymethacrylates and methacrylate polymers are used here for polymers whose repeat units derive from esters of methacrylic acid, and PMMA and PHEMA are the established member abbreviations. Methacrylates fall within the broader acrylic-polymer class and differ from acrylate polymers by the methyl group on the backbone carbon that bears the ester, so the poly(alkyl acrylate) family is a related but separate record. Poly(methacrylic acid) and its salts are often grouped with the polymethacrylates but are acids rather than ester polymers and are not members here. Ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymers used as ionomer precursors, and styrene- or butadiene-based copolymers that contain methacrylate units, are separate records.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Members are made by addition polymerization through the carbon–carbon double bond of the corresponding methacrylate ester, most often by free-radical chemistry. Radical routes are run in several media: one documented PHEMA preparation polymerizes the monomer in toluene with an azo initiator under nitrogen, and a patent describes precipitation or suspension polymerization of the same monomer. Controlled radical methods such as atom-transfer radical polymerization keep the same backbone while a catalyst system regulates chain growth, molar mass and chain ends, as published PMMA examples in aqueous emulsion and in a polar organic solvent show. Linear polymers and crosslinked hydrogel networks are different products, because network formation depends on added multifunctional comonomers and cure conditions. Initiator, medium, temperature, conversion and crosslinker level are therefore route choices rather than family constants.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Because the methyl group and the ester sit on the same backbone carbon, polymerization creates a quaternary carbon in every repeat unit, which separates methacrylate polymers structurally from acrylate polymers, whose corresponding carbon carries a hydrogen. The ester side group then sets the balance between hydrophobic and polar character, from the hydrophobic, glassy PMMA to the hydroxyl-bearing, water-swelling PHEMA. Tacticity, molar mass, comonomers and crosslinking are further variables that are not fixed at family level.

tradeNames.name: POKETONE
tradeNames.scopeNote: Hyosung trade name for its aliphatic polyketone engineering plastic made from carbon monoxide, ethylene and propylene. Grades and compounds differ, so cite the grade; the two-monomer ethylene–carbon monoxide copolymer is a separate entry.

tradeNames.name: Carilon
tradeNames.scopeNote: Shell trade name for the carbon monoxide/ethylene/propylene terpolymer it commercialized in 1996 and stopped producing in 2000; it identifies that historical product line.

sections.overview: This entry covers the aliphatic polyketone made by palladium-catalyzed terpolymerization of carbon monoxide with ethylene and a small proportion of propylene. Olefin-derived units alternate with carbonyl groups along the chain, and most olefin units come from ethylene, so the material is closely related to the alternating ethylene–carbon monoxide copolymer. The propylene units lower the melting point relative to that copolymer, which suits the terpolymer to melt processing as a semicrystalline engineering plastic. Hyosung’s POKETONE resins are made from these three monomers.
sections.history: Alternating olefin–carbon monoxide polymers became practical after Drent and co-workers reported highly efficient palladium–diphosphine catalysts in 1991. Shell commercialized a carbon monoxide/ethylene/propylene terpolymer under the Carilon name in 1996 but closed that production in 2000. Hyosung began producing aliphatic polyketone in 2013 and started its POKETONE commercialization plant at Yongyeon, Ulsan, in June 2015. These dates mark a catalyst discovery and two commercial production lines rather than a single invention date for the terpolymer.
sections.nomenclature: The canonical name states the three monomers. Suppliers and researchers often call this material simply aliphatic polyketone, a term also used for the two-monomer ethylene–carbon monoxide copolymer and for non-alternating ethylene–CO polymers, so the bare term needs its source context and is kept here only as a broad search term. POKETONE and the former Carilon are trade names for commercial terpolymers, not names of the class. Propylene–carbon monoxide copolymers without ethylene, and terpolymers made with higher α-olefins or styrene, are separate materials outside this entry.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The terpolymer is made from carbon monoxide, ethylene and propylene with cationic palladium(II) catalysts bearing bidentate diphosphine ligands, the catalyst family whose high activity was reported in 1991. In methanol-containing media a palladium methoxide species is the active site, and the chain grows by alternating insertion of carbon monoxide and olefin into palladium–alkyl and palladium–acyl bonds, with termination mainly by protolysis. Propylene reacts roughly an order of magnitude more slowly than ethylene, so the feed composition sets how much propylene enters the chain. Terpolymers with different proportions of ethylene–CO and propylene–CO units have been prepared in hydrocarbon media and, at much lower rates, in water with water-soluble palladium complexes. Catalyst, medium and feed ratio are route choices, so a laboratory recipe does not specify a commercial grade.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Olefin-derived units alternate with carbonyl groups, giving a 1,4-diketone backbone in which each propylene-derived unit carries a methyl group. Incorporating propylene lowers the melting point and the proportion of the α crystal form compared with the ethylene–carbon monoxide copolymer; the terpolymers studied for this effect contained about 1 to 7 mol% propylene. Hyosung contrasts its terpolymer engineering plastic, melting near 220 °C, with the fibre-forming copolymer near 260 °C, and attributes chemical and fuel resistance and gas barrier properties to its compact crystalline structure.
sections.applications: Hyosung lists food-contact parts such as conveyor components and water-purifier parts, gears and mining components, automotive connectors, and extruded pipe liners and food-packaging film among POKETONE uses. It cites chemical, impact and abrasion resistance, low water absorption and dimensional stability for them. These are supplier-reported application areas for its grades, not measured properties of the class.
sections.degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Batch pyrolysis of an ethylene–propylene-based aliphatic polyketone generated carbon monoxide, methane, hydrogen and light hydrocarbons, with ketones, cyclopentenones, furans and aromatic compounds in the liquid fraction; cyclization competed with chain cleavage.

Timescales: In that study a 250 g laboratory batch was heated from ambient to above 500 °C, and strong vapor production began about one hour into heating, near a 400 °C reactor temperature. This is an apparatus-specific observation, not a service-life value.

Environmental persistence: Inert thermal decomposition gives no environmental mineralization or disappearance time, and no ambient-fate data for the terpolymer were found in the reviewed open sources.
sections.recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical recycling has been demonstrated for composites of a commercial ethylene–propylene-based polyketone grade with 15 or 30 wt% short glass fiber: a 2025 study remolded fully recycled material after one and five cycles and found that fiber and matrix changes affected retained properties. Batch pyrolysis of an ethylene–propylene-based polyketone converts it to liquid, gas and solid fractions, a thermochemical route distinct from combustion for energy. Both are laboratory demonstrations on specified materials, not evidence of established collection or closed-loop recycling.
sections.healthSafetyAndRegulation: The cited batch-pyrolysis study shows that severe heating of an ethylene–propylene-based polyketone releases a complex gas and condensate mixture including carbon monoxide and light hydrocarbons; this reactor experiment is not an occupational exposure measurement during ordinary molding. HSE guidance supports controlling thermal history and fumes during extrusion, reprocessing, stoppages and cleanup, with the specific grade and its additives included in the assessment.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Propylene content, molecular mass, additives and reinforcement differ between grades, so properties and processing windows reported for one grade or compound do not describe the class. Data for the two-monomer ethylene–carbon monoxide copolymer, which melts higher and crystallizes differently, should not be transferred to the terpolymer, or the reverse.

reagents.detail: Palladium(II) salt with a bidentate diphosphine ligand and an acid, forming the active cationic complex.

reagents.detail: Methanol-containing solvent; hydrocarbon and aqueous media are also reported.

synthesisRoutes.conditions: Palladium-catalyzed terpolymerization of carbon monoxide, ethylene and propylene in a methanol-containing medium.
synthesisRoutes.mechanism: Alternating insertion at a palladium centre builds the chain. Carbon monoxide inserts into the palladium–alkyl bond to give an acyl, and an olefin then inserts into the palladium–acyl bond, so carbonyl and olefin-derived units alternate. Ethylene and propylene compete for the olefin insertion, propylene much more slowly, and protolysis of the active site mainly terminates the chain.

steps.title: Prepare the reaction
steps.body: Form the cationic palladium–diphosphine catalyst in the methanol-containing medium and charge carbon monoxide with the ethylene/propylene olefin feed.

steps.title: Grow the alternating chain
steps.body: Repeat carbon monoxide insertion into the palladium–alkyl bond and olefin insertion into the resulting palladium–acyl bond. The relative ethylene and propylene feed sets how many propylene-derived units enter the chain.

steps.title: Terminate and recover the product
steps.body: Chain growth stops mainly by protolysis of the palladium site; recover the precipitated terpolymer from the medium.
